body: Every position here is meant to follow from the premises below plus the evidence. To reject a conclusion, a critic has to show that it doesn't follow, or reject one of these premises and say which. Each premise links to its fullest defense.

Axiom 7, status: "I don't claim this as objective moral fact. It's a coherent system I choose to endorse and want enforced." Every legal order enforces norms on people who reject them, and a realist or a theist enforces the same rules under another label (Imposing it; Realists; Divine command).

Axiom 1: "subjective experience (first-order phenomenal consciousness) shall serve as the basis for moral status and the possession of negative rights." Nothing can matter to a being that experiences nothing, so experience is the precondition for anything mattering to anyone (Why sentience).

Axiom 2: "Any being, biological or artificial, that possesses first-order subjective experience is to be treated as a rights-bearer." Every narrower line, by species, contract, intelligence, or substrate, leaves out beings that can be harmed, infants included, for reasons that have nothing to do with harm (Contract, egoism, substrate).

Axiom 3: "A being on an undisturbed developmental trajectory toward sentience ... shall be granted significant moral weight proportional to the robustness of that trajectory." Left undisturbed, it becomes a being that can be harmed, and a voluntary act of procreation creates responsibility for it (Normative Ethics; Abortion).

Axiom 4: "A being that once possessed sentience retains residual moral consideration." Known wishes don't lapse when a person can no longer voice them, as advance directives already recognize (End-of-life care).

Axiom 5: "Practical determination of sentience shall follow the best available scientific consensus." Who can suffer is a question for evidence, not opinion, and where the evidence is unclear the rule leans toward consistency with the axioms, not toward convenience (Sentience Determination).

Axiom 6: "strong negative rights against interference and harm," working as "side-constraints" that give way only at "a clear threshold of rights violation by the agent." No total feels the suffering of the one sacrificed, and aggregation applied consistently would kill one patient to save five (Side-constraints). Rights are reciprocal, so a deliberate violator can't claim the protection he violated (Forfeiture).
Negative rights only: a positive right to goods compels someone else to provide them, which is itself interference (Negative rights).

Axiom 7, consistency: "All moral and political rules within this system must remain consistent with the prescribed primacy of subjective experience." A rule anyone demands for themselves binds them for everyone in the same position (Hare), so every hard rule has to follow from the axioms and the evidence (Coherence and hard rules).
Standard of proof: proof means testable, repeatable evidence or reasoning that others can check, for moral and factual claims alike (Meta-Ethics).
Each of these can look like a contradiction. Here is how each one follows from my framework.

Liberty versus the office bars and the mosque cap. The bars are prophylaxis, not punishment. They protect the rights order from ideologies that are hostile to it. No one would be fined, jailed, or silenced for belief. Only the four named ideologies meet the test, and adherence is defined by something checkable, never by ancestry alone (Oath of Office and Perjury). The office bar withholds a power no one has a right to, and the building cap falls on institutions that propagate the program, while existing buildings and private worship stay. Ordinary religious and political disagreement fails the four-part test (Where the line is).

Property versus the two exceptions. The exceptions follow from forfeiture (animal-industry firms violated rights) and from the excluded-ideology rules. They are not ad hoc breaks in the property right. Banning a harmful use without compensation is settled law, and the Fourteenth Amendment has already voided claims to property in sentient beings (Compensation).

A minimal state versus the sanctuary system and predator removal. Protecting rights is the state's core duty. The sanctuary system and predator removal are part of that job, not an expansion of it. "Minimal" means minimal in purpose, not in size, and both are built to shrink: no animal is bred into the sanctuaries, and predator numbers fall through fertility control. The full answer is in Purpose of the State.

Legal drug use versus capital punishment for large-scale distribution. Personal use affects only the person using. Large-scale distribution puts doses of unknown strength, often cut with fentanyl, into the hands of many people who cannot know what they are taking, which is why I believe it should be a capital crime. Sharing a known, tested dose with a consenting adult is not capital, because the recipient knows the risk he accepts. Where each line sits, and what would move it, is in Drug Policy.

A 12-week rights claim versus a ban from conception. Before 12 weeks a fetus on its way to sentience already carries significant moral weight (Axiom 3), and where science is unclear I err on the side of consistency with my axioms (Axiom 5). The ban from conception rests on both, and it is also a safeguard against documented drift past 12 weeks: Denmark, Norway, France, and Massachusetts Chapter 188. Before 12 weeks the ban protects no right of the embryo. It rests on that moral weight and on the responsibility created by voluntary procreation, which is why a pregnancy from rape is treated differently (Normative Ethics; Abortion and Bioethics).

Values, not ethnicity, versus group statistics. Group statistics never become verdicts on individuals; each person is judged on their own values and conduct. Group data may set defaults, such as priors, screening thresholds, and where police go, but it never decides anyone's guilt, punishment, or legal status, and every default can be rebutted by the person's own record. The operating rule, with worked cases, is in Group Statistics and Individual Judgment. How the immigration presumption fits that rule is in Group presumption and individual vetting. Stereotypes and prejudice aren't necessarily bad as long as they don't lead to rights violations. Pattern recognition is reasonable even when the person turns out to be harmless, such as wariness of a hooded Black man at night or a suspicious-looking Muslim on a plane. Statistics showing much higher criminality among Black Americans shouldn't be denied either. Pretending nothing is going on isn't virtuous, it's stupid. Wariness of that kind is private caution, which takes no one's rights; a state default may never rest on race (rules 4 and 6). Critics who use group statistics to prove discrimination already accept them as evidence (Group statistics).

Anti-realism versus strong moral rankings. Every ranking runs on my own prescribed scale, which is the stated basis of everything I write here. Why a prescribed system can still be enforced is answered in Meta-Ethics. A realist would enforce the same rules under a different label, and each hard rule has to follow from the axioms and the evidence (Realists; Coherence).

Conservation versus "no wilderness." Wilderness is obsolete. It is full of animal-rights violations and should be engineered by humankind. Preserved habitat stays, but it is managed against predation rather than left wild. Conservation in my sense protects the animals living in a habitat, not the predation in it. The methods are stated: captive predator lines end, non-threatening predators go to sanctuary, herbivorization is pursued where the science works, and every step is held to the stop rule (Hunting, Fishing, Pets, and Zoos; Burden of proof).

Backing Trump versus opposing his oversteps. Supporting the administration's direction while opposing its oversteps is ordinary support with limits. Each action is graded on its own, from Aligned to Opposed, and the running totals show both the direction and the dissents (Summary of Grades).

Shared ground with the Greens. The Greens are right only on animal rights. They're wrong on economics and on the other social issues. Even the Greens offer reforms, such as extending the Animal Welfare Act and replacing factory farms, not the day-one end of animal agriculture I want, so a Green vote would buy reform on animals at the cost of opposition on nearly everything else (Green Party).

Ranked choice and initiatives inside a restricted vote. How people vote is separate from how many vote. I believe the electorate should be drastically reduced, and those who qualify should vote by the best method. Where the franchise criteria come from, and what would change them, is in Epistocratic Republic and Qualified Franchise.

Feasibility versus accepted costs. Some of my positions can't be carried out today, and some carry real costs I accept rather than deny. Not possible today: cultivated meat at the scale and price of meat, fertility control for wild predators, and any gene drive in a wild vertebrate (What works now); and, without constitutional amendment or new Supreme Court rulings, the qualified franchise, mandatory death sentences, and public execution (Qualified Franchise, Mandatory Death Penalty). Costs I accept: scarce and costlier foods during the switch, lost jobs concentrated in farming counties, and the Sanctuary Levy (Sanctuary Plan); ecological risk from removing predators, held to the rule that no step causes more suffering than it prevents (Wild-Animal Predation); and extradition refusals and diplomatic friction (Immigration and Borders); and, if AI displaced nearly all work quickly, taxing capital beyond what "minimal" means today to fund the floor (AI and Automation). One gap I haven't closed: what enforcing the food ban will cost in inspectors, customs checks, and prosecutions has no estimate yet, and I flag it as Needs research (Enforcement). Where a tool doesn't exist yet, the duty uses the tools that do. Where a cost is real, I name it and say why the rights at stake outweigh it. Why I accept these risks at all: the status quo kills billions of land animals and over a trillion fish every year, so the burden of proof falls on keeping it, not on ending it (Burden of proof).

Each hard position names its own cost where I argue it: - Death where the victim lived: a proven offender who would never have offended again is executed too (Why death where the victim lived). - Finality: an error built on evidence that looked solid at trial, and that no new objective evidence exposes, will not be caught (New evidence after the verdict). - Compelled labor: the work is hard and unpaid (Compelled labor). - Qualified franchise: a capable citizen who skips the test goes unheard by choice (Why a license to vote). - Office bar: open adherents lose authority roles they could otherwise hold (The office bar and free speech). - Mosque cap: peaceful congregations cannot build new places of worship (Why cap mosques). - Group presumption: some applicants who would have been fine are turned away (Group presumption). - No compensation: shareholders, including fund savers, lose that value (No compensation). - Opt-in welfare: some people get less from the state than today's programs give (Opt-in welfare). - Research on offenders: some research will be slower or will not happen (Research capacity). - Predator removal: less carrion for scavengers, disease spread without predators, and herbivore overshoot, each watched under the stop rule (Risks I accept and watch).

Treaty law versus my rules. Exiting the ICCPR, possibly denouncing the Convention Against Torture, compelled labor for prisoners of war beyond Geneva's limits, and West Bank removals that conflict with Geneva IV Art. 49 and the Rome Statute all depart from treaties. Treaty law is not my moral standard: a rule is not right or wrong because a convention forbids it, any more than a punishment is wrong because other democracies dropped it (the same test as the death penalty). The standard is forfeiture by the person's own conduct, and every departure is individual, decided by a court or military tribunal, never en masse or by identity (Hostile conduct, removal, and entry). The United States should leave through its own constitutional procedure, because no nation is bound forever to a foreign committee's reading of a treaty it chose to join (Treaty exits). I acknowledge that Article 49's text bars individual transfers too, so this answers the charge of ethnic cleansing, not the treaty.

Due process versus emergency on-scene sentencing. Ordinary times get the 30-day capital trial and a unanimous jury. On-scene sentencing exists only inside a declared emergency over riots or violent crime that local policing can't contain, and the emergency expires on a fixed date unless the legislature renews it. It speeds up the process, not the standard of proof: the officer must be certain to the full capital standard, every case is recorded on body camera, a civilian court reviews it afterward, and an officer whose sentence the record doesn't support is charged as for murder. That is stricter than today's law, where Tennessee v. Garner already allows deadly force on probable cause (Emergency sentencing).

Double jeopardy versus a capital retrial after nullification. I allow one retrial, only after a finding of nullification, only in mandatory-death-penalty cases, and before a different jury held to the same unanimity rule and capital standard. Successive trials for the same act already exist: under the dual-sovereignty doctrine, which the Supreme Court declined to overturn in Gamble v. United States (2019), a state and the federal government may each prosecute the same conduct. I acknowledge this departs from the Fifth Amendment rule that an acquittal is final (Role of Juries).

Causal liability versus the secret ballot. Reparations are owed only by those who caused the harm. Lawmakers' votes and officials' enforcement acts are on the public record, so the people who passed or carried out a policy can be held liable now. Voters can't be, because the secret ballot records no one's vote, and I keep the secret ballot (Race and Diversity).

Free association versus birth-sex bathroom rules for private businesses. It is a mandate, and it rests on protection and privacy in multi-person rooms where people undress. It is not a new kind of rule: federal workplace law already requires toilet rooms "separate for each sex" in all places of employment (29 CFR 1910.141). Single-occupancy lockable rooms are open to anyone, so no one is left without access (Gender Identity).

Every position and conclusion here is mine. I used AI tools the way a writer uses an editor and a research assistant: to tighten wording, find and check sources, and attack my arguments with the strongest objections I could find. None of that makes a claim true or false. Each claim stands on its linked source or its reasoning, and the Sources boxes under each section let you check it yourself. Where data is missing I mark it Needs research, where I accept a cost I say so, and where my positions seem to pull against each other I answer it above.
Moral anti-realism: I claim no objective moral truth. I prescribe a sentience-centered system because it is the most coherent and stably consistent framework available.

Moral anti-realism is the view that there are no moral facts that hold independently of what anyone thinks or prescribes. I hold that view, so I prescribe a sentience-centered system because it is the most coherent and stably consistent framework available.
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Moral Anti-Realism
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Moral Realism
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Constructivism in Metaethics
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Moral Cognitivism vs. Non-Cognitivism

head: "Isn't morality subjective?"
body: It is a prescribed system (Moral anti-realism). Its authority rests on its coherence and on its practical necessity for protecting subjective experience, not on moral facts existing independently of human prescription.

head: "Why moral anti-realism?"
body: I don't claim moral facts independent of what anyone thinks or prescribes can be established, and I hold moral claims to the same standard of evidence I apply elsewhere. Three arguments support that judgment. They are reasons, not proof. The first is from disagreement: moral views differ deeply across cultures and eras in ways that are better explained by differing attitudes and interests than by some groups perceiving moral facts that others miss. The second is J. L. Mackie's argument from queerness: objective values would have to be facts of a very strange kind, prescriptions built into the world that motivate or bind anyone who grasps them. Nothing else in a naturalistic picture of the world is like that. The third is evolutionary debunking, developed by Sharon Street and Richard Joyce. Human moral attitudes were shaped by natural selection for survival and reproduction, not for tracking independent moral truth, so any match between them and such truths would be a coincidence. Rather than rest on facts I can't demonstrate, I defend the system on grounds that can be checked, set out in the answer above.

head: "What kind of anti-realism is it?"
body: A hybrid, which is a recognized position in metaethics. It is constructivist in the Humean sense: its rules are built from what beings actually care about, chiefly avoiding suffering, and the best set of rules is the one that is most coherent and stable. It is prescriptivist in form, in the tradition of R. M. Hare: its moral statements are universal prescriptions, rules that apply to everyone in the same situation, including the person who states them. And it has an expressive element: its judgments also express a settled attitude against harm to beings that can suffer.

head: "If there are no objective moral facts, why should anyone accept these rights?"
body: Critics claim that a framework without independent moral facts cannot bind anyone who rejects its starting point. No moral system meets that demand, realist ones included, because asserting that moral facts exist does not by itself persuade someone who denies them. What my framework delivers is what any moral system can actually deliver. My reasons are open to everyone. The system is coherent and stable, it protects every being that can be harmed rather than drawing arbitrary lines, and anyone who wants protection from harm has a reason to support a system that protects it. Those who accept it are motivated by recognizing that coherence and by cultivated character (Moral Motivation). Those who reject it are still bound by its enforcement, as people are under any legal order.

head: "If no moral system is objectively true, what licenses imposing yours?"
body: The same thing that licenses any legal order, minus the pretense of cosmic backing. Every legal order enforces some norms on people who reject them. Even the most permissive one enforces its ban on murder against the murderer and its property rules against the thief. Anti-realism doesn't create the problem of imposition. It only drops the claim that the universe signed off on the result. The real choice is which system is enforced, not whether one is. Declining to enforce is also a choice, and it has victims. Where the law won't stop an aggressor, the aggressor's will is imposed on the victim. Neutrality between the two isn't available. What licenses my system in particular is what it protects. Every being that can suffer already counts its own suffering against an outcome, from its own standpoint, before any theory is applied. That is the Humean constructivist starting point Sharon Street develops: reasons are built from what valuers actually care about. Hare's universalizability does the rest. Anyone who demands not to be harmed is, by the same logic, committed to that rule for everyone in the same position, and the position that matters is being able to suffer. My enforcement rests on protecting those who can be harmed, not on a claim of truth (Philosophy of Law). Realists face the same practical problem. They still impose on people who reject the facts they claim, and claimed objectivity hasn't produced agreement. A realist judge enforces the law on a defendant who denies its moral facts exactly as I would. My test is public and checkable: coherence, consistency, and testable evidence about who can suffer. Enforcement targets acts against others, not dissent. Anyone may reject the system in private belief, and no one would be fined, jailed, or silenced for belief. Nor does my prescription bind anyone on its own: a rule becomes punishable only once it is enacted and published through lawful process, and changes to the Constitution go through Article V (Ex post facto; Epistocratic Republic and Qualified Franchise). Nor is this a step anti-realists must refuse. J. L. Mackie denied objective values and still went on to build a practical morality, which he called "a device for counteracting limited sympathies," including a section on the right to life. Simon Blackburn's quasi-realism holds that an anti-realist can make and stand behind moral demands at full strength. R. M. Hare held that sincerely assenting to a moral judgment means prescribing action, for everyone in the same situation. Anti-realists who stop short of enforcement do so by choice, not because the view requires it. J. L. Mackie – Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong (1977) Simon Blackburn – Ruling Passions: A Theory of Practical Reasoning (1998) Sharon Street, Philosophy Compass – What is Constructivism in Ethics and Metaethics? (2010) Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Richard Mervyn Hare

head: "Wouldn't a moral realist reject the whole system?"
body: Not its content. Realists and anti-realists disagree about what moral claims are, not about which beings they protect. A realist still has to name a criterion for who counts, and every criterion faces the same test. Nothing can matter to a being that has no experience: a rock can't be wronged, because nothing is like anything for it. So sentience is not one criterion among many. It is the precondition for anything mattering to anyone, and a realist who holds that harm is objectively bad is already committed to it (Normative Ethics). The realist would call these rights true, and I prescribe them. A court enforces them the same way under either label. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Moral Realism

head: "Many systems are coherent. Does coherence alone license every hard rule in yours?"
body: No, and I don't claim it does. Coherence is a filter every rival has to pass, not the whole case. The case has three parts: The starting point is the one every valuer already shares: its own suffering counts against an outcome, from its own standpoint. Universalizability (Hare) rules out any exception that can't be stated without naming oneself, one's species, or one's group. Hare himself drew a preference utilitarianism from it, and I don't follow him there. Universalizability tests a rule's form, not its content, so it can't by itself choose between adding up welfare and protecting each being. The starting point chooses: suffering is felt by individuals, never by a total (side-constraints). Evidence settles the facts the rules apply to: who can suffer, and what a person did. Each hard rule is that chain applied. Capital punishment follows from forfeiture at the Axiom 6 threshold, held to the capital evidentiary standard (Evidentiary Standard). The office bar follows from the fact that an authority role is a grant of power, not a right (Excluded ideologies). The Sanctuary Plan follows from equal rights above the sentience threshold (Sanctuary Plan). So a critic who rejects a hard rule has two honest routes: show that it does not follow from the axioms and the evidence, which is a fair challenge on the merits, or reject an axiom and say which one. Disliking a conclusion is not a third route.

head: "People disagree about science too. Doesn't moral disagreement prove nothing?"
body: The realist reply has force. Disagreement alone does not show there are no facts, since disagreement exists in nearly every field, including those where everyone agrees there are facts. Realists also point to convergence on basics, such as condemning gratuitous cruelty. The anti-realist answer is about the kind of disagreement: scientific disputes tend to narrow as evidence accumulates and methods are shared, while basic moral disputes often persist among informed people who agree on every fact. I treat disagreement as evidence that weighs against realism, not as a refutation, and the convergence realists cite, on avoiding suffering, is exactly what my constructivism builds from.

head: "If objective values are 'queer,' aren't the norms of reasoning and mathematics queer too?"
body: Realists answer with a companions-in-guilt argument: the objection to moral facts would apply equally to facts that almost no one doubts, such as the norms of good reasoning or the truths of mathematics, so it proves too much. The parallel fails. Mathematical and logical norms are confirmed by their use in every successful field of inquiry and by results that anyone can check, while independent moral facts add no such checkable payoff. I rely on reasoning and evidence myself, not on independent moral facts, so I don't need the stronger claim.

head: "Doesn't evolutionary debunking undermine your own moral views too?"
body: It would, if I claimed my intuitions track moral truth. I don't. Realists answer debunking by arguing that evolution favored attitudes such as caring for others because those attitudes were in fact good, so the match is not a coincidence. Others point out that the same argument, pressed too far, would undermine trust in human reasoning in general. My case rests on coherence and on evidence about sentience, which are testable: whether a being can suffer is a scientific question, and whether a set of rules is consistent is a logical one. Debunking removes the case for realism. It does not remove the evidence that beings can be harmed or the reasons beings have to avoid harm.

head: "If there are no objective moral facts, isn't that relativism?"
body: No. Relativism says moral truth varies by culture or person, so no moral view is better than another. I deny independent moral facts, but I still prescribe one system and I want it enforced. The system is a hybrid: constructivist in the Humean sense, built from what beings actually care about, chiefly avoiding suffering, with the best set of rules the most coherent and stable; prescriptivist in the tradition of R. M. Hare, so the rules apply to everyone in the same situation, including me; and it has an expressive element, a settled attitude against harm to beings that can suffer. Those are reasons anyone can check, not a claim that every view is equally valid. Proof, as elsewhere, means testable, repeatable evidence or reasoning that others can check. Whether a being can suffer is a scientific question, and whether a set of rules is consistent is a logical one. I still draw hard, enforceable verdicts (Moral anti-realism). On art, I likewise reject the view that all output is equal (Artistry).
I'm an agnostic atheist: I hold no belief in gods, but I stay open in principle to evidence. That stance is personal. My moral system rests on the sentientist framework, not on theology.

I am an agnostic atheist. I do not believe in the existence of any gods, while remaining open to the theoretical possibility that evidence could change that assessment. I treat religious claims as unsupported by sufficient evidence. This stance is personal. My moral system is grounded in my prescribed sentientist framework, not in theology.
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Atheism
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Atheism and Agnosticism
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Religion and Morality

head: "Why agnostic atheism rather than atheism or agnosticism alone?"
body: The two words answer different questions. Atheism concerns belief: an agnostic atheist lacks belief in any god. Agnosticism concerns knowledge: the agnostic atheist does not claim to know with certainty that no god exists and stays open to evidence. The burden of proof rests on the claim that a god exists, as it does for any claim about what exists. Proof here means testable, repeatable evidence or reasoning that others can check. Revelation, scripture, or private experience alone does not meet that standard. The absence of sufficient evidence warrants withholding belief, not asserting the opposite as proven. Philosophers often use "atheism" more strictly, for the claim that no god exists, and on that usage the position is closer to non-theism. I use the wider sense of lacking belief.

head: "Without God, where does morality come from?"
body: From the prescribed sentientist framework, not from theology (Agnostic Atheism). Rights rest on sentience, the capacity to be harmed, which can be investigated by evidence whether or not a god exists. Grounding morality in a god's commands also raises an old problem: if something is good because a god commands it, the commands could have been anything. If a god commands it because it is good, its goodness does not depend on the command. Theists argue that without a god there is no moral authority beyond human prescription. I claim no more than that and need no more: the framework rests on reasons anyone can check (Meta-Ethics). A divine-command theorist faces three further problems before any command can do work. Which command. Scriptures that claim divine authority contradict one another on what is commanded, and none offers testable evidence that it alone is true (Agnostic Atheism). How it is known. A command reaches anyone only through a text, a tradition, or an experience that a human must interpret, so the believer relies on human judgment after all. Why it is good. Some theists answer the dilemma by grounding goodness in God's nature rather than his will, but calling that nature good already uses a standard of goodness that doesn't come from the command. My framework needs none of this. Whether a being can suffer is a question anyone can investigate, believer or not, and a believer who holds that suffering matters already accepts the premise my rights rest on. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Theological Voluntarism

head: "If free will is unresolved, how can anyone forfeit rights?"
body: Responsibility does not wait on a resolution of the metaphysical free-will debate. An agent who understood the act, foresaw the harm, and was not physically compelled still chose, whatever desires, upbringing, or illness shaped the choice, and forfeiture follows the deliberate violation. The full test, and where responsibility is absent, is in Free Will and Responsibility.

My ethics is a threshold sentientist deontology. I believe moral status and strong negative rights belong to every being with first-order subjective experience, biological or artificial. Those rights are side-constraints, not goals to maximize, and they give way only when an agent crosses a clear threshold of rights violation and forfeits the matching protections. I reject positive rights, with minimal tax-funded basic services as a narrow practical exception.
I prescribe that subjective experience (first-order phenomenal consciousness) shall serve as the basis for moral status and the possession of negative rights.
Any being, biological or artificial, that possesses first-order subjective experience is to be treated as a rights-bearer under my framework. Higher-order self-awareness is not required.

A being on an undisturbed developmental trajectory toward sentience (e.g., a healthy fetus in a living womb) shall be granted significant moral weight proportional to the robustness of that trajectory.

A being that once possessed sentience retains residual moral consideration. If sentience is permanently and irreversibly lost, decision-making authority transfers to next-of-kin, guided by respect for the former being’s known wishes and dignity.
Practical determination of sentience shall follow the best available scientific consensus. Where science remains unclear, decisions should err on the side of consistency with these prescriptions.

Under my framework, sentient beings are to be granted strong negative rights against interference and harm. These rights function as side-constraints that may be overridden only when a clear threshold of rights violation by the agent has been crossed (rights forfeiture). The direct imposition of severe, non-consensual risk of serious harm on others counts as crossing that threshold.

All moral and political rules within this system must remain consistent with the prescribed primacy of subjective experience. I don't claim this as objective moral fact. It's a coherent system I choose to endorse and want enforced.
Sentientist:

Moral status and full negative rights attach to beings capable of first-order subjective experience (Axioms 1-2). A being on a developmental trajectory toward sentience (Axiom 3) gets proportional moral weight, not the full negative-rights stack. I believe elective abortion should be banned from conception by constitutional amendment, on that moral weight and on Axiom 5's caution where science is unclear, with drift past week limits as a further safeguard, even though the rights claim starts at 12 weeks (Abortion ban (from conception); Abortion and Bioethics).
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – The Moral Status of Animals
Negative-rights focused:

Rights are side-constraints against interference and harm (Axiom 6). Positive rights are rejected. Minimal tax-funded basic services (education, public safety, infrastructure) are a narrow practical exception.
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Rights
Threshold deontologist:

Core rules against violating sentient rights hold until the Axiom 6 threshold is crossed, and the violator then forfeits corresponding protections. Fetal moral weight scales with proximity to sentience and is grounded primarily in the responsibility created by voluntary procreation. Duties to sustain another being arise only from voluntary responsibility. Where no voluntary act created the dependency, as in rape, withdrawing support differs from killing.
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Deontological Ethics

head: "How is sentientism here different from utilitarianism?"
body: Both start from subjective experience, but mine is a threshold deontology, not a calculation of total welfare: sentient beings hold negative rights that work as side-constraints, not goals to maximize, so no welfare total overrides them (see below).

head: "Why do rights rest on sentience?"
body: Subjective experience is what can be harmed: a being that feels has a life that can go well or badly for it. That is why the Axioms make first-order subjective experience, in any being, biological or artificial, the basis for moral status and negative rights, without requiring higher-order self-awareness.

head: "Why is sentience, rather than species, intelligence, or reason, the right basis for moral status?"
body: Because sentience is what makes harm matter to the one harmed. A being that can suffer has interests of its own. A being that cannot has nothing at stake in how it is treated. Jeremy Bentham put the test plainly: "the question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?" The alternatives draw the line arbitrarily. Species membership alone says nothing about whether a being can be hurt. Intelligence, rationality, and the ability to reciprocate duties fail what philosophers call the problem of "marginal cases." Infants and some severely disabled people lack them, yet almost everyone holds that they have rights, which shows the criterion is doing no real work. Sentience is also evidence-based and gradeable: the 2012 Cambridge and 2024 New York declarations on consciousness extend the evidence well beyond humans (Sentience Determination). Negative rights follow from that basis: if what matters is that a being can be harmed, the core claim it holds is not to be harmed by others. Critics object that sentience cannot be observed directly, so its borders, in insects or in artificial systems, stay uncertain. Uncertain borders call for graded weight and precaution, not for a criterion that's easier to measure but doesn't track what makes harm wrong.

head: "Why not limit rights to those who can make and keep a contract, or only to oneself?"
body: Because both lines fail the test that species fails: each leaves out beings that can be harmed, for reasons that have nothing to do with harm. Contract. Contract theories that give standing only to those who can bargain threaten, as the Stanford Encyclopedia puts it, "to leave many, such as the severely disabled, the global poor, and animals outside the realm of justice." Infants can't bargain either. Some contractarians bring such beings back through indirect duties owed to the people who care about them, which makes an unloved infant's protection depend on someone else's feelings. I reject that. Egoism. An egoist demands not to be harmed while keeping the liberty to harm others. Stated as a rule for everyone in the same position, that demand gives everyone else the same liberty against the egoist, so it can't be universalized (Meta-Ethics). Substrate. For the same reason the circle can't stop at biology. A being with first-order experience in silicon has as much at stake as one in flesh (Axioms, Axiom 2). Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Contractarianism Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – The Moral Status of Animals Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Egoism

head: "Why only negative rights, not positive rights?"
body: A positive right to goods or services would compel others to provide them, which is itself interference with those others. Positive rights are therefore rejected. The minimal tax-funded basic services in the summary above are a narrow practical exception, not rights (Political Philosophy).

head: "What makes rights side-constraints rather than goals?"
body: A goal is something to maximize, so one person's rights could be traded away whenever that raises the total. A side-constraint limits what any agent may do to any other, so the numbers never license harming an innocent (Conflicts Between Rights-Holders). The constraints give way only at the Axiom 6 threshold. The case against aggregation is concrete. In the standard Transplant case, a surgeon could kill one healthy patient and use his organs to save five. Aggregation, applied consistently, says to do it. Utilitarians who refuse do so by adding rules that work like side-constraints. Robert Nozick named the reason: "there is no social entity with a good that undergoes some sacrifice for its own good. There are only individual people, different individual people, with their own individual lives." Suffering is felt by individuals, never by a total, so no total can be the one harmed or the one repaid. A utilitarian who rejects side-constraints has to accept the transplant. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Consequentialism Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Robert Nozick's Political Philosophy

head: "Why can rights be forfeited at all?"
body: Rights are reciprocal. An agent who crosses the Axiom 6 threshold cannot claim the full protection of the rights it violated (Moral Psychology of Rights & Forfeiture). How a court finds forfeiture, scales it to the violation, and sets its duration is in General Rules of Forfeiture.

I ground rights in sentience, not in agency, so children and cognitively impaired adults hold full negative rights. Responsibility rests on agency (Theory of Agency), and a being that lacks agency at the act does not forfeit by that act the way a deliberate agent does. Permanent unremediable dangerous incapacity would be handled as defensive force against a permanent threat, not as act-forfeiture: confinement, then execution if no progress (Insanity Defense). Minors cannot consent to irreversible decisions about their bodies. Permanent loss of sentience falls under Axiom 4. For adult offenders, mental competence or intellectual capacity does not reduce the sentence for a deliberate violation, because my political concern is the outward violation (Criminal Justice & Security). Liability for minors scales with the severity of the crime (Juvenile Offenders).
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Moral Responsibility
Roper v. Simmons (2005) – Death penalty barred for offenses committed under 18

Forfeiture is triggered only when an agent crosses the threshold set in Axiom 6: violating another's negative rights through force or fraud, or directly imposing a severe, non-consensual risk of serious harm. What is forfeited corresponds to the violation and is applied proportionally. Proportionality is applied at the forfeiture decision. Once rights are forfeit, the sentence carried out within them is not a further injustice (Section 10). Forfeiture should be found by a court under due process, never by executive declaration, and its duration should follow the sentence. Rights forfeited for a finite sentence should be forfeited for its duration, and past the repeat-offender threshold or for capital offenses they should be forfeited for life. Some consequences outlast the sentence by rule, such as the bar on felons voting. The same logic scales to organized groups that systematically violate rights (Rights, Order, and Forfeiture at Scale).

Duration matters because repeat offending is common. Among prisoners released from 34 states in 2012, 62% were rearrested within three years and 71% within five, and property offenders had the highest rate, 78.3% within five years. Counted per person rather than per release, about one in three people who enter and leave prison go back to prison (Rhodes et al., using 13 years of data from 17 states). A third of everyone released returning to prison is the repeat population that duration rules exist for.
Christopher Heath Wellman – The Rights Forfeiture Theory of Punishment
Crime & Delinquency (Rhodes et al.) – Following Incarceration, Most Released Offenders Never Return to Prison (2016)
Bureau of Justice Statistics (Durose & Antenangeli) – Recidivism of Prisoners Released in 34 States in 2012: A 5-Year Follow-Up Period (2012–2017)

Some conflicts arise where no one has forfeited anything. Negative rights are side-constraints, so the default is that an innocent person may not be harmed to benefit another, even when the numbers favor it. Self-defense applies to the threat itself: force may be used to stop an attack in proportion to the danger, consistent with Authority & Civil Liberties, and the person defending is not required to absorb serious harm because the attacker lacks culpability.

Scarcity of rescue, such as the allocation of emergency medical care, is a question of positive aid rather than of violation. Allocating a limited resource by a fair, publicly known rule does not violate the rights of those who go without, because no one held a negative right to the resource. What remains forbidden is actively killing or injuring a bystander as a means to an end.
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Rights
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Self-Defense
Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia – Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Robert Nozick's Political Philosophy
See also: Regulation and Conservation · Genetic Engineering and CRISPR · Insanity Defense · Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

Animal agriculture and aquaculture ought to be banned outright and shut down immediately, with sanctuary for every animal still alive (Sanctuary Plan). I hold that sentient animals have rights on a gradient. Deliberately killing a high-sentience animal is murder, except euthanasia for the animal's own sake on a veterinarian's finding and by a veterinary professional. In my view hunting is murder, commercial fishing should be banned and shut down immediately, and cruelty causing lasting injury should be capital, with other grave cruelty in the grave tier: three marks: execution, experimentation, or life with labor. Other sections apply this ethic to their own fields.

Animal agriculture, commercial fishing, aquaculture, commercial breeding mills, and animal testing should be banned outright and instantly, because that is how my view stays sentientist. The philosophy itself is not phased in: there is no lag at all, they should shut down immediately, and every animal still alive should get sanctuary (Sanctuary Plan; Sanctuary forfeiture). Day-one is the position - not a headline softened by a gradual aside elsewhere.

Every animal alive at the shutdown should be kept alive and given sanctuary for its natural life. The day-one shutdown, conversion and liquidation, levy, adoption, worker, and handover rules are set out once in the Sanctuary Plan.

Property ranks among the strongest negative rights, and compelled liquidation without compensation is ordinarily a rights violation. Animal-industry firms forfeited those property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights. The Sanctuary Plan follows from that forfeiture, stated here the same way the excluded-ideologies amendment states its building and office bars (Excluded ideologies). Scope: domestic animal-agriculture, wild-capture commercial fishing, aquaculture, commercial breeding-mill, and animal-testing assets would be compelled to convert, divest, or liquidate. Owners and shareholders would receive no compensation; after workers' unpaid wages and creditors are paid, proceeds would go to the sanctuaries; a family on a liquidated farm would keep its house and house lot; land the sanctuaries need from owners outside these industries would be bought at fair value; the flat Sanctuary Levy (never above 3%, income above $75,000 single / $150,000 joint) would fund care and bond repayment. Those firms used the named assets to violate the rights of the animals they held, and so forfeited ordinary property remedies for those assets. Limit: the forfeiture would be one-time as to the shutdown and conversion, and the levy would end when the national sanctuary population falls below 1% of its starting animal units and the bonds are repaid. It is not a standing power to seize unrelated property or to liquidate firms outside the named industries. The general property rule stands for everything else.

Sentience exists on a gradient across species, and that gradient sets the moral weight of a being under the same scale used for murder in Criminal Justice & Security. Animals are graded into sentience classes. Deliberately killing a member of a high-sentience class outside self-defense is murder, an egregious rights violation that should be on the capital track with the same forfeitures as the murder of a human. Killing a member of a lower-sentience class should count as a mark against the offender. Placement in each class, including fish species by species, is set in the sentience classes. Predation violates its victim's rights even though the predator is not a moral agent (Wild-Animal Predation).

Hunting is murder. There is no subsistence or Indigenous exception. Self-defense and defense of rights cover an actual or imminent attack on a person or animal, and a clear disease or rights threat, including a statutory infestation under the pest rule in Sentience Determination, which limits lethal control to the occupying population (Hunting, Fishing, Pets, and Zoos; Infestation (pest)). Hunger or need is not self-defense. Defense of others covers any sentient victim: force may be used in proportion to the danger, and separation or containment comes first where it will work.

The ban on commercial fishing and aquaculture covers every sea animal in the sentience classes, from decapods in the high class to shrimp placed species by species. Bivalves are likely not sentient and sit in no sentience class; farming them ends with aquaculture for consistency, not as a sentience claim. Bycatch would end with the fishing ban. Other marine activity, such as shipping, dredging, and offshore energy, follows the least-harmful-method rule in Sentience Determination, the same rule as on land; and seafood imports should be banned.

Animal cruelty is extreme violence, intentional neglect, beating without drawing blood, or withholding food, water, or shelter as deliberate punishment (Animal Cruelty Law). Any of these against a higher-sentience animal should be capital if it causes lasting injury, physical or psychological, even when only one animal is harmed, as it is against a human. Otherwise it would fall in the grave tier: three marks at once, reaching the threshold: execution, experimentation, or life with labor, as the victim chooses. Cruelty to lower-sentience animals should not be capital, but it should be tracked and should count toward the repeat-offender threshold, weighted by severity. I would ban ritual slaughter outright.

The duty to protect covers all sentient animals. Within U.S. borders, the government has a duty to intervene to stop rights violations against animals. Protecting animals elsewhere is a virtue but not a duty of the American government. Predation and herbivore population control are decided in Cultural & Social Issues and in Wild-Animal Predation.
Animals cannot consent.

While an animal is alive, decisions about its care would be made by a guardian acting for the animal, not by next-of-kin. The next-of-kin rule in Axiom 4 would apply only after sentience is permanently and irreversibly lost. The owner would be the guardian by default and would decide routine vet care. Euthanasia and other major decisions should be allowed only for the animal's own sake, such as ending suffering, never for convenience, and only on a veterinarian's finding that it is in that animal's best interest. Even at home, if the guardian believes the animal is suffering, euthanasia still requires a veterinary professional, just as assisted death for humans requires a medical professional (Assisted Death).

The comparison to human assisted death concerns who carries it out, not who decides. A human may choose assisted death only as a competent adult. Animals cannot consent, so for an animal the guardian decides for it, under the stricter limits above.

An ownerless or wild animal has no guardian until someone takes it on. Anyone who wants to take an ownerless or wild animal under their responsibility is free to adopt it and becomes its guardian. Adoption would be the rule. There would be no state or sanctuary mandate. Animals alive when animal agriculture, fishing, breeding mills, and testing shut down are different: they would be kept in sanctuaries, and those that are safe to keep may be adopted only after the vetting in the Sanctuary Plan (background check, a home inspection that also sets how many animals a home may take, signed no-slaughter commitment, sterilization, registry ID, unannounced welfare checks, return rule; the adopter pays all care, with no stipend; never a sale).

Euthanasia that breaks these conditions is graded on a sliding scale. A genuine case where the animal is truly suffering, but the guardian ends its life at home without a vet, for example because they cannot afford the vet or do not want to make the trip, should carry a lesser, separate, non-capital penalty. The convenience there is the vet trip, not the killing, and real suffering is still required. A case that only looks like mercy, with no real suffering and no genuine basis, is cruelty, graded under the cruelty tiers above (Animal Cruelty Law). A case with clear intent to harm is murder. Killing for convenience stays murder. A parent who kills a sick child at home is wrong even if the child was going to die, and this needs a real block. But genuine euthanasia holds real mercy, so a capital line for every non-vet case would be too harsh.
Until the industry is shut down, I believe that if paying is the only way to save a sentient animal already headed to slaughter, the person should pay (Rescue Purchases).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Westland/Hallmark, 2008: undercover footage released by the Humane Society (an advocacy group; primary footage) showed workers shocking, kicking and ramming downed cows with a forklift to force them to slaughter. CNN (2008) – Video of workers abusing cows raises food safety questions

Recall: the plant's footage led to the largest U.S. meat recall, 143 million pounds, about 50 million of which had gone to school lunch and other federal nutrition programs. Congressional Research Service (2008) – Prepared for Members and Committees of Congress

head: "Sentience can't be measured directly. How does anyone decide which animals count?"
body: No one can observe another being's experience directly, in animals or in other humans, so the question is one of evidence, not proof. Researchers have built graded tests. A 2021 review for the UK government by Jonathan Birch and colleagues at the London School of Economics assessed over 300 studies against eight criteria, including nociceptors, integrative brain regions, responses to anaesthetics and analgesics, and trade-offs between the cost of a threat and the benefit of obtaining resources, and recommended that all cephalopod molluscs and decapod crustaceans be regarded as sentient in UK animal welfare law. I use the same approach. Species are placed on the sentience gradient by the best available evidence, and where evidence is uncertain, protection is extended rather than withheld, because wrongly denying a sentient being its rights is the worse error. I adopt that recommendation in the sentience classes. Insects are technically covered too, but they sit on a very low tier of the sentience scale, closer to potential sentience than established sentience, and are protected on a precautionary basis, with enforcement aimed at deliberate killing (Sentience Determination).

head: "Why should animals hold rights when they cannot hold duties?"
body: Rights rest on sentience, not on the ability to take on duties (Minors and Incompetent Adults). Infants and incompetent adults hold rights without moral agency, and sentient animals do too, weighted by their place on the sentience gradient.

head: "If rights come in proportion to sentience, how can killing a pig carry the same sentence as killing a person?"
body: While a human life is usually richer than a pig's, richness does not set the right not to be killed. I'm a threshold deontologist, not a utilitarian. The gradient decides which class a being falls in. It does not discount the right not to be killed once a being is in the high class (sentience classes). Above that threshold, the right against being killed is a full side-constraint, the same for every member. That is already how the law treats people: an infant, a person with severe dementia, and a philosopher have unequal cognitive lives and an equal right not to be murdered. A pig, a cow, or a chicken has a life that can go well or badly for it, and killing it takes all of that away, permanently. Below the threshold, the gradient sets the penalty, marks rather than death, and across every class it guides rescue priority, which is positive aid, not violation (Conflicts Between Rights-Holders). While most people's intuitions rank a human death far above an animal's, intuitions once ranked some humans above others too, and an intuition is not evidence of where the threshold lies. Proportionality in my framework means the punishment matches the violation, and killing a high-sentience being is the gravest violation it can suffer. The law already accepts the premise and then breaks it. Federal law punishes purposely crushing, burning, drowning, suffocating, or impaling a living mammal, bird, reptile, or amphibian with up to seven years in prison, then exempts "the slaughter of animals for food." The animal's experience is the same either way. The line follows the human purpose, not what is done to the animal. To reject my rule, a critic has to deny one of two premises: that a pig is in the high sentience class, which is a question of evidence (Sentience Determination), or that every being above the threshold holds an equal right not to be killed, which the law already applies to infants and to people with dementia. Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 48: Animal crushing

head: "Isn't this an extreme outlier, even among animal-rights positions?"
body: On penalties, yes, and I don't hide it. But being an outlier is a headcount, not an argument. The premise is not an outlier: in Gallup's 2015 survey, 32% of Americans said animals should have the same rights as people, 62% said they deserve some protection, and only 3% said they need little protection "since they are just animals." Federal law already treats crushing or impaling a living animal as a serious crime, then exempts slaughter for food (see the question above). My position is that premise held without the exception. Most animal-rights positions stop at the right and leave out the enforcement. I believe a right the law won't enforce protects no one, and that once a being is in the high sentience class, the penalty for killing it should not depend on its species. A critic who wants to show I'm wrong has to name the premise to drop, not count the people who share the conclusion. Gallup (May 18, 2015) – In U.S., More Say Animals Should Have Same Rights as People

head: "If animal farming is murder, are today's farmers, slaughter workers, and hunters murderers?"
body: The act is a rights violation now. But criminal punishment applies only to acts committed after the law that forbids them takes effect. The Constitution bars ex post facto laws, and I hold that rule on its own merits: my ethics are prescriptions I choose and want enforced, and a prescription becomes a punishable law only once it is enacted and published. So no one would be prosecuted for killing an animal before the ban, and every killing after it would be prosecuted under the sentience-graded rules. The bar on people who killed animals for a living working in hands-on care or adopting (Sanctuary Plan) would not be a punishment. It would be a fitness rule for the animals' safety, of the same kind as the adoption vetting. Cornell LII – Calder v. Bull, 3 U.S. 386 (1798)

head: "How is anyone supposed to know which animals are capital?"
body: The statute should list the classes, and the list should be published. The mental state required should be knowledge of the act: the offender knew they were killing that animal. Not knowing the list is no defense, any more than not knowing the murder statute is. A genuine, reasonable mistake about what the animal was, such as a thrown net that caught a bird hidden in it, goes to intent the same way it does with a human victim. The evidence behind the list is strongest for mammals and birds. For cephalopods and decapods, the list follows the Birch review described above and puts both in the high class, and the UK's Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 now covers both groups. For fish, Sneddon and colleagues found that rainbow trout have pain receptors much like those of mammals, and that a painful stimulus changed their behavior and physiology for a prolonged period. Fish species differ widely, which is why they are placed species by species rather than as one group. Sneddon, Braithwaite & Gentle, Proceedings of the Royal Society B – Do fishes have nociceptors? Evidence for the evolution of a vertebrate sensory system (2003) London School of Economics (Birch et al.) – Review of the Evidence of Sentience in Cephalopod Molluscs and Decapod Crustaceans (2021) UK Legislation – Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022, section 5

head: "Does killing rats or mice in a house count as murder?"
body: Rats and mice are high-class mammals (sentience classes), and pest status does not drop them a class: deliberately killing them outside self-defense or defense of rights is murder and should be on the capital track. What changes the analysis is a qualifying infestation under the pest rule above (Infestation (pest)). Separation and exclusion come first where they will work. A single animal passing through, or animals outdoors that are not occupying a qualifying site, do not meet the test, and kill campaigns against non-infesting wildlife in parks, fields, and islands should stay banned and are murder when the animals are high-class. Hunger, nuisance alone, or "they might show up later" is not the infestation test and is not self-defense.

head: "Plants respond to damage too. Why don't they count?"
body: Responding to damage is not experiencing it. Plants have no neurons and no centralized structure that integrates information into experience, and the plant biologists who reviewed the "plant neurobiology" claims concluded that plants neither have nor need consciousness. Under Axiom 5 the best available science decides, and it finds no subjective experience in plants. If the evidence changed, so would the classification. A plant diet also kills fewer plants than an animal diet, because farmed animals eat crops (Agriculture and Food Policy). Taiz et al., Trends in Plant Science – Plants Neither Possess nor Require Consciousness (2019)

head: "Harvesting crops kills field mice. Isn't a plant diet also killing?"
body: Some harvest kills are real. Steven Davis argued they could exceed the deaths from grazing cattle. That comparison counted totals rather than deaths per person fed, and it left out the cattle themselves. A diet that feeds crops to animals kills more field animals per person, because most feed calories are lost on the way. Incidental deaths in lawful harvesting are not deliberate killings and carry no criminal liability. The least-harmful-method rule above should govern them, and failing to use it should be punished. Davis, Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics – The Least Harm Principle May Require that Humans Consume a Diet Containing Large Herbivores, Not a Vegan Diet (2003) Matheny, Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics – Least Harm: A Defense of Vegetarianism from Steven Davis's Omnivorous Proposal (2003)

I believe a sentient being's right not to be killed does not disappear because a price is attached to them. If paying is the only way to get an animal out of slaughter, and someone refuses on principle, that animal dies for a rule it had nothing to do with. I believe the person should pay.

The usual argument in modern vegan thought is utilitarian: paying funds the system and creates demand for more animals. I reject that as a reason to let this animal die. Buying a spent hen or a cull cow already headed to slaughter barely changes supply, and it is not an order to breed more animals. It changes that animal's whole existence. A certain death here and now outweighs a speculative effect on future demand. Letting the animal die in order to send a message about demand to a farmer uses that animal as a means to an end. Rescuers already pay for veterinary care, transport, and feed, so money changing hands is not the line. The question is who gets paid.

This is about the world as it is now, while the industry still kills animals. It is not a change to the Sanctuary Plan. After the shutdown, animals in sanctuaries are already safe, and adoption from a sanctuary should never be a purchase (Sanctuary Plan).

I also draw a line about what is being paid for. I support paying to rescue an animal that is already doomed. I still oppose paying a breeder to produce a newly bred animal. "Adopt don't shop" is right when it means do not pay breeders to bring new animals into existence. It is wrong when it is used to refuse to buy an animal out of death.

head: "Doesn't paying the farmer fund the system and create more suffering later?"
body: That is the traditional vegan argument, and it is a utilitarian one: decline this purchase so that fewer animals are bred or raised later. My ethics is a threshold deontology, not a calculation of total welfare (Normative Ethics). Rights are side-constraints, not goals to maximize, so a living animal's right not to be killed is not traded away for a speculative drop in future supply. The purchase at issue is not an order for a new animal. A spent hen or a cull cow was already going to be killed. The money adds almost nothing to the farmer's incentive, because he would kill the animal anyway. The certain death of this animal is here and now. The demand effect is uncertain and later. I believe that is not a reason to walk away.

head: "If we shouldn't pay ransoms to kidnappers, why pay a farmer?"
body: Imagine a murderer who says: pay me, or I kill this person, and I will use the money to kill more people. I believe we should work to shut him down. But if there is no other way to save the person, I believe we should pay, because otherwise the person is just dead. A person's right to life does not disappear because their captor might profit, or because the captor will "do it again." If the police have no other way to save someone, they ought to pay the ransom. The usual reply is the no-concessions policy. The U.S. and U.K. governments refuse to pay ransoms to terrorist kidnappers, on the ground that paying makes their citizens more valuable targets later. That is the same utilitarian argument. Two points answer it. First, no-concessions is a policy for the state. It does not, in the United States, bar families from paying. In the June 2015 hostage policy review that produced Presidential Policy Directive 30, the White House stated that the Department of Justice "does not intend to add to families' pain in such cases by suggesting that they could face criminal prosecution." Second, the analogy is weaker than it looks. A terrorist seizes a person in order to collect. A farmer is not seizing animals in order to extract money from rescuers. He would kill them anyway, so the rescue payment adds almost nothing to his incentive to keep killing. White House (June 24, 2015) – FACT SHEET: U.S. Government Hostage Policy White House (June 24, 2015) – Presidential Policy Directive: Hostage Recovery Activities UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office – Kidnappings or hostages abroad
