Socialism is state or collective ownership of productive property, central planning in place of prices, and redistribution by force. I condemn it because it takes property and overrides consent from people who have harmed no one. Voluntary cooperatives, a flat tax, and a minimal floor for basic needs are not socialism.

Socialism meets the excluded-ideologies test: it takes property and overrides consent from people who have harmed no one. Its open adherents ought not to hold authority roles (Oath of Office and Perjury), and no one should be fined, jailed, or silenced for holding it. Social democracy I judge as too large a state, not as socialism (Socialism (excluded)). The economic case, the country records, and the comparisons are in Socialism.
See also: Socialism (economic case) · Communism · Cultural Marxism

Communism is the program of abolishing private property, with one party holding a monopoly of power. I condemn it because every state that built it banned rival parties, ran forced-labor camps, and caused famines and mass killings that cost millions of lives. Today it is carried mainly through cultural Marxism.

I judge communism by its program and its record. Marx and Engels described the goal as an association in which "the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all." They also wrote that the theory "may be summed up in the single sentence: Abolition of private property," to be achieved at first "by means of despotic inroads on the rights of property." Every state that acted on this program in the twentieth century gave one party a monopoly of power. It confiscated land and businesses, punished political opponents, and directed labor by force. The worst cases include the Soviet Gulag, the Soviet famine of 1931–34 including the Holodomor in Ukraine, China's Great Leap Forward famine, and the Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia. These are violations of the right to life, liberty, and property on a scale few other systems have matched. Communism is condemned at the same severity as Nazism, socialism, and Islam, without making belief in it a crime, and its organized violent groups treated as threats (Terrorism and Domestic Extremism).

The United States ought to treat communism the way it treats Nazism in everything the government does itself. State history standards ought to teach the crimes of communist regimes alongside the Holocaust, the nation ought to remember their victims, and no communist figure or regime ought to receive a public honor, name, statue, holiday, or public funding, just as no Nazi one does. Existing public honors, names, statues, and holidays for communist figures or regimes ought to be removed, as a Nazi one would not be left standing (Cultural Stance). That is the government speaking for itself. Private citizens keep their full right to praise Lenin or Mao, as they keep the right to praise Hitler (Free Speech and Censorship).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

North Korea: a UN Commission of Inquiry documented crimes against humanity driven by "policies established at the highest level of State," and called for referral to the International Criminal Court. UN News (2014) – UN-mandated human rights inquiry on DPR Korea documents 'widespread, systematic abuses'

Cambodia: the UN-backed tribunal convicted Khmer Rouge leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan of genocide in 2018. UN News (2018) – UN genocide adviser welcomes historic conviction of former Khmer Rouge leaders

China, 1989: a declassified British diplomatic cable put the Tiananmen crackdown death toll at at least 10,000. The figure is far above other estimates. BBC News (2017) – Tiananmen Square protest death toll 'was 10,000'

head: "Wasn't that not real communism, only distortions by Stalin, Mao, and Pol Pot?"
body: I judge the program and its results. The program itself called for abolishing private property and for "despotic inroads" to do it. The abuses followed from giving a state unchecked power over all property and labor, in countries with very different cultures and leaders. I judge a plan that has failed the same way in every state that tried it by that record.

head: "Didn't communist states also reduce illiteracy, expand health care, and industrialize?"
body: Whatever gains in literacy, health care, and heavy industry occurred, I don't accept trading some people's lives and liberty for others' gains, and market economies achieved these gains without camps or famine (Economic System). China's own reversal after the Great Leap, returning private plots and tools to peasants, is a concession from inside the system.

head: "Death-toll figures are disputed. Aren't critics inflating them?"
body: While critics claim the totals are inflated, the dispute is over how many tens of millions died, not whether they did. The widest total, the 85 to 100 million in The Black Book of Communism, was contested even by two of its own authors, so I set it beside the lower counts (Rationale). For the Great Leap famine, early demographic estimates were 16.5 to 23 million excess deaths, and later studies found 23 to 30 million. Western scholars put Gulag deaths from 1918 to 1956 at 1.2 to 1.7 million. Even the lowest figures describe deaths caused by state policy on a scale that settles the moral question.

head: "If communism is condemned, why not ban the party?"
body: Because the state ought to punish harm, not belief. The two civic disabilities for excluded ideologies are not penalties. Advocacy should be protected up to true threats and incitement to imminent violence, the same rule that applies to every ideology (Free Speech and Censorship). Punishing belief would copy the method being condemned.

head: "If communism is treated like Nazism, why not make glorifying it a crime, as some European countries do?"
body: Because in the United States glorifying Nazism is not a crime either, and I keep it that way. The law restricts only true threats and incitement to imminent violence, for every ideology (Free Speech and Censorship). Equal treatment applies to what the government itself does: what public schools teach, which victims the nation remembers, and whom it names, honors, or funds. The Supreme Court has held that a government choosing which permanent monuments to place on public land is speaking for itself, which the Free Speech Clause does not restrict, so none of this needs a new speech law.

head: "Isn't equating them wrong? Nazism aimed at extermination, while communism's deaths came from a failed utopian plan."
body: Defenders of the distinction point to intent: Nazism made killing a goal, while communism promised liberation. The record answers them. Soviet authorities blacklisted Ukrainian villages from food and barred starving peasants from leaving to find it, and a UN-backed tribunal convicted the Khmer Rouge's surviving leaders of genocide. A victim's rights are violated the same whether the regime that starved or shot them promised liberation or not, and the state's treatment of the two follows the victims, not the slogans.

I rest on individual negative rights to life, liberty, and property (Political Philosophy). Communist states removed all three as a matter of system design. The 1977 Soviet Constitution named the Communist Party "the leading and guiding force of Soviet society and the nucleus of its political system," which left no lawful route for opposition. Forced collectivization began in 1929. Peasants were made to give up land and property, and resisters and "kulaks" were deported. Britannica reports that between 1931 and 1934 at least 5 million people died of hunger across the USSR, including at least 3.9 million Ukrainians, and that Ukrainian villages were blacklisted from food and peasants were barred from leaving to seek it. Britannica puts the Gulag at about 5 million prisoners by 1936; the NKVD's own records, opened in the 1990s, are lower, about 1.2 million in its camps and labor colonies at the end of 1936, not counting prisons and deported "special settlers." Western scholars estimate 1.2 to 1.7 million Gulag deaths from 1918 to 1956.

In China, the Great Leap Forward caused what Vaclav Smil called the largest famine in human history. Demographic reconstructions put the toll at 23 to 30 million excess deaths, and Smil wrote that it was "largely a manmade catastrophe." Britannica gives a lower estimate of about 20 million. In Cambodia, Yale's Cambodian Genocide Program estimates that about 1.7 million people, 21% of the population, died under the Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979. A UN-backed tribunal later convicted the regime's surviving leaders of genocide and crimes against humanity.

The widest estimate comes from the authors of The Black Book of Communism, who put the cumulative toll of communist rule at between 85 and 100 million. The breakdown reported at publication in 1997 gave China 45 to 72 million and the Soviet Union about 20 million. Critics, including two of the book's own contributors, Nicolas Werth and Jean-Louis Margolin, objected to its editor's "obsession" with reaching a hundred million dead, and Werth counted 15 million Soviet victims. The dispute is over the size of the total, not its order: Werth's 15 million Soviet victims and the Great Leap's 23 to 30 million already come to 38 to 45 million before Cambodia, North Korea or anywhere else is counted.

Treating the two alike in the state's own conduct already has precedent. Congress authorized the Victims of Communism Memorial in Washington in 1993, and it was dedicated in 2007. Florida's History of Communism standards, approved in November 2025 under a 2024 law, take effect in its public schools in the 2026–27 school year. In 2019 the European Parliament, by 535 votes to 66, called on member states to make "a clear and principled assessment" of the crimes of the communist regimes and the Nazi regime, to commemorate 23 August as a day of remembrance for the victims of totalitarian regimes, and to put that history in school curricula. In Pleasant Grove City v. Summum (2009) the Supreme Court held that placing a permanent monument in a public park is government speech, not subject to scrutiny under the Free Speech Clause, so the government's choices about memorials and honors restrict no one else's speech.

Today communism is carried mainly through cultural Marxism, which I set out in its own section, with intersectionality, equal outcomes, anti-merit policy, and its acceptance among the young and in universities (Cultural Marxism).

The common thread is collective goals placed above individual rights. When the state owns all property and allows no opposition, a person has no legal defense against it. Famines then go unreported, and dissent becomes a crime. My answer is the opposite design: property rights, competing parties, and limits on state power, with belief itself left free.

Cultural Marxism is the critical theory of the Frankfurt School and its offshoots, which recasts class struggle as oppressed groups against oppressors and carries it into culture and education. I condemn it because it assigns a person's standing by group instead of by merit or conduct.

By cultural Marxism I mean a specific strand of Marxist thought: the critical theory of the Frankfurt School and the broader strands of critical theory that grew from it, such as critical theory applied to race, sex, and culture, which recast Marx's class struggle as a struggle between oppressor and oppressed groups and carry it into culture, institutions, and education. The lineage is documented in the school's own texts. Max Horkheimer's 1937 essay "Traditional and Critical Theory" defined the program against ordinary scholarship: critical theory "never aims simply at an increase of knowledge as such," but at "emancipation from slavery." The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy places the Frankfurt School in "the Western European Marxist tradition" and lists feminist theory, critical race theory, queer theory, and postcolonial theory as broader strands of critical theory. Herbert Marcuse's 1965 essay "Repressive Tolerance" carried the program into speech and schooling: "Liberating tolerance, then, would mean intolerance against movements from the Right and toleration of movements from the Left," including "the withdrawal of toleration of speech and assembly" from groups he opposed and "new and rigid restrictions on teachings and practices in the educational institutions." I hold this to be communism carried into culture. It sorts people into oppressor and oppressed groups and treats the freedom of those labeled oppressors as something to withdraw, the same assignment of standing by group that I reject in every excluded ideology. My claim is about these published ideas and their spread, never about anyone's ancestry or a secret plot.
I answer it with the merit rule, tests in selective admissions, and gifted programs, never with a penalty for belief.

head: "Isn't 'cultural Marxism' a conspiracy-theory label?"
body: Critics argue that it is. The philosopher Joan Braune calls it "an antisemitic conspiracy theory" in which "the Jewish Marxists of the Frankfurt School implemented a slow takeover of 'culture.'" I reject that theory as she describes it: I claim no plot and no secret coordination, and the ancestry of any Frankfurt School member has nothing to do with my judgment. My claim is about published ideas and their spread, and both are documented. The lineage runs from Horkheimer's 1937 program of critical theory, through Marcuse's 1965 call to withdraw toleration from the Right and to restrict teaching in schools, to the broader strands of critical theory the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy lists, and its spread is measured in the survey and faculty data. Marxist scholars use the term for their own tradition: the UCLA critical theorist Douglas Kellner wrote that cultural studies "had predecessors in a number of currents of cultural Marxism," naming Georg Lukacs, Antonio Gramsci, Ernst Bloch, Walter Benjamin, and T.W. Adorno among others. A name that Marxist scholars give their own tradition is not a slur when I apply it to the same tradition (Cultural Marxism).

head: "Isn't intersectionality only a descriptive legal tool for overlapping discrimination?"
body: Its defenders say it is. Crenshaw called it "a provisional concept" and built it from employment cases in which courts would not hear Black women's claims, and in that use it asks a court to hear a claim it was dismissing. I hold every individual claim of discrimination open to a court, whatever its source. The concept did not stay there, and Crenshaw did not mean it to. The 1989 article ends on "restructuring and remaking the world where necessary" and on "collectively challenging the hierarchy." "Mapping the Margins" defends identity politics against its critics and asks for finer group lines, not fewer: "The problem with identity politics is not that it fails to transcend difference, as some critics charge, but rather the opposite—that it frequently conflates or ignores intragroup differences." A framework that names, stacks, and ranks groups so that they can be empowered as groups is a program, not a description. The record shows where the program leads: racial preferences at Harvard and UNC struck down by the Supreme Court, test-free admissions at Thomas Jefferson that cut offers to Asian-American students, and eighth-grade algebra removed in San Francisco and restored ten years later (Anti-meritocratic beliefs in practice). Each came from the outcome-by-group logic of equal outcomes, not from a court's need to hear one plaintiff (Intersectionality).
The supporting record is collapsed below.

head: Intersectionality, equal outcomes, merit, and acceptance among the young

body: Intersectionality. The term comes from the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw. In "Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex" (1989) she argued that antidiscrimination law worked from a "single-axis framework" that erased claims by Black women, who can be harmed by race discrimination, sex discrimination, or both at once: "Discrimination, like traffic through an intersection, may flow in one direction, and it may flow in another." The same article went past that legal point. It pictured a basement holding everyone "disadvantaged on the basis of race, sex, class, sexual preference, age and/or physical ability," "stacked—feet standing on shoulders—with those on the bottom being disadvantaged by the full array of factors," and it called for "collectively challenging the hierarchy" and for "restructuring and remaking the world where necessary," beginning with those at the bottom. In "Mapping the Margins" (1991) Crenshaw wrote that the work "arises out of and is inspired by two emerging scholarly discourses," the first being "critical race theory," and Encyclopaedia Britannica describes that movement's "immediate precursor" as critical legal studies, "an offshoot of Marxist-oriented critical theory." I hold that intersectionality is the oppressor-versus-oppressed sorting of cultural Marxism with the groups stacked: it ranks a person's standing and claims by how many disadvantaged groups the person belongs to, and the person's own conduct drops out of the ranking.

From disparity to equal outcomes. Once every gap between groups is read as proof of oppression, the remedy becomes equal outcomes by group. Ibram X. Kendi states the logic plainly: "A racist policy is any measure that produces or sustains racial inequity between racial groups," "There is no such thing as a nonracist or race-neutral policy," and "The only remedy to racist discrimination is antiracist discrimination. The only remedy to past discrimination is present discrimination." Britannica records the central criticism of critical race theory as "interpreting racial inequity as proof of institutional racism." Equalizing outcomes by group requires handing out admissions, hiring, pay, and standing by group membership instead of by individual merit or conduct. That is the same assignment of standing by group that the excluded-ideologies test rejects, and it is why I hold equality of outcome to be discriminatory by definition (Race and Diversity). A gap between groups is a fact to be explained, not proof of who wronged whom, and measured achievement gaps that persist at equal family income are set out in Intelligence, Race, and Crime.

Anti-meritocratic beliefs in practice. The same logic is turned against merit itself. MIT's dean of admissions noted in 2022 that "the entire concept of 'merit'" "has been critiqued as merely laundering intergenerational privilege," and Kendi counts "standardized tests that produce racial inequities" among the things racist power calls "race neutral." Where that belief governed, it raised the bar for some applicants to lower it for others. In Students for Fair Admissions (2023) the Supreme Court's opinion noted that at Harvard an African American applicant in the fourth-lowest academic decile had a higher chance of admission (12.8%) than an Asian American applicant in the top decile (12.7%), and that at UNC, in the second academic decile from the top, 83% of Black applicants were admitted against 58% of white and 47% of Asian applicants. At Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in Virginia, after a board member demanded that the district "be explicit in how we are going to address the underrepresentation of [b]lack and Hispanic students," the board in December 2020 adopted an admissions policy that no longer relies on standardized tests. Asian Americans' share of offers fell from between 65% and 75% to 54.36%, and although the entering class grew by 64 seats, they were offered 56 fewer. The Fourth Circuit upheld the policy, and the Supreme Court declined review in 2024 over a dissent by Justice Alito, joined by Justice Thomas: "What the Fourth Circuit majority held, in essence, is that intentional racial discrimination is constitutional so long as it is not too severe." San Francisco's school board moved Algebra 1 out of eighth grade in 2014 to address racial gaps in advanced math. Stanford researchers later found the large racial and ethnic gaps in advanced math enrollment persisted, and in February 2024 the board voted 6 to 1 to bring the course back. The evidence on merit runs the other way. Dartmouth's faculty found that SAT scores alone explained about 22% of the variation in first-year grades and high school GPA alone 9%, and Dartmouth restored its testing requirement in 2024. MIT restored its own in 2022, finding that tests help it identify disadvantaged students who could not otherwise show readiness. Across Ivy-Plus colleges, Opportunity Insights found that students with a 1600 SAT earned first-year grades 0.43 points higher than students with a 1200, and that the scores show no calibration bias: students from less advantaged backgrounds do not outperform peers from more advantaged backgrounds with similar scores. A test that predicts equally well for every group measures merit, not privilege. The policy that follows is the merit rule, with tests in selective admissions and gifted programs and tracking.

Acceptance among the young and in universities. In the Cato Institute's March 2025 survey, fielded by YouGov, 62% of Americans aged 18 to 29 held a favorable view of socialism and 34% a favorable view of communism, against 43% and 14% of all adults. In the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation's 2020 survey, also fielded by YouGov and the latest edition of its annual report I could verify, 30% of Gen Z, then aged 16 to 23, viewed Marxism favorably and 28% communism, against 6% and 3% of the Silent Generation. Gallup's figures on young adults and socialism are in Public Opinion Trends. The faculty who teach them lean overwhelmingly one way. The Higher Education Research Institute's 2016–17 survey of 20,771 full-time undergraduate teaching faculty at 143 four-year institutions found 48.3% liberal and 11.6% far left, against 11.7% conservative and 0.4% far right. The liberal share was 48.8% in 2013–14 and 36.8% in 1989–90. Mitchell Langbert's study of 8,688 tenure-track, Ph.D.-holding professors at 51 of the top 66 liberal arts colleges found a Democratic-to-Republican registration ratio of 10.4 to 1, or 12.7 to 1 without West Point and Annapolis, and 39% of the colleges had no Republican faculty at all. Critics note that these surveys measure favorable views of labels that respondents define for themselves. Cato says its poll did not define socialism, and party registration is not critical theory. The label is the point: a third of young adults no longer treat communism as disqualifying, and the faculty who form them register Democratic at more than six times the 1.6-to-1 ratio Langbert found among Americans with some graduate education.

Islamism is the political project of ruling by Islamic law. I condemn it because where it holds power it punishes apostasy and blasphemy with death and gives women and non-Muslims lesser legal standing. Its jihadist wing is the deadliest source of terrorism in the world today.

Islamism seeks to make Islamic law the law of the state (Sharia as State Law). Where Islamist law is enforced, it punishes belief and speech through apostasy and blasphemy laws, imposes fixed (hudud) punishments such as stoning, flogging, and amputation, criminalizes consensual same-sex relations, and makes legal standing depend on sex and religion. Its jihadist wing pursues the same goal by terror. These are violations of the right to life, liberty, and equal standing that every sentient individual holds (Animal Rights and Sentientism). Islam, and Islamism with it, is condemned at the same severity as Nazism, communism, and socialism, without making belief in either a crime, and Islamism's organized violent groups treated as threats (Terrorism and Domestic Extremism). My separate critique of the faith's classical teachings is set out in The Islamic Faith in Practice.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Iran, 2022–24: a UN fact-finding mission found the repression of the protests that followed Jina Mahsa Amini's death in morality-police custody involved serious violations, many amounting to crimes against humanity. head: "How can Islam rank with Nazism when Nazism killed far more people?"
body: Nazism's toll is far larger, and I do not claim otherwise. It murdered six million Jews and millions of others in a few years (Nazism). My ranking is about the present: which ideology is killing the most people now, in the most places, and holding state power to punish belief. On that test Islam leads. The data are set out in Islam and Extremism.

head: "Isn't most terrorism in the West political rather than religious?"
body: Yes. In North America since 2007, politically motivated attacks outnumbered religiously motivated ones, 84 to 21, and 58 were linked to the far right. Most terrorism deaths, 98% in 2024, occur in countries at war. But in the West, every death from religiously motivated terrorism from 2007 to 2024, 494 in all, was caused by jihadists, and worldwide the four deadliest groups were all jihadist.

head: "If Islamism is condemned, why not ban it?"
body: Because the state ought to punish harm, not belief. The two civic disabilities for excluded ideologies are not penalties. Advocacy should be protected up to true threats and incitement to imminent violence, the same rule that applies to every ideology (Free Speech and Censorship). Punishing belief would copy the method being condemned, which is exactly what apostasy and blasphemy laws do.

Islamism removes rights I protect, both through state law and through terror. In 2019, 79 of 198 countries had laws against blasphemy and 22 had laws against apostasy, 13 of them in the Middle East and North Africa. In Afghanistan, Brunei, Iran, Mauritania, Nigeria, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia, blasphemy can carry the death penalty. The Library of Congress found in 2014 that Afghanistan, Brunei, Mauritania, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, the United Arab Emirates, and Yemen expressly make apostasy a capital offense. Brunei's 2019 revisions provided death for adultery, sodomy, and insulting the Prophet, and amputation for theft, according to the UN human rights office. These laws punish belief, identity, and speech, not harm.

The jihadist wing kills on the largest scale of any terrorist movement today. In 2024, Islamic State and its affiliates were the deadliest group, killing 1,805 people in 22 countries. Together with Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimeen, Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, and al-Shabaab, they caused 4,204 deaths, 80% of the terrorism deaths attributed to a specific group, and were active in 30 countries. The Sahel alone accounted for 51% of all terrorism deaths. Total terrorism deaths fell 13% in 2024 to 7,555.

The common thread with Nazism and communism is a doctrine placed above individual rights, enforced by the state or by terror against those who do not submit. My answer is the same in each case: rights held equally by every sentient individual, a state barred from punishing belief, and force reserved for those who violate others' rights.

Nazism ranked human beings by supposed race and used the state to strip, expel, and kill those it ranked lowest. I condemn it because it assigned rights by group identity instead of to every sentient individual, and murdered six million Jews and millions of others.

Nazism is incompatible with my framework at its root. Its core claim was a racial hierarchy in which "Aryan" Germans were superior and Jews and others were inferior. It turned that claim into law, took total control of the state, and then pursued conquest and extermination. I ground rights in sentience, which every person has equally, so any doctrine that assigns rights by race, ancestry, or disability contradicts my framework directly (Animal Rights and Sentientism). Nazism is condemned at the same severity as communism, socialism, and Islam, without making belief in it a crime, and its organized violent groups treated as threats (Terrorism and Domestic Extremism).

head: "Doesn't your own nationalism and civilizational language resemble it?"
body: No, and the difference is the test itself. Nazism assigned worth by blood. I judge compatibility by values that anyone of any ancestry can hold, and I protect every sentient individual's rights, including non-citizens' within U.S. borders (Western Values and Compatibility). It does not penalize belief and leaves removal to courts with due process, which is the opposite of the Nazi method.

head: "Why give Nazism its own topic when no serious movement defends it?"
body: Because it is the clearest case for testing a principle. Its racial laws, its "euthanasia" killings, and its genocide show what happens when a state decides some sentient beings have no rights. Naming the specific rules that made this possible shows why I put rights before the state, the majority, and the group.

Each stage of Nazi rule removed rights I protect. The Reichstag Fire Decree of February 1933 suspended constitutional protections for personal liberty, free expression, the press, assembly, and the privacy of mail and telephone, and let the regime jail opponents without charge. The Nuremberg Race Laws of 1935 limited citizenship to those "of German or related blood." They banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and other Germans and were extended to Roma and Black people. These laws punished identity, not conduct.

The "euthanasia" program began in 1939 and targeted institutionalized disabled people as "life unworthy of life." By T4's own count, 70,273 people were killed at six gassing centers from January 1940 to August 1941, and historians estimate about 250,000 deaths across all phases. The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum notes that T4's gas chambers and staff were later used for the killing centers of the Holocaust. The museum counts six million Jews murdered, about 2.7 million of them at killing centers and about 2 million in mass shootings. It also counts around 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war, around 1.8 million non-Jewish Poles, 250,000 to 500,000 Roma, and 250,000 to 300,000 disabled people. Lebensraum ("living space") policy planned the removal of Slavs and Jews from eastern Europe. Pre-invasion guidelines stated that "many tens of millions of people in this territory will become superfluous and will have to die or migrate to Siberia."
The lesson I draw is that rights ought to belong to every sentient individual and should not depend on the state, a majority, or a group's ranking. Nazism reversed every part of that rule.

I stand for strong individual liberties and property rights, with government limited to protecting sentient rights, public safety, and order. I want opt-in mechanisms where possible and harsh accountability for criminals and officials, and I am skeptical of overreach but support effective enforcement.

I believe the government should leave people alone unless they are actively harming others or about to do so. That is my core rule. Speech should stay free except for real threats and calls to immediate violence. Being watched while you are out in public is normal. Being tracked everywhere by permanent databases is not something we should accept lightly. Liberty comes first. The state ought to step in only to stop rights violations, and it has to justify every step it takes.

The state may use force only when it is necessary to stop people from violating the negative rights of others - mainly force, fraud, or the direct imposition of serious non-consensual harm. Liberty ought to be the default. Any mandate, speech restriction, or surveillance power should have to clear a high bar: it must be necessary, narrowly aimed at the actual problem, and temporary when the threat is temporary. Personal choices end when they cross into violating someone else’s rights, not merely when they create some diffuse or indirect effect.

head: "Doesn't almost every choice affect someone else? Where does that leave the line?"
body: Almost every choice has some effect on others, which is why indirect effect is not the test. The test is whether the choice violates someone's negative rights through force, fraud, or the direct imposition of serious non-consensual harm. A choice that others dislike, or that changes a social environment they would prefer to keep, does not meet that test. A choice that injures, defrauds, or directly endangers someone does.

I treat rights as side-constraints, not as goals that can be balanced away whenever a net benefit appears. The state does not get to override liberty simply because a policy is believed to be good for people overall. It acts when one person is violating, or is about to violate, another’s rights. The practical test used is simple: Is someone violating (or imminently about to violate) another’s negative rights? Is the response necessary and proportionate? If the answer to either question is no, the state should stay out.

Speech follows the same logic. The line is drawn at true threats and incitement to imminent lawless action. Once the state starts policing ideology, offense, or “misinformation,” it is no longer protecting rights, it is managing thought. That is incompatible with free inquiry and a limited role for government. The excluded-ideologies rule polices no one's speech or thought: it governs the state's own positions and the building of institutions, under one published test (Excluded ideologies).

Public surveillance sits in a middle position. There is no reasonable expectation of privacy against ordinary observation while walking down the street. Continuous bulk tracking and permanent facial-recognition databases are different; they concentrate power and change the relationship between citizen and state even if no traditional “search” occurs. NIST testing of face-recognition algorithms found false-positive rates that often differed by factors of 10 to 100 across demographic groups. I accept normal public-order policing while requiring tighter limits on the more sweeping technological versions.

The force or punishment used in reply to a rights violation is matched to the severity and nature of the violation: enough to stop it, deter it, and reflect the seriousness of what was done, but not wildly excessive relative to the harm.

Katz v. United States (1967) – Reasonable expectation of privacy

In my view government exists to protect rights and must justify every expansion. The branches should stay separate, new rules carry the burden of proof, and agencies cannot go beyond the laws that authorize them.

I hold government power to the same test applied to every use of coercion: it exists to protect sentient rights and must justify each extension. Separated legislative, executive, and judicial powers should be retained so that no single branch can expand state authority unchecked. The burden of proof ought to rest on any new regulation, not on the people regulated, and administrative rules should carry no more authority than the statutes that authorize them. Emergency authority should lapse automatically unless the legislature renews it. When a federal action is unconstitutional, the ruling should protect everyone's rights the same way, through class actions or fast Supreme Court review, so a right never depends on which district a person lives in. Single district judges should not set national policy by themselves.

head: "Doesn't a limited government struggle to act when needed?"
body: No. A limited government acts decisively within its core functions: defense, policing, courts, and the protection of rights. The limits apply to expansion beyond those functions, which should be justified rather than presumed.

The Constitution vests legislative power in Congress, executive power in the President, and judicial power in the courts (Articles I–III). In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) the Supreme Court overruled Chevron deference, holding that courts must exercise independent judgment on whether an agency acted within its statutory authority. That aligns with the rule that the burden of justification rests on the regulator, set out in Domestic Policy & Governance.

I oppose term limits on any elected office. Every elected office should run on a three-year cycle, with re-election on the table based on performance. Federal offices need a constitutional amendment to match that structure, including the presidency and Congress.

I oppose term limits on any elected office. Re-election should always be on the table based on performance: if they do a good job, voters can re-elect them and they continue; bad performance ends it. Somebody who is successful can stay indefinitely based on the people's want. This applies to all elected offices: the presidency, Congress (representatives and senators), governors, and every other elected position. Election cycles should be three years for every elected office. Keeping re-election always available kills lame-duck corruption, because the incentive to stay clean never drops; there is always another election coming.

head: "Don't term limits stop career politicians and corruption?"
body: No. Officials who cannot run again are lame ducks, and the accountability evidence runs the other way: Brazilian mayors who could seek re-election diverted about 27% fewer resources than mayors in their final term. Studies of U.S. state legislative term limits find turnover and a shift of influence toward governors, agencies, and lobbyists rather than a proven drop in corruption. Accountability comes from voters facing another election on a short cycle, not from a hard exit date.

head: "What about presidents who refuse to leave?"
body: Supporters of limits point to evasion: of 234 presidents in 106 countries who reached the end of their term limit since 2000, at least a third tried to stay on. That record argues for my system. Courts mostly failed to stop those attempts, and the ones that failed were stopped mainly by popular resistance, the same check a three-year election cycle puts in voters' hands at every election. The United States ought to keep that check live rather than create the lame-duck final term in which the audit evidence above finds more misuse of funds.

head: "Doesn't the Twenty-Second Amendment already limit the presidency?"
body: Yes under current law. This position replaces that structure: the presidency, like every other elected office, has no term limit and runs on a three-year cycle. Putting that in force for federal offices requires constitutional amendment, including changing or repealing the Twenty-Second Amendment and aligning House and Senate terms with the three-year cycle. Under U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton (1995), states cannot add congressional term limits on their own.

head: "Does the whole Senate turn over at once, and what about judges and state offices?"
body: No. Each Senate term lasts three years. The Senate stays staggered in thirds, with one class up every year on the three-year cycle, so there is always a fresh electoral check without the whole chamber turning over at once. Elected judges are on the same three-year cycle. States adopt the three-year cycle by changing their state constitutions, starting at the next regular election after adoption.

Accountability that never turns off beats a forced last term. Ferraz and Finan (2011) found Brazilian mayors eligible for re-election misappropriated about 27% fewer resources than lame-duck mayors in randomized federal audits. Alt, Bueno de Mesquita, and Rose (2011) found U.S. governors eligible for re-election outperformed term-limited governors on growth, taxes, spending, and borrowing costs. State legislative term-limit studies find higher turnover and a shift of influence toward governors and the bureaucracy, not a measured anti-corruption gain. So I reject adding term limits and shorten the cycle to three years so voters can act while the incentive to stay clean is still live. Changing presidential and congressional terms requires amendment; Thornton bars states from adding congressional qualifications on their own.

In my view defense, borders, and immigration belong at the federal level. Schools should be local with per-child state funding. Rights must apply the same everywhere, and programs ought to be opt-in rather than imposed from above.

Powers ought to be placed at the level closest to the people that can carry them out. National defense, foreign policy, immigration, border enforcement, and national election-integrity standards (ID, authentication, counting method) should be federal; states and localities should not be able to obstruct them, which is why I would abolish sanctuary policies. Schools should be run locally, with each state funding about $10,000 per child that follows the child to any public school in the state, and the federal Department of Education abolished. Programs funded by opt-in money follow the same principle: participation is chosen, not imposed from the top. Policing should be local by default. The federal government should reinforce or take over local police only where local authorities fail to stop violent crime or riots, under a time-limited emergency that Congress must renew. The District of Columbia, as a federal district, is Congress's direct responsibility.

head: "Doesn't local control produce unequal outcomes between places?"
body: Some variation is expected and acceptable. Rights protections apply equally everywhere. What varies is how localities choose to deliver services, and people and families can move or choose among providers.

The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people the powers not delegated to the United States. Immigration and naturalization are federal powers under Article I, Section 8, and in Arizona v. United States (2012) the Supreme Court held that federal immigration law preempts conflicting state measures. The education structure is set out in Domestic Policy & Governance.

Emergency powers must be necessary, narrow, and temporary. I would have them expire automatically unless the legislature votes to renew them, keep free speech working, and stop the state from keeping extra powers once the danger passes. During an emergency, charging, trial, and sentencing should move to the law enforcement officers or military handling it, so the people caught inside it are protected while it lasts.

I hold emergency powers to the same test as any mandate: necessary, narrowly aimed at the actual threat, and temporary. Every emergency declaration and every power exercised under it should expire automatically on a fixed date unless the legislature votes to renew it. Renewal ought to require a fresh justification on current evidence. In an emergency, charging, trial, and sentencing move to the law enforcement officers or military handling it (Gun Crime and Violence). In a declared state of emergency involving riots or violent crime that local policing cannot contain, the military and police handling it may impose and carry out a death sentence on the spot. The emergency does not lower the capital evidentiary standard: the officer should have to be certain of the act to that standard before acting. Every on-the-spot sentence should be recorded, including body-camera footage, and an ordinary civilian court should review the record after the emergency ends; an officer who carried out a sentence the record does not support ought to be charged as for murder. Speech should stay protected except for true threats and incitement to imminent violence. I reject open-ended emergency powers and the permanent expansion of state authority after the acute danger has passed.
My view: Emergencies add latitude: in an emergency, charging, trial, and sentencing move to the law enforcement officers or military handling it.

head: "Can a government respond fast enough to a real crisis under these limits?"
body: Yes. The executive can act immediately when a severe, direct threat appears. The limits govern duration, not speed: the powers lapse on their own unless the legislature affirmatively renews them, so extraordinary authority cannot continue by inertia.

head: "How are on-the-spot death sentences necessary and narrow?"
body: They should be allowed only inside a declared emergency over riots or violent crime that local policing cannot contain, and that emergency expires on a fixed date unless the legislature votes to renew it, so the power ends with the danger. It is narrow in who it reaches: only a person the officer is certain, to the full capital evidentiary standard, committed a capital act in front of the emergency response. The emergency speeds up the process, not the standard of proof. It is checked after the fact: every case is recorded on body camera, an ordinary civilian court reviews it once the emergency ends, the recording is published, and an officer whose sentence the record does not support is charged as for murder. A high-crime area that has no declared emergency gets intensive policing and full due process, not on-the-spot sentences. The standard is stricter than today's law. Under Tennessee v. Garner (1985), an officer may already use deadly force against a fleeing suspect on "probable cause to believe that the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury." My rule requires certainty to the capital standard, a recording, and a murder charge where the record falls short. The people it protects are the ones a riot reaches first: residents, shopkeepers, and bystanders who cannot leave and cannot wait for order to return. The two errors are not equal. An officer who acts without a record to support it is charged as for murder, while an offender who kills in front of the response and is left free to keep going takes lives that no later trial gives back. An officer certain to the full standard can still be wrong, and an on-the-spot sentence cannot be undone; the recording, the civilian review, and the murder charge keep that rare and punish it. Cornell LII – Tennessee v. Garner, 471 U.S. 1 (1985)
Graded: Alien Enemies Act invoked against Tren de Aragua

An emergency does not let the government close places of worship or ban gatherings in them as a class. Ordinary laws still apply to any building, such as fire codes, structural danger and active crime scenes. Worship may not be treated worse than comparable secular gatherings, and no general emergency order may single it out. If I were voting on Wisconsin Question 2, I would vote yes.

Under the National Emergencies Act, a declared emergency ends only by joint resolution or presidential proclamation, or if the President fails to renew it each year; Congress is directed to meet every six months to consider termination. The default favors continuation, and emergencies accumulate: as of October 2, 2026, 51 declared national emergencies were in effect. Automatic expiry with legislative renewal reverses the default, so the burden rests on continuing a power rather than on ending it.

I believe that once ownership is properly established, it is meant to last. The state may take property only for narrow public purposes and must pay full value. Ordinary zoning can exist, but rules that destroy the real value of ownership without payment should be treated as takings. Two cases fall outside that protection: one is barred by amendment, and in the other the owners forfeited it. Under the excluded-ideologies amendment, which uses the categories of the oath standard, places promoting anti-American or anti-constitutional causes, such as Nazi, communist, socialist, or Islamic sites, are barred from being built, rebuilt, expanded, or relocated, and no new mosques may be built (Excluded ideologies). Under the Sanctuary Plan, those industries would be shut down at once, with no compensation to owners or shareholders, because animal-industry firms forfeited their property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights. That forfeiture is one-time, and the general property rule covers everything else (Sanctuary forfeiture).
Intellectual property should be protected for practical reasons even though it rests on thinner foundations than physical property.

Owners should be able to use necessary force to stop theft or intrusion. Lethal force is available only when the intrusion is violent or carries a clear threat to persons or the security of the home. Pure non-violent theft is handled through restitution and criminal penalties, not lethal force. As population grows and time passes, adjustment should happen through voluntary exchange, denser development, and new value creation - not through political resetting of existing titles. I treat secure property rights as a basic condition for investment, agency, and a high-trust society.

I rank property rights among the strongest negative rights. Once ownership is legitimately acquired, it is permanent and may be defended with proportionate force. Eminent domain should be limited to narrow public-use cases with full compensation. I don't treat ordinary zoning as a taking, but regulation that eliminates the economically beneficial uses of property, or destroys the great majority of its value, is a taking and should require compensation. The first exception is the bar on building, rebuilding, expanding, or relocating places that promote anti-American or anti-constitutional causes, the four excluded ideologies of the oath standard - Nazism, communism, socialism, and Islam, all on the same terms; examples are a Nazi gathering place with its symbols, an anti-American communist stronghold, or an Islamic center or school; new mosques are also barred outright. The bar falls on the place and the symbols built into it, never on a person's belief, speech, or home practice (Excluded ideologies; Oath of Office and Perjury).

The second is the Sanctuary Plan: those industries should be compelled to shut down their animal operations, with no compensation to owners or shareholders. Animal-industry firms forfeited their property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights, so this is a one-time forfeiture, not a break in the property right. The full scope, conversion, land, levy, and worker rules are set out in the Sanctuary Plan and in Sanctuary forfeiture. The general rule still stands for all other property.

Intellectual property's foundations are thinner than physical property's, but I would protect it for practical reasons. As population grows and time passes, adjustment occurs through voluntary exchange, development, and new value creation rather than political resetting of titles.

head: "If ownership is permanent, doesn't that lock in past injustices and leave later generations with nothing?"
body: Permanence applies to legitimately acquired property. A title that rests on force or fraud was never legitimate, and the rights violation behind it can be answered through ordinary legal process. Later generations are not left with nothing: as population grows, adjustment comes through voluntary exchange, development, and new value creation. What I reject is political redistribution of titles that were legitimately acquired.

head: "Can an owner use property to harm the neighbors?"
body: No. Property is a negative right and stops where it violates others' rights. Pollution that harms others or imposes a severe, non-consensual risk of serious harm on them makes the polluter liable (Pollution and Liability).

head: "Why protect intellectual property if its foundations are thinner?"
body: It is protected for practical reasons of incentive and coordination, and subject to reasonable limits, rather than as a natural right equal to physical property.

My excluded-ideologies amendment covers Nazism, communism, socialism, and Islam, the four doctrines that meet the test in Excluded ideologies, but only for the bars on building, rebuilding, expanding, or relocating places and on holding office. For those bars it sets aside the First Amendment's speech and free exercise protections and the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), and it blocks any objection on viewpoint-discrimination or religious-liberty grounds. A constitutional amendment overrides any earlier provision or statute that conflicts with it, so no such objection can be raised against these bars. Everywhere else, speech and belief stay protected: holding or peacefully advocating any of these views carries no legal penalty.
Sources: Cornell LII – 42 U.S. Code § 2000cc

Secure property rights protect the ability to plan, invest, and build without constant fear that what has been created can be taken by force or by political decision. Evidence across countries and centuries shows that clearer, more stable ownership tends to produce more investment and higher incomes. Where ownership is insecure, people invest less, informal arrangements multiply, and conflict over resources becomes more common.

The idea that all land begins as government property until it is sold is set aside. The state’s role is to recognize and defend legitimate holdings once they exist, not to act as the original owner of every piece of territory. Once title is justly acquired, permanence is the default. Permanence does not freeze use. Owners remain free to sell, lease, subdivide, or redevelop. As population grows, rising demand raises the return to more intensive use. Land held in low-value ways faces growing market pressure to change hands or change use. Ownership protects the right to decide. It does not protect any particular use from competition.

head: What counts as legitimate holdings / just acquisition?

body: Legitimate (or “just”) acquisition means the holding was obtained without violating others’ negative rights. The main routes are:
First acquisition of something previously unowned (classic homesteading / effective occupancy and improvement).
Voluntary transfer from a prior legitimate owner (sale, gift, inheritance, exchange).
Rectification in limited cases where a clear prior rights violation can be traced and corrected (stolen property returned, etc.).
What is not legitimate acquisition:
Conquest or seizure by force
Fraud
Political grant that simply takes from one private party to give to another
“We voted to take it” without a narrow public-use justification and full compensation

I do not require a perfect historical genealogy back to the first human. In practice it operates with a strong presumption in favor of long-settled, currently recognized titles and a high bar for disrupting them. The key test is whether the current claim rests on a chain of voluntary transfers or original appropriation rather than on ongoing aggression or pure political allocation.

Eminent domain stays an exception. It is acceptable only for clear public-use projects and only with full compensation and strong safeguards. Expanding it to private economic development or general revenue goals turns a limited tool into a political transfer mechanism. I reject that expansion.

Zoning sits in the middle. Some basic coordination rules can reduce conflict without destroying ownership. When regulation becomes so heavy that formal title remains while the economically beneficial uses of the property are eliminated, or the great majority of its value is destroyed, the regulation functions as a taking and requires compensation.

Intellectual property rests on weaker ground than physical property. Ideas can be used by many people at once, and the boundaries are conventional. Protection is still maintained because limited exclusivity gives people reason to create and helps coordinate complex production. Because the justification is practical, the length and scope of protection remain open to evidence and adjustment.

Defense of property would follow ordinary proportionality. An owner should be allowed to use the force needed to stop the violation. Lethal force would be justified when the intrusion is violent or carries a clear threat to persons or the security of the home. Pure non-violent theft or conversion would not authorize lethal force. It would be handled through restitution and scaled criminal penalties. Once the immediate threat ends, the response would shift to recovery of the loss and proportionate punishment. This limit would govern an owner's immediate defense. The state's sentencing of repeat offenders after conviction is a separate matter, set out in Criminal Justice & Security. Proportionality would be applied at that forfeiture decision, not again within the sentence (Section 10).

As time passes and population increases, the state does not promise every person a land allotment. It keeps peaceful acquisition and voluntary exchange open, and it refuses to treat existing ownership as a pool that may be reallocated whenever demographic pressure rises. Larger populations are supported by denser development, technological improvement, and the creation of new forms of value - all of which function better when ownership is secure. Societies that have maintained relatively stable property rights while allowing markets in land and housing have generally absorbed population growth with rising average living standards. Systems that make ownership politically revisable in the name of access have more often produced both insecurity and poorer overall results.

Strong property rights shrink the realm of political allocation, encourage investment, and support a high-trust order. Weakening them for short-term flexibility or redistributive convenience reintroduces the uncertainty the institution exists to limit.

I believe people may use force to protect themselves or others anywhere, with no duty to retreat. An aggravated, avoidable killing is murder and goes to the mandatory capital track. Near-justified self-defense should be a lesser homicide with a lighter sentence set by the judge.

I believe a person may use force to stop an attack on themselves or on another person. There should be no duty to retreat and no location limit: the right applies at home, in a vehicle, and in public alike. Whether a killing in a claimed act of self-defense is lawful turns on an intent test. A killing that was aggravated and avoidable is murder and goes to the mandatory capital track. "Avoidable" means the attack had already been stopped or could have been stopped without killing; it never means the defender could have retreated. A killing in near-justified self-defense is a lesser homicide, with a lighter sentence decided by the judge. Defense of property follows the separate rule in Property Rights.

head: "Doesn't removing the duty to retreat everywhere invite needless killings?"
body: No. The absence of a duty to retreat does not protect a killer who acted with intent beyond defense. An aggravated, avoidable killing is murder and should carry the mandatory capital sentence, and a killing that came close to justified self-defense but fell short should still be punished as a lesser homicide.

head: "Doesn't the evidence show stand-your-ground laws increase homicides?"
body: The evidence leans that way. RAND's review rates as supportive the evidence that stand-your-ground laws increase total and firearm homicides. The position does not rest on that evidence; it rests on principle. Running should never be the first option for a person facing an attack, and a threat should never feel free to intimidate because its target is expected to retreat. The intent test is the safeguard: an aggravated, avoidable killing is still murder on the capital track.

head: "Who has to prove whether a killing was self-defense?"
body: The prosecution. It should have to prove intent for a lesser-homicide charge, and should have to prove any aggravating factor that moves a killing to the capital track, not just the act itself (Lesser Homicide).

As of January 1, 2025, 35 states had stand-your-ground statutes or statutes extending castle doctrine beyond the home, according to RAND. RAND also reports supportive evidence that these laws are associated with increases in total and firearm homicides; the intent test answers that risk by treating an aggravated, avoidable killing as murder under the mandatory penalty in Criminal Justice & Security. Qualification for gun ownership and red flag laws are set out in Cultural & Social Issues.

People, clubs, and religious groups should be free to choose whom they associate with. Association should stay free only so long as it violates no one's rights. Joining or organizing a group to commit or plan rights violations, such as a conspiracy, gang, or organized violent group, is not protected (Terrorism and Domestic Extremism). No one may be held in a group against their will. Employers and businesses open to the public should not be allowed to hire, fire, serve, or treat anyone differently for race, sex, sexual orientation, or another protected trait, in either direction. There should be no quotas or DEI preferences, though wide advertising is fine, with narrow carve-outs (Merit-rule carve-outs). Businesses should still be free to decline to create expressive work they object to. Outside employment and public business, I consider compelling association coercion. It needs the same high justification as any other use of state force.

I hold that private individuals and voluntary organizations have the right to decide whom they associate with in personal, religious, and club life. They should be free to include or exclude on any basis there. Employment and public business are different. Hiring, firing, pay, promotion, and service in a business open to the public should not turn on race, sex, sexual orientation, or another immutable or protected trait. Treating a person worse or better for what they are is a rights violation (Equal Treatment in Employment and Business). The rule should be symmetric. It should bar preferences and quotas, including private DEI preferences, as firmly as exclusion, with narrow carve-outs (Merit-rule carve-outs). Voluntary outreach that does not affect selection, such as advertising widely, should remain legal. Sex means biological sex: male, female, and rare intersex conditions. Gender identity is not a legal category. Outside those traits, employers and businesses would keep wide freedom to choose on merit, conduct, and fit. A business may decline to create expressive work it objects to. I reject broad mandates that police ordinary preferences in private social life.

head: Doesn't this lead to segregation, or discrimination?
body: Legal segregation and private freedom of association are not the same thing. Historical Jim Crow was primarily state-enforced separation: laws that required racial division and often forbade private integration. A pure association rule does the opposite. The state may neither compel association nor compel separation. In personal, religious, and club life, private parties may exclude or include and the law stays neutral. In employment and public business, one neutral rule bars treatment by protected traits in either direction. Markets and reputation raise the cost of widespread exclusion. Forced association can produce physical proximity without the trust that makes integration valuable. Every anti-discrimination regime still excludes. They simply transfer the decision from the rights-holder to the state. I reject state-mandated segregation. I permit voluntary sorting in private association. I treat exclusion or preference by protected traits in employment and public business as a rights violation.

head: "Could a business refuse service because of race?"
body: No. A business open to the public may not refuse a customer because of race, sex, sexual orientation, or another protected trait. An employer may not refuse a worker for those reasons either. A business may still decline to create a message or expressive work it objects to, whoever asks, as the Supreme Court held in 303 Creative v. Elenis. Private clubs, religious bodies, and personal relationships remain free to choose their members. The state itself may never compel separation.

Freedom of association follows from the same negative-rights logic applied to liberty and property. If people own their labor, their time, and their property, they must be free to decide the terms on which they share them. Forcing a private party to associate, serve, or employ against their will is a form of compelled labor or compelled use of property. That compulsion is justified only when it is necessary to stop a rights violation. It is not justified when it is intended to produce a preferred social pattern. Employment and public business are where I find such a violation. An employer or business that rejects or prefers a person for an immutable or protected trait judges them by group rather than by merit or conduct. Stopping that is the justification for the rule.

The historical and practical case for wide association rights is straightforward. Voluntary sorting allows cooperation among people who share values, risk tolerances, or purposes. It reduces conflict. It supports high-trust environments. It lets different communities test different norms. When the state overrides those choices in the name of inclusion or equity, it substitutes political allocation for private coordination. That often generates resentment and evasion rather than genuine integration.

Anti-discrimination rules are not rejected in every form. Rules that prohibit violence, fraud, or clear safety hazards fit inside the negative-rights frame. Refusing to serve someone who is actively threatening others is an example. In personal, religious, and club life, rules that treat ordinary preference or cultural affinity as illegal do not fit. In employment and public business, preference or exclusion by protected trait is barred because it judges people by group, including statistical discrimination by group. Once the law begins policing the reasons for private choices rather than the presence of force or fraud, it expands beyond protecting rights and into managing social outcomes. That expansion is inconsistent with limited government and with the priority given to negative rights.

Public accommodations and common carriers would follow the protected-trait rule like any public business. Beyond those traits, a business holding a genuine bottleneck position on essential services can be held to further narrow non-discrimination conditions. The burden would be on the state to show necessity and narrow tailoring.

Membership organizations, religious groups, and social clubs would keep the full right to choose their members. Religious bodies would choose their own clergy and religious roles. The right to exclude is what makes the right to include meaningful. Without it, association becomes a state-managed status rather than a private decision.
In short, I treat freedom of association as a core negative right. The state may intervene to stop rights violations. It may not intervene to force people into relationships they do not want.

To me, privacy means control over access to one’s body, home, private spaces, and personal information. Others should not get to enter, search, or collect without consent or a clear, limited legal process. Ordinary observation in public is acceptable. Turning public presence into permanent, identifiable records should be limited to public protection by the government and require opt-in for companies. Companies may offer services that involve data sharing, but the terms must be honest and the ability to decline must be real. Government access should be targeted and process-based, not open-ended. Privacy protects against intrusion while still allowing focused investigation when rights are actually being violated.

Privacy protects a person from non-consensual intrusion into their body, home, personal spaces, and personal information. The default ought to be control: others, including the state, should not get access without consent or a clear, limited justification tied to stopping rights violations. Ordinary observation in open public spaces carries no reasonable expectation of privacy. Entry into private spaces, searches of persons or belongings, and collection of personal data should all require either consent or proper legal process. Mass, open-ended collection of data or permanent surveillance systems that convert public presence into lasting records face a higher bar.

head: "Doesn't strong privacy protection just help criminals and block legitimate security needs?"
body: Privacy is not a right to hide criminal activity. Targeted investigation based on probable cause, warrants for specific places or data, and ordinary public observation remain available. The limit is on bulk, preemptive, or indefinite collection and on entering private spaces without process. Strong default privacy raises the cost of casual intrusion and mission creep while still allowing focused enforcement when force, fraud, or serious harm is actually at stake.

Privacy, in both its traditional and informational forms, protects the ability to maintain a personal domain free from unwanted interference. Without it, agency shrinks. If the state or private actors can enter the home, search the person, or compile detailed records of private life at will, the individual no longer sets the terms of access. That is a form of control even when no physical injury occurs.

The classic core remains the home, the person, and private papers or effects. Entry or search in these domains requires consent or a specific, evidence-based legal process. General warrants, open-ended authorization, or routine intrusion without individualized suspicion are incompatible with the right. This is ordinary negative-rights protection applied to physical space and personal boundaries.

Public space is different. What a person knowingly exposes to open view, like walking on a street, speaking in a park, or attending a public gathering, carries no reasonable expectation of privacy against ordinary observation. The problem arises when technology turns transient public presence into permanent, searchable, identifiable records. Continuous bulk recording, facial-recognition databases, and long-term tracking change the character of public life. They concentrate power and create lasting exposure that ordinary observation never did. The initial setting is public, but that shift justifies tighter limits.

Informational privacy follows the same logic. Personal data is not simply “out there” for the taking. Collection by the state or by companies requires clear notice and genuine consent, or a proper legal process when consent is absent. Hidden collection, vague terms, or designs that make refusal impractical undermine the condition that makes consent meaningful. Where a service is difficult to avoid, the demand for transparency and workable choices is higher. Data-driven services are not prohibited. It requires that they rest on agreement rather than default extraction.

State power receives the strictest application. Targeted collection under warrant for specific investigations fits inside rights-based enforcement. Open-ended bulk collection, indefinite retention of ordinary activity, or repurposing data for unrelated goals does not. Once detailed records on the population become routine, the capacity for abuse grows and becomes hard to reverse. A 2022 FISA Court opinion found that FBI personnel ran more than 278,000 noncompliant queries of Section 702 data, including queries tied to protest participants and campaign donors.

Privacy is therefore handled as a side-constraint on intrusion. It protects the home, the person, private spaces, and personal information from non-consensual access. It does not guarantee invisibility in public, nor does it block focused investigation of actual rights violations. The practical goal is to keep control with the individual by default while still permitting necessary, limited responses when force, fraud, or serious harm is at issue.

Facial recognition and social credit should be opt-in only. I'm fine with cameras in public, but companies must notify people and get their consent before using that footage for anything beyond viewing. Tech-government partnerships are acceptable to me if rights and consumer protections are respected.

People in public have no reasonable expectation of privacy, but facial recognition by companies should always be opt-in and never mandated; government use of public-space data for public protection follows Surveillance and Digital Technology below. Social credit systems should be opt-in and never mandated. I find partnerships between tech companies and government acceptable as long as sentient rights are respected and consumer protections are upheld. I accept surveillance in public areas. Any further data mining of public surveillance data by a company should require that the person be notified and opt into sharing before the data is used in any way beyond viewing.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.
NSA bulk phone records: a U.S. appeals court ruled in 2020 that the program exposed by Edward Snowden was unlawful. BBC News (2020) – NSA surveillance exposed by Snowden ruled unlawful

head: "If public spaces carry no expectation of privacy, why require consent for data mining?"
body: Being seen in public is different from having that footage processed, profiled, and traded. Viewing public surveillance should be permitted. Turning it into a data product about a specific person requires notice and opt-in consent. This keeps public safety intact while protecting individuals from commercial exploitation of their data.

head: "Doesn't public-area surveillance build a surveillance state?"
body: Viewing public spaces should be permitted because there is no reasonable expectation of privacy there. Mass, open-ended collection and permanent surveillance systems that turn public presence into lasting records face a higher bar (Privacy Rights), and any use of the data beyond viewing requires notice and opt-in. Facial recognition by companies and social credit systems are opt-in only.

My privacy rule distinguishes public presence from private data. The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches, and the Supreme Court has recognized that new technologies can intrude on privacy even when data is gathered in public or held by third parties, as in Carpenter v. United States on cell-site location records and Kyllo v. United States on thermal imaging. Consent-based rules for data use beyond viewing follow that line while allowing ordinary public surveillance for safety.

head: What is a social credit system?

body: A social credit system scores individuals based on behavior, finances, or compliance, and attaches rewards or penalties to the score. The position here allows such systems only on a voluntary, opt-in basis.

I believe data privacy must be respected and all data trading should be opt-in. Public-space data can be used for public safety, and companies handling it ought to be regulated.

All data privacy ought to be respected, and all data trading should be opt-in only. Government should regulate this and punish any transgressions, with fines scaled to income and wealth. Data acquired in public spaces carries no expectation of privacy protection and is used for public protection and the best interest of the people, and by companies only with notice and opt-in. Government should regulate any private company trading or accessing this encrypted data.

head: "If public data has no privacy expectation, why regulate companies' use of it?"
body: Public data may be used for public protection. Private trading of that data for commercial gain is a separate act, and regulation keeps it within consumer protections.

Personal data is an extension of the person, and its sale without consent is a rights violation. Public spaces carry no expectation of privacy, so public-safety use should be permitted. These rules match the positions in Privacy Rights and Surveillance State above.

head: Due Process and Rule of Law
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

body: Everyone should answer for what they do, and people with more power answer to a higher standard. Assets can be taken only to settle broken contracts or unpaid debts between private parties. I view bail with suspicion, and judges ought to be vetted more strictly so that repeat offenders are stopped.
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

head: Position
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

body: I hold all people liable for their actions. Higher elected officials and those with great responsibility should be offered more in salary but held to higher standards. Assets should be forfeitable when contracts are broken or debts go unpaid between private actors. I view the bail system with skepticism. Judges ought to be vetted far more stringently so that punishment is applied appropriately, because I treat repeat offenders causing great damage as something that should never happen. Death penalty and incarceration positions are set out in Criminal Justice & Security.
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

head: "Does limiting asset forfeiture to private disputes leave the state without tools against criminals?"
body: No. Forfeiture here is a remedy between private parties: a broken contract or an unpaid debt allows the injured party to recover assets. Punishment of criminals is handled through the criminal sentencing, restitution, and compelled-labor rules in Criminal Justice & Security, where offenders pay their victims from their own accounts and assets.
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

head: Rationale
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

body: Equal liability under law is the foundation of a high-trust society, and power that escapes accountability invites abuse. Greater authority therefore carries a stricter standard. Asset forfeiture in the civil-enforcement sense has drawn constitutional limits, including the Supreme Court's holding in Timbs v. Indiana that the Excessive Fines Clause applies to the states; restricting forfeiture to private contract and debt disputes keeps the remedy tied to an actual injured party. Federal pretrial release law already allows detention of defendants who pose a danger, which the Court upheld in United States v. Salerno. Repeat offending is a documented pattern in national recidivism data, which is why judicial vetting and sentencing aim at preventing it. Among prisoners released from 34 states in 2012, 62% were rearrested within three years and 71% within five years.
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

head: What is asset forfeiture?
topic: Due Process and Rule of Law

body: Asset forfeiture is the legal transfer of property to another party because of its connection to a wrong. Civil forfeiture lets the government take property tied to suspected crime, often without a conviction. The position here allows forfeiture only to satisfy broken contracts or unpaid debts between private parties.
