body: Defendants should be released before trial unless a judge finds they are dangerous or likely to flee. In my view money must not decide who stays in jail, and those held must be tried within 90 days or released while the charge stands.

An accused person has not been convicted and keeps their rights until a court finds otherwise. Pretrial detention should be allowed only on an individualized judicial finding that the person poses a serious danger to others or a real risk of flight, made at a prompt hearing with counsel. Detention should not be set by ability to pay. Detained defendants ought to receive swift trials so that detention does not become punishment before conviction.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Kalief Browder: held at Rikers Island for years without trial after a robbery arrest, reportedly beaten and kept in solitary, his case was dismissed in 2013. He killed himself in 2015. NPR (2015) – Kalief Browder, Jailed For Years Without Trial, Kills Himself

Waukesha, 2021: the man charged in the Christmas parade attack had been released on $1,000 bail, an amount the county's district attorney later called inappropriately low. NPR (2021) – Wisconsin Christmas parade case raises questions around bail

head: "Won't releasing defendants endanger the public?"
body: Those who pose a serious danger are detained. The rule removes wealth as the deciding factor: a dangerous person with money is not released, and a harmless person without money is not held.

head: "How swift is a swift trial?"
body: A detained defendant should be brought to trial within 90 days of arrest. Only the defendant should be able to ask for more time. The prosecution and the court should not be able to extend the deadline on their own. If the state misses it, the defendant should be released pending trial under ordinary conditions, and the charge should stand. Federal law already sets a similar clock. The Speedy Trial Act requires an indictment within 30 days of arrest and a trial within 70 days of indictment or first appearance, though it excludes many periods of delay and its remedy is dismissal rather than release. Detention never becomes an open-ended punishment before conviction.

A constitution may let judges deny release for the most serious charges, such as capital murder, terrorism and rape, as long as each denial is the judge's own finding about the particular defendant, made at a hearing with counsel and given in writing. No charge leads to detention automatically, and the 90-day trial limit still applies. Tennessee Amendment 1 allows courts to deny bail for a listed set of serious offenses and requires judges to record their reasons. If I were voting, I would vote yes.

At midyear 2023, 70% of people held in local jails had not been convicted of the crime they were held for. In United States v. Salerno (1987) the Supreme Court upheld federal pretrial detention based on a judicial finding of dangerousness after an adversarial hearing, which is the structure this position adopts. Speed matters because people admitted to jail from July 2022 to June 2023 spent an average of 32 days in custody before release.

I would bar the state from taking property from people who have not been convicted, except assets of foreign cartels formally designated as war enemies or Foreign Terrorist Organizations, which are seized as enemy property on the combatant track, and true contraband, which may be seized and destroyed or returned to owners. Domestic gangs and undesignated actors still require a conviction. The Sanctuary Plan also takes property without a conviction: animals are removed to sanctuaries, and those businesses are shut down with no compensation to owners or shareholders, because animal-industry firms forfeited their property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights (Sanctuary forfeiture). After a conviction, the offender's assets should go to the victims first. Leftover goes to a victim restitution fund, then the general treasury - no seizing agency keeps what it seizes. The government must prove the link by clear and convincing evidence, give notice within 7 days, and hold a hearing within 30 days before any sale.

I believe the state should not take property without a conviction. No property may be seized or forfeited absent a criminal conviction for the offense the seizure is tied to, except as set out below for designated enemy assets and true contraband. The government ought to bear the burden of proving that the property is tied to that offense by clear and convincing evidence, not a preponderance of the evidence. Owners should receive written notice within 7 days of any seizure and have the right to contest it at a hearing held within 30 days; no seized property should be sold or transferred before that hearing is decided. Assets should be forfeited when a person is convicted of a rights violation, and they should go first to restitution for the victims. After victims are fully paid, leftover forfeited assets go to a victim restitution fund, then the general treasury; no seizing agency keeps what it seizes. True contraband - items illegal to possess - may be seized without a conviction and destroyed, or returned to rightful owners if stolen. Lawful property is never forfeited without a conviction, and an owner may contest disputed status at the 7-day/30-day hearing. Assets of foreign cartels formally designated as war enemies or Foreign Terrorist Organizations are seized as enemy property on the combatant track, without a domestic civilian conviction, consistent with Foreign Policy & International Relations. Domestic gangs and undesignated actors still require a conviction and full due process. The one further exception is the Sanctuary Plan: animals are removed to sanctuaries without a conviction, and those businesses are shut down with no compensation to owners or shareholders, under the Sanctuary forfeiture; the conviction rule stands for everything else. Between private parties, assets can be forfeited when contracts are broken or debts go unpaid, through ordinary legal process.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Philadelphia, 2018: to settle a class action, the city agreed to overhaul civil forfeiture and create a $3 million fund for people whose property had been seized. City of Philadelphia (2018) – City Announces Settlement in Civil Forfeiture Class Action Suit

head: "Doesn't civil forfeiture help police take the profits out of drug and cartel crime?"
body: Taking the proceeds of crime is legitimate after a conviction. Taking property from people who have not been convicted of anything reverses the burden of proof and violates the property rights my view treats as among the strongest. Assets of foreign cartels formally designated as war enemies or Foreign Terrorist Organizations are seized as enemy property without a domestic civilian conviction — that is the combatant track, not civil forfeiture. Domestic gangs and undesignated actors still require a conviction and full due process. The Sanctuary Plan's removal of animals and compelled conversion of animal-agriculture and animal-testing businesses follows from forfeiture: those firms forfeited their property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights (Sanctuary forfeiture; Sanctuary Plan). See Foreign Policy & International Relations.

Property rights rank among the strongest negative rights (Property Rights), and the burden of proof rests on the state. Offenders' own pre-existing bank accounts and assets, along with forfeited property, pay restitution to victims and their families first; this is the offender's own existing resources, not payment for labor (Criminal Justice & Security). The Institute for Justice estimates that states and the federal government forfeited at least $68.8 billion between 2000 and 2019. The Supreme Court held in Timbs v. Indiana (2019) that the Excessive Fines Clause applies to the states.

I would require a unanimous jury of at least twelve to convict, in civil and criminal cases alike. A guilty plea cannot avoid the mandatory death penalty, and every plea offer should be made on the record. Juries can nullify, but a nullification acquittal in a mandatory-death-penalty case may be retried once before a different jury.

Unanimity. A unanimous jury should be required to convict. Reciprocity limits the protection a rights violator receives in sentencing and treatment once guilt is established. It does not lower the procedural bar for establishing guilt.

Plea deals. Pleading guilty to murder should not reduce or avoid the mandatory death penalty. A plea may affect only non-capital elements of a sentence. Every plea offer should be made on the record, with the offered terms disclosed to the court.
Civil juries. The same unanimity rule applies in every case, civil or criminal. Civil cases keep their lower standard of proof, but not a lower verdict threshold.
Jury nullification. Juries have the power to nullify. Judges should instruct juries to follow the laws given.

Retrial after nullification. If a jury acquits through nullification in a case carrying a mandatory death penalty, the state should be able to retry the case once before a different jury. This knowingly departs from the Fifth Amendment double jeopardy rule, under which an acquittal is final. Successive trials for the same act are not new: under the dual-sovereignty doctrine, which the Supreme Court declined to overturn in Gamble v. United States (2019), a state and the federal government may each prosecute the same conduct (Cornell LII – Gamble v. United States (2019)). My exception is narrower: one retrial, only after a finding of nullification, only in mandatory-death-penalty cases, before a different jury held to the same unanimity rule and capital standard.
Jury size. Twelve should be the minimum jury size, required alongside the unanimity rule. Six-person panels should not be permitted.

head: "Doesn't a unanimity rule let a single holdout block justice?"
body: The rule protects the innocent first. A conviction can lead to the capital track, so the standard of proof has to be met for every juror, not most of them. A hung jury allows a retrial. A wrongful conviction cannot be undone after execution.

If acquittals found to be nullification, the same finding that allows the one retrial, reach 5% of jury verdicts in mandatory-death-penalty cases, sustained over a five-year window, the nullification stance is revisited: from allowing nullification with judges not disclosing it, toward judges instructing juries that they may not nullify. Until that threshold is met, the current nullification and retrial rules stand. For context, federal juries acquitted in about 11% of jury trials in fiscal 2024 (159 of 1,491 defendants) and 12% in fiscal 2023 (184 of 1,596), against 14% in fiscal 2018. Those figures cover every offense and every reason for acquittal, including evidence that fails to convince, which is the system working. Counting all acquittals would likely trip the trigger before any nullification occurred, so only nullification acquittals count.

Twelve-person juries are more accurate and more representative. In Saks's 1977 mock-jury studies, as reported in Ballew v. Georgia, 12-person juries reached the correct verdict 83% of the time, compared with 69% for 6-person juries, in the student experiment, and 71% against 57% in the experiment with former jurors. In Ballew v. Georgia, the Supreme Court calculated that a group making up 10% of the community would be missing from 53% of 6-person juries; the same math puts that figure at about 28% for 12-person juries. A 1997 meta-analysis of 17 studies (Saks & Marti) found no significant difference in verdicts by jury size, but larger juries included more minority members and deliberated longer.

Most people treat a universal vote as what makes a country free. I don't. I support a constitutional republic with a qualified (restricted) franchise, also called an epistocratic republic or a limited democracy rather than a full democracy. The net-taxpayer and no-welfare rules are the stake qualification, and a voter license test on issues, civics, and laws is the competence qualification, so the laws that bind everyone are chosen by people who understand them. Ranked-choice voting and the Constitution stay.

I believe the United States should be a constitutional republic with a qualified (restricted) franchise. Epistocracy means rule by the knowledgeable, so the system is also an epistocratic republic, or a limited democracy rather than a full democracy. Elections, ranked-choice voting, and the Constitution would all stay. What would change is who holds the franchise. On top of voter ID and the felony bar (Voting and Elections), every voter should meet two qualifications:

Stake qualification: only net taxpayers would vote, and people living on personally directed transfers would not, because the franchise decides other people's money (net fiscal voting bar; welfare voting bar). This is a tax or stake qualification, close to what Aristotle called timocracy and to the property and taxpaying qualifications of the early American states.

Competence qualification: every voter would hold a voter license, earned by passing the voter license test on issues, civics, and the laws they vote on. This is the epistocratic part. The test would be a literal knowledge exam that gives you a voting license: passing it means you are qualified to make these decisions on behalf of the people. It would test deeper knowledge of:
all the candidates on the ballot;
the structure of government, including Congress (the Senate and the House);
the parties and how parties work;
some history of the administration;
the different policies that have been in place.

Passing it is not enough on its own: you also need to be a net positive taxpayer (the stake qualification above; net fiscal voting bar). If you are unqualified and cannot answer these questions, I don't believe you deserve to be voting, because you are not qualified to.

Together they require a stake in the system and a working knowledge of it. Of the classical constitutions, that is closest to Aristotle's polity (politeia), the mixed constitution between rule by the few and rule by the many.

Both qualifications need constitutional amendments. Federal law has banned literacy tests and similar tests nationwide since 1970, permanently since 1975, and the courts treat voting as a fundamental right, so the voter license belongs in the Constitution, not in a statute that a later Congress or a court could undo.

The fight will be over the design of the test, and the history earns that. Southern states used literacy tests, applied at local officials' discretion, to keep Black citizens from voting. So the test has to meet the same standard of evidence I apply everywhere else (Meta-Ethics): its questions should be neutral, public, and repeatable, with factual answers anyone can check, never opinions. Who writes it, how it is audited, and how pass rates are published are set out in Voting and Elections.

head: "Why epistocracy instead of direct democracy?"
body: I want a more intelligent voter base. Too many voters today are completely uninformed, and I believe the current voter base, and the democracy we have, is a complete failure. Direct democracy has one real strength: Swiss voters reject most proposals put to them, which makes the initiative a check on the legislature rather than a replacement for it. That is why I keep initiatives, but only for qualified voters (Qualified Citizen Initiatives). Beyond that check, I prefer epistocracy for three reasons: Majorities can vote away rights. Swiss men rejected women's federal suffrage in 1959, and Swiss voters approved a ban on building minarets in 2009. A majority vote cannot authorize violating an individual's negative rights, and that limit applies to every majority, including American ones (Qualified Citizen Initiatives; Sharia as State Law; Political Philosophy). Voters should know what they decide. Those who fail to meet the standard of knowledge of the government and the laws they vote on should not vote, so the people choosing the government understand it (Voting and Elections). The franchise decides other people's money. Initiatives decide taxes and transfers, and voting on a transfer involving yourself is a massive conflict of interest, so the net-taxpayer rule applies to them with equal force (net fiscal voting bar; Qualified Citizen Initiatives).

head: "Why should anyone need a license to vote?"
body: For the same reason we license drivers, doctors, and pilots: their choices put other people at risk. A driver endangers the people on the road. A voter helps choose the laws, taxes, and wars that bind everyone, including people who voted the other way or could not vote at all. Jason Brennan calls this the competence principle: it is unjust to force high-stakes decisions on people when those decisions are made incompetently or by an incompetent body. I accept it. If we ask a pilot to prove what they know before flying passengers, I believe it is reasonable to ask a voter to prove what they know before helping govern the country. The knowledge gap is real. In the 2025 Annenberg Constitution Day Civics Survey, 70% of U.S. adults could name all three branches of government, and 13% could not name any. Asked which rights the First Amendment protects, 79% named freedom of speech, but fewer than half named any of the other four. The voter license test asks for that kind of knowledge, and for knowledge of the laws voters decide (Voting and Elections). A license is not a judgment of anyone's worth. Everyone without one keeps every right a voter has except the vote, and the test is free and retakable, with free prep courses. The two errors are not equal. A capable citizen wrongly left off the rolls loses one vote among millions until a free retake, and keeps every protection the law gives. An uninformed vote helps set the taxes, laws, and wars that bind everyone, including the people who studied and the people who could not vote at all. A capable citizen who skips the test goes unheard by choice, since the test, the prep, and every retake are free. Jason Brennan, Philosophical Quarterly – The Right to a Competent Electorate (2011) Annenberg Public Policy Center – Americans' Knowledge of Civics Increases, Annenberg Survey Finds (2025)

head: "If not everyone can vote, is it still a democracy?"
body: Not a full one, and I don't claim it is. It keeps elections, ranked-choice voting, and a written constitution, so it is a republic, but its franchise is qualified rather than universal. The accurate name is a constitutional republic with a qualified franchise, or an epistocratic republic. The United States began with a qualified franchise too: many founding-era state constitutions limited the vote to people who owned a set amount of property, and some to those who paid taxes. No franchise is universal, including today's. The 26th Amendment protects the vote of citizens "eighteen years of age or older," and no state lets young children vote, because they are presumed not yet able to judge what they would decide. The question has never been whether to qualify the franchise, only how. Age is a proxy for competence. The voter license measures it directly, person by person, instead of inferring it from a birthday (Voting and Elections). National Archives – The Constitution: Amendments 11-27

head: "Isn't a voter license just a literacy test with a new name?"
body: Literacy tests were real tools of disenfranchisement, and I don't dispute that. They were left to local officials who chose whom to test and how to grade. The voter license test removes that discretion: one public question bank, factual answers anyone can check, the same test for everyone, free and retakable, with free prep courses, and with pass rates published by group (Voting and Elections). The country already gives a test of this kind to its newest citizens. The naturalization civics test draws 20 questions from a published list of 128, with an official study guide, and an applicant passes with 12 correct. A naturalized citizen has already shown the knowledge I would ask of every voter. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services – Study for the Test

head: "Qualified franchises have a dark history: literacy tests, poll taxes, property rules. Why would this one be different?"
body: I believe that history should be faced, not waved away. Louisiana's "interpretation test" required an applicant to "give a reasonable interpretation" of any clause of the state or federal constitution, and the Supreme Court found it "vested in the voting registrars a virtually uncontrolled discretion as to who should vote and who should not" (Louisiana v. United States, 1965). The Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed literacy tests as a prerequisite to voting. The Twenty-fourth Amendment barred poll taxes in federal elections, and Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966) struck them down in state elections, holding that "wealth or fee paying has, in our view, no relation to voting qualifications." The early American states limited the vote to property owners, and some to taxpayers. I don't defend any of those. I don't accept the alternative either. Universal democracy as it runs today produces rotted politics: power swings back and forth, and elections devolve into demographic voting blocs with no care for substance or for economic, social, or political theory. It is unfair to informed citizens to be ruled by people who know nothing about what they vote for. So the question is how to qualify the vote without repeating those abuses. Each abuse had a cause, and the design removes it: Discretion. Registrars chose whom to test and how to grade. Here there is one question bank, published in advance as a public study guide with free prep courses, factual answers anyone can check, the same test for everyone, free and retakeable, and any citizen can challenge a question in court as biased (Voting and Elections). Hidden targets. Southern literacy tests and poll taxes were used to keep Black citizens from voting. No rule here looks at race, religion, or ancestry. Pass rates are published by race, sex, age, and party, and if a group fails at a markedly higher rate and fixing biased questions cannot close the gap, the test is suspended. A price on the ballot. A poll tax charged people to vote. No one pays anything to vote here. The stake rule asks whether a person pays more in tax than they receive in personally directed transfers, and anyone can decline such a transfer to keep the vote (net fiscal voting bar). Easy entrenchment. Those rules came by state law and local practice. This one comes only through Article V, its definitions sit in the amendment itself, a change in tax or transfer law cannot change anyone's franchise status until after the next general election, and the amendment lapses unless it is re-ratified every 20 years. Losing more than the vote. Jim Crow disenfranchisement was part of a system that also denied Black citizens the equal protection of the law. Here everyone without the vote keeps every right a voter has except the vote itself, and no majority, qualified or not, may vote to violate an individual's negative rights. Harper is also why both qualifications need a constitutional amendment: under today's Constitution, the stake rule would not survive. Cornell LII – Louisiana v. United States, 380 U.S. 145 (1965) Cornell LII – Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections, 383 U.S. 663 (1966) Cornell LII – U.S. Constitution, Twenty-fourth Amendment National Archives – Voting Rights Act (1965)

head: "Aren't the franchise criteria just stipulated? Why these, and what would change them?"
body: Where they come from. Voting is not a negative right. It is a share in the coercive power the state holds over everyone else, so I hold it to my rule for all coercion: it is justified only as far as it protects rights (Political Authority and Coercion). Two things make a voter a danger to other people's rights. One is a conflict of interest over their money, which the stake qualification removes. The other is deciding laws without knowing them, which the competence qualification removes. The test also has to meet my standard of proof: factual, public, repeatable questions anyone can check. The rivals. Universal suffrage lets majorities vote away rights and lets voters decide transfers to themselves. Property or wealth qualifications measure the wrong thing. A renter who pays more in tax than they receive has the stake, and a landowner living on transfers does not. J. S. Mill's plural voting gave extra votes by occupation or degree. Those are proxies for knowledge. I judge each voter directly, by a test, not by a group they belong to (Group Statistics and Individual Judgment). Mill held both of my qualifications in the same chapter: "that the receipt of parish relief should be a peremptory disqualification for the franchise," and that no one should vote "without being able to read, write, and, I will add, perform the common operations of arithmetic." What would change them. Both rest on principle, not on a promised outcome, so a study of election results would not overturn them. What changes is how they apply. The stake bar lifts in any year a person is again a net taxpayer. Test questions are audited every cycle, pass rates are published by race, sex, age, and party, and any question one group fails at a markedly higher rate is reviewed for bias. If the commission cannot close such a gap by fixing biased questions, the test should be suspended until it can. John Stuart Mill – Considerations on Representative Government (1861), ch. 8: Of the Extension of the Suffrage

head: "How could a qualified franchise be adopted legitimately?"
body: Only through Article V, under today's rules. An amendment has to be proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or by a convention called on the application of two-thirds of the state legislatures, and ratified by three-fourths of the states, 38 of 50. Every past change to who may vote went the same way, including the 15th, 19th, and 26th Amendments. A qualified franchise ratified by those supermajorities would be as legitimate as the universal franchise it replaced. Imposed any other way, by statute, executive order, or force, it would not be, and I would not support it. I don't expect it soon: the world I wish for may never be reality, so I favor directional moves that close the distance, such as voter ID, though they are not the ideal itself. National Archives – The Constitution of the United States: Article V

Aristotle sorted constitutions by whether one, a few, or many rule, and by whether they rule for the common advantage. The correct form of rule by the many he called polity, and he describes it as a mixed constitution combining features of democracy and oligarchy, and where possible aristocracy, the best attainable for most cities. In the Nicomachean Ethics he names a constitution based on a property qualification "timocratic, though most people are wont to call it polity." The stake qualification is that property element in modern form, and the competence qualification adds the element of knowledge. Jason Brennan's Against Democracy (2016) is the modern case for epistocracy: it argues that democracy should be judged by its results and that no one has a fundamental right to a share of political power.

Section 4(a) of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 suspended literacy tests and similar devices for five years in the jurisdictions it covered, mostly in the South. The 1970 amendments extended the ban to every state until August 6, 1975, and the Supreme Court upheld it in Oregon v. Mitchell (1970). The 1975 amendments made the nationwide ban permanent. The ban is statutory: in Lassiter v. Northampton County Board of Elections (1959) the Court upheld a literacy test that was fair on its face. But the Court has called voting "a fundamental matter in a free and democratic society" (Reynolds v. Sims, 1964) and scrutinizes restrictions on it closely, and Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966) struck down wealth conditions on voting. That is why both qualifications belong in the Constitution, where neither a later statute nor a court can undo them.

Voters should have to show ID, mail-in ballots must be fully authenticated and encrypted, felons cannot vote, and only net taxpayers should vote. I support a constitutional amendment that would require passing a fair voter license test to vote. Political money ought to be limited to individual donations, and corporations do not get the voice of people.

Voter ID should be federally mandated. Mail-in voting ought to be reformed for complete authentication of the voter and transmitted through encrypted channels with world-class cybersecurity. Felons should not vote; a felony is any offense worth two or more marks, or any capital-tier crime (Felony and misdemeanor). Only net taxpayers should vote. A person is a net taxpayer for a year when two conditions both hold for the prior completed tax year: taxes paid exceed personally directed transfers received, and income-tax liability is positive; the bar lifts when a later year shows net taxpayer again.

Personally directed transfers means cash, food, housing, or non-emergency medical support funded by general taxation and paid into the person's budget — today's SNAP, TANF, SSI, housing vouchers, non-emergency Medicaid, and refundable tax-credit cash-outs, and under this framework the last-resort allowance, the earnings-only top-up, and any remaining means-tested floor. A refundable credit cash-out is only the amount paid when income-tax liability would otherwise be ≤ $0. The portion that offsets positive liability is tax reduction, not a transfer received. Non-refundable relief — exemptions, deductions, and non-refundable credits, including the mothers' income-tax exemption — is not received. Taxes paid means federal income tax, the employee share of payroll / FICA attributable to the worker, and state income tax. The employer share of FICA is remitted by the employer and does not count on the paid side of the franchise scorecard. Income-tax liability means federal and state income-tax liability after ordinary non-refundable credits, measured before the mothers' income-tax exemption: that exemption does not by itself fail the positive-liability gate when pre-exemption liability is positive. Payroll-only with zero pre-exemption income-tax liability does not clear the gate. Grandfathered Social Security and Medicare, unemployment insurance, veterans' benefits, private insurance, charity, mutual aid, emergency shelter, emergency medical care, K-12, roads, defense, and other universal or shared public goods do not count as transfers on the received side. Excluding grandfathered Social Security and Medicare from the received side does not waive the positive-liability gate: an SS-only retiree or other payroll-only adult with $0 pre-exemption income-tax liability fails, because the franchise tracks current net contribution to the tax system that funds transfers, not lifetime payroll history. The bar is a conflict-of-interest rule, not a punishment and not a rights forfeiture: the franchise decides other people's money, and people who are not net taxpayers cannot cast the deciding votes about it (Welfare and Entitlements).

The bar should be enacted by constitutional amendment, the same path as the voter license test, and it lifts when a later completed tax year shows the person is again a net taxpayer. The unit is the tax-filing unit. Spouses who file jointly share one net position and one liability status for that year, so a stay-at-home spouse on a joint return that is a net taxpayer with positive liability votes. I don't treat voting as a universal right. A constitutional amendment should require voters to pass a bipartisan, unbiased, thorough voter license test of political and social knowledge. Those who fail to meet the standard of knowledge of the government and the laws they vote on should not vote. Campaign finance ought to be reformed because money in politics is dangerous and disadvantages small candidates. Corporations do not have the voice of people, contrary to Citizens United, and finance should be limited to individual donations rather than organized donation campaigns. These limits apply to contributions to candidates and campaigns, not to independent speech.

head: "Is the voter license test a return to Jim Crow literacy tests?"
body: Critics point to literacy tests, which were administered selectively to exclude Black voters and are banned by federal law today. That record condemns discretionary local administration, which is exactly what this test removes: it is bipartisan, unbiased, and applied to everyone through a constitutional amendment, not through local officials. Its purpose is that those choosing the government understand the government and the laws they vote on, and it rests on that principle, not on a promised outcome.

head: "Why can't felons vote, even after their sentence?"
body: Some consequences of forfeiture outlast the sentence by rule, and the bar on felons voting is one of them (General Rules of Forfeiture). A felony here means any offense worth two or more marks, or any capital-tier crime. A misdemeanor, worth one mark or a fine without a mark, does not bar voting (Felony and misdemeanor).

head: "Why can only net taxpayers vote?"
body: Because the franchise decides other people's money. A person who is not a net taxpayer — whose personally directed transfers meet or exceed the taxes they pay, or who owes no income tax — and who then votes on the taxes and programs that move that money is voting on a transfer involving themselves. That is a massive conflict of interest. The bar lasts only while the prior completed tax year fails the net-taxpayer test, and it is not a punishment for poverty or a claim that non-payers lack judgment — it is an eligibility rule that removes the conflict. The rule protects the people who pay from having the amount set by those who receive it, and it protects recipients too, since the benefit does not depend on how anyone votes. The two errors are not equal. A person wrongly kept off the rolls loses the vote only until a completed tax year shows otherwise, and keeps every benefit and every right; a vote cast on one's own transfer helps set what is taken from others for one's own benefit. The law already draws this line for federal judges, who must step aside where they have "a financial interest in the subject matter in controversy." Cornell LII – 28 U.S.C. § 455: Disqualification of justice, judge, or magistrate judge

head: "Isn't that a poll tax by another name?"
body: No. A poll tax charged a fee to vote and was struck down in Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections. This rule charges nothing. It restricts the franchise to net taxpayers for the prior completed tax year, and it lifts when a later year shows net-taxpayer status again. It still goes through constitutional amendment, the same path as the voter license test, because franchise conditions of this kind should be fixed in the Constitution rather than left to statute.

head: "What about Social Security and Medicare?"
body: Grandfathered Social Security and Medicare do not count on the received side of the comparison. Those are contributory benefits people already paid into, not personally directed transfers chosen from general revenue — collecting them is not itself a franchise disqualifier (Social Security and Medicare Transition). That exclusion does not waive the other half of the test. Positive pre-exemption income-tax liability is still required. An SS-only unit with $0 pre-exemption liability fails even with no SNAP, TANF, last-resort, or other personally directed transfer on the received side. The franchise tracks current net contribution to the tax system that funds transfers, not lifetime payroll or transition-levy history.

head: "Can a retiree living only on Social Security vote?"
body: Not on Social Security alone. Grandfathered Social Security is not counted as received, so drawing it does not by itself fail the transfers side. The liability gate still applies: the prior completed tax year should show positive federal-plus-state income-tax liability measured before the mothers' income-tax exemption. An SS-only retiree — or any payroll-only adult — with $0 pre-exemption liability does not vote that year. If the same return shows positive pre-exemption liability for any ordinary reason (taxable portion of benefits, other taxable income, or a joint return that clears the unit's liability gate), the liability half is met and the rest of the net-taxpayer test applies as usual. Lifetime FICA or transition-levy payments do not substitute for current-year liability. The bar lifts when a later completed tax year shows net-taxpayer status again.

head: "How is net-taxpayer status measured?"
body: From the prior completed tax year. Personally directed transfers received that year — cash, food, housing, non-emergency medical support funded by general taxation, including the last-resort allowance, the earnings-only top-up, and refundable credit cash-outs — are summed and set against federal income tax, the employee share of payroll / FICA, and state income tax paid that year. The employer share of FICA is not counted. A refundable credit cash-out is only the amount paid when income-tax liability would otherwise be ≤ $0. Amounts that offset positive liability do not count as received. Non-refundable relief (exemptions, deductions, non-refundable credits), including the mothers' income-tax exemption, is not received. Non-emergency Medicaid is counted at the program's average cost per enrollee for the year. The unit should also show positive federal-plus-state income-tax liability measured before the mothers' income-tax exemption. That exemption does not by itself zero the gate when pre-exemption liability is positive. Payroll alone with zero pre-exemption income-tax liability fails. Sales and property taxes are not in the tax side. K-12, roads, defense, and other shared public goods are not on the received side. The tax-filing unit is the unit: joint filers share one net position and one liability status. Eligibility for elections in a given year uses the prior year's result.

head: "Don't the family credits and mothers' exemption knock parents off the voter rolls?"
body: No, not by tax reduction alone. The child credit, birth credit, and mothers' exemption exist to raise births under lower immigration. Non-refundable relief is not a transfer received. Refundable credits count on the received side only as cash-outs — the dollars paid when liability would otherwise be ≤ $0 — not as the portion that offsets tax still owed. The mothers' exemption does not by itself fail the positive-liability gate when pre-exemption liability is positive. SNAP, TANF, the last-resort allowance, the earnings-only top-up, and other personally directed transfers stay on the received side in full. A unit that is mostly cash-out or welfare still fails the net-taxpayer test. A working parent whose family package is tax reduction against positive liability does not lose the vote for that reason alone.

head: "Does a stay-at-home spouse lose the vote?"
body: No, not for unpaid home work alone. Spouses who file jointly share the tax-filing unit's net position and liability status. If the joint return is a net taxpayer with positive income-tax liability, both spouses vote. Private dependence on a spouse's earnings is not a claim on other taxpayers. A spouse who files alone with zero income-tax liability fails the positive-liability gate.

head: "Don't limits on political money restrict free speech?"
body: The limits apply to contributions to candidates and campaigns, not to independent speech. Finance should be limited to individual donations because corporations do not have the voice of people, and money in politics disadvantages small candidates.

head: "Doesn't voter ID suppress turnout, especially among minority voters?"
body: The best evidence says it does not. A nationwide study of 1.6 billion voter-file observations from 2008 to 2018 found that strict ID laws had "no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation." The same study found no effect on fraud, actual or perceived, so ID is justified here as a verification standard for every ballot, not as a fraud cure. The voter license test is a different matter: unlike ID, it is designed to exclude voters who fail it, and pass rates may differ by group. That is why its pass rates are published broken down by race, sex, age, and party, and any question that one group fails at a markedly higher rate is reviewed by the bipartisan commission for bias.

head: "Who writes the voter license test?"
body: A commission should write and maintain it. Each major party should hold an equal number of seats, an equal number of members should be drawn by lot from licensed voters who belong to neither major party (registered voters, for the first commission), and the chair should be drawn by lot from that group. Any change to the question bank should need a two-thirds vote, so no single faction can rewrite the test. The question bank should be published in advance as a public study guide with free prep courses, questions should test facts about the structure of government and the laws voters decide on, never opinions, and the test should be free and retakeable. Any citizen should be able to challenge a question in court as biased. The commission should audit the question bank each cycle, and pass rates should be published so anyone can check whether the test is excluding a group.

head: "Couldn't whoever controls the test or the net-taxpayer rule shut out opponents and entrench an oligarchy?"
body: That is the real danger of any qualified franchise, and the design is built against it. The test. A commission writes it, with equal seats for each major party, an equal number of members drawn by lot from licensed voters in neither, and a chair drawn by lot from that group. Changing the question bank takes a two-thirds vote. The question bank is public in advance, the questions are facts, never opinions, and the test is free and retakeable, with free prep courses. Any citizen can challenge a question in court. Pass rates are published by race, sex, age, and party, and if the commission cannot close a gap one group fails at a markedly higher rate, the test is suspended until it can (Epistocratic Republic and Qualified Franchise). The net-taxpayer rule. I believe the definition should be written into the amendment itself, not left to statute, so no majority can redraw it. Changing it should take a new Article V amendment: two-thirds of both houses and three-fourths of the states. The feedback loop. Qualified voters elect the lawmakers who set taxes and transfers, and taxes and transfers decide who qualifies. A majority could try to move opponents off the rolls by changing the zero bracket or handing them transfers. So a change in tax or transfer law should not change anyone's franchise status until after the next general election, and anyone should be able to decline a personally directed transfer to keep the vote. Elite overreach. A qualified electorate is bound by the same side-constraints as any other. No majority, qualified or not, may vote to violate an individual's negative rights, and everyone without the vote keeps every right a voter has except the vote itself (Epistocratic Republic and Qualified Franchise). The franchise decides who chooses among lawful policies, not whose rights count. Re-ratification. I believe the amendment should lapse unless it is re-ratified every 20 years under Article V: two-thirds of both houses and three-fourths of the states. If it is not re-ratified in time, universal suffrage returns at the next general election. Adoption. The whole system comes in only through Article V, and every condition sits in the Constitution, where courts enforce it. No mechanism is incorruptible, universal suffrage included, since majorities there can vote themselves other people's money. The test is whether abuse can be seen and stopped. Published pass rates, the suspension rule, court challenges, and fixed constitutional text make it visible and hard to do quietly. How many adults would qualify under both rules has no estimate yet (Needs research: share of adults who are net taxpayers and would pass the test).

Elections are only legitimate if every vote is cast by an eligible, verified voter. The Supreme Court upheld photo ID requirements in Crawford v. Marion County Election Board, and states have adopted ID rules widely. Nationwide panel data from 2008 to 2018 found strict ID laws did not lower registration or turnout for any group; ID is justified here as a verification standard for every ballot, not as a cure for measured fraud. The Court held in Richardson v. Ramirez that states may disenfranchise felons under the Fourteenth Amendment. A second eligibility rule follows the same logic as keeping the franchise off people who have not shown knowledge of the government they vote on: only net taxpayers cast votes about other people's money, because people who are not net taxpayers have a direct financial stake in how large personally directed transfers are and how heavy the tax burden is. The bar is temporary and aimed at that conflict, not at poverty as such. Measurement details — the tax-filing unit and joint returns, what counts as paid and received, the mothers' exemption, and grandfathered Social Security and Medicare — are set out in the position and the questions above (Births and Family Formation). The paid side counts only taxes the worker remits as income tax or as the employee share of payroll — matching how a W-2 reports them. Arguments that the employer share is economically incident on wages are economics, not the eligibility formula; the franchise scorecard stays auditable. Because Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections struck down poll taxes, and because wealth-linked franchise conditions are the kind of rule that belongs in the Constitution, the bar is proposed by constitutional amendment rather than statute. Federal law currently bans literacy tests nationwide, which is why a knowledge requirement is proposed through constitutional amendment rather than statute. The requirement rests on principle; the literacy-test history is why it is built around bipartisan authorship, a public question bank, and audit. Citizens United removed limits on independent corporate political spending; limiting finance to individual donations restores elections to individual citizens.

In Citizens United v. FEC (2010), the Supreme Court held that the First Amendment bars the government from limiting independent political expenditures by corporations, unions, and other associations. Direct contributions to candidates remain subject to limits.

Elections should require ID, authenticated mail ballots, and clean voter rolls, with money limited to individual donations. I want the rules set before each election.

Elections should be administered to ensure that only eligible voters vote and that every valid ballot is counted. Voters should show identification, mail-in ballots should be fully authenticated and encrypted, and people convicted of felonies ought to be removed from the rolls because they cannot vote. People who are not net taxpayers are likewise removed under the conflict-of-interest rule in Voting and Elections, and restored when a completed tax year shows they are net taxpayers. Political money should be limited to individual donations to candidates and campaigns. Election procedures ought to be fixed in law before each election rather than changed during it.

head: "Doesn't strict administration make voting harder?"
body: Identification and authentication protect each lawful vote from being diluted by an unlawful one. Every eligible citizen can meet the requirements, and confidence in the count is what makes the result legitimate.

Under the Constitution and federal law, the President is chosen by 538 electors, and a majority of 270 electoral votes is required to win. The administration rules above apply within that structure, and each state chooses its presidential electors by ranked-choice voting (Ranked-Choice Voting); the voting rights rules are set out in Voting and Elections. Term length, the absence of term limits, and the three-year election cycle for every elected office are set out in Term Limits.
National Archives – About the Electoral College
National Archives – The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription

In my view federal enforcement around an election must follow rules fixed before it. In the last 60 days there should be no bulk ballot holds, no eligibility questioning at voters' homes without a court order, and no overt steps against candidates unless a judge finds an immediate need.

Election procedures ought to be fixed in law before each election rather than changed during it (Election Administration), and the same should hold for federal enforcement around an election. Rolls should be cleaned by matching government records through each state's process before voting begins, and each person who registered or voted unlawfully should be prosecuted on individual evidence. Within 60 days of a federal election, no agency should demand that ballots be set aside in bulk, or send agents to voters' homes to question them about their eligibility, unless a court orders it for a named person on individual evidence. Overt steps against a candidate, such as searches, arrests or subpoenas that become public, also wait until after the election unless a judge finds an immediate threat to safety or evidence about to be lost; covert investigation continues throughout. These limits should be written in statute, so they apply the same way whichever party holds power.

The Justice Department's practice in recent history has been to advise prosecutors against overt investigative steps involving members of Congress or candidates within 60 days of an election. It is a practice, not a statute. In October 2026 a federal court enjoined election-related field interviews of likely citizens in nine states, and the Justice Department asked a court to hold back more than 20,000 California mail ballots before counting.

I believe districts should be redrawn once after each census, by fixed neutral criteria, without partisan data, and never mid-decade unless a court orders it.

Districts should be redrawn once after each census. The criteria ought to be fixed in law in advance: equal population, contiguity, compactness, and keeping counties and cities whole where possible (Election Administration). Mapmakers should not use party registration or past vote results. A map should not be redrawn mid-decade unless a court finds it unlawful. The maps, data and code should be published, and any voter may challenge a map in court. If I were voting, I would vote no on Missouri Proposition A, which keeps a 2025 mid-decade map; no on Maryland Question 3, which removes compactness, contiguity and boundary rules for congressional districts; and yes on Colorado Amendment 86, which requires commission and state supreme court approval for a mid-decade map and bars maps drawn to favor a party.

I would require ranked-choice voting for every election in the country, federal, state, and local. It runs on paper ballots, published rounds, fixed rules, and clear notice that partly ranked ballots can be exhausted. Its effects on turnout and polarization are mixed, and it does not guarantee a majority of all ballots.

The United States ought to require ranked-choice voting for every election in the country: federal, state, and local. Because the Constitution gives Congress power over federal elections but not over state and local ones, the United States ought to enact the requirement through a constitutional amendment, as with the voter license test (Voting and Elections). It should run on paper ballots, every round of the count should be published, the rules are fixed in law before the election (Election Administration), and voters are told plainly that a ballot ranking only some candidates may be exhausted before the final round.

head: "Doesn't ranked-choice voting guarantee a majority winner?"
body: No, only a majority of ballots still counted in the final round. Burnett and Kogan examined more than 600,000 ballots from four local elections and found that in every one the winner received less than a majority of all ballots cast, because exhausted ballots dropped out of the count. That limit is why exhaustion is disclosed to voters rather than hidden.

head: "Isn't it too confusing for voters?"
body: The evidence from Maine says mostly not. In the 2018 race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District, the Republican led the first round 46.33% to 45.58% and the Democrat won after transfers, 50.62% to 49.38%. Only 621 ballots, 0.21% of the total, were exhausted through apparent confusion. My voter license test (Voting and Elections) also means every voter has shown knowledge of the structure of government.

head: "Does it raise turnout or reduce polarization?"
body: Critics say ranked-choice voting has not delivered what its backers promised. On polarization the gain is modest: the National Conference of State Legislatures summarizes research on Maine as showing only a modest reduction. On turnout the critics are on weaker ground: a 2024 study using administrative turnout records found substantially higher turnout and more direct voter contact where it is used, while earlier work by Kimball and Anthony found negligible turnout effects outside the runoffs it replaces (Needs research: the turnout gain rests on one 2024 study). Neither result decides it. I would not require it for promised effects. I would require it because it lets voters rank every candidate and ends the spoiler problem.

head: "Doesn't a national requirement override the states?"
body: It does, by design. Seventeen states had banned ranked-choice voting by 2025, and a national standard replaces those bans. The rules I call for already set national standards for how votes are cast and verified, such as voter ID and authenticated mail ballots. How votes are counted is part of the same integrity standard, and a vote should not count differently depending on the state it is cast in. States keep running their own elections under that standard (Federalism). Voters have also shown support where it was tested: Alaska's 2024 measure to repeal its system failed by 743 votes after a recount, 50.12% to 49.88%. Alaska voters face a second repeal attempt, Ballot Measure 2, on November 3, 2026 (Ballot measures, November 3, 2026).

head: "Can't a decoy candidate with the same name split the vote?"
body: Under ranked-choice voting a decoy can't split a vote the way it can under plurality voting. A voter who ranks both candidates loses nothing, because a ballot for an eliminated candidate moves to the voter's next choice. The danger left is voters ranking only the decoy. That is handled before the election with clear ballot labels and a ballot-access rule against candidacies filed to deceive (Ballot Access and Deceptive Candidacies), not by holding up a count afterward (Suit to hold Alaska's Senate certification).

The United States ought to fix the integrity rules for every election, such as identification, authentication, and rules set in advance, and the counting method is part of those rules, so ranked-choice voting should be required everywhere. Ranked-choice voting also reduces the spoiler problem that keeps small candidates from competing, a concern I already raise about money in politics (Voting and Elections). Against that, it does not guarantee a true majority of all ballots, its counts take longer, and its measured effects on turnout and polarization are mixed. I accept those trade-offs for a count that lets every voter rank every candidate.

I see parties as private associations that choose their nominees by their own rules. A state may instead hold one all-candidate primary only if at least four candidates advance to a ranked-choice general election. I would not allow a top-two primary.

I hold that a political party is a private association, and its members should decide how it picks its nominees (Freedom of Association). A state may run a party's primary for it, but it may not force a party to accept nominees chosen by non-members. A state that prefers one primary open to every candidate may hold one, as long as at least four candidates advance to a general election decided by ranked-choice voting (Ranked-Choice Voting), as in Alaska. A top-two system leaves the general-election ballot with two names, which empties ranked-choice voting of any meaning and often leaves voters with two candidates from one party. If I were voting on Massachusetts Question 3, I would vote no.

I believe a candidacy filed to deceive voters, such as a stand-in with the same name, can be kept off the ballot under a rule written before the election and decided by a court before ballots are printed. Once votes are cast, they must be counted as cast.

Ballot access should be open to any good-faith candidate. The United States ought to let election officials refuse a candidacy filed to confuse voters, such as one that copies an incumbent's ballot name, party and branding, under a standard fixed in law in advance, with a prompt court review that finishes before ballots are printed (Election Administration). Ballots should list every candidate's full legal name and party. Once voting begins, the result ought to be counted as cast; no official or court should hold up certification on a guess about what voters meant. Ranked-choice voting limits the harm of any decoy that gets through (Ranked-Choice Voting).

States and localities may offer citizen initiatives and referendums. I support a constitutional amendment creating a national initiative for federal statutes and amendments, reaching the ballot with signatures from 1% (statute) or 2% (amendment) of qualified voters within 18 months. Measures should pass by more than half of the votes cast with no minimum turnout, and amendments also need a majority of the states, 26 of 50, each counted by its own voters. No initiative can override protected rights, and every measure faces court review. Only voters who meet the full election stack - ID, the voter license test, net-taxpayer status, and no felony bar - may sign and vote, under rules fixed in advance, and outcomes rest with those who vote.

I support citizen initiatives and referendums at the state and local level, and a national citizen initiative for federal statutes and constitutional amendments, enacted through a constitutional amendment. Each state should decide whether to offer its own initiatives and set its own signature thresholds. No initiative, state or national, should be able to override the rights I protect, such as negative rights, equal treatment, and due process. Every measure is subject to court review like any other law (Due Process and Rule of Law). Only voters who meet the same eligibility stack that governs every election may sign petitions and vote on measures: voter ID, the voter license test, net-taxpayer status for the prior completed tax year, and no felony bar (Voting and Elections; net fiscal voting bar; Election Administration). Initiatives decide taxes and transfers; the conflict-of-interest rule that bars non–net-taxpayers from candidate elections applies with equal force here. The rules for each measure are fixed in law before signatures are gathered. In this section, "qualified voters" means that full stack. A national initiative reaches the ballot with signatures from 1% of qualified voters in the last federal election for a federal statute, or 2% for a constitutional amendment, gathered within 18 months. These thresholds are my own choice, scaled from the Swiss model rather than taken from it. A measure passes by a simple majority of votes cast, more than half, with blank and spoiled ballots not counted and no minimum turnout. A constitutional amendment by initiative needs a double majority: a national popular majority plus a majority of the states, 26 of 50. A state counts toward that majority when its own voters approve the measure, as Swiss cantons do.

head: "Don't citizen initiatives let majorities vote away minority rights?"
body: It can, and Switzerland shows it. Swiss men rejected women's federal suffrage in 1959 by 66.9% and approved it only in 1971, with 65.7% in favor. The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden voted it down again in 1990, and the Federal Supreme Court imposed it on 27 November 1990 under the constitution's equality clause. In 2009 voters approved a ban on building minarets with 57.5% of the vote. That record is why initiatives here cannot override protected rights and stay subject to court review.

head: "Won't voters simply pass anything that is put to them?"
body: The Swiss record says no. Of 237 federal popular initiatives put to a vote since 1891, only 26 were accepted by the people and the cantons, about 11%. Voters reject most proposals, which makes the initiative a check on the legislature rather than a replacement for it.

head: "Doesn't low turnout let a small group decide?"
body: No. Average turnout in Swiss federal votes in 2009 was 46.1%, though the minaret vote that year drew 53.76%. There is no minimum turnout: a measure passes by more than half of the votes cast, with blank and spoiled ballots not counted. The goal is that the vote is held and open to every qualified voter — every person who clears the full election stack — even if only a small share takes part. Those unwilling to vote are subject to the choices of those who do, and the outcome rests with the participants.

head: "How can there be a national initiative under the Constitution?"
body: Only through a constitutional amendment. Article I vests federal legislative power in Congress, and Article V allows amendments only through Congress or a convention of the states, so the national initiative is created by an amendment ratified in the ordinary way. Once in place, it lets citizens propose federal statutes and constitutional amendments directly. A proposal reaches the ballot with signatures from 1% of qualified voters in the last federal election for a statute, or 2% for an amendment, gathered within 18 months. These figures are my own choice, scaled from Switzerland's 100,000 signatures in 18 months, not a Swiss rule.

head: "Wouldn't a national initiative let big states outvote small ones?"
body: Not on the Constitution. An amendment by initiative needs a double majority: a national popular majority and a majority of the states, 26 of 50, as Switzerland requires a majority of the people and of the cantons. A state counts toward that majority when its own voters approve the measure, just as the result of the popular vote in a canton determines that canton's vote. Article V already protects the states' role by requiring three-quarters of them to ratify amendments proposed by Congress. A federal statute by initiative needs a national popular majority and stays subject to the same rights limits and court review.

Each state sets its own amendment process, but more than half of the votes cast should decide, which is the same rule that ought to govern national measures. Requiring 60% lets 40% plus one block what most voters chose. Protected rights are guarded by court review (Due Process and Rule of Law), not by supermajorities. My national rule makes amendments harder in a different way: they need a majority of the states as well as a majority of the votes. If I were voting, I would vote no on North Dakota Measure 1 and no on South Dakota Amendment L.

Switzerland's system is the most developed model. A popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures within 18 months to force a national vote on a constitutional amendment. An optional referendum needs 50,000 signatures within 100 days to put a new law to a vote, and every constitutional amendment requires a double majority of voters and cantons. In the United States, 26 states provide a statewide initiative, referendum, or both. In Pacific States Telephone & Telegraph Co. v. Oregon (1912), the Supreme Court declined to hear a claim that Oregon's initiative process violated the Guarantee Clause, treating the question as one for Congress, so state initiatives stand. Initiatives fit my federalism and my preference for power held close to citizens (Federalism). The Swiss record also shows the risk: majorities have voted on the rights of minorities, and only a court restored women's vote in one canton. The initiative therefore ought to come paired with firm rights limits and the same voter qualifications that apply to every election: ID, the voter license test, net-taxpayer status, and the felon bar (net fiscal voting bar). At the national level the Constitution gives no initiative power today. So the United States ought to create one by amendment, with signature thresholds of 1% and 2% of qualified voters in the last federal election, my own figures scaled from the Swiss model. The double majority for amendments by initiative, 26 of 50 states counted by each state's own vote, keeps the states' role that Article V protects. Turnout is not a condition of validity: a vote open to every qualified voter is decided by more than half of the votes cast by those who take part.

I stand for strict separation of religion and government in the United States. Religions that do not violate sentient rights should be tolerated; those that do should be restricted or banned in their harmful aspects. Private conscience and association ought to be protected, and public institutions should remain secular.

Religion should stay out of government, and officials must not turn scripture into law. Adherents of the four excluded ideologies (Nazism, communism, socialism, and Islam) are barred from the sworn authority roles, and the state endorses no religion. I'd keep historic religious monuments but put up no new ones. Public schools should have no prayer. Private schools do as they like.

Religious doctrine should never be involved in a governmental body, and in the United States religion should be neither mandated nor involved in government. Elected officials who are religious may be influenced ideologically and philosophically by their faith, but no one should be forced to follow their scriptures, and religious mandates should not become law. Religious symbols already on public property may remain for historical significance, and historically significant religious structures should not be taken down, but new ones should not be added. Prayer should be excluded from government-run public schools. Private schools may do as they wish on religious practice. The state ought to stay religion-neutral: the excluded-ideologies test applies to any doctrine, religious or secular (Excluded ideologies), and the mosque rules that follow from it are set out in Religious Freedom.

My view: You are free to be a moderate, practicing Muslim, but I would not allow a Muslim into an authority role, and the state should never endorse Islam. The constitutional amendment designating excluded ideologies bars adherents of Islam, Nazism, communism, and socialism from authority roles, and covers all four on the same terms for the bar on building, rebuilding, expanding, or relocating their places (Property Rights; Excluded ideologies). Authority roles are the sworn positions listed under Oath of Office and Perjury, from public office and policing to the courts and K-12 curriculum authority. An accountant, grounds worker, or other non-authority public employee is not under that bar. I judge every other candidate by their record and commitments: support for state-enforced religious law, or for purging the press or police, rules a candidate out for my vote, whatever their faith.

head: "Does keeping historic religious symbols on public land contradict strict separation?"
body: No. Separation forbids the state from imposing religion, not from preserving its own history. A historic monument does not compel belief or practice. Adding new religious symbols would be a fresh act of government endorsement, which is why existing ones stay and new ones are not added.

The First Amendment bars establishment of religion and protects its free exercise. The Supreme Court held in Engel v. Vitale that state-sponsored prayer in public schools violates the Establishment Clause, and in American Legion v. American Humanist Association that a long-standing cross memorial could remain on public land given its history. The position follows both: no state-directed religious practice, and no removal of historic monuments.
