Socialism in its core sense, social or state ownership of the means of production and planning in place of markets, is antithetical to sentientism and negative rights, and a terrible idea: it takes property, forces redistribution, compels labor and speech, and suppresses dissent. Social democracy is different: the Nordic countries are market economies with large welfare states. I share the goal of a floor for basic needs but fund only a minimal one and leave the rest to markets and voluntary giving.

The word "socialism" covers very different systems, and I judge each by what it does to individual rights. In its core sense — social or state ownership of the means of production and planning in place of markets (Stanford Encyclopedia: "the bulk of the means of production is under social, democratic control") — three features are incompatible with my framework: (1) collective or state ownership of productive property imposed by force, including expropriation; (2) central planning that replaces prices and voluntary exchange; (3) compulsory redistribution beyond a minimal floor for basic needs. Each takes property or overrides consent from people who have harmed no one.

Social democracy keeps private ownership and markets and funds a large welfare state through taxes. The Nordic countries are in this category (Denmark's PM, 2015: "Denmark is far from a socialist planned economy. Denmark is a market economy."). Social democracy shares only the third feature, so I judge it as too large a compulsory state, not as socialism in the core sense (Nordic Social Democracy).

Socialism in the core sense is antithetical to sentientism and negative rights: it seizes property, forces redistribution, compels labor and speech, and suppresses dissent. Cases, calculation-problem argument, and country comparisons live in the Q&As, Rationale, and Comparisons — not repeated here. Shared ground I keep: a bare-minimum safety floor, voluntary cooperatives, and voluntary giving. Flat tax, named minimal welfare/top-up floor, and the time-limited Sanctuary Levy are not excluded socialism (Socialism (excluded)).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Venezuela, 2016: the ENCOVI living-conditions survey by three Venezuelan universities found 74.3% of the population lost an average of 8.7 kg (19 pounds) and about 9.6 million people ate two or fewer meals a day. CNBC (2017) – Venezuela’s crisis causes its people to cut meals and lose weight
My view: The right of citizens to simply be left alone is incomprehensible to socialists who are convinced they have a mandate to rearrange other people's lives.

head: "Isn't socialism just about fairness and helping people who are struggling?"
body: The government ought to fund a bare-minimum safety floor for basic needs through minimal necessary taxes, and anyone may give more voluntarily (Welfare and Entitlements). The disagreement is about means. Taking ownership of productive property, or compelling redistribution beyond that floor, uses force against people who violated no one's rights. The record of planned economies also suggests it leaves the poor worse off, not better.

head: "The Nordic countries are successful and socialist. Doesn't that disprove the critique?"
body: No, because they are not socialist in the core sense. Their own leaders describe them as market economies, and the Heritage Foundation's 2025 Index of Economic Freedom ranks Denmark 7th, Norway 9th, Sweden 12th, and Finland 13th in the world. What they add is high taxes and a large welfare state. I reject that compulsory scale too, but it's a different argument from the one against planning and state ownership. Their success tends to support markets with private property, which they kept.

head: "Venezuela failed because of oil prices and U.S. sanctions, not socialism."
body: They were shocks, not the cause. Oil prices fell sharply in 2014, and ECLAC links part of the 2020 drop to tighter U.S. sanctions on the public sector. But the IMF found that "economic mismanagement accelerated and amplified the economic collapse," and price controls were producing shortages of staples in 2007, during the oil boom. The IMF calls the result the largest collapse for a country not at war in almost half a century. The policies made the economy fragile before the shocks arrived.

head: "Isn't Cuba's poverty caused by the U.S. embargo?"
body: The embargo raises costs, but it is not the cause of Cuba's poverty. It has blocked most U.S. trade and investment since the early 1960s. Its extraterritorial provisions, such as the 1996 Helms-Burton Act, also raise costs for foreign firms and banks that deal with Cuba. But the embargo does not stop Cuba from trading with the rest of the world. The European Union describes itself as Cuba's main trade partner and largest foreign investor, and in the 1990s Spain, Canada, and China were among its leading partners. U.S. law has also allowed agricultural exports to Cuba since 2000. Through 1990 the Soviet Union provided more than $65 billion in aid and price subsidies, and the economy still shrank by roughly a third when that aid ended. Analysts of the 1990s crisis named the "inefficiencies of centrally planned economies" as its underlying cause. The embargo makes a weak economy worse. It does not explain why the economy is weak.

head: "Doesn't Cuba have excellent health care and literacy?"
body: Cuba reports high literacy, long life expectancy, and low infant mortality. These figures come from a government that controls statistics and the press, so researchers treat some of them with caution. A 2017 study in Demography found patterns in Cuba's records of fetal and newborn deaths consistent with misclassification. It estimated Cuba's infant mortality at about 9.0 to 10.1 per 1,000 live births, against the officially reported 5.8. Even taking the official figures at face value, I do not accept good services as justification for taking property and forbidding exit.

head: "Couldn't modern computers solve the planning problem?"
body: The argument does not depend on computing power. Hayek's point was that the knowledge an economy runs on is "dispersed bits of incomplete and frequently contradictory knowledge which all the separate individuals possess," much of it about local conditions and changing preferences that are never written down. Mises argued that without market prices for capital goods, planners cannot compare the costs of different uses of resources. Prices gather that information because people trade with their own resources. A computer can process data faster, but it cannot produce the prices that come from voluntary exchange.

head: "Is market socialism, with worker cooperatives competing in markets, also rejected?"
body: Not if it is voluntary. Workers may form cooperatives, own firms jointly, and compete in markets under my freedom of association. What I reject is making that model compulsory, by forbidding private ownership or seizing firms to convert them.

head: "Don't a tiny few seize the wealth that workers produce?"
body: Some large fortunes are inherited, and some are helped by political favors. That is why I reject taxpayer-funded corporate subsidies and would tax an heir's inherited gains when the assets are sold (carryover basis). But most of the largest American fortunes were built, not seized: Forbes classed 71% of its 2026 list of the 400 richest Americans as self-made, counting someone as self-made when they built most of the fortune themselves, even from a comfortable start. Those fortunes came from selling something millions of people chose to buy. A wage is the price a worker and an employer both accept. When the state sets a higher price than an employer can pay, the job does not happen (Labor and Unions). A fair share is what free people agree to, not what a planner decides. Forbes – Forbes Releases Its 45th Annual Forbes 400 Ranking Of Richest Americans (2026)

head: "Can the rise in hospital, college, and housing costs be directly associated with regulation, progressive tax policy, and the states involved?"
body: I believe it can be strongly associated with regulation and other government intervention, and with state policy especially in housing. I would not pin it directly on progressive tax rates. Mark Perry's "Chart of the Century" plots BLS consumer prices from January 2000 to December 2023. Hospital services rose 243.7%, college tuition and fees 184.7%, and housing 96.2%, against overall inflation of 82.4%. Televisions fell 97.9%, toys 73.5%, and computer software 72.4%. That is an earlier cut of the same BLS pattern I already calculate through September 2026 above. Mark J. Perry chart: U.S. price changes for selected consumer goods and services and wages, January 2000 to December 2023, from Bureau of Labor Statistics The association with government is not just a coincidence of labels. In healthcare, third-party payment (insurers and public programs) means the patient often never sees the price, so nobody in the transaction has a strong reason to hold it down (Healthcare). In college, federal lending and subsidies raise demand without freeing supply, and schools exposed to higher federal loan limits raised tuition (data in Higher Education). In housing, rules that restrict building and entry keep supply tight (Housing, Zoning, and Homelessness). The pattern matches the degree of government involvement: prices rose where the state pays, subsidizes, or regulates most heavily, and fell where firms compete for customers. Progressive tax policy is a weaker and more indirect link. A progressive income tax does not set hospital charges, tuition, or rents. It can affect where people live, how much they invest, and what they have left after tax, but that is not the same as directly causing those sector prices to rise. State differences are clearest in housing. Stricter zoning and other supply limits, which are common in more progressive coastal areas, keep housing scarce and expensive. Places that allow more building see more moderate prices. Healthcare and higher education also vary by state rules and subsidies, but the housing contrast is the sharpest. This is not the only cause. Labor-intensive services like hospital care, college, and child care can get more expensive even without new regulation, because wages in those fields have to keep up with the rest of the economy even when productivity grows slowly (Baumol's cost disease). Quality changes, technology, and demand also matter. Those caveats do not erase the main pattern: the sectors with the heaviest government involvement are the ones that ran far ahead of inflation. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics – CPI-U, U.S. city average; Mark J. Perry, American Enterprise Institute (chart of BLS prices, January 2000 to December 2023)

I protect property and voluntary exchange as extensions of the right not to be subjected to force (Political Philosophy). Socialism in the core sense removes both by design. It also faces a problem of knowledge that holds even under good intentions. Mises argued in 1920 that without market prices for the means of production, a planning authority cannot calculate which uses of resources are more or less valuable. Hayek added in 1945 that the relevant knowledge "never exists in concentrated or integrated form," and that prices are how a market economy uses it. The record of planned economies matches this reasoning (Economic System).

Venezuela is the most recent large case. Under Hugo Chávez the state took over the Orinoco oil projects of ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips in 2007. An international arbitration tribunal later found the Conoco takeover unlawful and awarded the company about $8.7 billion. Price controls on about 400 basic products, imposed from 2003, were followed by recurring shortages of milk, meat, and sugar. The IMF estimates that real GDP contracted by more than 75% between 2013 and 2021, which it calls "the single largest economic collapse for a non-conflict country in almost half a century." Hyperinflation began in late 2017, and ECLAC reported annualized inflation still at 1,198% in November 2021. By late 2025, UNHCR and the R4V platform counted nearly 7.9 million Venezuelan refugees and migrants worldwide.

Cuba is the longest-running case in the hemisphere. In 1960 the revolutionary government nationalized the banks, the foreign oil refineries, and the property of U.S. nationals. The U.S. Foreign Claims Settlement Commission later found 5,911 of those claims compensable, worth about $1.9 billion in principal. The state still owns most means of production and employs a majority of the workforce, according to the Congressional Research Service. Basic food has been rationed through the libreta ration book for decades. When Soviet aid ended, official statistics show GDP fell 34.8% from 1989 to 1993. Recent years have brought a second crisis. In 2021 the official consumer price index rose 77%, and economists estimate true inflation at 174% to 700%. In September 2024 the government cut the subsidized daily bread ration from 80 to 60 grams for lack of flour. In October 2024 the national grid collapsed, leaving the whole island without power. U.S. Customs and Border Protection recorded 224,607 encounters with Cuban nationals in fiscal 2022 and 200,287 in fiscal 2023. Cuba's own statistics office reports that the population fell to 9,748,007 at the end of 2024, 307,961 fewer than a year earlier, with net emigration of about 251,000 that year.

Social democrats share one premise with it: no one should lack basic necessities. The overlap ends there. It keeps only a bare-minimum floor funded by minimal necessary taxes, and it differs on scale and on compulsion. Help beyond that floor comes from markets, families, and voluntary giving, not from taking property.

The clearest tests are cases where similar people were divided between systems, or where one country changed systems. Critics note that none is a controlled experiment and that each has confounders, set out below; in every case the more market-oriented system or period outperformed the planned one. The Soviet Union and Mao's China are covered in Communism.

East and West Germany. The same nation, divided after 1945, ran a planned economy in the East and a market economy in the West. Before monetary union in 1990, IMF staff put East German labor productivity at 30% to 40% of the West German level. The German government's later account puts it at only about 20% to 25% in 1988. The two states had different occupying powers and foreign support, so not every gap is due to the economic system.

North and South Korea. In 2023 the Bank of Korea estimated North Korea's gross national income per person at 1.59 million won, 3.4% of South Korea's 47.25 million won. The estimate is uncertain because North Korea publishes almost no data, and both states relied heavily on foreign patrons. South Korea also grew under military rule before it democratized, so the comparison is about markets, not about democracy.

China after 1978. After China began market reforms, starting with returning farmland to individual households, GDP growth averaged over 9% a year. The World Bank credits China with lifting close to 800 million people out of extreme poverty, about three-quarters of the global reduction over that period. China remains a one-party state with a large state sector, so the gains came from introducing markets, not from changing the political system.

Vietnam after 1986. Before the Đổi Mới reforms, inflation reached 487% in 1986. After the country moved to market-oriented policies, growth averaged about 8% a year in the 1990s. The poverty rate fell from 58% in 1993 to 37% in 1998, and GDP per person rose from under $500 in 1986 to $5,066 in 2025, according to the World Bank. As in China, the ruling party kept its monopoly on power.

India after 1991. After a balance-of-payments crisis, India dismantled much of the "license raj" system of industrial licensing. Average tariffs fell from 80% in 1990 to 37% in 1996, and IMF research finds the reforms produced "decidedly more stable and sustainable growth from 1992 on." Rodrik and Subramanian note that India's growth had already accelerated around 1980, before the main liberalization, so 1991 deepened a change already under way rather than starting it.

Tanzania under Ujamaa. In 1973 the ruling party made it compulsory for rural Tanzanians to live in planned villages, and scholarly estimates put the number moved at about five million. Many farmers were moved far from their fields and trees. Purchases by the cashew authority fell from 140,000 tons in 1973 to 44,000 tons in 1978–79. By 1985, IMF staff report, agricultural production had been declining since the 1970s and cash-crop exports had fallen by half since 1970. Falling world crop prices and oil shocks contributed. After liberalization began in 1986, growth averaged about 7% a year from 2000.

Across countries. Single cases have confounders, so I also look at the cross-country record. Grier and Grier studied 141 countries from 1970 to 2015 and identified 49 sustained jumps in economic freedom. Compared with matched countries that did not reform, average annual growth ran about 2.1 to 2.9 percentage points higher over the next five years and about 1.0 to 1.9 points higher over ten. On their illustration, that leaves a reforming country roughly 16% richer after a decade. Critics note that reforms are not randomly assigned, and that the result is an average, not a guarantee for every country. The authors match on investment, institutions, human capital and other covariates, and the effect holds across their different thresholds and estimators.

I see the same pattern inside the United States. Prices have risen fastest where government pays, subsidizes or regulates most heavily, in hospital care, college, child care and rent, and have fallen or stayed far below inflation where firms compete for customers, in televisions, toys, software, phones and clothing (data below).

From January 2000 to September 2026, by my calculation from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' consumer price indexes (U.S. city average, not seasonally adjusted), hospital services rose 295%, college tuition and fees 196%, day care and preschool 166%, medical care services 152% and rent 149%, against 100% for all items. Televisions fell 98%, toys 72%, computer software 68% and wireless phone service 41%, while apparel rose 10% and new vehicles 26%, far below inflation. Critics note, as Our World in Data does, that medical services are not adjusted for quality. That caveat does not reach tuition, day care or rent, which rose 149% to 196% with no comparable quality claim. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics – CPI-U, U.S. city average, all items and component series (2026). Our World in Data – Price changes in consumer goods and services in the United States (2026)

head: Data: global poverty and extreme hunger

body: No matter which absolute line you pick, the share of the world living below it has fallen since 2000: Our World in Data / World Bank series show declines at $3, $5, and $10 a day (2021 PPP). Our World in Data – No matter what poverty line you choose, the share below it has declined globally

Extreme famine deaths and the share in extreme poverty collapsed as market growth and trade spread. China's post-1978 market reforms alone account for a large share of the global reduction (World Bank figures already cited above). Literal starvation deaths in the United States are rare. Food insecurity and malnutrition elsewhere remain real problems, which is not the same claim as "capitalism never feeds people."
I take this as evidence for markets and private property, not for a large compulsory welfare state. Planned systems produced the largest man-made famines of the twentieth century (Communism).

Unions should be voluntary, and no one should have to join or pay one to work. Licensing ought to exist only to prevent real harm to consumers. I oppose a minimum wage: pay is set by agreement, fraud and forced labor stay crimes, and the safety floor covers hardship.

I support the freedom of workers to form and join unions, and of employers and workers to bargain freely, under freedom of association. No one should be compelled to join or pay a union as a condition of work. Occupational licensing should meet the same burden of proof as any regulation: it is justified only where it prevents real harm to consumers, not to limit competition. I oppose any minimum wage. A minimum wage dictates the terms of a voluntary contract between a worker and an employer. How many jobs are lost is disputed, but it can price people whose labor is worth less than the floor out of work. Neither is consistent with negative rights. Wages ought to be set by agreement, including collective agreements reached by unions that workers join voluntarily. Low pay should be supplemented by the earnings-only top-up and hardship is covered by the bare-minimum safety floor, both set out in Welfare and Entitlements, not by price controls on labor. Fraud, coercion, wage theft, and forced labor should remain crimes. The abolition ought to cover state minimum wages too: rights do not change at state lines, and the top-up uses one national zero-bracket line.

head: "Doesn't banning compelled dues weaken unions?"
body: Unions remain free to organize and bargain. They keep members by delivering value, as any voluntary association does.

head: "Without a minimum wage, won't workers be exploited?"
body: Exploitation through force, fraud, or coercion should stay illegal: wage theft, deceptive contracts, and forced labor are rights violations and ought to be prosecuted. What ends is the state setting the price of a voluntary agreement. Workers keep the right to refuse a job, to quit, and to join a union and bargain collectively. Several of the highest-wage countries in Europe, including Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Austria, and Italy, have no national minimum wage. Wages there are set by collective agreements. Those agreements rest on very strong unions, which the law ought to allow only as voluntary associations, so the outcome in the United States would not simply copy theirs. People who still cannot earn enough are covered by the safety floor.

head: "Why abolish the minimum wage instead of keeping a small one?"
body: A floor of any size is a rule that two consenting adults may not agree on certain terms, and it hits hardest those whose skills are worth the least. The federal minimum already binds very few people: in 2024, 1.0 percent of hourly paid workers earned $7.25 or less. The safety floor, funded by minimal necessary taxes, handles hardship directly rather than through a price control that can price people out of work. How large that job loss is remains disputed in the research, and the abolition does not depend on its size.

head: "Isn't the minimum wage just a wage floor, not a ban on work?"
body: In price terms it is a floor: the law forbids a voluntary wage below a set price. When a worker's productivity is worth less than that floor, the job often does not exist at the legal wage. Employment effects are debated in size. The definition is not. I would abolish the floor because negative rights forbid the state from dictating the terms of a peaceful contract. I would cover hardship through the earnings-only top-up and the safety floor instead (Welfare and Entitlements).

head: "Without a minimum wage, how do low earners get by?"
body: Through pay set by agreement plus the earnings-only top-up built into the flat tax's zero bracket. A low earner's pay should be topped up through the ordinary tax return, and the top-up should shrink gradually as earnings rise, reaching zero at the zero-bracket line. So taking more hours or a raise would always leave the worker better off. The support would come through the tax system rather than from a rule that the employer must pay more, so no one would be priced out of a job (Welfare and Entitlements).

head: "Doesn't Acemoglu show that a minimum wage creates more good jobs?"
body: It is a serious case. In his 2001 model, firms that invest more in a job have to share more of the payoff in wage bargaining, so the market creates too many low-wage jobs. A wage floor can push hiring toward higher-wage jobs and raise average productivity. I grant that a floor can change which jobs get created. But the same model predicts more unemployment, and the paper says only that these rules "may improve welfare." It is a theory paper with no evidence that they do. It also does not answer my objection: a minimum wage overrides a voluntary contract, and wages ought to be set by agreement. Low pay is topped up through the tax return, and hardship is covered by the safety floor (Welfare and Entitlements).

Union membership was 9.9% of U.S. wage and salary workers in 2024 (14.3 million), with 32.2% in the public sector and 5.9% in the private sector, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. In Janus v. AFSCME (2018) the Supreme Court held that compelling public employees to pay agency fees violates the First Amendment. Freedom of association is set out in Authority & Civil Liberties.

In 2024, 82,000 U.S. workers earned exactly the federal minimum of $7.25 an hour and 760,000 earned less, together 1.0 percent of hourly paid workers, down from 13.4 percent in 1979. Most were young, and about two-thirds worked in leisure and hospitality, where tips may supplement wages. As of July 2026, Denmark, Italy, Austria, Finland, and Sweden had no national minimum wage, and in those countries, as in Iceland, Norway, and Switzerland, minimums are set by collective agreements for specific sectors. In 2022 the share of low-wage earners was 4.1 percent in Sweden, 6.5 percent in Finland, 8.8 percent in Italy, and 9.7 percent in Denmark, against 14.7 percent across the EU. Portugal, which has a statutory minimum wage, had the lowest share, at 1.8 percent, so the absence of a minimum wage does not by itself explain low-pay rates.

Defenders cite Cengiz, Dube, Lindner, and Zipperer, who studied 138 state minimum-wage increases and found that the overall number of low-wage jobs was essentially unchanged five years later. Neumark and Shirley's review of U.S. studies found the opposite in most of the literature: a clear preponderance of negative employment estimates, strongest for teens, young adults, and the less educated. The abolition does not rest on the employment evidence: I rest it on the right of workers and employers to set their own terms.

Big is not illegal in my view. Collusion, fraud, and coercion should be prosecuted, and genuine bottlenecks over essential services can be regulated.

I don't believe size alone justifies intervention. Firms that grow by serving customers better have violated no one's rights. I support intervention against fraud, collusion to fix prices or divide markets, and coercive conduct, and against genuine monopoly bottlenecks where refusal would leave people without reasonable alternatives for essential services. Any intervention carries the burden of proof, as all regulation does.

head: "Won't large firms abuse their power without stronger antitrust?"
body: Abuse through fraud, collusion, or coercion should be prosecuted. A large firm without such conduct faces competition and new entrants. Breaking it up for its size punishes success rather than wrongdoing.
The Sherman Act prohibits contracts and conspiracies in restraint of trade and monopolization (15 U.S.C. §§ 1–2). The bottleneck exception follows Authority & Civil Liberties.

I want a federal income tax with a large zero bracket, a short phase-in, then a single flat 20% (22% through 2041 with the transition surcharge), and capital income at a preferential flat 15% (17% through 2041). The base should be broad. Family measures are the named exceptions (Births). I'd have no sales tax or VAT, no estate tax, and local moderate property taxes. A transition levy (≤16% of wages) should replace FICA for grandfathered SS/Medicare and debt, and a Sanctuary Levy ≤3% on income above $75,000/$150,000 is time-limited (Sanctuary Plan). I support full expensing now and across-the-board employer payroll cuts as the levy steps down. The tax take should match essential functions only.
The tax system across all levels of government should be low, simple, and limited to funding core public functions.

At the federal level I would make the centerpiece a flat income tax with a large zero bracket and a short, transparent phase-in. Income below $42,000 for single filers and $84,000 for joint filers (adjusted for inflation) faces a zero rate. A linear phase-in then applies over the next $10,000 for single filers ($42,000 to $52,000) and $20,000 for joint filers ($84,000 to $104,000), so that the rate rises smoothly to the full flat rate of 20%. Income above the phase-in range faces that single flat rate. Capital gains and dividends receive a preferential but still flat 15% rate, which rises to the full 20% rate only if the automation trigger in AI and Automation is met. Through 2041 the 2-point transition surcharge applies to both rates, so the top rates are 22% on ordinary income and 17% on capital gains and dividends (22% if the trigger is met). I reject permanent progressive rate schedules, and the surcharge should go to the debt.
Most deductions, credits, and special preferences ought to be eliminated to keep the base broad and the rules simple.

Inherited assets should keep the original owner's cost basis (carryover basis) rather than a stepped-up basis. Today an heir's cost basis is "stepped up" to the value at death, so gains built up during the owner's life are never taxed. The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates this exclusion at $336 billion in forgone revenue for fiscal years 2024 to 2028. Under carryover basis the heir keeps the original cost basis and pays the flat tax only when the asset is sold. Nothing is taxed at death, so this is not an estate or inheritance tax, which I reject. JCT estimated that an earlier version of this change would raise about $105 billion over ten years. Joint Committee on Taxation – Estimates of Federal Tax Expenditures for Fiscal Years 2024-2028 (JCX-48-24); Congressional Budget Office – Change the Tax Treatment of Capital Gains From Sales of Inherited Assets. Carryover basis is also how capital income stays taxed as AI ownership grows (AI and Automation).

The exceptions are the family measures set out in Births and Family Formation and the earnings-only top-up in Welfare and Entitlements. How the family package counts under the franchise is fixed in net fiscal voting bar.
My view: Since restricting immigration will lower the population, we want as many things as possible to help parents and raise birth rates to replacement level (Immigration and Borders).

Secondary taxes (no VAT/sales; low corporate tax so business income is taxed once; transition levy; surcharge; Sanctuary Levy; permanent full expensing; local moderate property taxes; no estate tax; narrow excise and tariffs only), the two named time-limited exceptions to the single flat rate (the transition surcharge through 2041 and the Sanctuary Levy), and the essential-functions tax-take rule — including sanctuary care for the animals freed by the shutdown — are set out in In short and the example callouts above, not re-bulleted here.
My view: The honest way to keep promises to people who already paid in is one visible levy with a hard ceiling and a written end, not a hidden mix of taxes.

head: "How far below replacement is the U.S. birth rate?"
body: The U.S. total fertility rate was about 1.6 births per woman in 2024, a record low, against a replacement level of about 2.1. CDC/NCHS – Births: Final Data for 2024

head: "Are payroll tax cuts and full expensing just corporate subsidies by another name?"
body: No. A subsidy transfers taxpayer money to a business. A payroll tax cut or full expensing takes less of the business's own money and transfers nothing. Both are consistent with the rule that taxpayer money subsidizes no business unless taxpayers opt in, and both apply across the board rather than to chosen firms or groups. Full expensing applies now. Payroll tax cuts are a long-run goal as the transition levy steps down.

head: "Do these tax cuts stop outsourcing?"
body: No study measures whether any incentive reduces outsourcing itself. The evidence measures domestic employment and investment. Across-the-board payroll tax cuts and full expensing are the two broad tools with measured gains in U.S. jobs. Full expensing applies now. Payroll tax cuts are a long-run goal as the transition levy steps down.

head: "Doesn't the flat tax mostly cut taxes for the rich?"
body: In dollar terms, the largest cuts go to the highest earners: the top federal rate is 37% today, against a flat 20% here (22% through 2041 with the transition surcharge), and capital income keeps a preferential rate of 15% (17% through 2041). Lower earners gain through the large zero bracket and the earnings-only top-up, and parents at every income get a refundable credit per child (Births and Family Formation), so most low-income workers owe no income tax at all. I do not claim the change is neutral by income. It rests on principle: one rate for everyone above the zero bracket, with no penalty for earning more. My static model's household table in Fiscal Policy shows every household tested paying less federal tax than today. Those are my estimates, not official scores.

head: "Couldn't taxing billionaires pay for the government?"
body: Not for long. While $8.4 trillion is more than a full year of federal spending, and most wealth-tax proposals are yearly levies rather than one-time seizures, the yearly version raises little: Saez and Zucman estimated that Senator Warren's 2019 plan (2% a year above $50 million, 1% more above $1 billion) would raise about $2.75 trillion over ten years, about 1% of GDP a year, under a twentieth of federal spending at about 21% of GDP. But the fortunes themselves run out fast. Forbes counted 989 U.S. billionaires worth a combined $8.4 trillion on March 1, 2026. Federal outlays were $7.01 trillion in fiscal 2025, so taking every billionaire's entire fortune would pay for about 14 months of federal spending, once. Counting state and local governments, U.S. government spending ran at about $11.1 trillion a year in 2025 (BEA), which the same fortunes would cover for about nine months. Spending recurs every year. A fortune can be taken only once. That is one more reason I reject wealth taxes at every level, including California's Proposition 40 (State and Local Taxes).

head: Data: Verifying claims on US tax progressivity and billionaire effective rates

body: Core claim: US has (or "might have") the most progressive tax system among developed countries

This is well-supported by a November 2025 Fraser Institute study (Measuring Tax Progressivity in High-Income Countries (OECD)). It ranks 45 high-income OECD jurisdictions on structural measures of progressivity (spread between top and bottom combined marginal personal income tax rates, income level at which the top rate applies relative to average wages, size of basic exemptions relative to average wages, share of revenue from progressive personal income taxes, and share from generally regressive consumption taxes).
California ranks 1st overall.
Texas ranks 4th (the study was updated in December 2025 to correct an earlier ranking of 5th).

Taking the US high- and low-tax jurisdictions together, the United States ranks highest among the countries/jurisdictions examined - ahead of nearly all Canadian provinces and European systems (California ranks above every Canadian province; Texas ranks below Newfoundland & Labrador, 2nd).

Scandinavian countries (often cited as models) rank much lower (e.g., Finland ~36th, Norway ~37th, Sweden ~41st) largely because they rely more heavily on broad consumption taxes (VAT rates of roughly 20-25.5%) that fall more evenly or regressively across income groups, and their top income-tax rates apply at lower multiples of average wages.

This is consistent with older OECD analyses of household taxes showing the US collecting a larger share of taxes from the top 10% relative to their income share than most peer countries. The high ranking is driven primarily by relatively low effective burdens on lower- and middle-income earners (large standard deductions, credits, absence of a national VAT, and top brackets starting at high multiples of average wages) rather than uniquely high statutory rates on the rich. High earners still pay the large majority of federal individual income taxes.
Important caveats for accuracy:
The Fraser Institute ranking is based on tax structure (rates, thresholds, and revenue composition), not a full distributional analysis of every tax paid after transfers.

Results can differ under other definitions (e.g., including all state/local taxes, property taxes, payroll taxes, or focusing on the extreme top with unrealized capital gains). Some analyses (including certain ITEP state rankings or studies of the very top of the wealth distribution) show less progressivity once these factors are emphasized.
It does not measure total tax levels or the net redistributive effect of government spending.

The claim is therefore accurate as a description of the US system's position among developed countries on standard progressivity metrics, though "most progressive in the world" is a slight overstatement relative to the study's OECD scope. Fraser Institute – Measuring Tax Progressivity in High-Income Countries (OECD) (December 2025 corrected PDF)
Quoted figures from the @GunnelsWarren post

Billionaires 8.2%: This is the exact figure from a September 2021 White House Council of Economic Advisers / OMB report by Greg Leiserson and Danny Yagan. It is the estimated average federal individual income tax rate paid by the 400 wealthiest families over 2010-2018 on a broad income measure that includes unrealized gains from unsold stock (a Haig-Simons-style concept). It does not include corporate income taxes, payroll taxes, state taxes, or other levies. The report's own sensitivity checks put the rate at roughly 6-12% under varying assumptions. CEA/OMB – What Is the Average Federal Individual Income Tax Rate on the Wealthiest Americans? (2021)

More comprehensive measures: A 2025 NBER working paper by Balkir, Saez, Yagan, and Zucman (matching Forbes 400 data to tax returns) estimates the total effective tax rate for the top ~0.0002% (roughly the top 400) at about 24% of economic income in 2018-2020, compared with roughly 30% for the full population and about 45% for high labor-income earners. Corporate taxes form a substantial portion of the burden for this group (on the order of 9 percentage points in the study). Estimates vary with methodological choices around unrealized gains, corporate tax incidence, and income definitions. Shifting part of the corporate tax onto workers, as the CBO method does, lowers the top group's rate further. NBER – How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay? Evidence from Administrative Data (w34170)

Average worker 15.1%: This aligns with older OECD/Tax Foundation data for the income tax component of the tax wedge on a single average-wage worker (not the full effective rate). Full burdens for middle-income workers typically include employee payroll taxes (FICA ~7.65%) plus any state income or sales taxes, and federal individual income tax effective rates for many middle-income filers are often in the single digits to low teens after the standard deduction and credits. Tax Foundation – The U.S. Tax Burden on Labor, 2020; OECD – Taxing Wages 2026: The United States

The side-by-side comparison in the quoted post therefore mixes a selective individual-income-tax measure on a broad (including unrealized) income concept for billionaires with a different wage-focused measure for average workers. It is not a like-for-like comparison of total tax burdens.
Other elements
Federal minimum wage has remained $7.25 since 2009: Accurate. U.S. Department of Labor – History of Federal Minimum Wage Rates, 1938-2009
Large wealth increases for Musk, Bezos, and Zuckerberg since 2009: Directionally accurate (driven by equity valuations), though exact 2026 figures fluctuate with markets.

Summary: The central observation that the US tax system ranks as highly (or the most) progressive among developed countries on standard structural measures is supported by the recent Fraser Institute evidence and prior OECD work. The 8.2% vs. 15.1% framing is a real but incomplete and non-comparable statistic that excludes major taxes paid by the ultra-wealthy (especially corporate) and uses a broad income definition.

States set their own taxes (Federalism), and the same principles ought to apply at every level: flat, low and broad taxes, with no wealth tax, no graduated rates, no retroactive taxes, and moderate local property taxes tied to core services. A tax base should treat residents alike. If I were voting:

California: no on Proposition 3 (it makes the higher top income-tax rates permanent) and no on Proposition 40 (a one-time tax of up to 5% on covered assets over $1 billion, mostly for health care). SEIU-UHW is a primary backer. Calling the measure leverage or "blackmail" is opinion, but a union-backed wealth tax aimed at Medi-Cal funding is still a wealth tax, which I reject at every level. A Stanford/NBER analysis finds many billionaires would leave and that the net present value is often negative if the measure passes. Yes on Proposition 41 (audits of special-tax programs) and yes on Proposition 42 (it bars new taxes on owning financial assets and limits retroactive taxes). No on Proposition 43 (it requires two-thirds voter approval for voter-proposed local special taxes, while I hold that measures pass by a majority).
Colorado: no on Amendment 87 (graduated income tax) and yes on Proposition 136 (a 4.4% cap on income-tax rates).
Washington: yes on IP26-645 (it repeals the 9.9% tax on income above $1 million and bars state and local income taxes).

Florida: no on Amendment 3 (a $150,000 non-school homestead exemption in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028). It narrows the base, shifts the load onto renters, businesses and second homes, and gives new residents a smaller exemption for their first years.

High and complex taxes distort work, saving, investment, and compliance. U.S. federal revenue as a share of the economy has remained relatively stable for decades even when top statutory rates changed dramatically; very high rates do not reliably produce proportionally higher revenue. Federal revenue ranged from 14.2% to 18.5% of GDP during the 1950s, according to OMB, when the top rate was 91% or higher, and CBO puts the 50-year average at 17.3% of GDP. That top rate reached few people. The 91% bracket of 1950 began at $200,000 of income, about $2 million today, and the top 0.1 percent paid an average effective income tax rate of about 21%. So the 1950s show high statutory rates, not high rates actually paid. Flat-tax reforms in other countries have shown that simplification is workable and need not collapse collections. An IMF review of flat-tax adoptions found that personal income tax revenue rose in some countries, such as Latvia, Lithuania, and Russia, and fell in others, with total revenue effects that varied by country.

A large zero bracket increases take-home pay for lower- and middle-income households and supports private spending. A short linear phase-in removes the sharp notch that would otherwise encourage people to hold income just below the threshold. Lower marginal rates above the phase-in reduce disincentives to work and invest, though the measured gains from flat-tax adoptions abroad come mainly from simplicity and compliance, not faster growth. Reviews find no evidence that the rate cuts paid for themselves, and in Russia's 2001 reform the rise in income tax revenue came from better compliance rather than more work. Neither a sales tax nor a VAT is used, so no new consumption tax can grow quietly. Corporate and payroll taxes should not serve as primary redistribution tools. Property tax is retained at the local level because it is a practical and accountable way to fund local order and infrastructure. Eliminating it would require less accountable replacements. Estate taxes confiscate property that has already been taxed.

No study measures whether any incentive reduces outsourcing itself. The evidence instead measures domestic employment and investment, and the two broad tools with measured gains in U.S. jobs are across-the-board payroll tax cuts and full expensing. The government ought to apply full expensing now and treat payroll tax cuts as a long-run goal as the transition levy steps down. In Norway, the abolition of lower regional payroll tax rates showed that each 1-percentage-point payroll tax increase cut local employment by 1.37% while wages fell only 0.32%. So lower payroll taxes support employment where wages do not fully adjust. A Swedish payroll tax cut for young workers raised their employment by 2–3 percentage points with no change in net wages. Bonus depreciation raised eligible investment by 10.4% (2001–04) and 16.9% (2008–10), and areas more exposed to it gained employment at roughly $20,000–$53,000 of forgone revenue per job, though earnings per worker did not rise. Targeted hiring credits, Opportunity Zones, domestic-content procurement rules, and firm-specific deals show weaker, short-lived, or far more costly results, often above $110,000 per job.

This structure is sustainable only alongside spending restraint. It can support strong defense, core public goods, and a minimal safety floor. It cannot support the present long-term trajectory of major entitlement programs without reforming those programs. The tax rules and the commitment to a smaller federal government are designed to fit together.

K-12 is funded by each state from its general revenue at about $10,000 per child per year, and the money follows the child to any public school in the state (K-12 Funding). There should be no separate education tax. Private and religious schooling is paid by parents, and homeschooling families get a refundable federal credit (Homeschooling).

I believe we should balance the budget, minimize deficits, and pay down and eventually eliminate the national debt. Defense stays protected. Committed cuts come first; new entrants go on reformed tracks; grandfathered SS/Medicare is kept. A capped transition levy plus a 2-point surcharge (ends 2041) fund promises and debt, and a debt brake auto-corrects. Sanctuary bonds are the one stated deficit exception, repaid by the Sanctuary Levy (Sanctuary Plan). The flat tax alone does not balance today's budget - spending would have to fall to fit it. Numbers: Data callout (my static model, not official scores).

I believe a balanced budget is the proper target. Deficit spending should be minimized; the one stated exception is sanctuary bonds, which cover the early years of sanctuary care that liquidation proceeds do not and are repaid in full by the Sanctuary Levy (Sanctuary Plan). Long-term policy ought to aim at reducing and eventually eliminating the national debt. Owner income from federal land, minerals, energy, and spectrum should go first to the earnings-only top-up, and any remainder automatically to debt reduction (Economic System). Defense should be the top spending priority, with reductions coming from other areas.

My paydown order is committed cuts first, then the 30% nondefense cut, reformed tracks for new entrants with grandfathered SS/Medicare kept, CBO-scored Medicare savings, transition levy + surcharge, and the debt brake - scored in the Data callout. The aim is first to stop the debt growing faster than the economy, then to reduce it in dollars.

head: "Is eliminating the national debt realistic?"
body: It is a long-term aim, not an immediate demand. Balanced budgets stop the debt from growing, and sustained restraint reduces it over time. The direction matters as much as the timeline.

head: "Does the flat tax raise enough to balance the budget?"
body: Not on its own. Applied to IRS returns for 2023 and grown to 2026, my static estimate puts the 20% flat tax at about $1.9 trillion a year, or about 6.0% of GDP. That is roughly 71% of today's individual income tax. Heads of household use the single line, and capital gains and dividends are taxed at their permanent 15% rate. The 2-point surcharge through 2041 is counted separately below. The range is about 5.6–6.3% of GDP depending on income growth and capital-income treatment. That is why spending has to fall and why the transition levy exists. IRS SOI – Table 1.2, Tax Year 2023; IRS SOI – Table 1.4, Tax Year 2023

head: "Does the flat tax at least cover defense and interest?"
body: Only just, on my estimate. For fiscal 2026, CBO projects defense outlays of $885 billion (2.8% of GDP) and net interest of $1,039 billion (3.3%), together $1.92 trillion, or 6.1% of GDP. My static estimate of the 20% flat tax is about $1.9 trillion, or 6.0% of GDP, within a range of 5.6–6.3%. So the income tax roughly pays for defense and interest and nothing else, and at the low end of the range it falls about $0.15 trillion short. Fiscal 2026 $ billions % of GDP Flat income tax, 20% (my static estimate) about 1,900 about 6.0 Defense outlays (CBO) 885 2.8 Net interest (CBO) 1,039 3.3 Flat tax minus defense and interest about −25 about −0.1 Everything else CBO projects: Social Security 1,666, Medicare 1,063, Medicaid/CHIP/marketplace 845, other mandatory 955, nondefense discretionary 996 5,525 17.3 Other revenue today: corporate 404, customs 418, other 197 1,019 3.2 The rest closes through measures already on this page, set out in the answers below. The transition levy carries Social Security and Medicare for the protected generation, so they do not draw on the income tax. The committed cuts end SNAP, farm payments, and the Department of Education, and wind non-emergency Medicaid down to a residual. Other nondefense spending falls 30% over three years. Applied to CBO's $996 billion, that is about $300 billion a year once fully phased in. The 2-point surcharge through 2041 adds about a tenth of flat-tax receipts, roughly $0.19 trillion a year, because it is 2 points over the same base: a tenth of the 20% rate, and a little more on capital income at 15%. Corporate tax and other receipts cover what remains of core government. Interest is the item that shrinks only as the debt does, which is why the surcharge, the levy floor, and the debt brake all go to the debt first. CBO – The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036

head: "Who pays for the benefits already promised?"
body: The transition levy, which replaces today's payroll taxes. It is a temporary tax that pays off existing promises. In 2026 Social Security costs about $1.67 trillion and Medicare about $1.06 trillion. The levy pays only for people who are protected and for credits earned before the change. It applies to all wages because 17.4% of earnings sit above today's Social Security cap, and a wider base lets the rate stay lower for everyone under it. Nobody earns new benefits from it, and nobody is enrolled in anything by paying it: it is a debt to the people already promised, and it shrinks as they pass. SSA – 2026 COLA Fact Sheet; SSA – Fast Facts & Figures 2025

head: "Why does the levy stay at 12% after the protected costs fall?"
body: Because the debt still has to be paid. On my model, letting the levy fall as soon as the protected costs fall would leave deficits in the 2050s. Holding it at 12% until debt is below 60% of GDP, then stepping it down half a point a year, would balance the budget in 2050 and keep it in surplus after. The levy would never be higher than in year one.

head: "Where do the savings come from?"
body: Mostly from programs that end or shrink: non-emergency Medicaid, SNAP, farm payments, the Department of Education, and a 30% cut to other nondefense spending phased over three years. Spending lags appropriations: CBO estimates a one-third cut to transportation and education grants saves only $13 billion in its first year against $41 billion of funding cut. Medicare savings are counted only where CBO has scored them. Paying hospital outpatient departments site-neutral rates saves $156.9 billion over 2025–2034. CBO – Reduce Selected Nondefense Discretionary Spending; CBO – Site-neutral payments; CBO – Options for Reducing the Deficit: 2025 to 2034

head: "What stops the plan from drifting off course?"
body: A debt brake. Each year debt is compared with the legislated path, leaving out sanctuary bonds while the Sanctuary Levy repays them on schedule. For each point of overshoot, the next year's income surcharge rises half a point, up to two points. The brake should be suspended in a recession. If it stays on for three years in a row, Congress ought to pass spending cuts to close the gap, and the surcharge should then end. Surpluses, owner income left after the top-up, and Federal Reserve remittances should go straight to the debt.

head: "Does anyone pay more than today?"
body: Not in any household I tested, from the first year on (see the table below). The closest case is a self-employed worker earning $70,000, who pays about $77 less in the early years, because today's tax code gives them a 20% business-income deduction.

head: "What could go wrong?"
body: The biggest risks are the flat tax raising less than estimated, interest rates rising, and removals costing more than assumed. I assume about $15 billion a year above current law, which is about 876,000 removals at ICE's own $17,121 average. Penn Wharton's estimate of $70,236 per removal would make that cost about four times higher. MinnPost – Does each ICE deportation cost taxpayers at least $17,000?. Highest worker marginal rate on wages (worker share): 30.0% in 2027–2036 (22% income tax with the 2-point surcharge + 8%, the worker half of the 16% levy), 29.05% in 2041 (22% + 7.05%) and 26.0% in 2051 (20% + 6%). Above the Sanctuary Levy line it is 1.71 points higher while the levy runs on my middle case (31.71% in 2027–2036), and at most 3 points higher at its cap. Persistent deficits shift costs to future taxpayers and raise interest payments that crowd out other spending. Federal debt and interest costs have grown substantially. CBO projects debt held by the public to rise from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036, above the 1946 record of 106%, and net interest to rise from $1.04 trillion to $2.14 trillion over the same period. Fiscal restraint is consistent with my limits on government and my preference for low taxation. Federal debt passed 100% of the economy in 2013, when both debt and GDP were about $16.7 trillion. The debt has been eliminated before, briefly, in 1835.

On October 14, 2026, total federal debt was $40.33 trillion, of which $32.48 trillion was held by the public. In the first eleven months of fiscal year 2026, the government collected $4.85 trillion and spent $6.81 trillion, including $1.02 trillion of net interest, $1.53 trillion for Social Security, $0.98 trillion for Medicare, $0.93 trillion for other health programs, and $0.88 trillion for defense. My static model puts the 20% flat tax at about $1.9 trillion a year, as set out in the answers above. These are my static estimates, not official scores, and they ignore changes in behaviour and growth. They show that my tax and spending plans should move together: the rate cannot carry the budget alone, and spending has to fall by more than a third from today's level.

France shows where the other path leads. The cost of state services does not disappear when the state provides them: it is paid through taxes and payroll contributions and carried forward as debt, while results in the services themselves decline (data below).

head: Data: France's public spending, taxes and schools

body: INSEE puts French public spending at 57.2% of GDP in 2025 and general government debt (Maastricht definition) at €3,460.5bn at the end of 2025, 115.6% of GDP. France's tax revenue of 43.5% of GDP in 2024 was the second-highest of the 38 OECD countries, after Denmark, against an OECD average of 34.1%. In PISA 2022, French 15-year-olds' mathematics and reading results fell from 2018 and were among the lowest PISA has measured for France in all three subjects, with a mathematics drop of more than 20 points. Defenders of the French model point out that scores fell across most of the OECD after the pandemic. France's mathematics drop exceeded the OECD average of almost 15 points, and its reading decline began around 2012, years before COVID-19. Neither "the old" nor "immigrants" is a single root cause of France's crisis (News Commentary France view). Public debt around 119% of GDP, rising service costs, and suspended or fragile pension reform are the bond-market facts behind 2026 political turmoil. Balanced budgets keep money stable. My goal is price stability, and I treat inflation as a hidden tax. The Fed should be reformed, not abolished: one price-stability mandate under a rule, no deficit finance, lending only to solvent banks, no bailouts, a full audit, legal competing currencies, and any profits to debt reduction.

Stable money follows from fiscal restraint. With balanced budgets and debt reduction, the government does not rely on the central bank to finance deficits, and monetary policy aims at price stability. Inflation acts as an unlegislated tax on savings and wages, so preventing it is part of keeping the tax burden visible and matched to essential functions. I would reform the Federal Reserve, not abolish it. It should keep a single mandate, price stability under a published rule, and drop the employment mandate. It should not finance deficits or run asset purchases that work as deficit finance. As lender of last resort it ought to lend only to solvent banks, against good collateral, at a penalty rate, and never bail out insolvent firms, whose losses would otherwise fall on taxpayers who never consented. It should be fully audited in public. Competing private currencies should remain legal. Any profits it remits to the Treasury ought to go to debt reduction. Fed governors should be removable only for cause, such as misconduct or breaking the price-stability rule, proven with notice, the evidence and a hearing, and never for disagreeing with the President on interest rates. A Fed bound by one published rule needs no political steering, and that insulation keeps it from being pushed to finance deficits.

head: "Isn't some inflation needed to manage the economy?"
body: Price stability is the aim. Balanced budgets remove the main pressure for inflationary finance, and stable prices let people plan, save, and invest.

head: "Why not abolish the Fed?"
body: Before the Fed, money held its value over the long run but swung sharply, with frequent deflation and recurring bank panics in 1873, 1893, and 1907 that destroyed depositors' savings. The Fed's worst failure, the 1929 to 1933 collapse, came from its own discretion, as Ben Bernanke acknowledged in 2002. The lesson I draw is to limit discretion, not to remove the institution: a single price-stability rule, no deficit finance, and lending only to solvent banks. A return to gold is not favored, since countries that left the gold standard recovered from the Depression sooner.

Consumer prices rose 9.1% over the year ended June 2022, the largest 12-month increase since November 1981, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Balanced budgets are set out in Fiscal Policy. By the Minneapolis Fed's consumer price index, the standard deviation of annual inflation was about 5.7 points in 1801 to 1912 and about 1.5 points in 1984 to 2025. But prices rose about 32-fold from 1913 to 2025, so a 1913 dollar buys about 3 percent of what it did. NBER business-cycle dates show average contractions of 21.6 months in 1854 to 1919 and 10.3 months in 1945 to 2020, though Christina Romer found that older data overstate pre-1914 volatility. The Federal Reserve Act sets three goals: maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates. The Fed remitted $107.4 billion to the Treasury for 2021; since then its interest costs have exceeded its income, and its deferred asset stood at $243.5 billion at the end of 2025.

Government should be sized to its essential functions, with defense first. Work private firms can do ought to be contracted out, and I would abolish agencies without an essential function. Career staff get severance or placement help. Political appointees' roles end with the office.

I believe the size of government should follow from its functions. Spending and staffing ought to be matched to essential functions, with defense the top priority, and functions that private firms can perform should be contracted out, as government research already is. Agencies with no essential function, such as the federal Department of Education, should be abolished. When an agency is abolished, career staff who built their lives around these jobs deserve severance or placement help: that is the commitment side, honoring people who followed the rules. Political appointees are different; their roles end with the office, and I see no transition obligation to them.

head: "Doesn't contracting out reduce accountability?"
body: Contracts set measurable deliverables and can be ended. A contractor that fails should lose the work, which is a stronger check than the near-permanence of a public office.

head: "Should the government build new national monuments?"
body: Honoring veterans is worthy. A new monument should be paid for by private donors or opt-in funds rather than general taxes, because it is not an essential function that justifies compelled taxes. I believe the President should have discretion over monuments and improvements on federal property already under executive control. That discretion covers only property the executive already manages. It is not a power to take new land, spend money Congress has not appropriated, or go beyond the laws that authorize the executive (Government Structure and Checks).

In a realistic world, these programs phase out to bridge the gaps during the transition; that is why the phase-out window exists. The federal civilian workforce was about 2.3 million on September 30, 2024, according to the Office of Personnel Management. Government R&D through private contracts is set out in Bioethics, Progress, & Technology. I would defund NGOs that run on public money and end grants to nongovernmental organizations. A nonprofit should be paid only under a contract for an essential public service, with measurable deliverables, verified results and the right to end it for failure. No public money should pay for advocacy, lobbying, litigation or political campaigns, and no nonprofit is paid to pass public money on to others.

The government ought to defund NGOs that run on public money. A nonprofit that lives on taxpayer grants is a government program with the accountability taken out: it spends public money without answering to voters and without the deliverables a contract would impose. The United States ought to end every federal grant to nongovernmental organizations, at home and abroad, and the states ought to do the same.

The rule has four parts. (1) No grants: no grant, cooperative agreement or other transfer without deliverables should go to a nongovernmental organization. (2) Contracts only: where a nonprofit performs an essential public function, it should be paid under a contract that names the service, sets measurable deliverables, checks them independently, pays only for what was delivered, and can be ended for failure, as with sanctuary operators (Sanctuary Plan). Where the work is put out to bid, nonprofits and firms should compete on the same terms. Money that follows a person to the provider they use, such as per-child school funding or the last-resort allowance paying for a placement, is payment for a service, not a grant. (3) No advocacy money: no public dollar, under a contract or otherwise, should pay for lobbying, advocacy campaigns, litigation against the government, or political organizing. (4) No pass-through: no nonprofit should be paid to hand public money on to other organizations. The agency should pay the provider that does the work. Causes with no essential function can still be funded through opt-in, taxpayer-designated funds, as charitable foreign aid is (Fiscal Policy). Tax exemption for charities is a separate question and is not changed here.

head: "Don't NGOs deliver services cheaper and better than government?"
body: Supporters of NGO funding point to exactly that. If it is true, the contract rule costs them nothing: an NGO that really delivers more for less wins and keeps the contract on measured results, against public agencies and private firms alike. What ends is money handed over without competition or checked deliverables. Feeding Our Future, a Minnesota nonprofit that sponsored sites in the federal child nutrition program, went from receiving and disbursing about $3.4 million in federal funds in 2019 to nearly $200 million in 2021. It did so by opening more than 250 sites that filed fake meal counts, and it fraudulently obtained and disbursed more than $240 million, collecting more than $18 million in administrative fees for sponsoring them. Its founder was sentenced in May 2026 to 500 months in prison. A pass-through sponsor paid on self-reported claims is the model this rule ends.

head: "Won't cutting grants close charities that people depend on?"
body: Critics cite the Urban Institute's finding that, in every state, 60 to 86 percent of the nonprofits that received government grants would have run at a loss without them from 2021 to 2023. That measures dependence, not value. Urban itself describes it as a measure of grant dependence, not a prediction. A charity that cannot cover its costs without taxpayers is already a public program, so where its service is essential it moves to a contract, and the rest compete for voluntary giving, which reached $592.50 billion in 2024, and for opt-in funds. Grants end over the phase-out window, not overnight.

head: "Doesn't federal law already stop grants from paying for lobbying?"
body: Only narrowly. 31 U.S.C. § 1352 bars a recipient of a federal grant, contract, loan or cooperative agreement from using those appropriated funds to pay anyone to influence federal officials or Congress on a federal award. It restricts only the federal money itself and only lobbying on awards, so a grant still frees an organization's own money for advocacy, campaigns and lawsuits. Ending grants and barring advocacy spending under contracts closes that gap.

In a realistic world, these programs phase out to bridge the gaps during the transition; that is why the phase-out window exists. The scale is large. The Urban Institute counts more than 80,000 501(c)(3) charities, about a third of those that electronically filed a full Form 990, reporting government grants each year from 2021 to 2023, worth $304 billion in 2021, $294 billion in 2022 and $240 billion in 2023, more than double foundation giving. That total leaves out Medicare and Medicaid payments, so it understates public funding.

France shows how far the model can go. In 2024 the French state made 114,778 payments to associations worth €9.5 billion. Subsidies were €7.3 billion of it, 76.7%, while payment for services was €923 million, 9.7%. The largest subsidy streams ran through school education (€1,162 million), territorial cohesion (€983 million), solidarity and equal opportunity (€973 million), special social and pension schemes (€875 million) and labor and employment (€797 million).

Accountability runs through elected officials (Civil Service Protections). A grant moves public money beyond that line. A contract keeps it there, because the agency that signs it answers for the results and can end it. Paying NGOs to lobby, campaign or sue also makes every taxpayer fund political speech they may oppose, the same coercion I reject in mandatory redistribution (Welfare and Entitlements). Hiring should be by merit, and policy-setting jobs ought to answer to elected officials. Career staff cannot be fired for politics, but I want removal for poor performance or misconduct to be fast: notice, a 30-day decision, and one appeal decided within 90 days.

Federal hiring should be by merit, through open competition and tested qualifications, never by party or loyalty. Positions that set or direct policy ought to serve at the pleasure of elected officials, so voters can hold the people they elect responsible for what the government does. Career staff in non-policy roles should keep one firm protection: no one is hired, fired, or punished for party, political speech, or refusing an unlawful order. Removal for poor performance or misconduct ought to be fast and fair: written notice of the specific reasons, a chance to answer, a decision within 30 days, and one appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board decided within 90 days. The probationary period should be two years, with an affirmative decision required before it ends.

head: "Won't weakening protections bring back the spoils system?"
body: That is the strongest objection. Protections were built after the spoils era because jobs handed out for loyalty produced corruption and incompetence, and a workforce that can be fired at will can be pressured to serve a party rather than the law. The government ought to keep the part of the old settlement that answers this: merit hiring, and a ban on firing or punishing anyone for party, political speech, or refusing an unlawful order, enforceable in court. What it removes is delay. Reclassifying policy roles is legitimate only for positions that genuinely set policy. Using it to reach ordinary career staff would be the spoils system by another name.

head: "Is it really that hard to fire a federal employee?"
body: It is slow. The Government Accountability Office found that removing a poor-performing permanent employee can take six months to a year or longer, and that an appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board averaged 243 days in 2013. Agencies dismissed about 3,500 employees for performance or conduct that year, most during the probationary period, when appeal rights are limited. The delay discourages managers from acting at all.

Accountability runs through elected officials, so those who set policy answer to them (Public-Sector Size and Civil Service). Due process still applies to every removal (Due Process and Rule of Law), but process that takes a year protects poor performance more than it protects fairness. Keeping a hard line against political firing protects both the employee and the public from a workforce bent to party ends.

I would phase out existing benefits for people who followed the rules, with grandfathered Social Security and Medicare for life. Welfare should be cut to a bare-minimum floor for basic needs, with no compelled redistribution beyond that floor and other social programs opt-in, so no worker is made to fund programs they never chose. I support an earnings-only top-up paid through the tax return: 10% of earnings, peaking at $15,000 of earnings (at most $1,500 per worker), plus up to $1,000 more per child for up to three children, for all working parents, paid only on earnings. It is paid per worker and phases out on household income from $15,000 to $42,000 (married: $30,000 to $84,000). Legal residents and lawfully present non-citizens who pay taxes receive it on the same terms as citizens. For people who cannot work, the order is private disability first (by default), then charity, then a last-resort means-tested allowance ($575/$900 plus local rent). Failing the net-taxpayer test suspends the vote (net fiscal voting bar).

People who followed the rules and are on benefits should not be punished when the system changes to something better, so I would build in a phase-out period that honors existing commitments. The obligation is to the person, not to the old funding stream: a person's status, meaning their entitlement, is honored through the transition, while the funding sources behind those benefits may change.

I hold that failing the net-taxpayer test should suspend the franchise. A person cannot vote on the taxes and programs that move money to them if their personally directed transfers meet or exceed the taxes they pay, or if their pre-exemption income-tax liability is zero. That is a massive conflict of interest (Voting and Elections · net fiscal voting bar). Transfers include the last-resort allowance, the earnings-only top-up, and refundable credit cash-outs. Grandfathered Social Security and Medicare, shared public goods, and non-refundable relief such as the mothers' income-tax exemption are not counted as received. The benefit remains available. Failing the test suspends the vote until a completed tax year shows otherwise. The full counting rules, including joint filers and SS-only retirees, are at the voting-bar link above.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.
