Existing welfare and entitlement programs are aggressively reduced to bare-minimum safety nets. I reject mandatory redistribution beyond a bare-minimum floor. That floor should be funded by minimal necessary taxes as set out in Core Principles, and an opt-in funding model for remaining social programs is the preferred long-term structure. Benefits, when provided, cover only basic necessities and do not support comfort or lifestyle expansion. Privatization and structural reform of Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, and similar programs are pursued where feasible.

The bare-minimum floor has two income parts — the earnings-only top-up and the last-resort allowance for people who cannot work — each a narrow, named exception to the rule against compelled redistribution, alongside emergency shelter, emergency medical care, and the K-12 backstop. Layers run private disability → charity → last resort. The last-resort allowance is $575 a month (single) or $900 (couple) for non-housing needs, plus local HUD fair market rent (studio or one-bedroom), reduced when housing is shared. Non-housing indexed to inflation, housing to HUD's annual update. Other income reduces the allowance dollar for dollar. The first $100/month of earnings is ignored, then 50¢ per further dollar; in-kind charity does not reduce it. Asset test: home and one car exempt, plus $10,000 savings (single) or $15,000 (couple). Recipients are auto-enrolled in the opt-in public health plan under the same exception. Part B premium paid for grandfathered Medicare members; long-term care in kind with medical certification (home care preferred where cheaper; capped pay for family caregivers). A narrow allowance of up to $575 a month covers severely disabled children for disability-related costs only. Intake is by referral from shelters, hospitals, police, or charities, or by application at any shelter. Assessment within days by a licensed, neutral clinician; placement in the least costly safe setting with private or charity providers; shelter or hospital until placement; court-appointed guardian/advocate (preferably volunteer or charity) when needed. Non-citizens are ineligible for the last-resort allowance (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). Parameters and dollar amounts are also answered in the Q&As.

head: "Would cutting entitlements abandon people who paid into the system?"
body: No. People who followed the rules and are on benefits should not be punished when the system changes. There should be a phase-out period that honors existing commitments. The person's entitlement is honored through the transition, even as the funding behind it shifts. Privatization and restructuring are pursued where feasible, and a bare-minimum safety net covering basic necessities remains. What I reject is mandatory redistribution beyond that floor.

head: "Doesn't 'food insecurity' mean people are starving?"
body: No. USDA "food insecurity" is a survey measure of constrained or anxious access to food, not chronic starvation. NHANES patterns show food-insecure adults in the United States, especially women, have higher obesity rates than food-secure adults, not lower body weight. The bare-minimum floor covers basic food need. It is not sized as if the typical insecure household were wasting away. Nature Scientific Reports – food insecurity and obesity, NHANES-based analyses

head: "What happens if opt-in funding falls short?"
body: The program should scale to what its contributors fund. It should not fall back on general taxation. The bare-minimum safety floor for basic necessities should be funded separately by minimal necessary taxes, so a shortfall in an opt-in program should never remove that floor.

head: "Isn't the top-up redistribution?"
body: Yes. It would be funded partly from owner income and otherwise from general revenue, so it is a narrow, named exception to the rule against compelled redistribution, like emergency shelter, emergency medical care, and the K-12 backstop. It should be limited in three ways: it should be paid only on earned income, it should end at the zero-bracket line, and it should replace the minimum wage and separate wage-subsidy credits rather than adding to them. Redistribution beyond the named exceptions remains rejected.

head: "Why does the top-up include children?"
body: A worker supporting children has more to cover on the same pay, and the strongest evidence for earnings top-ups comes from working parents. The add-on would be modest and paid only on earnings, so it would reward work rather than having children. It would go to all working parents, married or single, with no marriage penalty, and it would stop at three children.

head: "Why per worker but phased out by household?"
body: Paying each worker keeps the top-up tied to that person's own work. Phasing it out on household income keeps it for households that are actually low-income: a teenager or second earner in a well-off household should get nothing. Because the married range is double the single range, a couple should neither gain nor lose by marrying, splitting, or combining households.

head: "What about people who can't work?"
body: They are covered in layers. Employers enroll workers by default in private disability insurance, and workers may opt out. The self-employed and people between jobs get the same choice through their tax return. The insurance is private. The state does not run it. Those within the grandfathered Social Security system keep that protection. People who can work some draw the earnings-only top-up on what they earn. Charity and mutual aid, including respite for family caregivers, come next. As a last resort, people with severe disabilities and the elderly poor receive a strictly means-tested allowance from general revenue, under the same backstop logic as grandfathered Social Security. It is checked by fraud enforcement and periodic medical reviews, and it is a narrow exception, not a general welfare entitlement.

head: "How much does the last-resort allowance cost?"
body: In 2025, SSI paid $64.85 billion to about 7.4 million people. Restricted to severe disability and the elderly poor, the allowance's cash cost is estimated to stay close to that, because the higher standard is offset by the narrower eligibility. Health coverage for recipients is the larger cost, but it replaces Medicaid spending for the same people rather than adding to it. These are estimates, not official scores.

head: "Won't a higher allowance invite fraud?"
body: It is checked by income and asset verification, fraud enforcement, and periodic medical reviews. Only severe disability should qualify, and fraud should be punished as theft. Income from any source reduces the allowance, so there is nothing to gain from hiding behind it while working.

head: "Why not one flat national amount?"
body: Rent is the largest cost and varies more than anything else. A studio in Los Angeles has a fair market rent of $2,079 a month, far above what one flat amount could cover without overpaying everywhere else. Tying the housing part to local rent pays what basic housing actually costs where the person lives, no more.

head: "Why does the allowance include health coverage?"
body: Severe disability and frailty mean ongoing care, not just emergencies. Emergency-only care would leave the people least able to provide for themselves without treatment for chronic conditions, which is often more expensive when it ends in the emergency room. Covering them inside the same narrow exception keeps everyone else's healthcare opt-in.

head: "Why are severely disabled children covered when parents are responsible for their children?"
body: Parents remain responsible for the ordinary costs of raising a child. A severe disability can add costs far beyond what any ordinary family budget can carry. The child allowance, up to $575 a month, covers only those extra costs, in severe cases, so that parents can keep caring for the child at home.

head: "What happens to an elderly person with no home and no family who needs care?"
body: A shelter, hospital, police officer, or charity refers them to the allowance office, or they apply at any shelter. Within a few days a licensed, neutral clinician assesses them, and once certified they are placed in the least costly setting that safely meets their needs, such as a studio with home care, assisted living, or a nursing home, run by private or charity providers. Until then they stay in shelter, or in hospital rather than being discharged to the street. If they cannot manage their own affairs, a court appoints a guardian or advocate, preferably a volunteer or a charity.

In a realistic world, these programs phase out to bridge the gaps during the transition. That is why the phase-out window exists. Mandatory redistribution takes from some citizens to fund others, which I treat as coercion beyond the state's core role. Major entitlement programs also face long-term funding shortfalls under current law, so structural reform is needed regardless. The 2025 Trustees Reports project Social Security's combined trust funds to be depleted in 2034, with 81% of scheduled benefits then payable, and Medicare's Hospital Insurance trust fund in 2033. An opt-in model lets those who wish to fund social programs above the floor do so, while the minimal floor for basic necessities stays funded by minimal necessary taxes. Voluntary giving alone could not yet carry the floor: SNAP benefits in FY2024 ($92.9 billion) exceeded all U.S. charitable giving to human services in 2024 ($91.15 billion).

An earnings-only top-up is the tool with the strongest evidence for low earners. Hoynes and Patel found that a $1,000 increase in the Earned Income Tax Credit raised single mothers' employment by 7.3 percentage points and cut the share of their families below the poverty line by 9.4 points. Paying it only on earned income matters: in the Seattle-Denver income maintenance experiment, which guaranteed income whether or not people worked, husbands cut their hours by about 9 percent and wives by about 20 percent. Delivering the top-up through the flat tax replaces the EITC's separate rules, which produce large errors. The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration reported that 27.3 percent of EITC payments in FY2024 ($15.9 billion of $58.4 billion) were improper. Improper payments will not vanish and should still be policed, but one return with one phase-out leaves fewer rules to get wrong. The top-up is far smaller than the EITC it replaces: the EITC paid about $69.6 billion to about 24 million claimants for tax year 2024, with a 2026 maximum of $7,316 for two children. I modelled the top-up on the Census Bureau's 2025 Current Population Survey microdata, applying the rules exactly as set out here to every household, with 2024 incomes carried forward to 2026 by wage and price growth. On my middle case it costs about $26 billion a year, about $17.5 billion for the base and $8 billion for the child add-on, paid to about 20 million households. Granted, survey data understate what the IRS pays out: the same data and method put the 2024 EITC at about $45 billion, against the $69.6 billion the IRS paid. My middle case scales the top-up up by the same ratio as the EITC's proper payments, the IRS total less the 27.3 percent paid improperly, bear to the survey figure, and it allows a small earnings response to the top-up's own rates. If the top-up instead runs over its survey estimate by the full EITC gap, improper claims included, and earnings respond more strongly, it costs about $36 billion. If the survey is right and only 85% of those eligible claim it, slightly more than the 81% who claim the EITC, it costs about $19 billion. The model counts every worker because the survey cannot separate workers without legal status, who would not receive it; about 9.7 million of them were in the workforce in 2023, so these figures overstate the cost by about $2 billion. Even at the high end it costs about half the EITC it replaces, which runs about $70 billion a year by 2026, so the replacement saves about $44 billion a year on my middle case ($34 billion to $51 billion). This is my own estimate, not an official score. Granted, by the same evidence a smaller credit gives weaker work incentives: the top-up pays a single parent of two at most $3,500, against $7,316 under the EITC. I accept that trade: the top-up keeps support tied to work and ends at the zero-bracket line, at a third to half the cost. The phase-out takes at most about 16.7 cents of each extra dollar, for a single parent of three, against 21.06 cents under the EITC for families with two or more children. The $1,000 add-on sits below the $1,700 refundable portion of the 2026 child tax credit (maximum $2,200 per child), which the flat tax also replaces. An amount above about $1,395 per child would push a single parent of three past the EITC's 21.06 percent.

In August 2026, 7.3 million people received Supplemental Security Income, averaging $738.73 a month, and 7.0 million disabled workers received earned Social Security Disability Insurance benefits averaging $1,635.90. The need is real: in 2023, 24.2 percent of working-age adults with disabilities living in the community were in poverty, against 9.9 percent of those without. Means-tested programs are also error-prone: SSI's improper-payment rate rose from 9.41 percent in FY2019 to 10.62 percent (about $6.5 billion) in FY2023, which is why the last-resort allowance carries fraud enforcement and periodic medical review. Work-focused design shrinks the group who cannot work at all. After the Netherlands required employers to attempt rehabilitation before a disability claim (2002) and replaced its disability law with one built around remaining work capacity (2006), new disability claims fell by about 25 and 21 percentage points respectively, and the caseload by more than 60 percent. Voluntary institutions once carried much of this load: by David Beito's conservative estimate, one in three adult American men belonged to a fraternal society in 1920.

The current federal SSI maximum is $994 a month for an individual and $1,491 for a couple in 2026. In December 2025, the average federal SSI payment was $688.47, and 7.39 million people received payments, 1.20 million aged and 6.13 million disabled, of whom 1.02 million were children. That is well below what basic needs cost. The 2026 poverty guideline for one person is $15,960 a year, about $1,330 a month. The USDA's Thrifty Food Plan alone costs $236.30 to $281.20 a month for an adult aged 51 to 70. HUD's fair market rent for a Los Angeles studio is $2,079. Health and care needs are larger still. Medicaid spent $27,361 per disabled enrollee and $20,305 per aged enrollee in FY2023. A semi-private nursing home room costs a national median of $9,581 a month, against $6,673 for a home caregiver 44 hours a week, which is why I prefer home care where it costs less. The Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 a month in 2026. The current administration's 2026 SNAP rules are graded in Current Administration: work requirements and categorical eligibility.

head: What is an opt-in funding model?

body: An opt-in model funds a program through voluntary contributions from those who choose to support it, rather than through mandatory taxes on everyone. A voluntary checkoff, where a taxpayer chooses to direct a contribution to a program, counts as opt-in.

Social Security and Medicare should become voluntary for new benefits: nobody is forced into the new system. A temporary transition levy, which replaces today's payroll taxes, pays off the benefits already promised and ends when they end. I would protect current retirees, and people within ten years of full retirement age, before the new system comes in, as an honored commitment, and they keep their benefits for life. The old system fades out only as fewer people remain in it. The separate basic safety floor stays. Employers should sign workers up for private retirement savings by default, and anyone can opt out.

Social Security and Medicare should become opt-in only. Participation and contributions for new benefits ought to be voluntary; no one should be compelled to join either program or to rely on it, and those who opt out arrange their own retirement savings and coverage. The transition levy is a temporary tax that pays off existing promises; it buys no new benefits and ends when they end (Taxation). Current retirees ought to be protected before the new system comes in: their benefits are an existing commitment that is not a rights violation, and existing commitments that aren't rights violations are honored during the transition to the new system. People within ten years of full retirement age should get the same protection as current retirees, grandfathered on current benefit formulas, as part of the same honored commitment. Grandfathered people should keep Social Security and Medicare for life. The old system phases out because fewer people remain in it, not because benefits end on a set date. This protection is part of the position, not a practical concession. The separate bare-minimum safety floor for basic necessities, defined in Welfare and Entitlements, is unaffected.

Employers should enroll workers by default in a private retirement savings account, and workers should be free to opt out. The self-employed make the same choice on their tax return. The state should not run or hold the accounts. I don't set the default contribution rate. One rule ties this to the disability-insurance default in Welfare and Entitlements: defaults apply only where a person mainly protects themselves, as with disability insurance and retirement savings. Anything that funds other people stays opt-in.

In a realistic world, many systems — like taxes, like education, like all the systems that would be changing — would have some gradual period of change for most of these changes to happen. That practical lag is a brief aside, not the main position.

head: "Doesn't moving to opt-in break the promise made to people who paid in?"
body: Current retirees are protected before the new system comes in, because existing commitments that aren't rights violations are honored during the transition. People who planned around the current system are not cut off, and the basic-necessities floor remains. Grandfathered people keep their benefits for life. The old system shrinks only as fewer people remain in it. The programs are also not financed for the long term under current law, so continuing them unchanged would itself break the promise of scheduled benefits.

head: "Who pays for the protected benefits, and what about people who paid in but are more than ten years from retirement?"
body: Protected benefits are paid first by opt-in contributions and then by the transition levy, which replaces today's payroll taxes and ends when the protected benefits end. The government ought to pay for the rest of the transition with spending cuts, not new debt. The retirement age rises two years, phased in, for people not yet 67, and protected benefits for people now aged 57–66 are reduced 15% above a means-test threshold. That is the price of keeping everyone else's promise without new debt. People more than ten years from full retirement age keep a credit for the contributions they already paid, payable at retirement.

head: "Won't moving to opt-in push the elderly into poverty?"
body: Critics warn that ending Social Security would push millions of older people into poverty, and the scale they point to is large. Social Security is the country's largest antipoverty program: in 2024 it moved 28.7 million people above the Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure line, 20.1 million of them aged 65 or older. Even with it, 15.0% of people 65 and older were poor under that measure in 2024. Without it, the Census Bureau estimates their rate would have been 32.7 points higher, about 47.7%. Benefit payments that year were about $1.47 trillion ($1,316.4 billion retirement and survivors, $155.0 billion disability), and the program costs about 5.3% of GDP in 2025. That is why the transition is built around the people at risk. Current retirees and everyone within ten years of full retirement age keep their benefits for life, so no one now old or nearly old loses income. Younger workers keep a credit for what they have already paid, and default enrollment in private accounts builds their own savings. The last-resort allowance remains for the elderly poor who still fall short. The price of that protection is that the benefits run for decades. The backstop should cover benefits on the order of today's payments at first, shrinking only as the grandfathered group shrinks, and the program is already short, with the combined trust funds projected to be depleted in 2034. For people who reach old age after the transition with too little saved, the allowance is thinner than a Social Security check by design: it is a bare-minimum floor, not a pension, and it still covers the elderly poor, because it is means-tested rather than earned. Any eligible elderly person below the line qualifies, whatever they paid in, and it pays for food, phone, transport, and personal needs plus local rent, rising each year with prices and rents (last-resort allowance).

head: "Isn't default enrollment a form of coercion?"
body: No. Nobody would be forced to save: opting out should be free and simple, and the money should stay in the worker's own private account. The default only changes what happens when a person does nothing. The evidence shows how much that matters. In Madrian and Shea's study of one large U.S. employer, 401(k) participation among new hires rose from 37% under opt-in to 86% under automatic enrollment. In Great Britain, where employers have enrolled workers automatically since 2012, 89% of eligible employees were saving into a workplace pension in 2024. More people with their own savings means fewer who end up relying on the last-resort allowance in old age.

Compelled contributions to retirement and health programs are redistribution beyond the floor, which I reject. The transition levy is different: it is a temporary tax that pays off promises already made, buys no new benefits, and ends when those promises end. Existing commitments that aren't rights violations are honored during the transition, which is why current retirees are protected before the new system comes in. The protection extends to people within ten years of full retirement age because the transition risk lands hardest on them. They have planned and paid in around the current system and have the least time left to build their own retirement savings and coverage. The programs also face shortfalls under current law. The 2025 Trustees Reports project Social Security's combined trust funds to be depleted in 2034, with 81% of scheduled benefits payable after that, and Medicare's Hospital Insurance trust fund in 2033. CBO projects Medicare spending to rise from 2.6% of GDP in 2025 to 5.2% in 2055. Structural reform is needed regardless; the government ought to set its direction toward voluntary participation. Default enrollment fills the gap that opt-in leaves, because inertia is strong: Madrian and Shea found that most workers hired under automatic enrollment also kept the default contribution rate and fund. That same finding is why I leave the default rate unset rather than picking a number the evidence does not single out; the rate will shape how much people save.

America should get back above replacement, 2.1 children per woman. I would do it with support that grows with family size, cheaper housing through freed-up building, and a higher-trust culture that honors marriage and children (phone-free schools, childhood-independence laws, car-seat mandate review), not with mandates or a large welfare state.

The U.S. fertility rate hit a record low of about 1.6 in 2024 and has been below replacement since 2008. Americans say the ideal family has 2.7 children, so most of the gap comes from obstacles, not from what people want. I believe the government's job is to remove the obstacles it controls: taxes on parents, housing scarcity, and school costs. Culture and faith, which matter most, ought to be carried by families, churches, and communities.

The fertility collapse is mostly a marriage collapse. Age-controlled marital fertility has held up or risen in some cells while marriage rates cratered. Fewer and later marriages drive the drop (data below). Policy that only writes checks without making early pairing easier will underperform. Money is a lever, not the whole cause. I treat higher trust — built through assimilation, values-tested immigration, and national cohesion argued elsewhere — as a natalist prior, not a measured policy lever with a published effect size on this page.

The package I support, evidenced in the Data callouts: a refundable child credit of $1,500 for the first and second child and $3,000 for the third and each later child. A one-time refundable $5,000 birth credit for third and later births; and no federal income tax on a mother's earned income for life after her fourth child, half after her third, on up to $30,000 of earnings a year. Under the net fiscal voting bar, non-refundable relief is not received, and refundable cash-outs count only when liability would otherwise be ≤ $0. The mothers' exemption alone does not fail the liability gate when pre-exemption liability is > $0. SNAP, TANF, the last-resort allowance, and the top-up count in full.

Housing: by-right starter homes and duplexes, including family-size units (3+ bedroom apartments, single-stair buildings, no bedroom-count caps), and repeal of minimum lot sizes and parking minimums. Work and money: childcare deregulation within safety limits, with home daycare by right. Growth and rising earnings for young adults through the flat tax and job growth; no federal paid-leave mandate on employers; and no marriage penalty anywhere in the tax code. Fertility: IVF legal and unrestricted, with no insurance mandate and honest age-and-fertility information in existing health education. Childhood: phone-free schools set by states and districts, Reasonable Childhood Independence laws on the Utah model, and state review of car-seat age mandates. The leaving-home, meeting-place, and career-path levers are in the notes below. Culture, faith, and marriage should be carried by families and churches, not the state. The United States ought not to use immigration to fill the gap. The nation should renew itself through its own families (Immigration and Borders).

I want young adults to be able to afford a place of their own in their early twenties, because people who move out tend to be the ones who marry and start families. The fix is supply, not subsidy: legalize small starter apartments, accessory dwelling units, shared and roommate housing, and by-right starter homes, so a first lease costs less.

In 2023, 57% of Americans 18–24 lived in a parent's home (53% in 1993), along with 21% of those 25–29 and 11% of those 30–34. Far fewer young adults are married or have kids than in 1993. Pew Research Center – Parents, Young Adult Children and the Transition to Adulthood (2024)

Worsening rent- and price-to-income ratios explain up to a quarter of the 9-point rise in young adults living with parents from 2000 to 2021. Real Estate Economics – Why do young adults coreside with their parents? (2024)

Moving out is strongly associated with marriage and childbearing, but a causal effect of living at home on family formation was not established. Jacinda Sze, University of Delaware – The Dynamics of Co-Residence, Wealth, and Family Formation (2025)

Supply that only makes living alone cheaper does less for births than family-size housing. Large-unit supply produced 2.3 times the births of equal-cost one-bedroom supply. Couillard – Build, Baby, Build
Evidence strength: moderate on housing costs leading to living at home. Weak on living at home leading to fewer births.

I want young people to meet each other face to face again. Government shouldn't run dating programs, but local rules shouldn't make it hard to open a café, bar, gym, club, or event space either. I support allowing mixed-use neighborhoods by right, simpler business and liquor licensing, and fewer permits for small venues and events.

Meeting online rose from 2% of heterosexual couples (1995) to 39% (2017). Meeting through friends fell from 33% to 20%, and meeting through family, church, and neighborhood has declined since 1940. Rosenfeld et al., PNAS – Disintermediating your friends (2019)
57% of single U.S. adults said they were not looking for a relationship or dates (2022 survey). Pew Research Center – 5 facts about single Americans (2023)

The drop in in-person social time is in the phones box above. Evidence strength: the decline in in-person meeting is well documented. No causal study was found showing that more venues raise marriage or births.

I want young people to be able to start a career, and a family, without spending their twenties collecting credentials. I support dropping degree requirements in federal hiring wherever a degree isn't truly needed, recognizing apprenticeships and skills tests as equal paths, and trimming occupational licensing hours. The government ought not to mandate anything on private employers. Earlier starts give couples more time to reach the family size they want, and this is good policy on its own.

Employers dropped degree requirements from far more job postings from 2014 to 2023, but hiring barely changed: only about 1 in 700 hires in 2023 went to someone who gained access that way. Burning Glass Institute & HBS – Skills-Based Hiring: The Long Road from Pronouncements to Practice (2024)

In Norway, two more years of compulsory school pushed first births later but did not lower completed fertility or raise childlessness. Black, Devereux & Salvanes – Education and Fertility: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
Competition for college slots helps explain why college-educated parents spend much more time on childcare since the mid-1990s. Ramey & Ramey, NBER – The Rug Rat Race

Evidence strength: weak. Longer schooling clearly delays births, but the best causal study finds no loss in completed fertility. No causal study was found linking apprenticeships or degree requirements to births.

Across 36 industrialized countries (1981–2009), national generalized trust combined with rising women's education is positively associated with completed fertility. High trust moderates the fertility decline as women's education expands, likely because trust makes parents more willing to rely on care outside the family. Aassve, Billari & Pessin, Social Forces – Trust and Fertility Dynamics

In 41 U.S. communities, more ethnically diverse areas showed lower trust in the short run, including trust within one's own group ("hunkering down"). Putnam argues successful immigrant societies overcome this by building broader shared identities. Putnam – E Pluribus Unum (2007)
These are correlations, not causal estimates. No study directly tests trust-building policy on births.
40.0% of U.S. births in 2023 were to unmarried women (1,440,031). CDC/NCHS – Births: Final Data for 2023

About 75% of the U.S. fertility decline since 2007 is attributable to fewer people being married at each age. Birth rates within marriage barely changed. Had marriage shares stayed at 2007 levels, fertility would be about 12% higher. Institute for Family Studies – Yes, Marriage Still Matters for Fertility (2025)

Red states have higher total fertility and smaller post-1990 declines than blue states on CDC state series. Most states are still below replacement, so "holding steady" overstates the red-state pattern. Culture and composition matter at least as much as any single policy. CDC – Fertility rates by state

head: Data: phones, social life, and dating

body: Ages 15–25 spent 21–23 fewer minutes a day in in-person social interaction in 2017 than in 2003. Twenge & Spitzberg, Journal of Applied Social Psychology – Declines in non-digital social interaction among Americans, 2003–2017 (2020)
Past-year sexual inactivity among U.S. men 18–24 rose to 30.9% in 2016–18. JAMA Network Open – Trends in Frequency of Sexual Activity, 2000–2018
Early iPhone access reduced births 4.5–8.0% among women 15–19 and 3.2–6.6% among women 20–24. NBER – Is the iPhone Birth Control? (2026)

head: Data: culture, media, and religious communities

body: In Brazil, the arrival of Globo soap operas showing small families lowered birth probability by 0.5–0.6 points a year. AEJ – Applied: Soap Operas and Fertility: Evidence from Brazil

Religious-community data (not policy): Israel's fertility rate was 2.85 in 2023; Haredi women averaged 6.8 children against 1.9 for secular Jewish women (2022–24). Israel CBS – Fertility of Jewish and Other Women in Israel by Level of Religiosity Utah's fertility rate fell to 1.801 in 2023 (10th). South Dakota was highest at 2.01. Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute – Utah's fertility rate dropped to 1.801 in 2023 For Georgia and Pew data, see the boxes below.

head: Data: parenting intensity and needless rules

body: Parents' childcare time rose sharply from the mid-1990s, twice as much for college-educated parents (9+ more hours a week for college-educated mothers), linked to competition for college slots. Ramey & Ramey, NBER – The Rug Rat Race

State car-seat age mandates cut third births: women with two children under the mandated age are 0.73 points less likely to give birth each year, about 8,000 fewer births in 2017 and 145,000 since 1980, against an estimated 57 child crash deaths prevented in 2017. Journal of Law & Economics – Car Seats as Contraception (2024)
Utah's 2018 law says letting a mature child walk to school, play outside, or stay home alone is not neglect. Utah Legislature – S.B. 65, Child Neglect Amendments (2018)
About one in five U.S. women 18–40 did not know aging affects fertility. Fertility and Sterility – Knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding conception and fertility (2014)

54% of women in IVF overestimated their chance of a live birth. Women over 40 were three times as likely to overestimate. McMahon et al., Human Reproduction – What do women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) understand about their chance of IVF success?

State infertility-insurance mandates raised births among women over 35 but did not raise completed fertility, partly because they led younger women to delay. SERIEs – Coverage of infertility treatment and fertility outcomes
U.S. total fertility rate 2024: 1,599.5 births per 1,000 women, a record low, down 23% since 2008. CDC/NCHS – Births: Final Data for 2024

Births in 2023 by birth order: 3,596,017 in total, of which 589,447 were third children and 464,156 were fourth or later children. Third-and-later births were 1,053,603, or 29.3% of all births. Fourth-and-later were 12.9%. CDC/NCHS – Births: Final Data for 2023, Table 3
Among mothers ages 40 to 44 in 2014, 24% had three children and 14% had four or more, down from 40% with four or more in 1976. Pew Research Center – Family Size Among Mothers

Ideal family size: 2.7 children on average in 2023, with 45% saying three or more; the 2.7 held again in 2025. Gallup – Americans' Preference for Larger Families Highest Since 1971; Gallup – Americans' Ideal Family Size Remains Above Two Children

head: Data: what the new measures cost (estimates)

body: These are my estimates from CDC birth counts, not official scores.
$3,000 credit for third and later children: about 1.05 million such births a year, over 18 years, is roughly 19 million children. The extra $1,500 each costs about $28 billion a year.
$5,000 birth credit for third and later births: 1,053,603 × $5,000 is about $5.3 billion a year.

Mothers' income-tax exemption: worth her full federal income tax after a fourth child and half of it after a third. The exemption applies to earnings: after a fourth child up to $30,000 of her earnings is exempt, and after a third half of that, up to $15,000. A single mother earning $60,000 owes $2,860 through 2041 (22% with the transition surcharge) and $2,600 after (20%). After a fourth child her taxable earnings fall to $30,000, below the $42,000 zero line, so the exemption is worth $2,860 a year through 2041 and $2,600 after. After a third child her taxable earnings fall to $45,000, inside the phase-in, where she owes $99 through 2041 and $90 after, so the exemption is worth $2,761 and $2,510. A national total is not yet estimated, because no current count of working mothers by family size was found.
Zoning reform, no leave mandate, no marriage penalty, and legal IVF cost the budget nothing.

Hungary: fertility rose from 1.23 in 2011 to 1.61 in 2021, then fell to 1.38 in 2024. Family spending was 3.1% of GDP by OECD data (2019). The government claims up to 5%. OSW – Hungary's ongoing demographic decline Demographers note much of the rise came from women no longer delaying births: mean age at first birth rose 2.6 years in 2000–2010 but only 0.7 years in 2010–2020. N-IUSSP – Evaluating pronatalist policies with TFR brings misleading conclusions

Hungary's tools: since 2020 mothers of four or more pay no income tax for life. From October 2025 the exemption covers employed mothers of three, and from 2026 it is phasing in for mothers of two. The CSOK Plus home loan (up to HUF 50 million at no more than 3%) is reduced by HUF 10 million for the second and each later child. Safe in Hungary – Family allowances About 57,000 mothers of four or more used the exemption in its first year. Index.hu – 57,000 mothers received the tax exemption

Poland: the 500+ child benefit raised births about 4.5% a month from 2016 through 2017, mostly third, fourth, and fifth children, with no effect on first births, and no effect by mid-2019. Studia Socjologiczne – In Search of Demographic Effects of the Family 500 Plus Program One estimate puts the cost of each extra birth at about $389,000. Gromadzki – Universal Child Benefit and Child Poverty Fertility still fell to 1.099 in 2024, a record low. bne IntelliNews – Poland's fertility rate sinks to just below 1.1
France: 1.62 in 2024, the lowest since the end of World War I. INSEE – Demographic report 2024
Nordics: Finland 1.25 and Norway 1.44 in 2024, despite generous leave and childcare. Nordic Statistics – Record low fertility in the Nordics
South Korea: 0.72 in 2023 and 0.75 in 2024, after more than 360 trillion won (about $270 billion) spent since 2006. Al Jazeera – How did South Korea start producing more babies after long decline?

Israel: 2.87 in 2024, the highest in the OECD. OECD Family Database – Fertility rates Secular and traditional non-religious Jewish women have averaged around 2.5 children, and above 2.2 combined. Taub Center – Israel's Exceptional Fertility (2018)

Georgia: after Patriarch Ilia II pledged in 2007 to personally baptize every third and later child of married Orthodox parents, the national fertility rate rose 17% (0.3 children per woman), and third-and-later births within marriage doubled among Orthodox women. Journal of Population Economics – Religiously inspired baby boom: evidence from Georgia

Cash: Quebec's Allowance for Newborn Children (up to C$8,000) raised fertility 12% on average and 25% for families eligible for the maximum. Each extra C$1,000 in the first year raised the chance of a birth by 16.9%. Milligan, NBER – Subsidizing the Stork Each additional child cost about C$15,000 in public funds. Milligan – Québec's Baby Bonus backgrounder By birth order the Quebec effect was 5% for first, 11% for second, and 85% for third births. Institute for Family Studies – Expand the Child Tax Credit

The 2021 U.S. child tax credit: a review of its effects found little evidence of a fertility response and judged one unlikely. NBER – The Effects of the 2021 Child Tax Credit on Child Developmental Outcomes A review of quasi-experimental studies found cash transfers have mainly temporary effects. Bergsvik et al., Population and Development Review – Can Policies Stall the Fertility Fall?

Housing: a 10% rise in home prices cut births 1% among non-owners while raising them 4.5% among owners. NBER Digest – The Impact of the Real Estate Market on Fertility One study estimates that if rents had not risen since 1990, about 13 million more children (11%) would have been born. Couillard – Build, Baby, Build: How Housing Shapes Fertility (Needs research: a second estimate of the rent effect on births; this figure rests on one study).

Marriage: from 2007 to 2017 the decline was concentrated among young and unmarried women, while married women's fertility rose. Buckles, Guldi & Schmidt, NBER – Fertility Trends in the United States, 1980-2017
Religion: Christians ages 40 to 59 have had 2.2 children on average, against 1.8 for the religiously unaffiliated. Pew Research Center – Religion, fertility and child-rearing

Economics explains only part of the decline: Kearney and Levine could not identify any period-specific social, economic, or policy change that statistically explains much of the U.S. decline since 2007. Recent cohorts are having fewer children over their whole childbearing years. Kearney & Levine – The Causes of Declining U.S. Fertility
Childcare prices: a 10% rise in childcare prices lowers birth rates 5.7% (about 4 births per 1,000 women ages 20 to 44). Dow – Childcare prices and fertility

Young-adult jobs: a 1-point rise in unemployment at ages 20 to 24 reduces completed conceptions by 14.2 per 1,000 women by age 40, mostly through more childlessness. Currie & Schwandt, PNAS – Short- and long-term effects of unemployment on fertility (2014) Shocks to men's earnings cut marriage and fertility (4.7 to 6.1 fewer births per 1,000). Autor, Dorn & Hanson, NBER – When Work Disappears: Manufacturing Decline and the Falling Marriage-Market Value of Young Men (2017)
Childcare: the national average price was $13,128 a year in 2024, 35% of a single parent's median income. Child Care Aware – Child Care in America: 2024 Price & Supply

head: "Don't baby bonuses mostly pay for births that would have happened anyway?"
body: Yes, which is why I aim the extra support at third and later children. In Quebec the response to third births was far stronger than to first births (85% against 5%), and in Poland the extra births were mostly third, fourth, and fifth children. Lyman Stone, Institute for Family Studies – Expand the Child Tax Credit: Pronatal Policy Works, and America Can't Afford to Forego It (2025). Bartnicki & Alimowski, Studia Socjologiczne – W poszukiwaniu demograficznych efektów rządowego programu „Rodzina 500 Plus” (In search of the demographic effects of the Family 500 Plus program, 2022)

head: "Hungary spent big and fertility is falling again. Doesn't that prove it fails?"
body: It shows money alone doesn't hold. Hungary reached 1.61 and fell back to 1.38, while Israel and Georgia show that faith and a culture that celebrates large families do more than any budget line. OSW Centre for Eastern Studies – Hungary's ongoing demographic decline: an increase in birth rates is the only hope (2025). Chung, Deopa, Saxena & Stone, Journal of Population Economics – Religiously inspired baby boom: evidence from Georgia (2025)

head: "Why not copy the Nordic model of long paid leave and state daycare?"
body: Finland is at 1.25 and Norway at 1.44 with that model. It hasn't held births up, and it needs mandates and taxes I reject. Nordic Statistics – Record low fertility in the Nordics

head: "Why exempt only mothers, and only after the third or fourth child?"
body: The mother carries the pregnancy and most of the early career cost, and the third and later child is where both the drop-off and the strongest response are. Hungary used the same design. Hungarian Government, Safe in Hungary – Family allowances

head: "Doesn't the net-taxpayer voting bar cancel the family credits?"
body: No. The bar targets conflict of interest over other people's money, not parenthood. Working parents whose family package is tax reduction against positive liability keep the vote. A household that draws SNAP, the last-resort allowance, or the earnings-only top-up, or that takes large cash-outs with little tax paid, still fails. The counting rules are in the net fiscal voting bar.

Americans still want 2.7 children and are having 1.6, so the problem is obstacles, not desire. The evidence points the same way across countries: cash raises births but costs a lot per extra child, the strongest response comes at the third child and later, and higher housing costs push births down. Spending on its own has failed in South Korea, Poland, and the Nordics. The countries that stay high, Israel and Georgia, do it through faith and a culture that prizes large families. So the state stays small: a low flat tax, support that grows with family size, cheaper housing through freed supply, and no mandates. The rest belongs to families and churches.

I believe both genetic parents who consented to the sex owe support. Civil orders should come first. Willful refusal after an order brings escalating penalties. A rape victim owes no duty from the rape. The rapist owes full support.

I hold that voluntary conception creates a support duty on both genetic parents who consented to the sex. Support should be enforced by civil order first; willful refusal after an order is a rights violation, a fraud on the child's claim, with escalating penalties; any fines are scaled to income and wealth. In cases of rape, the victim parent owes no duty created by the rape, and the rapist parent owes full support.

head: "Does a parent who was raped owe support?"
body: No. Duties arise from voluntary responsibility, and rape is not voluntary for the victim. The rapist parent owes full support.

Duties arise from voluntary responsibility, matching the voluntary-procreation responsibility in Ethical and Philosophical Framework. A parent who consented to the sex took on the child's claim; refusing an order to meet it defrauds the child. Rape is not voluntary for the victim, so no duty arises for the victim from it. The U.S. Census Bureau reports that in 2022 about one in four children under 21 lived with only one parent while the other parent lived outside the household.
U.S. Census Bureau (Liza C. Valle) – Custodial Parents and Their Child Support: 2022 (2025)
See also: Axioms

I'd leave housing mainly to property owners and the market. Basic zoning should be allowed, but rules that wipe out property value must be paid for, and housing subsidies need voluntary funding. The safety floor should offer emergency shelter only, not housing, and charities and private groups are free to run Housing First. Camping and drug use in public ought to be banned.

Housing supply ought to be governed by property rights and the market. Ordinary zoning that coordinates land use is acceptable, but regulation that eliminates the economically beneficial use of property, or destroys most of its value, is a taking and requires compensation. Population growth should be met through densification, development, and voluntary exchange, not political allocation of land. Housing subsidies should require taxpayer opt-in. For homelessness, the safety floor ought to provide emergency shelters only; it is not a housing program. The one exception is the rent component of the last-resort allowance for severe disability and the elderly poor (Welfare and Entitlements). Charities and private groups are free to run Housing First programs, and opt-in funding can support them; the public rent component stays limited to the last-resort allowance. Camping on public property should not be permitted, and public drug use should be prohibited.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Record homelessness, 2024: HUD reported more than 770,000 people homeless on a single night in January 2024, an 18% increase from 2023. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (2024) – HUD Releases January 2024 Point-In-Time Count Report

head: "If public camping is banned, where do homeless people go?"
body: To emergency shelter, which the safety floor would provide. The floor would cover a basic necessity, not long-term housing. Permanent housing would come from the market, opt-in programs, and private charity. Public spaces would remain open for everyone's use rather than becoming encampments.

head: "Doesn't Housing First work better than shelters?"
body: Supporters cite its housing results: a meta-analysis of randomized trials found Housing First participants about 2.46 times as likely to be stably housed, with fewer emergency-department visits and hospital stays, though no clear improvement in mental health or substance use. Results for its recipients do not make it a public duty. Housing First is a housing subsidy, so it is left to charities, private groups, and opt-in funding, which are free to run it. The public floor stays at emergency shelter, and the only public rent support is the last-resort allowance.

Secure property and open land markets are how societies have historically absorbed population growth with rising living standards (Authority & Civil Liberties). Homelessness has grown. HUD's 2024 point-in-time count found more than 770,000 people experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2024, an 18% increase from 2023. HUD attributed part of the rise to steep rent increases and years of under-building, along with migration and natural disasters. Supply restrictions that hold back building bear directly on the problem. Randomized trials show Housing First keeps more people stably housed than treatment-first approaches, which is why the government ought to leave charities and opt-in programs free to run it while the public floor stays at shelter. The basic-necessities floor is set out in Welfare and Entitlements, and the rule on public drug use in Drug Policy.

Blocking building is what pushes rents up, and a rent freeze adds a second shortage on top of the first: when rents are capped, owners take units off the rental market, so everyone still looking for a home faces fewer and costlier choices (data below). New York City has now frozen rents and is planning city-run grocery stores.

head: Data: rent control and housing supply

body: Findings as reported by the study's authors. The study covers rent control, not a rent freeze.

San Francisco, 1994 expansion of rent control: landlords whose buildings came under rent control cut their rental housing supply by 15%, by selling to owner-occupants and redeveloping, and the authors conclude that the lost supply likely drove up market rents, "ultimately undermining the goals of the law." Supporters of rent control point to the same study's finding that it lowered displacement of covered tenants from the city. That protection went only to tenants already in place, and everyone looking for a home afterward paid for it in a smaller, costlier rental market, which is why the answer is more building, not price caps. The government should not use taxpayer money to make home loans cheaper. Federal lending and loan guarantees must cover their own costs, below-market rates need opt-in funding, and I would cut rules that only add closing costs. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac should leave conservatorship only once fully capitalized, as private companies with no federal backstop.

Federal home lending should carry no hidden subsidy. Loans the government makes or guarantees ought to be priced to cover their own risk and costs, and any rate below that is a housing subsidy that requires taxpayer opt-in, like every other subsidy (Housing, Zoning, and Homelessness). Federal requirements that add cost without protecting the borrower or the taxpayer, such as duplicate reviews, unnecessary appraisals and mandatory products that automated checks can replace, ought to be removed. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac ought to leave conservatorship only once they meet the full capital rule, and then as private companies with no federal guarantee, explicit or implied; until then their guarantee fees ought to cover the full risk they place on taxpayers.

head: "Doesn't the federal guarantee keep mortgages affordable?"
body: Supporters argue that the backing behind Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac keeps the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage widely available at lower rates, and it does lower rates. The lower rate is paid for by risk that taxpayers carry without consent, which makes it a subsidy. The two companies are still in federal conservatorship, and at the end of the second quarter of 2026 their estimated capital ratios were about 2.84% (Fannie Mae) and 2.36% (Freddie Mac), below the Federal Housing Finance Agency's 4% leverage requirement and its 8% risk-based requirement. Releasing them before they meet that rule would leave taxpayers holding losses an undercapitalized company cannot absorb. Private lenders and securitizers can offer long fixed-rate loans priced to their real risk.
Congressional Research Service – Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac: Conservatorship Status and Related Directives, R46746 (Aug. 25, 2026)

I want people to choose between a publicly supported plan and private insurance. No one should be required to buy coverage, but the public plan has one yearly sign-up window and a modest surcharge for joining late.

Healthcare ought to be organized around freedom of choice. Individuals should be free to opt into publicly supported systems or purchase private coverage. I reject mandates. The voluntary public plan has one annual open-enrollment window, and people who join late pay a modest surcharge, modeled on Medicare Part B's 10 percent for each full year a person was eligible but not enrolled. No one should be required to join or penalized for staying out; the surcharge applies only to those who choose to join later. Emergency care should stay tax-funded, and people on the last-resort allowance should be enrolled automatically.

head: "Without a mandate, will healthy people avoid coverage and drive up costs?"
body: Critics warn of adverse selection, and Massachusetts shows the effect a mandate has: when it took effect, healthier people entered the individual market and average costs and premiums fell. The 2019 repeal of the federal penalty did not bring the collapse that warning predicts: some studies found no clear drop in coverage and others only a modest rise in people becoming uninsured. The government keeps choice and limits the problem without a mandate. The public plan has one annual enrollment window, and late joiners pay a modest surcharge, as in Medicare Part B, so people cannot wait until they are sick to sign up. No one is compelled to buy insurance.

head: "What about people who can't afford private coverage?"
body: They can opt into a publicly supported system. Emergency medical care would remain part of the safety floor, so no one in a genuine emergency would be left without care (Economic Orientation). People on the last-resort allowance for severe disability or old-age poverty would be enrolled in the public plan automatically, paid under that narrow exception (Welfare and Entitlements).

head: "Doesn't a majority support Medicare for All?"
body: KFF's September 2026 poll finds that 66% of adults favor a national health plan, sometimes called Medicare-for-all, in which all Americans would get their insurance from a single government plan, and 34% oppose it, the highest favorability KFF has recorded. When people hear claims about the plan, that share changes. After hearing it would "eliminate private health insurance companies," 52% favor it and 47% oppose it. Favor falls to 24% if the plan could lead to delays in getting some medical tests or treatment, and to 35% if most Americans would pay more in taxes. It rises to 75% if the plan would eliminate premiums and reduce out-of-pocket costs. I still oppose Medicare for All. People should choose between a voluntary public plan and private insurance, with taxpayers funding the public option only by choice, and Medicare voluntary for new entrants (Healthcare Funding; Social Security and Medicare Transition).

head: "Wouldn't Medicare for All save tens of thousands of lives a year?"
body: The best-known estimate, Galvani and colleagues in The Lancet (2020), calculates that "ensuring health-care access for all Americans would save more than 68 000 lives and 1·73 million life-years every year compared with the status quo." The evidence that coverage saves lives is real but uneven. In Oregon's 2008 Medicaid lottery, coverage "generated no significant improvements in measured physical health outcomes in the first 2 years," though it raised use of care, lowered depression and "nearly eliminated catastrophic out-of-pocket medical expenditures." In an IRS experiment that sent letters to 3.9 million uninsured taxpayers, the added coverage reduced mortality among middle-aged adults. Either way, the lives in that estimate come from covering the uninsured, not from making one government plan compulsory for everyone. My plan reaches the same people without the mandate: anyone may join the voluntary public plan, people on the last-resort allowance are enrolled automatically, and emergency care stays tax-funded (Healthcare). Single payer then adds the congestion and delays CBO projects (see the prior-authorization question below) on top of compelled funding. Choosing a voluntary plan over a compulsory one does not mean choosing more deaths.

head: "Wouldn't the taxes just replace premiums and copays?"
body: Yes. A single-payer plan would replace much of what people now pay in premiums, deductibles, and copays, so a taxes-only description is incomplete. In the same KFF poll, favorability rises to 75% when people hear that the plan would eliminate premiums and reduce out-of-pocket costs, and falls to 35% when they hear that most Americans would pay more in taxes. Those were asked as separate messages, not as one combined tradeoff. I still reject compelled funding. The public health option should be voluntary, with taxpayers funding it only by choice (Healthcare Funding).

head: "Would ending prior authorization and claim denials speed up care under Medicare for All?"
body: Prior authorization and claim denials do delay some patients. In the Commonwealth Fund's 2023 survey of adults in 10 countries, 27% of U.S. adults skipped a doctor visit because of the cost in the past year, against 8% in Canada and 7% in the United Kingdom, and 32% said insurance denied payment or paid less than expected, against 18% and 3%. CBO's 2020 and 2022 single-payer analyses project that under illustrative designs the amount of care used would rise, and in that sense overall access would be greater, but demand would exceed supply, with "increased congestion in the health care system - including delays and forgone care," especially when cost sharing and payment rates are lower. Access would rise for some who are uninsured or face high cost sharing today, and decline for some now on private insurance in congested areas. Among those who saw or needed a specialist, 46% in Canada and 42% in the United Kingdom waited two months or more for an appointment, against 16% in the United States; 9.6% and 10.7% waited a year or more, against 1.6%. I still oppose Medicare for All. People should choose between a voluntary public plan and private insurance.

Compelling citizens to buy a product conflicts with my limits on state coercion. Offering both public and private options keeps access while preserving choice. Federal health spending is a major driver of long-term budget pressure, which supports keeping public systems opt-in. CBO projects major federal health spending to rise from 5.8% of GDP in 2025 to 8.1% in 2055, with Medicare rising from 2.6% to 5.2% of GDP. Without a mandate, a voluntary plan risks adverse selection: Hackmann, Kolstad, and Kowalski found that the Massachusetts mandate brought healthier people into the individual market and lowered average costs and premiums. After the federal penalty was repealed in 2019, one study comparing states that kept their own mandates found no significant change in coverage or marketplace enrollment. Medicare Part B shows a non-mandate tool. Its late-enrollment penalty adds 10% for each full 12-month period a person was eligible but not enrolled, usually for as long as they have Part B. The public plan borrows that design in modest form.
Budget figures as reported by the cited sources. They bear on the budget pressure from public health spending noted in the rationale above.

While the Legislative Analyst's Office traces much of Medi-Cal's growth to deliberate choices to expand eligibility, provider payments and benefits, largely financed by federal matching funds, and expects federal changes in H.R. 1 to push about 1.2 million people off the program, most of them into having no insurance, the program remains the largest in the state budget: about $197 billion in total funds in 2025–26, more than half of it federal, with its growth recently outpacing the state's General Fund budget. Almost 15 million people, over one-third of Californians, are estimated to be enrolled. LAO – Considering Medi-Cal in the Midst of a Changing Fiscal and Policy Landscape (2025)

Cost per enrollee: most of the program's growth since 2005–06 comes from enrollment, which more than doubled, and from inflation. The real rise per person is moderate, about 1.8% a year, and the two years' budget totals are not compiled on an identical basis. It is still a rise. By my calculation from state budget figures, Medi-Cal spent about $5,100 per average monthly enrollee in 2005–06 ($34.9 billion for 6.81 million) and about $13,100 in 2025–26 ($194.5 billion for 14.84 million), about 43% more per person after adjusting for medical-care inflation, or 55% on the general CPI-U. Eliminating the asset limit for seniors also cost more than double its estimate. Citing those overruns and structural deficits, the state froze new enrollment of undocumented adults in comprehensive coverage from January 2026 and reinstated the asset limit. head: Healthcare Funding, Emergency Care, and Drug Approval
topic: Healthcare Funding, Emergency Care, and Drug Approval

body: The public health option should be voluntary, with taxpayers funding it only by choice. I count emergency care among the basic services taxes pay for. Drug and insurance rules ought to exist only to protect safety and stop consumer abuse, and nobody should have to buy insurance.
topic: Healthcare Funding, Emergency Care, and Drug Approval

head: Position
topic: Healthcare Funding, Emergency Care, and Drug Approval

body: The publicly supported healthcare option should be opt-in, and its funding ought to follow the rule for all programs beyond core services: subsidies require taxpayer opt-in. Emergency services belong among the core services funded by minimal necessary taxes. Drug and device regulation is legitimate for genuine safety and against anti-consumer practices, with the burden of proof resting on each regulation. Insurance regulation should be limited to preventing fraud and anti-consumer practices. No one should be required to buy coverage. Tax-funded research ought to be limited to defense, biosecurity and pandemic defense, and the government's own core functions. Other medical and scientific research, including disease research, should be funded by private money and taxpayer opt-in, under the same rules for every group, and research the government does fund must treat sex as a biological variable.
topic: Healthcare Funding, Emergency Care, and Drug Approval

head: "What happens to people who have no coverage and need emergency care?"
body: Emergency services are part of the core public functions funded by minimal necessary taxes. Current federal law also requires hospitals with emergency departments to screen anyone who arrives and to stabilize an emergency condition or transfer the patient appropriately, regardless of ability to pay. The government ought to keep emergency care within the safety floor while leaving routine coverage to individual choice.
topic: Healthcare Funding, Emergency Care, and Drug Approval

head: Rationale
topic: Healthcare Funding, Emergency Care, and Drug Approval

body: Most Americans already arrange coverage without a mandate: 92.0% had health insurance for some or all of 2024, with private coverage (66.1%) more common than public (35.5%). Federal health spending is the main driver of long-term budget pressure; CBO projects it to rise from 5.8% of GDP in 2025 to 8.1% in 2055. Keeping the public option opt-in prevents that pressure from becoming compulsory redistribution. The Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (1986) requires a screening examination and stabilizing treatment or appropriate transfer in hospitals with emergency departments, without delay to ask about payment. Drug regulation follows the same burden-of-proof rule as all business regulation in Infrastructure and Regulation. Federal law now permits non-animal alternatives in drug approval, consistent with Bioethics, Progress, & Technology.

body: Insulin: other countries regulate insulin prices and pay far less, and the 2023 U.S. cuts followed government action more than competition. In 2022, U.S. manufacturer list prices were 9.71 times those of 33 other OECD countries combined, and net prices after rebates 2.33 times. Lilly cut Humalog's list price 70%, to $66.40 a vial, ahead of the American Rescue Plan's removal of the cap on Medicaid drug rebates on January 1, 2024, a change one model projected would otherwise have cost Lilly about $430 million in added rebates that year. Novo Nordisk and Sanofi announced similar cuts the same month. Medicare has capped insulin copays at $35 a month since 2023, and California now sells interchangeable glargine at $55 for five pens under a state contract. What held the U.S. price up, though, falls within that drug-rule test. Until March 2020, copies of insulin could not be approved as biosimilars or as interchangeable products a pharmacist may substitute. The first interchangeable, Semglee, was approved in July 2021 after a switching study, and in 2024 the FDA, finding the risk from switching "insignificant," proposed that such studies generally no longer be needed. In 2020 a federal appeals court held that Sanofi had improperly listed, against competing glargine, a pen-mechanism patent that "does not mention insulin glargine or the Lantus SoloSTAR at any point". Suing on it had triggered an automatic 30-month hold on approval of Lilly's version, which launched in December 2016 under a royalty-bearing settlement. And a bipartisan Senate Finance Committee investigation found that manufacturers raised list prices in part to fund larger rebates to pharmacy benefit managers, who are also paid fees as a percentage of list price: the average net price of a Humalog pen fell from $28 in 2015 to $24 in 2018 while its list price nearly doubled, and uninsured and high-deductible patients may pay the full list price. body: I believe each state should fund basic K-12 education at about $10,000 per child (more for disability as each state sets from need, with pre-K left out). The money follows the child to any public school, district or charter, statewide. Parents should pay for private and religious schools, and homeschooling families get a fully refundable $1,000 tax credit per child. Schools ought to be run locally, with a curriculum that sticks to core skills and facts, not ideology. College should be paid for with personal loans, not federal ones, and state subsidies for colleges should end.

I'd have each state fund about $10,000 per child per year for basic K-12 education from its general revenue, roughly what Utah and Idaho spend, with an extra amount for students with disabilities that each state sets from actual need. The money follows the child to any public school, district or charter, anywhere in the state. Private and religious schools stay legal but get no public money; parents pay for them. Homeschooling families get a $1,000 tax credit per child per year. Pre-K is excluded.

The $10,000 per-child average is the level the evidence points to now - close to what Utah and Idaho spend - not a floor and not a slogan. It moves up or down only with outcome data; any change alters state tax calculations. Students with disabilities get an added amount each state sets from actual need; no fixed national figure. Publicly funded means publicly accountable: the money follows the child to any public school, district or charter, statewide. Private and religious schools should stay legal with no public funds; parents pay. Homeschooling families get a fully refundable $1,000 federal income-tax credit per child per year (Homeschooling); pre-K is excluded.
My view: Since restricting immigration will lower the population, we want as many things as possible to help parents and raise birth rates to replacement level (Taxation; Immigration and Borders).

head: "Is $10,000 per child enough?"
body: Utah spent $10,333 per pupil and Idaho $10,247 in FY2023, against a national average of $16,526, and both scored at or above the national results in 2024 NAEP eighth-grade math and reading (Utah 282 and 261, Idaho 278 and 261). New York spent $30,012 and scored 271 and 257. Critics answer that the states' student populations differ, so raw averages are not a clean test. The comparison holds within the same groups, where the low spenders still match or beat New York: in 2024 eighth-grade math, white students scored 289 in Utah and 284 in Idaho against 283 in New York, and Hispanic students 260 and 256 against 253. Across OECD countries, higher spending tracks math scores only up to about $75,000 per student over ages 6 to 15, and the United States spends more than $150,000.

head: "Doesn't more money raise outcomes?"
body: Researchers find gains on average: a review of U.S. school-spending evaluations finds that $1,000 more per pupil, sustained for four years, raises test scores by about 0.03 standard deviations and college-going by about 2.8 percentage points, with smaller effects for advantaged students. That is $4,000 per pupil for three-hundredths of a standard deviation, while Utah and Idaho match or beat far higher spenders near $10,000. I hold an average of about $10,000 per child as the level the evidence supports today. It is not fixed: if the data shows better outcomes from spending more, the level moves up, and if it shows the same outcomes from spending less, the level moves down. Any change in either direction alters the state tax calculations.

head: "If spending keeps rising and scores barely move, aren't schools just underfunded forever?"
body: "Underfunded" without a fixed definition is a slogan, not a budget. Real per-pupil spending has risen for decades while NAEP gains have been small. From FY1992 to FY2024 staff grew far faster than enrollment, and non-teaching staff grew fastest (data in "Where did the extra money go?"). Cross-state spending and NAEP results show a weak relationship once poverty and income are accounted for. Causal studies still find small average gains from sustained increases, on the order of a few hundredths of a standard deviation per $1,000 per pupil over several years. I do not claim the correlation is literally zero. I claim the United States already spends past the point where more money, without better use, reliably buys large score gains, which is why I hold about $10,000 per child as the working level and move it only with evidence (Education).

head: "Where did the extra money go?"
body: From FY1992 to FY2024, public school students rose 17.2% while all staff rose 51.5%. Teachers rose 33.4% and non-teaching staff 69.0%. Real spending per pupil rose 68% while real teacher pay fell 6%.

head: "Are public schools just a jobs program for adults?"
body: NCES staffing data shows schools adding staff far faster than students. From fall 2000 to fall 2022, enrollment rose 5%, teachers 10%, principals and assistant principals 39%, and district administrative staff 95%, reaching about 189,000 full-time equivalent (about 386,000 with principals). The extra money has gone mostly to adults outside the classroom, and it hasn't reliably bought score gains (data in "Where did the extra money go?").

head: "Why include charter schools?"
body: Charter schools received about 30%, or $7,147, less per pupil than district schools across 18 cities in 2019–20. CREDO's 2023 national study found charter students gained the equivalent of 16 more days of learning in reading and 6 in math per year than matched peers in district schools.

Current spending is $16,526 per pupil (Census, FY2023), and a large part of the growth since 1992 went to non-teaching staff rather than teachers. States near $10,000 per pupil, such as Utah and Idaho, match or beat higher-spending states on NAEP. Funding that follows the child to any public school lets families leave schools that fail them, and charter schools have delivered gains at lower cost. Keeping public money out of private schools keeps it publicly accountable.

In a realistic world, these programs phase out to bridge the gaps during the transition. That is why the phase-out window exists. Public K-12 schools collected about $981.8 billion in revenue in FY2023, or $19,871 per pupil: $443.3 billion state, $412.1 billion local, and $126.4 billion federal (12.9 percent). Spending was $18,905 per pupil in total expenditure and $16,526 per pupil in current expenditure. The largest federal K-12 programs that block grants would replace are IDEA Part B grants to states ($14.214 billion in FY2025) and Title I-A ($18.4 billion in FY2025).

The evidence that local control by itself improves results is weak. Funding matters from low baselines and in poorer districts — older finance-reform studies find a 10 percent rise in per-pupil spending across all twelve years of school linked to 0.27 more completed years of education and 7.25 percent higher adult wages, with larger effects for children from low-income families — but those wage effects do not license New York-level spend. The United States already spends past the point where more money, without better use, reliably buys large NAEP gains, which is why I hold about $10,000 per child as the working level and move it only with evidence. State funding of the per-child amount keeps the money guaranteed in poorer districts.
