I would abolish the federal Department of Education and put control local first. States should set minimum core-skill standards. Districts pick curriculum, limited to core skills and objective facts.

I would abolish the federal Department of Education outright and end its programs or return them to the states. States that structured budgets around the transitional block grants are not cut off cold; their commitments are honored through the phase-out window. Control ought to be local first. Local districts should run schools, and the state guarantees the per-child funding, with state and federal law limited to child protections such as security of children's personal information and training and oversight for childcare, minimum core-skill standards, fraud and safety rules for public funds, and the protection of gifted programs and ability tracking (Gifted programs and tracking). Charter schools set their own curriculum and remain publicly accountable; each private school sets its own curriculum. Public-school curriculum standards exist and carve away biases of any sort; private schools set their own. For public schools, states set minimum standards for core skills, and local districts pick curriculum and materials. Teaching should focus on core skills (literacy, numeracy, science, and civic knowledge) and be entirely objective about facts and subject knowledge, not ideological, with no forced patriotism. No framework should be banned by viewpoint, but critical race theory, like any contested framework, may be taught only as one framework among others, never as settled fact, and no student or teacher may be required to affirm it (Cultural Marxism).

Gifted programs and ability tracking should stay. Every public school district ought to keep them, open to every student by merit, and entry may be decided by a test. No public school, district or charter, may cut, merge, or close a gifted program or an ability track to even out results between groups, and admission to a selective public school follows the test requirement in Tests in selective admissions. Fully private schools, which take no public money, set their own programs and admissions, under the same bar on immutable traits as a requirement or a quota (The merit rule). San Francisco moved eighth-grade algebra to high school to address racial gaps and brought it back ten years later, and Thomas Jefferson High School dropped its admissions test and cut offers to Asian-American students (Anti-meritocratic beliefs in practice).

My view: Gifted students should absolutely not be dragged down by less intelligent kids. Grouping students by what they can do lets each one move at the pace they can handle, and holding the fastest back to narrow a gap between groups punishes individuals for an average they did not set (From disparity to equal outcomes).

head: "Doesn't tracking widen gaps between groups?"
body: Critics argue that it does, and San Francisco removed eighth-grade algebra on that ground. The gaps it aimed at persisted after the change (Anti-meritocratic beliefs in practice). A gap between groups is a fact to be explained, not a reason to hold back the student who is ahead. What helps the students behind is better teaching for them, not a lower ceiling for everyone else.

In a realistic world, many systems — like taxes, like education, like all the systems that would be changing — would have some gradual period of change for most of these changes to happen. Here that means transitional block grants that phase out. That practical lag is a brief aside, not the main position.

Education does not require a central ministry. Canada, Belgium, and Bosnia and Herzegovina have no national education ministry; Switzerland's cantons run its schools; Germany and Australia have national ministries but leave schools to their states. On PISA 2022, all five wealthy decentralized countries outscored the U.S. in math (Switzerland 508, Canada 497, Belgium 489, Australia 487, Germany 475, U.S. 465), while the U.S. scored 504 in reading, trailing only Canada (507) among them. Bosnia and Herzegovina did not take part in PISA 2022; in PISA 2018 it scored 406 in math and 403 in reading, far below the others. The comparison cannot show that decentralization causes these results, and Bosnia's scores show it does not guarantee them.

Local control would be chosen on grounds of accountability and closeness to the families affected, not on outcome evidence. Restricting curriculum to objective knowledge and skills would keep public schools from becoming instruments of ideology. Curriculum is already set locally in most of the country: local entities develop curriculum in 43 states, the state alone in one (Rhode Island), and both in five. Common Core has no official tracker. Roughly 30 states still use it in original, renamed, or revised form, and about 15 adopted and then repealed or replaced it.

Homeschooling should be fully allowed, with no school-performance testing. I want oversight to be tiered: clean households file an annual paper or virtual welfare check-in - no surprise entry. Complaint, prior-abuse history, or withdrawal-from-school after a CPS case triggers intensive unannounced visits. Homeschooling families would receive a fully refundable $1,000 federal income-tax credit per child per year (K-12 Funding).
Homeschooling should be fully allowed, with no testing requirement. Child-welfare oversight is tiered, not universal quarterly entry.

Clean households (no open complaint, no substantiated prior abuse in the household, no withdrawal from school that followed a CPS investigation or open case): one annual paper or virtual welfare check-in with a child-protection caseworker — confirmation the child is alive, reachable, and not reported missing or injured. no unannounced home entry on that track.

Triggered households (any of: a credible welfare complaint; substantiated prior abuse or neglect in the household; withdrawal from school after a CPS investigation or while a CPS case was open): intensive unannounced welfare visits by a child-protection caseworker, at random times, at a cadence the caseworker sets from risk (and at least as often as needed to clear or escalate the case). Visits check the child's welfare only, never schoolwork.
Homeschooling families would receive a fully refundable $1,000 federal income-tax credit per child per year (K-12 Funding).

Homeschooling carries no testing requirement because no study shows that state testing or progress reviews improve homeschool outcomes. The most comprehensive review of the research (Kunzman and Gaither, 2020) finds the literature cannot isolate the effect of homeschooling, let alone the effect of regulation. Where data cannot show either way, the less regulatory option applies. Private schools publish yearly results because parents choose among schools and need comparable information; a homeschooling family is not choosing among providers, so the same reason does not apply.

The real risk is abuse hidden behind a withdrawal from school. Knox et al. (2014) is a clinical series of 28 child-torture cases; 8 of 17 school-age victims (47%) had been removed from school and labeled homeschooled. That is a child-safety signal worth acting on when a trigger is present — complaint, prior abuse, or CPS-linked withdrawal — not a warrant for surprise state entry into every clean homeschool four times a year. An n=28 clinical series does not justify universal quarterly unannounced visits. The answer is tiered welfare oversight: annual paper or virtual check-in for clean households. Intensive unannounced visits when a trigger fires — not school-performance testing, and not surveillance of every family that educates at home.

Private and religious schools have the full right to exist and should be privately funded. I'd have them meet background-check, audit, and anti-fraud rules and publish a yearly norm-referenced test of their choice. Homeschooling keeps its testing exemption.

I believe private and religious schools have the full right to exist. They should be privately funded, with no public vouchers or education savings accounts. Private schools, religious schools, and any other privately funded education provider meet safety and fraud rules (background checks, financial audits, no fraud) and give a yearly nationally norm-referenced test of the school's choice, with results published. Homeschooling families are covered by the no-fraud rule and keep the testing exemption in the Homeschooling topic.

State law on education is limited to child protections, minimum core-skill standards, and fraud and safety rules; these rules apply them to privately funded schools without public funds attached. A test of the school's choice gives parents comparable results without imposing the state curriculum. Florida's tax-credit scholarship, where schools choose a nationally norm-referenced test, raised college enrollment to 57 percent from 51 percent, while Louisiana's state-test model left students 0.41 standard deviations lower in math after one year with no significant effect on college entrance. The two programs differ in many ways, so the comparison cannot isolate testing rules as the cause.
Urban Institute – The Effects of the Florida Tax Credit Scholarship Program on College Enrollment and Graduation
Abdulkadiroğlu, Pathak & Walters, NBER – Free to Choose: Can School Choice Reduce Student Achievement?
Erickson, Mills & Wolf, ERIC – The Effects of the Louisiana Scholarship Program on Student Achievement and College Entrance

Higher education sits outside public K-12 funding. I would make Pell Grants opt-in, end state subsidies, and stop new federal student lending. Existing loans and contracts are honored.

Higher education should sit outside public K-12 funding. Pell Grants ought to be converted to opt-in, taxpayer-designated funding through a voluntary checkoff. State subsidies for higher education should end. Existing commitments to higher-education subsidy recipients are honored through the transition window; they are not cut off cold. Student loans for college are personal loans, not federal loans from taxpayers; anyone who pursues higher education does so on a personal loan, not on the taxpayer's dime. New federal lending should stop, and existing federal loans should be collected on their current terms. Existing loan contracts, including forgiveness terms in force when they were signed, are honored, and no new forgiveness programs should be created.

head: "Won't ending federal student loans shut people out of college?"
body: College remains open to anyone who finances it through a personal loan. Ending federal lending and phasing out state subsidies removes the taxpayer from the risk of a borrower's degree choice, and the cost and value of each degree are settled between the student, the lender, and the college.

In a realistic world, these programs phase out to bridge the gaps during the transition; that is why the phase-out window exists. Pell Grants reached 7.3 million students in 2024-25 at a cost of $38.6 billion, with an average grant of $5,320 and a maximum of $7,395. State and local support for higher education totaled $149.2 billion in FY2025. Public Service Loan Forgiveness and related programs had discharged $93.4 billion for about 1.25 million borrowers through April 2026.

Federal student loans place the cost of a borrower's degree choice on taxpayers while any benefit stays private, which conflicts with my limits on redistribution and my emphasis on personal responsibility. The federal government is currently the main lender to U.S. college students through the Direct Loan program. Deming and Walters found that a 10% increase in public colleges' spending raised enrollment by about 3% and raised persistence and degree completion, while tuition cuts had no discernible effect on enrollment.
When the state subsidizes demand without freeing supply, prices rise, and federal student lending shows it (data below).
Findings as reported by the study's authors.

Federal loan-limit increases of 2007–08 and 2008–09: institutions more exposed to the higher federal loan maximums raised sticker-price tuition by about 60 cents for each dollar of increase in the subsidized-loan maximum, with smaller but positive effects for unsubsidized loans. The effect was strongest for more expensive degrees, private institutions and two-year or vocational programs. Defenders of federal lending point to the chance that colleges offset higher sticker prices with their own grants. For the institutions that report grant data (about 60% of the sample), the same paper finds the opposite: schools cut their own grants by about 20 cents per dollar of added subsidized lending, so the price rise is not offset, which is one more reason federal student lending phases out under my plan. Lucca, Nadauld & Shen, Federal Reserve Bank of New York – Credit Supply and the Rise in College Tuition: Evidence from the Expansion in Federal Student Aid Programs (Staff Report 733, revised 2017)
I see trade schools, apprenticeships, and certificate programs as equal pathways to a career, and they should operate under the same rules as college.
Trade schools, apprenticeships, and certificate programs ought to be equal pathways under the same rules.

Taxes should pay to keep core infrastructure safe and working. I would regulate businesses only for safety, serious environmental harm, worker exploitation, and consumer protection, and leave everything else to the market.

Core infrastructure should be maintained to safe and functional standards with tax revenue. I believe business regulation is legitimate only for genuine safety, prevention of serious environmental harm (as defined in Energy & Environment), prevention of clear worker exploitation, and protection against anti-consumer practices. Outside these domains, the market ought to operate freely.

head: "Who decides what counts as genuine safety or clear exploitation?"
body: The burden of proof rests on the regulation. A rule should show a real safety, environmental, worker-exploitation, or consumer-protection harm it addresses. Rules that cannot meet that test should be removed, and the market should govern everything else.

Roads, bridges, and water systems are public goods that markets do not reliably provide, and their condition directly affects safety. Regulation beyond clear harms raises costs and is prone to capture by established firms. Dawson and Seater find that federal regulation accumulated since 1949 has significantly reduced U.S. output growth. Djankov and colleagues find that heavier entry regulation across 85 countries goes with more corruption and larger unofficial economies rather than better goods. Limiting regulation to defined harms keeps government effective where it is needed and out of the way elsewhere.

Retribution, incapacitation, and the protection of victims' sentient rights ought to come first, with rehabilitation as secondary. I hold that those who murder; commit violent rape, child molestation, child rape, kidnapping, or human trafficking; distribute hard drugs on a large scale; give or sell any hard drug to a minor; or repeatedly violate the rights of others forfeit the protections they denied their victims. Punishment ought to be swift, certain, and public, and capital punishment ought to apply only where guilt is established beyond any real doubt. Enforcement ought to be heavy, with military-style action against cartels and high-crime threats.

Helping the poor and excusing crime are separate policies. I support the first through the basic-necessities floor and reject the second: offenders are not victims of society, poverty does not excuse a crime, and fusing the two insults the poor who never offend. Defending yourself against an attacker is not aggression (Self-Defense and Defense of Others). Studies that compare siblings, and experiments that hand out money at random, find that the link between low income and crime largely disappears (data below). Critics point to the study finding that 18-year-olds removed from Supplemental Security Income were charged with more crimes. That shows a floor of support keeps some people from turning to crime, which is what my floor is for. It does not make poverty an excuse for the crimes that are committed.
A one-glance view of the rules I set out in the topics below. The topics themselves govern. This table only collects them.

Voluntary murder; attempted murder; knowingly imposing an extreme risk of death · Capital · Capital evidentiary standard · Death (public), or the experimentation track · Victim; where the victim has died, the experimentation track by default, unless the victim's close family or friends step forward and choose (experimentation if they disagree); a judge when victims disagree or the victim is an animal
Violent rape, child molestation, child rape, kidnapping, human trafficking · Capital · Capital evidentiary standard · Death (public), or the experimentation track · Victim

Large-scale distribution of hard drugs: a statutory trafficking quantity, or organizing or leading a distribution operation (not legal marijuana or licensed clinical therapy) · Capital · Capital evidentiary standard · Death (public), or the experimentation track · Judge (no single victim)
Giving or selling any hard drug to a minor, at any quantity · Capital · Capital evidentiary standard · Death (public), or the experimentation track · Victim

Selling or giving another person an untested or unknown hard drug, below the large-scale threshold · Two marks · Ordinary conviction · Fixed-term hard labor with training, term set by the judge · Judge
Selling a known, tested dose of a hard drug to an adult, below the large-scale threshold · One mark · Ordinary conviction · Fixed-term hard labor with training, term set by the judge · Judge
Sharing a known, tested dose with a consenting adult, for no profit · Misdemeanor, no mark · Ordinary conviction · Income-scaled fine · Judge

Cruelty acts (extreme violence, intentional neglect, beating without drawing blood, deliberate withholding of food, water, or shelter) causing lasting injury · Capital · Capital evidentiary standard; lasting injury proven beyond a reasonable doubt by clinician evaluation · Death, or the experimentation track · Victim

The same cruelty acts without lasting injury · Grave: three marks at once · Lasting-injury findings below the capital tier by clear and convincing evidence · Execution, experimentation, or life with labor · Victim
Terrorism, material support, treason · Attempted-murder rules · Capital evidentiary standard · Death; otherwise secure confinement under compelled labor; never deportation instead · Court
Lesser crimes (for example theft) · One or two marks · Ordinary conviction · Fixed-term hard labor with training, term set by the judge · Judge

Third mark (repeat-offender threshold) · Threshold · Capital standard for the threshold offense to allow death or experimentation; otherwise life with labor · Execution, experimentation, or life with labor · Victim; where the victim has died, the experimentation track by default, unless the victim's close family or friends step forward and choose (experimentation if they disagree); a judge when victims disagree or the victim is an animal
Excessive self-defense close to justified · Lesser homicide · Prosecution proves intent · Lighter sentence · Judge

Killing without agency (insanity) · Confinement; counts as two marks (threat, not guilt) · Agency decided by a forensic panel and a judge · Confinement with treatment; execution only if no progress · Panel and judge
No crime; serious mental illness with danger or lost capacity · Civil commitment · Clear and convincing evidence at a hearing · Outpatient treatment first; review every six months · Court
Every capital sentence passes all of these before it is carried out:
Proof. Objective corroboration such as footage and physical evidence, not testimony alone; a case that falls short goes to the non-capital tracks (Evidentiary Standard).
Recordings. A recording counts only if its source and chain of custody are proven, and capital convictions and later-found errors are published every year (same section).
Trial. Thirty days at most, with no death row (Capital Trials).
Independent panel. Three reviewers outside the prosecuting office re-examine the full record before the sentencing date, and any one can take the case off the capital track (same section).
New evidence. New objective evidence of innocence gets an expedited review before the sentencing date, and for life on the experimentation track (same section).
Openness. Executions are public or openly recorded (Public Executions).
Errors. A wrongful conviction brings compensation and accountability (Wrongful Convictions and Compensation).
Findings as reported by the studies' authors. The income–crime correlation is real, the question is whether income causes it.

Sweden, 526,167 children born 1989–1993: children in the lowest family-income quintile were about 6.8 times as likely as the highest to be convicted of violent crime, but comparing siblings and cousins reduced the hazard ratio to 0.95 (95% CI 0.44–2.03). Sariaslan et al., British Journal of Psychiatry – Childhood family income, adolescent violent criminality and substance misuse (2014)

Finland, 650,680 people born 1986–1996: each $15,000 of family income at age 15 was linked to 23% fewer violent-crime arrests, but the link vanished within siblings (hazard ratios 0.99–1.00). Sariaslan et al., International Journal of Epidemiology – No causal associations between childhood family income and subsequent psychiatric disorders, substance misuse and violent crime arrests (2021)

Sweden, lottery players: randomly assigned lottery wealth had a small, statistically insignificant effect on winners' own conviction risk, ruling out effects one-fifth the size of the cross-sectional income gradient. Cesarini, Lindqvist, Östling & Schroeder, NBER – Does Wealth Inhibit Criminal Behavior? Evidence from Swedish Lottery Winners and Their Children (w31962)

Finland, 2017–2018: 2,000 randomly selected unemployed people received €560 a month unconditionally for two years. Crime perpetration and victimization were unchanged relative to 173,222 comparable people under the existing safety net. Aaltonen, Kaila & Nix, NBER – The Impacts of Guaranteed Basic Income on Crime Perpetration and Victimization (2025)

United States, 2007–2010: unemployment doubled from 5.0% to 10.0% and the poverty rate reached 15.1%, yet reported robberies fell 10.0% in 2010 (FBI UCR). That count is opportunity- and reporting-confounded in a recession. It is supporting color, not the causal weight. The sibling, lottery, and cash-experiment lines above carry that weight. FBI – Crime in the United States 2010, Robbery; Census Bureau – Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage: 2010

New Zealand, 1,000 children followed to age 32: low childhood self-control predicted adult criminal convictions independent of intelligence and social class, and children whose self-control improved had better outcomes. Moffitt et al., PNAS – A gradient of childhood self-control predicts health, wealth, and public safety (2011)

Liberia, 999 high-risk young men: eight weeks of cognitive behavioral therapy and a $200 cash grant each reduced crime and violence at first, but the effects faded. When cash followed therapy, crime and violence fell sharply for at least a year. Ten years later, men given therapy alone were 0.20 standard deviations less antisocial, and men given therapy plus cash 0.25. Blattman, Jamison & Sheridan, American Economic Review – Reducing Crime and Violence: Experimental Evidence from Cognitive Behavioral Therapy in Liberia (2017). Blattman, Chaskel, Jamison & Sheridan, AER: Insights – Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Reduces Crime and Violence over Ten Years (2023)

Not every study points one way. In the 1930s, cities that spent more on relief saw somewhat less property crime (about 1.5% less per 10% more spending). Johnson, Kantor & Fishback, NBER – Striking at the Roots of Crime (w12825). In the Moving to Opportunity experiment, vouchers to leave high-poverty neighborhoods cut girls' violent and property arrests, while boys' property arrests rose. Kling, Ludwig & Katz, NBER – Neighborhood Effects on Crime for Female and Male Youth (w10777) When a 1996 law led to more 18-year-olds being removed from Supplemental Security Income, those removed faced 20% more criminal charges over the next two decades, with income-generating charges up 60% and the yearly chance of incarceration up 60%. Deshpande & Mueller-Smith, Quarterly Journal of Economics – Does Welfare Prevent Crime? The Criminal Justice Outcomes of Youth Removed from SSI (2022)

I would execute nobody unless the proof is overwhelming and backed by objective evidence such as video and physical evidence, not just testimony. Because there is no long appeals process, the trial itself has to get it right.

I would allow execution only when guilt is absolutely clear, without a shadow of a doubt. Ordinary proof beyond a reasonable doubt is not enough for a capital outcome. The standard should require corroborating objective evidence: body-camera or surveillance footage, multiple eyewitnesses backed by camera footage, physical evidence such as a body, and similar proof that does not depend on a single witness or on inference alone. Cases that fall short of this bar should not go to the capital track.

head: "Innocent people have been sentenced to death. Doesn't any death penalty guarantee that the state will eventually kill an innocent person?"
body: Opponents cite Gross and colleagues (2014), who estimated that at least 4.1 percent of defendants sentenced to death in the United States are likely innocent. That figure indicts capital punishment as it currently operates, and this standard is built to remove its causes. Most known wrongful capital convictions rested on mistaken eyewitness identification, false confessions, unreliable informants, or flawed forensic testimony. Those are exactly the kinds of evidence a corroboration requirement excludes as a sufficient basis. I treat wrongful execution as a rights violation by the state, with full accountability for those responsible. No human process reaches zero error, and the claim is precise: restricting execution to cases with objective corroboration reduces the error rate far below the current system's. Abolition does not remove the error. It moves it. The same study found that "the great majority of innocent defendants who are convicted of capital murder in the United States are neither executed nor exonerated. They are sentenced, or resentenced to prison for life, and then forgotten." Years taken from an innocent person can't be returned either, so a critic who holds that any risk of an irreversible wrong forbids a punishment has to forbid prison too. The real question is how low the error can be driven, and the capital standard, the independent panel review, and the yearly error report are built to answer it (Capital Trials).

head: "With this many capital crimes and execution on the day of sentence, won't more innocent people die?"
body: The list of capital crimes is broad, but the capital track is narrow. A crime on the list goes to the capital track only when the proof meets the capital evidentiary standard: objective corroboration such as footage, physical evidence, and witnesses confirmed by recording. A case that falls short goes to the non-capital tracks, however grave the charge. Drug distribution is capital only at large scale, a statutory trafficking quantity or leading a distribution operation, or when any hard drug is given or sold to a minor (Quick Reference). More capital crimes should mean more cases screened against the bar, not a lower bar. The case for the sentence rests on desert, not deterrence (Deterrence). Speed removes the appeals, so the trial has to do their work, and recordings are now easier to fake. The federal courts' evidence rules committee has warned that AI deepfakes "can be extremely hard to detect" and "can be generated easily and inexpensively by any member of the public." I believe a recording should count toward the capital standard only if its source and chain of custody are proven, and a recording the defense shows may be fabricated should not count unless the prosecution proves it authentic. The state should also publish every year the number of capital convictions, the evidence each rested on, and every capital conviction later found wrong, so the error rate is measured rather than assumed. I don't claim zero error. A wrongful execution is a rights violation by the state, with full accountability for those responsible (Wrongful Convictions and Compensation). Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules – Report to the Standing Committee, December 1, 2025 (proposed Rule 901(c) on deepfakes)

A swift system with no long appeals is defensible only if guilt is certain at the front end. The longer the period between sentence and execution, the more the system relies on appeals to catch mistakes. The state ought to remove that period, so the burden moves to the trial itself. The evidentiary bar does the work that decades of appeals were meant to do.

Corroboration matters because the main sources of wrongful conviction are subjective. A recording, a body, and independent witnesses who agree with the recording are much harder to fabricate or misread than a single identification made under stress. The bar is deliberately strict. Its purpose is to make the capital track narrow, reliable, and limited to cases where the facts are not in serious dispute.

Evidence that establishes both the act and the identity of the offender without depending on a single uncorroborated source. Examples include body-camera or surveillance footage of the act, multiple eyewitnesses whose accounts are confirmed by camera footage, and physical evidence such as a body. A confession alone, a single eyewitness, or circumstantial inference alone does not meet the standard.
Gross, O'Brien, Hu & Kennedy – Rate of False Conviction of Criminal Defendants Who Are Sentenced to Death (PNAS, 2014)

In my view murder, violent rape, child molestation, child rape, kidnapping, human trafficking, large-scale distribution of hard drugs, and giving or selling any hard drug to a minor should be prosecutable no matter how much time has passed, as long as the strict evidence standard is met. Old convictions always count toward the repeat-offender threshold, and restitution and civil claims never expire: restitution is owed until it is paid. Other non-capital crimes should have tiered limits of 3, 6, or 20 years: under $500, $500 up to $10,000, and $10,000 and up.

There should be no statute of limitations for murder, violent rape, child molestation, child rape, kidnapping, human trafficking, large-scale distribution of hard drugs, or giving or selling any hard drug to a minor. I hold all people liable for their actions, and the passage of time does not restore rights that were forfeited by a deliberate violation. Old convictions ought to count toward the repeat-offender threshold indefinitely, with no time limit on the look-back. Restitution and civil claims should have no time limit either: restitution is owed forever until it is paid. Theft, fraud, and other non-capital crimes should have limitation periods that scale with severity and the value involved. Minor offenses (under $500) may be prosecuted within 3 years, mid-level offenses ($500 up to $10,000) within 6 years, and major offenses ($10,000 and up) within 20 years. The thresholds may be adjusted each year to rise with the national average wage.

head: "Doesn't evidence degrade over time, risking wrongful convictions in old cases?"
body: The protection against that risk is the evidentiary standard, not a deadline. A capital conviction should still require proof to the strict standard in Evidentiary Standard, however old the case.

Forfeiture follows from the act, not from how quickly it is prosecuted (Ethical and Philosophical Framework). Federal law already sets no limitation period for offenses punishable by death (18 U.S.C. § 3281). For non-capital crimes, the federal default is 5 years (18 U.S.C. § 3282). Norway scales its limitation periods by the maximum sentence, from 2 years for the least serious offenses to 25 years for the most serious, and France sets 20 years for serious crimes and 6 years for mid-level offenses. The dollar thresholds are set below what the typical full-time worker earns in the same time. The full-time median is $65,052 a year (about $1,251 a week), so $500 is under half a week's pay and $10,000 is about eight weeks. Because I rank retribution and incapacitation above rehabilitation, more serious offenses carry longer periods.
Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 3281: Capital offenses
Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 3282: Offenses not capital
Lovdata – Straffeloven § 86
Service-Public.fr – Justice pénale : quels sont les délais de prescription ?

head: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: Deliberate murder should be punished by death, and so should violent rape, child molestation, child rape, kidnapping, human trafficking, large-scale distribution of hard drugs, and giving or selling any hard drug to a minor proven to the same strict standard. Attempted murder and knowingly putting others at extreme risk of death should be treated the same way, even if no one dies; ordinary accidents should not. Killing or trying to kill a victim or witness should always be capital, and most abuse within families, which rarely meets the capital proof standard, should be punished on the non-capital tracks. I want the sentence fixed for adults, not left to a jury's sympathy, so equal crimes get equal sentences whoever the victim was, and the offender's mental state does not change it. Minors whose crimes are serious enough are sentenced like adults. Offenders pay restitution from their own assets. Current Supreme Court rulings forbid much of this, so I believe those rulings ought to change.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: Position
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: The capital offenses, attempted-murder / extreme-risk track, mandatory adult sentence, juvenile reach, restitution from the offender's own assets, and the conflict with current Supreme Court doctrine are in the In short above — not repeated here.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: I would also make four cruelty acts capital when done to a person if they cause lasting injury: extreme violence. Intentional neglect (a chosen pattern of keeping it up); beating without drawing blood; and psychological abuse (withholding food, water, or shelter, not out of neglect but as deliberate punishment). Lasting injury is harm, physical or psychological, that requires ongoing treatment, does not heal within a recovery period measured in months, or leaves permanent damage - including neglect and other acts that leave lasting psychological harm. At the capital tier, lasting injury (including psychological injury) should have to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt through evaluation by a licensed clinician for humans, or a veterinarian or veterinary behaviorist for animals, documenting harm that requires ongoing treatment, persists for months, or is permanent. Below the capital tier, lasting injury should have to be proven by clear and convincing evidence, with the same clinician or veterinary evaluation. Without lasting injury, those acts would fall in the grave tier: three marks at once, reaching the threshold - execution, experimentation, or life with labor, as the victim chooses. Beating means force beyond ordinary discipline: a closed fist, an object, or repeated strikes. A swat on the rear as ordinary discipline is not beating. See Animal Cruelty Law.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: I don't believe the offender's mental competence, intellectual capacity, or understanding of the proceedings should reduce the sentence, because none of these change what was done to the victim. Incompetence alone does not lead to execution. An offender who was completely unaware and incompetent ought to be removed from society, imprisoned or confined, because they are too dangerous to be around (Ethical and Philosophical Framework). But some offenders cannot be changed from incompetence and remain a threat: they are violent and show no sign of change. Such a person is a threat to society and should not be kept alive merely for the sake of keeping them alive. I believe they deserve to die. The same holds for an animal in confinement that remains a threat. See Insanity Defense.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: Attempted murder should stay on the capital track: I treat a deliberate attempt to kill as murder whether or not the victim dies. So is conduct that knowingly imposes an extreme, unjustified risk of death on others, where the person understands the danger and goes ahead anyway with blatant disregard for life and rights - even if no one is harmed. Street racing through traffic at extreme speed is one example. The test is awareness and severity: the person knew the danger and the risk was grave, not merely careless. Ordinary accidents and ordinary negligence should stay outside the capital track and be handled as lesser homicide.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: "Hasn't the Supreme Court already ruled that mandatory death sentences, executing the mentally incompetent, and executing for rape are unconstitutional?"
body: Yes. Under current doctrine all three are barred. Woodson v. North Carolina (1976) struck down mandatory death sentences for murder. Ford v. Wainwright (1986) and Atkins v. Virginia (2002) bar executing the insane and the intellectually disabled. Coker v. Georgia (1977) and Kennedy v. Louisiana (2008) bar the death penalty for rape where the victim was not killed. The position here does not pretend otherwise. It is a normative claim about what the law ought to be. Achieving it would require the Court to revisit those holdings or a constitutional amendment. The Eighth Amendment itself does not prohibit capital punishment; Gregg v. Georgia (1976) upheld it. The dispute is over which offenses and which offenders qualify, and that line has been drawn by the Court rather than by the text. On mandatory sentences the Court's own cases pull against each other. Furman v. Georgia (1972) struck down death sentences left to discretion. Justice Stewart wrote that they were "cruel and unusual in the same way that being struck by lightning is cruel and unusual," falling on "a capriciously selected random handful." North Carolina answered by making death mandatory for first-degree murder, and Woodson struck that down. I side with Furman's diagnosis. The arbitrariness critics rightly condemn lives in discretion, and a mandatory sentence behind a strict evidence bar removes it. Cornell LII – Furman v. Georgia, 408 U.S. 238 (1972) Cornell LII – Woodson v. North Carolina, 428 U.S. 280 (1976)
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: "Won't other countries refuse to extradite fugitives who face death?"
body: Many will. Under the U.S.-U.K. treaty, the United Kingdom may refuse extradition for a capital crime unless the United States assures it that the death penalty will not be imposed or carried out, and the United States has agreed to similar terms with France, Poland, Argentina, South Korea, India, and Peru. In Soering v. United Kingdom (1989), the European Court of Human Rights blocked an extradition to Virginia largely because of the years spent on death row. I abolish death row, but the treaty terms stay. I believe the United States should not give no-death assurances. A capital sentence should not depend on where the offender fled. The United States should renegotiate the treaty clauses that require such assurances, and until they change, I accept that some fugitives will not be returned. UK Government – Extradition Treaty between the United Kingdom and the United States, Cm 7146, Article 7 U.S. Senate Treaty Document 108-23 – Extradition Treaty with the United Kingdom, letter of submittal European Court of Human Rights – Soering v. the United Kingdom (1989)
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: "Most Western democracies have abolished the death penalty. Why go the other way?"
body: They have, and I don't treat their practice as the moral standard. A punishment is not right or wrong because the countries nearest to us adopted or rejected it. The standard I use is the victim's rights: a murderer who deliberately ends a life forfeits their own right to life, and the sentence answers what was done to the victim, not what is comfortable for the state (Moral Psychology of Rights & Forfeiture). The real constraint is accuracy, which is why the evidentiary standard comes first (Evidentiary Standard).
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: "Does forfeiture let the state add suffering beyond the sentence?"
body: No. Forfeiture would remove the offender's claim against the sentence the law should set: execution, the experimentation track under the rules in Section 10, or compelled labor. Within that sentence the forfeiture is complete. On the experimentation track the sentence is the research itself, and the subject's suffering in it is irrelevant: the law should set no limit on it (Section 10). They didn't care if their victim suffered, so the law ought not care about their suffering once their rights are forfeited. What forfeiture does not reach is harm outside the lawful sentence. Beatings, deprivation, or cruelty by guards or other inmates that the sentence does not call for remain rights violations against the offender and should be punished, because that harm would serve no sentence the law had set.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: "Isn't the death penalty applied with racial bias?"
body: The historical record supports the concern. A 1990 review by the Government Accountability Office covered 28 studies. In 82 percent of them, the race of the victim influenced whether a defendant was charged with capital murder or sentenced to death. Those who killed white victims were more likely to face death than those who killed black victims. Legally relevant factors such as prior record and heinousness did not fully explain the gap, and the effect was strongest at the earliest stages, when prosecutors decide whether to seek death and whether to accept a plea. The race of the defendant had a less clear effect. I answer this where the disparity arises. The death sentence should be mandatory once the capital evidentiary standard is met. So neither the prosecutor nor the jury chooses who among the guilty faces death, and plea bargaining cannot take a capital case off that track. Discretion still remains in investigation and charging, so charging decisions in capital-eligible cases should be audited and published by the race of victim and defendant.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: "Won't a death penalty for child rape stop families from reporting abuse, or push offenders to kill the child?"
body: The concern is serious. Most sexual abuse of children is committed by someone the child knows: in Bureau of Justice Statistics data, family members were 34 percent of the offenders against juvenile victims, and 42 percent for victims aged 6 to 11. In Kennedy v. Louisiana the Supreme Court reasoned that a capital penalty could discourage families from reporting an abuser who is a relative and could remove an offender's incentive to keep the victim alive. That is the Court's reasoning, not a measured finding. No study has measured either effect. I answer the second risk directly: killing or trying to kill a victim or witness is an automatic capital aggravator in every case. I'm also honest about the first. Most abuse inside families leaves no camera footage or independent physical proof, so under the capital evidentiary standard most family cases will be tried on the non-capital tracks, where they are still punished.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: "Why death for crimes where the victim lived?"
body: Because the sentence answers what was done to the victim, and because of who is left exposed if the offender lives to do it again. Violent rape, child rape, and trafficking leave the victim alive to carry the harm, and the next victim is a person no court has met yet. The risk is measured: in a federal nine-year follow-up of state prisoners released in 2005, released sex offenders were "more than three times as likely as other released prisoners to be arrested for rape or sexual assault (7.7% versus 2.3%)," and they were 5% of releases but 16% of the later arrests for rape or sexual assault. The two errors are not equal. The capital track opens only when the proof meets the capital evidentiary standard, so the error left on it is small and is reported every year (Capital Trials); a case that falls short still goes to the non-capital tracks. A lighter sentence for a proven rapist or trafficker puts the risk of a repeat on someone who never agreed to carry it. No law can pick out in advance the proven offender who would never strike again, and when it guesses wrong, the next victim pays, not the offender. Bureau of Justice Statistics (Alper & Durose) – Recidivism of Sex Offenders Released from State Prison: A 9-Year Follow-Up (2005-14) (2019)
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

head: Rationale
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: Under the rights-forfeiture principle, an agent who deliberately violates the most basic negative rights of another cannot claim the full protection of those same rights. Murder destroys the victim's subjective experience entirely and permanently. Rape is among the gravest violations of bodily integrity short of death. The response is matched to the severity of the act: proportionality in my framework means the punishment reflects the seriousness of the violation. For the worst violations, that is the most serious punishment available.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: The refusal to exempt incompetent offenders follows from where moral weight is placed. I'm concerned with outward rights violations, not with the inner condition of the violator. The victim is equally dead whether the killer understood the proceedings or not. Execution still requires agency: a person who was completely unaware and incompetent did not act as an agent, so they are removed from society, imprisoned or confined rather than executed. Discretionary sentencing introduces inconsistency: two offenders who commit the same act receive different outcomes depending on the jury, the county, and the quality of mitigation evidence. A mandatory rule treats like cases alike. The historical risk with mandatory statutes, noted in Woodson v. North Carolina, was that juries refused to convict to avoid the sentence. The clear-cut evidentiary standard narrows capital cases to those where guilt is not in serious dispute, which reduces that pressure.
topic: Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty

body: Restitution follows the same logic of reciprocity. The offender, not uninvolved taxpayers, should bear the cost of the harm. Where an offender is executed or serving a long sentence, restitution should be drawn from their own pre-existing bank accounts and assets, and forfeited property and assets should go to restitution, victims first. This is not payment for labor. It is the offender's own existing resources.

body: In my view a self-defense killing that went too far but was close to justified should be a lesser homicide with a lighter sentence set by the judge. The prosecution should have to prove intent, and should have to prove any aggravating factor for a capital charge.

I treat a killing in self-defense that was excessive but close to justified as a lesser homicide, with a lighter sentence set by the judge. No duty to retreat and no location limit should stay as they are. The prosecution ought to bear the burden of proving intent for the lesser charge, and of proving any aggravating factor that pushes a killing to the capital track, not just the act itself. Self-defense itself is set out in Section 3, Authority & Civil Liberties.

head: "Why not treat any killing beyond justified self-defense as murder?"
body: A person who was really under attack and went too far did not set out to violate anyone's rights. The aggressor started the encounter. Murder on the capital track requires a deliberate violation. A near-justified killing is still a wrong and should be punished, but more lightly, and the prosecution should have to prove the intent behind it.

Current federal law already separates killing with malice from killing without it: manslaughter is the unlawful killing of a human being without malice. The law ought to keep that line for self-defense that went too far, so a near-justified killing is not treated as murder on the capital track. The prosecution carries the burden on intent and on any aggravating factor that would move a killing to the capital track.
Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 1112: Manslaughter
See also: Self-Defense and Defense of Others

I hold that extreme violence, intentional neglect, beating without drawing blood, and withholding food, water, or shelter as punishment against a spouse or family member should be capital if they cause lasting injury. Otherwise they would fall in the grave tier, so each would count as three marks at once: execution, experimentation, or life with labor. Other domestic violence should be aggravated and carry an extra penalty. Capital rules apply as anywhere, and guns are removed only through a red flag court finding.

I believe violence by an aggressor toward their own spouse or family is worse than violence between strangers, because it betrays the people the aggressor is supposed to protect. Murder, attempted murder, violent rape, and kidnapping inside a household should be capital as anywhere else, and so should the four cruelty acts, extreme violence, intentional neglect, beating without drawing blood, and withholding food, water, or shelter as deliberate punishment, when they cause lasting injury. Without lasting injury, these acts, and other grave abuse that does serious harm without killing, often driven by anger, would fall in the grave tier: three marks at once, reaching the threshold: execution, experimentation, or life with labor, as the victim chooses. Beating a spouse without drawing blood should be capital if it causes lasting injury and otherwise should fall in the grave tier. Beating means force beyond ordinary discipline: a closed fist, an object, or repeated strikes; a swat on the rear as ordinary discipline is not beating. These offenders sit below the capital tier of serial killers, murderers, and rapists; their lifelong labor rests on their own forfeiture and is not ownership. Other domestic violence should be an aggravated offense, carrying an extra penalty on top of the penalty for the same act against a stranger. Protective orders should be issued by a judge on evidence, and firearms removed only through the red flag rule: a court finding that the person directly imposes a severe, non-consensual risk of serious harm on others (Gun Rights). Domestic violence convictions would count toward the repeat-offender threshold.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

France, 19 Dec 2024: a court in Avignon sentenced Dominique Pelicot to the maximum 20 years for aggravated rape after he drugged his then-wife Gisèle Pelicot and invited dozens of strangers to rape her over nearly a decade. All 50 co-defendants were found guilty, with terms of 3 to 15 years. BBC News – Gisèle Pelicot's ex-husband jailed for 20 years in mass rape trial

head: "Why punish violence against family more harshly than violence against strangers?"
body: The aggressor holds a position of trust and often power over the victim, who may depend on them and cannot easily leave. Abusing that trust is a further betrayal on top of the act itself. The same act would get the same base penalty, and the household setting would add to it.
In preliminary federal data for fiscal year 2024, domestic violence was recorded as a circumstance in 9% (16,101) of children's entries into foster care.
ACF Children's Bureau – The AFCARS Dashboard, FFY 2024
See also: Gun Rights

Human trafficking of adults or children, and kidnapping, are egregious rights violations, and I believe they must be capital. Consensual adult sex work should stay legal. Force, fraud, or coercion makes it trafficking.

Trafficking a person by force, fraud, or coercion, for labor or for sex, takes a person's body and labor without consent. Human trafficking, adult or child, is an egregious rights violation, and I would make it capital, as I would kidnapping (Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty). The same strict evidentiary standard applies.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Kansas, 7 Aug 2025: a federal judge sentenced six former members of a group to between five years' probation and 10 years in prison for a years-long conspiracy to compel the labor of children. A jury had convicted all six of forced labor conspiracy in September 2024 after a 26-day trial. U.S. Department of Justice – Six Former Cult Members Sentenced for Years-Long Forced Labor Conspiracy to Compel the Labor of Multiple Minor Victims

head: "Doesn't legal prostitution make trafficking easier?"
body: Legal, regulated prostitution among consenting adults is separate from trafficking (Drugs and Vice). Consent is the line: once force, fraud, or coercion enters, it is trafficking, and the regulated trade is where that line can be enforced in the open. Cross-country data do link legalization to larger reported trafficking inflows. My answer, strict licensing, verification of every worker, and capital penalties for trafficking, is set out in Drugs and Vice.

Federal law already makes sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion, and sex trafficking of any child, a federal crime. In preliminary federal child-welfare data for fiscal year 2024, sex trafficking was recorded as a circumstance in 570 entries into foster care.
Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 1591: Sex trafficking of children or by force, fraud, or coercion
ACF Children's Bureau – The AFCARS Dashboard, FFY 2024
See also: Drugs and Vice

I would set the age of consent at 18, except under the close-in-age exception below, and a minor cannot consent to sex with an adult. Young people close in age are exempt: up to two years apart if the younger is under 16, and up to four years if the younger is 16 or 17 and the older is no more than 19. No one 20 or older is ever covered. Violent rape, child molestation, and child rape proven to the strict standard should be punished by death. Statutory rape based on age alone, with no force or violence, should be a serious non-capital crime.

The age of consent should be 18, except under the close-in-age exception below. A minor cannot consent to sex with an adult, and sex with a person who cannot consent is rape. Minors should not be allowed to marry. A close-in-age exception ought to apply only in two cases: when both parties are minors, or when the older party is 18 or 19 and the younger party is 16 or 17. The gap may be no more than two years when the younger party is under 16, and no more than four years when the younger party is 16 or 17. The exception never covers anyone 20 or older. Violent rape, child molestation, and child rape should be capital: where established under the capital evidentiary standard, they should be punished by death, as set out in Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty. Statutory rape, meaning sex with a minor based on age alone with no force or violence, is not capital in my code. It is still a crime and still wrong, and it should go through the regular criminal justice system with a serious non-capital sentence.

head: "Should a teenage couple close in age be treated the same as an adult preying on a child?"
body: No. When both parties are minors, or the older party is 18 or 19 and the younger is 16 or 17, and they are within the allowed gap (two years if the younger is under 16, four years if the younger is 16 or 17), the close-in-age exception applies. The exception never covers anyone 20 or older.

head: "Why 18 rather than 16?"
body: Eighteen is the line for adulthood throughout my framework: minors cannot consent to irreversible decisions about their bodies and cannot marry. A single line avoids a patchwork of ages, and the close-in-age exception covers peers so teenagers are not treated as predators. The rule protects 16- and 17-year-olds from adults, the partners the evidence links to harm: girls under 18 with partners six or more years older had pregnancy rates 3.7 times higher than girls with partners within two years (Rationale below). The two errors are not equal. A line set too high makes an adult wait until a minor turns 18, while peers stay covered by the close-in-age exception; a line set too low leaves a 16-year-old open to an adult of any age.

Consent is what separates a lawful act from a rights violation, and I already hold that minors cannot enter certain binding agreements: they cannot marry (Cultural & Social Issues) and are excluded from assisted death. The same principle applies to animals, which cannot consent to sexual activity (Animal Cruelty Law). Federal law currently criminalizes sexual acts with minors aged 12 to 15 by a person at least four years older (18 U.S.C. § 2243). State ages of consent range from 16 to 18.

Research on teen sexual partners finds that harm clusters at age gaps of about five to six years or more and grows stronger the younger the teen. Girls under 18 with partners six or more years older had pregnancy rates 3.7 times higher than girls with partners within two years. No study identifies a single optimal gap. The sliding scale here, tighter for younger teens, is my own line drawn from that gradient, not a directly measured threshold. Most U.S. states with a close-in-age exception use a gap of two to four years, with four years the most common.

Ryan et al., Guttmacher Institute – Older Sexual Partners During Adolescence: Links to Reproductive Health Outcomes in Young Adulthood

I would ban all sexual contact between blood relatives, of any degree, including between consenting adults, as a precaution against reproduction. Between consenting adults it is a misdemeanor punished by an income-scaled fine plus labor for both partners. A third offense is one mark. I don't necessarily think incest is unethical in itself, but a child conceived even by accident would have to be carried to term, and legalizing it would lead to more children born to blood relatives, with serious genetic risk. Sex between a parent, step-parent, or similar guardian figure and their adult child is not valid consent. Blood relatives may not marry. Incest involving a minor is criminal under the rules already set out for child molestation, child rape, and statutory rape.

I would ban all sexual contact between blood relatives, of any degree, including between consenting adults, as a precaution against reproduction. I don't necessarily think incest is unethical in itself. But even accidental reproduction, though criminal, would have to be carried to term, because I am anti-abortion and a consensual pregnancy cannot be ended (Abortion and Bioethics). Legalizing it would lead to more children born to blood relatives, with serious genetic risk, which would be harmful to those children and to society. Step family is not under the blood-relative ban.

Offense: Consensual sexual contact between adult blood relatives is an offense meant to deter, not a mark. It is a misdemeanor punished by a fine plus labor, with the fine scaled to income so that it deters, and both partners are sentenced. A third offense becomes one mark.

Scope: The ban covers all sexual contact, not just intercourse, and every pair of blood relatives, including same-sex pairs and pairs who are infertile or past childbearing age. It is a blanket rule for consistency, not tailored to each couple's chance of conceiving.
Children: A child born to blood relatives has full rights, and both parents owe the normal support duties.

Parental figures: Sex between a parent, step-parent, or similar guardian figure and their adult child is not valid consent. A relationship that began with one person raising the other carries an added layer of lifetime grooming, or developmental romance, that turning 18 does not erase. A step-parent who joined the family after the child was already an adult is not a parental figure. Sex without valid consent is rape, so these cases fall under the rape rules, and where a parent and adult child are also blood relatives, the rape rule governs rather than the incest fine. Sex the adult child entered willingly, without force or violence, should be two marks, the same as statutory rape. Forced cases follow the violent-rape track in Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty. This applies equally to a step-parent who raised the child. A pregnancy from parental-figure sex the adult child entered willingly does not qualify for the rape exception to the abortion rules (Abortion and Bioethics), since the act was willing even though the law does not count it as valid consent. A pregnancy from forced parental-figure rape keeps the exception.

Minors: Incest involving a minor is criminal. A minor cannot consent to sex with an adult (Age of Consent), so a relative who has sex with a minor should be punished under the existing rules: violent rape, child molestation, and child rape proven to the capital evidentiary standard should be capital, and statutory rape based on age alone, with no force or violence, should be a two-mark crime. The close-in-age exception applies between relatives the same as between anyone else. A minor's pregnancy from sex with a relative keeps the abortion rape exception, since a minor cannot consent.
Marriage: Blood relatives should not be allowed to marry. Step relatives other than parental figures may (Marriage Law).
Sex without valid consent between relatives is rape, as it is between anyone else.

head: "What about the risk to children?"
body: The risk is real and large for the closest relatives. In four studies of 213 children of first-degree unions (parent and child, or brother and sister) compiled in the National Society of Genetic Counselors' 2002 review, 46% were normal; 11.7% had known recessive disorders, 16% congenital malformations or sudden infant death, 11.7% severe and 14.6% mild intellectual impairment. Those studies have serious ascertainment biases, such as young maternal age, parental disability, and uncertain paternity. In a Canadian study of 21 children identified from a history of incest, 9 (43%) had severe abnormalities. The risk falls sharply with distance: for first cousins the review put the added risk of a significant birth defect at 1.7 to 2.8 percentage points above the general population's. The rule protects the child who would be conceived, who has no say in the risk and, because a consensual pregnancy cannot be ended, would be born to carry it. The two errors are not equal: two consenting adults wrongly barred lose a sexual relationship and keep every other part of their lives together, while a child conceived under the risk carries it for life. The ban also reaches pairs who cannot conceive, the price of one clear line (Rationale below).

head: "What about power dynamics and grooming?"
body: Sex between a parent, step-parent, or similar guardian figure and their adult child is not valid consent, as set out above. Beyond that, consent obtained by force, threat, or from someone unable to consent is not valid consent, and sex with a minor is criminal regardless. Some laws go further for family authority figures: Ohio, for example, makes sex by a parent, stepparent, guardian, or person in loco parentis a crime of sexual battery regardless of age, while not otherwise criminalizing adult incest. In Stübing v. Germany, the German courts found that the defendant's sister, who was 16 when the relationship began and seven years younger, was "considerably dependent" on him, and the German government argued the incest law protected weaker partners from structural imbalance in families.

head: "Where is adult incest legal?"
body: In the United States, New Jersey does not criminalize incest between people 18 or older, and Rhode Island between people 16 or older. Both still bar incestuous marriage. New Jersey repealed its incest crime in 1978, and a 2024 bill (A4524) would recreate it. Ohio prohibits incest only in parent-child type relationships. Most other states criminalize it, with penalties such as up to 5 years in Florida and up to 10 in Pennsylvania. In Europe, according to the comparative survey in Stübing v. Germany, consensual sex between adult siblings is not a crime in France, the Netherlands, Spain, Portugal, Belgium, Luxembourg, Russia, Turkey, and others, while Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland, Denmark, and others criminalize it. All the systems surveyed bar siblings from marrying. In 2012 the European Court of Human Rights unanimously held that Germany's conviction of a man for consensual incest with his sister did not violate his right to private life, citing the lack of consensus among member states and a wide margin of appreciation.

The ban is a precaution, not a judgment that incest is wrong in itself. Because a pregnancy from consensual sex cannot be ended, any child conceived between consenting blood relatives, even by accident, would be born, and the genetic risk to that child is high for the closest relatives (see the risk figures above). Banning the sexual relationship prevents those conceptions rather than leaving them to chance. The rule is blanket, covering all sexual contact and every pair of blood relatives, including same-sex and infertile pairs, for consistency: a single clear line is easier to know and enforce than case-by-case judgments about fertility. Because the aim is deterrence, not punishment of a rights violation, the offense should be a misdemeanor punished by an income-scaled fine plus labor, becoming a mark only on a third offense. My worry that legalization would lead to more children born to blood relatives is a concern, not a measured finding; I found no reliable data on births to related parents in places where adult incest is legal. A parental figure's lifelong influence over a child voids consent in adulthood, and abuse of a child is among the most serious crimes in my framework.

The opposing case is serious. In Stübing v. Germany, the German Federal Constitutional Court's dissenting judge called eugenic aims an invalid objective for criminal law, and the applicant argued that people at higher genetic risk, such as known carriers, are not forbidden to have children. The Court's majority, and then the European Court of Human Rights, upheld Germany's ban as protecting the family, the weaker partner, and public health. The German government itself said genetic risk alone would not justify the ban but could support it.

I support hot-spot, harsh crackdowns in gang and high-crime areas, and high-rate violent offenders should be incapacitated under full due process outside a declared emergency. Riots and blockades should be shut down immediately. El Salvador-model sweeps belong only inside a declared, time-limited emergency (riots / grave national danger / completely rampant local crime), with on-scene charging, trial, and sentencing. In my view law enforcement exists only to protect victims of rights violations.

High-crime and gang areas ought to receive intensive policing with swift and brutal crackdowns. Incarceration should target the incapacitation of high-rate violent offenders and gang members, with hot-spot policing concentrated where violence clusters, all under full due process, with individual charges, counsel, and trial, outside a declared emergency. Riots, road blockades, and takeovers should be swiftly and brutally shut down. I support zero tolerance for criminals. The only focus of law enforcement ought to be protecting the victims of perpetrators who violate sentient rights.

I believe El Salvador-model sweeps are justified in a declared emergency over riots and political violence like the 2020 riots or major movements taking over the streets. Grave danger to the nation; or areas with extraordinary, completely rampant crime, such as neighborhoods and parts of the country whose violent-crime rates are many times the national rate. Each such emergency should be declared, time-limited, and lapse unless the legislature renews it (Emergency Powers). In those conditions, charging, trial, and sentencing move to the law enforcement officers or military handling the emergency. Outside those conditions, the rules above stay.

El Salvador's official homicide rate fell from a mid-2010s peak on the order of 100+ per 100,000 to roughly 2 per 100,000 (about 1.9 in 2024 on the government's series) after Bukele's gang crackdown—an extraordinary drop. That series is not a full body count: it has excluded gang members killed in confrontations in some accounting, and human-rights monitors documented more than 260 deaths in custody from 2022 to mid-2024. Disappeared persons and classification fights remain. Due-process costs are separate from the rate. AP – El Salvador homicides, gangs, Bukele (2024) · Cristosal – El silencio no es opción (2024) I cite the direction and scale as evidence that concentrated force against territorial gangs can collapse murder rates. Counting and custody caveats do not reverse that direction. I do not treat every tactic as a template for peacetime U.S. due process. My El Salvador-model sweeps stay inside a declared, time-limited emergency (Emergency Powers).

head: "Does mass incarceration fit with abolishing permanent incarceration?"
body: Incarceration here means removing high-rate violent offenders and gang members from the streets, not idle life sentences. Broad, El Salvador-model sweeps are reserved for a declared emergency over riots and political violence like the 2020 riots or major movements taking over the streets. Grave danger to the nation; or areas with extraordinary, completely rampant crime, such as neighborhoods and parts of the country whose violent-crime rates are many times the national rate. Each such emergency should be declared, time-limited, and lapse unless the legislature renews it (Emergency Powers). Those incarcerated fall under the same rules set out in the sections above: compelled labor, restitution to victims, and the capital track for murder, violent rape, child molestation, child rape, kidnapping, human trafficking, and repeat offenders.

head: "Do Black and white Americans commit crime at different rates?"
body: Yes, for violent crime. When white means non-Hispanic white, not white plus most Hispanics, Black Americans were arrested about 10 times as often for robbery and about 4 times as often for aggravated assault in the latest official recast (BJS 2018). A 2024 victim survey that already counts white as non-Hispanic white shows the same direction: Black offenders were about 2.9 times the non-Hispanic white rate for violent incidents overall. I don't use FBI tables that fold most Hispanics into "white" as a white-American crime rate. Most violent crime stays within one race. Full tables, misrecording, parental-income and test-score accounts, and the settled / contested / unresolved summary: Race and Violent Crime.

head: "What do the numbers say about gun deaths and gun crime in the U.S.?"
body: Most U.S. gun deaths are suicides, not homicides. In 2024, 44,447 people died from gunshot injuries: 62% were suicides and 35% were homicides. Gun homicides fell 27% from their 2021 peak, while the gun suicide rate is near its all-time high. Handguns are the weapon in most gun murders where the type is known. Rifles, including what are called assault weapons, are a small share. Most criminals who carry guns do not buy them from a store, and mass shootings are a tiny share of gun deaths. Estimates of defensive gun use vary widely and remain disputed. Gun deaths by type, 2024 (CDC) Type Deaths Share Rate per 100,000 (age-adjusted) Suicide 27,593 62% 7.6 Homicide 15,364 35% 4.7 Law enforcement 636 1% — Accidental 450 1% — Undetermined 404 1% — Total 44,447 100% 12.8 Guns were used in 76% of all homicides and 57% of all suicides in 2024. The gun homicide rate rose from 3.5 per 100,000 in 2014 to 6.7 in 2021, then fell to 4.7 in 2024; its record was 7.2 in 1974. The gun suicide rate was 7.6 in 2024, close to the record of 7.7 in 1977. FBI data come from police agencies that report voluntarily, so they run lower than CDC death-certificate counts. Where prisoners who had a gun during their offense got it, 2016 (BJS) Source Share Off the street or underground market 43% Family or friends (gift, purchase, or borrowed) 25% Found at the crime scene 7% Bought in their own name from a licensed dealer 7% Theft 6% Gun show 0.8% Any non-retail source 90% 21% of state and federal prisoners had a gun during the offense they were imprisoned for, and 13% used one. Defensive gun use Estimate Uses per year National Crime Victimization Survey (BJS) about 47,000 (235,700 over 2007–2011). About 1% of nonfatal violent crimes Range across studies (National Academies) about 108,000 (NCVS) to more than 3 million (Kleck and others) The National Academies called defensive gun use a subject of controversy. The NCVS asks only people who first report being victims of a crime, and private surveys ask everyone, which may overcount. The true number is unknown. Mass shootings. There is no single definition. The FBI counted 24 active shooter incidents in 2024, down from 61 in 2021, with 23 people killed, about 0.15% of gun homicides. The Gun Violence Archive counts any shooting with four or more people shot. By that measure 510 people died in 2024, about 3% of gun homicides. Other countries. In 2023, the U.S. gun death rate of 13.2 per 100,000 was among the highest in the world but below Venezuela (45.8), El Salvador (40.4), Colombia (21.7), Mexico (19.8), and Brazil (17.4). Its gun homicide rate of 6.2 was lower than in more than two dozen countries and territories, but its gun suicide rate of 6.7 was second only to Greenland's. Critics point out that suicides are the largest share of gun deaths. Policing gangs and hot spots does not reach them, and red flag laws reach only people who are flagged in time. Background checks at licensed dealers apply to only a small share of guns used in crime, since 90% come from non-retail sources, which argues for enforcement against illegal markets and straw purchases as well. The homicide data point my way: gun homicide is concentrated, falling, and mostly committed with handguns rather than rifles, which fits targeting violent offenders over broad restrictions.

head: "If reported crime falls, isn't that proof the city got safer?"
body: Not by itself. Reported crime is what reaches the police after people choose to report and after they change where they go, what they carry, and how much private security they buy. A drop can mean less predation, or it can mean more walls, more stay-home, and less reporting. I treat NCVS-style victimization and CDC homicide as the primary safety read. FBI reported series stay useful for volume and for gaps that victim surveys already corroborate (Gun Crime and Violence).

Gun violence is concentrated in specific areas and among gang networks, so enforcement is concentrated there. The evidence favors targeting over scale. The National Research Council found that the growth of U.S. incarceration probably reduced crime, but by an uncertain and likely modest amount, with diminishing returns as prisons grew and long sentences efficient only for very high-rate or dangerous offenders. A Campbell systematic review of 65 studies found that hot-spot policing produces small but significant crime reductions, with benefits spreading to nearby areas rather than crime simply moving. El Salvador's large-scale arrests of gang members under its state of exception, in place since 2022, show that gang incapacitation can be sustained. Outside a declared emergency, it is carried out here under full due process, with individual charges, counsel, and trial; in those conditions, I accept El Salvador-model sweeps. Official homicides fell to 1.9 per 100,000 in 2024, though that count excludes gang members killed in confrontations, and human-rights monitors documented more than 260 deaths in custody from 2022 to mid-2024. Riots and blockades violate the rights of people and property owners who did nothing wrong, and tolerating them invites more. Directing law enforcement only at those who violate sentient rights keeps state power aimed at actual harm. FBI national crime statistics track reported violent crime and are one enforcement-volume signal for these policies. Safety is judged by victimization (NCVS and similar surveys), hard-to-hide deaths (CDC/vital homicide), and whether people must fortify or avoid ordinary life to stay unharmed — not by reported street crime alone after avoidance.

head: What is meant by zero tolerance?

body: Zero tolerance means every offense in the targeted categories is met with enforcement and punishment, without informal leniency or warnings. Here it applies to criminals who violate others' rights and to riots, blockades, and takeovers.
