Race is also misrecorded in the data, mostly by counting Hispanic and other nonwhite people as white. Federal standards treat Hispanic as an ethnicity rather than a race, so most Hispanics are recorded as white, and they have treated Middle Eastern and North African people as white. A 2024 revision makes Middle Eastern or North African a separate category, with agencies given until 2029 to comply. A study linking court and prison records to Census data found that 17% of court defendants and 10% of prisoners carry a race label that differs from their Census identity. Courts recorded only 15–16% of Hispanics as Hispanic, and the most common error was recording a Hispanic person as white. Black people were recorded accurately more than 96% of the time. Researchers who removed Hispanics from national arrest figures found that the Black share of homicide arrests averaged 64% rather than 51% over 1980–2008, and that the Black–white homicide arrest ratio averaged almost 12 to 1 rather than 7 to 1.

Several factors explain part of the gap, but not all of it. In a Chicago study, parents' marital status, immigrant generation, and neighborhood conditions explained over 60% of the Black–white gap in violence, with neighborhood conditions mattering most. The remainder was unexplained. Parental income does not close the gap either. Among men counted in the 2010 Census at ages 27–32, 21% of Black men raised in the poorest 1% of families were incarcerated, against 6.4% of white men. Among those raised in the richest 1%, 2.2% of Black men were incarcerated against 0.2% of white men, the same rate as white men raised at the 34th percentile of parental income. The authors, Chetty, Hendren, Jones & Porter, attribute the gap to environmental factors outside the family rather than ability. They call their findings inconsistent with a cognitive-ability explanation because, at the same parental income, Black women earn about as much as white women while Black men earn far less, and they see no biological reason an ability gap would differ by sex. Incarceration rates are very low for women of both races, so that comparison rests mainly on earnings. The study measured parents' income and, for earnings, their marital status, education and wealth, but not the ability or behavior of the parents or their sons, so it shows that parental income does not explain the gap without settling what does.

Teenage test scores statistically account for much of the incarceration gap. In the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, Black men were about 3.5 times as likely as white men to have been incarcerated when surveyed, and about 1.8 times as likely once their Armed Forces Qualification Test scores were held equal. Roland Fryer, NBER – Racial Inequality in the 21st Century: The Declining Significance of Discrimination (2010). For murder and rape, the racial makeup of state prisons closely tracks the racial makeup of arrests, and victims' descriptions of offenders closely match arrestees. For drug, weapons and aggravated-assault offenses, which leave more room for discretion, it tracks less closely. Beck & Blumstein, Journal of Quantitative Criminology – Racial Disproportionality in U.S. State Prisons (2018). In federal cases, Black defendants received sentences almost 10% longer than white defendants arrested for the same crimes with the same records, mostly through prosecutors' mandatory-minimum charges. Rehavi & Starr, Journal of Political Economy – Racial Disparity in Federal Criminal Sentences (2014)

Antisocial behavior is moderately heritable within populations, about 41% across twin and adoption studies, but no study has tested whether genes contribute to the Black–white difference in crime, and current genetic scores are on average about 4.9 times less accurate for people of African ancestry than for Europeans. Rhee & Waldman, Psychological Bulletin – Genetic and Environmental Influences on Antisocial Behavior: A Meta-Analysis of Twin and Adoption Studies (2002); Martin et al., Nature Genetics – Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities (2019). Settling the genetic question, including what causes the group gap in IQ and test scores, needs research the current tools cannot yet do: within-family designs such as comparisons of siblings whose ancestry differs, admixture studies that properly control for environment, and genetic scores that predict equally well across ancestries. Until then, the data can neither show nor rule out a genetic share.

Summary of findings. Settled: for murder and rape, the imprisonment gap largely reflects an arrest gap that victims' reports confirm (Beck & Blumstein). The incarceration gap persists at every level of parental income, and the related earnings gap persists among boys raised in the same neighborhood (Chetty et al.). Disparities inside the justice system, such as longer federal sentences, are real but much smaller (Rehavi & Starr). Contested: why the teenage test-score gap that statistically accounts for much of the incarceration gap exists (Fryer), and how much father absence, peers and street culture cause the gap rather than reflect it. Unresolved: whether genes contribute to the group gap at all, and if so how much.

Arrests and known offenders are not the same as all offending, homicide offender race is unknown in about a fifth of cases, victim surveys exclude homicide, and the FBI's 2021 switch to a new reporting system makes year-to-year comparisons around that time unreliable. Every offender should be judged as an individual, by the same law.
See also: Intelligence, Race, and Crime · Race and Diversity · Worldview

No average tells anything about an individual, and every person should be judged by the same standards. Below I separate what is settled from what is contested and what is unresolved, and the bottom line says which is which.

Size and trend. On adult tests of general mental ability, the average Black–white gap is about 1.1 standard deviations, roughly 16 IQ points, though it is smaller in some settings, such as among applicants for more complex jobs. Roth, Bevier, Bobko, Switzer & Tyler, Personnel Psychology – Ethnic Group Differences in Cognitive Ability in Employment and Educational Settings: A Meta-Analysis (2001). Whether it has narrowed is disputed. Dickens and Flynn found Black Americans gained 4 to 7 IQ points on whites between 1972 and 2002; Rushton and Jensen replied that the gap still stands at about 1.1 standard deviations and that the gains came from a selected set of tests; in their rejoinder Dickens and Flynn put the current gap at about 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9 standard deviations at ages 4, 12 and 18. Dickens & Flynn, Psychological Science – Black Americans Reduce the Racial IQ Gap (2006); Rushton & Jensen, Psychological Science – The Totality of Available Evidence Shows the Race IQ Gap Still Remains (2006); Dickens & Flynn, Psychological Science – Common Ground and Differences (2006). School test gaps narrowed most before the late 1980s. On the long-term NAEP reading test, the gap at age 9 fell from 44 points in 1971 to 23 in 2012, and at age 17 from 53 points in 1971 to 20 in 1988 before widening to 26 in 2012; the math gap at age 13 fell from 46 points in 1973 to 28 in 2012. NCES – Digest of Education Statistics, Table 221.85; NAGB – NAEP Long-Term Trend 2012

At equal income. In the 2003 SAT cohort, Black students from families earning more than $100,000 averaged 490 in math and 495 in verbal, about the same as white students from families earning under $10,000 (478 and 480). The study's authors found family income affected scores nearly twice as much for Black students, and note that Black and white families with similar incomes tend to differ in other social and economic ways. Dixon-Román, Everson & McArdle, Teachers College Record – Race, Poverty and SAT Scores (2013). Hereditarian researchers read the persistence of the gap at equal income as evidence that it is not simply a matter of class. Environmental researchers read it as evidence that income alone misses wealth, neighborhood and schooling, the same point the Chetty study makes about incarceration.

IQ and crime within groups. IQ predicts official delinquency at least as well as social class or race does, and independently of both, and delinquents average about 8 IQ points below non-delinquents. Hirschi & Hindelang, American Sociological Review – Intelligence and Delinquency: A Revisionist Review (1977); Herbert C. Quay, NCJRS – Intelligence, in Handbook of Juvenile Delinquency (1987). It is not only that low-IQ offenders get caught: in a New Zealand cohort, delinquents who were never detected scored as low as those who were. Moffitt & Silva, Journal of Abnormal Psychology – IQ and Delinquency: A Direct Test of the Differential Detection Hypothesis (1988). Among 700,514 Swedish men, lower conscription IQ predicted violent convictions. The link shrank between full brothers (from −0.19 to −0.10), so part of it comes from family factors, but most of it remained, and the authors note that genes and traits such as impulsivity could not be separated out. Frisell, Pawitan & Långström, PLOS ONE – Is the Association between General Cognitive Ability and Violent Crime Caused by Family-Level Confounders? (2012)

How much of the crime gap it accounts for. In the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, 2.4% of white men and 13.1% of Black men of average age were interviewed in a correctional facility, and holding IQ equal cut that difference by almost three-quarters. Herrnstein & Murray – The Bell Curve, ch. 14 (1994). Fryer's analysis of the same survey cut the incarceration ratio from 3.5 to about 1.8 once teenage test scores were held equal (see Race and Crime). These are statistical accounts, not proof of cause: teenage scores partly reflect home, school and neighborhood, so holding them equal also holds equal some of the environment that may drive both scores and crime.

IQ and earnings. AFQT embeds home, school, and neighborhood, and residual gaps on hours and employment remain after controls. Equalizing teenage AFQT scores still accounts for all of the Black–white wage gap among young women and about three-quarters among young men. Among year-round workers in Herrnstein and Murray's NLSY cut, equalizing IQ left Black wages near parity with White wages. A raw group earnings gap is a fact to explain, not proof of present discrimination, and equal-outcomes remedies that ignore measured skills fail on that evidence (Equal outcomes; Merit rule). Neal & Johnson, Journal of Political Economy – The Role of Premarket Factors in Black-White Wage Differences (1996) · Herrnstein & Murray – The Bell Curve, ch. 14 (1994)

Admixture. One study tested whether genetic ancestry predicts IQ among African Americans. In 2,179 African Americans aged 8 to 21 in Philadelphia, more European ancestry predicted a higher general ability score. Controlling for parental education modestly weakened the link, and controlling for genetically predicted skin, hair and eye color did not. A European-derived education polygenic score predicted ability about half as well in African Americans as in European Americans, and the authors estimate it may "naïvely" explain as much as 20–25% of the gap. Lasker, Pesta, Fuerst & Kirkegaard, Psych – Global Ancestry and Cognitive Ability (2019). The result is unreplicated in a nationally representative sample, and the authors themselves say their design cannot rule out many kinds of environmental confounding and that their SES control, parents' education only, is partial. Critics add that ancestry can track unmeasured environment such as wealth, neighborhood and treatment by others. That polygenic scores built from European samples lose much of their accuracy in people of African ancestry (see Race and Crime); and that the paper appeared in a new, low-profile journal. A critique of related work by the same research group called it "a cautionary example of fringe science entering the mainstream." Giangrande & Turkheimer, Perspectives on Psychological Science – Race, Ethnicity, and the Scarr-Rowe Hypothesis (2021)

Flynn and environmental arguments. Test scores rose worldwide by about 2.8 full-scale IQ points per decade across 271 samples from 31 countries between 1909 and 2013, with gains slowing in recent decades. Pietschnig & Voracek, Perspectives on Psychological Science – One Century of Global IQ Gains: A Formal Meta-Analysis of the Flynn Effect (1909–2013) (2015). Gains that large within a few generations show that environment can move scores by amounts comparable to the group gap. Nisbett and colleagues add that adoption from working-class to middle-class homes raises IQ by 12 to 18 points and that the Black–white gap has shrunk by about 0.33 standard deviations, and they conclude that group differences in IQ are best understood as environmental in origin. Nisbett et al., American Psychologist – Intelligence: New Findings and Theoretical Developments (2012); Nisbett et al., American Psychologist – Group Differences in IQ Are Best Understood as Environmental in Origin (2012). Hereditarian researchers answer that IQ is highly heritable within both groups, about 0.61 for African Americans and 0.72 for European Americans in the Philadelphia sample, that the tests measure the same abilities in both groups, and that the gap is concentrated in general ability (Lasker et al.). Heritability within groups does not by itself show what causes a gap between them, and a rise in scores over time does not by itself show that the group gap has the same cause.

Bottom line. Settled: a Black–white gap in average tested ability exists, about one standard deviation in adults and smaller in young children. It persists at equal family income; IQ predicts offending within groups, not only detection; and test scores statistically account for much of the incarceration gap. Contested: how much the adult gap has narrowed, how much of the IQ–crime link is causal, and how much of the gap environment explains. Unresolved: whether genes contribute to the group gap. The only DNA admixture study points toward a partial genetic share but is unreplicated and cannot exclude environmental confounding, and settling the question needs the research set out in Race and Crime. No average tells anything about an individual, and every person should be judged by the same standards.
See also: Race and Diversity

I treat domestic terrorism as a serious threat. Public data can be used to track it, and companies can share flagged data if users agreed to it. Islamist, communist, socialist, Nazi, anti-Western, and anti-constitutional ideologies should be watched as threats, and I rank Islam, communism, and socialism as dangerous as Nazism: all four are Civilizational Risks at the same level.

Domestic terror threats ought to be taken extremely seriously. I support targeted surveillance drawn from public data to fight them, within the limits in Authority & Civil Liberties, and private companies may share flagged data with government agencies when users have given clear, specific, separate consent to government sharing, not consent buried in terms of service. Islamist, communist, socialist, and Nazi ideologies should be monitored and treated as threats, with Islam, communism, and socialism flagged at the same level of danger as Nazism. The four excluded ideologies are Civilizational Risks, all at the same level. By violence, Islam is the most dangerous today; communism, carried today mainly through cultural Marxism, is equally insidious and poisonous to civilization by its wide acceptance among the young and in universities (Cultural Marxism). Anti-Western and anti-constitutional ideologies should be treated as threats. Monitoring ought to use only public data and lawful process and impose no legal penalty for belief; the two civic disabilities for excluded ideologies are not penalties. Islamist sympathy toward foreign terror agents and anti-Western governments should be monitored, and it should be punished as a threat of terror only where it amounts to a true threat or incitement to imminent violence. I would punish terrorism, material support to a designated terrorist organization, and treason under the attempted-murder rules, whoever commits them: death where guilt meets the capital evidentiary standard (Evidentiary Standard), otherwise secure confinement under compelled labor (Compelled Labor). Any knowing support, proven by a documented money trail or communications, counts. Deportation should never be used instead of punishment (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Texas, 23 Jun 2026: eight defendants were sentenced to a combined 450 years over the 4 July 2025 attack on the Prairieland ICE detention center in Alvarado, in which an Alvarado police officer was shot. Benjamin Song received 100 years for attempted murder. The Justice Department described them as an antifa cell and called it the first sentencing of antifa-affiliated defendants since the group's designation as a domestic terrorist organization. New Orleans, January 1, 2025: a driver who had posted videos proclaiming support for ISIS killed 14 people on Bourbon Street. FBI (2025) – Investigative Updates on the New Orleans Bourbon Street Attack

Sydney, December 14, 2025: two gunmen, a father and son, killed 15 people at a Chanukah by the Sea celebration at Bondi Beach. The motive rests on police allegations not yet tested at trial, but the court documents describe an attack inspired by the Islamic State: police allege the pair planned it for months, recorded a video manifesto in front of an IS flag, and had a "tennis ball bomb" and IS flags in their car. Trappes and La Verrière, France, October 23, 2026: a gunman shooting from a car killed one man and wounded five people. France's anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating it as terrorist murder committed because of the victims' real or supposed race, ethnicity, nation or religion, and a copy of Mein Kampf was found in the suspect's home. The suspect does not contest the facts but contests their racist character. Nothing has been tested at trial (News Commentary). franceinfo (2026) – Ce que l'on sait de l'attentat raciste à Trappes et La Verrière

head: "Does monitoring ideologies conflict with free speech absolutism?"
body: Speech is protected up to true threats and incitement to imminent violence, the same as for any other ideology. Monitoring uses public data, where no expectation of privacy exists, and private data only through clear, specific, separate user consent. Islamist sympathy is monitored and punished as a threat of terror only where it amounts to a true threat or incitement to imminent violence. The government's disgust with Nazism, communism, socialism, and Islam is expressed in its official voice through official condemnation, no platforms, no funding, and no public honors. Condemnation punishes no one's belief.

head: "Is left-wing or right-wing political violence worse in the U.S.?"
body: It depends on what is measured. Right-wing extremists have killed far more people since 1990. Left-wing unrest caused far more property damage, and left-wing attacks have risen since 2016. No neutral source counts all political violence by side, so the figures below come from different datasets and cannot be added together. Islamist violence is left out here. Deaths Measure Right-wing Left-wing Ideologically motivated homicides, 1990–2020 (Duran, ECDB) 227 incidents, 523 deaths (168 in Oklahoma City) 42 incidents, 78 deaths Fatal extremist attacks, Sept 2001–2016 (GAO, ECDB) 62 incidents, 106 deaths No deaths Terrorist attacks and plots, 1994–May 2020 (CSIS) 57% 25% Terrorist attacks and plots, Jan–July 4, 2025 (CSIS) 1 5 Property damage Event Side Damage 2020 unrest tied to Black Lives Matter protests, May 26–June 8, 2020, 20+ states Left-wing Insured losses over $2 billion, the largest civil-disorder loss on record January 6, 2021, Capitol breach Right-wing $2,881,360.20 in losses (DOJ, as of Oct 2022) Charges Event Side Federal charges 2020 unrest tied to Black Lives Matter protests Left-wing More than 300 people by Sept 2020, about 80 for arson or explosives and 35 for assaulting officers January 6, 2021 Right-wing About 1,583 people, about 608 for assaulting, resisting, or impeding officers; about 140 officers assaulted Since 2016, left-wing attacks and property damage have risen markedly. CSIS counts about 0.6 left-wing attacks and plots a year from 1994 to 2000 and about 4 a year from 2016 to 2024, and in 2025 left-wing incidents outnumbered right-wing ones for the first time in more than 30 years. The 2020 unrest was the largest civil-disorder insured loss on record, and DHS reports that assaults on ICE officers rose from 19 to 238 over the same ten months of 2024 and 2025. The numbers remain small, and left-wing attacks remain far less lethal. Terrorism datasets undercount riot violence. CSIS generally excludes riots, and counts January 6 only in part, through premeditated attacks made under cover of the riot. The Duran and GAO counts cover only killings. The labels are also rough. About 94% of the 2020 demonstrations tied to Black Lives Matter involved no violence or destruction, and much of the damage came from looting with no clear ideology. Neither DOJ nor the insurers code events as left or right. Duran's far-left category includes Black separatists and anarchists, and his far-right category includes white supremacists, militias, sovereign citizens, and anti-abortion extremists. Only 8 of the more than 19,000 U.S. homicides in 2020 were ideologically motivated.

Terrorism is a direct attack on sentient rights and on the trust a free society depends on. Public spaces and public data carry no expectation of privacy, so using them for security is consistent with my privacy rules, while private data remains protected unless the user consents. Communism and Nazism are both treated as totalitarian ideologies that have produced mass killing, so they share the same threat level. Socialism in the core sense shares it: imposed by force, it strips the same negative rights, and the largest famines tied to central planning came under it (Socialism). Islam shares it too, and the four are Civilizational Risks at one level. That parity reflects each ideology's historical record, not current incident counts. Federal data currently show racially or ethnically motivated and anti-government violent extremists committing the most domestic-terror incidents, and violent movements of that kind fall under the anti-constitutional threats already monitored. Federal law defines domestic terrorism as dangerous criminal acts intended to intimidate civilians or coerce government, and the designation process for foreign terrorist organizations provides the basis for treating support of foreign terror agents as a threat.

head: How does U.S. law define domestic terrorism?

body: Under 18 U.S.C. § 2331(5), domestic terrorism covers acts dangerous to human life that violate criminal law, occur primarily within the United States, and appear intended to intimidate or coerce a civilian population, influence government policy by intimidation or coercion, or affect government conduct by mass destruction, assassination, or kidnapping.

I hold that mental illness does not undo a rights violation: a mentally handicapped person who kills still commits murder. Whether agency was absent should be decided by a panel of forensic psychiatrists and a judge, not a jury. An insane killer is confined, with labor or an asylum, and treated, with a first check within two years and yearly checks after. Three straight years with no progress means execution. Progress means a decade of confinement, then possible supervised release if neutral clinicians find genuine progress and the release standard is met. The killing counts as two marks, the same as lesser homicide, toward the repeat-offender threshold: as an unchangeable threat to be removed, not as guilt. In my view "incompetent to stand trial" is usually applied too broadly. For the large majority of capital crime the approach is arrest, convict, execute, and these confinement rules apply only to the truly incompetent, which is rare.

I hold that moral agency does not matter for whether a rights violation occurs: a mentally handicapped person who kills still commits murder. Whether agency was absent should be decided by a panel of forensic psychiatrists and a judge, not a jury. An insane person who kills ought to be confined. Those who are able do labor; those who cannot are confined in an asylum. All receive rehabilitation or treatment. The first evaluation comes no later than two years after confinement begins, and progress checks follow every twelve months. Execution follows only when the panel finds no measurable progress at three consecutive annual checks. If the panel is split, or the evidence is incomplete, the default is continued confinement and treatment, not execution; a single dissenting expert blocks execution, as one blocks release. If they make progress, they remain in confinement and serve their sentence: a decade of confinement. When the decade is up, a person who is still deemed viable, rehabilitated, and showing great, genuine progress, as judged by a board of neutral clinicians in the asylum, may be released back into society under supervision for a period. The burden for release sits entirely on the confined person: the panel should have to find by clear and convincing evidence that agency is restored and that the risk of violence is minimal, and a single dissenting expert blocks release. The killing still counts as two marks, the same as lesser homicide, toward the repeat-offender threshold in Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life. They count because the person is an unchangeable threat to be removed, not as a finding of guilt. An insane offender whose act is not a killing should receive no marks and should be confined in secure treatment until no longer dangerous. The decade-plus confinement and panel release should apply to killings. Insanity is not a defense to the act, but it changes the outcome: a killer found to lack agency is confined and treated rather than sentenced as guilty, and the killing counts toward the repeat-offender threshold as a threat, not as guilt.

"Incompetent to stand trial" is usually applied too broadly, so people who are competent get labeled incompetent. For the large majority of capital crime, I believe the approach should be arrest, convict, execute. For the truly incompetent, the rules above stand: confinement, progress checks, and possible release after a decade. That case is rare.

head: "Isn't it cruel to hold the mentally ill responsible?"
body: A rights violation is a violation whatever the offender's mental state. An insane person who kills should be confined and treated, and should be given the chance to make progress. Release should come only after a decade of confinement and a finding that agency is restored and the risk of violence is minimal. A person who makes no progress should be executed.

head: "Doesn't current law forbid executing the insane?"
body: Yes. Under current doctrine it is barred. Ford v. Wainwright (1986) bars executing the currently insane and Atkins v. Virginia (2002) bars executing the intellectually disabled. The position here does not pretend otherwise. It is a normative claim about what the law ought to be. Achieving it would require the Court to revisit those holdings or a constitutional amendment.

head: "If a being without agency forfeits nothing, how can the state execute an insane killer?"
body: The execution is not forfeiture. It is defensive force against an ongoing, permanent threat. Rights give way to force aimed at the threat itself, and the person defending does not have to absorb serious harm because the attacker lacks culpability (Conflicts Between Rights-Holders). That is not harming an innocent person to benefit another. The insane killer has already killed and remains the source of the danger, so he is the threat, not a bystander. The law first gives him every chance: confinement and treatment, a first evaluation within two years, then yearly checks, with a split panel or a single dissenting expert defaulting to continued confinement. When the panel finds no measurable progress at three consecutive annual checks, the threat should be treated as permanent. Lifelong confinement achieves absolutely nothing. It is a total waste of resources, time, and manpower, spent indefinitely on a threat that will never change. So once permanence is found, the United States ought to remove the threat from society for good, and the case is closed. The people this protects are the nurses, guards, and other patients who share a ward with a killer the panel has found will not change. The years of treatment, the yearly reviews, and the rule that any dissent means continued confinement keep an error here as unlikely as the evidence allows.
The confinement, progress, release, and marks rules, including the non-killing case, are set out in the position and the questions above.

Moral agency is irrelevant to whether a violation occurred (Ethical and Philosophical Framework). In practice the insanity defense is rare. An eight-state study found it was raised in one percent of all felony cases, and only 26 percent of those who raised it were acquitted as not guilty by reason of insanity. The Supreme Court held in Kahler v. Kansas (2020) that due process does not require a state to adopt any particular insanity test. Under Ford v. Wainwright (1986), current doctrine holds that the Eighth Amendment prohibits executing the insane.

Cornell LII – Atkins v. Virginia (2002)

I would set no fixed age of criminal responsibility. How severely a minor is punished should depend on how serious the crime was. Sentences are served as work with training, and a minor whose crime is serious enough reaches the capital tier or three marks like an adult. A capital sentence for a minor first requires a clinician's individual maturity assessment.

There should be no fixed age of criminal liability. I hold that minors have full negative rights and are liable for their actions, and the extent of that liability is driven by the severity of the crime. Custodial sentences for minors, like all custodial sentences, are served as compelled labor, with the vocational and educational training that applies at one or two marks. Juveniles fall under the same rules: a minor whose crime is serious enough reaches the capital tier or three marks like an adult. I would allow no juvenile exception to the mandatory capital rule in Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty. Before a minor reaches the capital tier, a licensed clinician conducts an individual maturity assessment. A minor found not to have acted with an adult's capacity for self-control and judgment is sentenced below the capital tier, by the judge in proportion to the harm.

head: "Current law forbids executing anyone for a crime committed under 18. Why allow it?"
body: Roper v. Simmons (2005) bars the death penalty for offenses committed under 18, and Miller v. Alabama (2012) bars mandatory life without parole for juveniles. I depart from Roper as a normative position, and achieving it would require the Court to revisit that holding or a constitutional amendment. I also depart from Miller: minors whose crimes are serious enough reach the capital tier or three marks under the same rules as adults. The rule protects the victims, who are no less dead or violated because the offender was 17, and the clinician's maturity assessment protects the minor: one who did not act with an adult's self-control and judgment is sentenced below the capital tier. A fixed age errs in one direction only, by treating every minor as immature however the crime was planned and carried out. A minor who plans and commits a murder with an adult's judgment has made an adult's choice, and is sentenced for it.

Responsibility under my framework follows agency, and a fixed age line treats a fifteen-year-old who plans a murder the same as one who shoplifts. Tying liability to the severity of the act keeps the response proportional to what was done to the victim. Applying the same rules to minors whose crimes are serious enough follows from liability scaling with the severity of the crime, as described in Ethical and Philosophical Framework. The training provisions in Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor apply most naturally to young offenders, whose working lives are longest.

Critics cite the developmental evidence, which on average points their way: self-control and judgment keep maturing into the mid-twenties, and most serious juvenile offenders stop offending. The Pathways to Desistance study followed 1,354 serious juvenile offenders for seven years and found that desistance tracked gains in psychosocial maturity, especially impulse control. Averages do not decide individual cases, and the position rests on principle. The individual maturity assessment answers the evidence case by case: liability still follows the act, but a capital sentence requires a finding that the particular minor acted with an adult's capacity.
Roper v. Simmons (2005) – Death penalty barred for offenses committed under 18
Miller v. Alabama (2012) – Mandatory life without parole barred for juveniles
National Institute of Justice – Pathways to Desistance From Crime Among Juveniles and Adults

No one should be confined for being homeless or mentally ill. In my view a court may commit a seriously mentally ill person only on clear and convincing evidence that they endanger others' rights or have lost the capacity to survive unaided, starting with outpatient treatment, reviewed every six months, and ending when the danger or incapacity ends.

Being homeless or mentally ill is not a crime, and I don't believe it is by itself grounds for confinement. A person with serious mental illness should be committed only on a judicial finding, by clear and convincing evidence at a prompt hearing with counsel. The court should have to find that, because of the illness, the person (1) has violated, attempted, or credibly threatened to violate the rights of others, or (2) lacks the capacity to understand their situation and is unable to secure food, shelter, or care needed to survive. The least restrictive effective option comes first: court-ordered outpatient treatment before inpatient confinement. Commitment is reviewed by a court at least every six months and ends when the person is no longer dangerous or has regained capacity, the same "until no longer dangerous" rule that governs insane offenders whose act was not a killing (Insanity Defense). A person with capacity who refuses treatment and harms no one ought to keep that choice. Camping and drug use on public property should stay prohibited for everyone under the ordinary rules (Housing, Zoning, and Homelessness).

head: "Isn't involuntary commitment a violation of liberty for people who haven't committed a crime?"
body: The objection targets a rule this framework does not have: liberty cannot be taken because someone is sick, poor, or unpleasant to see. In O'Connor v. Donaldson (1975) the Supreme Court held that a state cannot confine a non-dangerous person who can live safely in freedom, and I agree. Commitment should be allowed only on two grounds that fit its foundation. The first is danger to others, which is protection of other people's negative rights. The second is lost capacity: rights rest on sentience, not agency, so a person who cannot understand their situation is protected the way a child or incompetent adult is (Minors and Incompetent Adults), not punished. A capable adult who refuses help and harms no one is left free.

head: "Does court-ordered treatment actually work?"
body: Critics cite the OCTET randomized trial in England, where community treatment orders did not reduce readmission: 36% of patients were readmitted in both groups over 12 months. New York's assisted outpatient treatment program (Kendra's Law) was linked with fewer hospital admissions: about 25% lower odds during the first six-month order and over a third lower during renewals, in an observational study of 3,576 people. The evidence reads one way: court orders help when they bring intensive services with them, and do little alone. So outpatient orders under my framework come with assigned treatment and case management, and the program publishes its outcomes so it can be judged by results.

head: "How many homeless people does this concern?"
body: On one night in January 2024, 771,480 people were homeless in the United States, and 139,964 were reported as severely mentally ill, about 18%. Among the unsheltered, 67,235 of 274,224 were, about 25%. Most homeless people are not severely mentally ill, which is why mental illness is never a stand-in for homelessness.

I protect people from interference by others, so danger to others is the clearest ground for confining anyone. Lost capacity is the second ground because rights rest on sentience rather than agency: a person who cannot understand their situation is protected, as children are, rather than left to die in the street. The clear and convincing standard follows Addington v. Texas (1979), which set it as the constitutional minimum for civil commitment. The evidence on court-ordered treatment favors orders that carry real services, so the state ought to tie every order to them and measure the results.

Swartz et al., Psychiatric Services – Assessing Outcomes for Consumers in New York's Assisted Outpatient Treatment Program (2010)
Burns et al., The Lancet – Community Treatment Orders for Patients with Psychosis (OCTET): A Randomised Controlled Trial (2013)

head: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

body: I believe repeat offenders who keep committing crimes after being punished should lose their right to life once they reach three marks (marks are weighted by the crime, not counted per conviction: a grave crime counts as all three at once), provided they are still active. At least one earlier mark must fall within the ten years before the new crime. The victim chooses among execution, experimentation, or, if they are competent and well behaved, life with labor. When multiple victims disagree, or when the victim is an animal, a judge makes the decision instead of the victim. Where the victim has died, the experimentation track is the default unless the victim's close family or friends step forward and choose, and it stays the default if they disagree.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

head: Position
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

body: The repeat-offender threshold should be three marks: I hold that at three marks the offender forfeits the right to life. Marks stay on the record permanently, but the automatic threshold applies only to active offenders - when the threshold is reached by accumulating marks, at least one earlier mark should fall within the ten years before the new offense. A grave-tier crime that counts as three marks at once reaches the threshold on its own. The principle: someone who robs and steals again and again, and is caught each time, has shown that the community cannot be protected by ordinary sentences.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

body: Once the threshold is reached, I would allow three outcomes and let the victim choose among them: execution, experimentation on the experimentation track, or life with labor (open only to offenders judged competent and well behaved). When multiple victims disagree, or when the victim is an animal, a judge should decide instead. Where the victim has died, the sentence defaults to the experimentation track unless the victim's close family or friends step forward by the sentencing hearing and choose, and it stays there if they disagree. A later disqualifying act ends the labor status and results in execution. Execution and the experimentation track at the threshold require that the threshold offense be proven to the capital evidentiary standard in Evidentiary Standard. Where it is proven only beyond a reasonable doubt, the outcome is life with labor. Mark-tier definitions, labor rules, organ rule, and related ops are in the Mark tiers note below - not repeated here.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

head: Documented accounts

body: Charlotte, 2025: the man federally charged with fatally stabbing Iryna Zarutska on the light rail had court records listing 14 prior cases dating to 2011, including convictions for armed robbery, felony larceny and breaking and entering. head: "Executing someone for theft is wildly disproportionate. How can stealing ever justify death?"
body: The sentence does not answer the last theft by itself. It answers a pattern. A single theft should be punished with a finite sentence. The capital consequence should attach only after the offender has been convicted repeatedly, served sentences each time, and returned to violating others' rights. At that point the question is no longer what one theft deserves. It is whether the community must keep absorbing an offender who has shown, through repeated choices, that they will not respect the rights of others. Forfeiture in my framework scales with the pattern as well as the act. Repeated predation erodes the trust a free society depends on, and the state's first duty is to protect the innocent from that erosion. The pattern is real: of state prisoners released in 2008, 82% were arrested again within 10 years, and the people who pay for each further chance are the next victims, who were never asked. The ten-year activity rule already leaves out anyone whose record shows they stopped. Experimentation and life with labor also mean execution is not the only outcome at the threshold, and the choice among the three belongs to the victim. When multiple victims disagree, or when the victim is an animal, a judge makes the decision instead of the victim. Where the victim has died, the experimentation track is the default unless the victim's close family or friends step forward and choose, and it stays the default if they disagree.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

head: "Can three ordinary convictions really cost a life?"
body: Not on ordinary proof alone. Wrongful convictions are documented at scale (Wrongful Convictions and Compensation), and lesser convictions often come by plea, with less scrutiny than a capital trial. A life should not be forfeited on a weaker standard of proof than murder requires. So marks still count toward the threshold. But execution or the experimentation track at the threshold requires that the threshold offense be proven to the capital evidentiary standard: objective evidence such as video and physical evidence, not testimony alone. Where the threshold offense is proven only beyond a reasonable doubt, the offender is removed from society for life under compelled labor instead. The community is protected either way. Death is reserved for cases where the proof leaves no serious doubt.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

head: "Won't juries refuse to convict if repeat theft can lead to death?"
body: Critics point to history. Under England's "Bloody Code," stealing goods worth 40 shillings or more from a dwelling house carried a mandatory death sentence until 1827, and juries often valued the goods below the threshold, sometimes implausibly, to spare the defendant. The practice was called "pious perjury" and had broad judicial and public support. Such verdicts declined once the death penalty for those thefts was abolished. That history condemns death for a single theft, which this is not. Death never follows a single theft: it requires three marks after earlier convictions and sentences, so a jury decides only whether this theft was committed, not whether this person dies. And at the threshold the victim chooses among execution, experimentation, and life with labor, so a non-capital outcome remains available. The state ought to track acquittal rates in threshold cases, so any jury that balks shows up in the data.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

head: "Why does the victim choose, rather than the state?"
body: The violation was done to the victim, so the person harmed has the strongest claim to decide among the outcomes the law should allow. The state should set the limits: only the three outcomes should exist, life with labor should require a competent, well-behaved offender, and a judge should stand in where the victim cannot decide.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

head: "Can a victim choose mercy below the three outcomes?"
body: No. The threshold protects the whole community, not only one victim, from an offender whose pattern shows ordinary sentences do not work. Life with labor is the most lenient outcome available.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

body: The original threshold was a third theft conviction. Each theft conviction now counts as one mark.

body: As I would define them, a felony is any offense worth two or more marks, or any capital-tier crime. A misdemeanor is any offense worth one mark or a fine without a mark.

body: Every mark requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt (In re Winship, 1970): due process requires proof "beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime" charged.

body: Grave-tier crimes, including the four abuse acts without lasting injury against a human or a higher-sentience animal, count as three marks immediately.

body: Every sentence short of execution or experimentation includes hard labor, at every stage of the tracks.

body: Life with labor should be open only to offenders judged competent and well behaved. Competence should be decided at sentencing by the same forensic panel and judge as in Insanity Defense, and competence should be presumed unless the panel finds otherwise. Conduct should be reviewed by a judge every twelve months on the prison record. An offender on life with labor should be moved to experimentation or execution only on a judge's finding, by clear and convincing evidence, of a new crime or a serious disciplinary violation. Execution should also require that the threshold offense or the new crime meets the capital evidentiary standard. Incomplete evidence should leave the offender on life with labor.

body: Multiple victims may decide together. If they remain undecided, the judge is the arbiter. Where the victim declines, does not respond, or is incapacitated, or where there is no victim, the judge chooses at three marks. Large-scale distribution of hard drugs should be capital-tier, not a mark offense. With no single victim, the judge should choose between execution and the experimentation track. Giving or selling any hard drug to a minor is also capital-tier, at any quantity. Smaller drug transfers are mark offenses or a fine (Drug Policy).

body: Lesser tier: one mark for property crimes (theft, fraud, and similar) and lower-sentience animal cruelty, such as to lower-class fish. Two marks for cruelty to higher-sentience animals outside the four acts and short of lasting injury, such as to dogs, cats, or livestock.

body: The rights-forfeiture principle holds that those who refuse to respect the basic negative rights of others cannot claim the full protection of those rights. Repetition matters to that judgment. A first offense may reflect a single bad choice. A pattern of offenses, each followed by punishment and release, shows a settled disposition to treat other people's property and safety as available for the taking. Each release under that pattern exposes new victims to a known risk.
topic: Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life

body: The state exists first to protect negative rights. Continuing to release a known repeat predator into the community, or to house them indefinitely at public expense, is a failure of that duty. Once the number is fixed in statute, the threshold makes the consequence predictable in advance: every offender knows where the line is, and every conviction before it is an explicit warning. Property offenders reoffend at the highest rate of any group (78.3% rearrested within five years in BJS data), and California's three-strikes law cut arrests among offenders facing a third strike by 17–20%. The statutory number should be set with that evidence. The ten-year window follows the desistance evidence. Offending falls steeply with age, and most offenders stop. The National Research Council found long sentences efficient only for very high-rate offenders. So the threshold is aimed at people who are still offending rather than those who have aged out.

body: All fines, criminal, civil, and regulatory, should be scaled to the offender's income and wealth, for corporations as well as individuals, so that a fine is felt equally by rich and poor. I'd have individuals pay day fines: the number of days set by the offense, each day worth about half a day's net income plus about 0.05% of net wealth, and every fine sentence includes labor alongside the money, scaled to the severity of the offense. Corporations would pay up to 4% of global revenue, or their gain from the offense if higher, and the CEO would be personally responsible.

All criminal sanctions and fines should be scaled to income, including for corporations. A fixed fine that deters a low-income offender is a trivial cost to a wealthy one, and a fine meant to deter should be felt the same by both. The rule would cover every monetary sanction, criminal, civil, and regulatory. It would not change the mark system, the length of labor terms, or restitution, which is set by the harm done to the victim, not by the offender's means.
Basis: Fines should be scaled to income plus wealth, so that someone with large assets but little reported income is not let off lightly.

Individuals: Fines would be set in day-fine units and would be a pure percentage, with no fixed floor and no cap. The number of days would be set by the severity of the offense: 1 to 60 for misdemeanors, 61 to 360 for felonies. Each day fine would be about half a day's net income plus about 0.05% of net wealth, with a small deduction for each dependent. At the maximum of 360 days, the wealth share alone would come to about 18% of net wealth.

Labor: I believe labor should always be a factor. Every fine sentence for an individual would include a labor component alongside the money, not only as a fallback for non-payment. Labor would scale with severity, and would be hard on crime:
Misdemeanor · 1 to 60 · 30 days to 6 months
Felony · 61 to 360 · 6 months to 5 years

Where the offense also carries marks, this labor would be added on top of the mark's fixed-term sentence, not merged with it. The labor from a fine at the two-mark tier would be capped at 5 years. The judge would set the term within the range in proportion to the harm. Minor regulatory fines involving no wrongdoing would be exempt from the labor component.
As a guideline, misdemeanor labor would run about 3 days per day fine, at least 30 days and at most 6 months. Felony labor would run about 5 days per day fine, at least 6 months and at most 5 years.

Corporations: A corporation would be fined up to 4% of its global revenue, or its gain from the offense if that is higher, so that a fine would never cost less than the crime earned. I hold the CEO personally responsible, as they are ultimately responsible for the actions of the company: the CEO would serve the labor component and would be personally fined, scaled to their own income and wealth, alongside the corporate revenue fine. The law would default to the CEO because otherwise corporations would establish fault-officers by default who would be the ones to do labor if the corporation is indicted. Naming a designated fault-officer would not shield the CEO. Officers and controlling shareholders who authorized the violation would answer as well (Corporations as Moral Entities). For fines, a CEO who proves they acted to prevent or report the crime would not be held responsible for it. For marks, the CEO's own involvement should have to be proven beyond reasonable doubt, as my framework requires for any mark. The same default would apply to the heads of nonprofits and religious groups (High-Control Groups) and to the CEOs of foreign companies operating in the United States.

Civil and regulatory fines: A regulator or civil court should assign each violation a day count by severity within the misdemeanor range, 1 to 60 days, and the value per day should follow the offender's income and wealth like any other fine. Corporate civil and regulatory fines should use the revenue rule: a percentage of global revenue up to 4%, or the gain from the violation if higher. A violation serious enough for the felony range should be prosecuted as a crime.
Income on record: The latest income on record should be used, and the offender should have the right to appeal if it is outdated.
Non-payment: An unpaid fine would be worked off as additional labor. Refusing to pay or work it off would add a mark. Marks, labor terms, and restitution would not be changed by income.

head: "How do countries with income-based fines work?"
body: Finland and Germany use day fines. In Finland the court sets a number of day fines for the offense, from 1 to 120, and the amount of each is one sixtieth of the offender's average monthly net income after a basic deduction of €255, with a minimum of €6. In 2002 a Nokia executive was fined about €116,000 for riding a motorcycle at 75 km/h in a 50 km/h zone, 14 day fines based on 1999 income boosted by stock options. A court later cut it to about €5,900 using more recent income. Germany sets 5 to 360 daily rates, each based on the offender's average daily net income and set between €1 and €30,000, while leaving the offender the minimum needed to live on.

head: "How would this apply to corporations?"
body: Existing law already scales some corporate penalties to size or gain. The EU's data protection regulation sets fines for the most serious violations at up to €20 million or 4% of a company's total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding year, whichever is higher. The U.S. Sentencing Commission's guidelines for organizations set a base fine as the greatest of a table amount for the offense, the organization's gain from the offense, or the loss it caused, then multiply it by a culpability score.

head: "Do income-based fines deter?"
body: The evidence that exists supports it. In the first U.S. trial, in Staten Island from 1987 to 1989, average fines rose by 25%, yet collection did not suffer: 85% of day-fine cases under new collection procedures paid in full, against 76% of fixed-fine cases the year before. A 2026 study in The Review of Economic Studies, using Finnish speeding tickets that become income-based above 20 km/h over the limit, found drivers did not slow down to avoid the higher fine beforehand, but those who received a fine about €200 larger were about 15% less likely to reoffend over the next six months, an effect driven by high-income drivers that faded after a year.

A fine is meant to deter or punish. Its weight depends on what it takes from the person who pays it. A flat amount falls hardest on the poor and barely touches the rich. The same offense is then punished unequally. Scaling to income and wealth would make the sanction equal in effect. Counting wealth would keep people with large assets but low income from paying little. For corporations, the fine would be tied to global revenue, or to the gain from the offense if that is higher. That would keep a fine from becoming just another cost of doing business. The number of days would stay separate from the value of each day. That would keep the seriousness of the offense visible no matter who committed it. Every fine would also carry labor, so no one could simply buy their way out of a sentence. A corporation cannot serve labor, so the person at its head would. The CEO would be ultimately responsible for the company's actions. Personal liability would keep a corporate fine from being an expense paid with shareholders' money while those in charge face nothing. The law would default to the CEO, not to whoever the company names. That would keep corporations from installing fault-officers to take the labor. The reversed burden would be limited to fines. A mark would change a person's standing toward the repeat-offender threshold, so it would require proof of the CEO's own involvement. Fine labor would be added on top of mark labor, not merged with it. That would keep the fine from being free for anyone already sentenced to marks. Finnish evidence suggests larger fines on higher earners do reduce reoffending in the short term. The Staten Island trial found income-based fines could be collected as reliably as fixed ones.

head: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

body: No one should sit in prison for life with nothing to do. I want all prison sentences served as required, generally supervised hard labor on public projects, and sentences for first and second offenses made much longer. First and second offenders would get job training, may work for private employers, who would pay for the work into restitution while the offender is not paid, and could take cognitive-behavioral programs, all without shortening the sentence or using taxpayer money. Grave abuse that causes no lasting injury, such as beating without drawing blood, would fall in the grave tier, so it would count as three marks at once: execution, experimentation, or life with labor. Lesser crimes would be one or two marks, served for a fixed term. The Constitution's ban on involuntary servitude expressly allows it as punishment for a crime.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

head: Position
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

body: I would abolish idle permanent incarceration in its entirety. Life sentences served in a cell and indefinite warehousing of prisoners should end; every long-term sentence, including life with labor at the repeat threshold, would be served as work. Every custodial sentence ought to be served as compelled labor, generally under supervision, on government projects such as building, cleaning, and the production of goods. The labor would be hard labor: difficult, demanding work, not comfortable or easy. Sentences for first and second offenses should be greatly increased in length, so that early offenses are not treated as cheap strikes before the threshold. The training, private-employer, unpaid-offender, opt-in rehab, and three-tier (capital / grave / one-or-two-mark) rules are in the In short above - not repeated here. Rights forfeited by an offender should be forfeited for the duration of the sentence, and at the repeat threshold they should be forfeited for life. Rehabilitation should remain secondary to retribution, incapacitation, and victim protection: it would be mandatory on every labor sentence and would run inside it; it would never shorten it, and it would be paid by opt-in donations or private employers, never by taxpayers.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

head: "Isn't lifelong compelled labor just slavery? Doesn't the Thirteenth Amendment forbid it?"
body: The Thirteenth Amendment prohibits slavery and involuntary servitude "except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted." Compelled labor imposed on a convicted offender falls within that stated exception, so the Constitution does not forbid it. The moral objection is a separate question and deserves a direct answer. Slavery as historically practiced seized people who had violated no one's rights, on the basis of race, and held them and their children as property. Compelled labor here applies only to individuals convicted of violating others' rights, as a consequence of their own choices. Under the forfeiture principle, an offender's claim against compelled labor is lost through the violation, just as a claim to liberty is lost through imprisonment. At the threshold it is one of the victim's three options, alongside execution and experimentation, not an addition to them. Lifelong labor, whether for a grave-tier crime or at the repeat threshold, is still not ownership. The offender has forfeited their liberty for life through their own violations, each proven in court. At the threshold, it is one of the three outcomes that forfeiture of the right to life allows. It is offered only to offenders judged competent and well behaved, and only where the victim chooses it in place of execution or experimentation. Ownership is claimed over people who forfeited nothing, passes to heirs, and reaches the owned person's children. Lifelong labor reaches no one but the offender, ends with the offender's life, and leaves untouched every right the offender did not forfeit. The state holds a sentence, not a person. The offender's labor offsets the cost their crimes have imposed on the public.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

head: "Doesn't the Eighth Amendment forbid hard labor, public execution, and the experimentation track?"
body: It may, as courts read the ban on cruel and unusual punishment. I support amending or abolishing the Eighth Amendment as needed so that hard labor, public execution, and the experimentation track are permitted. The same holds for capital punishment of animal murder: Kennedy v. Louisiana limits death for crimes against individuals to crimes that take the victim's life, and no court has held that an animal's life counts, so the amendment ought to say that it does. Treaty conflicts are handled in Global Institutions.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

head: "If an offender's labor is compelled, isn't the state owning them?"
body: No. For lesser crimes, the offender forfeited their rights for a term the judge sets in proportion to the harm, with a known end date. When it ends, full rights should return. For grave-tier crimes and at the repeat threshold, where the victim chooses life with labor, the sentence is for life. It rests on the offender's own forfeiture: it reaches no one else and leaves every unforfeited right intact. Ownership is claimed over people who forfeited nothing and passes no judgment on what the person did. Assigning work to the sentenced is not new to limited government either: federal regulation already provides that "each sentenced inmate who is physically and mentally able is to be assigned to an institutional, industrial, or commissary work program." eCFR – 28 CFR § 545.23: Inmate work/program assignment
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

head: "Doesn't adding rehabilitation contradict ranking it below punishment?"
body: No. The ranking is unchanged: the sentence length, the labor requirement, and restitution are fixed at sentencing, and no program shortens them. Training and therapy take place within the term the offender already serves. They're included because they serve my own aims: an offender who reoffends less creates fewer new victims.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

head: Rationale
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

body: Idle incarceration costs the public heavily while giving nothing back to victims or the community. State and local governments spent $87 billion on corrections in 2021. The Federal Bureau of Prisons reports an average cost of $47,162 per federal inmate per year (FY2024), and Vera Institute data put the 2015 state average at $33,274. These averages include fixed costs such as facilities and administration, so removing one prisoner saves less than the average figure. Even so, a life sentence commits taxpayers to housing, feeding, and guarding an offender for decades, which is a burden on people who did nothing wrong.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

body: Compelled labor turns the sentence into productive work that offsets part of that cost. It is not claimed to pay for incarceration in full. The federal model, Federal Prison Industries, receives no annual appropriation and runs as a self-funding revolving fund. In fiscal year 2025 it employed 19,560 inmates and reported $14.98 million in net income, though it posted a $37.4 million loss from operations, made up by interest and other income. Its output is real but small relative to the cost of the prison system. The stronger case for structured prison work lies in outcomes: the Washington State Institute for Public Policy estimates that correctional-industries programs return about $4,975 in benefits per participant, largely through reduced reoffending.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

body: Longer sentences for early offenses address a gap the threshold would otherwise create. If only the threshold carried serious consequences, the first and second offenses would look cheap by comparison. Raising their cost means every offense carries weight, and the threshold is not the only deterrent in the system. Longer sentences also serve incapacitation and desert, not only deterrence, and they operate alongside the certainty measures in this section: expanded policing, swift trials, and execution on the sentencing date.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

body: Training within the labor term serves victims and public safety. A RAND meta-analysis found that incarcerated adults who took part in correctional education had 43% lower odds of returning to prison, a 13-percentage-point reduction in three-year reincarceration risk. Vocational training raised the odds of post-release employment by 28%. Cognitive-behavioral programs reduced 12-month reoffending from 40% to 30% on average across 58 studies, with the largest effects among higher-risk offenders. Lower reoffending means fewer new victims. Set against an idle cell, compelled labor leaves everyone it touches better off: victims receive restitution, taxpayers who did nothing wrong carry less of the bill, and the offender leaves with a work record and training instead of years of idleness. The work is hard and unpaid because it is part of the sentence.
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

head: What is compelled labor?
topic: Abolition of Permanent Incarceration and Compelled Labor

body: Required, generally supervised hard labor, difficult and not comfortable or easy, on government projects (construction, cleaning, production of goods, and similar tasks) performed by convicted offenders as their sentence. It would replace idle time in a cell. For lesser crimes (one or two marks) it would last for a finite term with a known end date. Grave-tier crimes would count as three marks, where life with labor is one of the victim's three options. Past the threshold, for offenders judged competent and well behaved, it would last for life.

head: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

body: Capital trials should take 30 days at most, and the sentence should be carried out the day it is handed down. I want no death row, so no victim's family waits decades for a sentence already passed. The strict evidence rule is what makes this speed acceptable.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

head: Position
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

body: Capital trials should be capped at a maximum of 30 days. I would abolish death row as a concept. The sentencing hearing is held on the same-day sentencing date, so the victim's choice deadline and same-day execution align; the replacement judge's 30 days is the stated exception. There should be no waiting period between sentencing and execution. The sentence ought to be carried out on the sentencing date, except where the offender is placed on the experimentation track under Section 10. It is carried out first for incapacitation and finality, so the threat ends the day guilt is settled; any added deterrence is a hoped-for benefit that research has not tested (Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment). Victim-choice, registry, refusing-judge, and pregnancy exceptions are in the note below - not repeated here. Nobody should be held for years or decades under a death sentence, except on the experimentation track, and nobody is held idle for life as a substitute for one.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

head: Victim choice, registry, refusing judge, pregnancy
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

body: Between execution and experimentation, the victim has priority in choosing. If the victim does not respond or does not care, research can proceed, with research firms requesting bodies through a registry system. A research firm's request never overrides a victim who chose execution. The victim's choice always wins. The victim should be notified at conviction and should have to choose by the sentencing hearing. No response by then should count as not responding. When multiple victims disagree, or when the victim is an animal, a judge makes the decision instead of the victim. Where the victim of a capital crime has died, as in murder, the sentence defaults to the experimentation track, with research firms requesting the body through the registry, unless the victim's close family or friends step forward by the sentencing hearing and choose between execution and experimentation in the victim's place. If the family and friends disagree, the sentence stays on the experimentation track. The same rule applies at three marks, where they may choose among the three outcomes. A judge should not be permitted to refuse this choice: choosing should be the judge's duty, and a judge who refuses should no longer be a judge. A refusal should send the case neither to the registry nor to execution by default. The refusing judge is removed through the judicial conduct process, and a replacement judge decides the case within 30 days, even if that pushes sentencing past the same-day date. This is an exception to same-day sentencing and execution. A pregnant offender should not be executed, or placed in any experiment that risks the fetus, until the child is born, because the fetus has violated no one's rights (Axiom 3). The sentence should be carried out after the birth, a second exception to same-day execution.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

head: "Doesn't removing the appeals process just mean executing people before their mistakes can be found?"
body: The tradeoff is explicit: a much narrower set of capital cases in exchange for finality within those cases. Appeals exist mainly because the trial is not trusted to reach the right answer. In the current system, the gap between sentence and execution often runs to decades. That gap brings cost and uncertainty without a reliable gain in accuracy, since most of the time is procedural. I address accuracy at the trial stage instead: only cases meeting the clear-cut evidentiary standard reach a capital verdict. If the evidence needs years of review to settle, the case does not belong on the capital track. The current wait has victims of its own. Prisoners executed in 2022 had been on death row for an average of 249 months, more than 20 years in which a victim's family waits for the end of a sentence a court has already passed. Finality spares them that, and the independent panel review below runs in every capital case whether or not anyone files for it. The cost of finality is stated plainly in the next answer.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

head: "What if new evidence of innocence turns up after the verdict?"
body: Errors do surface late. The Death Penalty Information Center counts at least 203 people sentenced to death in the United States since 1973 who were later exonerated. Many of those cases rested on evidence that looked solid at trial, such as a confession, an eyewitness, or forensic testimony. The law keeps one narrow door open. Between verdict and sentencing date, the defense may bring new objective evidence that was not available at trial, such as DNA, video, physical evidence, or proof that trial evidence was fabricated. It is heard in a single expedited review decided before the sentencing date. If the review finds the new evidence undermines the verdict, the sentence is suspended and the case is retried. No other appeal exists; the independent panel review below is a check the state runs on every capital case, not an appeal. Finality otherwise remains, and that has a cost I'll state plainly: an error built on evidence that looked solid at trial, and that no new objective evidence exposes, will not be caught. Requiring objective evidence for every capital verdict narrows that risk. It does not eliminate it. For an offender on the experimentation track, the same door stays open for as long as the offender lives: new objective evidence gets the same single expedited review, and if it undermines the verdict, the experimentation stops and the case is retried. Exculpatory evidence emerging during experimentation would be a very grave error, which is why the capital track demands extreme proof before anyone reaches it.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

head: "Who checks the case before the sentence is carried out?"
body: An independent panel of three should, in every capital case. All three members should come from outside the prosecuting office, with no part in the investigation or the trial, and at least one should be a forensic evidence specialist. Between the verdict and the sentencing date, inside the 30-day trial window, they should each re-examine, in parallel, the full record and every item of evidence the verdict rests on: where it came from, its chain of custody, and whether it meets the capital evidentiary standard (Evidentiary Standard). If any one member finds the standard is not met, the case leaves the capital track and is sentenced on the non-capital tracks. The review is not an appeal: the defense files nothing, it adds no time after the window, and if the standard is met the sentence is carried out on the sentencing date. The same review applies before the experimentation track begins. Once an impartial AI review is proven reliable, it should be added as a further check alongside the panel, not as a replacement for it.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

head: "Can objective corroboration really be checked within 30 days?"
body: Yes, because the 30 days cap the trial, not the investigation. Murder has no statute of limitations (Statutes of Limitations), so prosecutors can take as long as they need to gather and test the evidence before they charge. The standard itself is what makes the window workable: footage with a proven source and chain of custody, and physical evidence, are fixed before trial and can be checked by anyone, unlike a disputed confession or a lone eyewitness. A case that cannot be proven to the capital standard inside the window does not belong on the capital track, and goes to the non-capital tracks instead (Evidentiary Standard).
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

head: Rationale
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

body: Delay defeats both the retributive and the protective purpose of the sentence. A punishment carried out twenty years after the crime is disconnected from the act, burdens victims' families with decades of hearings, and costs the public far more than the sentence itself. The current system keeps the severity of the death penalty while removing its certainty and speed. That combination fails on every count: it is not swift, it is not certain, and it is enormously expensive.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

body: A fixed trial window with immediate execution keeps the formal finding of guilt by a court, which the rule of law requires, while removing indefinite delay. Organs should be usable from offenders on either track: at execution on the sentencing date, or from offenders on the experimentation track, as set out in Section 10. Combined with the evidentiary standard, it limits the death penalty to the cases where speed is justified because the facts are not in serious dispute. Capital trials under current rules have run well past 30 days (a California review cited by the state's 2008 commission put the average at 79 days). So the cap depends on the narrower capital track: only cases meeting the clear-cut standard qualify.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

body: The cost of delay is concrete. The Federal Bureau of Prisons puts the average annual cost of holding one federal inmate at $47,162 for fiscal year 2024. Across 45 states, Vera Institute data put the average at $33,274 per inmate in 2015. Every year a condemned prisoner spends waiting adds that cost again, on top of the cost of the appeals themselves.
topic: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row
