body: I believe public executions should return: executions ought to be public or openly recorded, so citizens can see what the state does in their name, and I accept both hanging and gunshot as methods. This changes nothing about the evidence or trial rules.

I back public execution. The state's use of lethal force ought to be visible to the citizens in whose name it is carried out, not hidden behind closed doors or presented as a quiet medical procedure. Public or openly recorded (including by livestream), hanging and gunshot as acceptable methods, and the rule that this changes nothing about the evidentiary standard, the trial process, or any other requirement are in the In short above - not repeated here. Emergency on-the-spot recording and publication are in the note below.
An on-the-spot execution in a declared emergency should be no exception: it should be recorded, and the recording should be published once the civilian court review is complete (Emergency Powers).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Fort Hood, Oct 2026: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, which he described as an act of jihad, would be public and livestreamed. On 15 Oct President Trump reversed this, saying the execution would proceed by firing squad as scheduled on 3 Dec at Fort Hood but would not be streamed, and that victims' families may watch in person. An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found eight in ten Americans opposed livestreaming it. ABC News – Trump announces Nidal Hasan execution 'will not be streamed'; NBC News – Trump says government won't livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
My view: Public executions should return.

head: "Isn't public execution barbaric spectacle? Shouldn't the state at least keep it out of sight?"
body: Keeping executions out of sight does not make them less real. It makes them less accountable. When the state takes a life, the public that authorized it has a claim to see what is done in its name. Secrecy allows both sides to avoid the reality: supporters avoid confronting what they support, and officials avoid scrutiny of how it is carried out. Transparency serves accountability first. If executions deter at all, they can deter only when people know they happen, but my case rests on desert, not deterrence (Deterrence). The Supreme Court made the same point about trials: "People in an open society do not demand infallibility from their institutions, but it is difficult for them to accept what they are prohibited from observing." The rule protects every person the state puts to death, and every defendant who may be next, because an execution held in the open cannot hide a botched method or a rushed case. Watching is never required: the execution is open to anyone who chooses to see it, in person or by recording, and no one is made to attend. The two errors are not equal. An open execution costs those who watch a hard sight; a hidden one leaves the method, and any error in carrying it out, to the word of the officials who did it. Cornell LII – Richmond Newspapers, Inc. v. Virginia, 448 U.S. 555 (1980)

head: "Doesn't research show that executions can increase murder?"
body: Some studies say so, and the finding is contested. Bowers and Pierce found about two extra homicides in New York in the month after an execution, from 1907 to 1963. Cochran, Chamlin, and Seth found more killings of strangers after Oklahoma resumed executions in 1990. Shepherd found that executions deterred murder in only a minority of states and were followed by more murders in many others. The National Research Council judged the whole literature, in both directions, not informative for policy (Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment). Those studies measured rare executions carried out years after the crime, after appeals that kept guilt in public dispute. My design is different: execution on the day of sentence, only on objective corroborated evidence, and in the open, so the public sees a punishment tied to a proven crime. The death penalty rests on retribution and incapacitation, not deterrence, so a brutalization finding would not change the sentence. It should still be measured: the state should publish homicide figures before and after executions every year, so the question can be tested on a swift and certain system for the first time. Bowers & Pierce, Crime & Delinquency – Deterrence or Brutalization: What Is the Effect of Executions? (1980) Cochran, Chamlin & Seth, Criminology – Deterrence or Brutalization? An Impact Assessment of Oklahoma's Return to Capital Punishment (1994) Joanna M. Shepherd, Michigan Law Review – Deterrence versus Brutalization: Capital Punishment's Differing Impacts among States (2005)

A government exercising its gravest power should do so in the open. Transparency is consistent with my broader demand for accountability of officials, who are held to higher standards than ordinary citizens. It also connects the punishment to its purpose: a sentence intended to show that grave violations bring certain consequences cannot show anything if it is hidden.
Britain ended public executions with the Capital Punishment Amendment Act 1868, which moved them inside prison walls. The United States ought to reverse that move toward secrecy.
legislation.gov.uk – Capital Punishment Amendment Act 1868

head: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

body: Studies cannot say whether the death penalty deters, partly because the current system is so slow and uncertain. My reforms aim to make punishment fast and certain, which is what deterrence research says matters most. I justify the death penalty mainly because offenders deserve it and can never harm anyone again, not because of deterrence statistics.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

head: Position
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

body: The empirical research on whether capital punishment deters murder is, at best, insufficient to support a conclusion either way. That is not evidence that the death penalty fails to deter. It is evidence that the studies cannot tell. The weakness of the findings largely reflects the system being studied: slow trials, decades of appeals, and uncertain outcomes. The reforms set out above (swift trials, no death row, execution on the sentencing date, and public visibility) are designed to make the punishment certain and swift, which are the conditions under which deterrence is most expected to operate. My justification for the death penalty does not depend on a deterrence claim. It rests on retribution, incapacitation, and the forfeiture of rights by those who commit the gravest violations.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

head: "If the research can't show that the death penalty deters, isn't the case for it gone?"
body: No. The National Research Council's 2012 review found that the existing studies are "not informative" about whether capital punishment increases, decreases, or has no effect on homicide rates, and recommended they not be used to inform policy in either direction. A finding that the research is uninformative is not a finding of no effect. The case for capital punishment here was never built on deterrence statistics. It rests on desert and protection: a murderer has forfeited the right to life, and an executed offender cannot harm anyone again. Deterrence is a possible additional benefit, not the foundation.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

head: "Doesn't the evidence say severity barely deters, so why make punishment harsher?"
body: Critics cite the deterrence research, which the National Institute of Justice summarizes plainly: the certainty of being caught is "a vastly more powerful deterrent than the punishment," and "increasing the severity of punishment does little to deter crime." That finding concerns severity in today's slow, uncertain system, and it does not touch the grounds my sentences rest on. They rest mostly on incapacitation: an executed or confined offender cannot violate anyone's rights again. They also rest on desert, meaning punishment matched to what the offender earned by the crime, regardless of whether it deters, and on rights forfeiture. Its deterrence strategy is certainty: heavy funding for police and investigation, swift trials, and fixed sentences that do not depend on discretion. My punishments are also far more severe than anything the research has studied: public executions, hard labor, and the experimentation track. The existing research has not tested punishments of this kind, and I expect them to add to the deterrence benefit.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

head: "Don't some studies show that each execution saves several lives?"
body: Some papers have claimed large, precise deterrent effects, but those claims have not held up. Donohue and Wolfers (2005) re-ran the leading estimates and found they were extremely fragile: small changes in sample, specification, or method produced dramatically different results, and they concluded there is "profound uncertainty — even about its sign." The National Research Council's 2012 review reached the same practical conclusion: the existing studies are not informative about whether capital punishment increases, decreases, or has no effect on homicide rates, and should not be used to inform policy in either direction. This position does not rest on a body count of lives saved. It rests on desert, incapacitation, and forfeiture, as in the questions above.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

head: Rationale
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

body: The National Research Council panel identified recurring flaws in the deterrence literature. Studies failed to account for the effect of non-capital alternatives such as life imprisonment. They relied on untested assumptions about how potential offenders perceive the risk of execution. Their results shifted with small changes in statistical specification. The panel concluded that this body of work cannot settle the question.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

body: The broader deterrence research points in a consistent direction. Daniel Nagin's reviews conclude that the certainty of apprehension and punishment has far more consistent support as a deterrent than the severity of punishment. The American death penalty as currently practiced is severe but neither certain nor swift. Execution is rare, comes decades after the crime, and is surrounded by uncertainty about whether it will happen at all. Under those conditions weak deterrence findings are what the theory would predict. Historical evidence also suggests visibility matters: Phillips (1980) found that homicides in London dropped in the weeks following heavily publicized executions, though the effect was short-lived and later weeks showed a rebound that appeared to offset it. Bailey and Peterson's monthly U.S. analysis of execution publicity from 1950 to 1980 found no deterrent effect. The position does not rest on deterrence.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

body: Critics read the null findings as proof that the death penalty does not deter. They show only that the existing studies never tested a swift, certain, public one. The case stands on other grounds. Retribution gives the offender what the violation deserves. Incapacitation ensures the offender never violates anyone's rights again. Reciprocity holds that those who reject the basic framework of non-aggression cannot claim its full protections. These justifications hold regardless of what future deterrence research shows.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

head: What is the difference between certainty and severity of punishment?
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

body: Certainty is the likelihood that an offender will actually be caught and punished. Severity is how harsh the punishment is if it happens. Deterrence research generally finds that certainty has a stronger and more reliable effect on behavior than severity. A harsh punishment that is unlikely or delayed for decades deters less than people expect.
topic: Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment

body: I treat convicting an innocent person as the state violating their rights. When a court or pardon board formally clears someone on new evidence, the prosecution should pay compensation. Ordinary acquittals are not compensated. Officials who caused the error through misconduct must be held liable.

A wrongful conviction is a rights violation by the state. I believe compensation is owed when an official finding, either vacatur of the conviction by a court or a determination by a pardon board, establishes the person's innocence based on evidence that emerged after the trial. The prosecuting authority should pay that compensation. An ordinary acquittal is not a finding of wrongful conviction and carries no compensation. Officials whose misconduct caused the conviction, such as fabricating or hiding evidence or coercing a confession, ought to be held liable under the higher standard applied to those with great responsibility. A wrongful execution should carry full accountability for those responsible.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.
Central Park Five: New York City reached a $40 million settlement with five men wrongfully convicted in the 1989 jogger case. NPR (2014) – Central Park Five Settlement: Was Justice Served?

head: "Why shouldn't everyone who is acquitted be compensated?"
body: Compensation is reserved for convictions later overturned on new evidence through a formal finding, where the record shows the state punished an innocent person. An acquittal means the state did not prove guilt to the required standard. It is the trial working as designed, not a finding that the state wronged the defendant.

Wrongful convictions are documented at scale. The National Registry of Exonerations recorded 3,767 exonerations in the United States from 1989 through 2025, and Gross and colleagues estimated that at least 4.1% of defendants sentenced to death are likely innocent. As of August 2026, 38 states and the District of Columbia had statutes compensating the wrongly convicted. Placing the cost on the prosecuting authority ties the consequence to the party that brought the case, and requiring a formal finding on new evidence separates proven errors from ordinary verdicts. Officials' heightened liability follows Authority & Civil Liberties.
National Registry of Exonerations – Exonerations in 2025
National Registry of Exonerations – Compensation
Gross, O'Brien, Hu & Kennedy – Rate of False Conviction of Criminal Defendants Who Are Sentenced to Death (PNAS, 2014)
See also: Due Process and Rule of Law

In my view offenders lose their rights when they violate others'. They should serve a fixed labor term set at sentencing without pay. Private-employer payments for the work and opt-in donations repay the victim, and their assets are used if they are serving a long sentence or executed. Taxpayers pay nothing except through voluntary donations.

%% AUTHOR NOTE (Oct 15, 2026): The assets rules are intentionally kept and must not be removed in any future pass that strips offender-wage references. When an offender is executed or serving a long sentence, restitution comes from the offender's own bank accounts and assets; forfeited assets also go to victims first. This money is not wages. %% I hold that offenders forfeit their rights when they violate the rights of others. At the three-mark threshold, the victim should choose among execution, experimentation, or, if the offender is competent and well behaved, life with labor (Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life). When multiple victims disagree, or when the victim is an animal, a judge would make the decision instead of the victim. Where the victim has died, the experimentation track is the default unless the victim's close family or friends step forward and choose, and it stays the default if they disagree. Restitution to the victim ought to be paid by the offender. The offender would serve a fixed compelled-labor term, set at sentencing in proportion to the harm. The offender would not be paid for that labor. What private employers pay for the work, together with opt-in donations, would be applied to restitution, and any unpaid balance would not extend custody. Where the offender is executed or serving a long sentence, restitution would be drawn from the offender's own pre-existing bank accounts and assets, and forfeited property and assets would likewise go to restitution, victims first. This is not payment for labor; it is the offender's own existing resources. Uninvolved taxpayers should fund no restitution beyond opt-in donations.

head: "What happens when an offender cannot pay?"
body: The sentence should be a fixed labor term set at sentencing. The offender should not be paid. What private employers pay for the work, together with opt-in donations, should go toward the debt. An unpaid balance should not extend custody. Where the offender is serving a longer sentence or is executed, the offender's own pre-existing bank accounts and assets should be used, and forfeited property and assets should go to restitution, victims first. This is not payment for labor. The cost should never shift to taxpayers who had no part in the crime.

The harm belongs to the person who caused it, so the duty to repair it does too. Forfeiture theory holds that those who violate others' rights lose the claim to the protections they denied. Federal law already recognizes the principle in part. The Mandatory Victims Restitution Act requires restitution for many federal crimes of violence and property offenses, and the Crime Victims' Rights Act guarantees victims full and timely restitution as provided by law. The position extends that principle by applying the offender's own pre-existing accounts and assets, forfeited property, private-employer payments for prison work, and opt-in donations to repayment and keeping uninvolved taxpayers out of it. Most offenders have few assets (federal prosecutors classed 91% of $110 billion in outstanding restitution as uncollectible in 2016), so private-employer payments for prison work and opt-in donations carry most of the load where assets fall short.

Restitution is payment ordered from an offender to a victim to cover losses caused by the crime, such as medical costs, lost income, and damaged or stolen property. It differs from a fine, which is ordinarily paid to the state.
Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 3771: Crime victims' rights
Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 3663A: Mandatory restitution to victims of certain crimes
Christopher Heath Wellman – The Rights Forfeiture Theory of Punishment
U.S. Government Accountability Office – GAO-18-203, Federal Criminal Restitution (2018)

I believe the justice system is first about protecting victims and the public and giving offenders what they deserve. Reconciling offenders with victims or reintegrating them would come second and would never change the sentence. Victims should be repaid by the offender. A victim may choose to meet the offender, but the meeting would never change the sentence.

I believe restorative justice is secondary to justice. Reconciliation between offender and victim, victim-offender mediation, and community reintegration may have a place, but they are not what punishment is for, and they would never come ahead of it. The criminal process exists first to protect the innocent, give offenders what their violations deserve, and remove ongoing threats. Restorative practices should run only inside a sentence already matched to the violation; they would never reduce or replace the sentence, the labor, or restitution. Victims would be owed restitution from the offender first, not a process designed around the offender's restoration. A victim may choose to meet the offender, for example to ask questions or hear an apology; the meeting would be the victim's option and would not alter the sentence. Reduced reoffending that follows from compelled labor is a welcome side effect, not a purpose of punishment.

head: "Doesn't restorative justice reduce reoffending and give victims a voice that punishment ignores?"
body: The state's criminal process is organized around justice, not around mediation. Supporters of restorative justice cite a Campbell review of face-to-face conferencing, which found a modest reduction in repeat offending, larger for violent crime, along with higher victim satisfaction and fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms among victims. Those gains do not require reorganizing justice around mediation, so the state keeps those programs inside the sentence, where conferencing can run without reducing it. Victims are given a direct material remedy through restitution paid from the offender's own assets, and the protection of the community is placed at the center of the process. Restorative programs that make the offender's reintegration the central purpose of the system put it in the wrong order. I place the victim's rights and the safety of everyone else first. Restoration comes second, inside the sentence, and the mandatory rehabilitation on every labor sentence is part of that second place.

Under my framework, a violation of negative rights calls for a response matched to the violation. Restorative approaches move the focus from what was done to the victim toward the future of the person who did it. The protective and retributive purposes of punishment are the basis of the system, so restoration can follow only inside a sentence already matched to the violation, never in place of it. A meeting chosen by the victim is a different matter. In randomized trials where victims chose to meet offenders, more victims were satisfied with how their cases were handled (60% versus 46%), and they reported fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms and less desire for revenge.

Strang, Sherman, Mayo-Wilson, Woods & Ariel, Campbell Systematic Reviews – Restorative Justice Conferencing (RJC) Using Face-to-Face Meetings of Offenders and Victims: Effects on Offender Recidivism and Victim Satisfaction (2013)

Police should get more money, more officers, and more respect, but officers who break the law should be punished more harshly than ordinary people. Outside investigators should handle misconduct, and every officer who deals with the public would wear a body camera. I would abolish qualified immunity. A good-faith defense would apply when the officer, in a split-second decision, relied on training, a supervisor's order, or a reasonable reading of unclear law, and would fail if the officer ignored clear precedent or obvious warning signs. Force should be necessary and proportionate, and today's rules are only a starting point. Patrol officers of either sex should have to meet the same high physical standard.

Police should be heavily funded and expanded, and officers well paid and well respected in proportion to the danger and responsibility of the work. That status ought to carry a higher standard: officers who break the law should face greater criminal liability and punishment than ordinary citizens. Funding, cameras, independent investigation, and the physical patrol bar are in the In short above - not repeated here.

I would abolish qualified immunity as currently formulated. In its place, a plaintiff should have to show that the officer's conduct was objectively unreasonable given what the officer knew at the time. A good-faith defense would apply when the officer, in a split-second decision, relied on training, a supervisor's order, or a reasonable reading of unclear law. It would fail if the officer ignored clear precedent or obvious warning signs. Current use-of-force standards are a starting point for reform, not the final word - Graham v. Connor and Tennessee v. Garner set the constitutional floor, not the ceiling. Force should be used only when necessary to stop a rights violation or an imminent threat, and only in proportion to it. Deadly force ought to be used only when necessary to protect life from an imminent threat of death or serious injury. Officers would use de-escalation and less harmful means when safe and feasible. Departments would plan operations to minimize the need for force; every use and display of a firearm would be reported. Patrol should require one high bar of physical fitness and strength for all officers. Those who do not meet it would be assigned to verbal confrontations in the field and administrative work, and female officers in this group would also handle interactions with women.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Minneapolis, 2023: after George Floyd's murder, the Justice Department found reasonable cause to believe the city and its police engaged in a pattern or practice of violating constitutional rights, including excessive force. U.S. Department of Justice (2023) – Investigation of the City of Minneapolis and the Minneapolis Police Department

Uvalde, 2022: the Justice Department's review found cascading failures in leadership, tactics and training, the most significant being treating the active shooter as a barricaded subject. U.S. Department of Justice, COPS Office (2024) – Critical Incident Review of the Response to the School Shooting in Uvalde, Texas

head: "Does higher liability for officers conflict with heavy funding and support for police?"
body: No. Pay, respect, and power are paired with stricter accountability, not shielded from it. Qualified immunity as currently applied under the "clearly established law" test lets officials escape personal consequences for rights violations, so I would abolish it and replace it with an objective-reasonableness standard and a narrow good-faith defense. I treat strong policing and strict liability as parts of the same commitment: enforcement exists to protect sentient rights, and an officer who violates them is held to account more severely, not less.

Policing is the main instrument for protecting sentient and property rights in daily life, and an understaffed or poorly paid force cannot provide that protection. The authority to use force is also the authority most open to abuse, so accountability ought to grow with power. Independent investigation removes the conflict of interest in departments judging their own officers. Body cameras create a record that protects both the public and officers acting lawfully; a randomized trial in Rialto, California found that shifts with cameras saw fewer use-of-force incidents and fewer complaints than shifts without them, though a larger trial of 2,224 officers in Washington, D.C. found no detectable effect on either, so I rest the case on the record itself, not on a change in behavior. The Supreme Court's test in Graham v. Connor asks only whether force was objectively reasonable to an officer on the scene, and that test alone is insufficient. State force should stop a rights violation and be necessary and proportionate, in line with the European Court of Human Rights' "absolutely necessary" standard and the UN Basic Principles, which allow lethal force only when strictly unavoidable to protect life. Federal records have missed more than half of police killings, so the current standards cannot be shown to be adequate. Wording alone does not change outcomes: California's 2019 "necessary" standard showed no measurable reduction in deadly force. Practice does: in a randomized trial in Louisville, de-escalation training cut use of force by 28%, and requiring officers to report every time they point a gun was linked to fewer deaths. Patrol work can require physically overpowering resisting suspects, so physical standards are set by the demands of the job.

Qualified immunity is a judge-made doctrine that shields government officials from personal civil liability under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 unless their conduct violated "clearly established" statutory or constitutional rights that a reasonable person would have known. It grew from Pierson v. Ray (1967) and took its modern form in Harlow v. Fitzgerald (1982). It concerns civil suits, not criminal prosecution.

On 17 October 2026 a nationwide day of protest in France, called by a leaderless "gilets jaunes" appeal and joined by student unions, labor unions and left parties, turned to looting, arson and attacks on police by evening. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez attributed the violence to "several thousand far-left individuals", later joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses". BBC News – Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting. By 18 October more than 2,000 people had been arrested nationwide and more than 600 police and gendarmes injured. Ouest-France – Violences du 17 octobre : quel est le bilan. In Paris, 517 people were in custody on 18 October, 171 of them minors, so most of those held were adults. franceinfo – Mobilisation du 17 octobre : 517 personnes actuellement en garde à vue après les violences commises à Paris, dont 171 mineurs
The full case, with the documented accounts, the groups that endorsed or called for the protests, commentary and my view, is in News Commentary.

I want police to get more money, more officers, and more respect, and officers who break the law should be punished more than ordinary citizens. Body cameras ought to be required everywhere. The worst crime areas would get militarized enforcement under zero tolerance, and theft and burglary should be treated severely.

Police should be heavily funded and expanded, and the responsibilities and dangers of the job very well paid and well respected. Officers who break laws ought to be held to higher criminal liability and punishment than regular citizens, and the same should apply to elected officials. I would mandate body cameras nationwide. Ultra-high-crime areas should receive militarized police enforcement, and high-crime areas increased enforcement with proper protections and punishments to destroy crime, under zero tolerance. Theft and burglary ought to be treated severely, and any erosion of a high-trust society by criminals and bad actors is addressed harshly. The full policing framework is set out in Criminal Justice & Security.

head: "Does militarized policing threaten civil liberties?"
body: Militarized enforcement should be limited to ultra-high-crime areas and comes with proper protections and punishments, including body cameras and higher criminal liability for officers who break the law. Criminals infringe on the sentient rights of others, and their victims are owed the utmost protection under the law. The civil liberties at stake are first of all the victims'.

Criminals infringe on the sentient rights of others, and their victims deserve the utmost protection under the law. A force with the funding, numbers, and standing to do that job is a precondition for the rest of my framework. Each additional police officer prevents an estimated 0.06 to 0.1 homicides, roughly one life saved for every 10 to 17 officers hired, and in per capita terms the lives saved are about twice as large for Black victims as for White victims. The same study found that added officers make more low-level "quality-of-life" arrests, with per capita increases 2.5 to 3 times larger for Black civilians, while arrests for serious index crimes fall, with per capita drops 4 to 6 times larger for Black arrestees. More enforcement of low-level offenses is part of what a larger force is for: it is the harsh response to erosion of a high-trust society that this framework calls for. Pairing that power with higher liability and recorded interactions keeps it accountable. Concentrating the heaviest enforcement where crime is worst directs state power at the places where rights violations actually happen.
Cornell LII – Fourth Amendment
Chalfin, Hansen, Weisburst & Williams, NBER – Police Force Size and Civilian Race
Chalfin, Hansen, Weisburst & Williams, American Economic Review: Insights – Police Force Size and Civilian Race (2022)
See also: Federalism (when federal forces may take over local policing)
See Foreign Policy & International Relations: Border Security and Immigration Enforcement.

I stand for a traditional nuclear family preference, free speech absolutism (with narrow exceptions), meritocracy, cultural compatibility for cohesion, and personal responsibility. I strongly oppose identity politics and progressive social engineering, and I am skeptical of mandates.

I believe the healthiest family is close to the traditional nuclear family, and I see traditional roles as best, but nothing should be mandated. Divorce should be allowed, and custody should have no default. A neutral court decides, considering the child's wishes.

Marriage and family have multiple definitions depending on one's culture and religion. I believe the healthiest family is something very close to the nuclear family: a mother and father, married and loyal to one another, with two to three children. Divorce should be allowed. Child custody should not default to either parent; if the parents cannot reach a resolution, a neutral court ought to arbitrate the dispute, informed by the child's privately expressed preference. Traditional roles, with a stronger male working while a female raises children, cares for the home, and supports the working man, I judge superior. But they should not be mandated in any way, and people ultimately live as they decide.

head: "Does favoring traditional roles conflict with individual freedom?"
body: No. The preference is a judgment about what constitutes the best-functioning society, not a rule imposed by law. Individuals remain free to structure their families and roles as they choose.

I treat the nuclear family as the structure best suited to raising children, and cohesive families support a high-trust society. Married parents are far more stable: about a quarter separate before a child turns 12, against about two-thirds of cohabiting parents, though part of the difference in child outcomes reflects who marries. The preference for traditional roles is a value judgment, not an empirical finding, which is why it is never mandated. A neutral custody standard avoids presuming either parent is more fit. Keeping traditional roles voluntary respects my commitment to individual liberty. The fertility drop since 2007 is mostly fewer marriages at each age, not a collapse of birth rates inside marriage (Births and Family Formation); that is one more reason I treat the nuclear married family as the healthiest default without mandating it.
Brookings – Cohabiting parents differ from married ones in three big ways
Institute for Fiscal Studies – Cohabitation, marriage, relationship stability and child outcomes: an update
See also: Births and Family Formation

Both sexes hold equal rights and should be judged by the same rules. I reject outcome-based feminism, sex quotas, and treating traditional roles as oppression, while traditional roles stay a preference, not a law.

Men and women hold the same rights, because rights rest on sentience, not sex (Animal Rights and Sentientism). I support equal treatment under law and reject the strands of modern feminism that seek equality of outcome between the sexes, rely on sex-based quotas or preferences, or treat traditional family roles as oppression. Traditional roles, with a working husband and a wife who raises children and keeps the home, I judge superior but would never mandate (Family and Gender). My abortion position also departs from mainstream feminism (Abortion and Bioethics).

head: Data: young women and young men

body: Survey and exit-poll figures as reported by the cited sources.

Gallup, ages 18–29, 2017–2024: 40% of young women identified as liberal, compared with 25% of young men. Young women's share rose from 28% in 2001–2007 and 32% in 2008–2016. Young men's held at 25–27%. Gallup – Exploring Young Women's Leftward Expansion

Same Gallup data, young women vs. young men: favor stricter gun laws 74% vs. 51%. Abortion should be legal in all or most cases 60% vs. 48%. Global warming is human-caused 86% vs. 71%. Prioritize the environment over economic growth 78% vs. 62%. Gallup – Exploring Young Women's Leftward Expansion
2024 national exit poll, ages 18–29: women voted 61% Harris, 38% Trump. Men voted 49% Trump, 48% Harris. CNN – National Exit Polls, 2024 Presidential Results

head: "Doesn't the pay gap prove women face discrimination?"
body: Mostly not. Most of the raw gap tracks differences in occupation, industry, hours, and the effect of maternity and children on mothers' careers. In 2025 women working full time earned 82.1% of men's median weekly earnings, and women working full time year-round earned 83.9% of men's median annual earnings. In Blau and Kahn's decomposition, occupation and industry were the largest measured factors in 2010, accounting for about half of the gap (51%), while work interruptions and shorter hours still mattered in high-skill jobs. Goldin finds that most of today's gap arises between men and women in the same occupation and largely begins with the birth of the first child, because many jobs pay disproportionately for long and particular hours. In Danish data, the arrival of children creates a long-run gender gap in earnings of around 20 percent, driven by time out of work, fewer hours, and lower wage rates after childbirth. A smaller residual remains: about 38% of the 2010 gap was not explained by measured factors. An unexplained residual is not proof of discrimination, but experimental evidence means discrimination "cannot be discounted." In one audit study, women applying to high-price Philadelphia restaurants were much less likely to receive job offers, while a nationwide experiment at 108 large U.S. employers found no significant average gap in callbacks between men and women, with some firms favoring men and others favoring women. The remedy I accept is equal rules, enforced against discrimination in either direction (Equal Treatment in Employment and Business), not outcome targets.

head: "Isn't preferring traditional roles itself sexist?"
body: No law follows from the preference. Women and men have identical rights and may arrange their lives as they choose. I'm only stating my judgment of which arrangement best serves families.

Equal rights and equal opportunity follow directly from my framework's foundations, so the earlier, legal-equality aims of feminism are compatible with it. The conflict is with outcome-based and identity-based approaches, which I reject for every group (Race and Diversity). The pay data show a persistent raw gap that is mostly explained by occupation, industry, hours, and the effect of maternity and children on mothers' earnings, with a smaller unexplained share, some of which experimental studies attribute to discrimination.

U.S. Census Bureau – Income in the United States: 2025

I see marriage as a legal contract between consenting adults, same-sex couples included. Minors should not be able to marry, and churches can decline.

I see civil marriage as a legal contract between consenting adults, and it should be recognized equally for opposite-sex and same-sex couples. The state ought to record and enforce the contract but not define its religious meaning, and religious bodies should remain free to perform or decline ceremonies. Minors cannot consent, so they should not be able to marry. Blood relatives should not marry; step relatives other than parental figures may (Incest). Divorce should be allowed, and custody follows the existing family rules.

head: Data: the marriage gap in voting and party

body: Survey and exit-poll figures as reported by the cited sources.

2024 national exit poll: married men voted 60% Trump, 38% Harris. Married women 52% Trump, 47% Harris; unmarried men split 48–48; unmarried women voted 61% Harris, 38% Trump. CNN – National Exit Polls, 2024 Presidential Results

Party identification (Pew, registered voters, 2023 data): 59% of married men and 50% of married women identify with or lean Republican. Never-married women are 72% Democratic and 24% Republican; never-married men 61% Democratic and 37% Republican. Pew Research Center – Partisanship by Gender, Sexual Orientation, Marital and Parental Status

Marriage by party: 65% of Republicans and 50% of Democrats were married in 2024, compared with 71% and 61% in 2000. Among Republicans ages 25–44, 55% of men and 63% of women were married. Institute for Family Studies – The Republican Marriage Advantage; AEI – Working-Class Realignment

head: "Should the state be in marriage at all?"
body: The state's role should be limited to recording and enforcing a contract, including property and custody consequences. It does not regulate the relationship itself.
In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) the Supreme Court held that the Constitution guarantees same-sex couples the right to marry. Family and custody rules are in Family and Gender.
Cornell LII – Obergefell v. Hodges (2015)

I believe elective abortion should be banned from conception by constitutional amendment. Sentience can begin as early as 12 weeks, and no one can pin down exactly when. Before then a fetus on its way to sentience already carries significant moral weight, and where the science is unclear I err on the side of consistency with my axioms. Countries that set a week limit keep raising it, so a line drawn at conception is the only one that holds. Rape and a threat to the mother's life are the exceptions.

My position is sentientist and affirms fetal rights. Sentience is the moral and rights theory: full negative rights attach when the fetus is sentient, and a fetus on an undisturbed trajectory toward sentience already carries significant moral weight (Axioms). The rights claim starts at 12 weeks, the earliest point in the published onset range (~12 weeks to after 24-28 weeks). I believe elective abortion should be banned from conception by constitutional amendment (Abortion ban (from conception)). Before 12 weeks the ban rests on two axioms. Under Axiom 3, a fetus on an undisturbed trajectory toward sentience carries significant moral weight. Under Axiom 5, where science remains unclear, decisions should err on the side of consistency with my axioms, and no one can pin down exactly when sentience starts. That is not a claim of full negative rights from conception. The ban is also a safeguard against drift, because countries that set a week limit keep raising it - Denmark and Norway from 12 to 18 weeks in 2025, France from 12 to 14 in 2022, Massachusetts Chapter 188 in 2026. I hold that a woman may not terminate a pregnancy that exists because of her own decisions. If the fetus is the product of rape, she ought to be freed of obligation, since she did not enter any agreement to raise it; voluntary sexual intercourse resulting in a fetus is what creates the responsibility. The exception does not cover sex an adult willingly entered with their parent or parental figure: the law ought to treat that as rape because consent is not valid (Incest), but the act was willing. Forced parental-figure rape keeps the exception, and so does a minor's pregnancy from sex with a relative, since a minor cannot consent.

head: Real-world example: Massachusetts Chapter 188 takes effect early (2026)

body: Healey framed this as an emergency for patients: she said further delay would "prolong uncertainty" and "risk further harm to the health and safety of women in Massachusetts," and she wrote that at least nine patients had been denied abortion care in the state since she signed the law in August. The repeal campaign can still seek a 2028 ballot question if enough signatures are certified.

I already hold that a woman may end a pregnancy that threatens her life. The prior Massachusetts statute already allowed abortion at or after 24 weeks for the patient's life or physical or mental health, and for a lethal fetal anomaly or a grave fetal diagnosis incompatible with sustained life outside the uterus. What Chapter 188 changed was the remaining limit: those four reasons are gone, and the physician's judgment stands alone. On November 6, 2026, Healey filed an emergency preamble with Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin. That made the law take effect immediately, before the ordinary 90-day clock, and blocked any attempt to suspend it while opponents pursue repeal. Sam Miele, chair of the Compassionate Care Coalition (Massachusetts Citizens for Life and Massachusetts Family Action), said the group dropped off 113,477 clerk-certified signatures that day - more than the 37,289 needed to put repeal on the 2028 ballot, and more than the 49,719 that would have been needed to suspend the law in the meantime. Galvin's office still has to certify the sheets. WBUR / State House News Service – Gov. Healey takes emergency action to block effort to suspend abortion law (2026)

This is the outcome I believe follows when abortion is allowed without a locked limit. A state that already allowed abortion after 24 weeks for set reasons now leaves those abortions to the physician's judgment, at a stage inside the published range for possible fetal sentience (~12 weeks to after 24-28 weeks), and used emergency procedure so voters cannot pause the change before 2028. That is why I believe elective abortion should be banned from conception by constitutional amendment: no one can pin down exactly when sentience starts, and countries that set a week limit keep raising it (Abortion ban (from conception)). Chapter 188 is evidence of that drift. The rights claim still starts at 12 weeks (Massachusetts Chapter 188).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Georgia, Aug 2022 (reported 2024): Amber Thurman, 28, died of sepsis after an incomplete medication abortion. Doctors waited about 20 hours to perform a D&C, a procedure the state's new ban had criminalized with few exceptions, and Georgia's maternal mortality review committee deemed her death "preventable". ProPublica – Abortion Bans Have Delayed Emergency Medical Care. In Georgia, Experts Say This Mother's Death Was Preventable.
U.S. reporting on reasons is incomplete. Figures below are from multi-state and survey sources, not a viral table.

Rape, incest, and life-of-mother exceptions are a small share of abortions in states that report reasons: typically under a few percent combined in Lozier Institute compilations of state data. Guttmacher's older national survey work likewise finds the large majority of abortions cited as elective reasons (timing, cost, partner, readiness), not rape or incest. Lozier Institute – Fact sheet: reasons for abortion · Guttmacher – Reasons U.S. women have abortions (2005)

I do not treat "rare exception" as an argument for elective abortion after sentience. The rape exception in my position follows the responsibility framework, not the size of the category. Exact viral percentages that claim incest at 0.001% or "no reason" at 92% are unsupported; use the sources above.

head: "Why ban before sentience?"
body: The rights claim starts at 12 weeks, the earliest point in the published onset range (~12 weeks to after 24-28 weeks). A fetus before that point does not hold full negative rights on my theory, but it is not without moral standing. I believe elective abortion should still be banned from conception, by constitutional amendment, on two grounds. Axiom 3 gives a fetus on an undisturbed trajectory toward sentience significant moral weight. Axiom 5 says that where science remains unclear, decisions should err on the side of consistency with my axioms, and no one can pin down exactly when sentience starts (Axioms). The ban is also a safeguard against drift: countries that set a week limit keep raising it. Denmark and Norway raised their limits for abortion on request from 12 to 18 weeks from 1 June 2025, and France raised its limit from 12 to 14 weeks in 2022. Massachusetts moved the same way in 2026. Chapter 188 of the Acts of 2026, signed by Governor Healey on 10 August, replaced the four permitted reasons for an abortion at or after 24 weeks (the patient's life, the patient's physical or mental health, a lethal fetal anomaly, or a grave fetal diagnosis incompatible with sustained life outside the uterus) with "the professional judgment of the physician," and ended the requirement that those abortions take place in a hospital. The House passed it 119–33 and the Senate 15–4. On 6 November 2026 Governor Healey filed an emergency preamble, so the law took effect that day and cannot be suspended pending a 2028 referendum (Massachusetts Chapter 188).

head: "Does a ban from conception mean rights start at conception?"
body: No. Sentience is the moral and rights theory, and the rights claim starts at 12 weeks. The earlier ban rests on the significant moral weight Axiom 3 gives a fetus on its way to sentience and on Axiom 5's rule to err on the side of consistency where science is unclear, since no one can pin down exactly when sentience starts. It is also a safeguard, because countries that set a week limit keep raising it. It is not a claim that a pre-12-week fetus holds full negative rights, and it is not revised by the animal sentience-class board (Abortion ban (from conception)). The two errors are not equal. If sentience starts earlier than anyone can now show, a later limit permits killing a being with rights; if it starts later, the ban holds a woman to a pregnancy she chose to risk, a burden that ends, against a life that does not come back. A pregnancy from rape is treated differently because that risk was never chosen (Abortion and Bioethics).

head: "What if the pregnancy threatens the mother's life?"
body: She may end it. A person is not required to absorb serious harm because the threat lacks culpability (Conflicts Between Rights-Holders). Where the fetus is viable, I prefer early delivery to termination.

head: "How is the rape exception established?"
body: By a report to law enforcement and a medical record. A criminal conviction should not be required first, because a trial cannot finish in time. A knowingly false claim is fraud and should be punished. The exception is responsibility-based: obligation arises from voluntary action, and rape involves none.

Sentient beings hold rights, and a sentient fetus is no exception. Expert estimates of when sentience begins range from about 12 weeks to after 24-28 weeks, depending on whether a mature cortex is required. No one can pin down exactly when sentience starts, and countries that set a week limit keep raising it, which is why I believe elective abortion should be banned from conception by constitutional amendment: the rights claim starts at 12 weeks, the bottom of the range, and the earlier ban rests on the moral weight of a fetus on its way to sentience (Axiom 3) and on erring toward consistency where science is unclear (Axiom 5), with drift as a further safeguard, not on a claim of full negative rights from conception. Voluntary sexual intercourse carries responsibility for the life it creates, which grounds the duty not to terminate. Where the pregnancy results from rape, no voluntary act created the duty to sustain the fetus, so the obligation does not arise; this follows the distinction I draw between withdrawing support and killing. After Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization returned abortion regulation to the states, laws vary widely, which is the setting in which the domino concern applies. In the U.S., most abortions occur early (92.8% at or before 13 weeks in 2022) and 1.1% at 21 weeks or later. The full framework is set out in Ethical and Philosophical Framework.
The responsibility framework holds that voluntarily engaging in sexual intercourse creates a duty toward a resulting fetus. Where intercourse was not voluntary, as in rape, no such duty arises.

In my view new technology should change abortion policy only if it reveals new rights violations. Sentience and responsibility remain the standard.

Policy should respond to advancing technology only where sentient rights are violated. The core sentience and responsibility framework ought to remain the standard as artificial wombs, earlier viability, and better sentience detection develop. New detection may refine how the standard is applied; it does not move the constitutional ban on elective abortion from conception, and it does not turn the pre-12-week protection into a claim of full rights from conception (Abortion and Bioethics).

head: "Would artificial wombs change the abortion debate?"
body: Only if they create or clarify sentient-rights violations. The standard remains sentience and responsibility. New technology informs how it is applied.

Technologies that extend viability or detect sentience earlier may refine where the line falls, but the principle does not change. Extra-uterine support research shows the direction of the technology: in 2017, an extra-uterine system kept extremely premature lambs developing normally for up to 4 weeks.

I support letting competent adults choose assisted death with a willing doctor, after an independent capacity check. Non-terminal cases wait 90 days, need two assessors, and get a documented offer of care. No one should be forced to help, taxpayers should not pay for it, minors should be excluded, and pushing someone toward death should be punished.

I believe a competent adult may choose medically assisted death with a willing provider, as a decision about their own body and life. No provider should be compelled to take part, and no taxpayer funding should be used. Minors ought to be excluded, as they are from all irreversible bodily decisions. Every request should require an independent capacity check by a second clinician. Where death is reasonably foreseeable (Track 1), a 48-hour waiting period applies, waivable when death is imminent. Where it is not (Track 2), the waiting period is 90 days, two assessors should have to agree, one a specialist in the person's condition, and the person should receive a documented offer of care and support. Whenever mental illness is involved, a psychiatric assessment should be mandatory; mental illness as the sole condition qualifies only if it is long-standing, assessed by a psychiatrist, and documented treatment attempts have failed. Cases should be reported publicly each year. Anyone who pressures or deceives a person into choosing death violates that person's rights and ought to be punished accordingly. Where sentience has been permanently and irreversibly lost, decisions belong to next-of-kin under Axiom 4, as set out in End-of-Life Care and Lost Sentience.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Canada, 2023: Health Canada reported 15,343 people received medical assistance in dying, 4.7% of deaths in Canada, an increase of 15.8% over 2022; 622 were cases where natural death was not reasonably foreseeable. Health Canada (2024) – Fifth Annual Report on Medical Assistance in Dying in Canada, 2023

head: "Won't legal assisted death pressure the sick, disabled, and elderly into dying?"
body: Voluntary choice by a competent adult is the condition. Pressure, deception, or coercion toward death is a rights violation in its own right and should be punished. No provider should be compelled, and no public money should pay for it, so there is no institutional incentive to steer people toward it. The law ought not to restrict assisted death to terminal illness. Instead it guards against drift with process: an independent capacity check, a 90-day wait, two assessors, and a documented offer of care for non-terminal cases, and psychiatric assessment whenever mental illness is involved. Oregon's data show why the concern is real. In 2024, 42% of those who died under its law listed being a burden on family, friends, or caregivers among their end-of-life concerns, though loss of autonomy, at 89%, was the most common.

head: "What does the data show where non-terminal assisted death is legal?"
body: Critics point to growth and to non-terminal cases, and the review data show the safeguards holding. In Canada, which allows both tracks, 16,499 people received assisted death in 2024, 5.1% of deaths, and yearly growth slowed from 36.8% in 2019–20 to 6.9%. Non-terminal (Track 2) cases were 732, or 4.4%. Those cases raise the concern my extra safeguards address: 44.7% cited isolation or loneliness, compared with 21.9% in Track 1, and only 23.2% received palliative care. Isolation was never the sole reason given, and 45 requests were refused for external pressure. Canada has twice delayed eligibility for mental illness alone, now set for March 17, 2027. In the Netherlands, 9,958 cases made up 5.8% of deaths in 2024, including 219 psychiatric and 427 dementia cases, and the review committees found six cases (0.06%) that failed the due-care standard. While critics argue that vulnerability is not captured by demographics alone, a 2007 review of Oregon and Dutch data found no heightened risk for the elderly, the poor, the disabled, or people with psychiatric illness, and my extra safeguards address the individual case.

head: "Why allow assisted death but not abortion?"
body: Assisted death is a competent adult's decision about their own body and life. Abortion of a sentient fetus ends another sentient being's life, one that exists because of the mother's own decisions. The line in both cases is the same: rights rest on sentience, and no one may end another sentient being's life without forfeiture.

Adults are free to make choices about their own bodies with willing providers, even choices others judge mistaken. That principle already governs adult transition in LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues. Negative rights protect a person against interference by others, and a competent person's own considered choice is not an interference. Oregon's experience shows the practice operating at small scale. In 2025, 637 people received prescriptions under the Death with Dignity Act and 400 died from ingesting the medication, about 1.0% of deaths in the state. Since 1997, 5,520 people have received prescriptions and 3,691 have died from taking them. Most had cancer (61%) or a neurological disease (14%), and the most common concerns were loss of autonomy (89%) and less ability to enjoy life (89%); 39.8% cited being a burden on family or caregivers. Jurisdictions that allow non-terminal cases, such as Canada and the Netherlands, show steady growth and some cases driven by isolation. So the law ought to allow any qualifying condition while adding time, a second specialist view, and a documented offer of care where death is not near.
