I believe patients decide their own care while they are conscious, and their written wishes must be followed. Once consciousness is permanently gone, the family should decide, guided by what the person wanted. Medical science decides when that point has been reached.

While a person remains sentient, their own decisions should govern their care, including refusing treatment. Advance directives and other known wishes ought to be honored. When sentience is permanently and irreversibly lost, the being keeps residual moral consideration, and decision-making authority, including whether to continue life support, passes to next-of-kin, guided by the person's known wishes and dignity (Axiom 4). Whether sentience is irreversibly lost is decided by the best available scientific consensus and accepted medical standards (Axiom 5).

head: "Who decides when a patient can no longer speak and has left no instructions?"
body: Next-of-kin decide, guided by what is known of the person's wishes and by respect for their dignity. Where the person left an advance directive, it governs. The decision ought to rest with the family rather than with the state, which intervenes only to protect a still-sentient person's rights.

Axiom 4 already sets the rule; this topic applies it to medical care. Current law offers the working standard. The Uniform Determination of Death Act defines death as the irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory functions, or of all functions of the entire brain including the brain stem, determined by accepted medical standards. In Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health (1990), the Supreme Court allowed a state to require clear and convincing evidence of an incompetent patient's wishes before life support is withdrawn. That shows why recorded wishes matter in practice. Assisted death for competent adults is covered in Cultural & Social Issues.
Uniform Law Commission – Uniform Determination of Death Act (1981)
Cruzan v. Director, Missouri Department of Health (1990) – Supreme Court opinion
See also: Assisted Death

I see male-female pairing as best, but same-sex marriage should be legal. I view transgenderism as a mental illness. Adults may transition privately, but not compete in opposite-sex sports or use opposite-sex multi-person bathrooms and changing rooms open to the public. Minors should get no transition treatment, and pronouns are never mandated. I would ban coercive or aversive "conversion" methods. Voluntary exploratory therapy for adults and non-affirming therapy for minors under parental authority should be allowed.

I believe the best outcome for society is male and female, naturally and biologically, but same-sex marriage should be legal. I would not mandate this belief, but male-male adoption raises concern for me because same-sex parents do not fully fulfill the best-case male/female dynamic of traditional parenting. I treat transgenderism as a mental illness and view the DSM's definitions of gender as ideologically driven; the illness should be treated rather than validated. Adults may transition, and private practices may train for and perform the surgery, as a freedom of both parties. Transgender individuals should not compete in their transitioned-sex sports in any case, minors should undergo no transgender treatment in any case, and every multi-person bathroom or changing room open to the public, in government or private facilities, ought to be separated by birth sex, while single-occupancy lockable rooms are open to anyone. Pronouns may be respected or not as each individual chooses and should never be mandated. Because I treat dysphoria as a mental illness rather than validating it, talk therapy aimed at reducing incongruence is ordinary treatment when it is voluntary. Coercive or aversive methods - force, electroshock, or any therapy a minor is compelled into against parental authority or an adult against their will - should be banned. Voluntary exploratory therapy for adults, and non-affirming / exploratory therapy for minors under parental authority, should be allowed; affirming medical transition for minors should remain banned.

head: "If transgenderism is a mental illness, why allow adults to transition?"
body: Adults are free to make choices about their own bodies with willing providers, even choices judged mistaken. The state should not validate or promote transition, and it should protect others where the choice affects them: in sports, bathrooms, and speech. Minors, who cannot consent to such decisions, should be excluded entirely.

head: "Isn't the DSM the scientific consensus? Why call its classification ideologically driven?"
body: The DSM is a consensus document, and the American Psychiatric Association states its reasons openly. In 2013 DSM-5 replaced "gender identity disorder" with "gender dysphoria" to "avoid stigma and ensure clinical care," stating that gender nonconformity "is not in itself a mental disorder" while keeping a diagnosis that preserves treatment and insurance access. The APA itself calls the diagnosis "a double-edged sword." The 2022 text revision changed "natal male" to "individual assigned male at birth" to use "less stigmatizing language." Reducing stigma and preserving coverage are social and practical aims, not new findings about causes or outcomes, so I treat the classification as a value judgment I may reject.

head: "What makes the DSM an ideologically captured text?"
body: I agree with the APA that homosexuality is not a disorder. But look at how psychiatry actually decides what counts as one: in 1974 its members put it to a vote, 5,854 to 3,810. In 2013 the DSM renamed "gender identity disorder" to "gender dysphoria" not because of any new discovery, but, in the APA's own words, "to avoid stigma and ensure clinical care," and it kept a diagnosis on the books so insurance would keep paying. In 2022 it swapped "natal male" for "individual assigned male at birth" for "less stigmatizing language." A manual that rewrites its categories to manage feelings and keep billing codes is not describing reality. It is doing activism with a medical letterhead. A male who believes he is a woman holds a false belief about his own body, and any honest manual would say so.

head: "Don't the major medical associations support gender-affirming care?"
body: Yes. The American Medical Association calls such treatment medically necessary and opposes laws that restrict it, and the American Psychiatric Association supports puberty suppression for youth when indicated. The question is what their guidance rests on. The Cass Review's systematic review of 23 guidelines found that few systematically reviewed the evidence and that most drew on two, WPATH's and the Endocrine Society's. Court documents reported by The BMJ show WPATH required Johns Hopkins reviewers it commissioned to use the data "for the benefit of advancing transgender health in a positive manner" and to seek board approval before publishing. The lead reviewer reported finding "little to no evidence about children and adolescents," and only two reviews were published. WPATH says it disputed only the timing of publication. The 2025 HHS umbrella review rated the evidence on psychological outcomes, quality of life, regret, and long-term health as very low quality. Endorsement by an association does not raise the quality of the studies underneath it.

head: "Doesn't childhood dysphoria usually persist?"
body: Follow-up studies suggest most cases do not. In a Toronto sample of 139 clinic-referred boys, 17 (12.2%) persisted and 122 (87.8%) desisted (Singh, Bradley, and Zucker, 2021). In a Dutch sample of 127, persistence was the minority outcome and was more likely with more intense dysphoria and among girls (Steensma et al., 2013). These studies have limits: they used older DSM criteria, 36.7% of the Toronto boys were below the diagnostic threshold, and they predate today's adolescent-onset caseload. Comorbidity is high: in Finland's adolescent service, severe psychiatric problems often preceded the dysphoria and autism-spectrum problems were very common (Kaltiala-Heino et al., 2015). That pattern supports treating the underlying distress first. Advocates cite a 2022 U.S. cohort of 317 children who had socially transitioned, 94% of whom identified as transgender about five years later (Olson et al.). The study followed only children who had already transitioned, so it cannot separate persistence from the effect of the transition itself. Transgenderism is a cultural mental illness propagated and supported by society, when it should instead be supported out of, not into.

head: "Hasn't the change in referrals just reflected greater acceptance?"
body: Advocates credit greater acceptance, but the researchers who documented the rise say the reasons "are not known," naming awareness, destigmatization, and social and media influences as possibilities (de Graaf et al., 2020). Referrals rose on a similar pattern across four Nordic countries and the UK, with natal girls predominating among adolescents. Whatever the cause, a fast change in who is referred argues for more diagnostic caution, not less. Several of the countries with the longest experience have pulled back. Sweden judged in 2022 that the risks of blockers and hormones for adolescents "are likely to outweigh the expected benefits," Finland made psychosocial support first-line, Norway's investigation board classed the treatments as investigational, and NHS England stopped routine prescribing of puberty blockers in March 2024, and in December 2024 the government made the under-18 ban indefinite, to be reviewed in 2027 (GOV.UK announcement).

head: "Why have trans identifications skyrocketed if this is just people finally coming out?"
body: Some of the rise is greater willingness to speak, and the main study of sudden teen onset relies on parent reports. The numbers still don't look like a hidden population stepping out. UK gender clinic referrals went from 51 in 2009, mostly boys, to 3,115 confirmed new cases in 2021/22, with about 73% female in a later audit. In 2023, 3.3% of U.S. high schoolers identified as transgender, triple the 1.1% of all adults, and about two-thirds of them were girls. In the parent-report study, 86.7% of the teens had more social-media use, trans-identifying friends, or both. The kids drawn in are disproportionately vulnerable: in Finland, 75% of teen referrals already had other psychiatric treatment and 26% were autistic, trans-identified people are three to six times as likely to be autistic, and clinic studies found sexual-abuse histories in 5-19%. I'm not talking about sexual grooming, but adults steering vulnerable children from troubled homes toward an irreversible identity follow the same pattern of isolating and shaping a child. This is not just acceptance. It is recruitment.

head: "Isn't sex a spectrum?"
body: No. Biological sex is defined by the type of gamete an organism is organized to produce, and there are two, small and large. No third gamete exists (Goymann, Brumm, and Kappeler, 2023). Some biologists argue sex is better described as a spectrum because of differences of sex development, and those conditions are real. They are variations in how the two-sex system develops, not additional sexes, so they do not change the binary. Law and public facilities that rely on sex therefore track biological sex.

head: "Isn't being trans about gender, not sex?"
body: Critics separate the two: sex is the body, gender is an inner identity or a social role. I think the distinction is hollow. Strip "gender" down and what's left is surface stereotypes - clothes, hair, makeup, mannerisms, interests. None of that is manhood or womanhood. A woman who hates dresses and fixes engines is still a woman. A man who loves fashion is still a man. Manhood and womanhood are lived through a sexed body: puberty, fertility, motherhood, fatherhood, and the vulnerabilities and strengths that come with each. Activists ask to be placed by sex while defining themselves by stereotype. That gives no claim to the word "woman," or to the spaces set aside for women. Either gender is stereotype, and changes nothing, or it is sex, and sex cannot be changed.

head: "Does medical transition change a person's sex?"
body: Hormones and surgery can change how a body looks. They cannot change what it is. Sex is set by which of two gametes a body is built to produce, and no drug or operation has ever turned a male body into one that makes eggs. A man is an adult human male and a woman is an adult human female. A "trans woman" is a male who has altered his appearance, nothing more. Law built on that fiction forces everyone else to pretend, in locker rooms, on playing fields, on birth certificates, and in courtrooms. That is why I reject the claim that anyone can change sex, or be treated as the other sex by law. Adults can do what they like to their own bodies. They cannot draft the rest of us into affirming it.

head: "If gender can be changed by self-identification, why can't race?"
body: Race is blurrier than sex, which only makes this harder for the other side. If saying "I am a woman" makes a male a woman, then saying "I am black" should make a white woman black. Ancestry is no more fixed than sex. The philosopher Rebecca Tuvel made exactly this argument in 2017: whatever justifies transgender identity justifies transracial identity just as well. Activists demanded her paper be retracted, and they never answered her logic. When Rachel Dolezal said "I identify as black," the country laughed, because everyone could see that wanting to be something doesn't make you that thing. The same reasoning applies to a male who says he is a woman. Either identity overrides biology in both cases or in neither. I say neither.

head: "Why is it offensive for a male to claim to be a woman?"
body: Adults may dress and speak as they like, and not every woman will take offense. The claim is still an insult to the people who live the sex being borrowed. A male who has never gone through a female puberty, never menstruated, never faced pregnancy or motherhood, and never lived with the ordinary female fear of sexual violence is not a woman, and a female who has never lived fatherhood or a male adolescence is not a man. That is not a feeling. It is a life. More than one in five U.S. women have experienced completed or attempted rape (CDC, 2023/2024). After puberty, males typically carry 15 to 20 times the testosterone of females, the basis of the male strength advantage (Handelsman et al., 2018). Sex is lived in the body. Claiming it without living it is an offense to everyone who does.

head: "Don't adults who transition report low regret and better well-being?"
body: Advocates cite low reported regret: a meta-analysis of 27 studies with 7,928 patients found about 1%, though its own authors note subjective measurement and a lack of standardized questionnaires (Bustos et al., 2021). Long-term outcomes are less clear. A Swedish cohort found post-surgery mortality 2.8 times and suicide 19.1 times that of controls, though it could not show what would have happened without surgery (Dhejne et al., 2011). A national Swedish study first reported reduced mental-health treatment after surgery, then issued a correction after reanalysis finding no advantage of surgery for mood or anxiety treatment or suicide-attempt hospitalization (Bränström and Pachankis, 2020). So the state ought to leave adult transition to adult choice without treating it as the established cure, and without public funding.

head: "You call dysphoria a mental illness and also oppose conversion therapy — which is it?"
body: Both, under a defined rule. Oppose means ban coercive and aversive methods: force, electroshock, or compelling a minor into any therapy against parental authority, or an adult against their will. Allow means voluntary exploratory talk therapy for adults who want to reduce incongruence, and non-affirming or exploratory therapy for minors under parental authority, consistent with treating the illness rather than affirming it. Affirming hormones or surgery for minors stay banned. Adult medical transition stays a private choice with willing providers, not a state-validated cure.

head: "Why not affirm a trans identity, as the person asks?"
body: The distress is real, some patients say affirmation helped, and the main follow-up study tracked only children who had already transitioned. We still don't affirm an anorexic's belief that she is fat, or remove a healthy limb for someone with body integrity dysphoria. We treat the disorder. Affirmation is not neutral kindness; it is an intervention. The Cass Review found no clear evidence that social transition in childhood improves mental health, found that children who socially transitioned were more likely to go on to medical treatment, and warned it may change the course of gender identity development. Of 317 American children socially transitioned early, 94% still identified as transgender about five years later (Olson et al., 2022). Affirm a child into an identity and expect it to stick. You treat a disorder. You don't build a child's life around it.

The state ought to protect adult liberty while refusing to compel others to affirm beliefs they do not hold. Sex-based categories in sports and bathrooms exist for fairness and safety, so they follow biological sex. Minors cannot consent to irreversible medical treatment, and the Supreme Court upheld a state ban on such treatment for minors in United States v. Skrmetti. England's Cass Review (2024) found the evidence base for youth gender medicine remarkably weak and recommended puberty blockers only within research protocols. My classification departs from the DSM-5-TR, which diagnoses gender dysphoria only where incongruence brings clinically significant distress. The departure rests on three points. First, the 2013 reclassification was justified by the APA in terms of stigma and access to care rather than new evidence about causes or outcomes. Second, the guidelines built on it have been judged weak by systematic review, and the evidence for treating minors has been rated low or very low quality by England's Cass Review, Sweden, and the 2025 HHS review. Third, sex is binary, defined by gametes, so an identity that contradicts it should be treated as a condition to be understood and treated, not as a fact the law must adopt. Counter-evidence is acknowledged: the AMA and the American Psychiatric Association support affirming care, and reported regret after adult surgery is low. Same-sex marriage remains legal under Obergefell v. Hodges, consistent with my limited role for the state in private relationships.

Columbia Law School's What We Know project reviewed 79 peer-reviewed studies. Of these, 75 found children of gay or lesbian parents fare no worse than other children. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Psychological Association agree. Supporting work includes Rosenfeld's 2010 census analysis, the National Longitudinal Lesbian Family Study (Gartrell and Bos), and studies of adoptive gay fathers by Golombok and by Farr and Patterson.

Three lines of research dissent. Regnerus (2012) reported worse outcomes for adults raised by a parent with a same-sex relationship. Allen, Pakaluk, and Price (2013) reanalyzed Rosenfeld's data and found children of same-sex couples 35% less likely to make normal progress through school. Allen also studied high school graduation in Canadian census data. Sullins (2015–2016) found emotional problems more than twice as common and attributed this to not living with both biological parents. Cheng and Powell (2015) reanalyzed Regnerus's data and found that at least a third of the respondents he counted as raised by a same-sex parent were misclassified, many having never lived with that parent or having lived with them for a year or less. Once corrected, the differences were small or absent.

Planned same-sex household studies do not settle the male-male adoption concern: the no-difference literature mostly uses small, self-selected samples of planned lesbian families. Breakup-contaminated designs cut the other way — dissenting studies often count a household as same-sex if a parent ever had a same-sex relationship, which mixes in children who went through family breakup — and the journal that published Regnerus released an audit concluding its peer review failed. Residual uncertainty stays. The preference for mother-and-father parenting stands on developmental priors and the family section, not on Regnerus alone, and male-male adoption remains the sharper concern.

No published study measures abuse rates in gay-father adoptive or foster homes. In the National Longitudinal Lesbian Family Study, 0 of 78 adolescents reported physical or sexual abuse by a parent or caregiver. In Regnerus's survey, 23% of respondents whose mother had a same-sex relationship reported ever being touched sexually by a parent or adult, against 2% from intact biological families. The question did not ask who did it, and Cheng and Powell's reanalysis found many of those respondents misclassified. The federal NIS-4 has no data specific to gay-father homes, so no national figure measures abuse in them.

Goldberg (2009) studied couples waiting to adopt. Among those with a sex preference, 46% of same-sex couples preferred boys, against 29% of heterosexual couples. Several studies find gay fathers do end up adopting boys more often. Whether this comes from parent preference or agency matching is unclear, and no data ties it to abuse. The pattern is noted as a point to watch, not as evidence of harm.

Every person is entitled to equal treatment under the law, and I support a plain equal-protection guarantee. I do not support writing gender identity or gender expression into a constitution as protected categories. Those categories would override the sex-based rules the law ought to keep for sports, multi-person bathrooms and changing rooms, and records. A rights clause should also not preserve preferences for some groups over others (Equal Treatment in Employment and Business). Vermont Proposal 4 does both, so if I were voting, I would vote no.

body: Public schools should stay out of gender-identity advocacy, never socially transition students, and never keep it from parents. No one should be compelled to use pronouns. I'd have ID, prisons, and shelters follow birth sex, adult transition gets no public money, military service follows ordinary medical standards, and government buildings fly official flags only.

head: Position
topic: Gender Identity in Schools and Institutions

body: This section applies LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues to public institutions. Public schools should teach core skills and objective facts without ideological instruction in either direction (Education), so gender-identity advocacy does not belong in the public curriculum. Schools should not socially transition students and should never withhold a student's gender-identity concerns from parents. No student, teacher, or public employee should be required to use another person's chosen pronouns. Government identity documents ought to record birth sex, with no change of marker. Prisons and shelters should house people by birth sex. No public money should fund adult transition. Transgender people should be able to serve in the military under the same medical-fitness standards as any other condition, set by the military. Government buildings ought to fly official flags only.

head: "Isn't refusing chosen pronouns harassment?"
body: Pronouns may be respected or not as each person chooses, and that freedom is never mandated away. Compelling speech is coercion, and the Supreme Court has limited compelled expression in 303 Creative v. Elenis. Threats and incitement remain unprotected as with any other speech (Free Speech and Censorship).

head: "Doesn't telling parents put some students at risk?"
body: Parents hold primary responsibility for their minor children, and a school that hides a significant psychological matter from them takes a decision that is not its own. Where a school has evidence of abuse, the ordinary child-protection process applies, as it does for any other concern. The HHS review found that the evidence does not show clear benefit from social transition in minors.

head: "Why birth sex on ID instead of gender identity?"
body: Documents record facts the state relies on, and sex is a biological fact defined by gametes (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues). The same record then governs sex-separated facilities consistently.

head: "Why must private businesses separate multi-person bathrooms by birth sex? Isn't that a mandate?"
body: It is, and it rests on protection and privacy: multi-person bathrooms and changing rooms are places of undress where people are most exposed. Direct data on assault are thin. A Massachusetts study of public-record incident reports found that gender-identity nondiscrimination ordinances were not related to the number of safety or privacy incidents, which were exceedingly rare either way (Hasenbush, Flores, and Herman, 2019). The rule therefore rests on privacy and protection rather than a measured crime effect. Single-occupancy lockable rooms are open to anyone, so no one is left without access. The rule protects anyone undressing in a shared room, women and girls above all, who should not have to judge a stranger's intentions in the one place they are most exposed. The two errors are not equal: a trans person keeps access to a birth-sex or single-occupancy room, while someone exposed without consent in a changing room loses a privacy that cannot be given back. It is also not a new kind of rule. Federal workplace law already requires toilet facilities "in toilet rooms separate for each sex" in all places of employment, except rooms used by one person at a time that lock from the inside. head: "Isn't housing trans women in men's prisons dangerous for them?"
body: Prisons owe safety to every inmate. Housing stays by birth sex. Separate protective units should be allowed inside the male and female prisons, assigned by individual risk such as small build, a history of being abused, or sexual orientation. They add protection within each sex's prison and are not a third category. Federal prison-rape standards already require screening on similar factors, including physical build, prior sexual victimization, and being perceived as gay, lesbian, or bisexual.

body: History and civics ought to be taught unmodified, and I want more curriculum on taxes, government, how society works, and jobs.

History and civics should be taught unmodified. The curriculum ought to add more instruction on taxes, government, how society works, and jobs. Charter schools set their own curricula and remain publicly accountable; private schools set their own curricula.

head: "Who decides what counts as unmodified?"
body: Public standards are set locally and published so parents can see them. Families who disagree may choose a private school or homeschooling.

head: "Is critical race theory taught in public schools?"
body: Not as doctrine. Critical race theory is an academic framework from legal scholarship whose core claim is that racism is "embedded in legal systems and policies," not only in individual bias. Public schools teach history unmodified, including slavery, Jim Crow, and the civil rights movement, as facts. They do not teach critical race theory, intersectionality, or any other ideological framework as settled truth, consistent with a curriculum limited to core skills and objective facts (Education). Some platforms call for closely related content: the Green Party would "Teach all students about white supremacy and intersectionality." Several states have passed laws on the subject, though Brookings found most of them never name critical race theory.

head: "Doesn't 'unmodified' history still leave out African and Arab roles in the slave trade?"
body: Unmodified means the full record, not a single villain. Public schools ought to teach the Atlantic trade as a system: European demand and shipping, and African kingdoms and middlemen—including Dahomey, Asante, and Fante networks—as essential suppliers on the coastal side, plus the separate Arab/East African trades, U.S. emancipation through the Civil War, Jim Crow, the civil rights movement, and Black achievement. "Primary brokers" is fair for the African supply side and incomplete without European demand. That is history as fact, not critical race theory as doctrine. A curriculum that casts only one group as eternal oppressor fails the unmodified test the same way a curriculum that erases slavery would.

In 2022, 13% of eighth graders performed at or above proficient in U.S. history and 22% in civics on the National Assessment of Educational Progress. Education structure is set out in Domestic Policy & Governance.

The institutions that tell the story pick the villain. Schools, universities and publicly funded culture that teach a single oppressor-and-oppressed lens train students to cast the capitalist, the employer, the landlord and "the rich" as villains, and a generation taught one lens applies it everywhere, to housing, to climate and to conflicts abroad. That is why no ideological framework is taught as doctrine and civics is taught unmodified.
Teaching only a domestic oppressor lens while skipping African supply-side kingdoms or the Arab trade is the same selective storytelling I reject.

I believe speech must be fully protected except for true threats and incitement to imminent violence. Private platforms set their own rules. Misinformation should be answered by platforms and individuals, not the government.

I hold free speech absolutely: no one should be fined, jailed, or removed for any opinion, and the only speech the law should punish is true threats and incitement to imminent violence that infringe on others' sentient rights. The two civic disabilities for excluded ideologies govern who holds authority roles and which institutions may be built, not what any person may say or believe (Excluded ideologies). Separate from speech restrictions, minors' access is limited by law in two areas: pornography, as set out in Pornography and Minors' Access, and social media accounts, as set out in Minors and Social Media. Adults' speech and access are unaffected. Private platforms are private and should be free to restrict speech under their own codes of conduct and terms of service, just as a homeowner may remove someone from a private home for speech the owner does not approve. Misinformation is the responsibility of the private platform or, in public, of individuals to debunk as factually false. Peaceful protest is protected speech and assembly. Once a protest turns to looting, arson or attacks, it is a riot, and it should be met with immediate enforcement and serious prison time for those who took part. Organizers and endorsers ought to be criminally liable only if they planned or incited the violence. Otherwise their endorsement is speech, which others are free to condemn.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

United Kingdom, 17 Oct 2024: Lucy Connolly was jailed for 31 months after pleading guilty to inciting racial hatred over an X post on the day of the Southport killings calling for "mass deportation now" and for hotels housing asylum seekers to be set on fire. The post was viewed about 310,000 times. Crown Prosecution Service – UPDATED WITH SENTENCE: Childminder admits inciting racial hatred over social media post; BBC News – Politician's wife Lucy Connolly jailed for race hate post

head: "Does letting private platforms moderate undermine free speech absolutism?"
body: No. Free speech is a protection against government censorship. A private platform setting its own rules is exercising property rights, the same way a homeowner controls who speaks in their home. The state's only role in speech is to restrict true threats and incitement to imminent violence. Limits on minors' access are set out separately.

head: "Is hate speech protected?"
body: Yes, legally. The only speech restricted is true threats and incitement to imminent violence. Private platforms may still remove it under their own terms, and misinformation is answered by platforms and individuals, not the government.

head: "Don't limits on minors' access contradict free-speech absolutism?"
body: They are separate from speech restrictions. They limit minors' access to pornography and to social media accounts. Adults' speech and access are unaffected.

head: "Is self-censorship among professors overblown?"
body: No. In a 2021 anonymous survey, 470 of 4,603 invited U.S. psychology professors answered, 92.6% of them at or left of the political midpoint. Those more confident that controversial conclusions were true were more reluctant to say so in a professional setting, which can make a field look more settled than the private beliefs are. Professors reported substantial fear of social-media attacks, ostracism, and pejorative labels if they stated their own empirical beliefs, and tenured faculty reported as much self-censorship and as much fear, including of being fired, as the untenured. A larger 2024 faculty survey found the same pattern across departments: 35% had recently toned down their writing for fear of controversy, against 9% of social scientists asked the same question at the end of the McCarthy era. Public universities are the government. The law should not punish a professor for a research conclusion any more than it punishes any other opinion.

Speech does not violate sentient rights unless it threatens or incites violence. The Supreme Court's standard in Brandenburg v. Ohio protects advocacy unless it is directed to and likely to produce imminent lawless action, which closely matches the line drawn here. Federal law already protects platforms' ability to moderate content on their own terms.
Cornell LII – First Amendment
Supreme Court of the United States – Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969)
Cornell LII – 47 U.S.C. § 230: Protection for private blocking and screening of offensive material
Perspectives on Psychological Science – Taboos and Self-Censorship Among U.S. Psychology Professors (Clark et al., 2024)
Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression – Silence in the Classroom: The 2024 FIRE Faculty Survey Report

No one may use force or the threat of force to stop a lawful talk or event. In my view the state should protect the event and prosecute the force. It must not cancel the speech to keep the peace.

I hold free speech absolutely, and that includes the speech a crowd hates. A mob that burns, blocks or attacks to stop a speaker has used force against the speaker's and the audience's rights, and the threat of that force is not a reason to shut the event. Public universities and police ought to protect a lawful event rather than cancel it, and those who use force should be prosecuted for the force, never for their opinions. Peaceful counter-protest is protected the same way.
See also: Case: France riots, 17 October 2026 (Bilbao talk cancelled after riots)

Adult pornography made with consent should be legal. Anything involving minors or non-consent must be prosecuted. I support a law prohibiting minors' access, with parental and device tools layered on top.

I believe adult pornography produced with the consent of adults is protected expression. Material involving minors or non-consenting people is a rights violation and should be prosecuted. A law ought to prohibit minors' access to pornography, and parental and device-level tools are a layer on top of it. The law and the tools are not mutually exclusive.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

United Kingdom, 2025: under the Online Safety Act, around 6,000 sites allowing pornography began checking that UK users are over 18. Experts questioned how easily the checks could be circumvented. BBC News (2025) – UK to see 6,000 porn sites verifying user age, Ofcom says

head: "Doesn't keeping it from minors burden adult speech?"
body: Adults keep full access. The same principle already keeps gambling and other vices from minors without banning them for adults.

In Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (2025) the Supreme Court upheld, 6–3, a Texas law requiring age verification for commercial sites with substantial sexual material, applying intermediate scrutiny. Free speech limits are set out in Free Speech and Censorship, and vice rules in Drugs and Vice.
Cornell LII – Free Speech Coalition, Inc. v. Paxton (2025)

Following Australia's model, I would bar minors under 16 from holding social media accounts. Going one step further than Australia, 16- to 18-year-olds should have access only with parental opt-in. I rest the rule on parental authority, not on proven harm.

Social media should follow Australia's model for under-16s: minors under 16 should not hold social media accounts. Australia sets no rule for 16- and 17-year-olds; I would allow access from 16 to 18 only by parental-consent opt-in. Opt-in consent for data collection should apply everywhere, given by parents for their children.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Australia, 2024: parliament approved a ban on social media accounts for children under 16, with fines of up to A$50m for non-compliant companies. BBC News (2024) – Australian social media ban on under-16s approved by parliament

head: "Doesn't this take the decision away from parents?"
body: Under 16, the rule is the same for every family. From 16 to 18, parents decide through opt-in consent.

head: "Is there proof that social media harms teenagers?"
body: Critics cite the National Academies, which found in 2023 that the research does not support the conclusion that social media causes changes in adolescent health across the population, while noting possible harms and benefits for individual teens. The ban never rested on population-level harm. It rests on parental authority: children cannot consent to contracts or data collection on their own, and the rule backs parents against platforms built to hold a child's attention.

Since December 10, 2025, Australian law has required age-restricted social media platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent Australians under 16 from creating or keeping accounts, according to Australia's eSafety Commissioner. In 2024, 16% of U.S. teens said they use TikTok almost constantly and 15% said the same of YouTube, according to the Pew Research Center. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine concluded in 2023 that the evidence does not show social media causing population-level changes in adolescent health. The age limit is grounded in parental authority over minors, not in a proven harm.
eSafety Commissioner (Australia) – Social media age restrictions
Pew Research Center (Faverio & Sidoti) – Teens, Social Media and Technology 2024
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine – Social Media and Adolescent Health (2023)

I want no quotas, no DEI preferences, and only merit in hiring and admissions. Reparations should be paid only by the responsible government, charged to those who voted for it, and expire after some generations. More unbiased research on group differences is needed. The current evidence on IQ and crime is set out in Criminal Justice & Security. In my view race carries real patterns that shouldn't be ignored or politically corrected away, without that meaning race-based policy. Profiling by police, aimed at those who fit the statistics and data, should not be stopped, and random checks are also allowed.

There should be absolutely zero hiring quotas based on innate characteristics, which are fundamentally racist and sexist. I would abolish government DEI programs. Equality of outcome is discriminatory by definition, and equality of opportunity should be the goal. Meritocracy ought to be the only relevant factor in hiring and admissions, public and private, with narrow carve-outs (Merit-rule carve-outs) (Equal Treatment in Employment and Business). Reparations should be paid only by the offending government, and only where a causal link runs from the electorate's voting decisions to the candidate or administration responsible. Those whose vote is on record as electing the offending government are liable for the reparations tax, and those who did not vote for it are not. Reparations ought to apply only for a limited number of generations, expiring once enough time has passed. I believe more unbiased scientific research on racial IQ is needed. Race doesn't matter in itself; culture and assimilation do. But race carries real patterns that shouldn't be willfully ignored or politically corrected away, without that meaning race-based policy. Profiling by police and law enforcement is acceptable and should not be stopped. It is justified because it targets the people who fit the statistics and data: a hooded young Black man fits them in a way an elderly white woman does not. Random checks should also be allowed.

I would end every federal DEI program by closing it outright, through Congress or a rewrite of the grant rules that applies to everyone. The government may decide what it funds. It may not cancel a researcher's grant inside a program because of the views the researcher holds, since that turns funding into a penalty on speech, which my absolute free-speech rule forbids (DEI grant cancellations).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Supreme Court, 2023: the Court held that Harvard's and UNC's race-conscious admissions programs violate the Equal Protection Clause. Supreme Court of the United States (2023) – Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, No. 20-1199

head: "How could voter records determine reparations liability when ballots are secret?"
body: The position ties liability to a voter's recorded support for the responsible government. Where no such record exists, liability cannot be assigned. The principle is that only those causally responsible pay. Implementing it would require a record of votes that current secret-ballot systems do not keep, so the mechanism is a statement of principle and does not change the secret ballot. Part of it can be applied today: legislators' roll-call votes and officials' enforcement acts are on the record, so those who enacted or carried out the policy can be held liable now. Voter liability waits on a record the secret ballot doesn't keep.

head: "Without DEI, what stops discrimination in public institutions?"
body: Merit. Meritocracy is the only relevant factor in public hiring and admissions, so neither preference nor exclusion by innate characteristics is permitted. Equality of opportunity should be the goal. I reject equality of outcome as discriminatory by definition.

head: "What makes research on group differences unbiased, and how is misuse prevented?"
body: Unbiased means open data, preregistered methods, and peer review, with any public funding opt-in. No finding about a group changes anyone's rights, which rest on sentience, and in hiring and admissions individuals should be judged by merit, not by group averages.

head: "If more unbiased research on group differences is needed, why is it scarce?"
body: Because many scholars will not say what they think. Interviews with 41 psychology PhDs pointed to genetic, evolutionary, or other natural explanations of group differences in outcomes such as intelligence and crime as the most taboo topics. In the follow-up survey of 470 professors, self-censorship was common, and those who leaned toward the claims were the most silent. That is the climate I want the open, preregistered work I already described to be free of. The evidence I already use is in Intelligence, Race, and Crime.

Judging people by innate characteristics in hiring, admissions, and business violates the principle of individual responsibility at the core of my framework. The Supreme Court held in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard that race-conscious admissions violate the Equal Protection Clause. Defenders of racial preferences cite California, which ended race-based admissions at its public universities under Proposition 209 in 1998: Bleemer (2022) found that underrepresented minority applicants then enrolled at less selective colleges, earned fewer degrees, and earned about 5% less a year at ages 24 to 34, driven by Hispanic applicants. That finding measures what a preference gave one group; it does not make the preference just. Every seat awarded by race is a seat denied to another applicant for the same innate trait, which is the discrimination the Court struck down. The law ought to ban race preferences in all hiring and admissions, public and private. Merit admission does not depend on group outcomes; equality of opportunity is the goal. Liability for reparations follows the same principle: those who caused the harm pay, and those who did not are not charged. Unbiased research aims at an honest account of group differences, without race-based policy built on them.

head: What is equality of opportunity versus equality of outcome?

body: Equality of opportunity means everyone is judged by the same rules and standards. Equality of outcome means adjusting rules or results so that groups end up with similar results.

head: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

body: Employers and businesses, public or private, must not treat anyone better or worse for race, sex, or sexual orientation: no firing for being gay, no firing a transgender worker for traits or conduct that would be accepted in the other sex, and no quotas or DEI preferences, with narrow carve-outs (Merit-rule carve-outs). Wide advertising is fine, I would abolish government DEI, and freedom of association covers private life, not jobs and public business.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: Position
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

body: One symmetric rule should govern employment and public business. Hiring, firing, pay, promotion, and treatment of workers or customers by race, sex, sexual orientation, or another immutable or protected trait is a rights violation. That holds for private employers and businesses as well as government, with narrow carve-outs (Merit-rule carve-outs). For government as an employer, the oath-standard exception also applies. Anti-American and anti-constitutional beliefs, namely Nazism, communism, socialism, and Islam, all on the same terms, bar authority roles (Freedom of Association, Oath of Office and Perjury). Private employers are unchanged by that oath exception. Religion stays a protected trait. Adherence to an excluded ideology (Excluded ideologies) is a chosen commitment judged by one published test, not an immutable trait. The rule cuts both ways. No one may be fired for being gay. A transgender worker may not be fired for traits or conduct that would be accepted in a worker of the other biological sex, because that is discrimination by sex. No one may be hired or promoted through a quota or DEI preference. Government DEI offices, diversity statements, and mandatory diversity training should be abolished. Voluntary outreach that does not affect selection, such as advertising widely, should stay legal. Sex means biological sex: male, female, and rare intersex conditions. Gender identity is not a legal category and is not a protected trait. Freedom of association covers personal, religious, and club life, not employment and public business (Freedom of Association).
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

body: The merit rule. I hold that merit is the one legitimate basis for hiring and admissions, public and private. Race, sex, ethnicity, and other immutable traits should never be a requirement or an effective quota in any law or policy. Any rule that makes them one is unjust. Judging a person by status rather than by merit or conduct is a status harm. It violates that person's equal negative rights. It is the same assignment of standing by group that the excluded-ideologies test condemns. The law ought to bar the use of these traits in selection, and nothing more. The rule would impose no outcome requirement and no quota. A workforce or a class that does not mirror the population would break no law. A rule that is neutral on its face but designed to reach a racial or sex balance is covered too, as Thomas Jefferson High School's test-free admissions were (Anti-meritocratic beliefs in practice). Disparate-impact liability ought to be repealed in every law, not only in employment. A rule that makes unequal group results the offense requires equality of outcome (From disparity to equal outcomes). Intentional discrimination stays unlawful, including any neutral-looking rule designed to reach a racial or sex balance. Current statutes, cases, and recent executive and agency actions are in the box below.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: Current law: disparate-impact liability, Title VII, and admissions
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

body: Under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(k), and since Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971), a neutral employment practice that causes a disparate impact on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin is unlawful unless the employer shows it is "job related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity." Griggs held that "good intent or absence of discriminatory intent does not redeem" such a practice. The Supreme Court allowed the same liability under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act in Smith v. City of Jackson (2005). It held the liability "cognizable under the Fair Housing Act" in Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project (2015). Executive Order 14281 (2025) made it "the policy of the United States to eliminate the use of disparate-impact liability in all contexts to the maximum degree possible." The Justice Department removed disparate-impact liability from its Title VI regulations in December 2025. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau amended Regulation B in 2026 to state that the Equal Credit Opportunity Act "does not provide that the 'effects test' applies." An executive order and agency rules can be reversed by the next administration. None of them changes the statutes as the Court has read them, so the repeal ought to be written into law. Current law already reaches much of this. Title VII bars employment discrimination by race, color, religion, sex, and national origin at employers with fifteen or more employees. Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) held race-conscious admissions unlawful at a public university and at a private college receiving federal funds.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

body: Carve-outs. Three narrow carve-outs apply. Employers with fewer than fifteen employees, the threshold Title VII already uses, would be outside the merit rule for hiring only. Choosing who joins a household or a shop of a few people is close to personal association. Firing, pay, promotion, and service to the public would stay covered for every employer. No employer of any size may fire anyone for being gay or for their race. Sex or race may be a requirement where it is a genuine, essential part of the role. Examples include casting an actor to portray a real or historical person, or a character of that race or sex. Hiring a model for a specific look; and staffing a locker room with an attendant of the same sex. It never applies to ordinary jobs, and it is never a quota or a balance target. This goes beyond Title VII, which allows a job-requirement exception for sex, religion, and national origin but none for race. Religious groups may hire by their faith for religious roles, meaning clergy and religious leaders, under the ministerial exception (Religious Freedom). Ordinary jobs at those groups would stay under the merit rule. This is stricter than current law. 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-1(a) and § 2000e-2(e)(2) let religious organizations and religious schools prefer members of their own faith for all jobs. The law ought to limit that preference to religious roles.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

body: Tests in selective admissions. Every selective public school ought to require a standardized test score for admission. So should every selective college or university that receives federal funds, meaning one that ranks applicants for a limited number of seats. The test should be the SAT or ACT, or an equivalent national exam for applicants schooled abroad, alongside auditions or portfolios where the school's work calls for them. Grades vary from school to school. A common test lets an applicant from any school show what they can do. Dartmouth's and MIT's own data, and the Opportunity Insights study across Ivy-Plus colleges, show that scores predict college performance and help identify disadvantaged students who would otherwise be missed (Anti-meritocratic beliefs in practice). A fully private school that takes no public money stays free to set its own admissions. The bar on immutable traits as a requirement or a quota still covers every school. Test-free admissions designed to change the racial mix fall under the merit rule (The merit rule).
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: "Doesn't a merit rule for private employers take away an owner's freedom to choose?"
body: It takes away one choice only: selecting by race, sex, or another immutable trait outside the narrow carve-outs. The owner stays free to hire for skill, for fit with the work and the team, and at whatever pay the two sides agree, and to set every standard of the job. The state does not pick the hire, require any outcome, or audit the mix of the workforce. Freedom of association protects whom people befriend, worship with, or admit to their clubs (Freedom of Association). A job is an exchange of labor for pay, and judging the other party to it by status is a status harm the law ought to stop. The small-employer carve-out keeps hiring at the household and the very small shop, where work and personal life overlap, outside the rule. Once someone is hired, firing, pay, and promotion stay covered (Merit-rule carve-outs).
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: "Doesn't banning private DEI preferences violate freedom of association?"
body: Freedom of association protects whom people befriend, worship with, or admit to their clubs. An employer or a business open to the public is not choosing companions. It is judging workers and customers, and judging them by group rather than merit or conduct is the rights violation the rule stops. The same reasoning that bars firing a worker for being gay bars hiring a worker through a racial or sex quota. A rule that banned one and allowed the other would not be neutral.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: "Isn't this just existing civil-rights law?"
body: Partly. Title VII already bars employment discrimination by race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. The Supreme Court held in Bostock v. Clayton County that firing someone for being gay or transgender is sex discrimination, reasoning that the employer penalizes in one sex what it accepts in the other. The law ought to apply that reasoning through biological sex alone and not recognize gender identity as a legal category. In Ames v. Ohio Department of Youth Services (2025) the Court held unanimously that majority-group plaintiffs face the same standard as anyone else. The law ought to add an explicit statement that preferences are barred as firmly as exclusion. My rule departs from current law in three places (The merit rule; Merit-rule carve-outs): disparate-impact liability is repealed in every law; religious groups may hire by faith only for religious roles, not for every job as 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-1(a) now allows. And race may be a requirement where it is a genuine, essential part of the role, such as casting an actor, which Title VII does not allow.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: "Don't diversity trainings reduce bias?"
body: Supporters cite lasting effects on knowledge: a meta-analysis of 260 samples found them, while effects on attitudes faded. Effects were larger when training was sustained and combined with other measures (Bezrukova et al., 2016). A network meta-analysis of 492 studies found changes in implicit bias were weak and generally produced trivial changes in behavior (Forscher et al., 2019). Dobbin and Kalev reported that mandatory training often fails to increase managerial diversity and can provoke backlash. My objection is to judging people by group, not to training as such: private voluntary training that does not affect selection stays legal.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: "Can employers, landlords, or insurers use group statistics?"
body: No. Race carries real patterns that shouldn't be ignored, without that meaning race-based policy: employers, landlords, and insurers judge each person on their own record, not on race or sex averages. The exceptions are real sex-based facts, such as life expectancy in actuarial tables, and fitness tests applied the same way to everyone. Current federal law is stricter on one point: in Los Angeles Department of Water and Power v. Manhart (1978), the Supreme Court barred employers from charging women larger pension contributions based on longer average life expectancy.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: "Does merit-only admission apply to private colleges?"
body: Yes. Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) held race-conscious admissions unlawful at Harvard, a private college receiving federal funds, and at the University of North Carolina. The law ought to extend the merit rule to all private colleges, with no race or sex preference. Single-sex colleges may remain, since they exclude by a defined mission rather than ranking applicants by group.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: "Isn't wide advertising a form of preference?"
body: No. Outreach widens who applies without changing who is selected. Selection itself should turn on merit.
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

head: Rationale
topic: Equal Treatment in Employment and Business

body: Judging individuals by group membership conflicts with the individual responsibility at the core of my framework (Political Philosophy). Applying one rule in both directions keeps it neutral and avoids treating any group's claim as special. The evidence on DEI training is mixed rather than uniformly negative, but I don't rest my case on that evidence: even an effective group-based preference treats individuals unequally.

body: Qualified citizens should be able to buy guns, with background checks and red flag laws aimed at stopping bad actors. I'd set a higher bar for concealed carry. Explosives should be banned or limited to construction, and full automatics heavily restricted.

Guns should be available for purchase by those who are qualified. Background checks and red flag laws ought to keep bad actors from acquiring firearms. Concealed carry should require a higher level of qualification than open carry. Assault weapons are vaguely defined, and handguns are more dangerous because they are easy to conceal. High-ordnance explosives should be banned or heavily restricted to construction work. Full automatics should be heavily restricted but potentially available to extremely trained or vetted individuals.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Highland Park, 2022: police had responded in 2019 to a report that the future July 4 parade shooter threatened to kill everyone in his home and seized 16 knives, a dagger and a sword. He was not arrested, no one sought a red-flag order, and he later obtained a firearm ID card with his father's sponsorship. NPR (2022) – Illinois' gun laws failed to stop the Highland Park shooter from getting weapons

head: "Do red flag laws violate due process?"
body: No, when a judge issues the order. A red flag order removes firearms only on a court finding that the person directly imposes a severe, non-consensual risk of serious harm on others, the forfeiture threshold in Section 1. It is never an executive declaration. A judge may issue a short emergency order before the hearing, and the person then has a prompt hearing where the order should have to be justified. The position supports red flag laws as part of qualification, alongside strong support for the right of qualified citizens to own guns.

head: "Why are handguns treated as more concerning than assault weapons?"
body: Assault weapons are vaguely defined, while handguns are more dangerous in practice because they are easy to conceal. In FBI data for 2019, handguns were used in about 91% of firearm murders where the type of gun was known, and rifles of every kind in about 5%. That is why concealed carry should require a higher level of qualification than open carry.

Self-defense protects sentient rights, and the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms, as held in District of Columbia v. Heller and New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Safeguards target the people and weapons most likely to cause harm. RAND's review of the research finds moderate evidence that background checks reduce firearm and total homicides, limited evidence that extreme risk protection (red flag) orders reduce suicides, and inconclusive evidence on their effect on violent crime. It also finds supportive evidence that shall-issue concealed-carry laws increase homicides, which fits the higher bar for concealed carry. In FBI data for 2019, handguns accounted for 6,368 of the 6,977 firearm murders where the type was recorded. Federal law already restricts machine guns heavily, which the position retains with a path for highly vetted individuals.

I believe marijuana should be legal and hard drugs legal for private, personal use, but no drug, marijuana included, may be used in public or while a minor is present, and no one may be impaired around a minor. Large-scale distribution of hard drugs is capital, and sharing a known, tested dose with a consenting adult is not. Prostitution should be legal and regulated, and adults can gamble. Impaired drivers ought to lose their license for ten years to life. The drug war should target cartels with military force, including war with governments that refuse to help.

I don't condone widespread use, but marijuana should be legal. Hard drugs should be legal for private, personal use. No drug, marijuana included, may be used in public areas or while a minor is also present in the same private home or area, and no one may be impaired or altered by any drug while in the presence of a minor. Large-scale distribution of hard drugs should be a capital crime (Drug Policy). Prostitution should be legal, less clandestine, and regulated to prevent exploitation of prostitutes. Consensual, regulated sex work is distinct from trafficking, which should be capital (Human Trafficking). Gambling should be regulated only to keep it from minors; adults may gamble. Driving while intoxicated or under the influence of hard drugs ought to result in license revocation for a minimum of ten years, up to permanently. The drug war should focus less on domestic addicts and more on the offensive obliteration of drug cartels by force, treating them as terroristic entities endangering the country's safety. Joint operations with compliant Central and South American governments are best, and if they do not comply, war with those governments is justified to eradicate the cartel problem. Refusal to act against cartels operating against the United States ought to be treated as hostility, consistent with Foreign Policy & International Relations.

head: "Is legalizing prostitution compatible with preventing exploitation?"
body: Legal prostitution brings the trade into the open, where regulation can address exploitation directly. A clandestine trade leaves workers without protection. Regulation targets the rights violation, exploitation, rather than the voluntary exchange.

head: "Don't countries that legalize prostitution see more human trafficking?"
body: The best cross-country evidence says they do. Cho, Dreher, and Neumayer found that countries with legalized prostitution report larger human trafficking inflows, apparently because a larger market outweighs the shift toward legal workers. Prostitution should stay legal because consenting adults may trade, and I would answer the trafficking risk directly: every business should be strictly licensed, every worker's age, identity, and consent should be verified, and trafficking should be a capital crime (Human Trafficking).

Adult choices that harm only the chooser fall outside the state's coercive role, while driving impaired endangers others and should be punished severely. Harsher DUI sanctions measurably reduce repeat offending (Washington State data show drops of up to 17% at the 0.08 threshold); the ten-years-to-life term is a protective judgment beyond what studies have tested. Cartels murder and corrupt on a scale that threatens national security, and the United States designated several cartels as Foreign Terrorist Organizations in 2025. The Supreme Court's decision in Murphy v. NCAA allowed states to legalize sports betting. Related positions are set out in Drug Policy.
Supreme Court of the United States – Gonzales v. Raich, 545 U.S. 1 (2005)
Supreme Court of the United States – Murphy v. NCAA, 584 U.S. 453 (2018)

Using drugs privately should be legal, but not while a minor is present or while impaired around a minor. Using them in public should be banned, and large-scale distribution of hard drugs is a capital crime. Smaller transfers fall on lower tiers. Adults obtain hard drugs only through licensed clinical channels or by producing their own, never from a shop. I would treat cartels as terrorists and destroy them with military force.

Marijuana should be legal, and other drugs legal for private, personal use. No drug may be used while a minor is also present in the same private home or area, and no one may be impaired or altered by a drug while in the presence of a minor. Drug use in public areas should be prohibited. The state ought not to pursue prohibition. Cartels should be designated as terroristic national-security threats and destroyed with military force. Enforcement resources ought to move away from private users and toward the organizations that traffic drugs through violence. Large-scale distribution of hard drugs should be a capital crime. Distribution means any transfer of a hard drug to another person: sale, gift, sharing, or carrying it for someone else. Large-scale means a quantity at or above a threshold fixed in statute for each drug, or organizing or leading a distribution operation. I believe the thresholds should follow the top federal tier, 21 U.S.C. § 841(b)(1)(A): for example, 1 kilogram of a heroin mixture, 5 kilograms of a cocaine mixture, or 400 grams of a fentanyl mixture. Organizing or leading should follow 21 U.S.C. § 848: a series of drug felonies by someone who organizes or manages five or more others and draws substantial income from it. Proven to the capital evidentiary standard, the sentence is death, the same as for the other capital crimes (Mandatory Death Penalty). The ground is the same as for every capital act that knowingly imposes an extreme risk of death: a trafficker puts doses of unknown strength, often cut with fentanyl, into the hands of many people who cannot know what they are taking, at a scale where deaths are close to certain. Cartel violence along the supply chain makes the harm larger, but it is not the reason. Below that scale the tiers step down. Selling or giving another person an untested or unknown hard drug is two marks, because it still imposes a severe, non-consensual risk. Selling a known, tested dose to an adult is one mark, because there should be no commercial market. Sharing a known, tested dose with a consenting adult, for no profit, is a misdemeanor punished by an income-scaled fine without a mark. A known, tested dose is one whose identity and strength have been verified, by a clinical label or a drug-checking test, and disclosed to the recipient. Fentanyl and its analogues never count as a known, tested dose outside clinical supply. Knowingly passing off fentanyl as another drug stays capital at any quantity, as knowingly imposing an extreme risk of death (Crimes and Outcomes). Giving or selling any hard drug to a minor is capital at any quantity. There should be no commercial market for hard drugs and no licensed shops or retail sellers. Hard-drug use is a personal endeavor, and an adult may obtain hard drugs lawfully in only two ways. The first is licensed clinical supply, through medical or therapeutic channels under clinical supervision, never a storefront; the most lethal synthetics, such as fentanyl and its analogues, are available only this way. The second is personal production for one's own use. Producing more than a personal quantity counts as distribution. Legal, regulated marijuana and prescribed clinical psychedelic therapy in a licensed setting are not covered, and private, personal use and possession stay legal.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Oregon, 2024: after Measure 110 decriminalized possession, lawmakers rolled it back and made small-amount possession a misdemeanor again. OPB (2024) – Drug possession is a crime again in Oregon. Here’s what you need to know

Cartels as terrorists, 2025: the State Department designated Tren de Aragua, MS-13, the Sinaloa Cartel, CJNG and four other groups as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. U.S. Department of State (2025) – Designation of International Cartels

head: "Does legalizing private use contradict a hardline stance on crime?"
body: No. Private drug use by an adult does not by itself violate the sentient rights of others. Prohibition has failed to stop it, and it has fed the black market that funds cartels. The hardline stance is aimed at rights violators. Cartels that murder, traffic, and corrupt governments should be treated as terrorist enemies. Public use that imposes on others remains banned, as do use and impairment around minors. Legal private use narrows enforcement to where harm to others actually occurs.

head: "Why use the military against cartels?"
body: Cartels are designated as terroristic national-security threats: they murder, traffic, and corrupt governments. They are rights violators at scale, and organized groups that systematically violate rights may be met with decisive force (Political Philosophy). In Mexico, drug-related violence rose substantially after close elections of mayors from the party leading the crackdown, as rival traffickers fought over territory the crackdowns had weakened (Dell, 2015). That is a finding about Mexican state capacity: cartels are embedded in Mexico, and the Mexican state cannot govern those territories effectively. It has no bearing on U.S. firepower if the United States gets involved.

head: "Didn't Oregon's decriminalization raise overdose deaths?"
body: Critics cite one study of Oregon's Measure 110 that estimated a 23% rise in unintentional overdose deaths, about 182 more deaths in 2021. Two JAMA studies found no significant effect once fentanyl's spread is accounted for. Either way, the rights line stands: private adult use harms no one else. The law ought to keep sale capital and keep the bans on public use and on use or impairment around minors.

head: "Why legalize private drug use rather than only decriminalize it?"
body: Decriminalization would still treat private use as an offense, handled by fines or administrative penalties, and private use by an adult does not by itself violate anyone else's rights. Legal private use puts the line where harm to others begins: in public, around a minor, behind the wheel, and at the point of sale. Marijuana goes one step further, with a legal, regulated market that takes that trade away from cartels. For other drugs there is no commercial market. Supply is clinical or personal, and any other transfer should be capital (Drug Policy).

head: "If using hard drugs is legal, how can large-scale distribution be capital?"
body: Use and distribution are different acts. Use risks only the user's own life, and that is his to risk. Large-scale distribution knowingly imposes an extreme risk of death on many people, the same ground that makes any act knowingly imposing an extreme risk of death capital: a trafficker's buyers cannot know the dose or whether it is cut with fentanyl. Sharing a known, tested dose with a consenting adult is different, because the recipient knows the risk he accepts, so it is not capital. The right to use is real, not a legal fiction, because the United States ought to leave two lawful sources open: licensed clinical supply under medical supervision, and personal production for one's own use. It ought not to license commercial sellers or shops. A retail market would turn a personal choice into a promoted trade and normalize drug culture. Supervised medical heroin in Zurich coincided with new regular heroin users falling from about 850 a year to about 150, while British Columbia's take-home prescribing was followed by more opioid-poisoning hospitalizations, so supply stays supervised. Prohibiting use is not the goal. It fails, and it reaches an act that harms no one else.

head: "Why is the capital line drawn at large-scale distribution, and what would move it?"
body: Where it comes from. Axiom 6 counts directly imposing a severe, non-consensual risk of serious harm on another person as crossing the forfeiture threshold, and knowingly imposing an extreme risk of death sits on the capital tier with murder (General Rules of Forfeiture; Crimes and Outcomes). A trafficker's supply is that risk at scale: buyers cannot know the dose or the cut, and across thousands of doses deaths are close to certain. Consent covers only a risk a person can know, so a buyer can't consent to a cut no one told him about. Below that scale the risk reaches fewer people, and with a known, tested dose the recipient accepts a known risk, so the tiers step down: two marks for an untested or unknown drug, one mark for selling a known, tested dose, and a fine for sharing one. Use stays legal because a risk to oneself violates no one's rights. The rivals. Prohibiting use punishes an act that harms no one else, and prohibition has fed the cartel market. A licensed commercial market turns a personal choice into a promoted trade. Supervised supply has the better record (Zurich against British Columbia, above). Ordinary prison terms for traffickers would punish this one kind of extreme risk of death more lightly than every other kind, with no principle for the difference. Death for every transfer would treat a friend who shares a known, tested dose with a consenting adult like a trafficker, though the friend imposes no non-consensual risk. What would move it. The line follows the risk of death, so the list of hard drugs should follow the evidence. Cannabis is already off it. A drug should come off if evidence showed that handing it to someone no longer carries an extreme risk of death, and a new drug should go on when evidence shows it does. The list and the large-scale quantity thresholds should be fixed in statute and revised by an expert board on the best available evidence, as the sentience classes are, with a change applying only to acts after it takes effect. Deterrence studies would not move the line, because the sentence rests on desert, incapacitation, and forfeiture, not on deterrence (Deterrence and the Justification for Capital Punishment).

I limit state coercion to protecting the rights of others, and private consumption falls outside that line while public use spills onto others. Portugal decriminalized the personal possession of all drugs in 2001, replacing criminal penalties with administrative responses, and the European drug agency's country reports track that model. I go one step further for private use, making it legal rather than an administrative offense, and keep the bans on public use, use around minors, and sale. On cartels, the United States designated several cartels and transnational gangs, including the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación, as Foreign Terrorist Organizations in February 2025, following a January 2025 executive order. That designation treats cartels as security threats rather than ordinary criminal enterprises, which matches my position.

head: What is the difference between decriminalization and legalization?

body: Decriminalization removes criminal penalties for using or possessing drugs, though use can still be restricted or handled through civil or administrative measures. Legalization makes production and sale lawful and regulated. My position is that marijuana should be legal and other drugs should be legal for private, personal use, obtained only through licensed clinical supply or personal production, without a commercial market or shops. Use should be barred in public and while a minor is present in the same private home or area, and no one should be impaired or altered by a drug in the presence of a minor.
