I believe a cohesive, patriotic culture is best, and multiculturalism works only with shared values. I see some immigrant cultures as compatible and others not, and being Muslim creates a rebuttable presumption of failing the values test. History should be taught straight, and America is exceptional because of liberty, rights, and opportunity.

I believe a patriotic nation that is culturally cohesive in its values is the best result for cohesion. Multiculturalism can work only if the cultures share important common values; many legally immigrated Mexican and South American families are compatible because of shared family and religious values. I judge Islamic and third-world African cultures incompatible with Western society, clashing with values such as human rights and civic responsibility; individual immigrants should be judged through values vetting. History should be taught unmodified and objective. American exceptionalism rests not on America as such but on what America stands for: liberty, freedom, rights, and great financial opportunity.

head: "Does cultural compatibility contradict civic nationalism?"
body: Civic nationalism unites people around shared values, and cultural compatibility is the condition for sharing them. Cultures that hold the same core values integrate. Those that clash with them do not. The test is values, which is why compatible immigrant communities are welcomed and Muslim applicants start with the burden of proving compatibility.

A high-trust society depends on shared norms, and cohesion is easier where citizens hold common values. Teaching history without modification gives citizens an accurate basis for national identity. Grounding exceptionalism in principles rather than in nationality alone makes it a standard the country should live up to. Robert Putnam's 2007 study found that in the short run, residents of more ethnically diverse U.S. neighborhoods showed lower trust, even of their own group, and less community cooperation. He also found that successful immigrant societies overcome this by building shared identities, which is the role shared values play here.
Robert D. Putnam, Scandinavian Political Studies (2007) – E Pluribus Unum: Diversity and Community in the Twenty-first Century
Assimilation is paramount to me, and English should be the shared civic language. Private language use is free.

I hold that cultural assimilation is paramount, and a shared language is central to it. English should be the common language of civic life, and immigrants ought to learn it as part of joining the shared Western value structure. Private use of any language is free.

head: "Isn't expecting English unwelcoming?"
body: A common language lets every citizen take part in public life, work, and civic debate. It is an invitation to full membership, while private life remains free.
Executive Order 14224 (March 1, 2025) designated English as the official language of the United States. Assimilation is set out in Foreign Policy & International Relations.
The White House – Designating English as the Official Language of the United States
See also: Immigration and Borders

I hold that deliberately killing a sentient animal outside of self-defense is murder, graded by the animal's sentience: high-sentience animals are on the capital track, and killing lower-sentience animals is still punishable and counts as marks against the offender. Hunting is murder, an egregious rights violation on the capital track, and animal agriculture should be abolished. Pets can be kept if their rights are respected, commercial breeding mills should be banned with animal agriculture, and killing a high-sentience pet for convenience is murder. Lethal pest control should be allowed only against an actual or imminent attack or a clear disease or rights threat - including a statutory infestation in a dwelling, food store, or medical facility - with the least-harmful method required. Preventive area-wide extermination of non-infesting high-sentience wildlife is not allowed. Zoos should become sanctuaries where non-threatening predators eat lab-grown meat. Herbivorization methods are under study. Animal cruelty is graded by severity: the most extreme, violent cruelty that causes lasting injury is on the capital track, and lesser cruelty is tracked and counts toward the repeat-offender threshold.

I hold that sentient animals within U.S. borders have negative rights, and the government has a duty to protect them. Animals are graded into classes by sentience (sentience classes). Deliberately killing a high-sentience animal, the capital class, is murder, treated the same as in the human context: it goes on the capital track, and the same forfeitures that apply to human murder apply here. Killing a lower-sentience animal is not capital, but it is still punishable and counts as marks against the offender as a lesser offense. Killing an animal in self-defense or defense of rights is not illegal. That covers an actual or imminent attack, or a clear disease or rights threat, including a statutory infestation: a high-class pest population occupying a dwelling, food store, or medical facility in a way that foreseeably spreads pathogens or destroys necessary stores. Hunger or need is not self-defense; only killing outside those bounds is murder. Rats, mice, and pigeons stay in the high class; pest status does not demote them (sentience classes). Lethal infestation control should use the least-harmful method that works; preventive area-wide extermination of high-class animals that are not occupying a qualifying site remains murder. I consider hunting murder: it is an egregious rights violation and belongs on the capital track. Fishing that kills sentient animals is classified the same way. Animal agriculture should be abolished immediately, and lab-grown meat is the goal and the replacement, scaling up over time (Animal Rights and Sentience Technology). Companion animals may be kept where their rights are respected. Zoos ought to operate as sanctuaries: animals are kept for their own protection, not for display at their expense, and non-threatening predators held in sanctuary are fed lab-grown meat for the rest of their lives. Confined predators that remain violent and cannot be helped fall under the execution rule in Criminal Justice & Security.

My view: Nature needs to be civilized more than it needs to be "protected". In its current state, quadrillions of animals die every year, often painfully, and conservation often gives no consideration to the welfare of the animals living inside it. Individual welfare should come before "nature".

head: "Isn't hunting necessary to control herbivore populations once predators are removed?"
body: Removing predators does raise the question of herbivore populations, and the answer cannot be to kill the innocent animals I protect. Once predators are removed, herbivore populations should be controlled. Predator removal should start with odd-order predators to avoid a trophic cascade that could harm the herbivores below them. Nature should be herbivorized through bioengineering, with outcomes scientifically tested: infertility to stop predator species from breeding, bringing the environment fully under human dominion so wilderness no longer exists, and keeping animals in sanctuaries. Many of these methods are still in their infancy and need to be studied. Herbivorizing nature and reducing predation is central to my framework, because predation and sentient rights are so intertwined.

head: "What herbivorization methods are being proposed?"
body: Many of these methods are still in their infancy and need to be studied. Methods proposed for study include: Selective breeding of animals over generations for the ability to live on plants. CRISPR gene drives to herbivorize predators. Tunable gene drives that regulate fertility across species. Single-sex gene drives, so predator species die out painlessly. Supplementary feeding of herbivores to reduce competition. Plants engineered so herbivores cannot overgraze them. Sterilization. Plant-based diets for predators. A model sanctuary for wild animals. AI monitoring of wild animals. No outside proposal has laid out an order for phasing predators out, so the odd-order predator approach above stands as the plan.

head: "What works now, and what waits on research?"
body: Works now: Ending the breeding of predators held under human control, so captive lines end. This needs a law, not new science. Sanctuary or confinement for non-threatening predators, fed without killing other animals. Fertility control for herbivores, so removing predators does not lead to overpopulation. EPA has registered the GonaCon immunocontraceptive vaccine for white-tailed deer (2009), for wild and feral horses and burros (2013), and for prairie dogs. PZP held the Assateague horses at zero population growth within 2 years (Evidence: Herbivorization). Waits on research: Fertility control for wild predators. None of the registered wildlife contraceptives is for a predator. Gene drives, including herbivorizing and single-sex drives. No gene drive has been released into the wild in any vertebrate, and the two most advanced vertebrate systems, both in house mice, have not reached full proof of concept in the laboratory. Selective breeding of predators for plant diets, and lab-grown meat at the scale needed to feed confined predators. The duty uses only tools that pass testing. A method that never passes is never used, and the duty is carried out with the tools that work, within the bound that no step causes more suffering or more rights violations than it prevents (Wild-Animal Predation).

head: "What about ecosystem collapse, omnivores, and cats?"
body: Ecosystem collapse. I take the hazard seriously, and the program is built around it. Predators feed scavengers, move nutrients, and can slow disease, and herbivores without predators can overshoot their range. So herbivore numbers are held by fertility control before predators are removed in an area, each loss is monitored, and no step may cause more suffering or more rights violations than it prevents. Nature is still not my standard: where it can be reordered without breaking that rule, it should be. The risks and the stop rule are set out in the next question. Omnivory. Predation is defined by the act, not the species label. Herbivores that kill animals, such as deer eating nestling birds, fall under the same duty and the same herbivorization methods, weighted by the sentience of the animals they kill. Cats. Obligate carnivores need specific nutrients, such as taurine, that synthetic or plant-based diets can supply. Each companion animal's diet is set by veterinary judgment of its health, and sentience science decides which prey species count.

head: "Has anything on this scale been done, and what could go wrong?"
body: Not on this scale, and I don't pretend otherwise. The largest federal wildlife fertility-control program, the Bureau of Land Management's for wild horses and burros, treated 1,038 mares in fiscal 2024 and 921 in fiscal 2025, with PZP and GonaCon. No gene drive has been released into the wild in any vertebrate. The program starts from tested tools used at small scale and grows only as they prove out. Risks I accept and watch: Scavengers and nutrient cycling. Predator kills feed ravens, eagles, coyotes, bears, and others, and return nutrients to the ground. In Yellowstone, wolf kills became a steady food supply for scavengers through the winter. Fewer kills mean less carrion. Disease. Predators can take sick animals first. A modeling study of chronic wasting disease in deer found that selective predation by wolves could slow the disease. Without predators, disease has to be found by monitoring and handled by veterinary care. Herbivore overshoot. Yellowstone's elk rose from about 3,000 to about 22,000 after culling stopped and before wolves returned (Yellowstone Wolves). That is why herbivore fertility control comes first. The stop rule. No step may cause more suffering or more rights violations than it prevents (Wild-Animal Predation). The day-one tools stay day-one: no breeding of captive predators, and sanctuary for non-threatening predators. Removal in the wild and every engineered method should start in pilot areas, with herbivore fertility control already working there, and with herbivore condition, disease, scavengers, and vegetation monitored and reported every year. A method should expand beyond its pilot areas only after a published review shows it causes less suffering than it prevents, and each year's report should give the program's cost alongside its results. A step that breaks the stop rule should be halted, and reversed where it can be, before the program goes further. The program has no fixed budget cap or end date, because a duty does not expire, but its size is set by evidence: it grows only as each tool proves out. Bureau of Land Management – Wild Horse and Burro Program Data: Fertility Control Treatments Wilmers et al., Journal of Animal Ecology – Trophic facilitation by introduced top predators: grey wolf subsidies to scavengers in Yellowstone National Park (2003) Wild et al., Journal of Wildlife Diseases – The role of predation in disease control: a comparison of selective and nonselective removal on prion disease dynamics in deer (2011)

head: "What is the long-term future of predator species?"
body: The duty to stop predation should apply instantly. Within U.S. borders, predation is a rights violation that the government should stop now, not someday (Wild-Animal Predation, Animal Rights and Sentientism). Methods under the day-one duty: Within U.S. borders the duty to stop predation should be immediate. Preferred tools, not a soft delay of the duty: stop breeding predators held under human control. Let captive predator lines end rather than restock them; and pursue herbivorization where the science works, in line with gene-drive methods under study and Pearce's proposal of "rewriting the vertebrate genome" (see Evidence: Herbivorization). Those are how the duty is carried out — not a gradual aside that treats the ban as optional.

head: "What about people who hunt or fish to feed their families?"
body: Killing a sentient animal for food is murder, graded by sentience. Self-defense against an immediate attack remains, as for humans (Section 1). But a predator that can be separated or contained may not be killed for being dangerous by nature. Separation and containment come first. I allow no subsistence exception, and no Indigenous exception whatsoever.

head: "Don't tribes have treaty rights to hunt and fish?"
body: Many do, and the Supreme Court enforces them: in Herrera v. Wyoming (2019) it held that an 1868 treaty hunting right survived Wyoming's statehood. But Congress can abrogate an Indian treaty right by a clear statement (Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, Menominee Tribe v. United States). The law ought to do exactly that, expressly, for every right to hunt or fish sentient animals. There is no Indigenous exception, because the animal killed is the same animal whoever kills it. Supreme Court of the United States – Herrera v. Wyoming (2019) Cornell LII – Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903) Cornell LII – Menominee Tribe v. United States, 391 U.S. 404 (1968)

head: "Tens of millions of Americans hunt or fish. Are you putting them all on the capital track?"
body: In 2022, 14.4 million Americans hunted and 39.9 million fished. Every one of them who kept killing high-sentience animals after such a ban took effect would commit murder and should be treated as a murderer. No one should be prosecuted for a hunt or a catch before the ban (Animal Rights and Sentientism). The law should be published, licenses should end on day one, and the line should be clear, so continuing would be a choice made in full knowledge. The capital evidentiary standard still applies: no one should be executed on a game warden's word, only on objective evidence such as video and physical evidence. Critics warn that a law this far from current practice invites juries to refuse to convict, as English juries did under the Bloody Code. The state ought to track acquittal rates in these cases as it does at three marks (Repeat Offenders). Widespread killing does not make the killing anything less than murder. It makes enforcement more urgent. The rule protects the animals, who hold the same right not to be killed whether one hunter or millions take part. A hunter who stops loses a hobby; the animal he would have shot keeps its life. Anyone who keeps killing after the ban has chosen murder, and is sentenced for it. U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service – 2022 National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation

head: "How is animal cruelty punished?"
body: Under Animal Cruelty Law: cruelty to animals in the applicable sentience classes should be capital if it causes lasting injury and otherwise should be grave abuse (three marks: execution, experimentation, or life with labor). Below that, cruelty should be non-capital but tracked and should count toward the repeat-offender threshold. Companion animals should be on the same tiers.

head: "What about the trade in wild and exotic animals?"
body: Capturing wild animals to sell them, and the commercial trade in wild-caught animals, fall under the same ban as commercial breeding mills: they treat sentient beings as stock. Exotic-pet owners are in the same category as any other pet owner: as long as the animals are safe, they may foster and keep them. Anyone who takes an ownerless or wild animal under their responsibility may adopt it and becomes its guardian (Animal Rights and Sentientism). Most infectious diseases in people can spread from animals, so the trade also carries a public-health cost.

head: "Can people keep pets, and what about commercial breeding?"
body: Companion animals may be kept where their rights are respected. Commercial breeding mills fall under the animal-agriculture ban: I would ban them outright. Killing a high-sentience companion animal for convenience is murder, and the cruelty tiers apply to companion animals the same as to any other sentient animal. Euthanasia is not murder only when it is for the animal's own sake, never for convenience, on a veterinarian's best-interest finding, and carried out by a veterinary professional, even at home (Animal Rights and Sentientism). noteNo wind-downThere is no lag here: commercial breeding mills should shut down immediately along with animal agriculture, and the animals in them should be adopted out where possible, after the same vetting as farm animals, and the rest go to sanctuary (Sanctuary Plan).

head: "Is pest control allowed?"
body: Lethal control of sentient pests should be allowed only to stop an actual or imminent attack on persons or animals, or a clear disease or rights threat. A clear disease or rights threat includes a statutory infestation: when a high-class pest population occupies a dwelling, food store, or medical facility in a way that foreseeably spreads pathogens or destroys necessary stores, lethal control of that occupying population is lawful self-defense / defense of rights (Infestation (pest); Animal Rights and Sentientism). Separation, exclusion, and other non-lethal methods come first where they will work. When lethal force is used, the least-harmful method that works should be required, and control is graded by sentience class like every other killing of a sentient animal. Rats, mice, pigeons, and every other high-class pest stay in the high class - pest status does not demote them. Qualifying infestation control is not the banned "preventive extermination." What stays banned is preventive area-wide extermination of high-sentience animals that are not occupying a qualifying site: outdoor kill campaigns, park or field sweeps, and island-wide rodent eradication dressed up as pest control are murder when the animals are high-class. Hunger, nuisance alone, or fear that pests might arrive later is not self-defense and is not an infestation.

head: "What counts as an infestation?"
body: Occupation of a dwelling, a food store, or a medical facility by a high-class pest population in a way that foreseeably spreads pathogens or destroys necessary stores. Those three sites only. A food store means a structure used to store food for persons or animals under care (a pantry, warehouse, or similar). Open fields, pastures, parks, and general agricultural barns that are not food stores do not qualify. A passing animal, or animals outdoors that are not occupying a qualifying site, do not qualify. Once the test is met, lethal control of the occupying population at that site is lawful defense of rights under the rules above. It is not a warrant to clear the neighborhood.
Fishing, companion animals, breeding mills, euthanasia, pest control, zoos, and the cruelty tiers are set out in the position and the questions above, and cruelty in full in Animal Cruelty Law.

Rights rest on sentience, not species (Ethical and Philosophical Framework). Killing a sentient animal for sport or food violates its rights in the same way I treat any other killing of an innocent. So the same murder rules, self-defense exception, and forfeitures apply as in the human context. Grading by sentience sets the severity of the offense. I treat predation as a rights violation even when the predator lacks agency, and within U.S. borders the government intervenes by placing non-threatening predators in sanctuary or confinement and feeding them lab-grown meat (Wild-Animal Predation). Sanctuary works for predators because their violence can be subdued: a predator can be contained, separated from other animals, and fed. A violent human, short of permanent sedation, requires far more maintenance and is much harder to manage, which is why violent humans face the forfeiture tracks rather than sanctuary. Herbivore populations and sanctuary lands receive priority protection (Energy & Environment). About 15.9 million people held paid hunting licenses in 2024, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, so ending hunting is a large change. The evidence for herbivorization is set out below.

Jeff McMahan argues that "we have reason to desire the extinction of all carnivorous species," provided herbivorous species replace them "without ecological upheaval involving more harm than would be prevented." David Pearce proposes "reprogramming or phasing out" predators. He writes that the abolitionist project "entails ecosystem redesign, cross-species immunocontraception, marine nanorobots, rewriting the vertebrate genome," and names "the extinction - or genetically-driven behavioural modification - of members of the cat family" as its most controversial case. Removing predators has already helped native species on islands. Across 251 eradications of invasive mammals on 181 islands, 236 native species benefited and 7 were harmed, and four threatened species improved their IUCN category while none got worse (Jones et al. 2016). New Zealand's Predator Free 2050 program, which targets possums, rats, and mustelids, had over 2.5 million hectares under sustained suppression and 122,110 hectares free of all three target groups and defended against reinvasion as of June 2025. Two of its seven 2025 goals were achieved. Contraception works on single herds but lowers numbers slowly. PZP immunocontraception of the Assateague horses was 92–100% effective each year and reached zero population growth within 2 years, but the herd fell only 22.8% (175 to 135) by year 11 because treated mares lived longer. No gene drive has been released into the wild in any vertebrate. The two most advanced vertebrate systems, both in house mice, have not yet reached full proof of concept in the laboratory, according to the 2026 Gene Drive Monitor survey. Without population control, removing predators shifts herbivores to food limitation: they increase, overgraze, and vegetation declines (Hairston, Smith & Slobodkin 1960). That is why herbivore control goes together with predator removal.

Wolves were eradicated from Yellowstone by the 1920s. Park managers held elk to about 3,000 by culling until 1969; after culling stopped, elk peaked at about 22,000 in 1994, and between 1995 and 1997, 41 wolves were reintroduced. A 21-year study of 113 aspen stands found that elk density was 8.6 to 9.5 times stronger than wolf predation risk as a driver of browsing, and about 20 to 28 times stronger for young aspen growing out of elk reach. Herbivore numbers, not elk's fear of wolves, drove both the damage and the recovery (Brice et al. 2025). Recovery took more than a decade: browsing did not begin to decline until 2008. Lower elk numbers alone did not restore willows. In a 20-year experiment, willows reached the heights of a restored community only where simulated beaver dams were present and browsing was reduced. A reorganized community of large herbivores, with bison as a relatively invulnerable prey species, suppressed willow growth (Hobbs et al. 2024). Yellowstone supports controlling the whole herbivore system: every herbivore species, not one, along with the conditions plants need to recover.

I define animal cruelty as extreme violence, intentional neglect, beating without drawing blood, or withholding food, water, or shelter as deliberate punishment. Any of these against a human or a higher-sentience animal should be capital if it causes lasting injury, even against a single animal, and otherwise is grave abuse (three marks: execution, experimentation, or life with labor). Against lower-sentience animals it counts as marks. It counts toward the repeat-offender threshold, and ritual slaughter ought to be banned with no religious exemption. I would ban all sexual acts with sentient animals, forced or not, because animals cannot consent and allowing any form would leave a gray area for abuse. Non-forced acts carry one mark, fixed-term labor with mandatory rehabilitation, an income-and-wealth day fine that goes first to the animal's care, and a ban on keeping animals.

I hold that cruelty to a sentient animal is a rights violation and should be a crime. Animal cruelty is any of the following: 1. extreme violence; 2. intentional neglect, a chosen pattern of keeping it up; 3. beating without drawing blood; 4. psychological abuse, withholding food, water, or shelter, not out of neglect but as deliberate punishment. Beating means force beyond ordinary discipline: a closed fist, an object, or repeated strikes. A swat on the rear as ordinary discipline is not beating. If any of these acts is done to a human or to an animal in the higher sentience tier, it should be capital if it causes lasting injury, physical or psychological; otherwise it falls in the grave tier: three marks at once, reaching the threshold: execution, experimentation, or life with labor, as the victim chooses. Marks are uniform across victims: the same act carries the same marks whether the victim is a person or a higher-sentience animal. Lesser cruelty, harm to a higher-sentience animal outside the four acts and without lasting injury, such as a single strike causing pain or abandonment, is two marks; cruelty to a lower-sentience animal is one mark. Cruelty to lower-sentience animals is not capital; it counts as marks against the offender. The same intent test that governs crimes against humans applies: what matters is whether the offender acted voluntarily and knew what they were doing. Moral agency is irrelevant to whether a violation occurred, but where agency is absent, no forfeiture-based punishment follows. The same sentience-based classes used for killing animals apply. Cruelty to high-sentience animals in the capital class should be capital if it causes lasting injury and otherwise should be grave abuse (three marks: execution, experimentation, or life with labor). Cruelty to lower-sentience animals is a lesser offense that counts as marks against the offender. Animal cruelty counts toward the repeat-offender threshold, with its weight depending on severity. Extremely severe, violent cruelty that causes lasting injury should be capital even when only one animal is harmed, just as violent torture of a single human should be capital; it does not require large numbers. Torturing large numbers of animals should likewise be capital outright, with no lesser classification. Mass neglect, meaning neglect of multiple animals at once or a sustained pattern, should be capital when it causes lasting injury, physical or psychological, and otherwise grave abuse (three marks). Intentional neglect of a single higher-sentience animal without lasting injury is grave abuse (three marks), the same as for a person, and neglect of a lower-sentience animal counts as marks. Ritual slaughter should be banned, with no religious exemption. Euthanasia that meets the living-animal rule in Animal Rights and Sentientism is not cruelty. Euthanasia that breaks those conditions is graded on a sliding scale. A genuine case of real suffering where the guardian skips the vet, the convenience being the vet trip and not the killing, carries a lesser, separate, non-capital penalty. A cover case with no real suffering is cruelty under these tiers, capital if it causes lasting injury and otherwise grave abuse (three marks: execution, experimentation, or life with labor); clear intent to harm is murder.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Michael Vick, 2007: the NFL quarterback was sentenced to 23 months for a dogfighting conspiracy that involved gambling and killing pit bulls. Sentences like this are far below the position's standard. NPR (2007) – Vick Sentenced to 23 Months for Conspiracy

Animals cannot consent to sexual activity. I would ban all sexual acts with sentient animals. The ban itself makes no distinction between forced and non-forced acts. Forced acts are graded under the cruelty tiers. Non-forced acts carry a separate, lesser penalty. The ban follows from the consent principle in Age of Consent.

head: "Shouldn't cruelty to animals be punished less severely than violence against people?"
body: Sentient animals hold the same negative rights as people, so the same cruelty acts should get the same penalties against a higher-sentience animal as against a human: they should be capital if they cause lasting injury, and grave abuse (three marks: execution, experimentation, or life with labor) otherwise. Severity should be graded by the animal's sentience, not by species membership. The rule protects victims who cannot speak for themselves: an animal cannot report abuse, testify, or leave the person hurting it. The two errors are not equal. The capital track requires the act proven to the capital evidentiary standard and lasting injury proven beyond a reasonable doubt through a veterinarian's or veterinary behaviorist's evaluation, and a case that falls short goes to the lower tiers; a light sentence leaves the offender free to reach the next animal, which again cannot ask for help.

head: "Is soring a show horse animal cruelty?"
body: Yes. Deliberately injuring a horse's legs or hooves so it steps higher in the ring is violence against a sentient animal for a ribbon, and it is graded under the same cruelty tiers as any other abuse. Inspection ought to be done by inspectors independent of the shows and their owners, never by people the industry appoints.

head: "How is animal cruelty punished?"
body: Any of the four cruelty acts (extreme violence, intentional neglect, beating without drawing blood, or withholding food, water, or shelter as deliberate punishment) against a higher-sentience animal should be capital if it causes lasting injury, even when only one animal is harmed, the same as against a human. Without lasting injury it should fall in the grave tier: three marks at once, reaching the threshold: execution, experimentation, or life with labor, as the victim chooses. Cruelty to lower-sentience animals is non-capital but tracked in the system, and cruelty convictions count toward the repeat-offender threshold. This matches the murder rules in Criminal Justice & Security and the threshold in Repeat Offenders, and replaces treatment of animal cruelty as an ordinary crime. Companion animals are included on the same tiers (Hunting, Fishing, Pets, and Zoos).

head: "Why ban it if the animal isn't forced?"
body: Animals cannot consent. With non-consenting people, the main problem is psychological damage, which can be severe, especially for the young. That harm dynamic is not exactly the same with animals. Even though animals can't consent, if they are not being sexualized in an abusive manner, the sexual activity itself does not create psychological danger to the animal, and sexual activity is a strong biological drive for them. So there is a difference between forced bestiality, where someone forces an animal, penetrative or otherwise, and cases where someone lets an animal do something to them. It is not as clear-cut as human sexual consent. I don't see a problem with the second category in itself. But societally, if any form were allowed, it would be too much of a gray area for people to abuse animals. So the ban is flat and covers all sexual acts with sentient animals.

Forced sexual acts with sentient animals should be treated as cruelty and should be graded under the cruelty tiers above, by severity and sentience class. Non-forced acts should still be banned and should carry a separate penalty, lighter than for forced acts, which should go through the cruelty tiers: one mark. A fixed-term labor sentence with mandatory rehabilitation and a known end date; an income-and-wealth day fine, which should go first to the animal's care, then to the victim restitution fund, and never to the seizing agency; and a ban on keeping animals. Fines can be substantial. Bestiality and neglect are separate harms: the sex act is one violation of the animal's dignity, and neglect is a failure of care on top of it. Marks should stack only when both are charged, so the same suffering is not punished twice. Neglect should be charged separately only when it is a distinct failure of care, not the harm of the act itself. Forced bestiality should follow the same rule: the force should be graded under the cruelty tiers (capital with lasting injury, otherwise grave abuse, three marks), and distinct neglect should stack on top.
The cruelty tiers, marks, and the forced versus non-forced sexual-act penalties are set out in the position, the questions above, and the penalties note.

Sentient animals hold negative rights within U.S. borders, so deliberately inflicting suffering on one is an outward rights violation, which is what my criminal law would punish (Criminal Justice & Security). Because those rights are the same rights humans hold, the same cruelty acts that should be capital against a human should be capital against a higher-sentience animal, with severity graded by sentience under Animal Rights and Sentientism. Religious practice does not exempt anyone from rights protections (Religion & Secularism). Federal law already criminalizes certain acts of animal crushing and torture under the Preventing Animal Cruelty and Torture Act (18 U.S.C. § 48).

I stand for America First realism with selective Western imperialism. The United States should prioritize its sovereignty, security, cultural cohesion, and manufacturing strength. It ought to engage forcefully against direct threats (especially Iran and extremist Islam) while avoiding open-ended nation-building, and participate in alliances and institutions only when they clearly serve American interests.

The U.S. should intervene where its safety is at stake, especially against Iran. I view nation-building skeptically because it usually fails. Openly hostile cultures may be confronted and defeated. Non-hostile ones should be left alone.

The United States should involve itself directly in areas of interest that strengthen the country's safety, such as intervention against Iran, a direct enemy and belligerent extremist force. I view nation-building and regime change with skepticism because of their track record of efficacy. I favor Western imperialism and colonialism that destroy openly hostile cultures whose governing norms violate sentient rights, which is what I mean by ethically inferior. Imperialism here means defeating and containing the threat, without governing the territory. Non-hostile cultures should be left alone in the majority of cases. When U.S. action takes control of a foreign country's assets or revenue, they ought to be held in trust for its people, with public audits, spending only for their benefit, a fixed end date unless Congress renews it, and creditors' claims settled in court.

head: "Doesn't favoring imperialism against hostile cultures contradict skepticism of nation-building?"
body: No. Nation-building tries to reconstruct a society into a friendly democracy, which has repeatedly failed. Action against openly hostile cultures aims at defeating the threat, not at remaking the society in America's image. The line is drawn by hostility: hostile forces are confronted, non-hostile ones are left alone.

head: "Who decides that a culture is hostile, and by what test?"
body: Conduct decides, not ethnicity or religion. A regime or movement is openly hostile when its governing institutions attack or sponsor attacks on the United States or commit systematic rights violations. Ethically inferior means governing norms that violate sentient rights. The President and Congress make the determination under their war powers. In real time, the President may act alone only to repel an attack under way or imminent, or to protect U.S. forces and citizens. That is the immediate response already allowed in Emergency Powers. A sustained campaign to defeat and contain a regime or movement needs Congress's authorization within 30 days, or it ends on a fixed date. That is shorter than the 60 days plus 30 for withdrawal in today's War Powers Resolution. When the evidence of attack or sponsorship is incomplete, the default is defensive action only: interception, protection of forces, sanctions, and intelligence gathering. A regime or movement is designated openly hostile, and offensive action begins, once the attack or sponsorship is attributed to its governing institutions on evidence the President certifies to Congress.

head: "Isn't 'ethically inferior and openly hostile' a stipulated test?"
body: Where it comes from. Both halves come from my axioms. "Ethically inferior" ranks governing norms on the one scale I use everywhere: whether they violate sentient rights. "Openly hostile" is conduct: governing institutions that attack or sponsor attacks on the United States or commit systematic rights violations. Organized groups that systematically violate rights may be met with decisive force, the same forfeiture rule I apply to individuals, scaled up (Rights, Order, and Forfeiture at Scale). Both halves are required. A culture I rank low that is not hostile is left alone. The rivals. Nation-building measures success by remaking a society, and its record in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Libya is failure. Pure non-intervention leaves attackers unanswered and the people they attack unprotected. Ethnicity or religion as the test would judge by identity, not conduct. What would change it. The test turns on conduct, so a designation should change with conduct. When the evidence of attack or sponsorship is incomplete, action stays defensive, and a sustained campaign ends unless Congress authorizes it within 30 days. A designation should lift once the governing institutions stop attacking or sponsoring attacks and stop systematic rights violations, confirmed on the same kind of evidence the President certified to designate them.

Foreign policy exists to protect the security, prosperity, and continuity of the United States. Realist thinking holds that great powers should act when core interests are at stake and stay out when they are not. Recent efforts in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Libya showed that military victory is often achievable while building a stable, friendly state almost never is. Iran funds and directs proxy forces that have attacked U.S. troops and allies, pursues nuclear capability, and has plotted assassinations on U.S. soil, which makes it a concrete security problem rather than a distant one.
Nation-building is the use of military and civilian power to construct or reconstruct a state's political institutions, economy, and security forces, usually after a war or regime change.

I believe the U.S. should join alliances only when they make the country safer and must never give up its sovereignty. It should stay diplomatic but not bow to allies or foreign courts.

The United States should not be part of or a contributor to any alliance that erodes the nation's sovereignty or the best interests of its people. It ought to join alliances that increase the security and interests of the nation. I support diplomacy and foreign relations, but national principles come first, and the United States should not capitulate to allies' demands or submit to any foreign tribunal. It should take territory only with the consent of its people and their government, by purchase or treaty. With allies, security needs ought to be met first through basing and defense agreements. Threats and tariffs against a friendly country should be a last resort, justified only when the security concern is overwhelming and truly justified.

head: "Does conditional membership weaken the credibility of alliances like NATO?"
body: Alliances are valuable because they serve the security of their members. Membership on the condition that it serves American interests is the same calculation every ally makes. Credibility comes from strength and clear interests, not from unconditional commitment.

The federal government's first duty is to its own citizens, and alliances are tools toward that end. NATO's collective-defense commitment under Article 5 serves U.S. security where it deters common threats. Sovereignty means U.S. actions answer to U.S. law and voters, not to foreign bodies.
NATO – Collective defence and Article 5
Cornell LII – U.S. Constitution, Article II

American manufacturing comes first for me, imports should come with matching exports, and I treat tariffs cautiously. Outsourcing should be restricted only where it involves a country judged to be a national security threat, such as China. China is a dangerous rival, and trade with it should continue only on reciprocal terms.

American manufacturing should be bolstered wherever possible. Every import brought into the country ought to have a deal structure under which the United States also exports to that partner, keeping trade mutually beneficial. I believe tariffs are good in theory and questionable in practice. Domestic trade should be prioritized and incentivized through tax and regulatory relief only, such as full expensing and the long-run payroll tax cuts in Domestic Policy & Governance. Outsourced labor should face regulations and restrictions only where it involves a country determined to be a national security threat to the United States; China is one example. I treat China as a dangerous rival, and trade with it should continue under these same conditions. Tariffs are taxes and belong to Congress. The President should impose them only under clear, narrow statutory authority, for a stated national-security or leverage purpose, and for a fixed period.

head: "Do restrictions on outsourcing conflict with your free-market position?"
body: No. I support free markets at home, and outsourcing restrictions should be limited to countries determined to be national security threats to the United States, such as China. Reciprocity requirements and these narrow restrictions protect the industrial base the country needs to defend itself. The broad work of making U.S. labor cheaper is done through full expensing now and across-the-board payroll tax cuts in the long run, as the transition levy steps down, set out in Domestic Policy & Governance. Tariffs are approached with caution because their practical effects are mixed.

head: "Don't Americans pay for tariffs?"
body: Mostly, yes. Studies of the 2018 tariffs found they passed almost completely into the prices Americans paid for imported goods, so the cost fell on U.S. buyers rather than on foreign exporters. That is why I treat tariffs as good in theory, as leverage and as protection for strategic industries, and questionable in practice. The preferred tools for supporting American industry are full expensing and, in the long run, payroll tax cuts.

A manufacturing base is a strategic asset in war and crisis. The United States runs a large goods trade deficit with China, and the FBI identifies China's intelligence and economic espionage as a major threat. Reciprocity keeps trade beneficial to both sides rather than one-directional. The practical case against broad tariffs is measured. The 2018 tariffs passed through almost completely to U.S. import prices, with the full cost falling on domestic buyers and a loss in U.S. real income of about $1.4 billion a month by the end of 2018.

head: Coastal Shipping and the Jones Act
sub: Coastal Shipping and the Jones Act

body: I believe support for American shipbuilding should come through tax and regulatory relief, not through a mandate that every cargo between U.S. ports ride on a U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed ship and that raises what Americans pay for fuel and goods. Where the military needs ships and crews it cannot buy in time of war, Congress ought to fund that need directly and in the open. Any waiver should be set by Congress or expire on its own, not renewed indefinitely by the executive.

body: I support sanctions and trade limits that target adversaries like China, Russia, and Iran, working alongside military deterrence.

Economic tools ought to serve national security. Trade should be reciprocal, and restrictions should apply to adversaries and national-security threats such as China, Russia, and Iran, including limits on outsourcing and technology transfer. Sanctions should be used where they weaken an enemy's capacity to threaten the United States, alongside military deterrence rather than in place of it.

head: "Do sanctions actually work?"
body: Not alone. They are one tool that raises an adversary's costs and limits its access to technology and finance, used together with deterrence. Across 204 sanctions episodes studied by the Peterson Institute, sanctions were at least partly successful in 34%, succeeding about half the time for modest policy goals but in about 31% of attempts at regime change or democratization.

The International Emergency Economic Powers Act authorizes the President to regulate economic transactions to deal with an unusual and extraordinary foreign threat once a national emergency is declared (50 U.S.C. § 1701). Under the emergency-powers rule in Authority & Civil Liberties, such declarations lapse unless the legislature renews them.

Foreign aid must serve America's own security and interests. In my view aid that is purely charitable should be paid for only by people who choose to give, not by required taxes.

Foreign spending ought to advance the security and long-term interests of the United States. Assistance that serves that purpose, such as support for allies against shared threats or efforts that counter adversaries, should be judged under the same national-interest test as alliances and institutions. Charitable aid that serves no American interest is redistribution abroad and ought to be funded only through taxpayer opt-in or private giving.

head: "Won't cutting aid cede influence to China and other rivals?"
body: Aid that counters adversaries or secures American interests passes the national-interest test and can continue. What does not pass is charity carried out with compelled tax money. Americans who want to fund humanitarian work abroad remain free to do so, through opt-in programs or private giving.

head: "Doesn't cutting aid cost lives?"
body: It can. The State Department credits PEPFAR, the U.S. HIV/AIDS program, with saving 26 million lives since 2003. I do not deny that. It rests on principle: compelled taxes do not fund charity abroad any more than at home. Programs like PEPFAR continue where they pass the national-interest test, and otherwise through opt-in funding and private giving, which remain open to everyone who wants to keep them going.

The state's primary duty is to its own citizens, as set out in Ethical and Philosophical Framework, and I reject mandatory redistribution at home. Applying the same rule abroad keeps policy consistent. Foreign aid accounts for about 1% or less of the federal budget, and U.S. global health funding was $12.4 billion in FY2024. The amounts are small relative to the budget, so the question is one of principle: whether compelled taxes should fund charity abroad. The opt-in model is defined in Domestic Policy & Governance.

I believe the U.S. should join global institutions only when they help it and never submit to international courts or law over its own.

Participation in global institutions follows my position on alliances: the United States should contribute only to those that benefit it and serve its best interests. It may contribute, but it should not be held to any standard, tribunal, or global court for its sovereign actions or capitulate to any international law. The United States ought to follow its own law and what is best for its people and shared values, and no globalist bureaucrats or courts should dictate its conduct. Treaties the United States has ratified remain binding as U.S. law until it exits them through its own constitutional procedure. The United States should stay in the UN and other bodies where participation benefits it. The rejection of foreign tribunals applies to every nation's sovereignty, not only America's. The United States should not recognize or cooperate with the International Criminal Court. Sanctions on its officials ought to be kept for concrete acts against Americans or allied personnel, such as warrants or arrests, not for the court's existence or general investigations.

head: "Does rejecting international law isolate the United States?"
body: No. The United States can cooperate with any institution that serves its interests. What it rejects is surrendering authority over its own actions to foreign bodies that answer to no American voter.

head: "Doesn't this let the U.S. ignore treaties it signed?"
body: No. A treaty the United States has ratified is U.S. law and is followed until the country exits it through its own procedure. What I reject is a foreign court or body claiming authority over U.S. actions.

Some ratified treaties conflict with my positions, and the United States ought to exit them before those positions take effect. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, ratified by the United States in 1992, says in article 7 that "no one shall be subjected without his free consent to medical or scientific experimentation," and article 4(2) allows no derogation from it. The U.S. reservation to article 7 limits only "cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment" to what the Fifth, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendments forbid. It does not reach the experimentation clause. The U.S. reservation to article 6 keeps capital punishment for anyone "other than a pregnant woman" under "existing or future laws," but the Human Rights Committee reads article 6 to allow death only for crimes "involving intentional killing" and to bar new capital offenses after ratification. So the United States ought to withdraw from the Covenant through its own constitutional procedure before the experimentation track and the new capital offenses take effect. While the Covenant has no withdrawal clause and the Committee holds that no state may leave it, the United States still ought to leave, because no nation is bound forever to a foreign committee's reading of a treaty it chose to join. The Convention Against Torture can be denounced under its article 31, effective one year after notice, and the United States ought to denounce it too if its definition of torture is read to reach the experimentation track. Leaving the Convention does not lift the bar on removing any resident to torture, which the law ought to hold in statute.

Sovereignty means accountability to one's own citizens. The United States is not a party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. Institutions such as the UN operate under a charter that lets members participate without surrendering domestic authority. The American Service-Members' Protection Act of 2002 (22 U.S.C. 7421 et seq.) bars U.S. cooperation with the International Criminal Court and authorizes the President to use "all means necessary and appropriate" to free U.S. and allied personnel it detains.

The United States should not be bound by the WHO. I'd cooperate on specific health work, such as surveillance data sharing, where Americans clearly benefit, with voluntary funding tied to results.

The United States should not be a member bound by the World Health Organization's rules, regulations, or pandemic agreements, consistent with Global Institutions. It may cooperate with the WHO and other health bodies case by case through specific agreements, such as disease-surveillance data sharing, where the benefit to Americans is clear. Any funding should be voluntary, targeted to named programs, and tied to published results. Domestic defense against pandemics, natural or engineered, is the government's own duty (Pandemics and Biosecurity).

head: "Doesn't leaving the WHO weaken the world's early warning against pandemics, including for Americans?"
body: Supporters of membership point to disease surveillance: disease does not stop at borders, and the WHO coordinates reporting and response among nearly every country. Cooperation does not require membership. The United States ought to keep that benefit by cooperating on surveillance and data sharing through specific agreements, without being bound to the organization's rules. Membership has not guaranteed good performance. The Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response found that the COVID-19 outbreak likely met the criteria for a global emergency at the WHO committee's first meeting on January 22, 2020, but the declaration came only on January 30.

head: "How much does the United States pay?"
body: More than any other country. The United States contributed $1.284 billion in the 2022–2023 biennium, 15.6% of the WHO's revenue. Most of it was voluntary and earmarked. The assessed contribution has been set at the 22% maximum share of member assessments.

The United States ought to take part in global institutions only where they serve the national interest, and never submit to their authority. Health cooperation serves that interest when it is specific and measured; open-ended membership and funding do not guarantee results, as the 2020 delay showed.

I see a culturally similar society as strongest, so immigration should be limited to people who fit Western values and assimilate, with American labor needs as a secondary criterion. Entry should be closed by default, open only through named paths in statute, each under the same values vetting: family, employment, seasonal work, students and visitors, refugee resettlement, and asylum, which is one category of application, not a pass to enter. The diversity visa lottery should end. I want less immigration from Muslim-majority countries. Being Muslim carries a presumption against admission, which an individual applicant can overcome only with verified evidence of conduct and record. The border must be heavily secured, with lethal force when necessary, and illegal immigrants removed by force. Refugee resettlement is a national-interest privilege. Residents who are removed keep the bars against return to persecution or torture; people denied at the border or applying for asylum do not. Birthright citizenship should end by amendment for future births.

I believe cultural cohesion in values should be the aim. Measured diversity–trust links are real but small on average and strongest for trust in neighbors; that is a reason for vetting and assimilation priority, not a diversity compliment. Culture-mashing raises tribalism and clashes of ideals - so I hold that immigration is not a virtue and not a protected entitlement. Entry should be closed by default, open only through named entry paths set in statute, each under the same values vetting. Starting from today's categories, these are the paths I would name:
Family: spouses, minor children, parents, siblings, and adult children of citizens, and spouses and minor children of green-card holders.

Employment, permanent and temporary, including H-1B: only for American labor needs the domestic workforce cannot meet first (Skilled-Worker Visas). Investment may count as one factor after vetting, never as a purchase of status (Investor Visas).
Seasonal work: temporary farm and non-farm seasonal visas, under the same labor-needs-first rule.

Students and visitors: study, business, and tourist visas. Student visas ought to carry a fixed term set by Congress, with an extension granted for documented academic progress and a fresh values check, rather than an open stay that lasts as long as a program does (see Fixed terms for foreign students). Work on a student visa ought to be limited to training the degree program requires, set by statute or published rule; any other work goes through the employment path, open only for labor needs the domestic workforce cannot meet first.

Refugee resettlement: a national-interest privilege, not a right, under the same vetting. It is sad, but protecting non-citizens from persecution abroad is not the purpose of the U.S. government; a refugee applicant who fails vetting is simply not admitted (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents).

Asylum: claims made here or at the border should continue to be heard under the same vetting. Asylum is one category of application, not a pass to enter and not a duty to protect. Entry requires meeting the same assimilation and values standard as every other path; a claimant who fails vetting is simply not admitted.
The diversity visa lottery should end.

Every path carries the same conditions: individual values vetting, with the Muslim and listed-country presumptions where they apply; no entry from places under the hard entry ban (asylum claims from those places are still heard under the same vetting, and a claimant who passes it may enter), and no lottery or open channel from listed places (Questionable Compatibility); and residence conditional on self-support, passing the English and civics test within two years, and obeying the law.

My selection order: Western-values fit and assimilation first; American labor needs second. I want less immigration from Muslim-majority countries. Muslim identity carries a rebuttable presumption of incompatibility, overcome only by clear and convincing verified conduct and record, never by self-declaration: acceptance of constitutional supremacy over religious law, equal rights for women and non-Muslims, freedom to leave the faith, and rejection of violence (Islam and Extremism). Border force, removal, birthright abolition going forward, and refugee resettlement are covered in In short. Resettlement is a national-interest privilege under the same values vetting. Persecution abroad gives an applicant no claim on the United States: its government exists to protect its citizens, not non-citizens.

head: Data: Norway, crime and immigrant background

body: Official statistics as reported by the cited sources. The spread by country of origin bears on vetting for values and on assimilation, the primary criteria in my position above.

Charges, 2020–2023: these are charges, not convictions. Statistics Norway made no full adjustment for age and sex, giving separate rates for men aged 15–24 as its like-for-like comparison; and sexual offences had the lowest immigrant share of any offence group, 12% of charges against 20% for all offences. On that like-for-like comparison, the overrepresentation is large and growing. Among men aged 15–24, immigrants had just over 550 charges per 1,000 over the four years and Norwegian-born children of immigrants about 630, against just over 280 for the rest of the population, an overrepresentation of 96% and 124%, up from 53% and 59% in 2015–2018. In Oslo the rates were 820 and 910 against 210. Young male immigrants from Iraq and Somalia had close to 1,200 per 1,000. Those from the Philippines had 170. Across all ages, immigrants received 20% of the charges in cases decided by the justice system and Norwegian-born children of immigrants 5%. SSB – Siktelser og siktede personer etter innvandringsbakgrunn (2024)

Oslo assault rape (overfallsvoldtekt), police 2010–11: That is not a claim that 100% of all rapes were by non-Western migrants. Overall identified rape suspects were mixed by origin; socio-economic controls shrink some gaps; and Oslo police did not stop publishing rape statistics afterward—the 2011 report itself is the source. For the narrow category of identified assault rapes over a multi-year window, Oslo police reported that identified perpetrators were overwhelmingly of non-Western appearance/origin (media summary of the "Rape in the global city" series). That is the prior I use for stranger-assault risk and assimilation. NRK – Reagerer på norsk voldtektsfakta (2011) · Oslo Police – Voldtekt i den globale byen (2010/2011 series)

Unit warning: these are charges, not convictions, and are not on the same scale as Denmark's age-adjusted conviction indexes in the next box. Use each country's within-country gap and origin spread. Do not mash Norway charge multiples and Denmark conviction indexes into one comparative number.

head: Data: Denmark, crime and immigrant origin

body: Official Justice Ministry / Statistics Denmark pattern as reported by the cited sources. Third-party relative-rate charts are not a substitute for the ministry's age-adjusted indexes.

Penal crime, men, 2024: Statistics Denmark's age-adjusted index (all men = 100) puts male immigrants from non-Western countries at 137 and male descendants from non-Western countries at 245. Men of Danish origin are at 92. Among male descendants the highest indexes are for origins in Lebanon (386), Somalia (316), Syria (312), Morocco (299) and Pakistan (287).

Trend: crime is falling in every origin group. Among men born in 1997, 26% of immigrants, 27% of descendants and 9% of men of Danish origin had a penal-code conviction by age 26, down from 41%, 35% and 17% for men born in 1987. The gap narrowed but did not close.

Why it matters here: the spread by origin, as in the Norway box above, bears on country-level priors and on assimilation, the primary criteria in my position. France restricts official ethnicity statistics in a way Denmark does not. That gap is one reason European capitals cannot all be compared the same way.

Public finances: Denmark's Finance Ministry found that immigrants and their descendants together cost the public finances a net 16 billion kroner in 2019, about 21,000 kroner a person. Immigrants from Western countries paid in a net 52,000 kroner a person. Immigrants from the Middle East, North Africa, Pakistan and Turkey (MENAPT) cost a net 74,000, and their descendants 109,000. Part of the descendants' figure reflects age, since most are still children. Adjusted to the age profile of people of Danish origin, MENAPT descendants still cost about 53,000 kroner a person, while Western descendants turn positive. Over a projected lifetime, the ministry put people of non-Western origin at a net cost of about 31,000 kroner per year lived in Denmark and people of Western origin at a net gain of about 20,000. Finansministeriet – Indvandreres nettobidrag til de offentlige finanser i 2019, revideret (2023) · Folketinget – Finance Minister's answer to UUI question 141 (2025)
Data om udlændinge (datau.dk), citing Statistics Denmark – Udlændinge og kriminalitet (Indvandrere i Danmark 2025, pp. 112–121)
Justitsministeriet – Kriminalitet og herkomst 2023
Household means-tested use as reported by the cited source. Definitions and methods are contested. This is a noisy prior, not the removal test and not the franchise test.

Legal immigrant–headed households (CIS definition): the Center for Immigration Studies' analysis of Survey of Income and Program Participation data puts about 51% of households headed by legal immigrants on at least one major means-tested program, against about 37–38% of native-headed households. The basket typically includes Medicaid, cash welfare, food assistance, and related programs (including EITC and school meals in some CIS tables). Cato and others dispute the household unit and the program mix. CIS – Welfare Use by Immigrants and the U.S.-Born

What that number is not: it is not a measure of adult dependency, not a count of named adult recipients, and not the rule that removes a resident or suspends a vote. Citizen-child benefits, household-level credits, and school meals can put a household in the CIS tally even when the adult immigrant is not a named recipient of the transfers that trigger removal or the net-taxpayer bar.

What I take from it: even under the narrower reading, legal-immigrant-headed households show higher program use than native-headed households under CIS's definition. That directional gap is one more reason admission is a privilege under values vetting, and why nationality and welfare rules sit upstream of individual cases. Prefer named-adult rates where available. The operative tests remain named-recipient personally directed transfers: green-card and visa holders who take cash welfare, SNAP, housing aid, or non-emergency Medicaid are removed after a court finding (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). The franchise turns on the net-taxpayer rule in Voting and Elections. I do not use stacked "remigration savings" graphics as accounting.

head: "Doesn't the Fourteenth Amendment guarantee birthright citizenship?"
body: Yes, as currently interpreted, which is why abolition is proposed through constitutional amendment. The Supreme Court read the Citizenship Clause to cover children born on U.S. soil in United States v. Wong Kim Ark. The change applies only after the amendment, leaving existing citizens' status untouched.

head: "Isn't lethal force at the border excessive?"
body: No, because it is held to clear limits. I want the border protected, with lethal force when necessary, and necessary should mean one of two things. The first is the rule for any use of deadly force: an agent reasonably believes the person poses an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury to the agent or to someone else. That is already Department of Homeland Security policy, and it tracks Tennessee v. Garner (1985). The second goes beyond current policy and should be rare: a mass, coordinated push to force through the border, an invasion-style breach. Ceuta shows what that looks like. On July 30 and 31, 2026, about 50,000 people by the Spanish government's count, and about 60,000 by the count of Ceuta's president, crossed from Morocco into Spain's enclave of Ceuta in about 24 hours, by land and sea, some swimming or wading and some scaling the border fence, into a city of 85,000. At least 57 people died, a toll Spain later raised to 72 on its side of the border. Spain's prime minister called it "a violation of Spain's territorial integrity." Ceuta saw a smaller rush in May 2021, when about 8,000 people entered in two days. Other pushes have been openly violent. In June 2022, between 1,500 and 2,000 migrants, some carrying sticks, stormed the fences at Melilla, Spain's other enclave. In March 2020, after Turkey opened its side of the border, migrants throwing stones and wielding metal bars tried to force their way into Greece at Kastanies. A border that can be overrun that way is not defended. Border agents should wear body cameras, as I require for ICE officers, and should answer under the objectively unreasonable standard I set for every officer in place of qualified immunity (Police Power and Accountability). Illegal entrants who are caught should be removed by force.
