head: "Doesn't the economy need immigrant labor?"
body: Supporters of high immigration point to the budget: the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the 2022–2026 immigration surge would reduce federal deficits by about $0.9 trillion over 2024 to 2034. That gain does not decide admission. My position rests on social cohesion, not on economics: I treat a shared culture of values as worth more than the fiscal gain. Labor needs are met first through the domestic workforce, with full expensing and, in the long run, lower payroll taxes making American labor cheaper, and immigration that remains is selected first through values vetting and assimilation, then by American labor needs.

head: "Don't undocumented immigrants pay more in taxes than they cost?"
body: No. They pay real taxes, about $96.7 billion in 2022 by ITEP's estimate, much of it through sales and property taxes and payroll taxes for programs they cannot draw on. The claim leaves out the spending side. States and localities pay for schooling their children, plus health care, shelter, and justice costs, and those costs exceed what they collect. The National Academies found the first generation costs state and local budgets more than natives do, mainly through education. CBO found the 2021–2023 surge cost states and localities a net $9.2 billion in 2023. The size of the gap depends on the population estimate, whether U.S.-born children are counted, and whether broader economic effects are included. The direction does not change.

head: Data: fiscal impact of unauthorized immigration

body: Taxes paid: ITEP estimates undocumented immigrants paid $96.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2022 ($59.4 billion federal, $37.3 billion state and local) on a population of 10.9 million. They often pay higher effective state and local rates than top earners because of sales taxes and limited access to credits. ITEP – Tax Payments by Undocumented Immigrants

Restrictionist upper bound: FAIR puts the net cost at about $150.7 billion at the start of 2023: $182.1 billion in gross spending minus $31.4 billion in taxes. Education is the biggest cost, followed by health care and justice. FAIR counts about 15.5 million illegal aliens plus about 5.4 million U.S.-born children. Cato and others say it inflates population and costs and undercounts taxes and economic effects. FAIR – The Cost of Illegal Immigration to American Taxpayers 2023

National Academies (2017): first-generation immigrants have a less favorable net fiscal impact than natives, driven mainly by state and local spending on their children's education. The second generation is among the strongest net contributors. Federal effects are closer to neutral or positive over long horizons. NASEM – The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration

CBO (June 2025), 2021–2023 surge, state and local budgets in 2023: revenues rose $10.1 billion, mostly from sales tax. Spending rose $19.3 billion, chiefly for K-12 education, shelter, and border security. That leaves a direct net cost of $9.2 billion, or $9.8 billion on CBO's broader measure. CBO – Effects of the Surge in Immigration on State and Local Budgets in 2023

head: "How does an applicant overcome the presumption?"
body: By evidence of conduct and record, not by declaration. Every immigrant goes through individual values vetting. Two groups start with the burden on them: Muslim applicants, and applicants from countries where Islamist movements govern or where survey data show majority support for state-enforced religious law. To overcome it, the applicant should have to show by clear and convincing evidence all five of the following: Constitution over religious law: acceptance that the Constitution and civil law override any religious law, including in family, inheritance, and criminal matters. Equal rights: acceptance of equal legal standing for women and for non-Muslims and nonbelievers. Freedom to leave the faith: acceptance that anyone may leave or change religion, or criticize it, without penalty. No violence: rejection of violence for religious or political ends, with no membership in, support for, or funding of a designated terrorist or Islamist organization. A verifiable record: a record of conduct that matches 1–4 and can be checked. Evidence that counts: criminal and security record checks. Public-data review of the applicant's own posts, publications, and affiliations, within the public-data limits in Surveillance and Digital Technology; memberships, donations, and employers; prior lawful residence and compliance with the law in a country that meets these standards; and sworn references who can be checked. A structured interview and a sworn statement should be required, but they are never enough on their own. The statement would be made under the perjury rules in Oath of Office and Perjury, so a lie found later would be fraud, which is conduct and a ground for removal. Who decides: a consular or USCIS officer trained for values vetting would decide first. A denial would get one review by a second officer, on the written record. The applicant would carry the burden throughout. Being Muslim would set where the burden starts. It would never be the test itself, and an applicant of any faith who fails 1–5 would be refused. Passing vetting would admit a person. It would not lift the excluded-ideologies amendment, which bars adherents of Islam, as it bars adherents of Nazism, communism, and socialism, from authority roles (Oath of Office and Perjury). Nor would passing vetting lift the mosque bar: no new mosques may be built, and existing mosques would stay capped with no expansion, relocation, or rebuilding (Religious Freedom).

head: "Why this compatibility test, and what would change it?"
body: Where it comes from. Entry is a privilege, not a right, so refusing it takes nothing anyone holds. The test checks the same values my rights framework rests on: the Constitution over religious law, equal rights for women, non-Muslims, and nonbelievers, freedom to leave a faith, and rejection of violence. High-trust societies protect negative rights better in practice, and that trust rests on shared norms (Sovereignty and Borders). The rivals. Open borders treat entry as a right, which I reject. Selection by labor needs alone ignores whether a newcomer accepts the rights order. I keep labor needs, but second, after values. Selection by ethnicity or ancestry judges people by what they cannot change and says nothing about their values. What would change it. A place comes off the list when it meets none of the grounds in consecutive annual reviews, and for the polling ground that means open support for genocidal attacks below 1% (Questionable Compatibility). Any individual can overcome the presumption with verified conduct and record. The presumption for being Muslim rests on what the faith teaches, so I would revisit it only if those mainstream teachings changed (Group Statistics and Individual Judgment).

head: "What stops officers from abusing the presumption?"
body: The rules are written so that abuse leaves a record. The five points are named in advance, and an applicant of any faith who fails them is refused, so being Muslim sets where the burden starts but is never the test itself. Every decision is made on a written record, and a denial gets a second officer's review on that record. Sworn statements fall under the perjury rules, for officers' records as well as applicants' statements. On top of that, I believe every denial should state in writing which of the five points failed and on what evidence. Denial rates should be published every year by post, by officer, and by nationality. An inspector general independent of the deciding agency should audit a random sample of approvals and denials each year. An officer who denies on grounds outside the five points, or falsifies a record, should be removed from vetting and prosecuted for the falsification. Admission decisions themselves stay outside court review, as they are under current law, because admission is a privilege; removing a resident still takes a court finding (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). Cornell LII – Department of State v. Muñoz, 602 U.S. 899 (2024)

head: "Won't this damage relations with Muslim-majority allies?"
body: Some, and I accept that cost. Governments may answer with visa limits of their own, and some cooperation may cool. Three things limit the damage. The presumption is individual and rebuttable, so citizens of any country who meet the five points are admitted. A place comes off the list when it meets none of the grounds in consecutive annual reviews, so every government has a clear path off it. And alliances should serve U.S. interests: a partner that works with the United States against terror does so because it serves its own interests too, and that does not end over visa policy. Diplomatic and official visas follow treaty obligations and are not immigration, so vetting does not close embassies or bar officials doing state business. The Supreme Court upheld entry limits on several Muslim-majority countries in Trump v. Hawaii (2018). Cornell LII – Trump v. Hawaii, 585 U.S. 667 (2018)

head: "Immigrants commit less crime than natives. Why prioritize removal?"
body: The data do show lower crime among undocumented immigrants: in Texas arrest records, which check the immigration status of every arrestee, undocumented immigrants had considerably lower felony arrest rates than native-born citizens. Incarceration is not the same as offending, but the national record points the same way: immigrants have had lower incarceration rates than the U.S.-born for 150 years, and by 2020 they were 60% less likely to be incarcerated, and 30% less likely than U.S.-born whites, a gap that has widened since 1960 and that the authors find is not explained by immigration policy or by immigrants' observable characteristics. Removal does not rest on crime rates. It rests on the rule of law and on sovereignty: a nation decides who enters and stays, and entering or remaining illegally is itself the violation of that law.

head: "Aren't undocumented immigrants law-abiding?"
body: No. Lower arrest rates are one thing. Being law-abiding is another. Entering without inspection is a federal crime under 8 U.S.C. § 1325, and staying past a visa's terms makes a person removable under 8 U.S.C. § 1227. Either way, the person is breaking immigration law from the first day. Unlawful presence also tends to bring more violations with it. Working without authorization breaks the employment rules of 8 U.S.C. § 1324a, which usually means showing an employer a forged or borrowed green card or Social Security number. Using a false Social Security number is a felony under 42 U.S.C. § 408(a)(7). Using fraudulent immigration documents is one under 18 U.S.C. § 1546. And using another person's identity is aggravated identity theft under 18 U.S.C. § 1028A when it is tied to such a felony. Many people stay below the threshold for arrest, but that is not the same as obeying the law. The law ought to be enforced as written, and removal should follow.

head: Data: unlawful entry, presence, and the violations that follow

body: Statutes as published. Prosecution rates vary by administration and district.
Improper entry: entering or attempting to enter at a place other than a port of entry, or evading inspection, is a misdemeanor for a first offense, up to 6 months. Cornell LII – 8 U.S.C. § 1325
Reentry after removal: a felony, up to 2 years, and up to 20 years for those with an aggravated-felony record. Cornell LII – 8 U.S.C. § 1326

Overstay and status violations: being present in violation of law, or failing to keep the status a person was admitted under, is a ground for removal. This is civil, not criminal. Cornell LII – 8 U.S.C. § 1227
Unauthorized employment: an employer may not knowingly hire an unauthorized alien and must check identity and work-authorization documents on Form I-9. Cornell LII – 8 U.S.C. § 1324a

Document and identity fraud: forging, using, or possessing false immigration or work documents, and making false statements on Form I-9, are felonies. Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 1546 · Falsely representing a Social Security number: 42 U.S.C. § 408(a)(7) · Aggravated identity theft adds a mandatory 2 years: 18 U.S.C. § 1028A

How common SSN misuse is: SSA's actuaries estimated that in 2010, about 1.8 million unauthorized workers used a Social Security number that did not match their name, and about 0.7 million more held SSNs obtained with fraudulent birth certificates (most before 2001). That is roughly a third of the estimated 7 million unauthorized workers. Another 3.9 million worked off the books. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary – Actuarial Note 151 (2013)

Skilled-worker visas would follow the same order as all immigration: every applicant would pass the same individual values vetting first, and American labor needs would be a secondary criterion after values and assimilation, met first through the domestic workforce.
Official figures and studies as reported by the cited sources.

The cap: the Immigration Act of 1990 set the annual H-1B cap at 65,000. Congress raised it temporarily to 115,000 for FY1999–2000 and to 195,000 for FY2001–2003. It returned to 65,000 in FY2004. Since FY2005 a further 20,000 visas have gone to holders of U.S. master's or higher degrees. Universities and affiliated nonprofit and government research organizations are exempt from the cap. Congressional Research Service – Temporary Professional, Managerial, and Skilled Foreign Workers (R47159)

Demand: for FY2026, USCIS counted 343,981 eligible registrations for the 85,000 capped visas and selected 120,141. Eligible registrations peaked at 758,994 for FY2024. After that, a rule counted each worker only once. USCIS – H-1B Electronic Registration Process

Wage-weighted selection: a rule published December 29, 2025 weights the lottery by the wage offered: four entries at the highest wage level (IV) down to one at the entry level (I). It was first used for FY2027, whose selection was completed March 31, 2026. Federal Register – Weighted Selection Process for Cap-Subject H-1B Petitions · USCIS: FY 2027 H-1B Initial Registration Selection Process Completed

The $100,000 payment: a September 2025 proclamation required an added $100,000 for new H-1B petitions for workers outside the United States. A federal judge in Massachusetts ruled it unlawful on June 8, 2026, and on July 24, 2026 the First Circuit refused to pause that ruling while the government appeals. Reuters – Trump's $100,000 H-1B visa fee is unlawful, US judge rules (2026) · Reuters: Appeals court rejects Trump bid to halt $100,000 H-1B visa fee ruling (2026)

Effect on other workers: across 219 U.S. cities from 1990 to 2010, Peri, Shih and Sparber found that H-1B-driven growth in foreign STEM workers raised wage growth for college-educated natives (7–8 points per 1-point rise in foreign STEM employment), with no significant effect on native employment. At the level of the hiring firm, the lottery evidence points to displacement: comparing firms that won and lost H-1B lotteries, Doran, Gelber and Isen found that each additional H-1B visa crowded out about 1.5 other workers at the winning firm and had at most a modest effect on its innovation. Journal of Labor Economics – STEM Workers, H-1B Visas, and Productivity in US Cities (2015) · Journal of Political Economy: The Effects of High-Skilled Immigration Policy on Firms (2022)

I judge the H-1B program by what it does now, not by the exceptional people it admitted decades ago. The firm-level lottery evidence (data above) finds that each added H-1B visa crowded out about 1.5 other workers at the winning firm, which is why American labor needs are met first through the domestic workforce. Critics cite the city-level finding that foreign STEM workers raised wage growth for college-educated natives. That is an average across cities, and it does nothing for the workers displaced at the firms that win the visas.

Shared values make trust and cooperation possible, which is why I favor cohesion over diversity. Critics cite the fiscal gain from immigration, which CBO put at about $0.9 trillion in lower deficits over 2024 to 2034; cohesion outweighs it. At the state and local level, unauthorized immigration is a net cost, driven mainly by schooling. Federal law already sets grounds for inadmissibility, so vetting for values extends an existing power. Critics note that no study shows values screening predicts later conduct. The vetting does not need one: it rests on the principle that a nation may choose members who share its values. The measured link between diversity and lower trust is real but small on average, strongest for trust in neighbors. About 9% of U.S. births in 2023 (roughly 320,000) were to unauthorized or temporary-status mothers. Enforcement positions are set out in Border Security and Immigration Enforcement. Denmark's crime-by-origin pattern and the higher CIS household-level means-tested use among legal immigrant–headed households in the U.S. (data above) are noisy priors for screening, not proof that every applicant fails and not a substitute for named-recipient tests at removal or at the ballot. They are why nationality and welfare rules sit upstream of individual cases under my compatibility bar (Questionable Compatibility; Western Values and Compatibility).
Birthright citizenship is automatic citizenship for anyone born on a country's soil, regardless of the parents' status. In the United States it rests on the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause.

My list has two tiers. Places on grounds A or B (the regime or dominant faction backs genocidal attacks, or 5% or more of people openly support them) should face a complete entry ban by nationality or place of origin, with no case-by-case visa path. The ban lifts only when open support stays below 1% in consecutive annual reviews and no authority there endorses such attacks. Places on grounds C-I, or added for security, are of questionable compatibility: free or open immigration is off, and anyone from them is admitted only case by case, starting from no. The list is a prior, not a verdict on any person. A place is listed on any one of nine grounds: genocidal attacks backed by its regime or a dominant faction 5% or more open support for such attacks state sponsorship of terrorism unresolved ethnic cleansing state war crimes, or a pattern of state killing and torture with impunity Islamist governance or majority support for religious law death for apostasy, blasphemy, or homosexuality terrorist cartel or gang control state denial of women's civil equality Findings must be verified by the United States, and the list should be reviewed every year.
The United States ought to keep this list. It has two tiers, and they are not the same.

Hard ban (grounds A and B). Entry should be banned completely, by nationality or place of origin, from any place whose regime or dominant factions wage or celebrate attacks that target civilians for genocide or ethnic cleansing, or where reliable polling shows 5% or more of the population openly supporting such attacks. When the people who hold power or set the norm openly back genocidal attacks, screening cannot reliably sort the hostile from the rest, because hostility is common, rewarded, and easy to conceal, and one wrong admission can cost lives. A/B places are therefore not priors for case-by-case screening - there is no case-by-case visa path from them. A place comes off the hard ban only when open support stays below 1% in consecutive annual reviews and no governing authority or dominant faction there still endorses such attacks (Hostile conduct, removal, and entry). West Bank and Gaza, Iran, Yemen, Lebanon, Sudan, Burma, China, Afghanistan, and every other A/B listing sit on this tier.

Questionable Compatibility (grounds C–I, plus security adds). Free or open immigration from these places should be off. No visa class, lottery, or open channel ought to admit anyone from them as a matter of course. Each applicant should be decided case by case, starting from no and carrying the burden of showing fit. I hold that entry is a privilege, not a right (Hostile conduct, removal, and entry), and a nation owes admission to no one whose society is hostile to it or incompatible with the values it rests on: individual negative rights, liberty, religious freedom with separation of church and state, and the rule of law (Western Values and Compatibility). Each of these grounds marks a place whose laws, rulers, or prevailing culture reject those values or wage violence against civilians. Where that is true, ordinary screening is less trustworthy, so the default flips: the United States ought not to carry the risk unless an individual case clears it.

A place should be listed if it meets any one ground, and come off only when it meets none of them in consecutive annual reviews. For the polling ground that means open support below 1%, and for every ground it means no governing authority or dominant faction there still does what put it on the list. I count a poll answer that calls such an attack "correct" or "legitimate" as open support. Every finding must be verified by the United States government. A foreign or international finding counts only once the United States has confirmed it on the evidence, and I reject findings I judge unfounded, such as the claim that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza (Israel and the Middle East). Beyond the grounds, the government and its immigration enforcement may add a place to the list or set a listing aside as security requires.
Compatibility bar

I treat nationality as a prior on cultural fit. The question at the border is not whether a place has been proven hostile, but whether it has shown it is compatible, so a presumption against entry is the default and clearance is the exception. A place stays clear only if it fails none of these hard bars:
No open majority, or 5% or more celebrating, for genocidal attacks on civilians (A, B).
No state death penalty for apostasy, blasphemy, homosexuality, or leaving Islam (F, G).
Women's civil equality not denied by the state as a formal baseline (I).
No terrorist cartel or gang the United States lists holding territory or working with the state's collusion (H).
Not a pattern, documented by the United States, of state unlawful killings and torture with impunity (E).

I don't use gay rights as a baseline metric. Women's civil equality is one. Clearing a place clears no person: every individual from a clear place should still be screened. A place goes under review when it fails no hard bar but its polling or religious-freedom record is weak or out of date.
The grounds
A. Genocidal attacks backed by those in power: the regime or a dominant faction wages or celebrates attacks that target civilians for genocide or ethnic cleansing.
B. Open support: reliable polling shows 5% or more of the population openly supporting such attacks.
C. State sponsor of terrorism: the United States designates the state as a sponsor of terrorism, or it knowingly hosts the leadership of a designated terrorist group.
D. Unresolved ethnic cleansing: forces of the state or its allies drove out a population for its ethnicity within the last ten years, and the victims have not been allowed to return in safety.

E. State war crimes or killing with impunity: the state's own forces commit murder, torture, rape, or deliberate attacks on civilians as a pattern, on a finding verified by the United States. Or the State Department's annual human rights report finds credible reports of both unlawful killings and torture by the state and finds the government took no credible steps to identify and punish the officials responsible. A government credited with credible steps does not meet this ground.

F. Islamist governance or religious law: an Islamist movement governs the state or a large share of its territory, or polling shows a majority of the population wants religious law made the law of the land.
G. Death for faith or homosexuality: the law punishes apostasy, blasphemy, or homosexuality with death.

H. Terrorist cartel or gang control: a cartel or gang the United States designates a Foreign Terrorist Organization or Specially Designated Global Terrorist holds substantial territory in the country, or operates with the effective collusion of the state or with impunity from it, as found by the United States government.
I. Women's civil equality denied: the state denies women civil equality in law as a formal baseline, such as male guardianship over adult women or unequal legal standing in court.

Illegal immigrants should be removed by force, the border heavily fortified, and lethal force allowed when necessary. I would abolish sanctuary cities. ICE should grow, and its officers should wear body cameras.

Illegal immigrants should be removed from the country by force. The border ought to be heavily secured and fortified, and border crossings defended with lethal force when necessary. I would abolish sanctuary cities at the federal level. ICE should be expanded in size, with one reform: all officers wear body cameras.

head: "Can the federal government abolish sanctuary cities without violating states' rights?"
body: I treat abolishing sanctuary jurisdictions as enforcing a federal responsibility that local governments have no authority to obstruct. Immigration and border control are federal powers, as the Supreme Court affirmed in Arizona v. United States. Federal law already bars state and local governments from restricting their officials from sharing immigration-status information with federal authorities under 8 U.S.C. § 1373.

head: "Isn't a 'know your rights' video just legal information?"
body: People may know the law. What I reject is a city government using its official channel to train the public on how to frustrate federal removal while it runs as a sanctuary jurisdiction. Immigration enforcement is a federal power (Border Security and Immigration Enforcement). Local obstruction is why sanctuary cities are abolished under my rules. A hotline that steers encounters away from cooperation is anti-enforcement policy dressed as civics.

head: "What about people who have worked here for years and broken no other law?"
body: Many of them are good neighbors and hard workers, and theirs are the hardest cases. But sympathy for a person cannot decide whether the law applies to that person. Immigration law decides who joins the political community. If that is settled by who managed to arrive and whose story moves us most, the citizens' consent is replaced by the fact of arrival. Hard cases are exactly where a rule has to hold, or it is not a rule. The 1986 amnesty was sold as a one-time fix: it legalized about 2.7 million people, the unauthorized population fell to about 1.9 million in 1988, and it then rose to about 12.4 million by 2007. Analysts also blame weak workplace enforcement and few legal channels for low-skilled work, but the amnesty did not end illegal immigration, and I believe a second one would invite the next wave. Removal applies to long-settled workers as to anyone else, with full due process (Due Process and Rule of Law). Migration Policy Institute – At Its 25th Anniversary, IRCA's Legacy Lives On (2011); Congressional Research Service – Unauthorized Aliens Residing in the United States: Estimates Since 1986 (RL33874, 2014)

A nation that cannot control who enters cannot enforce its own laws or decide who joins the political community, and the high-trust society I aim for depends on enforced law. Unlawful entry is a violation of the nation's law, and removal should be the remedy. Sanctuary policies place local politics above federal law and shield people the law requires to be removed. Expanding ICE gives enforcement the capacity it lacks, and the body-camera requirement applies the same accountability standard set for police. Official city coaching on how to meet ICE without cooperating is the sanctuary model in practice, not a neutral public-service announcement. ICE and CBP publish enforcement and encounter statistics that document the scale of the task.

A sanctuary city or jurisdiction is a local government that limits cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, for example by refusing to honor ICE detainer requests or restricting information sharing with federal authorities.

A church, mosque, synagogue or temple is not a sanctuary from the law. Immigration officers should be allowed to make arrests at or near a house of worship as they may anywhere else, and no congregation should be allowed to hide a person from removal. Entering a place of worship while a service is under way would need a judicial warrant, hot pursuit, or an imminent threat to life. These limits would be fixed in written rules published in advance, not left to a supervisor's case-by-case discretion. Every arrest would still carry full due process (Due Process and Rule of Law).

The fortified border should cover its whole length, including stretches with few crossings (Border Security and Immigration Enforcement). Where a barrier crosses protected-species habitat, a national park or a wildlife corridor, it should be built alongside nature rather than through it (Conservation vs Development): sited and designed to let wildlife pass, and paired with sensors and patrols where a solid wall would cut habitat in two. A waiver of environmental or wildlife law for barrier construction should cover only the project area, should be published with the crossing data that supports it, and should end when construction ends.

Status should never be sold. In my view investors must pass the same vetting as everyone else. Afterward, investment with a proven lawful source and audited job creation may count as one factor.

Immigration status should never be sold. An investor ought to go through the same individual values vetting and civics requirements as every other applicant (Immigration and Borders). Investment may count as one factor for an economic visa only after vetting is passed, and only with proof that the money was lawfully obtained and audited proof that the promised jobs were created. A payment or gift to the government should buy no place in line.

head: "Investors bring capital and jobs. Why not welcome them?"
body: They can be welcome, on the same terms as everyone else. The objection to selling status is that wealth says nothing about whether a person shares the values I admit for, and it opens a path for money of unknown origin. The record bears this out. The Government Accountability Office found that the EB-5 investor program faced fraud risks unique to it, including difficulty verifying that invested funds were lawfully obtained and schemes to defraud investors, and that the government's reports of the program's economic benefits were not reliable. Investment is a real benefit, so it may count once vetting is passed. It is never a substitute for vetting.

Admission is a privilege granted to those who fit the shared value structure (Western Values and Compatibility). Selling status replaces that test with wealth, and the EB-5 record shows the fraud risks that come with it.

head: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

body: Green card and visa holders should be removed, after a court finding by clear and convincing evidence, if they take cash welfare, SNAP, housing aid, non-emergency Medicaid, or the last-resort allowance, fail the naturalization English and civics test within two years, or are convicted of any crime above a basic infraction. Refugees go to a safe third country, never to persecution or torture. These bars are for residents: anyone lawfully living here who is removed or deported, including a resettled refugee, keeps them. People denied at the border or applying for asylum do not; the government exists to protect its citizens, not non-citizens, so the American taxpayer has no duty to protect or shelter them or to fund or arrange their transfer. Someone who entered unlawfully and claims asylum from inside the country is an asylum seeker, not a resident. No one should be removed for opinions or speech. I believe terrorism, material support, and treason should be punished, not deported: death where the capital standard is met, secure confinement under compelled labor otherwise, for citizens and non-citizens alike. I support a constitutional amendment adding forfeiture of citizenship for dual nationals so convicted, never leaving anyone stateless and never applied retroactively.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: Position
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

body: I hold that lawful residence for a non-citizen is a conditional privilege: self-support, integration, and obeying the law. The rule covers green card and visa holders already here, and reaches only conduct after it takes effect. The three removal grounds, the refugee safe-third-country path, the speech bar, and the clear-and-convincing court finding are in the In short above - not repeated here. Each case should still require written notice, a hearing before a judge, the chance to present evidence, and federal-court review (Due Process and Rule of Law). A third country should count as safe only after review of that person's case, not on diplomatic assurances alone.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

body: Terrorism, material support to a designated terrorist organization, and treason should never be handled by deportation instead of punishment, citizen or not. They ought to be prosecuted as crimes and treated as attempted murder is: death where guilt meets the capital evidentiary standard (Mandatory Death Penalty; Evidentiary Standard); secure confinement under compelled labor where proven beyond a reasonable doubt but short of that standard (Compelled Labor). Any knowing support counts, not only an attack. For a capital sentence the support should have to be a documented money trail or communications meeting the capital standard. Deportation would only move the threat elsewhere and let it return; punishment ends it.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

body: A dual national convicted of one of these offenses should also forfeit U.S. citizenship as an added penalty alongside the sentence, never in place of it - equally for dual nationals by birth and by naturalization, only for conduct after enactment, and never leaving anyone stateless. The law names offenses, not religions. Because the Supreme Court holds that citizenship cannot be taken without the citizen's consent, the forfeiture ought to be enacted by constitutional amendment, and the removal rules for non-citizens by statute.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Isn't 'failing to integrate' too vague to enforce?"
body: It would be if it meant attitudes or lifestyle, so it does not. The only test is the one the country already uses for new citizens: federal law requires naturalization applicants to show "an understanding of the English language" and knowledge of U.S. history and government. A resident who cannot pass that test within two years of admission has not met the condition. Broader standards, such as hostility to the country's way of life, are left out because they cannot be measured and would turn removal into a penalty for speech (Free Speech and Censorship).
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Isn't removal for any theft too harsh?"
body: Residence is a privilege extended on condition of obeying the law, and a resident who steals has broken that condition. Basic infractions such as traffic tickets are excluded so that the rule reaches crimes against people and property, not paperwork. Current law already makes many non-citizens deportable for crimes. This rule removes the gaps and the discretion, with a conviction and a court finding required in every case. The rule applies the same way to a long-term green-card holder with citizen family: residence was granted on the same condition, and the rule reaches only conduct after enactment, so every resident knows the terms in advance. Family members who are citizens keep their citizenship and may choose to stay or to leave. The rule protects the citizens who extend the privilege, who should not be the ones to pay when its terms are broken, and the lawful residents who keep those terms, whose standing should not be judged by those who don't. The two errors are not equal. A resident removed in error loses residence here, after notice, a hearing, and federal-court review; a resident who keeps offending and stays leaves the risk with people who never agreed to carry it. The condition was known when residence was granted, and a family that wants to stay together can leave together.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Doesn't the Constitution forbid stripping citizenship?"
body: For involuntary loss, yes, which is why this part requires an amendment. In Afroyim v. Rusk (1967) the Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment defines "a citizenship which a citizen keeps unless he voluntarily relinquishes it," and in Vance v. Terrazas (1980) it required proof of intent to give up citizenship. In Trop v. Dulles (1958) a plurality held that stripping citizenship as punishment was cruel and unusual, noting that "statelessness is not to be imposed as punishment for crime." The amendment answers the first point directly and the second by limiting the rule to dual nationals, so no one is left without a country. The forfeiture is added to the criminal sentence, death or secure confinement, and never replaces it. Current law already revokes citizenship obtained by fraud, where naturalization was "illegally procured or ... procured by concealment of a material fact."
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Can lawful residents be deported for using benefits or committing crimes without an amendment?"
body: Yes, with full due process. The Supreme Court upheld deporting long-time legal residents in Harisiades v. Shaughnessy (1952), treating deportation as a civil matter rather than punishment. In Zadvydas v. Davis (2001) it held that "the Due Process Clause applies to all persons within the United States, including aliens, whether their presence is lawful, unlawful, temporary, or permanent," which is why every case here goes through a hearing, the clear-and-convincing standard, and court review. Existing law already points this way. A non-citizen who becomes "a public charge" within five years of entry from causes not shown to have arisen after entry is deportable. Most qualified non-citizens are barred from federal means-tested benefits for their first five years.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Don't immigrants use less welfare than natives?"
body: Measured per person and counting Social Security and Medicare, yes: the Cato Institute finds immigrants consumed 24% less in welfare and entitlement benefits per capita than the native-born in 2023, $8,234 against $10,772. That total is driven by the old-age programs people pay into, where natives are older. On means-tested programs, the Center for Immigration Studies finds that 51% of households headed by legal immigrants used at least one major program in 2024, against 37% of U.S.-born households. That household figure is a noisy prior — CIS's unit includes child-linked benefits and, in some tables, refundable credits and school meals — not a measure of adult dependency and not the removal test. Part of the gap is benefits received for U.S.-born children, which my removal rule does not count. The rule asks whether the named resident is supporting themselves on personally directed transfers, case by case. The franchise uses the same named-recipient / tax-unit logic under net fiscal voting bar. Cato Institute – Immigrant and Native Consumption of Means-Tested Welfare and Entitlement Benefits in 2023 Center for Immigration Studies – Welfare Use by Immigrants and the U.S.-Born, 2024 (2026)
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Isn't it unfair to people who paid taxes and lost a job or fell ill?"
body: The rule should apply only to benefits received after it takes effect, so no one should be removed for past use that was lawful when it happened. Emergency care should never be counted, and a U.S.-citizen child should keep any benefit the child qualifies for without putting the parent's residence at risk. Residents would know the condition in advance and could protect themselves through work, savings, private insurance, or sponsors. The last-resort allowance should not be available to non-citizens (Welfare and Entitlements). A resident who needs long-term support can return to the country of citizenship.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Doesn't removing refugees violate the ban on returning people to persecution?"
body: Not when they go to a safe third country. Federal law bars removal to a country where a person's "life or freedom would be threatened" because of race, religion, nationality, social group, or political opinion, though that bar has exceptions for serious criminals and security threats. A separate statute, section 2242 of the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998, makes it "the policy of the United States" not to return anyone to a country "in which there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture," and its regulations bar removal where torture is "more likely than not," with no such exceptions. That statute takes its terms and its regulations from the Convention Against Torture, so the law ought to write the torture bar for residents into the Immigration and Nationality Act on its own terms, using the federal criminal code's definition of torture, so that it holds whether or not the United States stays in the Convention (treaty exit). Removal to a third country that will receive the person meets both bars. Federal law already lists additional countries to which a person may be removed when the first choice will not accept them. The review protects people the United States already took in to live here, resettled refugees included: removing them must never deliver them to persecution or torture, and a third country counts as safe only after review of that person's case. The two errors are not equal: a careful review costs time, while a removal to the wrong country can cost a life no later ruling returns. The duty runs to residents only. People denied at the border or applying for asylum are not owed U.S. protection, shelter, or a funded transfer (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents).
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Isn't death for material support far beyond current law?"
body: Yes. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2339B, knowingly providing material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization carries up to 20 years in prison, or any term of years or life "if the death of any person results." I go further on principle. Money and communications are what let a terrorist organization kill, so I treat knowing support as taking part in its attempts at murder. Because the penalty would be death, the proof should be a documented money trail or communications that meet the capital evidentiary standard, with no conviction on inference alone. Cases proven beyond a reasonable doubt but short of that standard would go to secure confinement under compelled labor.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "The immigration courts are already overwhelmed. How can they handle removal for every theft?"
body: They cannot as they stand. At the end of August 2026 the immigration courts had 3,092,988 pending cases, even after closing 899,741 cases so far in fiscal year 2026, and new removal grounds would add to that load. The United States therefore ought to pair the rules with capacity: dedicated removal courts, separate from the asylum backlog, hear these cases. They should be funded with enough judges, interpreters, and public defenders to decide cases within 180 days from notice. For crime cases, the removal hearing would be joined to the end of the criminal sentence, since the conviction already establishes the ground. A deadline without the judges to meet it would trade due process for speed, which the United States ought not to allow.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Doesn't this create two classes of citizens?"
body: No. Every offender, citizen or not, would face the same criminal punishment for terrorism or treason: death where the capital standard is met, secure confinement under compelled labor otherwise. The only difference would be the added forfeiture of citizenship for dual nationals, which would exist for dual nationals alone so that no one becomes stateless.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: "Why the focus on Islamist terrorism if the law is religion-neutral?"
body: Because the data put it first, though not alone. The Global Terrorism Index 2026 found that four jihadist organizations, the Islamic State, JNIM, the Pakistani Taliban, and al-Shabaab, caused 3,869 deaths in 2025, 70 per cent of all terrorism deaths worldwide. In the West, 527 of 990 terrorism deaths over the past two decades, 53 per cent, occurred in religiously motivated attacks, and almost all of those were caused by jihadist groups or individuals. The same report records the counter-trend. Religious attacks were just over ten per cent of the 1,449 Western attacks since 2007, 30 per cent had a political motivation and 32 per cent no single clear ideology, politically motivated attacks rose by almost 20 per cent in 2025, and the high-profile attacks that year included the assassination of Charlie Kirk. A law that names offenses rather than faiths covers every one of these threats.
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

head: Rationale
topic: Removal of Non-Citizen Residents and Loss of Citizenship

body: I treat immigration as a privilege the nation grants to those who fit its shared values, with assimilation paramount (Immigration and Borders; Language and Assimilation). Federal law already reflects the self-support condition. A non-citizen who becomes a public charge within five years of entry is deportable, and qualified non-citizens who entered on or after August 22, 1996 are generally barred from federal means-tested benefits for five years. Federal housing assistance is limited to listed categories of non-citizens. The public-charge rules for admission have shifted with administrations: a 2019 rule stopped being in effect on March 9, 2021, and a 2022 rule similar to the 1999 guidance took effect on December 23, 2022. Writing the condition into statute, with a court finding by clear and convincing evidence in every case, makes it stable. The design adapts two pledges from Britain's Restore Britain party: to deport a legally resident foreign national who "lives in social housing, claims benefits," "fails to integrate," or "commits crime" (Restore Britain – Reverse Mass Immigration), and to strip citizenship from "dual-national Islamic extremists" (Restore Britain – Make Britain Safe Again). The United States ought to narrow both: the benefits are listed, integration is a two-year test, every removal needs a court finding, and the citizenship penalty follows a conviction under religion-neutral offenses and never leaves anyone stateless (United Kingdom). The safe-third-country rule keeps the United States within its obligations against returning people to persecution or torture without granting refugees more than safety. Terrorism is different in kind. An attack meant to kill is an attempt at murder, and I treat attempted murder as capital (Terrorism and Domestic Extremism); deporting a terrorist would only move the threat abroad, where it can plan again, while execution or secure confinement ends it. I keep citizenship forfeiture as an added penalty for dual nationals so that an offender's tie to the country ends with the crime. The Court's reading of the Fourteenth Amendment in Afroyim means involuntary loss requires an amendment, and my concern for rights means the amendment should require a criminal conviction and should never create statelessness. The offenses are religion-neutral, but the emphasis on Islamist terrorism follows the data. Jihadist groups caused 70 per cent of terrorism deaths worldwide in 2025 and most terrorism deaths in the West over two decades, while political and mixed-ideology attacks are more numerous in the West and rising. Removal for belief or speech is excluded because I protect expression even when it's hostile.

body: Cartels should be treated as terrorists and destroyed, ideally together with the local government. A government that refuses to help can face war, but my goal is to defeat the cartels, not to run the country. I see many Latin American immigrants as good fits because of shared values.

Drug cartels should be treated as terrorist national-security threats and destroyed by force. Joint operations with compliant Central and South American governments, including Mexico, are my preferred route. A government that refuses to act against cartels operating against the United States ought to be treated as hostile, and I believe war with that government is justified to eradicate the cartel problem. Action should aim at defeating the threat, not at governing territory or rebuilding states. Immigrants from the region should be vetted individually, and I judge many Latin American families compatible because of shared family and religious values. A foreign leader who directs or shelters cartels or terror groups against the United States may be captured to stand trial in U.S. courts. That targets the person driving the threat and is not nation-building, and the United States should not then govern the country.

head: "Wouldn't military action in Mexico risk a disastrous war with a neighbor?"
body: Joint operations with a cooperating government come first, and most cartel action is meant to be carried out that way. War is reserved for a government that refuses to act against organizations killing Americans. Even then, the goal is to destroy the cartels, not to occupy or rebuild the country, in line with the skepticism of nation-building in Interventionism vs Non-Intervention.

Cartel-supplied drugs kill Americans at a scale comparable to war. CDC provisional data show an estimated 70,735 drug overdose deaths in 2025, of which 38,506 involved synthetic opioids, mainly fentanyl, down from about 81,300 in 2024 and a peak of about 112,400 in the 12 months ending August 2023. In 2025 the United States designated Cartel de Sinaloa, CJNG, MS-13, Tren de Aragua, and other groups as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, which aligns legal treatment with the threat. Domestic enforcement is set out in Drug Policy, and the war position in Cultural & Social Issues.

I back Israel as the first line of Western defense against the Islamic Republic of Iran and regional terror. The Iranian regime and its state-sponsored, anti-Western terror allies — Hezbollah, the Houthis, Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and the rest — ought to be destroyed, sparing ordinary Iranians. Extremist Islam eliminated; Hamas condemned as a terrorist organization. A two-state solution is not viable, and Gaza should likely be dissolved. A negotiated middle ground on the West Bank would be best but is unlikely. Failing that, its armed threat should be forcibly removed and the territory walled off from Israel entirely. Palestinian civilians should not be targeted, the hostages should be returned, and the war in Gaza is categorically not a genocide. Israel defends negative rights against an ideology that rejects them.

We should be supporting Israel as the first line of Western defense against the Islamic Republic and the forces of terror in the region. Extremist Islam should be eradicated. More force should be used toward Iran, and I judge the current administration too soft. Iran's people should be spared, but the Islamic regime should be obliterated along with all allies of state-sponsored, anti-Western terror. Destroying the regime should not be followed by nation-building or occupation. Israel should be supported as far as it serves U.S. security. The allies list, FTO designations, October 7 facts, Hamas condemnation, civilian-protection rules, hostage demand, and the judgment that the war is not a genocide are in the In short above and the Q&As below - not repeated here. Israel defends negative rights against an ideology, Islam, that rejects them.

A two-state solution is not viable, and Gaza should likely be dissolved — see In short. On the West Bank: a negotiated middle ground would be best but is unlikely. Failing that, the armed threat should be forcibly removed and the territory walled off from Israel entirely, separated by hard security, with violence met by force against those who commit it. Israel would be justified in annexing the land outright once the armed threat is removed. People in the West Bank who choose to join Israel and assimilate properly should be accepted. Those who refuse and remain hostile, as found individually by a court or tribunal under the conduct test in Hostile conduct, removal, and entry, should be forced out. Under current polling, the West Bank and Gaza belong on the entry-ban list (Hostile conduct, removal, and entry). Given how widely hostility runs there, hostile conduct of that kind amounts to a security threat, and a nation's security and duty to its citizens override the negative rights of foreign security threats (Sovereignty and Borders). International law should be disregarded here, since a nation follows its own laws, not foreign tribunals, and a nation should exit any treaty that ties its hands against such threats (Global Institutions). I prefer separation to indefinite control because a perpetual security state is costly and dangerous and not in Israel's best interest.

Israel is a democratic Western society, mostly, and Palestine is not. Palestine is incompatible with the West and, by extension, an enemy of the United States. Israel is the barrier against barbarians who want the destruction of the West and the largest force in the region against Islamism, so we should aid and support it as necessary.

I am skeptical of politically charged alignment with the Palestinian cause. Left-wing politicians and progressives have rallied behind "Free Palestine," and a lot of misinformation and propaganda spread by Hamas itself is eaten up by pro-Palestinian audiences in Europe and the United States. That is not to discount Israeli propaganda either. Detail and cases are in the Q&A below.

head: "Can the Iranian regime be destroyed without harming its people?"
body: The United States ought to make sparing the Iranian people a requirement while targeting the regime and its terror allies. The distinction between a hostile government and the population it rules is central: the enemy is the regime and its proxies, not Iranians.

head: "What is the history of the conflict?"
body: A short timeline. Where accounts differ, both are given. Period Events Antiquity Jewish kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Jerusalem was David's capital (10th century BCE) and was destroyed by Babylon in 587/586 BCE and by Rome in 70 CE after a Jewish revolt. Ottoman era (1516–1917) Palestine was under Ottoman rule for four centuries. In 1914 its population was about 690,000: 535,000 Muslims, 70,000 Christians, and 85,000 Jews. The first Zionist agricultural settlement was founded in 1882. 1917–1922 The Balfour Declaration backed "a national home for the Jewish people" without prejudice to "the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities." Palestinian Arabs believed Britain had promised them independence in the Hussein-McMahon correspondence. The League of Nations approved the British Mandate in 1922. 1920s–1930s Riots in 1920, 1921, and 1929. The 1929 violence killed some 250 people, and the Shaw Commission attributed it to Arab fears of Jewish immigration and land purchases. Jewish immigration rose sharply after 1933. The Arab Revolt of 1936–39 followed, and in 1937 the Peel Commission judged the Mandate unworkable and recommended partition. 1947–1949 UN Resolution 181 (November 29, 1947) recommended partition. The Jewish leadership accepted it and Palestinian Arab leaders and Arab states rejected it. Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, and Arab states invaded. Armistices in 1949 left Egypt holding Gaza and Jordan the West Bank. About 750,000 Palestinians became refugees (the Nakba). Israel then estimated no more than 550,000 and Arab states 750,000–800,000. Historians debate how much of the flight was expulsion and how much was flight from fighting. 1948–1970s About 856,000 Jews lived in Arab countries in 1948 and about 26,000 by 1976. Iraq's community of about 135,000 fell to a few hundred. About 586,000 went to Israel between 1948 and 1972, and most of the rest to France, Britain, and the Americas. Causes are disputed: Israel points to riots, anti-Jewish laws, and confiscations, while Arab governments have said the Jews left by choice. 1967 After Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran and UN forces withdrew, Israel fought Egypt, Jordan, and Syria (June 5–10) and took Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan. UN Resolution 242 called for withdrawal from territories occupied in exchange for peace. The Arab League's Khartoum resolution answered: "no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it." 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked on October 6. The war ended in an Israeli military victory under UN Resolution 338. 1978–1979 Camp David Accords (September 1978) and the Egypt–Israel peace treaty (March 26, 1979); Israel returned Sinai. 1982 Israel invaded Lebanon on June 6 after the shooting of its ambassador in London; the PLO left Beirut. Lebanese Christian militiamen, allowed by Israel into the Sabra and Shatila camps, massacred Palestinian civilians. 1987 The First Intifada began. Hamas emerged in Gaza from the Muslim Brotherhood. 1993–1995 The Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority. Prime Minister Rabin was assassinated by an Israeli extremist in November 1995. 2000 Camp David talks failed. Accounts differ on why; President Clinton blamed Arafat. The Second Intifada began after Ariel Sharon's Temple Mount visit and lasted until about 2005. 2005 Israel withdrew its troops and settlers from Gaza but kept control of its airspace, sea access, and most crossings. 2006–2007 Hamas won the 2006 legislative election and refused the Quartet's conditions (recognize Israel, renounce violence, accept past agreements). In June 2007 it seized Gaza by force from Fatah, and Israel and Egypt imposed tight restrictions on movement in and out of Gaza. Egypt kept the Rafah crossing mostly closed and cracked down on tunnels, though Israel accused it of tolerating smuggling. 2008–2021 Major wars in 2008–09, 2012, 2014, and 2021, each ending with little change. In 2014, according to the UN commission of inquiry, Palestinian groups fired 4,881 rockets and 1,753 mortars at Israel; 2,251 Palestinians (1,462 of them civilians), 67 Israeli soldiers, and 6 civilians in Israel were killed. 2020 The Abraham Accords normalized Israel's relations with the UAE and Bahrain (September 15, 2020), Morocco (December 22, 2020), and Sudan (January 6, 2021). 2023–2025 The October 7 attack and the war in Gaza; the October 2025 U.S.-brokered ceasefire and hostage deal (see below). My view: This history shows Palestinian and Arab leaders rejecting partition and recognition several times, which is part of why a two-state solution is not viable.

head: "What happened on October 7, 2023?"
body: Hamas led an attack from the Gaza Strip into Israel, beginning with a barrage of more than 3,000 rockets. More than 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals were killed, including 46 U.S. citizens, and Hamas and other groups seized some 251 hostages. The Congressional Research Service notes allegations of sexual violence during the assault. The State Department designated Hamas a Foreign Terrorist Organization on October 8, 1997. Iran has provided material support to Hamas for decades. Rocket fire on this scale was not new, but the war multiplied it. In the 2014 Gaza war, Palestinian armed groups fired 4,881 rockets and 1,753 mortars toward Israel, according to the UN Commission of Inquiry. In the 11-day May 2021 conflict, Israel said about 4,360 rockets were fired from Gaza, about 680 of which fell short inside the Strip (Reuters). For October 7 itself, the IDF puts the barrage at 5,000 or more. By the war's first anniversary, the IDF counted about 26,240 rockets, missiles, and drones fired at Israel: 13,200 from Gaza, 12,400 from Lebanon, 400 from Iran in two direct attacks in April and October 2024, 180 from Yemen, and 60 from Syria (Reuters). By October 2026 its count had reached about 31,540: about 10,200 from Gaza, 20,000 from Lebanon, 1,200 from Iran, 90 from Yemen, and 50 from Syria. These are IDF figures. The 2026 Gaza total is lower than the 2024 one, which suggests a change in counting method, and the IDF does not count launches that fell short or failed to reach Israel, which it says number in the thousands. Documented accounts (individual reported events, not statistics): Nova music festival: the attack on the festival ended with 364 people murdered and 44 taken hostage. The BBC Storyville film reconstructs it from survivor testimony and footage. BBC (2024) – Surviving October 7th: We Will Dance Again Sexual violence: a UN mission led by Pramila Patten found "reasonable grounds to believe" that conflict-related sexual violence, including rape and gang rape, occurred in at least three locations, while saying its full scope would need a fully-fledged investigation. It also found two widely repeated allegations at Be'eri unfounded.
