head: "Is it a genocide?"
body: It is categorically not a genocide. Israel has the military power to level Gaza if that were its aim, and the numbers do not reflect genocide or ethnic cleansing. Gaza's population did not dip anywhere near the proportions other genocides do relative to the population. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated about 2.13 million people at the end of 2025, about 10.6% below its pre-war projection, a figure that counts deaths, departures, and fewer births. Case Killed Targeted population Share killed Holocaust, European Jews (1933–1945) about 6 million about 9.5 million (1933) about 2 in 3 Rwanda, Tutsi (1994) more than 500,000 Tutsi minority about 3 in 4 in the one province studied in detail Cambodia, Khmer Rouge (1975–1979), all groups about 1.7 million whole population about 21% Srebrenica, Bosnian Muslims (1995) 7,000–8,000 men and boys about 40,000 about 1 in 5 Gaza, health ministry count reported by UN OCHA (to October 2026) 74,250 about 2.2 million before the war about 3.4% Gaza, Lancet estimate (October 2023 to June 2024 only) 64,260 about 2.2 million before the war about 2.9% The Gaza figures include combatants, and the Lancet estimate covers only the first nine months. The Armenian genocide is left out for lack of a neutral demographic estimate I could verify. Under the Genocide Convention, genocide turns on intent to destroy a group "in whole or in part," not on a set share killed. International tribunals require that the targeted part be substantial, judged by its size relative to the group and other factors. exampleDisputed counts and reviewsOthers disagree, and the legal question is unresolved. South Africa brought a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice in December 2023. The Court ordered provisional measures in January, March, and May 2024 but has not ruled on the merits. It set deadlines for further written pleadings running to May 2029, and Israel has objected to the Court's jurisdiction. In September 2025, a UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejects. No independent count separates combatants from civilians. A peer-reviewed study in The Lancet, by researchers at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, estimated 64,260 traumatic-injury deaths from October 2023 to June 2024, about 41% more than the Gaza health ministry reported; 59% of deaths with known age and sex were women, children, and older people, and the study did not estimate how many were combatants. A household survey published in The Lancet Global Health in 2026 estimated about 75,200 violent deaths through January 5, 2025, about 3.4% of the pre-war population, and found 56% were women, children, or people over 64. A re-analysis in the same journal found interviewer-level deviations and said dropping two outlying teams lowers the estimate by about 16,000. A 2024 modeling study in Frontiers in Public Health estimated that combatants were 12.7% of deaths in 2023, an estimate built on health ministry data and Israeli claims. Israel's military has claimed about 17,000 Hamas fighters killed by October 2024. Some statistics have been revised or disputed. In May 2024 the UN switched its breakdown of Gaza deaths from the Hamas-run Government Media Office, which put women and children at 69%, to health ministry data on identified bodies, where they were 52%, while saying the overall toll had not changed. In June 2024 the IPC's Famine Review Committee found a famine analysis by FEWS NET, the USAID-funded early-warning network, not plausible given uncertain and non-convergent evidence, and a separate review that month found the evidence did "not indicate that Famine is currently occurring," while warning of a high risk. In August 2025 the Committee did confirm famine, "with reasonable evidence," in Gaza Governorate as of August 15, with about 514,000 people in catastrophic conditions and famine projected to spread to Deir al-Balah and Khan Younis. The IPC later added an addendum clarifying the malnutrition data it used after questions were raised about its methods. Israel's COGAT rejected the finding as relying on "partial and unreliable sources, many of them affiliated with Hamas." In December 2025, after the October ceasefire improved aid access, the IPC classified no area of Gaza in famine, though it put the whole Strip in Emergency (Phase 4) and about 1.6 million people in Crisis or worse. Cutting the other way, the Lancet capture-recapture study and the Lancet Global Health household survey both estimated more violent deaths than the health ministry reported, not fewer. My view: Palestinian reporting and the UN are biased against Israel, and I weigh their findings with that in mind. UN, USAID, and certain neutral-party statistics may have been ideologically driven or manipulated to align with the genocide claim, since aid and diplomatic groups have an interest in ending armed conflict.

head: "Is a two-state solution viable?"
body: It is not, and Gaza should likely be dissolved, since it has proven time and again hostile and uncooperative toward Israel. Palestinian opinion is divided: in an October 2026 poll by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, 53% of Palestinians supported a two-state solution on the 1967 lines and 44% opposed it.

head: "Do Palestinians support Hamas and October 7?"
body: Many do. In polls by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, the share of Palestinians calling Hamas's decision to launch the October 7 attack correct was 71% in March 2024 and 53% in October 2025, 59% in the West Bank and 44% in Gaza. In the October 2025 poll, nearly all respondents said they did not believe Hamas committed the atrocities against civilians shown in international media. Support for Hamas as a party has since fallen, to 19% in October 2026. Before the war, an Arab Barometer survey taken from September 28 to October 8, 2023 found 21% support for Hamas. It rose to 43% by early December 2023 but never reached a majority in the West Bank or Gaza. In a 2009 Pew Research Center survey, 97% of Palestinians held an unfavorable view of Jews. No newer neutral survey on that question was found. This support reflects open hostility and racism toward Jews and Israel.

head: "What does Hamas say it wants?"
body: Its founding 1988 charter opens with the quote "Israel will exist and will continue to exist until Islam will obliterate it," states that "there is no solution for the Palestinian question except through Jihad," quotes a hadith calling on Muslims to kill Jews hiding "behind stones and trees," and cites the forged "Protocols of the Elders of Zion." Its 2017 policy document says its conflict "is with the Zionist project not with the Jews because of their religion," rejects "any alternative to the full and complete liberation of Palestine, from the river to the sea," refuses to recognize Israel, and calls a state on the 1967 lines only "a formula of national consensus." On October 24, 2023, Hamas official Ghazi Hamad said on Lebanese television that October 7 "is just the first time, and there will be a second, a third, a fourth." These words are why I condemn Hamas as a terrorist organization.

head: "Who funds Hamas?"
body: The State Department says Iran gives Hamas money, weapons, and training, up to about $100 million a year in combined support to Palestinian militant groups. It also found "no evidence that Iran knew about" October 7 in advance. CRS cites a 2024 estimate that Hamas's yearly revenue tops $1 billion, about $360 million of it from taxes on goods entering Gaza, with foreign sources including Iran and private entities in Qatar, Turkey, and other states.

head: "How has Hamas governed Gaza?"
body: Hamas has held no election since 2006. CRS calls it Gaza's "de facto authoritarian ruler." The State Department reported that as of November 30, 2023 Hamas courts had sentenced 25 people to death, 13 for "collaboration," and carried out executions without the PA approval required by Palestinian law. It also reported that from January to September 2023 Hamas detained 60 Palestinians for political affiliation, criticism of Hamas, or suspected collaboration, and reported violence against LGBTQI+ people. During the 2014 war, Hamas's armed wing claimed the firing-squad executions of 21 alleged collaborators.

head: "What about the occupation and settlements?"
body: In a July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found, 11 votes to 4, that Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza is unlawful and must end "as rapidly as possible," and, 14 to 1, that Israel must stop new settlement activity and evacuate settlers. Advisory opinions are not binding. Vice-President Sebutinde dissented on every point, and Judges Tomka, Abraham, and Aurescu dissented on the core findings. The UN human rights office, citing the Israeli group Peace Now, put the settler population in 2023 at about 465,000 in the West Bank and 230,000 in East Jerusalem. UN OCHA counted 509 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank and East Jerusalem in 2023, the deadliest year since its records began in 2005, and before October 7 counted 26 Israelis killed in the West Bank. Forcible transfer of a civilian population is prohibited under the Fourth Geneva Convention (Article 49) and the Rome Statute. Article 49 reads: "Individual or mass forcible transfers, as well as deportations of protected persons from occupied territory to the territory of the Occupying Power or to that of any other country, occupied or not, are prohibited, regardless of their motive." Israel's position is that the Convention does not apply de jure to the West Bank, citing "the lack of recognition of the territory as sovereign prior to its annexation by Jordan and Egypt," and that it applies the Convention's humanitarian provisions in practice. The argument traces to Yehuda Blum's 1968 Israel Law Review article "The Missing Reversioner," which concluded that Jordan had no valid title to the territory and so the law of occupation did not apply. The International Court of Justice rejected that view in its 2004 advisory opinion on the West Bank barrier, finding the Convention applicable in the territories Israel occupied in 1967, "there being no need for any enquiry into the precise prior status of those territories." Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs separately argues that Article 49(6), on moving an occupier's own civilians in, does not reach voluntary Jewish settlement. My view: Forcing hostile residents out conflicts with Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention and the Rome Statute, and the Court found Israel's presence unlawful. I hold my position anyway, for two reasons. First, treaty law is not my moral standard. A removal is not right or wrong because a convention forbids it, any more than a punishment is right or wrong because other democracies dropped it (the same test I apply to the death penalty). The standard is whether the person has forfeited his protection by his own conduct (forfeiture). Second, every removal I support is individual: a court or military tribunal decides it on the person's own conduct, never in a mass action and never by ethnicity, religion, or any other identity (Hostile conduct, removal, and entry). I acknowledge that Article 49's text bars individual transfers too, so this answers the charge of ethnic cleansing, not the treaty. The opinion is advisory and drew dissents on its core findings, and a nation follows its own laws, not foreign tribunals (Global Institutions). Nor do I want indefinite control: a perpetual security state is costly and dangerous and not in Israel's best interest, so I prefer a negotiated middle ground and, failing that, separation behind hard security, with force aimed at those who commit violence. Residents who choose to join Israel and assimilate are accepted. Only those who refuse and remain hostile are forced out, because given how widely hostility runs there I treat hostile conduct as a security threat (Sovereignty and Borders; Hostile conduct, removal, and entry). The rule protects Israelis within reach of attack and the residents who choose to join and live in peace beside them. The two errors are not equal: a person wrongly removed loses a home, while a person wrongly left in place who acts on his hostility takes lives that cannot be returned. Removal follows each person's own record, and Israel carries the treaty and diplomatic cost of acting.

head: "Does the Palestinian Authority reward attacks?"
body: The 2018 Taylor Force Act bars most U.S. economic aid to the Palestinian Authority until it ends payments to people jailed for, or killed while committing, attacks and to their families. In April 2026 the State Department said it could not certify that the payments had ended. Citing Israel's foreign minister, it said the PA paid $156 million in 2025, $126 million to prisoners and released prisoners and $30 million to families of attackers who died, now through a new welfare agency. On schooling, a 2021 EU-commissioned study of PA textbooks by Germany's Georg Eckert Institute found they met UNESCO standards on themes such as human rights but also contained "anti-Semitic narratives and glorifications of violence." It found no direct calls for violence against Israelis and said 2020 revisions reduced some escalatory content.

head: "Why are you skeptical of the Free Palestine movement?"
body: I am skeptical of politically charged alignment with the Palestinian cause. Left-wing politicians and progressives have rallied behind "Free Palestine" as a cause, and a lot of misinformation and propaganda spread by Hamas itself is eaten up by pro-Palestinian audiences in Europe and the United States. That is not to discount Israeli propaganda either. examplePolls, campuses, and documented casesSome documented cases support the concern about Hamas. After the October 17, 2023 blast at Gaza's al-Ahli hospital, Hamas officials blamed an Israeli airstrike and cited about 500 dead. A U.S. intelligence assessment judged Israel was not responsible and estimated deaths at the low end of 100 to 300, and the New York Times said its early coverage "relied too heavily on claims by Hamas." In May 2024 the UN changed its breakdown of Gaza deaths from figures of Hamas's Government Media Office, which put women and children at 69%, to health ministry data on identified bodies, where they were 52%. The UN said the overall toll had not fallen and that women and children were still about 60% if the identified breakdown is applied to all deaths. Misinformation and covert influence run both ways: Meta removed an Israeli network, which it linked to the Tel Aviv firm STOIC, of 510 fake Facebook accounts that targeted U.S. and Canadian audiences and U.S. lawmakers, and a separate Iranian network posing as Israelis. U.S. opinion has split along party lines: in Gallup's February 2026 poll, 65% of Democrats sympathized more with the Palestinians and 17% with the Israelis, while 70% of Republicans sympathized more with the Israelis. Overall, Americans sided with the Palestinians 41% to 36%, the first time in Gallup's series since 2001. Pew found in September 2025 that 84% of Americans viewed Hamas unfavorably, including wide majorities of both parties, so sympathy for Palestinians does not mean support for Hamas. In Western Europe, YouGov's May 2025 EuroTrack found more people sided with the Palestinians than the Israelis in all six countries polled: Britain 32% to 14%, Spain 33% to 15%, Italy 31% to 7%, Denmark 28% to 18%, France 24% to 18%, and Germany 18% to 17%, with a fifth to two-fifths unsure in each. On U.S. campuses, the Crowd Counting Consortium at Harvard and the University of Connecticut logged more than 3,700 days of pro-Palestine protest at 525 schools from October 7, 2023 to late May 2024, with property damage, mostly graffiti, on 33 of them and police injuries on 8, and 3,645 arrests. It found protesters were injured by police or counter-protesters about as often as protesters caused property damage. ACLED found 97% of U.S. student demonstrations from October 7, 2023 to May 3, 2024 were peaceful, meaning they involved no serious violence or property damage. The protests were nonviolent for the most part, sure, but they were often aggressive and fascistic against others. In one documented case, a federal judge found in August 2024 that "Jewish students were excluded from portions of the UCLA campus because they refused to denounce their faith," noting that UCLA did not dispute it, and ordered the university not to allow campus areas to be closed to Jewish students, including over their beliefs about Israel (Frankel v. Regents of the University of California). Documented accounts (individual reported events, not statistics): Hospital coverage (Hamas misinformation): after the al-Ahli blast, The New York Times said its early coverage "relied too heavily on claims by Hamas" and "left readers with an incorrect impression about what was known." NPR (2023) – Media backtracks on Gaza hospital blast after relying on Hamas as source Columbia University, April 30, 2024 (aggressive protests): police cleared protesters who had occupied Hamilton Hall. NPR reported about 300 arrests in New York that night. NPR (2024) – New York police arrest 300 people as they clear Hamilton Hall at Columbia University

head: "Is Israel racist against Arabs?"
body: It is not. Arab citizens make up about 21% of Israel's population (2.15 million at the end of 2025), vote, and sit in the Knesset, and in 2021 the Arab party Ra'am became the first independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition. In 2022 Khaled Kabub became the first Muslim to hold a permanent seat on Israel's Supreme Court, which has had an Arab justice since 2003. All earlier Arab appointees were Christian. In 2021/22 about 60,600 Arab students made up 18% of students in Israeli higher education, against 21% of the population, up 133% over the decade. Large gaps remain: the OECD found that Arab-Israelis' hourly wages are about half those of non-Haredi Jewish men, and attributed the gap to education, language, location, and "partly also possible discrimination," citing audit studies that found discrimination against Arab-Israelis in hiring for some services and in rental housing. The State Department reported that planning for Arab areas lags far behind Jewish municipalities, leaving about 50,000 Arab families in unpermitted homes, and that the 2018 Nation-State Law downgraded Arabic from an official language. The OECD found Arab-Israeli women have the lowest employment rates of any group, and that gaps in schooling, Hebrew fluency, and distance from jobs explain much of the wage gap. In medicine, a 2024 peer-reviewed study found that in 2023 Arab citizens made up 25% of Israel's employed physicians, up from 8% in 2010, 27% of nurses and dentists, and 49% of pharmacists, compared with 16% of all employment. Military and police service is uneven. Druze and Circassian men are conscripted. Bedouin, other Muslim, and Christian Arab citizens may volunteer. An IDF colonel who heads the minorities department told The Jerusalem Post in 2025 that Druze enlistment had reached 85% since October 7, that Bedouin service was just over 60%, and that Christian Arab enlistment had tripled in a year, but that Muslim soldiers still number only a few dozen and Christian soldiers a few hundred. Calcalist, citing IDF and national civil service data, reported that in the 2022–23 service year 481 Arab citizens enlisted in the IDF (433 Muslims and Bedouin, 48 Christians) and 3,319 joined civilian national service. In the Israel Police, ministry data reported in 2026 show 3,294 new officers in 2025, of whom 96 were Muslim, 2 Bedouin, and 12 Arab Christian, down from 165, 7, and 59 in 2023, even as overall recruitment rose. These counts exclude the Druze.

head: "Does Israel protect civilians in Gaza?"
body: Palestinian civilians should not be targeted. Hamas endangers them by operating among them. A 2019 case study by the NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence found that Hamas has used human shields since 2007, launching rockets and placing military infrastructure in or near residential and commercial areas. An analysis in the West Point Combating Terrorism Center's CTC Sentinel reports that Hamas dug its tunnel network near and under schools, mosques, and UN facilities. Israel has issued evacuation orders and warnings before strikes, including "roof knocking," though a 2009 UN fact-finding mission questioned how effective such warnings are when there is little time or no safe place to go. Israel allows aid into Gaza, and patients are evacuated for treatment abroad through Israeli crossings: the World Health Organization counted more than 10,700 medical evacuations by the end of 2025. Israeli authorities and some U.S. investigations say Hamas often steals or diverts aid. The U.S. evidence is mixed: the USAID Inspector General is investigating credible allegations of Hamas diversion and theft, while an internal USAID review of 156 reported incidents of loss or theft of U.S.-funded aid found no evidence that Hamas benefited. The UN's tracking system reported that 88% of UN aid trucks entering Gaza from May 19 to August 22, 2025 were intercepted, taken "either peacefully by hungry people or forcefully by armed actors," without attributing the losses to Hamas. Israel's military has claimed, based on its intelligence, that Hamas diverted up to 25% of aid. Hamas denies it, and neither claim has been independently verified. U.S. intelligence, in an assessment declassified in January 2024, said it was confident that Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad used Gaza's al-Shifa hospital complex to command forces and hold at least a few hostages, and that they largely evacuated it days before Israeli troops entered. The evidence was not released. In 2014, UNRWA reported finding weapons hidden in one of its vacant Gaza schools and condemned it as a flagrant violation of its premises. A UN board of inquiry later identified them as a mortar tube and mortar rounds. On UNRWA, the UN's oversight office reviewed Israel's allegations against 19 of its roughly 13,000 Gaza staff and found that evidence, if authenticated, could indicate nine may have taken part in October 7; they were fired. An independent review led by former French foreign minister Catherine Colonna found UNRWA's neutrality rules the most elaborate in the UN system but in need of improvement, and that Israel had not provided evidence for its broader claim that many UNRWA employees belong to terrorist groups. After the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation began distributing food in May 2025, the UN human rights office counted at least 1,373 Palestinians killed while seeking food by July 31, 859 of them near its sites, most by the Israeli military.

head: "What about the hostages?"
body: All hostages should be returned to Israel. Hamas released the last 20 living hostages on October 13, 2025 under a U.S.-brokered ceasefire, and the remains of the last deceased hostage, Ran Gvili, were recovered on January 26, 2026, leaving no hostages in Gaza. Israel gave Hamas many chances at a deal that Hamas refused. Date Proposal Outcome November 24 – December 1, 2023 Truce mediated by Qatar, Egypt, and the U.S. Agreed. Extended twice; 105 hostages released for 240 Palestinian prisoners before fighting resumed May 31, 2024 Three-phase plan announced by President Biden as an Israeli offer Endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2735 (14–0, Russia abstaining); the U.S. said Israel had accepted and called on Hamas to accept. Netanyahu said the war would not end until Hamas was destroyed, and Hamas demanded a permanent ceasefire and full withdrawal August–September 2024 U.S. "bridging proposal" Not agreed. CRS reported that both sides resisted proposals, Netanyahu insisted on keeping the Philadelphi Corridor, and the White House called Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar "the big obstacle" January 15, 2025 First phase of the three-phase deal Agreed. Ceasefire began January 19 with 33 hostages to be released, but the later phases were not completed October 2025 Phase one of the U.S. 20-point plan of September 29, 2025 Agreed. The plan called for all hostages returned within 72 hours, 250 life-sentence prisoners and 1,700 Gaza detainees released, Hamas barred from governing Gaza and disarmed, and Israel not to occupy or annex Gaza; all living hostages were released October 13, and Hamas has refused to disarm The record shows Hamas rejecting or delaying several proposals, and Israeli leaders also resisting terms that would end the war before Hamas was defeated.

head: "What has the war cost Gaza?"
body: As of October 2024, more than 41,000 Palestinians in Gaza had been killed, according to the Hamas-controlled health ministry, whose count does not separate combatants from civilians. About 90% of Gaza's roughly 2.1 million residents had been displaced, most facing acute shortages of food, water, and medical care. Israel claimed to have killed about 17,000 of Hamas's estimated 25,000 to 30,000 fighters, and at least 346 Israeli soldiers had died in ground operations. These figures are from the Congressional Research Service as of October 2024. By October 2026 the health ministry count reported by UN OCHA had reached 74,250, still without separating combatants (see the table under "Is it a genocide?").

head: "How much military aid does the U.S. give Israel?"
body: Under the 2016 Memorandum of Understanding covering FY2019 to FY2028, the U.S. pledged, subject to appropriation, $38 billion in military aid: $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing grants and $5 billion for missile defense, or about $3.3 billion and $500 million a year. After October 7, Congress added emergency aid, including $3.5 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $5.2 billion for missile defense and the Iron Beam laser system in April 2024. Israel is the largest cumulative recipient of U.S. foreign assistance since World War II. I support this aid as far as it serves U.S. security (Foreign Aid).

Iran funds, arms, and directs proxy forces that attack U.S. troops, shipping, and allies, and it has plotted assassinations on U.S. soil. Its proxies have killed and attacked Americans for more than four decades. Hezbollah's 1983 suicide truck bombing of the U.S. Marine barracks in Beirut killed 241 U.S. service members. In 2023 Iran-aligned militias in Iraq and Syria, including Kata'ib Hezbollah, attacked U.S. forces with drones Iran supplied, and since 2023 the Houthis have launched hundreds of attacks on commercial ships in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden and on the U.S. service members defending them. Hamas is among the groups it has supported, and its October 7 attack killed more than 1,200 people in a single day. Israel confronts these forces directly, which serves U.S. interests. Destroying the regime removes the source of the threat rather than managing its symptoms.

The United States ought to designate as a terrorist organization every Muslim Brotherhood chapter shown to support Islamist terrorism or to organize violence, and keep the remaining chapters under close watch, designating any chapter as soon as the evidence shows it has crossed that line. The Brotherhood's ideology and network have produced one terrorist group after another; the record of named spin-offs and chapter conduct is in the Q&A and Rationale below. A legal political wing does not exempt a chapter that is shown to be dangerous. Executive Order 14362 set this chapter-by-chapter process in motion, and four chapters have been designated so far: Lebanon, Egypt, Jordan and Sudan (Muslim Brotherhood chapters designated). I would only designate the dangerous chapters, while watching the rest; those chapters, like the Islamist terror groups they back, are among the enemies met with proactive eradication (Islam and Extremism).

head: "Aren't some Brotherhood chapters peaceful political parties?"
body: Defenders point out that some chapters run as legal political parties and say they have renounced violence. Jordan's Islamic Action Front won 31 of 138 seats in the 2024 parliamentary election. Its secretary general calls it an independent party with "no relationship with any other organisational body" and says it is "committed to order, the law, and the provisions of the constitution," and the Jordanian Brotherhood says it is "committed to its peaceful approach." A party front does not shield a chapter with a record like Jordan's. In April 2025 Jordan's intelligence service arrested 16 people over plots involving explosives, automatic weapons, rocket manufacture, a rocket hidden ready to launch, and a drone project. A week later Jordan outlawed the Brotherhood, closed its offices, seized its assets and raided the Islamic Action Front's headquarters, and the interior minister said members had tried to remove and destroy documents from the Brotherhood's headquarters. In January 2026 the Treasury found that Jordanian Brotherhood members, working with entities abroad, had manufactured rockets, explosives and drones, run recruitment operations and raised money illegally, and designated the chapter for material support to a designated terrorist group. Jordan's chapter had a party that won seats and a peaceful public line while its members were building rockets, and that is exactly why the chapters not yet designated stay under close watch: designation follows as soon as the evidence does. Other chapters keep armed wings of their own. The Lebanese chapter reactivated its armed wing, the al-Fajr Forces, after October 7, 2023 and fired rockets into northern Israel in coordination with Hezbollah. The Sudanese chapter runs an armed wing, the al-Baraa Bin Malik Brigade, whose fighters have carried out mass executions of civilians and summarily executed people based on race, ethnicity or perceived affiliation with opposition groups. The governments closest to the movement treat it as a terror threat: Egypt declared it a terrorist group in December 2013, Saudi Arabia in March 2014, and the UAE listed "the Muslim Brotherhood (MB) organisation and groups" as terrorist in November 2014.

Designating U.S. organizations. The United States ought to designate a domestic organization as terrorist only on its own record of supporting terrorism or organizing violence, by the same evidence test I apply to each Brotherhood chapter, and only the federal government ought to make that designation, so one standard covers the whole country.

The Brotherhood's record is wider than any one group. The 9/11 Commission found that Osama bin Laden "relies heavily" on the Egyptian writer Sayyid Qutb, "a member of the Muslim Brotherhood" executed in 1966, who taught that all Muslims as he defined them must take up arms and that any Muslim who rejects his ideas is "just one more nonbeliever worthy of destruction." The State Department records that the Egyptian Brotherhood produced Egyptian Islamic Jihad, which assassinated President Anwar Sadat in 1981 and, led by Ayman al-Zawahiri, merged with al-Qa'ida in 2001; Gama'a al-Islamiyya, whose spiritual leader served a life sentence for his role in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing; HASM, whose 2019 car bomb outside a Cairo hospital killed at least 20 people; and Liwa al-Thawra, which assassinated the commander of the Egyptian army's Ninth Armored Division in 2016 and bombed a police training center in Tanta in 2017. Palestinian Islamic Jihad and Hamas also emerged from the Brotherhood; Hamas's 1988 charter states that it "is one of the wings of Moslem Brotherhood in Palestine." The United States has designated every one of these groups as terrorist.

The record of each chapter is what decides its designation, and the designated chapters have such records. The Lebanese chapter's al-Fajr Forces fired rockets into Israel in coordination with Hezbollah after October 7, 2023. In July 2025 the Lebanese Army dismantled a covert military training camp that included its militants; and its secretary general has pushed for a more formal alignment with Hezbollah's axis. The Sudanese chapter has contributed upwards of 20,000 fighters to Sudan's war, many trained and supported by Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Executive Order 14362 states that a senior leader of the Egyptian chapter called on October 7 for violent attacks on U.S. partners and interests, and the Treasury found that in mid-2025 the Egyptian chapter took funding from a terrorist group's military wing to destabilize the Egyptian government and that, in 2024, would-be fighters needed Brotherhood connections in Egypt to reach Gaza. Jordanian Brotherhood leaders, the order states, have long given material support to Hamas's militant wing. In the United States, a federal jury in Dallas in 2008 convicted the Holy Land Foundation and five of its leaders of funneling about $12.4 million to a designated terrorist organization. The government's evidence showed that the foundation was the chief fundraising arm of a committee the Brotherhood set up in the U.S. for that purpose. Each of these findings is tied to a named chapter or network. A chapter with no such record yet is watched, not designated.
A state-level case applying this test to a U.S. group is in News Commentary.

Russia is an aggressor, and I believe the U.S. should help those who fight it. Russia and China ought to be treated as enemies to the extent they try to destabilize the U.S., countered with intelligence, cybersecurity, and strength.

Russia is an aggressor, and I believe it should be fought by helping the countries that fight it. Russia and China are enemies insofar as they seek to destabilize the United States. Intelligence and cybersecurity ought to be advanced to counter their growing presence. Hostility should be met with strength and force.

head: "Does supporting Ukraine conflict with avoiding foreign entanglements?"
body: Helping countries that fight Russia weakens a U.S. adversary without committing American troops to nation-building. It fits the realist test: Russia and China seek to destabilize the United States, so countering them serves national interest.

Great-power rivals pose the most serious long-term threats to U.S. security. Russian and Chinese intelligence and cyber operations target American institutions and industry, which is why intelligence and cybersecurity are priorities. Deterrence through strength discourages aggression.
FBI – The China Threat

head: India, Africa, and the Global South
topic: India, Africa, and the Global South

body: I want ties with India, Africa, and the Global South to serve U.S. interests, help move supply chains away from China, and avoid nation-building.
topic: India, Africa, and the Global South

head: Position
topic: India, Africa, and the Global South

body: Relations with India, African states, and the wider Global South should follow the realist test: they ought to serve U.S. security and economic interest. Because China is an adversary, trade and supply chains should be shifted away from it toward partners that do not threaten U.S. security. Partnerships ought to be reciprocal and should not involve nation-building.

head: "Why engage these regions at all?"
body: They offer alternative supply chains and markets as outsourcing to China is restricted, and denying China influence there serves U.S. security.

head: North Korea and Nuclear Rogue States
topic: North Korea and Nuclear Rogue States

body: North Korea's arsenal should be deterred and contained. I'd take preventive action only when it can be done safely.
topic: North Korea and Nuclear Rogue States

head: Position
topic: North Korea and Nuclear Rogue States

body: I believe deterrence is the main safeguard against states that already hold nuclear weapons, such as North Korea. Their arsenals cannot be uninvented, so the United States should maintain a credible deterrent and alliances that contain them. Preventive military action against a nuclear program should be taken when it can be done safely; where a state already holds deliverable weapons, deterrence and containment govern.
topic: North Korea and Nuclear Rogue States

head: "Why not strike North Korea's arsenal?"
body: Preventive action applies when it can be done safely. Against an established arsenal, a strike risks nuclear retaliation, so deterrence is the safer course.

topic: North Korea and Nuclear Rogue States

body: SIPRI estimates that North Korea holds about 50 nuclear warheads and enough fissile material for up to 90. The preventive-action rule is set out in Nuclear Weapons and WMD.

body: I'm fine with current high military spending, and it can rise if needed. Homeland defense comes first, but global reach and swift strikes are part of protecting it.

Current military spending is very high, and I find it acceptable. The empirics of military spending are beyond what is asserted here, but if more firepower is needed or a visible shortfall appears in campaigns, it should be raised. Homeland defense should always come first, but global power is often bound up with homeland protection. Offensive deterrence and swift strikes go hand in hand with protecting the country. Spending ought to stay within the balanced-budget and spending-restraint goals in Domestic Policy & Governance.

head: "Why maintain global power projection if homeland defense comes first?"
body: Threats are easier to stop far from home. Global reach and swift strikes deter enemies before they can threaten the homeland, which makes projection an extension of defense.
The United States has the largest military budget in the world, and that capacity underwrites deterrence. Projection and rapid strike capability prevent distant threats from becoming close ones.
SIPRI – Military Expenditure Database
I see cyber and intelligence capabilities as a core defense priority. Autonomous weapons should be developed, with humans keeping judgment over lethal force.

Intelligence and cyber capabilities should be advanced as a core part of defense, so that the United States can deter and answer attacks on its networks and infrastructure. Autonomous weapons ought to be developed to keep pace with adversaries, under the same defensive logic as defensive AGI, with human judgment retained over the use of lethal force.

head: "Doesn't autonomy risk losing control of weapons?"
body: That is why human judgment over lethal force should be retained. Falling behind adversaries carries its own risk.

DoD Directive 3000.09 (January 25, 2023) requires autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems to allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force. Defensive AGI is set out in Bioethics, Progress, & Technology.

The Outer Space Treaty should stay as the civil baseline but be read to allow defense, with clauses that block missile defense renegotiated or exited. I allow defensive space weapons and disfavor first-strike weapons. Civil spaceflight stays private, the only funded government space program is military, and business subsidies are opt-in only.

I would keep the Outer Space Treaty as the baseline for peaceful civil use, interpreted to allow defensive systems, with renegotiation or exit from clauses that block missile defense or hostile-denial. Defensive space weapons, such as missile defense and defensive anti-satellite systems, should be allowed; I disfavor offensive first-strike space weapons. Human spaceflight should stay fully privatized, the only funded government space program should be military under the Space Force and the Department of Defense, which may contract private firms, and there should be no business subsidies except taxpayer opt-in.

head: "Doesn't the Outer Space Treaty ban weapons in space?"
body: It bans nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit and military bases on celestial bodies. It should be kept as the civil baseline and interpreted to allow defensive systems. Clauses that block missile defense should be renegotiated or exited.

This follows my view that military power serves the defense of the country (Military Spending and Projection), opt-in subsidies, and human judgment over force, as in Cyber Warfare and Autonomous Weapons. Article IV of the Outer Space Treaty bars placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit and bars military bases and weapons testing on celestial bodies. Article XVI allows any party to withdraw on one year's written notice. Privatized civil spaceflight is set out in Space and Exploration.
UNOOSA – Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space (Outer Space Treaty)
See also: Space and Exploration

In my view civilians are absolutely protected, except foreign actors who have forfeited protection as set out in Sovereignty and Borders (conduct test). Prisoners of war keep their Geneva rights, except where those conflict with the compelled-labor rule, and should be held in a separate military setup. But those a tribunal finds took part in hostilities can be put to compelled labor like domestic prisoners.

Civilians ought to be absolutely protected and given full rights protections, except foreign actors who have forfeited protection as set out in Sovereignty and Borders (conduct test). Prisoners of war should get basic protections and treatment similar to how the United States treats its own prisoners, including labor, but foreign captives should be held in a separate military setup. Labor is my preferred placement for them. I would refuse Geneva compliance only where the Convention conflicts with my compelled-labor rule: a prisoner whom a military tribunal finds, under due process, took part in hostilities against the United States has crossed the forfeiture threshold in Section 1 and may be assigned compelled labor on the same terms as domestic prisoners, beyond the Convention's limits on the kinds of work and its pay requirements. A rights violator past that line loses the corresponding protections. A prisoner who has not crossed it keeps every protection the Convention gives.

head: "Doesn't departing from Geneva on labor invite enemies to mistreat captured Americans?"
body: Civilians remain absolutely protected, except foreign actors who have forfeited protection by hostile conduct (Hostile conduct, removal, and entry), and prisoners of war receive basic protections and treatment similar to how the United States treats its own prisoners. The only departure is compelled labor for prisoners a military tribunal finds took part in hostilities. Every other prisoner keeps every protection the Convention gives. The standard is the same one applied at home, not a lower one invented for foreigners. Reciprocity is a practical consideration, but the United States ought not to let a treaty set the terms; U.S. law and the rights framework do.

head: "If civilians are absolutely protected and beliefs are never grounds for removal, how can hostile West Bank residents be forced out, and their population barred from entry? Isn't that ethnic cleansing?"
body: The two rules govern different people. Inside the United States, opinions, beliefs, and speech should never be grounds for removal (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). That rule should protect people the government governs. Abroad, a civilian should keep full protection unless he forfeits it by his own conduct against the threatened nation (Sovereignty and Borders). Hostility means conduct, not identity: membership in, or material support for, an armed group that targets civilians. Public calls for genocide or ethnic cleansing; or taking part in or organizing violence against civilians. Ethnicity, religion, ordinary speech, and private opinion alone should never count as hostility. Why the hostile are forced out. A person found hostile has forfeited his protection against the nation he threatens, and that nation has the right and the duty to defend its people from him. Removal should be the remedy that fits the threat. He has shown, by his own conduct, that he will act to harm the nation's civilians. Letting him stay keeps an active threat among the people it targets, and indefinite detention would be a costly, permanent security state, the very thing separation is meant to end. Removal ends the threat at its source without taking his life. Once a court or tribunal finds him hostile, he should be forced out. A later offer to assimilate does not reopen the case, because a promise from someone already proven hostile is not a security guarantee. The nation's security and its duty to its citizens override the negative rights of a foreign security threat, so forcing him out wrongs no one. Why entry is barred to the whole population. No foreigner has a right to enter another nation. Entry is a privilege the nation grants on its own terms (Sovereignty and Borders). The United States, and any nation such a population threatens, ought to keep a ban list and impose a complete entry ban, by nationality or place of origin, on two kinds of place. The first is any place whose regime or dominant factions wage or celebrate attacks that target civilians for genocide or ethnic cleansing. The second is any place where reliable polling shows 5% or more of the population openly supporting such attacks. When the people who hold power or set the norm openly back genocidal attacks, screening cannot reliably sort the hostile from the rest, because hostility is common, rewarded, and easy to conceal, and one wrong admission can cost lives. The line sits at 5% because even one person in twenty openly backing the slaughter of civilians is a risk no nation's citizens should be made to carry. Waiting for a quarter or a majority would mean acting only after the hostility is overwhelming. The West Bank and Gaza qualify on both counts: Hamas, a dominant faction, waged October 7 and celebrates it, and support for the attack runs far above 5% (PCPSR polling). The full list, including further grounds for a ban, is in Questionable Compatibility. The list is reviewed every year. A place comes off only when both conditions are met: reliable polling shows open support below 1% in consecutive annual reviews, and no governing authority or dominant faction there still endorses such attacks. The lift point sits far below the trigger so that a small or passing dip does not reopen entry. Support should fall to a level where hostility is rare enough that individual screening can reliably catch it again, and the people in power should have stopped endorsing it. The ban is tied to measured support and to what the authorities there do, not to ethnicity or religion, and it applies to any place that crosses the same line. Why none of this is ethnic cleansing. Ethnic cleansing drives people from their homes because of who they are. The entry ban removes no one from anywhere. It declines to admit people the nation has no duty to admit, on a measured security risk that applies equally to any place that crosses the same line. Forced exit applies only to individuals a court or military tribunal finds hostile by clear and convincing evidence, the removal standard, not the capital one. Residents who are not found hostile and choose to assimilate stay, whatever their ethnicity or faith. October 7 targeted people for being Jewish. This targets no one for being Palestinian.

The Third Geneva Convention of 1949, to which the United States is a party, states that "prisoners of war must at all times be humanely treated" (Article 13), that they "shall not be interned in penitentiaries" except in their own interest (Article 22), and that the detaining power "may utilize the labour of prisoners of war who are physically fit" (Article 49). I depart from the Convention only where its labor limits conflict with the compelled-labor rule, and only for prisoners past the forfeiture threshold. Labor by prisoners of war rests on two grounds. Their detention as captured combatants permits labor, as the Convention itself does for physically fit prisoners (Article 49). Labor is assigned after a military tribunal finds, under due process, that the prisoner took part in hostilities against the United States, consistent with the forfeiture rule in Section 1. Compelled labor for domestic prisoners is set out in Criminal Justice & Security.

I put defense first in the budget, including care for injured veterans.
Defense should be the top budget priority, and the care owed to those injured in service is part of the cost of defense.
Nuclear weapons cannot be uninvented, so I see deterrence as the main safeguard. Enemies should be stopped from getting them by military force when it can be done safely.

Nuclear proliferation is unfortunate but can never be reversed, since progress will always be made with all technologies. I believe mutual deterrence is the only way to prevent catastrophe. Enemies should be militarily prevented from advancing nuclear capability when the United States can do so safely.

head: "Isn't preventive military action against proliferation destabilizing?"
body: Action is taken only when it can be done safely. Allowing hostile regimes to acquire nuclear weapons is far more destabilizing, because deterrence depends on rational actors and some enemies are openly committed to destroying the West.

head: "Didn't the 2015 nuclear deal already stop Iran's program?"
body: It paused parts of the program, on a timer. Under the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, Iran kept 5,060 operating centrifuges at Natanz and could enrich to 3.67 percent. The Fordow site kept 1,044 centrifuges, with no uranium allowed there for 15 years. The main limits ran 10 to 15 years, and the 15-year limits would have expired on January 16, 2031. A deal that leaves the enrichment machinery in place and lets the limits lapse buys time without ending the capability. That is why enemies are stopped from advancing nuclear capability by force when it can be done safely. By 2025 Iran was enriching at about 60 percent, and the IAEA reported serious non-compliance. Those later facts are why a rented pause is not enough (War with Iran; War with Iran, October 2026).

Nine states possess nuclear weapons, and the knowledge cannot be removed from the world. Deterrence has prevented nuclear war among major powers since 1945. Preventing hostile regimes such as Iran from acquiring weapons keeps deterrence workable.
Mutual deterrence is the condition in which each side can inflict unacceptable retaliation on the other, so that neither has an incentive to strike first.

I support a practical, gradual transition guided by free-market innovation and sentient-rights considerations. Policy should avoid disruptive mandates and taxpayer-funded subsidies. It ought to prioritize human (and herbivore) welfare over apocalyptic framing while conserving nature where it does not conflict with rights or development.

Climate change is real and nearly all recent warming is human-caused (IPCC), but it is not apocalyptic under the IPCC AR6 scenario ranges I treat as the central case (serious harm, not civilization collapse). Any shift to greener infrastructure should be slow and market-driven, with no mandates and no source forced off early, so energy supply is not disrupted. Animal agriculture ought to be banned and shut down immediately as a rights violation, which also cuts a material share of human-caused warming (~12% FAO livestock agrifood systems, 2015 baseline).

The climate varies naturally, but the IPCC finds that essentially all warming since the late 1800s is human-caused. The threat is real but not apocalyptic: under AR6, long-term (2081–2100) global warming versus 1850–1900 is very likely about 1.3–2.4°C in a low-emissions case (SSP1-2.6, best estimate 1.8°C), about 2.1–3.5°C in an intermediate case (SSP2-4.5, best estimate 2.7°C), and about 3.3–5.7°C in a very high-emissions case (SSP5-8.5, best estimate 4.4°C). Likely global mean sea-level rise by 2100 versus 1995–2014 is about 0.32–0.62 m (SSP1-2.6), 0.44–0.76 m (SSP2-4.5), and 0.63–1.01 m (SSP5-8.5) under medium-confidence ice processes. That is serious, uneven harm - coasts, heat, extremes - not human extinction or civilization collapse as the central projection. Low-likelihood ice-sheet outcomes under very high emissions can go higher; if credible evidence shows extreme unjustified death-risk to future sentient beings, greenhouse-gas limits should tighten under Pollution and Liability, still without energy mandates or early forced shutdowns of reliable supply. Policy ought to support long-term wellbeing of sentient individuals without upending energy supply chains. Any transition to greener infrastructure should come slowly, through markets and private innovation, with no mandates and no early forced shutdowns (Grid Reliability and Permitting). Ending animal agriculture, which should be banned as a rights violation and shut down immediately (Agriculture, Grazing, and Habitat), also cuts livestock agrifood-system emissions; the ban rests on rights, and the climate gain is a side effect.

head: "If climate change is real, why not act faster?"
body: In my judgment, rapid transition would disrupt energy supply chains that sentient beings depend on, causing harm of its own. That is a judgment about risk, not a measured cost estimate. A slow, market-driven shift addresses the problem without that disruption.

head: "Doesn't carbon pricing cut emissions?"
body: Carbon-pricing advocates cite a 2024 meta-analysis of 80 evaluations covering 21 schemes, which found emissions cuts of 5% to 21% in the 17 schemes with significant effects, or 4% to 15% after correcting for publication bias. A cut bought with a government-imposed price on energy is still imposed. The shift to greener energy stays slow and market-driven, with no mandates and no source forced off early, so energy supply is not disrupted.

head: "What about catastrophic tail risk?"
body: Present agents ought not to impose extreme, unjustified risk of death on future sentient beings (Duties to Future Generations). If credible evidence shows that risk, the harm-based greenhouse-gas limits in Pollution and Liability can be tightened in proportion to it, with the burden of proof on the rule. That still means no energy mandates and no early forced shutdowns of reliable supply.

The IPCC attributes recent warming to human activity: it puts the human-caused rise from 1850–1900 to 2010–2019 at about 1.07°C (likely 0.8–1.3°C), out of about 1.1°C observed, with natural drivers contributing between −0.1°C and +0.1°C. It projects the scenario ranges above. FAO's 2023 Pathways towards lower emissions assessment (GLEAM) puts livestock agrifood systems — farm gate, land-use change tied to feed, and key supply-chain steps — at about 6.2 GtCO₂eq in the 2015 reference year, about 12% of anthropogenic greenhouse-gas emissions. That is a material share, not the largest human driver (fossil energy is larger). The 2006 Livestock's Long Shadow figure of about 18% and its livestock-versus-transport comparison are not used here; that comparison mixed a full livestock life-cycle with direct transport emissions only and was later corrected in the literature. The ~12% figure links the sentientist case against animal agriculture to the climate question as a side effect. Measured transition balances long-term wellbeing against present needs.
