I believe climate adaptation should be practical. Owners carry the risk of where they build, subsidies need opt-in funding, the 18 percent flood insurance cap should be removed, and emergency rescue stays public.

Climate change is real but gradual, so adaptation should be handled as a practical matter. Taxpayer subsidies for risk, including subsidized insurance for building in high-risk areas, ought to require opt-in funding like any other subsidy. Owners should bear the risks of where and how they build, and private insurance should price those risks. I would remove the 18 percent statutory cap on annual flood-insurance premium increases.

head: "What happens to people hit by a disaster?"
body: Emergency response, rescue, and public safety remain government functions. What changes is the long-term subsidy of rebuilding in high-risk places, which shifts costs to taxpayers who did not choose the risk.

head: "Should firefighting be exempt from pollution rules?"
body: No. Fighting wildfire is an emergency function, and retardant should stay available because fire kills animals as well as people. Drops in waterways and protected habitat ought to stay off-limits except to save lives, and an agency that kills fish with a drop ought to answer for it like any other polluter (Pollution and Liability). The current administration's one-year exemption is graded in Current Administration.

The National Flood Insurance Program owed the Treasury $22.525 billion after borrowing $2 billion on February 10, 2025, according to the Congressional Research Service. Under FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0, about one-third of National Flood Insurance Program policyholders already pay full-risk premiums, and 9 percent will eventually need increases of more than 300 percent, according to the Government Accountability Office. Annual increases for most policyholders are limited to 18 percent by statute; GAO estimated it would take until 2037 for 95 percent of current policies to reach full-risk premiums, leaving a $27 billion premium shortfall. Because the cap keeps premiums below the real risk for more than a decade, it should be removed. Any assistance for policyholders comes only through opt-in funding, not taxpayer subsidies. The no-subsidy rule is set out in Subsidies and Mandates.
U.S. Government Accountability Office – Flood Insurance: FEMA's New Rate-Setting Methodology Improves Actuarial Soundness but Highlights Need for Broader Program Reform (GAO-23-105977, July 31, 2023)
Congressional Research Service (Horn) – National Flood Insurance Program Borrowing Authority

I welcome awareness efforts. My contribution is the immediate ban on animal agriculture, which also removes a material share of human-caused emissions (~12% FAO livestock agrifood systems, 2015 baseline; critics note other FAO and inventory boundaries put the share higher or lower - livestock remains material either way). The U.S. should follow climate accords only when they match reasonable U.S. law and do not restrict Americans' freedom.

I can support international efforts to raise awareness of human-induced climate change. Animal agriculture should be banned and shut down immediately as a rights violation (Sanctuary Plan); ending it also cuts the livestock agrifood-system share of emissions (~12% of anthropogenic GHG in FAO's 2015 Pathways baseline), so the ban serves sentient-rights protections and the climate at once. Critics note that FAO livestock shares move with the system boundary and baseline year - an older FAO estimate put livestock nearer 14.5% of anthropogenic emissions, and other inventories attribute less once land-use change is allocated differently. Under any of those accountings livestock remains a material share; the Pathways 2015 baseline of about 12% is the figure I use, and the ban is driven by the rights violation first - the emissions cut is a concurrent benefit, not the ground. The United States should not be beholden to any accord that goes against the freedom of its people and nation. Accords that align with reasonable U.S. conservation and regulatory laws for the public safety of sentient beings can be followed. Policy that infringes on rights-respecting citizens should not be mandated.

head: "Does withdrawing from accords undermine global climate efforts?"
body: Accords consistent with reasonable U.S. conservation and safety law can be followed. What I reject is binding commitments that override the freedom of Americans.

Sovereignty applies to climate policy as to foreign policy. The Paris Agreement relies on nationally determined contributions, which shows that climate commitments can be set by each nation's own priorities.
UNFCCC – The Paris Agreement
Food and Agriculture Organization – Pathways towards lower emissions (2023)
Food and Agriculture Organization – New FAO report maps pathways towards lower livestock emissions (2023 newsroom)
Fossil fuels should stay where they work best while renewables grow through private innovation. I oppose forced phase-outs.

Fossil fuels should remain for now while greater effort goes into renewables. Fossil fuels may continue in industries that benefit most from them, while other industries move to renewables that suit them better. I don't support entire forced phase-outs; renewable technology ought to advance through incentivization and innovation by private companies.

head: "Does keeping fossil fuels slow the transition?"
body: Each industry uses the energy source that serves it best, and private innovation makes renewables competitive on their merits. Forced phase-outs impose costs before alternatives are ready.

Fossil fuels still supply most U.S. energy, so abrupt phase-outs would disrupt the economy. Technology learning and competition have lowered the cost of utility-scale solar by about 85% since 2010, and unsubsidized solar and wind now compete on cost, which supports a transition led by innovation rather than mandate.
U.S. Energy Information Administration – U.S. Energy Facts Explained
Lazard – Levelized Cost of Energy+ (June 2025)
PMC – Levelized cost-based learning analysis of utility-scale wind and solar in the United States

Any shift toward cleaner energy should be slow and market-driven, with no mandates and no early forced shutdowns. I'd encourage nuclear power mainly by cutting red tape, with any public money coming only from taxpayers who choose to chip in. Renewables are welcome but not required, and energy markets ought to stay competitive without taxpayer subsidies.

I accept a gradual, market-driven shift toward cleaner energy sources, with no mandates and no source forced to shut down early (Grid Reliability and Permitting). Nuclear power should be incentivized, first through deregulation such as streamlined licensing and permitting. Any public financial support for nuclear ought to be drawn only from taxpayers who opt in to fund it; no taxpayer should be compelled to subsidize nuclear or any other energy industry. Renewables may be encouraged but should not be mandated. Energy markets ought to remain competitive and consumer-oriented, without taxpayer subsidies (absent opt-in) or coercive industrial policy.

head: "Does incentivizing nuclear contradict opposition to subsidies?"
body: No. Nuclear is incentivized first by removing the regulatory and permitting obstacles that add to its cost and delay, and any public money comes only from taxpayers who opt in, consistent with Energy & Environment. Nuclear is singled out because of its safety record and reliability. Energy policy is set out further in Energy & Environment.

A reliable, affordable energy supply underpins economic growth, so transition should not disrupt it. Nuclear power produces large amounts of low-carbon electricity with one of the lowest death rates per unit of energy of any source. Construction cost is the largest barrier to new reactors, so streamlined licensing works alongside standardized designs and market competition rather than replacing them. Competitive markets drive innovation more efficiently than mandates.
U.S. Department of Energy – Advantages and Challenges of Nuclear Energy
Our World in Data – What are the safest and cleanest sources of energy?
U.S. Energy Information Administration – U.S. Energy Facts Explained
MIT Energy Initiative – The Future of Nuclear Energy in a Carbon-Constrained World (2018)
See also: Subsidies and Mandates · Graded: Wind turbine imports found a security threat (S12)
I believe nuclear power should expand because it is proven safe, with strict safety standards.
Nuclear power should be expanded because it has been proven safe. Safety remains crucial, as it is everywhere else.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Vogtle, 2024: Unit 4 entered commercial operation, making Vogtle's four units the largest nuclear power plant in the United States. U.S. Energy Information Administration (2024) – Plant Vogtle Unit 4 begins commercial operation

Fukushima: UNSCEAR reported that no adverse health effects among Fukushima residents have been documented that could be directly attributed to radiation from the accident. UN Information Service Vienna (2021) – A decade after the Fukushima accident: Radiation-linked increases in cancer rates not expected to be seen

head: "What about accidents like Chernobyl and Fukushima?"
body: Accidents show why safety standards are crucial, not why nuclear power should be abandoned. Measured by deaths per unit of energy, nuclear is among the safest sources available: about 0.03 deaths per terawatt-hour, counting Chernobyl and Fukushima, against 0.02 for solar, 0.04 for wind, 2.8 for gas, and 24.6 for coal.

Nuclear power has one of the lowest death rates per unit of energy produced of any source and emits very little carbon. Our World in Data puts it at about 0.03 deaths per terawatt-hour, close to solar (0.02) and wind (0.04) and far below gas (2.8), oil (18.4), and coal (24.6). It provides steady output that intermittent sources cannot, making it central to a gradual clean-energy transition.
Our World in Data – What are the safest and cleanest sources of energy?
Our World in Data – Death rates per unit of electricity production
U.S. Department of Energy – Advantages and Challenges of Nuclear Energy
Nuclear power should expand, spent fuel must be stored safely, recycling can develop, and I'd put storage sites in low-density areas.

Nuclear power should be expanded, and spent fuel managed under the same safety standards that make nuclear power safe. Storage and recycling technologies should be allowed to develop under deregulation, and storage sites ought to follow the development rule: low-density areas away from protected species.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.
Finland: Onkalo is designed to hold spent nuclear fuel deep in bedrock for 100,000 years. BBC Future (2023) – Finland's plan to bury spent nuclear fuel for 100,000 years

head: "Isn't waste the unsolved problem of nuclear power?"
body: Spent fuel has been stored safely for decades. Allowing recycling and permanent storage to develop removes regulatory obstacles rather than technical ones.

The Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982 makes the federal government responsible for permanent disposal of spent fuel (42 U.S.C. § 10131). About 97,061 metric tons of commercial spent fuel were in storage at the end of 2024, 46,864 tons in dry storage and 50,197 tons in pools, according to a U.S. Department of Energy inventory. Siting follows Conservation vs Development.
Cornell LII – 42 U.S.C. § 10131: Findings and purposes
U.S. Department of Energy via OSTI – Spent Nuclear Fuel and Reprocessing Waste Inventory
For me reliability comes first: no source should be forced off early, and permitting ought to be streamlined while environmental protections stay.

A reliable grid comes first. No source should be forced off the grid before replacements are ready, and permitting ought to be streamlined so that new generation and transmission can connect. Regulation should carry the burden of proof, and nuclear power in particular should be deregulated and expanded.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Texas, February 2021: Winter Storm Uri forced the largest manually controlled load shed in U.S. history and more than 4.5 million Texans lost power, some for four days. Freezing and fuel issues caused 75.6% of generator outages. FERC (2021) – Final Report on February 2021 Freeze Underscores Winterization Recommendations
Deaths: Texas health officials confirmed 246 storm-related deaths. Texas Department of State Health Services (2021) – February 2021 Winter Storm-Related Deaths – Texas

head: "Doesn't faster permitting harm the environment?"
body: Protections for sanctuary lands, protected species, and public health remain. Streamlining removes delay, not those standards.

head: "Don't AI data centers use too much power and water?"
body: They use a growing share. U.S. data centers used 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4% of the nation's electricity, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects 6.7% to 12% by 2028. The IEA expects U.S. data centers to use more electricity by 2030 than aluminium, steel, cement, chemicals and all other energy-intensive industries combined. Their direct water use was about 66 billion liters in 2023. Most of their water footprint, nearly 800 billion liters, comes from the power plants that supply them. The answer is supply, not bans: permitting ought to let new generation connect, and water is allocated as property within health standards (Water Resources and Rights).

Nearly 2,600 GW of generation and storage capacity was waiting in U.S. interconnection queues at the end of 2023, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation projects summer peak demand to rise by about 224 GW through 2035 and flags the MISO and PJM regions for seasonal shortfall risk. The no-phase-out rule is set out in Energy Mix.
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory – Queued Up: 2024 Edition
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory – 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report
IEA – Energy and AI: Executive summary (2025)
North American Electric Reliability Corporation – 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment
I support no energy subsidies of any kind, green or fossil, unless taxpayers opt in, and no mandates. The market should drive the energy mix.

Government subsidies for green technology, fossil fuels, refining or any other energy source mean taxpayer money, which I consider theft; the government should subsidize nothing unless taxpayers opt in. There should be no mandates. Goals can exist, and competition booms in the free market.

head: "Without subsidies, can clean technology compete?"
body: Free-market competition drives advancement, and taxpayers who want to support green technology can opt in. I reject using mandatory taxes to pick winners.

Compelled funding of private industries violates property rights and distorts markets. Competition rewards technologies that deliver value at the lowest cost, which is how energy innovation advances most reliably. The Energy Information Administration counted $183.3 billion (2022 dollars) in federal energy subsidies over FY 2016 to 2022, 46 percent of it for renewables, and 70 percent delivered through the tax code.
U.S. Energy Information Administration – Federal Financial Interventions and Subsidies in Energy in Fiscal Years 2016–2022
See also: Graded: Defense Production Act funds for refineries · America First Seafood Strategy

Pollution that harms people violates their rights. I'd limit it to what public-health standards allow, make polluters pay for the damage, and count greenhouse gases as pollution above the natural baseline, regulated as harm, without energy mandates or early forced shutdowns.

Pollution that harms others, or directly imposes a severe, non-consensual risk of serious harm on them, violates their negative rights. It should be regulated to a level that meets consumer and public-health standards, and polluters ought to be liable for the harm they cause to people and property. Greenhouse gases count as pollution to the extent that emissions exceed the natural baseline; the natural contribution is not attributed to anyone. Greenhouse-gas rules should be harm rules, not energy mandates: they ought to limit emissions in proportion to the harm shown, never prescribe a fuel, technology, or energy source, and set compliance periods long enough that no source is forced off early and reliable supply is not disrupted (Climate Change; Grid Reliability and Permitting). Each environmental rule should carry the burden of showing the harm it addresses.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

East Palestine, Ohio, 2023: the NTSB found the vent-and-burn of hazardous tank cars after the Norfolk Southern derailment was "unnecessary." NTSB (2024) – Failed Wheel Bearing Caused Norfolk Southern Train Derailment in East Palestine, Ohio

head: "Doesn't pollution regulation conflict with your skepticism of regulation?"
body: No. Preventing serious environmental harm is one of the four domains where business regulation is legitimate. The burden-of-proof rule still applies: a pollution rule should show the harm it prevents, and rules that cannot should be removed.

head: "How can anyone be liable for diffuse greenhouse-gas harm?"
body: Where harm cannot be traced to a specific emitter, emissions above the natural baseline are handled by the harm-based limits above rather than by individual lawsuits. Traceable harm to persons or property remains liable in court.

Axiom 6 treats the direct imposition of severe, non-consensual risk as crossing the forfeiture threshold, and property rights protect owners against physical invasion of their land and bodies. Air pollution is the clearest documented case. EPA's peer-reviewed second prospective study estimated that the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments would prevent over 230,000 early deaths in 2020, with central benefits exceeding costs by more than 30 to one. Climate has a natural baseline, and only the human-caused share above it is counted as pollution; the IPCC finds that share is essentially all recent warming. Rules with demonstrated effects meet the burden of proof in Domestic Policy & Governance.
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency – Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act 1990–2020, the Second Prospective Study
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency – Summary of the Clean Air Act
See also: Infrastructure and Regulation
Environmental rules should protect sanctuary lands and herbivore populations, and I want pollution regulated to keep people healthy.

Environmental regulations should exist on the specific grounds of conserving and maintaining sanctuary lands and herbivorous animal populations. Pollution and waste ought to be regulated to a level that meets consumer and public health standards.

head: "Why protect herbivores specifically rather than all wildlife?"
body: Herbivores can live without causing harm to other sentient beings, so the government ought to give their populations and habitats priority protection. This follows from the sentientist ethic set out in Ethical and Philosophical Framework.

head: "Should the law protect animals killed by habitat loss or accidents, not just hunting?"
body: Yes. An animal killed by the destruction of its habitat, or by a strike the actor could foresee, is as dead as one that was targeted. Whoever causes that death ought to answer for it, as polluters do (Pollution and Liability), graded by sentience class and by intent: deliberate killing is murder. Foreseeable, avoidable killing is a lesser, non-capital liability.

Regulation is justified where it protects sentient beings from harm. Pollution harms public health, which grounds rules like the Clean Air Act. Conservation regulation centers on the populations I value most. About 12.9% of U.S. land and inland waters is currently protected and managed mainly for biodiversity, the baseline sanctuary policy builds from.
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency – Summary of the Clean Air Act
Cornell LII – 16 U.S.C. § 1531: Endangered Species Act findings and purposes
U.S. Geological Survey – Analysis of Updated USGS Database Finds Increase in America's Lands and Waters Managed for Biodiversity
See also: Graded: Endangered species "harm" narrowed

I believe nature should be preserved where rights are not violated. Mining and extraction belong in quarries and lower-density places such as deserts, away from the habitat of protected species, and development ought to be built alongside nature instead of destroying it.

Nature should be preserved so long as sentient rights are not violated. Resource extraction should generally take place in quarries and lower-density areas such as deserts, sited away from the habitat of protected species such as the desert tortoise. Technology ought, for the most part, to be built in and alongside rights-respecting nature rather than demolishing it.

head: "Doesn't any development harm wildlife?"
body: Development should be directed toward low-sentient-density areas to minimize harm, and I prefer integration with nature over demolition. The aim is to minimize rights violations, not halt development.
The sentientist framework weighs harm to sentient beings, so where development occurs matters. Concentrating extraction in areas with few sentient animals limits the harm of growth.
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service – Western Solar Plan: desert tortoise update (2024)
See also: Border Barriers and Protected Habitat · Graded: Big Bend border wall
In my view water rights are property, pollution of water is a violation, and markets should allocate water within health standards.

I hold that water rights are property rights, to be held, traded, and protected like other property. Polluting another's water is a rights violation under the pollution rule, with liability for the harm. Water should be allocated through property and markets rather than political rationing.

head: "Won't markets leave people without water?"
body: Markets direct water to its most valued uses and reward conservation. Public health standards for drinking water remain.
Western states generally allocate water under prior appropriation, in which rights rest on beneficial use and seniority. Pollution liability is set out in Pollution and Liability.
Cornell LII – Prior appropriation doctrine

I would ban animal agriculture outright and shut it down immediately, with no wind-down. Every animal alive at the shutdown should be kept alive and given sanctuary for its natural life under the Sanctuary Plan, which also sets out what happens to the firms, the land and the workers. Federal grazing permits are revoked on day one, habitat rules protect sanctuary lands and herbivores, and lab-grown meat is the goal and the replacement. It may not meet demand at the same cost right away and scales up over time. The ban does not wait for it (Agriculture and Food Policy).
Animal agriculture should be banned outright and shut down immediately. Farming sentient animals for food is a rights violation, so the ban should not be phased in, and there should be no wind-down.

head: How this gets done: the Sanctuary Plan

body: There is no wind-down. The shutdown, the care and adoption of every animal alive at that moment, the conversion, divestment or liquidation of the firms, the land, the workers, enforcement, and the Sanctuary Levy that pays for it are all set out once, in the Sanctuary Plan.

Habitat protection centers on sanctuary lands and herbivore populations. No grazing permits should be issued on federal land, and existing permits should be revoked on day one. They should not be an honored commitment, and grazing should not displace protected herbivore habitat.

My view: Slaughterhouses and animal farming shouldn't exist in 2026, which follows my sentientist view. Animal agriculture should shut down immediately, with no transition. Lab-grown meat might not be able to replace the demand right away at the same cost, but it is the goal and the replacement, and it will scale up over time.

head: "Doesn't this hurt ranchers?"
body: Yes, ranching should end. A ranch that earns most of its revenue from animals should convert fully to plant-based farming or cultivated-meat research, or be liquidated, and its owners should receive no compensation. What is left after creditors should go to the sanctuaries. Keeping every animal alive comes first. There is no retraining or job-placement program: ranchers and farm workers find new jobs or can apply for sanctuary jobs under the worker rules in the Sanctuary Plan. Public sanctuary land serves the herbivore populations it protects.

head: "Animal agriculture is a huge industry. Won't ending it do serious economic damage?"
body: The industry is large. U.S. cash receipts from animals and animal products were a record of about $303.7 billion in 2025 and are forecast at $287.3 billion in 2026, more than half of all $540.3 billion in farm cash receipts, and the losses to producers, workers, and farm communities would be real. But economic value does not decide whether a practice violates rights. Britain did not weigh slavery's profitability against its wrong when it abolished slavery in 1833. It ended it, and the £20 million it raised, about 40% of government spending that year, went to compensating enslaved people's owners rather than to keeping the system. I draw the same line, with one difference: the industry gets no compensation, and what is left after creditors goes to the animals, in the sanctuaries. The precedent for that difference is American: Section 4 of the Fourteenth Amendment held every claim "for the loss or emancipation of any slave" "illegal and void" (Fifth Amendment question). Regulatory barriers to lab-grown meat and plant-based food are cleared so replacements scale up as animal products leave the market (Bioethics, Progress, & Technology). The full costs and funding are in Sanctuary Plan.

head: "How big is the shock, and how long does it last?"
body: Large, but bounded, and I don't hide either part. About 558,000 people worked in animal slaughtering and processing in September 2026, and farms and aquaculture operations raising animals averaged about 271,000 payroll jobs in 2025, before counting owners and family who work their own farms. That is about 830,000 payroll jobs against roughly 160 million on U.S. nonfarm payrolls, but the loss is concentrated: USDA counts 354 farming-dependent counties, 329 of them rural, and just over half are in the Great Plains, where cattle, corn, soybeans, and wheat make up much of what is produced. What the plan already does. Workers' unpaid wages and benefits are paid first from every liquidation. A farm family keeps its house and house lot. Landowners outside the industry are paid fair value for land the sanctuaries need. Former workers may apply for sanctuary care jobs under the worker rules, except anyone who killed animals for a living. There is no retraining program, and owners and shareholders get nothing (Sanctuary Plan). Land. Grassland pasture and range covered about 659 million acres in 2017, 29% of U.S. land. Federal grazing permits end on day one, and that land is managed as herbivore habitat. Sanctuary land, 46 to 183 million acres across my cost cases, stays with the animals and becomes protected habitat once they no longer need it. Land a receiver sells, and pasture owned outside the industry, goes to any lawful use, including crops where the soil allows. Food. The shortfall is in particular foods, not in calories, because the grain and soy now fed to animals are freed for people. Scarcity and higher prices for some foods should last only while supply chains, plants, and diets reorganize and replacements scale up. Nutrition is covered: the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics holds that planned plant-based diets are adequate at every stage of life, and food-safety rules ought to require B12 fortification of staple plant foods (Agriculture and Food Policy). If this were a farming operation on the same scale with humans instead of animals, there would be no debate over shutting it down on day one. There would be no critique and no debate. It would close immediately. No one would ever ask, "What about the jobs?" or "What about the impact on the economy?" This is a human rights issue, the same as it should be a sentient rights issue. It closes immediately, without cost deciding whether it closes and with no wind-down. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics – Animal slaughtering and processing employment, series CEU3231160001 U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics – Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, NAICS 112, 2025 annual average USDA ERS – County Typology Codes, 2025: Descriptions and Maps University of Missouri RaFF – Consistency and Change in Demographic Patterns in Farming-Dependent Counties (2025) USDA ERS – Major Uses of Land in the United States, 2017

head: "Dairy, eggs, wool, and honey don't kill the animal. Are they banned too?"
body: Yes, as commercial animal agriculture. Every one of them depends on breeding animals for use, which ends on day one, and commercial dairy and egg production kill the animals they can't use, such as male calves and male chicks, and send spent animals to slaughter. Once the food ban takes full effect, selling or possessing dairy, eggs, or honey should be banned as well, and sanctuary operators and adopters may not sell or use animal products (Sanctuary Plan). Companion animals, including horses kept where their rights are respected, remain under Hunting, Fishing, Pets, and Zoos.

head: "Prohibition failed. Won't a meat ban just create a black market?"
body: Some of it, yes. Alcohol Prohibition did not end drinking: Miron and Zwiebel estimate consumption fell to about 30% of its earlier level at first, then recovered to 60–70%. A meat ban will have smugglers and backyard slaughter too. Two differences matter. Prohibition banned an act between consenting adults, while every black-market slaughter kills a victim, which is why it is prosecuted as murder, graded by sentience, rather than as a vice offense. And raising an animal for slaughter takes space, feed, and time, so it is far easier to detect than a still. Even on Prohibition's own numbers, a ban cut consumption by a third or more, and each animal not killed is a life not taken. Miron & Zwiebel, NBER – Alcohol Consumption During Prohibition (1991)

Killing sentient animals for food violates negative rights, so animal agriculture should be banned on the same sentientist ground as other deliberate killings outside self-defense (Animal Rights and Sentientism). The 2025 federal grazing fee is $1.35 per animal unit month (AUM) on about 18,000 Bureau of Land Management permits, while private grazing leases the same year ran from about $11 to $47.50 per AUM. About 12.9% of U.S. land and inland waters is protected and managed mainly for biodiversity, as cited in Regulation and Conservation. Congress can reach even home-raised animals under the Commerce Clause, as Gonzales v. Raich (2005) held for home-grown marijuana, and protecting negative rights is the government's first duty.

I support a day-one shutdown of animal agriculture, wild-capture commercial fishing, aquaculture, commercial breeding mills, and animal testing - no wind-down. Every animal alive that day should be kept alive in sanctuary (then licensed nonprofit care) or adopted under strict vetting, with no breeding. Industry equity converts or is liquidated without shareholder compensation; workers' unpaid wages are paid first, and the proceeds fund care. Sanctuary bonds plus a flat Sanctuary Levy (never above 3%, income above $75,000 single / $150,000 joint) fund the run-down. The levy ends on the published population + repayment trigger. No compensation is owed because those firms forfeited their property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights (Sanctuary forfeiture). Ops detail: Adoption · Handover · How many · Costs · Levy. On my middle case, care costs about $349 billion in the first year and $50 billion by year ten, as the animals die naturally, and the levy runs at 1.71% from 2027 to 2040; a single filer earning $150,000 pays about $1,200 a year (Costs, Levy).

My plan is an immediate shutdown with no wind-down. On day one, all animal agriculture, wild-capture commercial fishing, aquaculture (including farmed crustaceans and, for consistency, farmed mollusks), commercial breeding mills and animal testing should stop. Nobody should breed, slaughter, catch or test on another sentient animal after that day. Experimentation on offenders who have forfeited their rights should continue under Animal Rights and Sentience Technology; it is not animal testing.

Keeping every animal alive comes first. No animal alive at the shutdown should be killed. Because no new animals are born, the sanctuary population and cost fall every year. Inland fish and crustacean farms should convert on site. Ocean farms should stay under the same keep-alive rule even where counts and costs are incomplete. Farmed mollusks, such as oysters, clams, mussels and abalone, should end with the rest of aquaculture for consistency, not because I claim they are sentient; I believe bivalves likely are not. The 2023 Census of Aquaculture counted 1,140 U.S. farms selling mollusks, with $575.5 million in sales, including 900 oyster farms, 373 clam farms and 30 mussel farms. My estimate of a year's throughput, not a headcount: those farms sold about 1.58 billion food-size mollusks, mostly oysters (about 553 million), hard clams (about 553 million), Manila clams (about 247 million) and mussels (about 201 million). Stock already in the water should be left unharvested and gear should be decommissioned. Numbers, gaps, and accepted risks: How many animals.

How care, adoption, state-to-nonprofit handover, firm conversion and liquidation, land, foreign firms, workers, enforcement, food-possession marks, funding, and the levy work is set out once in the subsections below — not repeated here. Shareholders and owners of animal-agriculture equity should get no compensation. Workers' unpaid wages should be paid first; a family on a liquidated farm should keep its house and house lot.

Forfeiture: The Sanctuary Levy, compelled conversion and liquidation, and taking industry property with no compensation to shareholders follow from forfeiture: animal-industry firms forfeited ordinary property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights, as set out in Sanctuary forfeiture. The levy is time-limited and ends on the published condition. I do not treat this as a standing power to seize unrelated property.
Day-one shutdown is the position. The middle and high cost cases are incomplete until the gaps below are filled. They are risks I accept, not reasons to phase the ban.

Farmed crustaceans. No reliable point-in-time headcount. The 2023 Census of Aquaculture counted 848 U.S. farms selling crustaceans, with $175.7 million in sales, but it counts farms and sales, not animals. My estimate of a year's throughput, not a headcount: those farms sold about 1.81 billion food-size crawfish (93.6 million pounds, about 19 to the pound) and about 67 million food-size saltwater shrimp (2.8 million pounds), roughly 1.9 billion crustaceans a year. Sanctuary care cost is unestimated; cost cases leave them out (Needs research: inventory + care cost).

Ocean fish / crustacean farms. No reliable U.S. site count. Commercial finfish net pens in state waters operate only in Maine and Hawaii; Washington emptied its last ones in 2023 and has banned them on state-owned aquatic lands. Sanctuary staffing and logistics for any ocean farms are a huge undertaking with no timed plan yet (Needs research: site inventory + staffing model).

Medical supply. Heparin from pig intestines and egg-based flu vaccine (~72% of 2025–26 U.S. supply) end with the ban. Egg-free flu vaccines and non-animal anticoagulants exist. My estimate of the flu gap: of about 154 million doses projected for 2025–26, about 111 million were egg-based and about 43 million cell-based or recombinant, so egg-free output would have to rise about 3.6-fold. The largest cell-based plant, CSL Seqirus in Holly Springs, North Carolina, is rated for 150 million pandemic doses within six months of a declaration, but those are single-strain pandemic doses, not three-strain seasonal ones, so they do not set a seasonal timeline. U.S. heparin is still sourced only from pig intestines; bioengineered heparin has reached pilot scale and is not yet approved. There is no published replacement timeline here — only the duty to clear every barrier starting day one (Needs research: timed scale-up path). Owning day-one means stating these gaps in the open. It does not mean a gradual agriculture wind-down.

head: "Doesn't the Fifth Amendment require just compensation when the government takes property?"
body: Not when the law bans a harmful use. In Mugler v. Kansas (1887) the Supreme Court upheld Kansas's prohibition of alcohol without compensation to a brewer whose plant lost most of its value, holding that banning a use injurious to the public is not a taking. Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992) still requires compensation for a total wipeout unless background principles of law already forbade the use. The law ought to declare, as part of the ban, that killing sentient animals for food is such a forbidden use. Courts may still order compensation for the land and buildings that pass to the sanctuaries without payment. The fair-value purchases from owners outside the industry already reduce that risk. The country has ended property in sentient beings without compensation before: Section 4 of the Fourteenth Amendment bars any government from paying "any claim for the loss or emancipation of any slave" and declares all such claims "illegal and void." Either way, the uncompensated transfers of industry assets rest on forfeiture, because those firms forfeited their property protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights, and the levy is a time-limited tax (Sanctuary forfeiture). Neither falls under ordinary eminent-domain practice. Cornell LII – Mugler v. Kansas, 123 U.S. 623 (1887) Cornell LII – Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council, 505 U.S. 1003 (1992) Cornell LII – U.S. Constitution, Fourteenth Amendment, Section 4

head: "A corporation is not a moral agent, and farming was legal before the ban. How can a firm forfeit anything?"
body: Two different things are going on, and neither is a punishment. First, no one is punished for what was legal before the ban; the ex post facto rule covers every farmer and shareholder (Ex post facto). Second, a company's assets answer for what was done with them, as they answer for its debts and torts (Corporations as Moral Entities). Shareholders lose the value of shares in a business whose use is banned, and their other property is untouched; a farm family keeps its house. That is the loss Mugler upheld for a brewery built in 1877, before Kansas adopted prohibition, worth $10,000 for brewing and no more than $2,500 after: "A prohibition simply upon the use of property for purposes that are declared, by valid legislation, to be injurious to the health, morals, or safety of the community, cannot, in any just sense, be deemed a taking or an appropriation of property for the public benefit." What forfeiture adds is why the owners have no claim on what remains: the assets were the instruments of the violation, so the proceeds go to the animals (Sanctuary forfeiture).

head: "Won't the import bans break WTO rules?"
body: The WTO allows measures "necessary to protect public morals" under GATT Article XX(a). In EC–Seal Products (2014) the Appellate Body upheld the EU's ban on seal products on animal-welfare moral grounds while faulting how its exceptions were applied. A ban with no exceptions, applied the same to domestic and foreign products, as this one is, removes the flaw the EU's had. If a panel still ruled against it, the ban stands. The United States follows its own law (Global Institutions). World Trade Organization – DS400: European Communities — Measures Prohibiting the Importation and Marketing of Seal Products

head: "Heparin and most flu vaccines come from animals. Do they end too?"
body: Yes. Heparin sold in the U.S. is made from pig intestines, and about 72% of the 2025–26 U.S. flu vaccine supply was made in chicken eggs. An innocent animal may not be harmed for another's benefit, however large the benefit (Conflicts Between Rights-Holders), so these supplies end with the rest of animal agriculture and the import ban. The cost is real: heparin is a standard blood thinner for surgery and heart attacks. Egg-free flu vaccines already exist: CDC says the remaining share of the 2025–26 supply after that 72% is cell-based or recombinant. Non-animal anticoagulants also exist already. Fondaparinux (Arixtra), a synthetic Factor Xa inhibitor first approved in 2001, is on the U.S. market for some surgical and thromboembolism uses, but it is not a published substitute for every use of heparin from pig intestines. The government ought to clear every barrier to scaling these replacements, starting on day one. There is still no published timeline for replacing the egg-based majority of flu vaccine or for a full-scale non-animal heparin supply. That is an accepted risk with a Needs-research placeholder for a timed replacement path — not a claim that the middle Sanctuary cost case already covers medical supply, and not a reason to delay the ban. head: "Is there a timeline, or only a day one?"
body: There is an order, and only the first step is a date. I believe the sequence should be written into the law, so no step in it can become a wind-down: Day one. Animal agriculture, wild-capture commercial fishing, aquaculture, commercial breeding mills, and animal testing stop. Breeding stops, so the number of animals can only fall. Federal grazing permits and fishing and aquaculture licenses and quotas are revoked. Every animal alive that day is kept in state-run emergency sanctuary or adopted under strict vetting, and food from any animal killed after that day is banned (Enforcement). First month. Animal-derived food made before the shutdown may still be sold and held. After one month, selling or possessing any food from a killed or farmed animal is banned. First three years. Firms convert, divest, or are liquidated, and the proceeds arrive over these years (Liquidation, conversion and land). Bonds carry the early peak in care costs. I expect most sanctuary sites to pass from the state to licensed nonprofit operators within one to three years (Handover). Until the last animal dies. The Sanctuary Levy pays for care, with unannounced welfare checks for each animal's life, and it ends on its published population and repayment trigger. Land the animals no longer need becomes protected habitat. What is not yet timed is the build-out behind day one: the staff, feed, and sites for the emergency phase (Needs research: emergency-phase staffing and logistics). The shutdown does not wait on it.

head: "Aren't the unintended consequences of an immediate ban and a predation program too risky?"
body: I believe the burden of proof falls on the status quo, not on ending it. Today's system is not a safe baseline. It is the largest ongoing rights violation on earth. In 2024 about 78.5 billion chickens and 1.49 billion pigs were slaughtered worldwide. Farmed fish killed for food numbered an estimated 78–171 billion in 2019, and wild fish caught an estimated 1.1–2.2 trillion a year on average over 2000–2019. Each year of delay is another year of that toll, and with fish counted it runs into the trillions. Nature is not the gentle alternative either. Wild birds alone number about 50 billion. Because most species reproduce by having many offspring, the overwhelming majority of wild animals die shortly after they come into existence, mostly by starving or being eaten alive (Horta; Ng). Across billions of animals, that is the normal course of life in the wild, and today no one is obliged to stop it. I would not accept a human atrocity on this scale continuing until every consequence of ending it had been modeled, and I don't accept it here. When the harm of acting is uncertain and the harm of not acting is certain and immense, uncertainty is a reason to act carefully, not a reason to wait. Acting carefully is built in: Numbers only fall. Breeding stops on day one, and every animal alive that day is kept alive (Sanctuary Plan). Predation is staged. Herbivore fertility control comes first, predator removal starts in pilot areas, and herbivore condition, disease, scavengers, and vegetation are monitored and reported every year (Hunting, Fishing, Pets, and Zoos). The stop rule. No step may cause more suffering or more rights violations than it prevents. A step that breaks it is halted, and reversed where it can be (Wild-Animal Predation). What I reject is the reverse burden: that those ending the killing must prove a perfect outcome in advance, while the killing itself needs no defense. Our World in Data (FAO data) – Animals slaughtered for meat Mood et al., Animal Welfare – Estimating global numbers of farmed fishes killed for food annually from 1990 to 2019 (2023) Mood et al., Animal Welfare – Estimating global numbers of fishes caught from the wild annually from 2000 to 2019 (2024) Callaghan, Nakagawa & Cornwell, PNAS – Global abundance estimates for 9,700 bird species (2021) Oscar Horta, Télos – Debunking the idyllic view of natural processes: population dynamics and suffering in the wild (2010) Yew-Kwang Ng, Biology and Philosophy – Towards welfare biology: evolutionary economics of animal consciousness and suffering (1995)

There should be no retraining or job-placement program. Workers should find new jobs, or apply for sanctuary jobs under strict rules. I would be very worried about people who killed animals for a living moving straight into caring for them, so:

Anyone who killed animals for a living should be barred from hands-on animal care at any sanctuary and from adopting. That covers slaughter and kill-floor workers, commercial fishing crews, fish-farm harvest staff, and lab staff who killed test animals.

Other former animal-agriculture workers may take care roles only after vetting at least as strict as an adopter's: a background check, a check of the animal-cruelty and animal-harm records, interviews and references, and a supervised probation period. Their work should then be checked by unannounced welfare inspections of the animals in their care, and any violation should mean removal.
Workers who never handled animals, such as drivers, office staff and maintenance workers, may take sanctuary jobs that involve no animal care.

Inspections, the import bans on animal products and seafood, and the sentience-graded penalties in Criminal Justice & Security should apply to anyone who keeps operating after the shutdown. No one should be prosecuted for farming, fishing, slaughter or testing before the shutdown; criminal penalties reach only acts after it (Animal Rights and Sentientism). A buyer who knowingly commissions or pays for the killing of an animal after the shutdown is an accessory to that killing, graded by the animal's sentience like the killer. Food from an animal killed after the shutdown should be banned from day one. Other animal-derived food made before the shutdown, including meat, fish, dairy, eggs, and honey, may still be sold and held for one month after the shutdown begins. From then on, selling or possessing any food from a killed animal or from a farmed animal should be banned, whenever it was made; that covers dairy, eggs, and honey, not only meat and fish. Each sale, possession, or eating of banned food should be one mark, and the product forfeited. Sanctuary hens' eggs stay with the hens, and nothing from a sanctuary is sold. The mark does not replace the accessory rule: a buyer who paid for a killing after the shutdown answers for that killing as well. What enforcement will cost in inspectors, customs checks, and prosecutions has no estimate yet (Needs research: inspection and customs staffing and cost).

Farm animals could be adopted by people who would kill them for meat at home, so every adoption should be vetted first. Breeding-mill dogs, cats and other companion animals should go through the same steps. Each step should be passed before an animal leaves a sanctuary:

Background check. Every adult in the household would be checked against the national records of animal-harm marks, convictions and earlier adoption violations. Any animal-harm mark or conviction would disqualify the household, and so would any adult barred from animal care under Workers.

Home and facility inspection. An inspector would check the space, shelter, fencing, heating, water and access to a veterinarian against the needs of that species, before approval. The inspection would set how many animals the home may take.

Signed no-slaughter commitment. The adopter would sign a commitment never to kill, sell, breed or use the animal for food or products. Euthanasia should be allowed only under the veterinary rule above.

Sterilization before release. Every adopted animal would be sterilized before it leaves the sanctuary. An animal for which sterilization is medically unsafe would be placed only in a home that keeps it apart from animals it could breed with, and the inspection would check for that.

ID and registry. Every adopted animal should carry a permanent ID and be entered in a national sanctuary registry, which would record its guardian and where it lives. A move or a transfer to another guardian should go through the registry and the same vetting. A death should be reported to the registry with a veterinarian's certificate.
Unannounced welfare checks. Inspectors would visit without notice, first within the opening months and then at least once a year for the animal's life.

Return rule. A guardian would be able to return an animal to a state sanctuary at any time, with no penalty. An animal would be removed and returned if a welfare check fails, the commitment is broken, or the guardian can no longer care for it.

No sale, no stipend. Adoption should never be a purchase. No price should be paid for an adopted animal, no adopted animal should be sold, and the adopter should pay for its feed, housing and veterinary care.

This rule is for sanctuary adoption after the shutdown, when the animal is already safe. It is not a bar on paying to get an animal out of slaughter while the industry still operates (Rescue Purchases).

Killing an adopted animal would be treated under the existing murder rules in Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty and the cruelty rules in Animal Cruelty Law, graded by the animal's sentience like any other killing of a sentient animal. An unreported death would be investigated as a possible killing.

I am skeptical of state-run sanctuaries. The state should run them at first only because a rights violation this atrocious, egregious and monumental was happening nationwide, so every sanctuary starts as a place of emergency. Once the emergency phase is over, the sanctuaries would pass to private nonprofit operators while the animals are still alive. How much government stays involved would follow one test: whatever is in the best interest of the victims, the animals.

Emergency phase. The state should run every sanctuary itself at first. The emergency phase should end site by site: each site should pass to a licensed operator once that operator passes accreditation, and the state should keep running any site that has none. I expect most sites to transfer within one to three years.

Sanctuary license. Only nonprofits should be allowed to hold a sanctuary license. The license should set the care standards, sterilization, the adoption vetting above and unannounced inspections. A licensed operator should not be allowed to sell animals or animal products and should not breed any animal, and it should hire care staff only under the rules in Workers.

Site-by-site handover. Each site would pass to a licensed operator by contract. The state should pay the operator a fixed amount per animal per year from the Sanctuary Levy. The payment should stay steady and should not be cut as donations come in, because a shortfall in donations would fall on the animals. Operators may take donations on top. An operator that fails should lose the site, back to the state or to another licensed operator.

Two layers of oversight. An independent accreditation body should accredit every operator, as the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries does for sanctuaries today, and state inspectors should check every site as well. When animals are at risk, the state should step in.

Land. Operators should get the right to use the land, never ownership, for as long as any animals remain on it. Sanctuary land should not be sold. Once the animals no longer need it, it should become protected habitat, and conservation trusts may hold it.

The end. When the levy ends, the Sanctuary Endowment should pay the remaining operators until the last animal dies. After that, the sanctuaries should become ordinary private charities under ordinary animal-welfare law. An operator that carries on as a private charity once its land becomes habitat needs land of its own. If the endowment ever runs short, the general-revenue backstop in The Sanctuary Levy still applies.

Contracting out work that private organizations can do is my general rule for government (Public-Sector Size and Civil Service). The per-animal payment is payment to a contractor for a service, the care the state would otherwise provide itself, not a subsidy. It is the same money the state would spend caring for each animal, so the handover does not change the levy.

On a typical day the United States holds about 86.2 million cattle, 74.3 million hogs, 384.3 million laying hens, about 1.74 billion meat chickens, 97.3 million turkeys, 5.0 million sheep and 2.5 million goats. It also holds 775,297 research animals covered by the Animal Welfare Act, and by one estimate more than 100 million lab mice and rats a year. Each year about 9.69 billion chickens and 189 million turkeys are slaughtered. Farmed crustaceans have no point-in-time count. The USDA's 2023 Census of Aquaculture counts those sold in a year: about 1.81 billion crawfish from 750 farms, nearly all in Louisiana, and 67.1 million saltwater shrimp from 36 farms, with far smaller numbers of softshell crabs and freshwater prawns. How many are alive on those farms on any given day is not reported, and I found no reliable figure for what their sanctuary care would cost, so I do not estimate it, and the cost cases below leave them out.

Laying hens (all layers) · 384.3 million · 1 Sep 2026
Pullets for laying-flock replacement · 144.0 million · 31 Dec 2022

The crawfish and shrimp rows count animals sold per year, not animals alive on a given day like the cattle and hens rows.

Worldwide in 2024 there were about 1.58 billion cattle, 962 million pigs, 1.36 billion sheep, 1.19 billion goats and 29.6 billion poultry. That year about 78.5 billion chickens and 1.49 billion pigs were slaughtered. Farmed fish killed for food number an estimated 78–171 billion a year, midpoint 124 billion (2019).

Most of these animals are young, because the industry kills them young. Natural lifespans run to about 15–20 years for cows, 10–12 for pigs and sheep, 6–8 for ducks and up to 8 for chickens. Meat chickens and turkeys are bred to grow so fast that their bodies give out early, so most would live only a short time even in sanctuary.

I estimate the cost in three cases. Each case adds up feed at 2026 USDA prices, veterinary care, medication, bedding and heat, caretaker wages at the BLS rate for farm animal workers, and one-time costs for sterilization and for converting housing. Each animal is kept until its natural death. Adopted animals would lower these costs, and I do not count them.
Low · $155 billion · $67 billion · $5 billion · $665 billion
Middle · $349 billion · $143 billion · $50 billion · $1.58 trillion
High · $1.09 trillion · $341 billion · $162 billion · $4.51 trillion
In every case, cattle account for about three-quarters of the cost, because they are numerous, large and long-lived.

A liquidated firm should be sold off by a court-appointed receiver. The money should be paid out in this order: the receiver's costs, workers' unpaid wages and benefits, secured lenders against their collateral, taxes, and other creditors. Whatever is left, which would have gone to shareholders, should go to the sanctuaries instead. A firm that converts should keep the assets it uses in its new business and should sell the assets that only served animals, and that money should also go to the sanctuaries after the lenders secured on those assets are paid. The animals themselves should not be part of any estate; they should go to sanctuary, and neither should a farm family's house and house lot. Lenders should get no special protection: a loan the sale cannot cover is a loss, as in any failed business. A lender that earns most of its revenue from animal-agriculture loans should itself be a covered firm, and every other lender should divest the line by making no new loans to it.

The value left after creditors comes mostly from ranch and farm land, not from the meatpackers. Once the ban is in force, slaughter plants, poultry houses and brands built on animal products are worth little, and most large processors would owe more than their assets bring. Pasture also loses value without grazing. I assume forced sales bring about 40–60% of today's value for pasture, 70–85% for cropland, 5–15% for animal buildings and 30–45% for machinery.
Low · $290 billion · 46 million acres · 19 million acres, $37 billion
Middle · $196 billion · 92 million acres · 37 million acres, $73 billion
High · $97 billion · 183 million acres · 73 million acres, $147 billion

The land figures assume 0.5–2 acres per cow, with hay brought in, and smaller yards for pigs, sheep and goats. Poultry would stay in the existing houses. I assume about 40% of that land is held by owners outside the industry and would be bought at the 2026 USDA average pasture value of $2,000 an acre. The rest would come from firms that convert or are liquidated, with no payment. The proceeds would arrive over the first three years. The land would never be sold back. Once the animals no longer need it, it would become protected habitat, so the plan counts no income from land sales.

The Sanctuary Levy is a single flat rate on income above its own line: $75,000 for single filers and heads of household, $150,000 for married couples filing jointly. It phases in over the next $10,000 ($20,000 joint), as the flat tax does, so there is no cliff. Grandfathered Social Security benefits are not counted. Anyone at or below the line pays nothing. On IRS data for 2023 grown to 2026, that base is about $6.49 trillion a year.

Liquidation proceeds and sanctuary bonds would cover the early years, so there would be no tax spike. The levy would be held level for its whole run, which would keep the rate as low as possible. It would be recalculated every year and may only be lowered. It would never be above 3%. Once the bonds are repaid, it would fall to the rate that covers that year's care alone. It would be legally dedicated to sanctuary care, bond repayment and the closing endowment, and to nothing else.
Low · 0.66% · 2027–2036 · $75 billion · $8.4 billion
Middle · 1.71% · 2027–2040 · $435 billion · $12.5 billion
High · 3% (the cap) · 2027–2055 · $2.48 trillion · none needed

On the middle case, a single filer earning $150,000 pays about $1,200 a year, and a married couple earning $200,000 pays about $680. Single filers at or below $75,000 and couples at or below $150,000 pay nothing.

When it ends. The end date is not fixed. The levy should end when the national sanctuary population falls below 1% of its starting animal units and the sanctuary bonds are repaid. The population is counted in animal units rather than heads, using the head counts that define a large animal feeding operation under EPA rules: 1,000 cattle, 2,500 pigs, 10,000 sheep, 55,000 turkeys, 82,000 laying hens and 125,000 meat chickens each count as 1,000 units. So a cow counts as 1, a pig 0.4, a sheep or goat 0.1, a turkey about 0.018, a laying hen about 0.012 and a meat chicken 0.008. Counting this way means a few million short-lived birds cannot keep the levy alive, and the threshold tracks what the animals actually cost to keep. The sanctuaries start with about 139 million animal units, so the threshold is about 1.4 million. On my middle case it is crossed around year 14, when the animals still alive cost about $2.5 billion a year.

The 3% cap. On the low and middle cases the cap never binds. On the high case, repaying the bonds by the 2044 threshold would need about 4.3%, so the levy stays at 3% past the threshold until the bonds are repaid, about 11 more years. The cap holds; the term stretches.

The last animals. In its final year the levy would fund a Sanctuary Endowment equal to five years of care at the threshold level. The endowment would be held in Treasury securities and would pay for the last animals until the final one dies. Anything left over would then go to the debt. If it ever runs short, the remaining care would come from general revenue, as an ordinary cost of the sanctuaries. When the levy outlasts the animals, as on the high case, it would pay their care directly and no endowment would be needed.
The bonds. On all three cases the bonds would be repaid in full by the levy. Sanctuary bonds would sit outside the debt brake's path while they are repaid on schedule (Fiscal Policy).

body: Under the convert, divest or liquidate rule, a firm such as a grain trader with a meat division would divest only that line. A foreign-owned firm's US operations would be liquidated, and the firm would then be barred from operating in the United States or doing business with U.S.-held companies. head: "Why not let the industry wind down over ten years?"
body: Because every year of wind-down means more animals bred and killed. With an immediate shutdown, no new animals are born. The cost falls every year as the animals alive today live out their lives.
sub: What converts and what is liquidated

head: "Doesn't taxing people and taking companies without compensation violate property rights?"
body: The levy is a time-limited tax to fund sanctuary care, and I accept that cost. Taking industry assets without compensation does not break the property-rights part of my negative-rights view: animal-industry firms forfeited those protections by using their assets to violate animals' rights. That forfeiture is stated in Property Rights and Civil Asset Forfeiture. The general rule still stands for everything else. Shareholders of firms built on a rights violation would get no compensation. What their firms are worth after creditors would go to the animals those firms held. No compensation is also the choice that spares people who did nothing wrong. Paying owners would mean charging taxpayers, most of whom never ran or profited from the industry, or shrinking what goes to the animals, which moves the cost of the wrong off the people who profited and onto people who did not; that is the trade Britain made in 1833 (Agriculture, Grazing, and Habitat). The people hurt by the change through no choice of their own come first instead: workers' unpaid wages and benefits are paid before any lender, and a farm family keeps its house (Liquidation, conversion and land). Shareholders, including savers who hold these firms through funds, lose that value, as any investor in a business built on violating rights should expect.
sub: What converts and what is liquidated

head: "Why are landowners outside the industry paid?"
body: A landlord who rented pasture to a feedlot, or a crop farm that kept a few cattle, did not run the industry and is not a covered firm. The sanctuaries would buy what they need from them at fair value for a practical reason, to reduce backlash, legal challenges and delay so the land is secured quickly, not because the payment is owed.

head: "What stops someone adopting an animal and killing it?"
body: The vetting above: a background check, a home inspection, a signed no-slaughter commitment, sterilization, a registry ID, and unannounced welfare checks for the animal's whole life. No one should be able to buy an animal. Killing one is murder or cruelty under the rules I set out.

head: "What happens to the workers?"
body: There should be no retraining or job-placement program. Workers should find new jobs, or apply for sanctuary jobs under the rules in Workers. Anyone who killed animals for a living should be barred from animal care, and other former animal-agriculture workers should be hired for care only after strict vetting.

head: "Does this end experimentation on offenders?"
body: No. "End all testing" means all animal testing. Experimentation on offenders who have forfeited their rights should continue under Animal Rights and Sentience Technology.

body: Breeding should stop on day one, so the number of animals can only fall. The cost is highest in the first year and shrinks as animals die of natural causes. In the middle case the cost per animal is about $1,800 a year for a cow, $920 for a pig and $30–35 for a chicken. The industry's own remaining value pays first, through liquidation and conversion proceeds. Bonds absorb the early peak, so the levy stays level at about 1.71% of income above the levy line on my middle case, and the 3% cap holds even on the high case. Setting the levy line at $75,000 single and $150,000 joint keeps the cost off low- and middle-income households. Ending the levy at a population threshold, with an endowment for the tail, keeps people from paying a broad tax for a few remaining animals. The middle case leaves farmed crustaceans, ocean-farm sanctuary costs, and medical-supply replacement out; those are accepted risks above, not hidden in the levy math.

I want no farm subsidies without opt-in funding, and food safety held to health standards. Lab-grown meat is the goal and the replacement for animal agriculture: it may not meet demand at the same cost right away, it scales up over time, and regulation should not block it.

Farming should receive no taxpayer subsidies without opt-in funding, consistent with the rule for every industry: no taxpayer money goes to farm, grazing, fishing or fish-farming businesses except through taxpayer opt-in, like any subsidy. Food safety should be regulated to consumer and public health standards, and food-safety rules ought to require vitamin B12 fortification of staple plant foods. Lab-grown meat is the goal and the replacement for animal agriculture, which should shut down immediately (Sanctuary Plan). It may not meet demand at the same cost right away; it scales up over time, and regulation does not block it from competing.

head: "Won't farmers fail without subsidies?"
body: Farms compete like other businesses. Opt-in funding remains available for those who choose to support agriculture, and consumers are protected by safety standards rather than by subsidies.

head: "What if lab-grown meat cannot meet demand when the ban starts?"
body: At first it may not. Cultivated meat has not yet been made at industrial scale at the price of conventional meat, and investment in it fell in 2024 (Good Food Institute – 2024 State of the Industry: Cultivated meat, seafood, and ingredients). The FDA itself says manufacturers are generally still "working on scaling up their processes to consistently produce amounts large enough to be competitively priced," and it completed the first U.S. pre-market consultation only in November 2022. The ban does not wait for it, because it rests on the animals' rights, not on a substitute being ready (Agriculture, Grazing, and Habitat). Plant-based food is already sold at scale, the regulatory barriers to both are cleared, and lab-grown supply scales up over time as private innovation brings its cost down. U.S. Food and Drug Administration – Human Food Made with Cultured Animal Cells

head: "Won't an overnight ban leave the country short of food?"
body: Not of calories. Feeding crops to animals wastes most of them: worldwide, 36% of crop calories go to animal feed, and only 12% of those feed calories reach people as meat, milk, and eggs. Ending animal agriculture frees that grain, soy, and land for people. The change will not be seamless. Supply chains, processing plants, and diets built around animal products will not reorganize overnight, and some foods will be scarce or expensive before they adjust. Prices of meat substitutes and some plant proteins will rise at first, and households will feel it. The ban still does not wait, because it rests on the animals' rights, and the government ought to clear every regulatory barrier to plant-based and cultivated food so supply follows quickly. Cassidy et al., Environmental Research Letters – Redefining agricultural yields: from tonnes to people nourished per hectare (2013)

head: "Can everyone, including children and pregnant women, eat healthily without animal products?"
body: Yes, with planning. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics holds that appropriately planned vegetarian diets, including vegan diets, are healthful and nutritionally adequate at every stage of life, including pregnancy, lactation, infancy, childhood, and older age. Critics point out that vitamin B12 has to come from fortified foods or supplements, and that iron, calcium, iodine, omega-3s, and vitamin D need attention, most of all for infants, pregnant women, and the elderly. That is why food-safety rules ought to require B12 fortification of staple plant foods, so no one has to plan it alone. Melina, Craig & Levin, Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics – Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: Vegetarian Diets (2016) NIH Office of Dietary Supplements – Vitamin B12: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals

Commercial fishing and fish farming of sentient animals should be banned outright and shut down immediately, with no wind-down, under the Sanctuary Plan. Farmed fish alive at the shutdown are kept alive and given sanctuary. Farmed crustaceans are kept alive the same way. Farmed mollusks end with the rest of aquaculture for consistency, not as a sentience claim. Licenses and quotas are revoked on day one. Firms that earn most of their revenue from fishing or aquaculture convert fully to cultivated seafood or plant-based alternatives, or are liquidated, with no compensation to shareholders. The ban covers shellfish, bycatch, and seafood imports. In my view the best available science decides which fish are sentient, cultivated seafood is the replacement, and fish and the oceans fall within the future reordering of nature against predation.

Commercial fishing and aquaculture of sentient animals should be banned outright and shut down immediately. Catching or farming sentient animals for food is a rights violation, so the ban should not be phased in, and there should be no wind-down.

Fish should follow the same sentience gradient as the murder rules in Criminal Justice & Security: killing higher-sentience fish should be on the capital track, and killing lower-sentience fish should be punished and should count as a mark against the offender.

head: How this gets done: the Sanctuary Plan

body: There is no wind-down. Like land-based animal farming in Agriculture, Grazing, and Habitat, wild-capture commercial fishing and aquaculture should shut down immediately. No fishing operations, vessels, fish farms, or hatcheries should operate after day one, and existing fishing licenses, quotas, and aquaculture licenses should be revoked. They are not an honored commitment, because catching or farming sentient animals is a rights violation. Every farmed fish alive at the shutdown is kept alive and given sanctuary, with no breeding or stocking. Farmed crustaceans are kept alive the same way. Farmed mollusks end too, for consistency, not as a sentience claim: those already in the water are left unharvested, and the farms are decommissioned. Every domestic company, vessel owner, fish farm, supplier or lender that earns most of its revenue from fishing or aquaculture converts fully to cultivated-seafood research or plant-based alternatives, or is liquidated. Others divest only that line. Shareholders get no compensation. After workers and creditors are paid, the proceeds go to the sanctuaries. Foreign firms may not operate in the United States or do business with US-held companies. There is no retraining or job-placement program. Workers find new jobs or can apply for sanctuary jobs under the worker rules in the Sanctuary Plan. Inspections, the seafood import ban, bycatch bans, and the sentience-graded penalties in Criminal Justice & Security apply to anyone who keeps operating. The full plan is in Sanctuary Plan.

Which fish are sentient follows the best available science. Crabs, lobsters, crayfish, and other decapod crustaceans sit in the high class, and shrimp are placed species by species, like fish (sentience classes). Bivalves, such as oysters and mussels, are also covered by the ban for consistency, not as a sentience claim; I believe they are likely not sentient, so they sit in no class (Sentience Determination). Bycatch ends with the fishing ban. Non-fishing marine activity, such as shipping, dredging, and offshore energy, should use the least-harmful method that works, such as speed limits and routing around whales, under the same rule as on land (Sentience Determination). Failing to use it should be punished, and unavoidable incidental deaths carry no criminal liability. Wild oysters and mussels keep filtering water when no one harvests them, so the ban costs those waters nothing; only the farms end. Imports of wild-caught or farmed seafood should be banned. Subsidies follow the opt-in rule in Agriculture and Food Policy. The long-term replacement is cultivated seafood produced through private innovation. In the bioengineering future of predation abolishment and the reordering of nature against predation and suffering, fish and the oceans are classified within that framework.

head: "Are fish even sentient?"
body: Sentience is determined by the best available scientific consensus, as for any being (Ethical and Philosophical Framework). Species that the best available science identifies as sentient are protected.

Animal agriculture and aquaculture should be abolished because they kill sentient beings that hold negative rights; farmed and wild-caught sentient fish fall under the same rule. Because every catch is a killing of a sentient being, the ban is the position. Subsidies follow the opt-in rule set out in Subsidies and Mandates. I treat predation as a rights violation (Wild-Animal Predation), and the oceans are included in the future reordering of nature against predation and suffering. The scale is significant: in 2022, U.S. commercial fishermen landed 8.4 billion pounds of seafood valued at $5.9 billion, and U.S. aquaculture produced an estimated 663 million pounds valued at $1.7 billion.
