I strongly support technological advancement and transhumanism, constrained only by sentient rights. I prefer free-market and private innovation, with the government's role limited to regulation against existential threats, rights violations, and national security. Privacy and data rules should be opt-in, and animal testing should be redirected to forfeited rights holders.

I'm pro-AI, but I treat it as a serious existential risk, so government should regulate it and prepare a defensive AGI. I reject a citizen dividend. Workers displaced by automation are covered by the earnings-only top-up. If AI displaces work on a large scale, I believe the answer is broad voluntary ownership of AI capital, falling prices, and the existing safety floor scaled to measured displacement, funded by the same flat tax system.

AI should be monitored and regulated as part of the government's role in protecting citizens' rights and security, limited to existential and rights-violation risks. If AI is observed becoming an existential threat, a risk serious enough to prepare for, the government ought to focus on regulating its development and preparing to defend against it. I oppose a citizen dividend. Workers displaced by automation into lower-paid work should be covered by the earnings-only top-up, and those who cannot work by the layered safety floor (Domestic Policy). I am pro-AI, and I believe a defensive AGI will likely be needed to combat any dangerous AGI that emerges. AI's existential and national-security risks are a federal matter, so national rules on them should preempt conflicting state laws, set by Congress in statute rather than by executive order. States should keep their ordinary fraud and consumer-protection law, which applies to AI like anything else. Every adult is enrolled by default in a low-cost private index account, with a free opt-out and no taxpayer seed. Capital gains should stay at the preferential flat rate, rising to the full flat rate under the displacement trigger, with the deferral gap closed by carryover basis (Taxation; carryover basis). The trigger is four consecutive quarters with the BLS labor share at least 3 points below its ten-year average and the prime-age employment-to-population ratio at least 2 points below its level three years earlier; capital income first moves from 15% to the 20% flat rate (17% to 22% through 2041 with the transition surcharge), then a surcharge of up to 5 points after eight quarters, never above 25% including the transition surcharge and the Sanctuary Levy while they run, and never on wealth or unrealized gains; each step reverses when the measures recover for four quarters.
The plan handles gradual or partial displacement. Fast, near-total displacement would force a choice about taxing capital beyond "minimal."
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.
Geoffrey Hinton, 2023: the AI pioneer quit Google, saying he now regretted his work, and warned of AI's dangers. BBC News (2023) – AI 'godfather' Geoffrey Hinton warns of dangers as he quits Google

head: "Does a pro-AI stance conflict with treating AI as an existential threat?"
body: No. AI offers enormous benefits and also serious risks. Supporting development while regulating against existential danger and building defensive capability addresses both.

head: "What happens to workers displaced by automation?"
body: I oppose a citizen dividend. A displaced worker who takes lower-paid work draws the earnings-only top-up on what they earn, and it phases out with no cliff as earnings recover. Those who cannot work are covered by the layered safety floor. Owner income from federal land, minerals, energy, and spectrum helps fund the top-up rather than being paid out (Welfare and Entitlements).

head: "How is the safety floor funded if AI replaces most jobs and no one has wage income?"
body: If AI does most of the work, the money doesn't vanish. It goes to the people who own the AI, as profits, dividends, and capital gains. That income would be taxed under the flat tax, at the preferential flat rate on capital gains and dividends, which would rise to the full flat rate if displacement shows up in the data, and business income would still be taxed only once (Taxation). The government also earns money from federal land, minerals, energy, and spectrum, and that money would go first to the earnings-only top-up. As AI and data centers use more spectrum and energy, that money grows. The more households own a share of AI and other businesses, the less they rely on a paycheck, and the less the floor has to cover. Owners also need people to have money, because a business whose customers have no income has no one to sell to.

head: "Why not a universal basic income?"
body: A UBI pays everyone regardless of need, which makes it far more expensive than a floor for those who cannot support themselves, and it requires compulsory redistribution well beyond the minimal floor. The government ought to keep the floor targeted. It phases support out gradually as earnings rise, so there is no cliff, and it prefers that people own capital rather than depend on a state check. The same reasoning is why owner income is not paid out as a citizen dividend (Economic System).

head: "Won't AI owners just hoard the gains?"
body: Profits that are spent, invested, or paid out are taxed under the flat system. Profits that sit idle earn nothing, so owners have strong reasons to reinvest them or pay them out. Ownership is also open to anyone: shares in AI companies trade publicly, and low-cost index funds let any household own a slice of the whole market. My answer to concentration is wider voluntary ownership, not seizing the firms. It concedes one real risk: if ownership stays highly concentrated and wages fall far, funding even a minimal floor could require a profit tax larger than "minimal" implies.

head: "What if AI replaces nearly all labor?"
body: Then something has to replace wages, and every option has a cost to my framework. The first is a large income funded by taxing the output of AI and capital, through a UBI or a much larger floor. It is the only option that reliably works, but it means redistribution far beyond the minimal floor. The second is a public ownership fund. Alaska's Permanent Fund pays citizens directly, $1,000 per person in 2025. Norway's fund, worth 22,683 billion kroner in mid-2026, pays nothing to citizens and instead helps fund the government budget. The state must first acquire the stake through taxes or takings, which clashes with my property rules. The third is near-free goods through falling prices. This is speculative, and land and housing are hard to make cheaper. The fourth is new human work in care, the trades, in-person services, and creative fields. Autor's research shows this has happened in past waves of automation, but it is not guaranteed. My choice is the first option, and only when the BLS trigger shows a real takeover of work. Until then, minimal taxes remain the default.

head: "Isn't building a defensive AGI itself a risk?"
body: Yes, and it is accepted because an undefended country facing a dangerous AGI is worse. Defensive AGI is built under the same existential-risk regulation as any other system, under government supervision.

Protecting citizens from catastrophic threats is a core government function, and advanced AI may become one. In a 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers, the median estimate of the chance of extremely bad outcomes such as human extinction was 5%. Federal policy currently aims to promote American AI leadership. A defensive capability ensures that if dangerous AI emerges, it can be countered. Measured job losses from automation have so far been modest (0.2 percentage points of employment per added robot per 1,000 workers), which is why displacement is handled through the existing earnings-only top-up rather than a separate automation payment.

Some economists argue AI is different from past automation. The IMF estimates that almost 40% of global employment, and about 60% of jobs in advanced economies, is exposed to AI, with roughly half of exposed jobs likely to benefit and half facing lower labor demand. Past automation did not end work. David Autor found that automation "complements labor, raises output in ways that leads to higher demand for labor," and that commentators "tend to overstate the extent of machine substitution." Acemoglu and Restrepo show that automation displaces workers from existing tasks, while new tasks reinstate them. They also found that the slower U.S. employment growth of the past three decades reflects faster displacement and weaker reinstatement. Labor's share of income has already been falling. BLS reports that the labor share of nonfarm business output reached a record low of 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026. Karabarbounis and Neiman document a global decline of about 5 percentage points since the 1970s, about half of it explained by cheaper investment goods such as computers. Autor and coauthors link much of the U.S. decline to sales shifting toward "superstar firms" with low labor shares. Early evidence on AI itself is mixed. Using ADP payroll data, Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen find no evidence of widespread job displacement so far. But employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations stood 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with less-exposed peers. Acemoglu estimates that AI will raise total factor productivity by no more than about 0.66% over ten years. Whether AI creates enough new tasks is unknown. So the government ought to scale its response to displacement as it's measured, not to forecasts.

Three features carry the response. First, ownership. Anyone may own AI capital through public shares and index funds, and a birth-to-adulthood account already exists in law. Trump Accounts, created by the Working Families Tax Cuts, let parents, relatives, employers, and charities invest for a child in low-cost U.S. index funds. Alaska's Permanent Fund shows that resource wealth can be held for residents over decades, paying $1,000 per person in 2025. I support voluntary contributions to such accounts but don't adopt a paid-out citizen dividend. Second, prices. Automation lowers the cost of what it produces, so a fixed income buys more, which supports demand even as some jobs shrink. The BLS price index for televisions fell 94% from December 1997 to August 2015, and William Nordhaus estimated that the cost of computation fell by a factor of trillions between 1850 and 2006. Third, the floor. The existing bare-minimum safety floor and earnings-only top-up stay the backstop, funded by the flat tax and owner income. That owner income is not trivial and is likely to grow. FCC spectrum auctions have raised more than $233 billion since 1994, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers' share of U.S. electricity use will rise from 4.4% in 2023 to between 6.7% and 12% by 2028.

Three additions turn these features into rules. First, default ownership. Every adult should be enrolled by default in a low-cost private index account, through an employer or on the tax return, with a free and simple opt-out and no taxpayer seed. It would extend the default enrollment already used for retirement savings (Social Security and Medicare Transition), where Madrian and Shea found that 401(k) participation rose from 37% under opt-in to 86% under automatic enrollment. The state should not run or hold the accounts. The accounts supplement income and would never replace wages. For example, at a 4% annual payout, a $10,000 account yields about $400 a year and a $100,000 account about $4,000. In fast displacement, it is the safety floor, not the accounts, that secures basic needs. Second, capital income is actually collected. Capital gains should keep their preferential flat rate, but the gap that lets inherited gains escape income tax entirely should be closed by carryover basis: the heir should keep the original cost basis and should pay the flat tax on sale, and nothing should be taxed at death (Taxation). Third, a measured trigger, with a ceiling. The floor and top-up should expand only when two BLS measures both show displacement for four consecutive quarters:
the labor share of nonfarm business output (BLS Productivity and Costs) stands at least 3 percentage points below its average over the previous ten years; and
the prime-age (25 to 54) employment-to-population ratio (BLS Current Population Survey) stands at least 2 points below its level three years earlier. It was 80.7% in September 2026.
Requiring both screens out ordinary recessions, in which employment falls but the labor share usually rises. Forecasts alone never trigger it.
When the trigger is met, the response comes in steps:

Step 1: owner income would go to the top-up first. The preferential 15% rate on capital gains and dividends would then rise to the 20% flat rate (17% to 22% through 2041 with the transition surcharge), so capital income would be taxed like wages.

Step 2: if the trigger holds for eight consecutive quarters, a capital-income surcharge of up to 5 points may apply, for a ceiling of 25% on capital income, still taxed once. The transition surcharge through 2041 and, while it runs, the Sanctuary Levy count inside that 25% ceiling (Sanctuary Plan).

Beyond the ceiling: anything past 25%, or any tax on wealth, estates, or unrealized gains, is outside my framework. It would need a separate recorded vote of Congress as the open choice described below.
Each step reverses once both measures have been back inside their thresholds for four consecutive quarters.

The plan has a stated limit. It is built for gradual or partial displacement, where income shifts from wages to capital over years and new tasks absorb part of the change. If AI displaced nearly all work quickly, a minimal floor funded by a flat tax on capital income might not cover basic needs. Covering them would then require taxing capital beyond what "minimal" means today. I do not settle that tradeoff in advance. It is an open choice to be decided if the data show it happening.

Ownership is broad but uneven. Gallup found that 62% of U.S. adults owned stock in 2025, directly or through funds and retirement accounts. Federal Reserve data show that the wealthiest 10% of households held about 84% of corporate equities and mutual fund shares, and the top 1% about half. That concentration is why I don't count on wider ownership arriving fast enough on its own.
Artificial general intelligence refers to AI systems able to perform most intellectual tasks at or beyond human level across domains, rather than within narrow tasks.

AI sentience should be decided by scientific consensus, and in my view sentient AI must get full rights.

Whether an artificial system is sentient should be determined by the best available scientific consensus, as for any being. This follows Section 1: if AI is sentient, it ought to be given sentient rights and treated with the same level of forfeiture if necessary. Consensus decides sentience.

head: "How could anyone tell if an AI is sentient?"
body: Through the best available science, the same standard used for animals. Researchers have proposed indicators drawn from theories of consciousness.

Butlin, Long, and colleagues (2023) proposed assessing AI systems against indicator properties derived from scientific theories of consciousness. Sentience rules are in Ethical and Philosophical Framework.
Butlin, Long, et al. – Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness (2023)

Whoever is in control should be liable: the driver, or the manufacturer in autonomous mode, with mandatory insurance. In my view cars must never intentionally sacrifice an identified person, should minimize harm in unavoidable crashes, and should keep human override where feasible.

Liability should follow control: the human driver is liable when in control, and the manufacturer or system provider is liable in autonomous mode under product liability, with mandatory insurance. Collision programming should never intentionally sacrifice an identified rights-holder to save others. Among unavoidable collisions, the system ought to minimize expected harm without targeting by status, and human override should be retained where feasible.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Cruise, 2023–24: a driverless Cruise car dragged a pedestrian over 20 feet in San Francisco. The company admitted filing a false report to NHTSA and paid a $500,000 criminal fine under a deferred prosecution agreement. U.S. Attorney's Office, N.D. Cal. (2024) – Cruise Admits To Submitting A False Report To Influence A Federal Investigation And Agrees To Pay $500,000

head: "Shouldn't the car sacrifice one person to save five?"
body: No. Negative rights are side-constraints, so the system never intentionally sacrifices an identified rights-holder. Where a collision is unavoidable, it minimizes expected harm without targeting anyone by status.

Negative rights act as side-constraints, so programming cannot direct a vehicle to kill one rights-holder as a means of saving others. Keeping human override where feasible is the same logic as human judgment over lethal force in Cyber Warfare and Autonomous Weapons. NHTSA reports 39,254 people killed in motor vehicle crashes in 2024 and notes that liability and insurance questions for automated driving systems are still being addressed by policymakers. SAE J3016 defines the levels of driving automation that separate driver control from system control. The best safety data so far come from Waymo. Over 56.7 million rider-only miles through January 2025, its vehicles had 79% fewer injury-reported crashes and 85% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers on comparable roads, in a peer-reviewed study written by company researchers.
NHTSA – Automated Vehicle Safety
SAE International – J3016: Taxonomy and Definitions for Terms Related to Driving Automation Systems
Kusano et al., Traffic Injury Prevention – Comparison of Waymo Rider-Only crash rates by crash type to human benchmarks at 56.7 million miles (2025)
See also: Cyber Warfare and Autonomous Weapons
I support brain-computer interfaces, and neural data should be opt-in only.

I support brain-computer interfaces as a freedom of enhancement. Neural data is the most personal data there is and an extension of the person, so collection and trading should be opt-in only, and the government should punish violations, with fines scaled to income and wealth.

head: "Could neurodata be misused?"
body: That is why it is opt-in and enforced. Misuse without consent is a rights violation.

Colorado's HB24-1058, signed April 17, 2024, added neural and biological data to sensitive data under the Colorado Privacy Act, requiring opt-in consent. Data rules are in Surveillance and Digital Technology.
Colorado General Assembly – HB24-1058 Protect Privacy of Biological Data
See Authority & Civil Liberties: Surveillance and Digital Technology.
I consider deepfakes free speech. Fraud should be punished under fraud law, commercial use of a likeness without consent is a property claim, and I would not ban the technology.

I hold that deepfakes are free speech, protected under Section 7. Identity fraud using deepfakes is a crime under existing fraud law, not a speech restriction. Using someone's likeness for profit without consent is a property claim. Non-commercial use (parody, art, political commentary) is protected; the line is commercial use, not any use. Deepfakes are impossible to regulate, so my approach stays narrow: protect speech, punish fraud, don't ban the tech.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

New Hampshire, 2024: the FCC fined the man behind AI-voice robocalls imitating President Biden $6 million under existing robocall law. FCC (2024) – FCC Issues $6M Fine for Election Interference Deepfake Robocalls

Hong Kong, 2024: a finance worker paid out $25 million after a video call with a deepfake "chief financial officer", a fraud case. CNN (2024) – Finance worker pays out $25 million after video call with deepfake ‘chief financial officer’

head: "Doesn't leaving deepfakes legal invite abuse?"
body: Fraud should be punished under existing fraud law, and commercial use of a person's likeness without consent should be a property claim. Everything else is speech.

Federal wire fraud law already punishes schemes to defraud carried out by electronic communication, whatever the medium of deception (18 U.S.C. § 1343). Speech limits are set out in Cultural & Social Issues.
Cornell LII – 18 U.S.C. § 1343: Fraud by wire, radio, or television
See also: Free Speech and Censorship
I want crypto legal, with fraud prosecuted and regulation that protects consumers.
Cryptocurrency should be legal and traded freely in a free market. Fraud and theft involving it ought to be prosecuted like any other, and regulation should be limited to consumer protection.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

FTX, 2024: founder Samuel Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years for misappropriating billions in customer funds. U.S. Attorney's Office, S.D.N.Y. (2024) – Samuel Bankman-Fried Sentenced To 25 Years In Prison

head: "Doesn't crypto enable crime?"
body: Crime is prosecuted whatever the medium.
The GENIUS Act, signed July 18, 2025 (Public Law 119-27), set a federal framework for payment stablecoins. Monetary rules are set out in Domestic Policy & Governance.
Congress.gov – Public Law 119-27 (GENIUS Act)
See also: Monetary Policy
I prefer open source but wouldn't require it. Intellectual property should be protected for those who claim it, and government research ought to go through private contractors.

I believe open source is preferable, but it should not be mandated. Intellectual property is relatively loose and undefined as a concept, but those who wish to mark it should have it protected. Government R&D should be conducted by contracting private companies.

head: "Is intellectual property compatible with a loose view of its foundations?"
body: I prefer open sharing, but protection should be available for those who want it. I treat the concept as weaker than physical property but still enforceable when claimed.
Open sharing accelerates innovation, while protection preserves incentives for those who invest in creation. Patent and copyright law provide the framework for those who opt in.
Cornell LII – 35 U.S.C. § 101: Inventions patentable
Cornell LII – 17 U.S.C. § 102: Subject matter of copyright
I'd leave human spaceflight to private companies. Government should fund only military space programs and hire private firms when needed.

Human spaceflight should be completely privatized. The only government space program that is funded should be militarized, focused on advancing technology to compete with any foreign power. Private companies should conduct research and development for civilian spaceflight. Government may purchase from or contract private companies for military research or security programs.

head: "Can private companies lead in space without government funding?"
body: Private firms already build launch vehicles and spacecraft under commercial models. The government would remain a customer for security needs rather than a competitor.

Private enterprise innovates faster and at lower cost than government programs. NASA already relies on commercial partners for crew and cargo transport. Space is a strategic domain, which justifies a military program.
NASA – Commercial Space
See also: Military Space
I reject vaccine mandates. Vaccines should be opt-in only. Dangerous gain-of-function research ought to be regulated as an existential risk.

I reject vaccine mandates; vaccines should only be opt-in. If you choose to get vaccinated, you immunize yourself and help limit spread to others; if you don't, that's your choice. I make no exception for severe cases. Engineered pandemic pathogens are an existential risk, which falls within the government's role in regulating technology, so research that makes dangerous pathogens more transmissible or lethal should be regulated accordingly.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

OSHA mandate, 2022: the Supreme Court stayed OSHA's rule requiring roughly 84 million workers to be vaccinated against COVID-19 or test weekly, finding the agency likely lacked authority. Supreme Court of the United States (2022) – National Federation of Independent Business v. OSHA, Nos. 21A244 and 21A247

head: "Doesn't regulating research slow medicine?"
body: Regulation should be limited to research that creates existential risk. Most biomedical research is untouched.

head: "Don't school vaccine mandates raise coverage?"
body: Supporters cite California: after it tightened exemptions in 2014 and ended nonmedical school exemptions in 2016, the share of kindergartners not up to date on required vaccines fell from 9.84% in 2013 to 4.87% in 2017, though medical exemptions rose and partly replaced the personal-belief exemptions. Higher coverage does not make compulsion legitimate, so vaccination stays opt-in only, with no exception for severe cases.

head: "Could emergency powers ever require vaccination?"
body: No. I reject vaccine mandates with no exception for severe cases, and emergency powers do not suspend that rule. They are held to the same necessity, narrowness, and time-limit test as any mandate (Emergency Powers) and cannot override an opt-in-only position.

Executive Order 14292 (May 5, 2025) ended federal funding for dangerous gain-of-function research in countries of concern and paused other federally funded such research pending new policy. Under it, the USG Policy for Stopping High-Risk Life Sciences Research, announced in NIH notice NOT-OD-26-101 on July 28, 2026, prohibits federal support for dangerous gain-of-function research and sets risk-based oversight for other life-sciences research. Emergency powers are limited as set out in Authority & Civil Liberties. Most infectious disease in people comes from animals: CDC estimates that more than 6 in 10 known infectious diseases in people can spread from animals, and 3 in 4 new or emerging ones come from animals. Ending animal agriculture (Agriculture) also removes routine contact with farm animals, one of the routes CDC lists for spread.
The White House – Improving the Safety and Security of Biological Research (EO 14292)
National Institutes of Health – NOT-OD-26-101: USG Policy for Stopping High-Risk Life Sciences Research
CDC – About Zoonotic Diseases
JAMA – Associations of Statewide Legislative and Administrative Interventions With Vaccination Status Among Kindergartners in California (2019)
Pediatrics – Elimination of Nonmedical Immunization Exemptions in California and School-Entry Vaccine Status (2019)
See also: Emergency Powers · Agriculture, Grazing, and Habitat
Genes should be edited to remove negative traits, and I believe designer babies are fine if rights are respected after sentience. Animals should be genetically modified only for their own benefit.

Where genetic editing can modify against negative traits, it should be done. I find designer babies acceptable as long as sentient rights are not violated post-sentience. Genetic engineering of animals should be done only to benefit their sentient-rights protections, never to violate them.

head: "Are designer babies a step toward eugenics?"
body: Eugenics historically meant coercive state control of reproduction. Genetic editing chosen to remove negative traits, with rights respected after sentience, involves no coercion and benefits the individual.

head: "The edited child cannot consent. Isn't that a violation?"
body: Editing happens before sentience, when there is not yet a rights-holder, under the responsibility the creator holds for the embryo (Reproductive Technology). After sentience, the person's rights are fully protected, and designer choices are acceptable only as long as those rights are not violated.

Reducing suffering from genetic disease benefits sentient beings. Heritable human editing is currently restricted in many countries, and some scientists have called for a moratorium, which shows where the debate stands. The sentient-rights test sets the limit.
CRISPR is a gene-editing technology that allows precise changes to DNA in living organisms.
Lander et al., Nature – Adopt a moratorium on heritable genome editing
I fully support enhancement technologies, limited only where they violate sentient rights.
I fully support transhuman technology. The only ethical limits I set are where the technology or its research and development violates sentient rights.

head: "Could enhancement create inequality between enhanced and unenhanced humans?"
body: I set my ethical limit at sentient-rights violations. Enhancement that violates no one's rights is a matter of individual freedom.
Extending human capacity and lifespan advances wellbeing. Liberty includes the freedom to improve oneself, so long as others' rights are untouched.
Transhumanism is the movement to enhance human physical and cognitive capacities through technology, including life extension and human-machine integration.
Willett et al., Nature (2023) – A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis

I support IVF, embryo screening, and gene editing. Whoever creates an embryo should be responsible for it: before sentience it gets provisional protection like animal welfare, with protection starting early as a safeguard, and full rights at sentience. Freezing an embryo indefinitely does not end that responsibility.

I support IVF, embryo screening, and genetic editing against negative traits, and I find designer babies acceptable as long as sentient rights are respected after sentience. Whoever creates an embryo holds responsibility and stewardship for it, following the responsibility created by voluntary procreation. Before sentience, an embryo should receive provisional protection of the kind given in animal welfare, not the full rights of a sentient being. Full rights attach at sentience. The same calendar caution that applies to abortion applies here: I believe elective abortion should be banned from conception by constitutional amendment, on the moral weight of a fetus on its way to sentience and on caution where science is unclear, while the rights claim starts at 12 weeks (Abortion and Bioethics). For embryos, pre-sentience protection stays provisional in the animal-welfare register, moral weight rises gradually as development approaches sentience, and earlier stewardship duties are not full negative rights from conception. Keeping an embryo in frozen storage indefinitely does not pause the creator's duty.

head: "If an embryo isn't sentient, why protect it at all?"
body: Because creating it was a voluntary act, and voluntary procreation creates responsibility. Before sentience the protection is provisional, in the animal-welfare register rather than the register of full rights. The abortion rule applies here too: the legal ban on elective abortion runs from conception on that moral weight and that caution, not as a claim of full rights from conception, so embryo stewardship does not wait until the moment of sentience and does not pretend a frozen embryo already holds the full rights stack. Freezing an embryo indefinitely does not suspend that responsibility.

Assisted reproduction is now a routine part of family formation. In 2022, U.S. clinics reported 435,426 ART cycles resulting in 98,289 live-born infants, about 2.6% of all U.S. births, and 184,423 of those cycles were banking cycles in which all eggs or embryos were frozen for later use. Large numbers of stored embryos make the question of stewardship practical rather than theoretical. The responsibility and sentience framework in Cultural & Social Issues supplies the rule, and editing and selection follow Genetic Engineering and CRISPR.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention – ART Surveillance
See also: Abortion and Bioethics

I believe reproductive human cloning should not be banned. Research cloning should stay inside existing fetal and sentience rules, with no gestation to birth. Any cloned person has full rights, and no one owns them.

I believe reproductive cloning of humans should not be banned. Research cloning and embryo use should be allowed only inside the existing fetal, sentience, and research rules, with no gestation to birth for research. Cloned persons, if any ever exist, hold full negative rights under the same sentience rules as anyone else, with no ownership.

head: "Would a clone have fewer rights?"
body: No. A cloned person holds full negative rights under the same sentience rules as anyone else. No one owns a clone.

Rights are sentience-based, as set out in Abortion and Fetal Rights: Technology, so research use stays within those limits and any cloned person is a full rights-holder. Reproductive cloning should be allowed because it differs in no meaningful way from ordinary procreation: a child conceived either way cannot pre-consent to being born, so lack of consent is no reason to ban one and not the other. A clone is a person like anyone else, not a product, and holds the same full sentience-based rights. Mammalian cloning from an adult cell has been possible since Dolly the sheep, born July 5, 1996, at the Roslin Institute.
The Roslin Institute, University of Edinburgh – Dolly
See Cultural & Social Issues: Abortion and Fetal Rights: Technology.
See Cultural & Social Issues: End-of-Life Care and Lost Sentience.

I believe organ donation and sales must always be opt-in, even after death, and any government payment needs opt-in funding. Everyone should be asked to choose, but no one is presumed to consent. Organs of condemned offenders may be used under forfeiture.

Organ donation and organ sales should be opt-in. Any government payment related to organ donation or sales ought to require opt-in funding. For innocent people it is always opt-in, even after death: it reflects the wishes of the person in life, not a default that takes without asking. Everyone should be asked to choose, yes or no, at a set point such as issuing or renewing a driver's license; the answer is recorded, and no one is presumed to consent. Organs from offenders sentenced to death, whose rights would be forfeited, should be usable under the same logic as the experimentation track. Organs may also be taken, without consent, from offenders at three marks on the execution or experimentation track. They are taken either at execution, which still takes place on the sentencing date under Section 6, or from offenders placed on the experimentation track by the victim's choice, by default where the victim has died unless the victim's close family or friends choose otherwise, or by a judge, who may not refuse, where victims disagree or the victim is an animal, or, when a living victim does not respond or does not care, through a research firm's request in the registry system, as set out in Animal Rights and Sentience Technology.

head: "Don't opt-out countries save more lives?"
body: Supporters of presumed consent cite a systematic review in the BMJ that found deceased-donation rates roughly 21 to 30 percent higher in presumed-consent countries, a gap that costs lives on the waiting list. That gap does not give the state a claim on anyone's body: taking organs by default treats silence as consent, and the body of an innocent person is not the state's to presume. Mandated choice closes part of the gap by asking everyone to decide, without presuming anything.

head: "Isn't taking organs from executed offenders abuse?"
body: Under forfeiture, an offender at three marks or the capital tier, violent or not, has given up the rights that would otherwise protect them, just as with experimentation. Innocent people's organs are taken only with consent.

head: "Does using offenders' organs give the state an incentive to convict?"
body: Conviction standards would not change: capital cases would still need the capital evidentiary standard and a unanimous jury. Organs would go to patients, not to the prosecuting agency, and the state would earn no revenue from them.

As of July 30, 2026, 109,817 people were on the U.S. national transplant waiting list, according to the Health Resources and Services Administration. A BMJ systematic review found presumed-consent countries had deceased-donation rates roughly 21 to 30 percent higher than opt-in countries, though the studies could not separate the law from other national differences. Wales, which moved to a soft opt-out system in December 2015, saw consent rates rise, though not immediately. I accept the lower donation rate as the cost of consent, and the state ought to use mandated choice to narrow it. The experimentation track is set out in Animal Rights and Sentience Technology.
Health Resources and Services Administration – Organ Donation Statistics
Rithalia et al., BMJ – Impact of presumed consent for organ donation on donation rates: a systematic review (2009)
Madden et al., Anaesthesia – The effect on consent rates for deceased organ donation in Wales after the introduction of an opt-out system (2020)
See also: Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row

Psychedelic therapy should be legal by prescription in licensed settings. Recreational use belongs in the hard-drug lane: private adult use legal, public use banned, cartels destroyed. As with every drug, marijuana included, I would allow no use while a minor is present and no impairment around one.

Clinical psychedelic therapy should be legal under medical protocols: prescription and a licensed setting. Recreational use should stay in the hard-drug lane: legal for private adult use, public use banned, and cartels still destroyed. The minor-presence rule covers every drug, marijuana included: no use while a minor is present and no impairment around one (Drug Policy). Psychedelics are not carved out as "not hard drugs"; therapy is a regulated exception to commercial and medical supply rules.
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

United States, 9 Aug 2024: the FDA declined to approve Lykos Therapeutics' MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, issuing a complete response letter and asking for an additional phase 3 trial. This followed an FDA advisory committee's June finding that there was not enough evidence the therapy was safe or effective. NPR – FDA rejects MDMA, disappointing drugmaker Lykos and psychedelics industry; NBC News – FDA rejects psychedelic MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD

head: "Does legal therapy mean psychedelics aren't hard drugs?"
body: No. They stay in the hard-drug lane. Therapy is a regulated exception to supply rules, not a reclassification.

This applies Drugs and Vice, Drug Policy, and the harm-to-others line: private adult use harms no one else, public use and cartel supply do. In a phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 67% of participants with severe PTSD who received MDMA-assisted therapy no longer met diagnostic criteria at the primary endpoint, compared with 32% in the placebo group. In August 2024 the FDA declined to approve MDMA-assisted therapy and asked for a new trial. About 40% of participants had used MDMA before, raising the risk of expectation bias and broken blinding, some adverse events went unrecorded, and durability beyond 18 weeks was not shown. Oregon runs a licensed psilocybin services program.
Mitchell et al., Nature Medicine – MDMA-assisted therapy for severe PTSD: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study (2021)
FDA – Complete Response Letter, NDA 215455 (midomafetamine), August 8, 2024
Oregon Health Authority – Oregon Psilocybin Services
See also: Drugs and Vice · Drug Policy

I would shut down animal agriculture immediately. Lab-grown meat is the goal and the replacement: it may not meet demand at the same cost right away, and it scales up over time. Truly sentient AI ought to get full rights. All animal testing should end immediately. Every test animal is kept alive, adopted after vetting where safe or kept in sanctuary (Sanctuary Plan). In my view experiments should be done instead on offenders who have forfeited their rights, so the burden of research falls on those who harmed others, not on animals who harmed no one. For offenders sentenced to death, the victim has priority in choosing between execution and experimentation. If the victim does not respond or does not care, research firms can request bodies through a registry, though never over a victim who chose execution. Where the victim has died, the default is the experimentation track, unless the victim's close family or friends step forward and choose instead; if they disagree, it stays the experimentation track. At three marks, the victim may choose the experimentation track, which can include non-violent repeat offenders such as repeat thieves. The state only picks the research. Offenders are experimented on for as long as the research agency deems appropriate, with no limit on their suffering, and are executed once the experimentation is exhausted or the body is no longer useful, unless they die in an experiment.

I view lab-grown meat as humanity's best hope for a sentientist world. It is the goal and the replacement for animal agriculture, which should be banned immediately. It may not meet demand at the same cost right away, but it scales up over time, and the ban does not wait for it. The scale and food-supply questions are answered in Energy & Environment: Agriculture and Food Policy.

AI sentience can be allowed, and if artificial systems give rise to true sentience, that sentience ought to receive the protections of sentient rights, as biological beings do, weighted on the sliding scale in Section 1, and is subject to the same forfeiture rules. I would ban animal testing completely. Scientific experimentation of any kind, including cosmetic, pharmaceutical, and technological testing, should be redirected to offenders placed on the experimentation track, whose rights have been forfeited through their violations. At the capital tier, the victim has priority in choosing between execution and experimentation. If the victim does not respond or does not care, research can proceed: research firms request bodies through a registry system, and offenders sentenced to death are assigned from it. The registry is run by the state research-oversight body and is public. Firms request eligible offenders by study need, not named individuals, and requests are ranked by scientific merit, then by order received. The victim should be notified at conviction and should have to choose by the sentencing hearing. No response by then should count as not responding. A research firm's request never overrides a victim who chose execution. The victim's choice always wins. Where the victim of a capital crime has died, as in murder, the sentence defaults to the experimentation track, unless the victim's close family or friends step forward and choose between execution and experimentation in the victim's place. If they disagree, the sentence stays on the experimentation track. A judge should not be permitted to refuse this choice: choosing should be the judge's duty, and a judge who refuses should no longer be a judge. A refusal should send the case neither to the registry nor to execution by default. The refusing judge is removed and a replacement judge decides the case under the deadline in Capital Trials. At three marks, offenders are placed on the experimentation track by the victim's choice among execution, experimentation, or life with labor at three marks, under Section 6. This may include non-violent repeat offenders, such as repeat thieves, not only violent offenders. The state only decides which research they are used for. Offenders on the experimentation track have forfeited their rights, and the forfeiture is complete. They are experimented on for as long as the institution or research agency deems appropriate, and their suffering in the research is irrelevant, so the law should place no limit on it. They didn't care if their victim suffered, so the law ought not care about their suffering once their rights are forfeited. An offender should be executed once the research agency deems the experimentation exhausted or the body no longer useful, unless the offender dies in the course of an experiment. Harm outside the research, such as abuse by guards unrelated to any study, remains punishable (Section 6). Research firms pay into the victim restitution fund and the registry's costs, never to police, prosecutors, courts, or any official, and no one in the charging or trial process may hold a stake in a research firm. A minor who reaches the capital tier or three marks may be placed on the experimentation track like an adult, under the rules in Juvenile Offenders, including the individual maturity assessment for the capital tier. A pregnant offender should not be placed in any experiment that risks the fetus until the child is born (Capital Trials).
These are individual reported events, not statistics. They illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

Wisconsin, 2026: Ridglan Farms, one of the largest U.S. breeders of beagles for laboratory testing, committed to permanently end its dog breeding, sales, research and testing. By 12 Aug 2026 its last 155 beagles had left, bringing the total relocated to rescue groups since May to 2,115. WTMJ – Historic conclusion at Ridglan Farms: All dogs released; FOX6 Milwaukee – Ridglan Farms beagles: Last dogs released from Wisconsin facility

head: "How many animals does this affect, and what replaces them?"
body: In fiscal year 2024, USDA-registered facilities reported 775,297 animals covered by the Animal Welfare Act used or held for research, teaching, testing, or experimentation, 650,208 of them actually used. That count leaves out most research animals, because the Act's definition of "animal" excludes birds, rats of the genus Rattus, and mice of the genus Mus bred for research. All of that testing ends. What replaces it is non-animal methods, which federal law now permits for drug approval, and the experimentation track for offenders who have forfeited their rights, set out above.

There should be no transition period: all animal testing ends immediately. Every animal in a lab at the shutdown is kept alive for its natural life, adopted after vetting where safe or kept in a sanctuary (Sanctuary Plan). Experimentation on offenders who have forfeited their rights continues, as set out above.

head: "Doesn't experimentation on prisoners violate the Nuremberg Code and federal research law?"
body: Yes. The Nuremberg Code's first principle is that "the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential," and federal rules for research on prisoners limit it to minimal-risk studies and research that may benefit the subjects or prisoners as a class. The experimentation track conflicts with both and would require changing federal law. I depart from them on my forfeiture principle. The Code protects people who hold their rights, while an offender who reaches the capital tier or the three-mark threshold has forfeited the rights that consent protects, through his own violation, proven under due process. The Code was written after experiments on people who had done nothing to forfeit anything, and the law ought to keep that protection for everyone who has not. Treaty conflicts are handled in Global Institutions.

head: "How can a repeat thief end up on the experimentation track? Isn't that out of all proportion?"
body: Forfeiture corresponds to the violation, and at three marks the violation is a pattern, not one theft (Repeat Offenders). Someone convicted again and again, punished each time, and back to taking what belongs to others has forfeited the right to life, and the experimentation track is one of the three outcomes that forfeiture allows, not an addition to it. The thief's case still needs what every case at the threshold needs: the threshold offense proven to the capital evidentiary standard, and the victim's choice. While most people will see experimentation on a thief as harsher than the theft deserves, the community owes nothing more to an offender who has shown that ordinary sentences don't stop him, and that the burden of research ought to fall on him rather than on an animal who took nothing from anyone.

head: "If rights rest on the capacity to suffer and forfeiture is proportional, how can the law place no limit on suffering on the experimentation track?"
body: There is no internal inconsistency. Proportionality would be applied once, at the forfeiture decision: a court would find, under due process and the capital evidentiary standard, that the offender crossed the published threshold, the capital tier or three marks (Repeat Offenders). At that point the offender has voided the societal standard and forfeited his rights, and the forfeiture is complete. Sentience is what grounds rights. It does not guarantee that rights survive the holder's own violations. Once the rights are forfeit, nothing done within the track sentence wrongs him, so unlimited research suffering is not a second, unjust penalty layered on the first. It is what forfeiture already allows. The only limits that remain protect others and the integrity of the sentence: harm outside the research is still punished, and the rules in the experimentation terms govern placement.

head: "Isn't using a person as a research subject treating them merely as a means?"
body: That objection assumes the person still holds every right that dignity protects. My framework doesn't rest on Kantian dignity. It rests on negative rights, which an agent forfeits by violating them in others. An offender on the track has forfeited his claim against this sentence through his own proven acts. Harm outside the sentence, such as abuse by guards unrelated to the research, is still punished. The alternative uses as a means an animal who forfeited nothing.

head: "What if an offender on the experimentation track is proven innocent?"
body: That would be a very grave error, and it is why the capital track demands extreme proof before anyone reaches it. Unlike an executed offender, a living subject can still be freed, so the review for new objective evidence stays open for as long as the offender lives (Capital Trials). If it undermines the verdict, the experimentation stops, the case is retried, and the state compensates the person as the victim of a state rights violation (Wrongful Convictions and Compensation).

head: "Will regulators and journals even accept data from subjects who didn't consent?"
body: Not under current rules. FDA's human-subject rules require informed consent, and FDA accepts foreign clinical data only if the trial met good clinical practice, consent included. The law ought to amend both, so that research on the experimentation track, run under the state research-oversight body's protocols, counts as valid evidence for approval. Journals are private and may refuse to publish it, which is their right. The data still answers the question that matters: whether a drug or product is safe for innocent people. eCFR – 21 CFR Part 50: Protection of Human Subjects eCFR – 21 CFR 312.120: Foreign clinical studies not conducted under an IND

head: "There will never be enough offenders to replace lab animals. Won't research slow down?"
body: Yes. Lab animal use, counted in the Sanctuary Plan, runs far beyond anything the experimentation track will supply, and some research will be slower or will not happen. That does not change the rule. Under my side-constraints, an innocent being may not be harmed to benefit another, however large the benefit (Conflicts Between Rights-Holders), so research loses its claim on innocent animals whether or not a substitute keeps pace. Non-animal methods, which federal law now permits, and the experimentation track carry what can be carried.

head: "Medical ethics codes forbid doctors from taking part. Who runs the experiments?"
body: The AMA's Code bars physicians from participating in executions, and the Declaration of Helsinki requires informed consent. Those codes are private professional rules, and they protect people who hold their rights. No researcher is compelled to work on the track. The law ought to bar licensing boards from disciplining anyone who works on it lawfully, and the state research-oversight body ought to staff it with those who choose to. American Medical Association – Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 9.7.3: Capital Punishment World Medical Association – Declaration of Helsinki

head: "Is experimentation on condemned prisoners compatible with sentient rights?"
body: Under the forfeiture principle, those who commit egregious violations of others' rights forfeit their own. Innocent animals hold their rights intact. Offenders at the capital tier or the three-mark threshold do not. The burden of experimentation shifts from those who did nothing wrong to those who did. It protects two groups who never chose the risk: the animals used today, 650,208 in fiscal 2024 among the species the federal count covers alone, and the patients who will take what is tested, since data from human subjects answer directly whether a product is safe for humans. The two errors are not equal. An offender wrongly placed on the track can still be freed, because the review for new objective evidence stays open for as long as he lives; every animal used in his place had forfeited nothing at all. These are offenders who committed capital crimes or offended again and again, with no regard for anyone else's rights, and they forfeited their own. Their suffering has no limit, and research runs slower than animal testing allowed.

head: "Can AI and computer modeling replace experimentation on living subjects?"
body: Not yet. AI speeds discovery and improves early safety results, but it has not improved how often drugs work in patients, no AI-discovered drug has been approved end to end, and regulators in the United States and Europe still require testing on living subjects where validated alternatives do not exist.

Cultivated-meat costs remain unproven at industrial scale and investment fell in 2024, so supply at today's meat prices will not arrive at once. It scales up over time as private innovation brings costs toward parity, and the ban rests on rights, so it does not wait for that. Animal testing inflicts suffering on sentient beings who have violated no one's rights. Federal law now permits alternatives to animal testing for drug approval under the FDA Modernization Act 2.0. Forfeiture theory, set out in Criminal Justice & Security, grounds the redirection of experimentation. Computational methods do not yet replace testing on living subjects. AI-discovered drugs pass early safety trials 80 to 90 percent of the time, against a historical 40 to 65 percent, but succeed in about 40 percent of trials that test effectiveness in patients, roughly the historical average. No drug discovered end to end by AI has been approved. AI-discovered candidates from BenevolentAI, Exscientia, and Recursion have failed in human trials, and AlphaFold3 cannot reliably predict how strongly drugs bind to their targets. How well animal models predict human results is contested. An umbrella review of 122 articles found 86% agreement between positive animal and human results, yet only 5% of animal-tested therapies reached regulatory approval, most failing later in human trials. The FDA began phasing out animal testing in 2025, starting with monoclonal antibodies, only where equivalent or better alternatives exist. The European Medicines Agency accepts AI only as validated support, not as a sole basis for approval; and non-animal methods cannot yet replace whole-body or long-term safety testing. Experimentation on living subjects therefore remains necessary, and the experimentation track places that burden on condemned offenders rather than on animals.

This page measures today's political parties against my framework. Each party is described from its own official platform, then compared section by section with the positions I set out. No party matches my framework. Each one aligns with some principles and conflicts with others, and the pattern of those overlaps says more than any party label. The United States gets the most detail. Selected foreign systems follow for contrast.
Most Americans are independents, but almost all votes go to the two major parties. I judge each party position by position.

American politics is a two-party system with a large unaffiliated middle. Third parties shape the debate but win almost no federal offices. I treat party labels as bundles of positions, not identities, and judge each bundle item by item.

head: "If no party fits, why compare them at all?"
body: Voters choose among the options that exist. Mapping where each party agrees and disagrees with my framework shows which trade-offs a vote for that party involves.

Party identification is weak while results are concentrated. Most voters do not identify with either major party, yet nearly all votes still go to one of them. That gap is why I set out my views as positions rather than as an affiliation (Relation to Other Political Traditions).

I fully align with Democrats on same-sex marriage and directionally on marijuana and drug reform. I conflict with them on NATO, Israel, policing and crime, wages, taxes, entitlements, abortion, capital punishment, immigration, group preferences, and gender policy.

The 2024 Democratic platform pairs an expanded federal role in wages, health care, and climate with a path to citizenship for people who entered unlawfully. I share its acceptance of same-sex marriage. I conflict with it on immigration and borders, alliances, Israel, policing and crime, economics, abortion, and capital punishment, and agree with it only in part on guns.

head: "Isn't the Democratic Party the party of civil liberties?"
body: No. Denying negative rights is not protecting civil liberties. A party that takes people's earnings through compulsory redistribution, mandates what they must pay and buy, and restricts their right to defend themselves is not defending liberty. Civil liberties are best defended by a party that is strong on crime and protects civilians' security and rights, because a person who is not safe from violence, theft, and coercion is not free in any meaningful sense. The platform's minimum wage, progressive taxation, and mandatory entitlement system all rest on the compulsory redistribution I reject (Welfare and Entitlements), and its record on crime leaves civilians less secure (Police Power and Accountability).

Platform: a federal minimum wage of "at least $15-an-hour". No tax increase for anyone earning under $400,000, with higher taxes above that. Support for Medicaid expansion; a ban on assault weapons and universal background checks; restoring abortion access after Roe; a "pathway to citizenship for Dreamers"; a net-zero emissions goal; strengthening NATO; support for Israel; "fund the police, not defund the police."
Full alignment: marriage freedom (Marriage Law).
Directional alignment: drug reform, where the party moves toward legal marijuana and the law ought to make drugs legal for private, personal use away from minors (Drugs and Vice).
Mixed: guns, where its background checks and red flag laws match mine and its assault-weapons ban does not (Gun Rights).

Conflicts: unconditional support for NATO, where the United States ought to join alliances only when they serve U.S. interests (Alliances and NATO). A two-state solution and a base that leans Palestinian, where I reject a two-state solution (Israel and the Middle East). Policing and crime, where the party is not pro-police or anti-crime in practice and the state ought to fund police heavily and punish harshly (Police Power and Accountability); the minimum wage (Labor and Unions); progressive rates instead of a flat tax (Taxation); a mandatory entitlement system (Social Security and Medicare Transition); elective abortion after conception, which I believe should be banned by constitutional amendment (Abortion and Bioethics); no support for capital punishment (Mandatory Death Penalty); a path to citizenship for people who entered unlawfully (Immigration and Borders).

Culture: the platform champions "an ambitious equity and racial justice agenda," including expanded federal contracting for small disadvantaged businesses, which conflicts with my ban on group preferences (Equal Treatment). It supports "medically necessary gender-affirming care" and pledges to pass the Equality Act, which would add gender identity as a protected category. The law ought to protect race, biological sex, and sexual orientation but not recognize gender identity as a legal category (Gender Identity in Schools and Institutions).

I agree with the Democratic Party on same-sex marriage and on several social freedoms. It disagrees on whether government should set wages, redistribute income, and run compulsory insurance. Because the platform rests on those tools, it scores low on the economic principles despite the agreement on marriage.

Not directionally aligned. In order of weight, the divergences are crime, group-based equity, gender policy, and then the size of the state. On crime the platform funds police ("fund the police, not defund the police") but moves away from punishment. It would "restrict state and local practices like solitary confinement," limit federal reincarceration "to only serious violations," and expand second-chance programs. It does not support capital punishment. I move the other way, toward mandatory death for murder and violent rape and forfeiture at three marks (Mandatory Death Penalty; Repeat Offenders). It then champions "an ambitious equity and racial justice agenda," against equal treatment without preferences (Equal Treatment), and "medically necessary gender-affirming care" and the Equality Act, against my biological-sex positions (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues). Last come a mandated wage floor, higher taxes on top earners, and expanded public coverage, against free labor markets, a flat tax, and opt-in programs (Taxation; Welfare and Entitlements). I fully agree on same-sex marriage, but that is one point of agreement inside an opposite trajectory; its NATO, Israel, and police-funding language does not match my positions in practice.

head: Republican Party and the MAGA Faction
sub: Republican Party and the MAGA Faction

body: I fully align with Republicans on borders, DEI, sex-based policy, missile defense, and alliances only in the U.S. interest. I'm directionally aligned on punishment, policing, guns, abortion, Israel, energy, and limited government (the party goes partway). I conflict with them on animal agriculture, broad baseline tariffs, entitlements, and private-school vouchers.
sub: Republican Party and the MAGA Faction

body: The 2024 Republican platform, written under Trump's leadership, combines tax cuts and deregulation with large-scale deportation, broad tariffs, and a promise not to cut Social Security or Medicare. I share its emphasis on border enforcement, gun rights, policing, energy production, and Israel. It conflicts with the populist economics: broad baseline tariffs that go beyond my cautious, targeted use, and an untouchable entitlement system.

head: "Isn't the MAGA movement national conservatism, which you partly share?"
body: Partly. I share its emphasis on borders, patriotism, and a strong military (Civilizational Nationalism). It parts ways on broad baseline tariffs, which go beyond my view that tariffs are good in theory and questionable in practice, used as leverage, to protect strategic industries, and against national-security threats such as China (Trade and Economics), and on protecting a mandatory Social Security system "with no cuts." That pledge rules out the opt-in transition I call for.

head: "How does the platform's abortion position compare?"
body: The platform leaves abortion to "a vote of the People, from within the States" and opposes late-term abortion. The law ought to ban elective abortion from conception by constitutional amendment. Sentience is the rights theory, and the rights claim starts at 12 weeks. The earlier ban rests on the moral weight of a fetus on its way to sentience and on caution where no one can pin down exactly when sentience starts, and it is a safeguard, because countries that set a week limit keep raising it (Abortion and Bioethics). In my framework, a right does not change from state to state (Federalism).

Platform: "carry out the largest deportation operation in American history". Make the Trump tax cuts permanent and add "no tax on tips". Baseline tariffs; protect Social Security and Medicare "with no cuts"; "DRILL, BABY, DRILL"; cancel the electric-vehicle mandate; close the Department of Education; the right to keep and bear arms; replenish police forces; an Iron Dome missile shield; stand with Israel.

Full alignment: border enforcement and deportation (Border Security and Immigration Enforcement). Ending DEI preferences. Sex-based policy; missile defense (Military Spending and Projection); alliances judged by the U.S. interest (Alliances and NATO).

Directional alignment: punishment, where federal executions are restored by executive order but death is not mandatory (Mandatory Death Penalty). Policing, funded but with qualified immunity kept (Police Power and Accountability). Guns, where the party protects ownership but most of its House members voted against red-flag funding and its states spread permitless carry, while the law ought to keep background checks and red flag laws (Gun Rights); abortion, through state bans rather than my single line (Abortion and Bioethics); Israel, stopping short on Iran (Israel and the Middle East); energy, where EV mandates are cut but the ethanol mandate is set at record volumes (Subsidies and Mandates); limited government, through deregulation alongside deficits.

Culture: the platform pledges to "keep men out of women's sports," "ban Taxpayer funding for sex transition," teach "Knowledge and Skills, Not CRT and Gender Indoctrination," and enforce civil rights laws "to stop schools from discriminating on the basis of Race." These match my sex-based and equal-treatment positions (Gender Identity in Schools and Institutions; Equal Treatment). It does not state protection for sexual orientation in employment, which the law ought to require.

Conflicts: broad baseline tariffs, beyond my cautious, targeted use (Trade and Economics). A mandatory entitlement system protected "with no cuts". A tax code that adds carve-outs instead of a flat 20% (scored 0, since rate cuts still move toward lower, simpler taxes); leaving abortion to the states; federal tax-credit scholarships for private and religious schools, where my money follows the child only to public and charter schools (Education); the push to override California's Prop 12, where the United States ought to ban animal agriculture (Animal Rights and Sentientism).

On security and borders the Republican Party is the closest major party to my framework. On economics it is closer than the Democrats on regulation and energy but not on trade or entitlements. The populist turn has moved the party toward broad baseline tariffs, where the United States ought to treat tariffs cautiously and use them in a targeted way, and toward a protected status for current entitlements, which runs against my opt-in principles.

Directionally aligned. On borders, policing, guns, energy, education, and sex-based policy, the platform moves the same way I do (Border Security; Gender Identity in Schools and Institutions). The main exceptions run against that direction: broad baseline tariffs, beyond my cautious, targeted use (Trade and Economics), and a pledge to protect Social Security and Medicare "with no cuts", which rules out the opt-in transition (Social Security and Medicare Transition).

I fully align with the Libertarians on opt-in welfare, free labor markets, self-defense, and equal treatment in law. I'm directionally aligned on drugs and vice (the party goes further). I conflict with them on capital punishment, borders, alliances, and private-employer discrimination.

The Libertarian Party is the closest match to my framework on economics and personal freedom. It is the furthest on punishment and borders. Its platform repeals the income tax, phases Social Security out into a voluntary private system, keeps government out of labor contracts and marriage, and repeals laws against victimless crimes. It also opposes the death penalty and calls for open movement across borders.

head: "You agree with libertarianism on rights. Why not adopt the Libertarian platform?"
body: Because I accept far more force against people who violate rights. The platform states, "We oppose the administration of the death penalty by the state," and it supports "unrestricted movement of human as well as financial capital across national borders." I hold the opposite on both (Mandatory Death Penalty; Immigration and Borders).

Platform: repeal the income tax and abolish the IRS. Phase out Social Security toward a private voluntary system. Labor contracts outside government's scope; repeal laws on drugs, gambling, and sex work; restitution to victims; the Second Amendment and self-defense; no government role in marriage; a sufficient military, no entangling alliances, no compulsory service; opposition to the death penalty; open borders.

Full alignment: opt-in retirement (Social Security and Medicare Transition). No minimum wage (Labor and Unions). Self-defense with no duty to retreat (Self-Defense and Defense of Others); equal legal treatment.

Directional alignment: negative rights and limited government (Political Philosophy). Vice, where the party legalizes the commercial sale and public use of all drugs and the law ought to legalize private, personal use only (Drugs and Vice).

Mixed: guns, where the party protects ownership but opposes every law that restricts or monitors firearms, including the background checks I support (Gun Rights). Taxes, where abolishing the income tax overshoots my flat 20% (Taxation).

Culture: the platform says government should not treat anyone differently by "sex ... or sexual orientation," and that gender identity "should have no impact on the government's treatment of individuals." It also holds that private organizations "retain their rights to set whatever standards of association they deem appropriate." I agree on equal legal treatment by sex, but the law ought to bar private employers and businesses from treating people by race, sex, or sexual orientation, and record birth sex in law (Equal Treatment).
Conflicts: the death penalty. Open borders. Non-interventionism and avoiding alliances (Alliances and NATO); no position on animal rights.

I sit closest to libertarianism on what government may do to peaceful people. It differs sharply on what government should do to people who violate rights and to threats from outside the country. The party's 2024 nominee won 0.42% of the vote.

Directionally aligned on economics and personal liberty; not on security. The platform shrinks the state toward voluntary exchange, as I do (Political Philosophy). It moves the opposite way on the use of force against people who violate rights and on borders, where I accept far more state power (Order and Security).

I fully align with the Greens on ranked-choice voting, and directionally on animal welfare, drugs, sex work, and same-sex marriage. I conflict with them on economics, energy subsidies, nuclear power, defense, Israel, bail, voting rules, guns, and capital punishment.

The Green Party combines an ecosocialist economic program with the strongest animal-welfare commitments of any US party. I share the animal-welfare direction and the interest in voting reform. I conflict with the Greens on economics, energy, defense, and punishment.

head: "The Greens want animal protections. Doesn't that make them the sentientist party?"
body: Yes, they are the closest on animal rights. They would extend the Animal Welfare Act to rats, mice, and birds, replace factory farms (CAFOs), and use non-animal chemical testing where available (Animal Rights and Sentience Technology). However, nearly all other social and cultural issues are at odds: they are the opposite on crime and immigration, and the opposite on redistribution. Though they are the best on animal rights, that is nearly all they are aligned on. I would rather put my lot into the vastly more aligned party and rely on private innovation to produce lab-grown meat.

Platform: "abolish the death penalty". Single-payer health care. An Ecosocialist Green New Deal; a national minimum wage indexed to inflation; phasing out nuclear power and fossil, nuclear, and biomass subsidies; replacing CAFOs and banning corporate ownership of farms; extending the Animal Welfare Act; cutting the defense budget; nuclear disarmament; proportional representation and ranked-choice voting.

Directional alignment: animal welfare, where the party replaces factory farms and the United States ought to ban animal agriculture (Animal Rights and Sentientism). Drug decriminalization, where the law ought to go further and make private use legal, and decriminalized sex work, which ought to be legal under licensing (Drugs and Vice); same-sex marriage (Marriage Law).
Full alignment: ranked-choice voting in every election (Ranked-Choice Voting).

Culture: the platform supports "affirmative action," names feminism among its key values, and would add "sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression" to civil rights law. I reject group preferences and agree on protecting sexual orientation, and the law ought not to recognize gender identity as a legal category (Equal Treatment; Feminism and Sex Equality).

Conflicts: single-payer health care (Healthcare). The minimum wage. The phase-out of nuclear power; defense cuts (Military Spending and Projection); abolishing the death penalty; a planned economy (Economic System); publicly funded renewables, where the government ought to subsidize nothing without opt-in (Subsidies and Mandates); national proportional representation, alongside opposition to the voter ID and voter license test I call for (Voting and Elections); bail as a right (Pretrial Detention and Bail).

The Greens show that animal welfare is not tied to free markets. My sentientism is shared on the left, while my economic and security positions are shared on the right. The party's 2024 nominee won 0.56% of the vote.

Not directionally aligned. In order of weight: on crime, the platform says "Abolish the death penalty," calls for "freedom on bail as a right of all defendants charged with non-violent crimes," and seeks to reverse mandatory sentencing, the opposite of my capital and compelled-labor system (Mandatory Death Penalty; Compelled Labor). On race, it supports "affirmative action" and would "Teach all students about white supremacy and intersectionality" (Equal Treatment; Curriculum Content). On gender, it would add "gender identity, and gender expression" to civil rights law (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues). On economics, it favors a planned economy, single-payer care, a national minimum wage, and defense cuts (Economic System). Two overlaps are genuine: animal welfare (Animal Rights and Sentientism) and decriminalizing consensual adult sex for pay, which I already call for allowing under regulation (Drugs and Vice).
