head: Democratic Socialists of America and the Progressive Wing
sub: Democratic Socialists of America and the Progressive Wing

body: I conflict with DSA at the foundation: on property, taxation, policing, prisons, bail, borders, the Senate, Israel, and gender policy. I align only directionally on drug decriminalization and marriage.
sub: Democratic Socialists of America and the Progressive Wing

body: The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is not a ballot party. It is an organization whose members, including Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, mostly run as Democrats. Its program calls for collective ownership of major industries, wealth taxes, abolition of police and prisons, open migration, and abolition of the Senate. It conflicts with my framework at the foundation.
In the 2026 midterms, DSA-endorsed candidates won 7 of the 10 House races they contested (Midterm elections).

head: "Is democratic socialism just Nordic-style social democracy?"
body: No. DSA states, "We want to collectively own the key economic drivers ... such as energy production and transportation," and its program calls for "public ownership of the largest corporations and essential industries." Nordic social democracies keep private ownership and market economies (see Part B). DSA's goal is a different economic system (Economic System).

head: "Does the progressive wing share the full DSA program?"
body: Not necessarily. Many progressive Democrats back Medicare for All and a Green New Deal without endorsing police abolition or public ownership of industry. This page scores DSA's written program, not every progressive politician.

head: "Why do progressive politicians as a group run against your positions?"
body: Because their shared commitments start from the opposite premises, and the gaps can be ranked. First is crime, where the two are opposite. The state ought to impose death for murder and violent rape (Mandatory Death Penalty), forfeiture at three marks (Repeat Offenders), compelled labor for every custodial sentence (Compelled Labor), no duty to retreat (Self-Defense), and larger, better-funded police (Police Power and Accountability). Progressive platforms would abolish the death penalty, widen bail and shorten incarceration, and, in DSA's case, move "towards fully abolishing the police and prison system." Second is group identity: DEI preferences and critical race theory's account of racism as embedded in law and institutions, against one rule for every individual (Equal Treatment). Third is how prevalent gender identity has become in progressive politics, against my biological-sex positions (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues). After those come property, taxes, and the size of the state. I treat property as a negative right (Property Rights). Progressives favor public or collective ownership of key industries. I would set a flat tax and a limited state (Taxation). They favor progressive and wealth taxes to fund a larger state. Some overlaps exist, such as decriminalizing drug use (Drug Policy), detention not set by ability to pay (Pretrial Detention and Bail), and, among Greens, animal welfare. Ending qualified immunity is a surface agreement with the opposite purpose: I pair it with stronger policing, progressives with shrinking it.

Program: "Demilitarize police departments, disempower police unions, and redirect funding to public services as steps towards fully abolishing the police and prison system". End qualified immunity. "Abolish ICE ... Legalize migration, grant amnesty for all immigrants ... end visa caps and quotas"; "abolish the Senate"; proportional representation; public ownership of the largest corporations; "aggressive wealth taxes"; Medicare for All; a Green New Deal; "End all military and economic aid to Israel." DSA reports more than 95,000 members.
Directional alignment: drug decriminalization (Drugs and Vice); same-sex marriage (Marriage Law).
Surface only: ending qualified immunity, which I pair with heavily funded police while DSA pairs it with cutting police budgets "annually towards zero" (Police Power and Accountability).

Culture: the program calls for ending restrictions on "gender expression and transition" and describes current law as "patriarchal restrictions" on family life, while asking to "ban sex discrimination." I agree on banning sex discrimination but hold that sex is biological and that minors receive no transgender treatment (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues).

Conflicts: collective ownership (Property Rights). Wealth taxes (Taxation). Abolishing police and prisons (Order and Security); open migration and amnesty; abolishing the Senate (Federalism); ending aid to Israel; single-payer health care; "Freedom for all incarcerated people" and the end of cash bail, where the state ought to detain anyone found dangerous (Pretrial Detention and Bail).
I begin with negative rights and private property. DSA begins with collective ownership. The two disagree at the foundation, and almost every later position follows from that.

The disagreement can be ranked. Crime comes first, because the two are opposite. The law ought to make murder and violent rape capital (Mandatory Death Penalty), should forfeit the right to life at three marks (Repeat Offenders), serves every custodial sentence as compelled labor (Compelled Labor), recognizes no duty to retreat (Self-Defense), and funds larger, better-paid police (Police Power and Accountability). DSA's program would "Demilitarize police departments, disempower police unions, and redirect funding to public services as steps towards fully abolishing the police and prison system," and the Green platform says "Abolish the death penalty."

Second is group identity. DEI preferences and the premise of critical race theory, that racism is "embedded in legal systems and policies" rather than only in individual bias, organize politics around groups. The law ought to apply one rule to every individual and bar treatment by race, biological sex, or sexual orientation in either direction in employment, admissions, and business (Equal Treatment). Third is the prevalence of gender identity in progressive politics: DSA would end restrictions on "gender expression and transition," against my position that sex is biological and that minors receive no transgender treatment (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues).

The economic divergences follow. On property, DSA's goal of public ownership of "the largest corporations and essential industries" overrides the owner's rights that I treat as basic (Property Rights). On the size of the state, "aggressive wealth taxes" and Medicare for All require a larger and more redistributive government, against my flat tax, opt-in programs, and limited state (Taxation; Welfare and Entitlements).

Some agreements are surface only. Both would end qualified immunity, but for opposite purposes: the state ought to hold officers to a higher standard while expanding and funding police, and DSA treats it as a step toward shrinking and abolishing them (Police Power and Accountability). Both would stop setting detention by ability to pay, but the state ought to detain anyone found dangerous (Pretrial Detention and Bail). These agreements are narrow and do not change the overall direction.

Not directionally aligned. In order of weight, DSA runs opposite to my framework on crime, group identity and race, gender policy, and then property, taxes, and the size of the state. Its points of agreement are narrow and do not change that direction.

I fully align with the Constitution Party on phasing out Social Security, borders, and sex-based policy. I'm directionally aligned on capital punishment, abortion, and limited government (the party goes partway or further). I conflict with them on religion in law, same-sex marriage, tariffs in place of a flat tax, the Federal Reserve, and private-employer discrimination.

The Constitution Party seeks to "restore the American system of law and justice to its Biblical foundations and to limit the federal government to its constitutional boundaries." It matches my framework on limited government, borders, and phasing out Social Security. It conflicts on religion in law and, more mildly, on replacing the income tax with tariff revenue rather than a flat tax.

head: "Isn't this the closest party to you on borders and crime?"
body: On borders, yes: it calls for the return of all illegal aliens, an immigration moratorium, and troops at the border. It supports "capital punishment where appropriate," which is close to my position. But its stated goal of grounding law in the Bible conflicts with my separation of church and state (Role of Religion in Government).

Platform: replace income, payroll, and estate taxes with tariff-based revenue. End the Federal Reserve. Phase out Social Security while meeting obligations already incurred; leave the United Nations; eliminate foreign aid; oppose abortion; return all illegal aliens, impose an immigration moratorium, and station troops at the border.
Full alignment: phasing out Social Security while honoring past obligations. Border enforcement (Immigration and Borders); sex-based policy.

Directional alignment: capital punishment "where appropriate", where the law ought to make it mandatory (Mandatory Death Penalty). Protecting fetal life, though the platform allows no rape exception, offering "compassionate care" "instead of the further violence of abortion", while I free the woman of obligation after rape (Abortion and Bioethics). Limited government, grounded in Scripture; skepticism of global institutions (Global Institutions).
Mixed: guns, where the party's absolutism overshoots my background checks and red flag laws (Gun Rights).

Culture: the platform rejects "legal favor or special protection" for homosexual and transgender people. I agree on not recognizing gender identity in law, but the law ought to protect sexual orientation in employment and public business, and I avoid that wording (Equal Treatment).

Conflicts: biblical foundations for law. Opposition to same-sex marriage. No employment protection for sexual orientation; tariff-based revenue in place of a flat income tax (Taxation; Trade and Economics); ending the Federal Reserve (Monetary Policy); eliminating all foreign aid (Foreign Aid); no position on animal rights.

The Constitution Party agrees with me on many policies but disagrees on their basis. It grounds rights in the Creator and law in Scripture. I ground rights in sentience, and religion ought to stay out of government. The party's 2024 nominee received 12,786 votes.

Directionally aligned on policy; not on foundations. On borders, capital punishment, phasing out Social Security, and sex-based policy, the platform moves the same way. It differs on why: it grounds law in Scripture, while I ground rights in sentience, and religion ought to stay out of government (Role of Religion in Government). It also rejects protection for sexual orientation, which I call for (Equal Treatment).

head: Public Opinion Trends: Socialism and Islamism
sub: Public Opinion Trends: Socialism and Islamism

body: Positive views of socialism among all Americans were flat at 35% to 39% from 2010 to 2025, then rose to 43% in 2026. The change is concentrated among Democrats, younger adults, and, most recently, independents; Republicans are at 14%. DSA's self-reported membership rose, fell, and rose again, and a DSA member won New York City's mayoralty in 2025. Islam is growing in the U.S., now about 1% of adults, mainly through immigration and higher birth rates. I believe general Islamic population growth, not just conversion, is extremely dangerous to the cohesion of our nation. There is no reliable national U.S. trend data on acceptance of Islamist ideas.

body: These are the measured trends. My views of socialism and Islam are set out in Socialism and Islam and Extremism.

head: "Is acceptance of socialism rising?"
body: Overall, only recently. Gallup's rating of socialism stayed between 35% and 39% from 2010 to 2025 and reached 43% in August 2026, the first reading above 39%. Through 2025 the stability hid a split: Democrats rose from 50% to 66% while Republicans fell from 19% to 14%. The 2026 rise came entirely from independents, from 37% to 45%. Capitalism's rating fell from 61% in 2010 to 54% in 2025 and was 55% in 2026. Among Democrats it fell from 51% to 35%. Pew's surveys moved the other way over a shorter span, with positive views of socialism falling from 42% in 2019 to 36% in 2022.

head: "Are young Americans more socialist?"
body: Yes. In Gallup's 2026 poll, adults 18 to 34 viewed socialism more positively than capitalism, 57% to 43%, while those 55 and older favored capitalism 65% to 34%. In Pew's 2022 survey, 44% of adults 18 to 29 viewed socialism positively and 40% capitalism, the lowest capitalism rating of any age group.

head: "How large is DSA?"
body: By its own counts, DSA had about 5,000 members for decades and grew to a peak of just under 79,000 members in good standing in 2021, then fell to about 51,000 by October 2024. Its dues-paying membership rose to 92,912 by December 2025 during Zohran Mamdani's campaign, according to DSA data reported by City & State. The New York City chapter more than doubled, from 5,910 to 13,145. These are self-reported figures.

head: "How did Mamdani win New York?"
body: In the June 2025 Democratic primary, Mamdani led the first round with 43.8% and won the final ranked-choice round over Andrew Cuomo with 56.4%, according to the certified results of the New York City Board of Elections. In the November general election he received 1,114,184 votes on the Democratic and Working Families lines, about 51%, to 906,614 for Cuomo, running as an independent, and 153,749 for Republican Curtis Sliwa.

head: "Is Islam growing in the U.S.?"
body: Yes. Pew estimated 2.35 million Muslims of all ages in 2007, 2.75 million in 2011, and 3.45 million in 2017, about 1.1% of the population, growing by roughly 100,000 a year. Pew projects that Muslims will pass Jews as the second-largest U.S. religious group around 2040 and reach 8.1 million, or 2.1% of the population, by 2050. The 2020 U.S. Religion Census counted 2,771 mosques with about 4.45 million adherents, an increase of nearly 700 mosques and 1.9 million adherents since 2010. Its adherent count uses a different method and runs higher than Pew's estimates. General Islamic population growth, not just conversion, is extremely dangerous to the cohesion of our nation. Survey shares of adults remain about 1%: Pew's Religious Landscape Study found 0.9% in 2014 and 1% in 2023–24, and Gallup's combined 2020–2024 data found 0.9% (0.8% in 2016 and 2017). Pew notes that the 2023–24 study was conducted mainly online and on paper, while earlier waves were by telephone, so comparisons with earlier years should be made cautiously. Gallup finds Muslim identification higher among younger adults, 1.9% of Gen Z and 1.4% of millennials. The growth comes mainly from immigration and births. Pew found 58% of U.S. Muslim adults were born abroad and another 18% are children of immigrants, and Muslims ages 40 to 59 average 2.4 children against 2.1 for all Americans. Pew also reports that conversions into and out of Islam roughly balance.
These are individual reported events, not statistics.

head: Data: blocking friends over politics (U.S., post-2016)

body: Blocking a friend over politics is not a crime and not a reason for viewpoint-based speech law. In PRRI's December 2016 survey, 30% of Democratic women said they had blocked, unfriended, or stopped following someone on social media because of politics, against 10% of Republican women; 14% of Democratic men against 8% of Republican men (overall Republicans about 9%). One-sided social enforcement is a cultural cost of politicized identity, and a reason I refuse equal-outcomes ideology that turns disagreement into moral contamination (Speech; Equal outcomes). Here I compare my framework with parties and governments abroad. The comparisons cover the European Union, Nordic social democracy, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and Singapore and Japan.

The European Parliament elected in 2024 is led by the center-right European People's Party (188 seats), followed by the Socialists and Democrats (136). The national-conservative groups, Patriots for Europe (84), European Conservatives and Reformists (78), and Europe of Sovereign Nations (25), together outnumber the Socialists. The Union pools trade and regulation across member states, which I view cautiously as a supranational layer above national self-government (Global Institutions).

2024 seats: EPP 188, S&D 136, Patriots 84, ECR 78, Renew 77, Greens/EFA 53, Left 46, ESN 25, non-attached 33. The rise of the national-conservative groups mirrors the populist turn among American Republicans.

Using the same order as the US profiles (crime, then DEI and critical race theory, then gender policy, then property, taxes, and the size of the state), no EU group is fully aligned, because of crime. The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights states, "No one shall be condemned to the death penalty, or executed," so every party that accepts the Union's legal order rejects my capital punishment (Mandatory Death Penalty). On gender, the Commission's LGBTIQ equality strategies, now renewed for 2026 to 2030, move toward legal recognition of gender identity, against my biological-sex positions (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues). The national-conservative groups (Patriots, ECR, ESN) are the closest on borders and national sovereignty, the area where I'm most skeptical of the Union (Global Institutions).

Closest alignment: the national-conservative groups (Patriots for Europe, ECR, ESN), for their emphasis on borders and national sovereignty. Conflict: like every group, they operate within a Charter that bars the death penalty.

The Nordic countries combine market economies and private ownership with large, tax-funded welfare states. Denmark has the highest tax-to-GDP ratio in the EU. Wages are set mainly through collective agreements rather than a statutory minimum wage. This model is the strongest argument that a generous welfare state can coexist with free markets. I still reject it because the welfare state is compulsory (Welfare and Entitlements). It also shows how DSA's program differs from social democracy: the Nordic countries kept private ownership.

Not directionally aligned on the size of the state; partly aligned on crime in Sweden. The large compulsory welfare state runs against my framework (Welfare and Entitlements). On crime, Sweden's 2022 Tidö Agreement between the Moderates, Christian Democrats, Liberals, and Sweden Democrats called for "dubbla straff för gängkriminella" (double penalties for gang criminals), an end to sentencing discounts for offenders over 18, and tougher penalties for violent and sexual crimes. Doubled gang sentences took effect in August 2026. That moves in my direction on punishment, but no Nordic party proposes capital punishment (Mandatory Death Penalty).

Closest alignment: the Sweden Democrats and their Tidö partners (Moderates, Christian Democrats, Liberals), whose agreement produced the crime package. Conflict: the welfare state they govern within stays compulsory and tax-funded.

Labour won 411 seats in 2024 with 33.7% of the vote. The Conservatives won 121 seats with 23.7%, and the Liberal Democrats 72 with 12.2%. A large majority on a third of the vote shows how first-past-the-post voting turns pluralities into majorities, the same mechanism behind the American two-party system (Voting and Elections). Like the US, Britain has a right-of-center and a left-of-center party, with a third party far underrepresented relative to its vote share.

On gender, the most important British development came from the courts rather than the parties. In For Women Scotland v The Scottish Ministers (2025), the Supreme Court held unanimously that "sex," "man," and "woman" in the Equality Act 2010 "refer to biological sex," which matches my definition (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues).

Closest alignment: Restore Britain, led by Rupert Lowe, is the closest on crime. It pledges to "Hold a Binding Referendum on Restoring the Death Penalty," saying "It is just to execute those guilty of the most heinous crimes," and to "Deport All Illegal Migrants" (Restore Britain – Make Britain Safe Again; Restore Britain – Reverse Mass Immigration; Mandatory Death Penalty). It also aligns on residency and citizenship. It would deport a legally resident foreign national who "lives in social housing, claims benefits," "fails to integrate," or "commits crime," and would strip citizenship from "dual-national Islamic extremists" (Restore Britain – Reverse Mass Immigration; Restore Britain – Make Britain Safe Again). The United States ought to adopt both in adapted form: listed benefits, a two-year English and civics test, removal for any crime above a basic infraction, and a court finding by clear and convincing evidence. On extremists it ought to go further than deportation: terrorism and treason are punished by death or secure confinement, with citizenship forfeiture added for dual nationals, under religion-neutral offenses and without statelessness (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). Conflict: it describes Britain as "a Christian nation" (Restore Britain – Reverse Mass Immigration), where religion ought to stay out of government (Role of Religion in Government). Reform UK is next. Its 2024 contract promised "Prison for violent crimes and possessing a knife," to "Scrap all Diversity, Equality and Inclusion (DE&I) roles and regulations," and "No gender questioning, social transitioning or pronoun swapping" in schools (Equal Treatment; Gender Identity in Schools and Institutions). Conflicts: it makes no death-penalty pledge, and replacing the Equality Act outright would leave open whether sexual orientation stays protected in employment, which I call for.

In the 2025 federal election the CDU/CSU won 28.6% (CDU 22.6%, CSU 6.0%) and the Alternative for Germany (AfD) came second with 20.8%. Proportional representation lets a populist-right party grow inside parliament instead of inside an existing party, as MAGA did inside the Republican Party. Germany's federal structure is closer to the American model than most European systems (Federalism).

Crime: no German party is aligned, because the Basic Law states, "Capital punishment is abolished" (Mandatory Death Penalty). Gender: the 2024 Self-Determination Act, which lets people change their legal sex entry by declaration, passed 372 to 251 with the SPD, Greens, FDP, and Left in favor. The CDU/CSU and the AfD voted against. On that question the CDU/CSU and AfD move with my framework and the governing coalition of the time moved against it (LGBTQ+ and Identity Issues).
Closest alignment: the CDU/CSU and the AfD, which both voted against the Self-Determination Act. Conflict: neither can propose capital punishment under the Basic Law.

Switzerland limits the power of parties through direct democracy. A popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures within 18 months to force a national vote on a constitutional amendment. An optional referendum needs 50,000 signatures within 100 days to put a new federal law to a vote. Citizens can overrule what parties agree on in parliament. I protect rights from majority votes, but of the systems on this page, it is the closest to my preference for decentralized power under citizen control (Federalism).

The Swiss People's Party (SVP) is the closest on crime and borders. Its 2010 initiative for the automatic deportation of foreigners convicted of serious crimes passed with 52.91% of the vote and a majority of cantons. The Social Democrats, Greens, FDP, and CVP opposed it (Border Security).
Closest alignment: the SVP, for its record on deporting foreign offenders and on borders.

Both countries have long been governed by a dominant party and both keep capital punishment. Singapore's People's Action Party won 87 of 97 seats with 65.57% of the vote in 2025. Singapore carried out at least 9 executions in 2024, mostly for drug offences, against 25 in the US. Japan's Liberal Democratic Party has governed almost continuously since 1955, though it lost its lower-house majority in 2024. Japan retains the death penalty but carried out no executions in 2024. I share their emphasis on order. I share Singapore's death penalty for selling hard drugs, but conflict with it on executing for cannabis, which ought to be legal; in 2023 Singapore executed Tangaraju Suppiah for abetting the trafficking of about 1 kg of cannabis (Drug Policy).

Crime: both countries keep capital punishment under their long-governing parties, the closest match to my framework on this page (Mandatory Death Penalty); Singapore also uses it for drug offences, which I share for large-scale hard-drug distribution but not for cannabis. Gender and marriage: in 2022 Singapore's Parliament repealed Section 377A, which criminalized sex between men, 93 to 3, a move toward my framework. It also added Article 156 to the Constitution so that no fundamental-liberties challenge can invalidate a law defining "marriage as a union between a man and a woman," which conflicts with my marriage freedom (Marriage Law).

Closest alignment: Singapore's People's Action Party and Japan's Liberal Democratic Party, the long-governing parties under which capital punishment is kept. Conflicts: Singapore executes for cannabis trafficking and protects a man-woman definition of marriage from constitutional challenge.

No American party matches my positions. Republicans score highest (+9): they lead on borders, DEI, sex-based policy, and defense, and move my way on punishment, policing, guns, and abortion, though they keep qualified immunity, defend animal agriculture, and fund private schools through tax credits. The Libertarian and Constitution parties tie (+3). The Libertarians match on economics and personal freedom but oppose the death penalty and leave private employment unprotected. The Constitution Party matches on borders, punishment, and sex-based policy but grounds law in religion and rejects protection for sexual orientation. Democrats follow (−10), agreeing on marriage and drug reform but opposing me on crime, alliances, Israel, economics, group preferences, and gender policy. The Greens and DSA conflict most (−13). DSA and the Greens run further than the Democrats on punishment and feminism, the Greens also on guns, and the Greens are the only party that moves my way on animals.

Each US party is scored on sixteen core principles of my framework, using its official platform or program together with its officeholders' record and its base's stance. Each party is graded against the realistic options, not against a perfect match: a party that moves my way earns alignment, and conflict is reserved for parties that move the opposite way. On the eleven general rows, +1 means the party moves my way, 0 means it is mixed or silent, and −1 means it moves the opposite way. The crime row (mandatory death penalty, firm punishment) and the four culture rows (DEI and group preferences, gender and transgender policy, feminism, and protected traits) are double-weighted from −2 to +2: ±2 for full alignment or full conflict, ±1 for directional. An unweighted total, counting only the sign of each row, is shown beneath the weighted total. The culture rows are measured against my equal-treatment rule: race, biological sex, and sexual orientation are protected in either direction, gender identity is not a legal category, and there are no DEI preferences. Scores are summed. Against progressive politics, I rank my divergences in this order: crime first, then DEI and critical race theory, then gender policy, then property, taxes, and the size of the state. Apart from the double weighting, the total shows how many principles a party shares, not how important each one is, so it should be read alongside the profiles above. Under the earlier equal-weight scorecard of twelve rows the totals were Democrats −7, Republicans +2, Libertarians +3, Greens −5, DSA −6, Constitution +3.

head: "Isn't the scorecard self-serving? Of course you rank parties by how close they are to you."
body: Yes, by design. The scorecard measures alignment with my framework, not which party is better in general, and a reader who holds different principles would score the parties differently. What keeps it honest is the method. Each score rests on the party's own platform and its record in practice, the rows and weights are published, mixed or silent positions score zero, each party is graded against the realistic options rather than against a perfect match, and conflicts are listed even for the parties that score highest, such as the Republican platform's protection of officers from lawsuits. The double-weighted rows score −2 to +2, ±2 for full alignment or full conflict and ±1 for directional. The unweighted totals count only the sign of each row, so readers can see what the weights change. Without them Republicans still lead (+7), the Libertarian and Constitution parties tie (+3), Democrats follow (−8), and the Greens and DSA tie at the bottom (−9).

November 17, 2026 · Grade: Directionally aligned (details differ)
Status as of Nov 18, 2026: Open. Preliminary injunction and stay; the case continues in the district court.

Since 1991 the federal government has counted any internship or practicum a certified school authorizes for academic credit as curricular practical training (CPT), work that foreign students on F-1 visas may do as "an integral part of an established curriculum." In broadcast messages of August 12 and 24, 2026, the Student and Exchange Visitor Program told schools that training counts only if it is required of every student in the degree program, not elective training taken for credit, and warned school officials of civil and criminal liability. Schools responded by denying or rescinding CPT and changing curricula. Immigration and Customs Enforcement counted 140,775 student visa holders authorized for CPT in 2024, according to Reuters. On November 17, 2026, in Association of American Universities v. Department of Homeland Security (D. Mass., No. 1:26-cv-14520), Judge Julia E. Kobick stayed both broadcasts and barred the government from applying their reading to the plaintiffs' members. She found the change likely arbitrary and capricious because the agency departed from its long-standing position "without acknowledging, let alone explaining, the change or considering serious reliance interests." The government had argued the messages "merely implement the correct reading of the existing regulation."

A student visa is for study, and work for foreign nationals belongs to the employment path, which opens only for labor needs the domestic workforce cannot meet first (Immigration and Borders; Skilled-Worker Visas (H-1B)). Confining student work to training the degree actually requires keeps the visa to its purpose, and protects American graduates competing for the same internships. The objection is that elective internships are part of a real education and that schools relied on the old reading for 35 years. Reliance is a reason to change the rule in the open, not a reason to keep it: an elective placement for credit is still a job, and a credit-bearing elective is the easiest place to pass off work as study. The method lost, and it should have. A policy that reverses three decades of practice belongs in a published rule or a statute, with notice and a date set in advance, not in a broadcast email threatening school officials with prosecution for approvals they gave under the old reading. This builds on Fixed terms for foreign students struck down.

body: A Homeland Security rule published July 17, 2026 would have ended "duration of status," which lets foreign students (F), exchange visitors (J) and foreign journalists (I) stay as long as they keep their status and progress in their programs. In its place it set fixed admission periods capped at four years for students and exchange visitors, with extensions granted at the agency's discretion. It also limited changes of program and joint degrees. The department said fixed terms would let it check periodically whether these visitors are complying and reduce overstays. On November 16, 2026, in Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. Department of Homeland Security (D. Mass., No. 1:26-cv-13799), Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV vacated the rule. He had already postponed it in September. He found the rule exceeded the department's authority and wrote, "Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity—providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States—that Congress sought to permit and encourage."
sub: Fixed terms for foreign students struck down

body: Student visas are one of the named entry paths I keep, and every path runs under values vetting (Immigration and Borders). A fixed term with a check before any extension fits that: a visitor is re-examined rather than admitted once and left alone for as long as a program runs. The objection is that four years is too short for many degrees and that discretionary extensions disrupt honest students. That objection lands on the details, not the direction. An extension tied to documented progress and a fresh values check answers it. Rules on changing majors or joint degrees do nothing for vetting, and the court was right that they reach past the purpose of the visa. The cleaner route is for Congress to write fixed terms and periodic re-vetting into the statute, so the policy does not depend on a rule a court can set aside.

sub: Labor test for employer-sponsored green cards

body: The Labor Department proposes to rebuild the labor market test that employers must pass before sponsoring a foreign worker for a green card (permanent labor certification, or PERM). It would eliminate Schedule A, the list of occupations exempt from the test, which has named only nurses and physical therapists since 1991. The department says the Immigration and Nationality Act requires a finding that no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers exist for each position, so it cannot exempt a whole occupation, and that more than 2,000 comments on an earlier request for information offered no reliable method to keep the list. The rule would also strengthen recruitment requirements, add safeguards for U.S. workers laid off by the sponsoring employer or by third-party staffing firms, widen notice of filing to U.S. workers, and write electronic filing into the regulations. It cites Executive Orders 14159 and 14431.
sub: Labor test for employer-sponsored green cards

body: American labor needs should be met first through the domestic workforce, and only then by immigration, which I rank behind values fit and assimilation (Skilled-Worker Visas (H-1B); Immigration and Borders). A test applied to each job, rather than a standing exemption for whole occupations, does that. The strongest objection is the nursing shortage: the Health Resources and Services Administration projects a 10% shortfall of registered nurses in 2027, 24% outside metropolitan areas. The rule does not bar foreign nurses. Where no qualified American applies, the test certifies the job, so a real shortage shows up in the recruitment results. What ends is certification without looking, on a list the department says it could not verify.

body: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration withheld 4% of New York's fiscal 2027 federal-aid highway funds, about $73.5 million, because the state issued commercial driver's licenses to non-domiciled immigrants that stayed valid for five or eight years instead of expiring with the holder's lawful-presence documents. In an audit sample of 200 such licenses, 101 outlasted the documents; about 32,600 New Yorkers held one. The agency conceded that the regulations in force when it audited New York contained no expiration-matching requirement. That requirement came later, in a final rule published February 13, 2026, and effective March 16, 2026, after an earlier interim rule was stayed by the D.C. Circuit. In State of New York v. U.S. Department of Transportation, the Second Circuit (Judge Nathan, joined by Judge Merriam) granted New York's petition and set the determination aside. Judge Schwartz concurred in the judgment only, writing that the case turns on the text alone. The Transportation Department said, "We've put a stop to the madness," and says about 30,000 such licenses have been canceled nationwide.
sub: Highway funds withheld from New York over immigrant truck licenses

body: A license that lets a non-citizen drive a truck for years after his lawful presence ends is a work permit the law does not give him, and the law ought to be enforced as written (Immigration and Borders). The current rule, which requires these licenses to expire with lawful presence, is the direction I want. But agencies cannot go beyond the rules that authorize them, and a penalty for breaking a requirement that was not yet written fails that test (Government Structure and Checks). The court was right, and the rule now in force fixes the gap the proper way.

sub: Citizenship checks for HUD housing aid

body: HUD's final rule under Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980 requires every applicant and recipient in covered housing programs to prove U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status, at any age, ending the exemption for people 62 and older. Prorated aid to "mixed" families, where some members are ineligible, becomes temporary pending verification instead of running indefinitely, and a deferral of termination of up to 18 months stays available. HUD estimates that about 20,000 mixed-status families received assistance in December 2024, about 78 percent of them with children. It rejected grandfathering current families because low turnover would delay moving the aid to fully eligible families on waiting lists by more than a decade.
sub: Citizenship checks for HUD housing aid

body: Non-citizens should not draw housing aid. A green-card holder who takes it should be removed after a court finding (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents), and the safety floor ought to offer emergency shelter, not housing (Housing, Zoning, and Homelessness). Verifying status before paying is the direction I want. Commenters warned that mixed-status families, most with children, would be evicted. HUD's answer holds: there is more demand than aid, so every subsidy kept by an ineligible household is one denied to an eligible family on the waiting list. The details differ: I hold that a U.S.-citizen child keeps any benefit the child qualifies for, while this rule ends a mixed family's whole subsidy after the deferral.

In a 60 Minutes interview recorded November 6 and aired November 8, President Trump said his deportation policy was "too tough" on people "that had good jobs" whose one violation was that "they came into the country illegally," and said he would "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats. Asked whether a deal could create legal status for undocumented workers, he said yes. CBS News exit polling found 58% of midterm voters thought the administration's immigration actions had gone too far. Hours after the interview was recorded, he named Stephen Miller, an architect of his enforcement strategy, as White House chief of staff in place of Susie Wiles.

The United States ought to remove illegal immigrants by force, and entering without inspection is a crime from the first day, whatever job a person holds afterward (Border Security and Immigration Enforcement). The claim is that long-settled, tax-paying workers are the wrong target. I believe a legal-status deal rewards the violation and invites the next wave, as the 1986 amnesty did. So far this is a statement, not an order, and the Miller appointment points the other way. I would grade any actual legalization proposal on its text.

Status as of Nov 8, 2026: Open. On November 2, in Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans v. Edlow, No. 1:26-cv-14817-MJJ (D. Mass.), Judge Myong J. Joun extended the October 27 administrative stay through December 4, 2026 and reset the §705 stay hearing to November 24 (government opposition due Nov 13, reply Nov 20). No newer order found on November 8. This is not a ruling on the merits.

On October 14, 2026, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services issued an interim final rule, effective that day, that cuts the time a refugee has to answer a Notice of Intent to Terminate from 30 days to 10, so the agency can end refugee status faster when it finds the person was not a refugee at the time of admission. The Department of Homeland Security estimated the rule could reach as many as 186,000 refugees. On October 27, U.S. District Judge Julia Kobick in Boston paused the rule through November 6 to preserve the status quo until the case is heard by another judge.

Ending status that was obtained by fraud or error matches my position that lawful residence is a conditional privilege (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). Critics say ten days is too short to gather records from abroad. The deeper problem is who decides: my rule is that every removal case should get written notice, a hearing before a judge, the chance to present evidence, and federal-court review, with refugees sent only to a safe third country. An agency notice with a ten-day answer window and no judge is not that process. The United States ought to end fraudulent refugee status through a court finding by clear and convincing evidence, and move those cases quickly once a judge rules.

Texas, No. 26A500).

body: Ending a mechanism that parks removal cases indefinitely fits my position that people here illegally should be removed (Immigration and Borders). The challengers' strongest point is the method: the government agreed with the plaintiff to have a court void its own rule and forbid any future one, the result they call "egregious collusion." That point holds. A rule the government no longer wants should be repealed in the open through the rulemaking process, with public notice and a stated reason, not through a same-day settlement that also binds future administrations. I support the outcome and reject the route.

body: Since July 8, 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has treated people who entered without being admitted, including those arrested in the interior after years in the country, as "applicants for admission" held under 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A), who "may not be released from ICE custody except by [discretionary] parole" and get no bond hearing. The Board of Immigration Appeals adopted that reading in Matter of Yajure Hurtado (2025). On October 23, 2026, the full Fifth Circuit, in Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara (No. 26-50183), held that three men who had lived in the United States unlawfully for many years had no due-process right to individual hearings on danger or flight risk before being detained pending removal, and that the length of their detention raised no constitutional problem. It reversed a divided panel that had required hearings within 90 days and vacated the district courts' releases. Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the court. Judges Southwick and Higginson were among the dissenters.
sub: No bond hearings for unlawful entrants upheld

body: Holding people who entered unlawfully while their removal is decided fits my position that illegal immigrants should be removed (Immigration and Borders), and the court is right that Congress, not judges, sets these rules. The critics' strongest point is that people here for a decade are held with no hearing at all. Their unlawful entry is the same act whether it was last month or ten years ago, and detention pending removal is not punishment. Where the details differ is time. My rule for anyone detained is that the state moves fast: a detained defendant is tried within 90 days (Pretrial Detention and Bail), and the ruling sets no limit on how long removal proceedings may run while a person is held. The United States ought to pair mandatory detention with a fixed deadline for deciding the case.

body: October 21, 2026 · Grade: Directionally aligned (details differ)
Status as of Nov 11, 2026: Open. On November 9 the Supreme Court stayed the district court's injunction pending a petition for certiorari; construction may resume.

In 2026 the Secretary of Homeland Security issued three waivers under section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act for border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector of Texas, which takes in 517 miles of the Rio Grande, almost a quarter of the southwest border: Secretary Kristi Noem's of February 17 (about 164 miles of barrier), and Secretary Markwayne Mullin's of May 15 (roads and about 17 miles of vehicle barrier inside Big Bend National Park) and July 27 (about 160 miles in the Big Bend and Del Rio sectors). Each found the area one "of high illegal entry," citing more than 89,000 apprehensions between ports of entry in the sector from 2021 to 2025, and waived, within the project areas, laws including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. The May and July waivers also list the National Park Service Organic Act. On October 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone halted all construction in the sector "until and unless" the government complies with those laws. Her October 14 opinion found the challengers likely to win under the major questions doctrine: over thirty years the sector's annual apprehensions ran between 0.3% and 2.2% of the border-wide total, and "the Big Bend Sector has the lowest rate of illegal entry along the entire U.S.-Mexico border." On October 21 the Solicitor General asked the Supreme Court to stay her order and summarily reverse it (Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, No. 26A560). The application argues that the statute allows only constitutional claims against a waiver, and that "leaving a 300-plus-mile gap in border defenses would act as a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors to exploit as other routes close off." On November 9, 2026, the Supreme Court granted the stay in an unsigned opinion, with Justice Jackson noting she would deny it, and declined to summarily reverse. It held the government "exceedingly likely to prevail" on its argument that the district court lacked jurisdiction, because the challengers' claim, "however it is labeled," alleges only that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority: "There is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim." It also cited the government's sworn estimate of "nearly half a million dollars in costs per day" that cannot be recouped, and held that Congress's waiver provision "reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction" over the aesthetic, recreational and environmental harms the challengers alleged. Construction may proceed while the government's petition for certiorari is pending.

The court's evidence holds on its own terms: by apprehensions, in total and per mile, Big Bend is the least-crossed sector on the border, and the waivers set aside wildlife law inside a national park. That finding goes to whether the statute's "areas of high illegal entry" reaches this sector, which is now before the Supreme Court. My position is a heavily secured and fortified border along its whole length, not only in its busiest sectors (Border Security and Immigration Enforcement), so building here is the direction I want. The details differ on habitat. The United States ought to build in and alongside nature rather than demolishing it, and site extraction away from protected species' habitat (Conservation vs Development). A blanket waiver of wildlife law across a national park does not meet that. My rule for barriers in protected habitat is in Border Barriers and Protected Habitat. The Court's ruling settles who may hear the challenge, not whether a blanket waiver inside a national park is good policy, so my habitat objection stands.

On January 20, 2025, the Department of Homeland Security rescinded the long-standing "sensitive locations" policy, letting immigration officers use "discretion" and "common sense" to make arrests at places such as churches, mosques and synagogues. ICE now lets supervisors approve operations "at or near" them case by case. On October 20, 2026, in Mennonite Church USA v. DHS, a 2–1 panel of the D.C. Circuit (Judges Pan and Wilkins; Judge Rao dissenting) held that 27 Christian and Jewish groups likely have standing to challenge the change and sent the case back to the district court to reconsider a preliminary injunction. The policy stays in effect for now.

The United States ought to remove illegal immigrants forcefully and allow no sanctuary that obstructs federal law (Border Security and Immigration Enforcement, Federalism), and a place of worship should not shield anyone from the law. That matches the direction of the rescission. The government also ought to require due process in each case (Due Process and Rule of Law), and the policy leaves the limits to supervisors' discretion rather than fixed rules, so the details differ. My rule for arrests at places of worship is in Enforcement at Houses of Worship.

September 29, 2026 · Grade: Directionally aligned (details differ)
Status as of Nov 16, 2026: Open. Respondents' brief is due November 16, the reply brief December 1, and argument is set for December 9.

In Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., the Supreme Court stayed a district court judgment that had vacated the administration's guidance on removing people with final orders to countries not named in those orders, and agreed to hear the case, with argument set for December 9, 2026. Under the guidance, people can be sent to countries that have promised not to persecute or torture them without further steps. For other countries, the government gives notice and generally waits at least 24 hours for a fear claim. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson would have denied the stay.

Removal to a safe third country matches my position (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). It differs in detail: the United States ought never to return anyone to persecution or torture, and ought to require notice and a real chance to be heard (Due Process and Rule of Law), and a 24-hour window, or none where the country has given assurances, may fall short of that: a third country ought to count as safe only after review of the person's case, not on assurances alone (Removal of Non-Citizen Residents). body: Proclamation 10903 invokes the Alien Enemies Act of 1798, declaring that Tren de Aragua, a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization, is carrying out an "invasion of and predatory incursion into the United States." It makes Venezuelan citizens 14 or older who are members of the group, are in the United States, and are not naturalized or lawful permanent residents liable to be "apprehended, restrained, secured, and removed." In A.A.R.P. v. Trump (2025) the Supreme Court barred removals under the Act of the detainees in a Northern District of Texas class case while appeals ran, and sent back the question of what notice is due. In August 2026 the full Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal as moot without reaching the merits, because the named detainees had already been removed under ordinary immigration law. On October 21 the government stipulated that it would not remove any member of the proposed class under the Act until the courts finally decide the Proclamation's legality or the case ends. On November 6 the district court let three detainees replace the removed plaintiffs. Class certification and summary judgment are pending. On November 12 the Justice Department dropped its Ninth Circuit appeal of an injunction barring such removals of a class held in the Central District of California.
sub: Alien Enemies Act invoked against Tren de Aragua

body: Members of a foreign terrorist gang who are here illegally ought to be removed, by force where needed (Border Security and Immigration Enforcement), and the Proclamation spares citizens and green-card holders. Ordinary immigration law already removes people here illegally, as the removal of the named plaintiffs shows, and the government ought to rely on it, with a court finding in each case. Wartime and emergency powers ought to be narrow and to rest on Congress's vote (Emergency Powers).

November 13, 2026 · Grade: Directionally aligned (details differ)
Status as of Nov 15, 2026: Open. The third 90-day extension starts November 16, 2026. Covered cargo must be loaded by 11:59 p.m. ET on February 14, 2027.

The Jones Act requires cargo moving between U.S. ports to travel on ships built in the United States, owned by U.S. companies and crewed by Americans. In March 2026, a month after the war with Iran began, the administration waived it to lower fuel and fertilizer prices. In August it extended the waiver but made decisions case by case. On November 13, Customs and Border Protection announced that Homeland Security had approved a third 90-day extension of the March 17 waiver at the Department of War's request. A shipper must apply first. The Maritime Administration checks whether a U.S.-qualified ship is available, and the Department of War decides whether the voyage is covered. Reuters calls it the longest waiver in the law's history. Bloomberg, citing government data analyzed by the Cato Institute, counts 338 voyages on foreign ships since March. Shipbuilders opposed any extension.

The waiver moves in the direction I want. I believe support for American shipbuilding should come through tax and regulatory relief, not through a mandate that every cargo between U.S. ports ride on a U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed ship and that raises what Americans pay for fuel and goods (Coastal Shipping and the Jones Act). Lifting that mandate for fuel and fertilizer shipments is regulatory relief. The details differ: this is a rolling executive waiver, renewed a third time, rather than a change in law set by Congress or a waiver that expires on its own (Emergency Powers). Where the military needs ships and crews it cannot buy in time of war, Congress ought to fund that need directly and in the open.

Status as of Nov 14, 2026: Open. Optional for states. Runs through June 30, 2027.

Under the 2025 reconciliation law, certain Medicaid applicants and enrollees ages 19 to 64 must meet a work requirement starting January 1, 2027, unless excluded: 80 hours a month of work, community service, a work program or half-time schooling, or a set monthly income. On November 13, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services offered states an optional "hold harmless" period through June 30, 2027. States that use it will check whether each person meets the requirement or is excluded, but "will not deny applications or disenroll otherwise eligible individuals solely for failure to meet the requirement." The agency also urged states to verify work and exclusions from data they already hold before asking people for paperwork.

Welfare ought to be a bare-minimum floor, and non-emergency Medicaid is a program the United States ought to wind down (Welfare and Entitlements). A work rule for adults who can work is a step in that direction, and I graded the same rule for SNAP as directionally aligned (SNAP work-requirement rule). This guidance lets states run the rule for six months with no consequence for ignoring it. Defenders say states need time to fix their systems so that people who are working, or are exempt, are not cut off by a paperwork error. That is a real risk, and checking the data a state already holds before asking for paperwork is the right fix for it. But that fix applies from the first day. It does not require suspending the consequence for everyone, including people the state's own data show are not working. The grade is directional because data-first verification is sound administration.

Status as of Nov 11, 2026: Open. Proposed rule. Comments close December 10, 2026.

The Department of Agriculture proposed rules to write the 2025 reconciliation law's SNAP changes into regulation. Adults subject to the time limit can receive SNAP for only three months in 36 unless they work or train 20 hours a week. The law raised the top age for that limit to 64, lowered the child exception so only parents of children under 14 are exempt, and ended the exceptions for homeless people, veterans and young adults leaving foster care. States can now get area waivers only where unemployment is over 10 percent, not for a shortage of jobs (Alaska and Hawaii have their own test). Beyond the law, the department proposes stricter data rules for waiver requests and would drop "imminently homeless" from the definition of a homeless individual. It says the changes keep the program focused on "self-sufficiency for those who can work."

Requiring people who can work to work or train before drawing food aid is the direction I want: welfare ought to be a bare-minimum floor, and food aid paid from general taxes is a transfer the United States ought to phase out (Welfare and Entitlements). Work rules for able-bodied adults move SNAP toward that floor. The details differ in two places. My plan replaces SNAP with an earnings-only top-up and a last-resort allowance for people who cannot work, rather than keeping the program with tighter rules. And the change applies to people already enrolled, while I hold that people who followed the old rules get a phase-out period that honors their existing benefits.

November 10, 2026 · Grade: Directionally aligned (details differ)
Status as of Nov 12, 2026: Open. Proposed rule. Comments close December 10, 2026.

The Department of Agriculture proposed limiting SNAP's categorical eligibility to households that receive TANF assistance itself. Under current rules, any non-cash benefit or service from a TANF-funded program can make a household eligible, so states can skip SNAP's federal asset test and enroll households above its income limits, under gross-income limits as high as 200 percent of the poverty line. The department estimates that 3.2 million households, 6.3 million people, would leave SNAP by fiscal 2029 because their income or resources exceed the federal limits, and that federal benefit spending would fall by about $44.6 billion over fiscal 2027–2031. About 1.78 million children would lose automatic free school meals, though about 97 percent would still qualify on income.

Food aid ought to go only to people who meet the program's own tests, and in my plan it is replaced by a bare-minimum floor (Welfare and Entitlements), so closing this route is the direction I want. Critics say it cuts six million people from food aid. By the department's own count, those are households whose income or resources exceed the limits Congress set, and nearly all of the children keep free or reduced-price meals on income. The details differ in the same two places as the work rule: I would replace SNAP rather than tighten it, and people enrolled under the old rules ought to get a phase-out that honors their existing benefits.

October 22, 2026 · Grade: Directionally aligned (details differ)

Executive Order 14438 of October 22, 2026, "Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People," directs the Federal Housing Finance Agency to have Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac pilot automatic cancellation of mortgage insurance once a borrower's equity, measured at current market value, meets the requirement, for mortgages made after the pilot is established. To turn the pilot that accepts an automated title review in place of a lender's title insurance on refinances into a nationwide program, with the savings passed to borrowers; and to consider waiving appraisals and cutting fees on refinances that lower the monthly payment. It sets up a Task Force on Manufactured Housing Innovation, due to report in 180 days, to remove "Federal requirements and duplicative reviews that unnecessarily impede" factory-built housing, to study conditioning federal grants on state and local adoption of standardized permitting, and to prepare legislative recommendations, building on Executive Order 14394 (Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Home Construction, March 13, 2026). Section 5 directs the Secretaries of Agriculture and Veterans Affairs, under 42 U.S.C. 1490a(a)(1)(B) and 38 U.S.C. 3762(c)(1), to "reduce the interest rates charged on single-family home loans made directly by their respective departments."

Cutting fees, paperwork and duplicate federal rules that add to the cost of a home is the direction I want: housing supply is a market matter, and regulation that only raises the price of building or buying should go (Housing, Zoning, and Homelessness). It also serves my goal of young adults affording a home early (Births and Family Formation). The details differ in two places. Lowering the rate on loans the government makes directly is a housing subsidy paid by every taxpayer, and federal home lending ought to cover its own costs, with any below-cost rate funded only by taxpayer opt-in (Government Home Lending). And tying federal grants to local permitting rules reaches into land use that belongs to states and localities (Federalism). The task force only studies this so far.

Federal law already ends private mortgage insurance automatically once the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the home's original value. Measuring equity at current value lets owners in rising markets drop it sooner, at no cost to taxpayers. The home builders' trade group, the National Association of Home Builders, estimates that regulation makes up 23.8% of a new home's price, about $93,870. A trade group has a stake in that number, and the exact share is contested. That does not change my conclusion: rules that protect no one add cost at any share, and removing them lowers the price without a subsidy. Cheaper direct federal loans do the opposite and move the cost onto every taxpayer.

After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026, that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs (Reciprocal tariffs), the President imposed a 10% global import surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows up to 150 days. It expired on July 24, 2026. On July 23 he imposed tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on all goods from 60 economies under Section 301, after the U.S. Trade Representative found they had not banned, or not effectively enforced bans on, imports made with forced labor, with exemptions for some products and for USMCA-compliant imports. A separate Section 301 action sets 25% on Brazil. Under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, duties of 50% apply to select Canadian goods in three disputes (motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages and dairy), with no USMCA exemption and on top of any Section 232 duties. Section 232 national-security tariffs continue on steel, aluminum, copper, autos, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, lumber and other goods. On October 23, 2026, a proclamation swapped some products under the Canadian motor-vehicle duties, removing plywood, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment and packing crates and adding certain valves, carpets and waste products, effective October 30.

Defenders point out that each of these laws, unlike IEEPA, was written by Congress and requires a finding or an investigation before duties are imposed. That is true, and it is why the grade is directional rather than full opposition. It does not meet my rule. I hold tariffs to be good in theory but questionable in practice, used cautiously and targeted at leverage, strategic industries and national-security threats, and set by Congress, with executive tariffs only under clear, narrow statutory authority, for a stated purpose and a fixed period (Trade and Economics). A global surcharge under a balance-of-payments law, which the government's own brief to the Federal Circuit said had no "obvious application" to trade deficits, is not narrow authority. Punishing forced labor is a sound purpose, but a flat rate on every good from 60 economies taxes far more than the goods made with forced labor. And 50% duties on an ally's goods are the broad tariffs I reject, not targeted leverage against a threat.

Status as of Nov 5, 2026: Open. Greenland's parliament approved the agreement 16–0 on November 3. The Danish parliament is expected to vote on November 19.

The United States, the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland signed an agreement in New York amending the 1951 agreement on the defense of Greenland. It allows the United States to modernize and expand Pituffik Space Base and to establish new Defense Areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig on terms still to be mutually agreed, lets either party propose further Defense Areas, and lets U.S. aircraft fly over and land anywhere in Greenland and U.S. public vessels move undersea in its territorial waters. It bars states outside NATO from military installations or a persistent military presence in Greenland, and bars investors from states outside NATO, NATO partners and the EU from control, significant influence or sensitive access in critical infrastructure and resource extraction unless the parties agree. It names a Golden Dome defense system as a shared interest, reaffirms "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark" and the Greenlandic people's "right to self-determination," has no end date, and requires an independent Greenland to remain in NATO and take on Denmark's obligations under it. No territory changes hands and the agreement grants no U.S. resource rights. It enters into force only after Greenland's and Denmark's parliaments approve it. Greenland's parliament debated it on October 12, 2026 and referred it to committee.

I support this agreement for U.S. security. It expands U.S. defense where Russia and China seek a foothold, keeps their militaries and capital out of a strategic territory (Russia, Ukraine, and China/Taiwan, Sanctions and Economic Statecraft), makes room for missile defense (Military Space), and comes through an alliance that makes the United States safer without giving up its sovereignty (Alliances and NATO). I want the United States doing what it needs to for its own security. I dislike the pressure tactics and threats against a friendly country that came before it, and I would prefer it had been reached more diplomatically (Interventionism vs Non-Intervention, Sovereignty and Borders). If the security concern is overwhelming and truly justified, I would still get behind that justification, which is why I land on Mixed rather than lower. The way it was pursued keeps it from Aligned. The earlier threats toward Denmark are recorded in News Commentary.

Status as of Nov 18, 2026: Open. On November 17 U.S. aircraft struck a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Iran's Qeshm Island, which a U.S. official called self-defense after Iran's third claimed drone attack on a U.S. radar in Bahrain. On November 18 Bahrain and Kuwait said they intercepted Iranian attacks, including drones Iran said it aimed at U.S. air defenses at Kuwait's Ali Al-Salem Air Base. No deal or vote in Congress.

On February 28, 2026, U.S. and Israeli forces began striking Iran: Operation Epic Fury (United States) and Operation Roaring Lion (Israel). President Trump said the goal was to "eliminate imminent threats from the Iranian regime," and U.S. officials named destroying Iran's ballistic missiles and navy and ensuring it does not acquire a nuclear weapon. U.S. strikes hit missile and drone sites, air defenses, naval assets, the military industrial base and command centers of the military and the IRGC. Israel killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and dozens of senior military and political leaders, and his son Mojtaba Khamenei was selected to succeed him on March 8. Iran attacked Israel, Gulf states, bases with U.S. forces and commercial shipping, cutting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. A two-week ceasefire on April 7 was followed by a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports from April 13. A memorandum of understanding signed June 17 committed the United States to end the blockade, waive oil sanctions and release frozen funds, and, in a final deal to be negotiated within 60 days, to "terminate all types of sanctions" and develop a $300 billion regional plan "for the reconstruction and economic development" of Iran. Iran reaffirmed that it "shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons." After Iranian attacks on shipping, the United States resumed strikes, President Trump declared the memorandum "over" on July 8, the blockade returned on July 14, and in August the Treasury launched "Operation Economic Outcast" to "sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime." The Congressional Research Service counts 18 U.S. service members killed and 824 wounded as of September 15, and cites the rights group HRANA's count of 3,636 Iranians killed by April 7, including 1,701 civilians, and a Congressional Budget Office estimate of $38 billion in operating costs as of August 1. On February 28 a U.S. Tomahawk missile reportedly struck a school in Minab and killed more than 150 people, mostly children. A preliminary military investigation reportedly found the United States responsible, having used outdated targeting information. Congress has not authorized the war. The House adopted three concurrent resolutions directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. The Senate passed one joint resolution, S.J.Res. 185, and agreed to one of the House's, H.Con.Res. 86.

The costs are documented: American and Iranian lives, a school strike that the military's own preliminary inquiry reportedly attributes to U.S. error, almost eight months without authorization from Congress, a June memorandum that committed to lifting every sanction in a final deal, and an Iran that, though weakened, still attacks shipping. Against them stands what the war has done to the regime: its supreme leader and dozens of senior leaders killed, its missile, air-defense and naval forces struck, and its ports blockaded. That is the direction I want. The United States ought to act directly against Iran, a direct enemy, and I want the Islamic regime destroyed and its people spared, with no nation-building or occupation afterward (Interventionism vs Non-Intervention, Israel and the Middle East). Enemies are stopped from advancing nuclear capability by force when it can be done safely (Nuclear Weapons and WMD). The details differ in three places:
Congress. The President may act alone only against an attack under way or imminent. A sustained campaign needs Congress's authorization within 30 days or it ends. This one has none.

Civilians. Civilians are absolutely protected, except foreign actors who forfeit protection by hostile conduct (Hostile conduct, removal, and entry; Laws of War), and sparing Iran's people is a requirement. The Minab investigation should be finished and published.

The June memorandum. Lifting all sanctions and a $300 billion reconstruction plan run against my use of sanctions alongside military deterrence (Sanctions and Economic Statecraft) and against my rule of no nation-building once the regime is destroyed. I judge the current administration too soft on Iran, and the memorandum is the clearest case.

body: In 2025, federal agencies cancelled research grants to University of California researchers because of the recipients' "perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints," in the Ninth Circuit's words. On May 26, 2026, in Thakur v. Trump (No. 25-4249), the Ninth Circuit upheld the order to restore those grants. It held that the government may create or end a funding program but may not cancel grants inside a program to suppress viewpoints it disfavors. body: I would abolish government DEI programs (Race and Diversity), so ending federal money for them is the right goal. The method lost, and on my own terms it should have. I hold free speech absolutely (Free Speech and Censorship), and the court's line holds up: a government that funds a program may stop funding it, but cancelling individual grants because of the views their recipients hold makes the grant a penalty on speech. The way to end DEI funding is to close those programs openly, through Congress or by rewriting the grant rules for everyone, and let the courts see a neutral rule rather than a list of disfavored views. This builds on Ending DEI preferences.

body: Executive Order 14168 directed the Attorney General to ensure that "no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate's appearance to that of the opposite sex." In February 2026 the Bureau of Prisons adopted a policy, which it says it reached "independently" of the order on the basis of "the latest scientific information" and prison-security concerns, ending sex-trait-modification surgery, hormone therapy for gender dysphoria and "social accommodations" such as wigs, makeup and chest binders. The Bureau continues mental-health treatment for gender dysphoria, and inmates already receiving hormones get an individual tapering plan. On August 26, Senior U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth barred the Bureau from enforcing the policy in a class action brought by three inmates, and a divided D.C. Circuit panel declined to pause his order. On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court denied the administration's request for a stay in Trump v. Kingdom (No. 26A416), without explanation. Justices Thomas and Alito would have granted it. The policy stays blocked while the case continues.
topic: Culture: Equal Treatment, Sex, Speech, and Religion

body: Three courts have left the block in place, and the inmates argue that withdrawing care risks worsening dysphoria, depression, anxiety, self-harm and suicide. The district court's 2025 injunctions rested on administrative law, finding the Bureau had not reasonably explained its change, and the Supreme Court gave no reasons. None of these orders holds that public money must fund transition. My position is that no public money funds adult transition and that prisons house people by birth sex (Gender Identity in Schools and Institutions). The Bureau's policy applies that in federal prisons, where the taxpayer pays for every inmate's care, while keeping mental-health treatment and a taper for those already on hormones. This builds on Biological sex in federal policy.

sub: Horse soring inspections returned to industry

body: November 13, 2026 · Grade: Opposed
sub: Horse soring inspections returned to industry

body: Status as of Nov 13, 2026: Open. Proposed rule. Comments close December 14, 2026.
sub: Horse soring inspections returned to industry

body: The Department of Agriculture proposed withdrawing what remains of its May 2024 Horse Protection rule, which targeted "soring," the deliberate injuring of a horse's legs or hooves to exaggerate its gait in shows. In January 2025 a federal court in Texas vacated the rule's ban on action devices, pads and substances for Tennessee Walking Horses and racking horses, along with its new inspection and appeal procedures. The court upheld the rule's replacement of industry-appointed inspectors (Designated Qualified Persons) with inspectors the Department trains and authorizes. The proposal drops that replacement too and keeps the industry inspectors, adding conflict-of-interest screening, training and evaluation by equine veterinarians, and required blood and pastern-swab testing. A horse found sore would be disqualified only from the class in which it was inspected, not the whole event. The Department says program funding has stayed flat since 2024, and that fewer than 1 percent of potentially qualified veterinarians showed interest in becoming inspectors.
sub: Horse soring inspections returned to industry

body: Soring is deliberate cruelty to a sentient animal, and under my rules it should be a crime (Animal Cruelty Law). The Department's own record cites conflicts of interest in the industry inspector system, found by its inspector general and the National Academies, and this proposal keeps that system. Defenders say the 2024 rule overreached and a court agreed. The court struck the device ban and the appeal procedures, but it upheld independent inspectors, and the Department is giving those up by choice. Disqualifying a sore horse from one class still lets it compete in others at the same show. Blood testing and conflict screening point the right way. They do not change the decision to hand inspections back to the industry, so I grade this Opposed. This follows Companion animal welfare enforcement.

sub: Grazing rules on national forests rewritten

body: The Department of Agriculture proposed the first full rewrite since 1977 of the rules for livestock grazing on the National Forest System, which has about 96 million acres of grazing allotments. The proposal would update permit issuance and eligibility, set a framework for responding to drought and wildfire, allow "targeted" and "outcome-based" grazing projects under temporary permits, make fee-setting consistent across the 16 contiguous Western states and the national grasslands, and add a surcharge on livestock a permittee leases from others. It follows a March 2026 Forest Service–BLM agreement to prioritize vacant and closed allotments and "maximiz[e] grazing flexibilities."
sub: Grazing rules on national forests rewritten

body: The United States ought to issue no grazing permits on federal land and revoke the existing ones on day one (Agriculture, Grazing, and Habitat). This rule writes livestock deeper into forest management, and the agreement behind it puts vacant and closed allotments first. Defenders say targeted grazing cuts wildfire fuel, but the wild herbivores my sanctuary plan protects graze the same land without anyone raising animals for slaughter. The leasing surcharge raises the price of one arrangement and ends none. This builds on Support for ranchers and livestock markets.
