body: November 10, 2026 · Grade: Mixed
sub: Fire retardant exempted from water-pollution rules

body: Status as of Nov 11, 2026: Open. The exemption runs through November 10, 2027.
sub: Fire retardant exempted from water-pollution rules

body: Under section 313(a) of the Clean Water Act, President Trump exempted federal firefighting, including aerial fire-retardant drops by the Forest Service, the Interior Department, other agencies and their contractors, from federal, state, interstate and local water-pollution requirements for one year, finding it in the "paramount interest of the United States." Two sections of the Act, on performance standards and toxic pollutants (33 U.S.C. 1316 and 1317), still apply. The White House says a district court ruling in Forest Service Employees for Environmental Ethics v. U.S. Forest Service requires a permit for retardant that reaches water, and that the Forest Service has not been able to get one. The Forest Service's avoidance maps, which bar drops in waterways and protected-species habitat except where lives or public safety are at stake, stay in place. From 2012 to 2019 the agency made about 56,868 retardant drops; 248 of them (0.43 percent) landed in water.
sub: Fire retardant exempted from water-pollution rules

body: Fighting fire is an emergency function that stays with government (Adaptation and Disaster Policy), and wildfire kills animals as well as people, so keeping retardant in the air is the right goal. The method is the problem. Retardant that lands in a stream kills fish, and fish are sentient beings whose deaths count under my rules (Commercial Fishing and Aquaculture). Polluters ought to answer for the harm they cause (Pollution and Liability), and the government ought to hold itself to that rule rather than waive it for itself. Defenders say the permit could not be obtained in time and that, without the exemption, retardant use in the 2027 season was legally uncertain. The agency's own record answers that: fewer than half a percent of drops reach water, and the avoidance maps already keep tankers off streams except to save lives, so a permit or a narrow statute could keep retardant flying while keeping the agency liable for any fish kill it causes. The goal is right and the blanket waiver is wrong, so I grade it Mixed.

body: October 23, 2026 · Grade: Opposed
Status as of Nov 15, 2026: Open.

On October 23, 2026, the administration released the America First Seafood Strategy, required by Executive Order 14276 (Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness, April 2025), and launched Seafood.gov.

Harvest and fishing grounds: NOAA will work with the regional fishery councils so that catch limits "reflect the best available science," and will "restore access to productive fishing grounds where supported by data." This builds on the proclamations of April 2025, February 2026 and June 2026 that reopened all Marine National Monuments to commercial fishing.
Aquaculture: clearer standards for "responsible expansion of domestic aquaculture" in federal waters.

Labeling and promotion: the Food and Drug Administration issued draft guidance on voluntary U.S.-origin statements such as "U.S.-Caught" (comments by December 28, 2026), placed 11 foreign firms on import alert after finding short-weighted imported seafood, and agencies will launch an "Eat American Seafood" campaign and buy more American seafood.
Imports: tighter import monitoring against illegal fishing and mislabeled seafood.

Processing loans: USDA made at least $5 billion available through its new Strengthening Processing for U.S. Ranchers (SPUR) Guaranteed Loan Program. It guarantees 90 percent of commercial loans of up to $175 million to expand meat, poultry and seafood processing, with a possible two-year deferral of payments.
NOAA says the strategy "relies on existing statutory authorities and programs rather than new spending initiatives."

Every part of the strategy grows what I would end. Commercial fishing and aquaculture of sentient animals, and of bivalves for consistency, should end immediately, shellfish included, and seafood imports should be banned (Commercial Fishing and Aquaculture). Raising catch limits, reopening protected waters and expanding fish farms all go the other way. The loan guarantees also reach meat and poultry plants, and I would end animal agriculture rather than expand its slaughter capacity (Agriculture, Grazing, and Habitat). A federal guarantee leaves taxpayers holding most of the risk on loans of up to $175 million to chosen firms, which breaks my rule that no industry should be subsidized unless taxpayers opt in (Subsidies and Mandates).

The case for the strategy is food security and protecting American fishermen from subsidized foreign competitors. Food security doesn't depend on killing sentient animals. Plant-based food is already sold at scale, and cultivated seafood is the long-term replacement through private innovation (Sanctuary Plan). On foreign competition, the strategy only screens imports, while I would ban seafood imports outright. The overlap is only in direction: I am against seafood imports for the animals' sake, not to protect an industry I would close. This builds on Saltwater angling and Support for ranchers and livestock markets.

head: Wind turbine imports found a security threat
sub: Wind turbine imports found a security threat

body: October 22, 2026 · Grade: Mixed
sub: Wind turbine imports found a security threat

body: Status as of Oct 28, 2026: Open.
sub: Wind turbine imports found a security threat

body: A proclamation of October 22, 2026, under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, accepts the Commerce Secretary's finding that imports of wind turbines and their parts "threaten to impair the national security." The findings name cybersecurity flaws in imported networked inverters that "could allow remote access and interference with United States power systems," radar clutter that affects air traffic control and defense, rising dependence on imported components, and wind's intermittency, which the Secretary found "diverts the United States electrical grid from more reliable energy sources." It imposes no new duty yet: it directs Commerce and the Trade Representative to negotiate agreements with trading partners and report within 180 days, and says the President "may consider alternative remedies." Wind components made largely of steel, aluminum or copper already carry those metals' section 232 tariffs.
sub: Wind turbine imports found a security threat

body: Keeping networked equipment from threat countries out of the power grid is a real security need, and restricting a threat country's technology is how I handle trade with one (Trade and Economics). Radar interference with defense is a fair concern too. The proclamation goes past that. It treats a power source being intermittent as a national-security threat, which is the government picking the energy mix. My position is that the market should drive the mix and no source should be forced out (Energy Mix). The security problem is narrow (the inverters and controls, and siting near radar), and the remedy ought to be narrow too: rules on the equipment and its origin, not trade action against wind as a whole. No duty has been set, so the grade may change with the remedy.

body: October 22, 2026 · Grade: Mixed
sub: Defense Production Act funds for refineries

body: Status as of Nov 18, 2026: Open.
sub: Defense Production Act funds for refineries

body: On October 22, 2026, the Department of Energy announced up to $150 million in Defense Production Act Title III funding "to expand domestic petroleum production, storage, and logistics at refineries across the United States," which it expects to raise refining output "by millions of gallons per day." The money comes from $1 billion Congress appropriated for energy projects critical to national security. Recipients have not been chosen. The funding rests on Presidential Determination No. 2026-11 of April 20, 2026, which found domestic petroleum production, refining and logistics capacity "essential to the national defense" under the energy emergency of Executive Order 14156 and waived the Act's usual preconditions. The White House posted a determination under the same title on October 22. The President announced the funding at a rally in Sioux City, Iowa, with diesel and gasoline prices high during the war with Iran.
sub: Defense Production Act funds for refineries

body: More domestic fuel supply fits my position that fossil fuels should stay where they work best and that no source should be forced out (Energy Mix), and fuel for the armed forces is a defense need. The method runs against me. Handing taxpayer money to chosen refiners is a subsidy, and the government subsidizes no energy source unless taxpayers opt in (Subsidies and Mandates). The better route to more refining is cutting the permitting delays the determination itself names (Grid Reliability and Permitting). It also rests on an energy emergency with no end date, which my rule does not allow (Emergency Powers). This builds on National energy emergency.
sub: Defense Production Act funds for refineries

body: The case for the money is real: U.S. refining capacity fell during 2025, to 18.16 million barrels per calendar day at 130 operable refineries on January 1, 2026. The shortfall is the reason to remove what causes it. Refiners close or never expand because of permitting time and regulatory cost, and $150 million spread across chosen firms changes neither for the industry. Permitting reform does, and it costs taxpayers nothing.

Executive Order 14433 directs disease-focused suppression of ticks and mosquitoes through land management, natural predators, and non-chemical controls.

Protecting people from disease and preferring non-chemical methods fit my least-harm rule for insects (Sentience Determination). Relying on natural predators conflicts with my position on predation (Wild-Animal Predation).

September 21, 2026 · Grade: Mixed
Status as of Nov 9, 2026: Open.

On September 21, 2026, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced steps under the Animal Welfare Act: a 2027 proposal to strengthen care standards for dogs, more than 2,000 "regulatory refresher mailings" to dog-breeding facilities, a new Animal Protection Bureau of enforcement specialists, a planned 20% increase in Inspector General agents working on animal fighting and other matters, and a review within six months of every dog breeder who surrendered a USDA or equivalent state license in the past two years. USDA reported that in 2026 it denied or terminated 8 dog-breeder licenses, suspended 6 and revoked 5, and with the Justice Department pursued a serious-danger case against a breeder. On October 6, in Iowa, Rollins said of past practice, "those days are over. We are now in the active process of shutting down these puppy mills." In the ASPCA's pending suit over USDA's licensing of Iowa breeders, including Steve Kruse (ASPCA v. Vilsack, D.D.C. No. 1:24-cv-02682), USDA's lawyers argue, as Iowa Capital Dispatch reports, that none of the Act's enforcement provisions are mandatory, that enforcement is at the agency's discretion, and that the case is moot because three of the breeders no longer hold licenses.

USDA's argument follows settled law: since Heckler v. Chaney (1985), an agency's decision not to enforce is presumed to be committed to its discretion and unreviewable, unless the statute itself sets guidelines for enforcement. The enforcement record is also real: in June 2026 the Justice Department obtained a restraining order against one of the Iowa licensees and inspected her kennel, and after the county sheriff seized her dogs she was charged with 34 counts of neglect, to which she has pleaded not guilty. Stronger enforcement against cruel breeders points my way, since I treat cruelty to a sentient animal as a rights violation and a crime (Animal Cruelty Law, Animal Rights and Sentientism). Two things pull the other way. The United States ought to shut commercial breeding mills down outright, not license them under better standards (Sanctuary Plan). And under a law that leaves enforcement wholly to the agency, no one can compel it to act on documented violations. My rule making enforcement a duty is in Animal Cruelty Law.

September 14, 2026 · Grade: Opposed
Status as of Nov 12, 2026: Open. In force since September 14, 2026; challenged in court.

The Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service rescinded the regulatory definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act, effective September 14, 2026. Since 1981 (FWS) and 1999 (NMFS) it had covered significant habitat modification or degradation that actually kills or injures listed wildlife, and the Supreme Court upheld it in Babbitt v. Sweet Home (1995). The same day, FWS Director Brian Nesvik issued a memorandum adopting Justice Scalia's dissent in that case: "take" now reaches only "an affirmative act that is intentionally and purposefully directed at a particular animal." Under it, a ship that strikes a whale by accident has not taken it, and felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled to kill them. NOAA's general counsel issued an identical memorandum. On November 11, 42 members of Congress (41 Democrats and one independent) asked Interior and Commerce to explain the legal basis by November 30.

My rules protect each sentient animal, not a species count (Bear baiting), and an animal killed by a foreseeable strike or by the loss of its habitat is just as dead as one shot. Whoever causes that harm ought to answer for it, the way polluters do (Pollution and Liability, Regulation and Conservation). The agencies argue that after Loper Bright a regulation cannot reach past its statute, and I agree that rules carry no more authority than the law behind them (Government Structure and Checks). The statute itself puts "harm" and "kill" in the definition of "take," though, and the Supreme Court upheld the habitat definition. If the reading is doubtful, Congress ought to write habitat protection into the Act, not leave whales and bats exposed while the agencies narrow it.

body: The administration plans a 250-foot arch on Memorial Circle, across the Potomac from the Lincoln Memorial near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, more than 80 feet taller than the Arc de Triomphe. On November 5 the National Capital Planning Commission approved it 8–4 and the National Park Service approved the project. About an hour later Judge Tanya Chutkan of the federal district court in Washington barred the Park Service from starting work for 14 days, in consolidated suits by veterans and an architectural historian and by the District of Columbia and Virginia. The administration cites a 1925 law authorizing the Arlington Memorial Bridge. Chutkan wrote that "the sheer improbability that a 100-year-old statute would contain authority, unknown to every previous administration, to erect a 250-foot arch at a principal location in the Nation's capital indicates how far Defendants must stretch," and noted that Congress has authorized other commemorative works in the capital but not this one. The Justice Department put construction at 33 to 39 months. The National Endowment for the Humanities has reserved $2 million in special-initiative funds and $13 million in matching funds for the arch. No total cost has been disclosed.
sub: Triumphal arch blocked pending court review

body: I am not opposed to the arch. Honoring veterans is worthy, and a monument on federal land falls within presidential discretion over federal property (Public-Sector Size and Civil Service). That discretion covers only land the executive already manages, here Park Service land at Memorial Circle, and not anything beyond the laws that authorize the executive (Government Structure and Checks). I would prefer it be paid for by private donors or opt-in funds rather than general taxes, because it is not an essential function. The National Endowment for the Humanities has reserved public special-initiative and matching funds, so the funding is not fully private, which is why the grade is directional. Defenders say Congress already authorized it in 1925. Congress authorized a bridge, and no administration in a century read that law to cover an arch. That statutory hook is thin, but it is not a reason for me to oppose the project itself.

body: Status as of Nov 13, 2026: Open. The government's petition for a writ of certiorari in National Park Service v. National Trust for Historic Preservation, No. 26-599, was filed November 5 and docketed November 6. The Trust's response is due December 7. The Supreme Court's August 31 stay of the district court's injunction remains in effect. As of November 13 the docket showed no further filings.
sub: White House ballroom petition at the Supreme Court

body: In October 2025 the government began replacing the White House East Wing. Demolition of the existing wing was completed in December 2025. Construction of a new East Wing followed, including a below-ground military installation and a 90,000-square-foot above-ground ballroom that the government says is paid for with private donations. The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued. On March 31, 2026, the district court preliminarily enjoined further above-ground work except as "strictly necessary" to protect the White House, the President, and his staff, while allowing the below-ground military work to continue. On August 7 a divided D.C. Circuit panel (Judges Millett and Garcia; Judge Rao dissenting) affirmed, holding that the government "very likely lack[s] statutory authority to construct the ballroom," and that "whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide." The court cited 40 U.S.C. §8106, which bars erecting a structure on federal grounds in the District of Columbia "without express authority of Congress," and stayed its mandate 14 days to allow Supreme Court review.
sub: White House ballroom petition at the Supreme Court

body: On August 31 the Supreme Court, over a dissent by the Chief Justice joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson, stayed the injunction pending a petition for certiorari. The per curiam opinion held that the government is likely to show the Trust lacks Article III standing, because the injury claimed by a single member, Alison Hoagland, is "offense, disagreement, or distaste" at the design, which the Court has not treated as a concrete and particularized injury. The Court wrote, "Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government's East Wing project." Senior officials told the Court the height and mass of the planned ballroom are "crucial" to shield the underground installation, and the Solicitor General later told the Court the project is "roughly 70% complete." The November 5 petition asks the Court to summarily reverse the D.C. Circuit or to grant review.
sub: White House ballroom petition at the Supreme Court

body: Private funding is the right way to pay for a White House improvement that is not an essential function (Public-Sector Size and Civil Service). Security work at the White House, including a below-ground military installation, is a function of defense, which I put first, and the district court's injunction already left that work in place. I believe the President should have discretion over privately funded improvements to the White House. That discretion covers only the White House grounds the President already controls, and not anything beyond the laws that authorize the executive (Government Structure and Checks). Defenders say the Court has already all but decided the case, and that stopping work now would leave a half-built structure and weaken security. The August 31 stay decided standing, not legality. I still support the project on the merits.

body: November 5, 2026 · Grade: Aligned
Status as of Nov 9, 2026: Open.

Using the Antiquities Act (54 U.S.C. §320301), President Trump proclaimed the Oval Office (Room 110), the Outer Oval Office (Rooms 106 and 108) and the Cabinet Room (Room 105) a national monument. The National Park Service will manage it, and any action that would "substantially alter or demolish" the rooms first requires documentation, review and consideration of alternatives. The proclamation keeps the President's power to redecorate and choose furnishings. Trump said the designation means his redesign "won't be able to be taken down or destroyed, touched or anything else."

I am not opposed to this. I believe the President should have discretion over the White House workspace already under his control, including a designation that documents the rooms while keeping the power to redecorate and choose furnishings. That discretion covers only rooms the President already controls, and not anything beyond the laws that authorize the executive (Government Structure and Checks). The Antiquities Act is an unusual vehicle for that, and the White House is already a National Historic Landmark managed by the Park Service. Those are reasons the route is odd, not reasons I oppose the designation. A future President can undo it with a proclamation of their own.

October 28, 2026 · Grade: Directionally opposed

Status as of Nov 15, 2026: Open. On November 14 Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order that keeps East Potomac Park and its golf course open to the public through November 28, 2026, or until further order. The Justice Department has appealed her tree-removal injunction.

Interior ended the National Links Trust's lease for Washington's three Park Service golf courses on December 30, 2025. On October 28, 2026, the Park Service signed a new lease for the other two, and the Justice Department told the court that the Service would submit a Tom Fazio design for a "World Class, championship-level golf course" to the National Capital Planning Commission and then close East Potomac Park south of Buckeye Drive. The closure covers the 124-year-old public course along with Hains Point, the seawall promenade, trails, fishing areas and picnic grounds, and it lasts until the superintendent lifts it. The Service cites a May 2026 assessment that found 110 deficiencies at the course, 69 of them Critical or Urgent, and a promenade that floods more than 30 times a year. At an October 19 hearing, a senior Justice Department official told the court "there is no plan to close the course." Judge Reyes found that the government had removed hundreds of trees to carry out the redesign and "bypassed the National Environmental Policy Act." She barred further removal and on November 9 refused to stay that order. The Park Service then set the closure for 9 p.m. November 15, citing the end of the course operator's contract and a failing seawall. On November 14 Judge Reyes blocked it. She found those explanations "pretextual": the Park Service has treated the whole seawall as a hazard since 2019 and fenced off its unsafe parts rather than closing the park, and three days before deciding to close it the Service let more than thirty thousand people run a marathon along the same perimeter. She held that the closure likely violates the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. The order keeps the course and the park south of Buckeye Drive open during their usual hours. It allows closures for seawall repair or an imminent safety threat, with notice to the court within 24 hours, and it does not require the government to offer golf or hire an operator. A Justice Department spokesperson said, "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue."

Fixing a failing public asset is reasonable, and the Park Service's inspection record supports real repairs. But government ought to be sized to its essential functions (Public-Sector Size and Civil Service), and a course built to host major championships is not one of them. Defenders say the course is unsafe and the President is fixing it. The safety record justifies repairs. It does not justify closing the whole southern park, seawall and trails included, for a redesign the government told the court did not exist. People with more power answer to a higher standard (Due Process and Rule of Law), and the executive answers to the courts (Government Structure and Checks). The grade is directional because the repairs are needed.

body: October 26, 2026 · Grade: Directionally opposed
sub: Firing of prosecutor Maurene Comey ruled unlawful

body: Status as of Nov 18, 2026: Open. The Justice Department says it will appeal. The court reserved judgment on her First Amendment claim.
sub: Firing of prosecutor Maurene Comey ruled unlawful

body: On July 16, 2025, the Justice Department fired Assistant U.S. Attorney Maurene Comey, a criminal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York for nearly ten years and the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, by an email that terminated her "[p]ursuant to Article II of the United States Constitution and the laws of the United States" and gave no other reason. The Department later said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi directed it. The Department argued that the Attorney General could remove her at will and that Congress cannot limit the removal of federal prosecutors at all. On October 26, 2026, in Comey v. Department of Justice (No. 25-cv-7625), U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman held that the firing violated the Civil Service Reform Act, which allows removal "only for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service" and only after notice and a chance to be heard, as well as the separation of powers and her Fifth Amendment due-process rights. He wrote that the Department's Article II argument "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent" on Congress's power to limit the removal of inferior officers, and ordered retroactive reinstatement and back pay through December 20, 2025, when she took another job. He did not decide her claim that she was fired because of her father or her perceived politics. A Department spokesperson said it "disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."
sub: Firing of prosecutor Maurene Comey ruled unlawful

body: The government ought to let elected officials control the people who set policy, and the Attorney General and the U.S. Attorneys, who direct prosecutions, serve at the President's pleasure for that reason. Career staff are different: no one is fired for party or political speech, and removal for poor performance or misconduct comes with written reasons, a chance to answer, a decision within 30 days and one quick appeal (Civil Service Protections). The Department's strongest point is that prosecutors wield the executive power itself, so the President must be able to remove any of them. A line prosecutor carries out charging policy that politically accountable officials set and can change at will. Control runs through them, not through firing career staff without a stated reason. Here the Department gave none, no notice and no hearing, and claimed a power to do the same to every prosecutor in the country. That is the at-will reach into ordinary career staff that my rule calls the spoils system by another name, and it fails my due-process rule whatever the motive was (Due Process and Rule of Law). Whether she was fired because of her father is not proven, and I don't treat it as proven. The grade may change after the appeal. The same at-will theory, applied to policy-influencing positions, is graded in Schedule Policy/Career.

body: Status as of Nov 18, 2026: Open. On November 17 NBC News projected Mary Peltola the winner with a majority of first-choice votes, so the race needed no ranked-choice tabulation, and the case the suit targeted, a loss Sen. Sullivan would have won with Daniel J. Sullivan's votes, did not arise. The appeal is pending in the Ninth Circuit. Certification is due November 25.
sub: Suit to hold Alaska's Senate certification

body: On October 22, 2026, the Justice Department sued Alaska and its election officials in federal court (United States v. State of Alaska, No. 3:26-cv-00376, D. Alaska). The complaint says Daniel J. Sullivan, a first-time candidate in the U.S. Senate race, is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan," Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, and that his "sole purpose" is to help Democrat Mary Peltola. Alaska's Division of Elections had found in June that his candidacy was filed "to confuse or mislead" and kept him off the ballot, but a state trial court reversed it and the Alaska Supreme Court summarily affirmed. The suit, brought under the National Voter Registration Act's purpose of protecting "the integrity of the electoral process," asks the court to bar certification of any result in which Sen. Sullivan loses but would have won had every vote for Daniel J. Sullivan gone to him, pending an investigation into whether those votes "were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan." In the August primary Peltola had 49.5%, Sen. Sullivan 41.4% and Daniel J. Sullivan 2.5%. On the sample ballot he appears as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no party listed, above "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent." President Trump said of the suit, "I'm the one that said, 'do it.'" Sen. Lisa Murkowski said the department "should never have filed this lawsuit."
sub: Suit to hold Alaska's Senate certification

body: On November 1, Judge Sharon L. Gleason dismissed the suit, holding that the Justice Department lacked standing because it "failed to satisfy its burden to show that its alleged injury is redressable by a court order." She wrote that it offered "no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy." The department appealed the same day, saying the court had not disputed its claim that Daniel J. Sullivan "entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters." It had amended the suit to cite a New York Times report that people tied to Peltola's campaign helped recruit him, which her campaign denies, and it is separately investigating the matter criminally. No one has been charged. On November 9 voting-rights groups, including the League of Women Voters and Common Cause, moved to dismiss the appeal. As of that date the department had not asked the appeals court for an injunction.
sub: Suit to hold Alaska's Senate certification

body: A candidacy filed to fool voters is a fraud on them, and a state should be able to keep one off the ballot under rules written in advance. Alaska's own election director found exactly that. So the concern is real. The remedy is what I oppose. Election rules are fixed in law before each election, not changed during or after it (Election Administration), and this suit asks a court to hold up a count only if one named candidate loses, then to guess what voters "meant." Ranked-choice voting, which I would require everywhere, already answers the spoiler worry: a voter who ranks both Sullivans loses nothing, because a vote for an eliminated candidate moves to the voter's next choice (Ranked-Choice Voting). Supporters of the suit will say a one-in-forty share could swing a race decided by a point or two. If so, the fix is a clear ballot-access rule before the next election, not a federal suit under a voter-registration law to reach into a state's certification (Federalism). It also runs against my rule for federal enforcement near an election (Federal Enforcement Near Elections). The grade is directional rather than full opposition because the decoy problem it points at is genuine. My rule for deceptive candidacies is in Ballot Access and Deceptive Candidacies.

body: October 21, 2026 · Grade: Mixed

Status as of Nov 13, 2026: Open. Judge Chutkan's November 2 injunction in League of Women Voters v. DHS, No. 26-cv-3602 (D.D.C.), still bars the government from sending lists of alleged noncitizen voters to election officials. It does not bar individual SAVE checks or prosecutions. I found no appeal of it. The California Nurses Association injunction on field sweeps ran until polls closed on November 3.

Resolved (ballot-demand suit, Nov 10, 2026): On November 6 the Justice Department voluntarily dismissed United States v. California, No. 2:26-cv-12025 (C.D. Cal.), saying the relief it sought was "no longer available" once the challenged ballots were commingled with others. On November 10 Judge David O. Carter closed the case, writing that it "attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike." The Supreme Court had denied DOJ's emergency application in United States v. California, No. 26A624 (Nov 2).

On August 31, 2026, according to the court's account of the record, the Department of Homeland Security issued an internal "Surge Initiative Guidance" directing Homeland Security Investigations agents to prioritize field investigations questioning people about their voter eligibility in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. The target lists drew on about 48.2 million records DHS received "through independent sources" and 50.6 million voter-roll records from the Justice Department, taken from commercial copies for states that would not share their rolls. During the surge, agents were to complete at least 40 reviews, taking no more than twelve minutes to clear a person from a list. On October 15 the Justice Department sued California, asking the court to make the state set aside, before counting, the mail ballots of more than 20,000 people it calls "likely noncitizens" and to verify their citizenship. On October 21, in California Nurses Association v. Mullin (N.D. Cal.), Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín enjoined election-related field operations and interviews in the nine states that involve people DHS knows, suspects or should reasonably suspect are U.S. citizens, until polls close on November 3. The judge stayed the order until 5 p.m. on October 23 to allow an appeal. The plaintiffs posted the required $100 bond on October 22, and as of that evening the public docket and news reports showed no appeal or stay from the Ninth Circuit. In the California ballot suit, Judge David O. Carter did not rule by the noon October 22 deadline the Justice Department asked for. That night the Department filed notice that it was appealing what it called a "constructive denial" to the Ninth Circuit, and on October 23 it asked for an injunction pending appeal.

The California list has documented errors. Los Angeles County found that only 7,035 of the names had addresses in the county. In a sample of 200, 112 registrations were already canceled or inactive, and where birthplace was meaningfully recorded, 38.9% said they were born in the United States. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said, "There may be some names on there who it turns out ultimately are citizens, we're not perfect." The same week, the Justice Department charged 28 people on the list, all lawful permanent residents. The injunction cites another federal court's finding that noncitizen voting is "exceedingly rare."

Rare is not never, as the charges show, and clean rolls are my position: elections are run so that only eligible voters vote and every valid ballot is counted (Election Administration). I graded the order that sends states lists of confirmed citizens Aligned (Citizenship verification in elections), and prosecuting each person who registered or voted unlawfully fits the same rule. Two parts run against it. Election procedures are fixed in law before each election rather than changed during it, and a demand three weeks before Election Day to hold back 20,000 mail ballots, on a list the government says may include citizens, would change the count during the election and hold up valid ballots. Judge Sanchez, concurring in the Ninth Circuit's dismissal, made the same point I make: asking a federal court to dictate a state's handling of ballots in the middle of an election invites 'disorder and confusion.' Questioning citizens at home on twelve-minute database checks is also not the record matching that cleans a roll. My rule for enforcement near an election is in Federal Enforcement Near Elections.

body: A presidential memorandum creates a committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook made false statements on mortgage documents and to report whether there is "cause" to remove her. It follows Trump v. Cook (June 29, 2026), in which the Supreme Court, 5–4, left her in office pending litigation, holding the Fed's for-cause protection valid and finding she had not been given notice, the evidence, or a chance to respond. The committee gives her the evidence in advance and holds a closed, transcribed hearing at the White House on November 5, 2026, lasting no more than four hours. On October 13, Cook's lawyer, Abbe Lowell, wrote that she cannot attend on November 5 because of official Fed meetings in Europe, that the earliest workable date is after the Fed's December 8–9 meeting, and that the committee is "demonstrably biased," citing member Kevin Hassett's earlier public statement that the President had cause to fire her.
sub: Inquiry into Fed Governor Lisa Cook

body: Notice, the evidence, and a chance to respond match my due-process requirements (Due Process and Rule of Law). I hold that Fed governors may be removed only for cause, proven with notice, the evidence and a hearing, and never for disagreeing with the President on rates (Monetary Policy). The inquiry is framed around cause, which matches my rule. Whether the allegations meet that standard is not yet decided. It differs in detail: the hearing is closed, run by a White House committee rather than an independent body, and capped at four hours.

body: March 31, 2026 · Grade: Aligned

Status as of Nov 14, 2026: Open. The Justice Department did not appeal Judge Carl Nichols's preliminary injunction, which bars the Postal Service mail-ballot rule for all federal elections, including 2028. Twelve Republican state attorneys general began an appeal on November 12.

Executive Order 14399 directs federal agencies to compile and send states lists of confirmed citizens to verify voter rolls (section 2) and directs the Postal Service to write rules for mail ballots (section 3). On June 25, 2026, a federal court in Massachusetts declared both sections void for the midterms. On August 24 the Supreme Court stayed that judgment, finding the states likely lacked standing and their claims were not yet ripe, so no injunction now blocks the citizen lists. The Postal Service's final mail-ballot rule of August 21 was enjoined, and on September 14 the Supreme Court refused to stay that injunction, so the rule does not apply to the November 3 election. A separate injunction by Judge Carl Nichols in Washington, D.C., blocks the rule for all federal elections. He found that "no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule." The Justice Department let its deadline to appeal pass on November 12.

Matches my rule that only qualified citizens with ID should vote (Voting and Elections). The citizen lists I graded stand. The blocked mail rule is a separate measure and does not change this grade. Enforcement on the eve of the 2026 midterms is graded separately in Voter-status sweeps and ballot demands.

Status as of Oct 23, 2026: Resolved.
In Trump v. CASA, arising from challenges to Executive Order 14160, the Supreme Court held that federal courts generally may not issue universal injunctions.
Outcome (June 27, 2025): Decided. The ruling governs remedies in later cases, including the class-wide injunction affirmed in Trump v. Barbara.

The ruling is procedural. The United States ought to keep court review of executive action (Due Process and Rule of Law), and the ruling narrows the remedy without removing that review. I hold that a single district judge should not set national policy, and that a ruling against an unconstitutional action should still protect everyone, through class actions or fast Supreme Court review (Government Structure and Checks). The ruling matches the first point and leaves class actions open. It differs in detail because it does nothing to speed Supreme Court review. The class-action route it left open is the one that stopped the birthright order: in Trump v. Barbara (June 30, 2026) the Court affirmed a class-wide injunction (Birthright citizenship order).

body: The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule, which it says was "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council," to stop companies headquartered in China, Macau or other arms-embargoed countries (Country Group D:5) from renting advanced American chips through data centers in third countries. Exporting those chips to a data center that supplies significant computing power to such companies now requires a license, and data centers already serving them must obtain one within 90 days; commercial recommender systems are exempt. The rule also requires a license to ship the most advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil unless the buyer is headquartered in the United States and meets reporting requirements, tightens the presumptions for chip foundries and packagers, and formally rescinds the never-enforced AI Diffusion Rule. It follows the Nvidia scandal: Megaspeed, a Singapore company that was one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia, is under U.S. criminal investigation for allegedly smuggling American chips into China, and Treasury Secretary Bessent blamed Commerce for not acting against it sooner.
sub: Remote access to advanced AI chips restricted

body: Restrictions on technology transfer should target adversaries and national-security threats such as China (Sanctions and Economic Statecraft), and AI's national-security risks are a federal matter (AI and Automation). Closing the rental route to chips that cannot be shipped to China directly is that. The details differ in two places. The new license requirement falls on trading partners that are not adversaries, where I would restrict trade only for a national-security threat (Trade and Economics); a case for it rests on documented diversion through those countries, and the Singapore case supports it for that route. And the rule took effect before any public comment. The rescission of the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule only formalizes what Commerce announced in May 2025; that rule was never enforced.

It keeps the statutory definition of artificial intelligence, leaves existing regulations, contracts and grants unchanged, and directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology to propose, within 60 days, legislative language for a federal definition.

body: Nov 2025: Texas Governor Greg Abbott proclaimed the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and the Muslim Brotherhood foreign terrorist organizations under state criminal law and transnational criminal organizations under state property law. The proclamation barred CAIR from buying land in Texas and let the attorney general sue to shut it down. It called CAIR a "successor organization" to the Brotherhood and cited its listing as an unindicted co-conspirator in the Holy Land Foundation Hamas-financing case. CAIR's Texas chapters challenged it in federal court, and the state sued to ban both groups. The federal government has never designated CAIR. CAIR's documented record includes the unindicted co-conspirator listing in the Holy Land Foundation case and the FBI's suspension of formal engagement over that evidence (El-Sayed case). Their platform rests on compulsory redistribution: a federal minimum wage, progressive taxes instead of a flat tax, and a mandatory entitlement system. They are not pro-police or anti-crime in practice, they want a path to citizenship for people who entered unlawfully, they lean toward a two-state solution on Israel, and they push group preferences and gender identity as a legal category. body: 23 Oct 2026: at about 10:30 a.m., a gunman firing from a car shot people at several places in Trappes and neighboring La Verrière (Yvelines), west of Paris, killing Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French mixed-martial-arts fighter of Congolese origin, and wounding five others, including a girl of about 12 hit by eight bullets, according to the mayor of La Verrière. The suspect, a 39-year-old man named by prosecutors and the press as Kévin T., was arrested in Coignières about twenty minutes after the shooting began. The National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) opened an investigation for murder and attempted murder "in connection with a terrorist enterprise," with the aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed because of the victims' real or supposed race, ethnicity, nation or religion. Investigators found a Sten-type submachine gun in his car and found his apartment booby-trapped with three gas bottles wired to a timer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said, "It is clearly a terrorist crime." President Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack" and "a turning point in the life of our Republic," saying the victims "were targeted because of their supposed color and religion." franceinfo – Un mort et plusieurs blessés graves, un suspect arrêté, "un crime terroriste"... Under my rule a mental illness does not undo the killing: a panel of forensic psychiatrists and a judge decides agency, and "incompetent" is usually applied too broadly (Insanity Defense). I hold the rioters of 17 October and this gunman to the same rule: force against people who did nothing is a rights violation, whoever uses it and whoever it is used on (France riots).

body: My view: Murdering mourners at a funeral to terrorize a religious minority is murder and terrorism, and both carry the death penalty under my rules at the capital evidentiary standard (Murder, Rape, and the Mandatory Death Penalty; Terrorism and Domestic Extremism). A verdict about three weeks after arrest is within the 30-day cap I set for capital trials. Where I differ is what comes after: Jordan sends the sentence to an appeals court and holds the men until it rules, while I would abolish death row, carry out the sentence on the sentencing date, and keep only a narrow review for new evidence (Capital Trials and the Abolition of Death Row).

21 Oct 2026: the Financial Times, citing three people familiar with the plans, reported that Israel had prepared several days of strikes for the weekend of 10 October on Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure including power plants, and did not go ahead because President Trump opposed resuming the war before the U.S. midterms. Before that weekend Trump had posted, "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections." Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, "We are just as prepared for diplomacy as we are for war," and that indirect talks continue over a seven-day ceasefire proposal Iran made in September, which Trump rejected. 13–14 Nov 2026: Reuters reported, citing three people familiar with the matter, that President Trump told senior advisers he may hold off on attacking Iran if there are no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis, and that he has not made a final decision. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Erdogan urged him not to resume attacks; Trump told Stephen A. Smith, "I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly." A third aircraft carrier is moving into the region. A White House official said the President "is the architect and sole decision-maker." 14–15 Nov 2026: The Revolutionary Guard's navy said two more tankers struck mines on 14 November on what it called an "unauthorised" route through the Strait of Hormuz, and that two others turned back after warnings. Early on 15 November the Guard said it launched six drones at a U.S. radar at Bahrain's Riffa Air Base, its second claimed attack on Bahrain in three days. Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued its first public alerts since September, the Bahrain Defence Force said it intercepted the attack, and the Foreign Ministry said it holds Iran "fully responsible," calling the strikes "a resumption of Iran's aggression against Bahrain and other countries in the region." 15–16 Nov 2026: The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt entered U.S. Central Command's area, joining the USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush, the first time since the Iraq war that the United States has had three carriers in the region, according to Euronews. 16–17 Nov 2026: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it launched drones at a U.S. radar at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base, its third claimed attack on Bahrain since 13 November. 17–18 Nov 2026: A U.S. military official said American aircraft carried out "precision strikes" on a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz "in self-defense," in response to "IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets." The strike came hours after Iran's third claimed attack in less than a week on a U.S. radar in Bahrain, all of which U.S. officials said were intercepted. On 18 November Bahrain and Kuwait said they intercepted Iranian attacks; Iran's army said its drones "targeted Patriot air defence systems" at Kuwait's Ali Al-Salem Air Base, and Kuwait's foreign ministry called the attacks "a dangerous escalation." What happened (sourced): As of 5 November 2026, a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran had sent the United States a nuclear proposal through Qatar, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran's seven demands; Iranian forces said at least five tankers were damaged by mines or fire in and near the Strait of Hormuz. My view: I want more force used against Iran and judge this administration too soft on it (Israel and the Middle East). If a strike was held back for the midterms, that is the softness I object to; if it was held back to seek Congress's authorization first, that is what my rule requires. Netanyahu's stated aim, toppling the regime, matches mine, that the Islamic regime be destroyed, with no nation-building or occupation afterward. Three of my rules apply to any campaign in November. It needs Congress's authorization: a sustained campaign must be authorized within 30 days, and after almost eight months there is none (Interventionism vs Non-Intervention). Iran's people must be spared (Laws of War), so strikes on power plants and other infrastructure that civilians depend on have to meet that requirement. And the Minab school investigation should be finished and published.
A return to a JCPOA-style rented pause is not a win. The 2015 deal left the enrichment plant in place on a timer (Nuclear Weapons and WMD).

Iran's threat to strike airports, pipelines and civilian targets across the Gulf is a threat to commit the war crimes my rules forbid, and it is one more reason the regime has to go (Laws of War). The administration says the Navy can hold the blockade "for the foreseeable future." A blockade is an act of war, and an envoy now saying the war could run another year, after an original estimate CBS reports as "four to five weeks," is what a war without Congress's authorization looks like: no defined aim, no end date and no vote. If the administration means to strike "fairly soon," it ought to put that to Congress first, as my 30-day rule requires (Interventionism vs Non-Intervention).

Iranian plots to kill American officials abroad are acts of war against the United States, and they are one more reason the regime has to go (Israel and the Middle East). A "little Epic Fury" announced at a campaign rally is not how a war decision should be made. If the options on the table include striking Kharg Island, which carries most of Iran's oil exports, that is a decision for Congress under my 30-day rule, and any strike on infrastructure civilians depend on has to meet my laws-of-war standard (Interventionism vs Non-Intervention, Laws of War).

The President is right not to announce timing. Surprise is part of fighting a war. Whether to resume a sustained campaign isn't his decision alone. After almost eight months it needs Congress's authorization under my 30-day rule (Interventionism vs Non-Intervention). Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz in exchange for ending the blockade would swap one pressure for another and leave both the regime and its nuclear program in place. I want the regime gone, not a return to the June memorandum (S12 entry, Israel and the Middle East).
A sustained new campaign after nearly eight months needs Congress's authorization under my 30-day rule (Interventionism vs Non-Intervention).

"Total victory" is the right aim if it means the regime is gone, which is my aim (Israel and the Middle East). Rezaei's refusal to give up the enriched uranium shows why a pause that leaves the stockpile in Iran is not a win (Nuclear Weapons and WMD). Declaring victory is not the same as authorizing the war, and after more than eight months the campaign still needs Congress's vote.

Walking away without a deal leaves the enriched uranium in Iran, at a site the IAEA cannot even locate. Holding the money and the strait is leverage, not an outcome. The aim I set is the regime gone and its nuclear capability stopped by force where it can be done safely (Nuclear Weapons and WMD). If the President now judges the war over, he should say so formally. If he doesn't, he owes Congress a vote.

Iran's refusal to let inspectors in until the war "has permanently ended" is the same problem as Rezaei's refusal to give up the uranium: any pause that leaves the stockpile uninspected leaves the aim I set unmet (Israel and the Middle East).

body: The law: most federal crimes must be charged within five years, and naturalization-fraud crimes within ten (18 U.S.C. § 3291). The civil statute for revoking naturalization "procured by concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation," 8 U.S.C. § 1451, sets no deadline, and a person who derived citizenship through a parent's naturalization loses it if the parent's is revoked on those grounds. Revocation requires evidence that is "clear, unequivocal, and convincing" (Fedorenko v. United States, 1981), and a criminal conviction requires that the illegal act played a role in obtaining citizenship (Maslenjak v. United States, 2017). body: My view: If anyone, in Congress or not, gained status or citizenship by lying on immigration papers, that is a serious crime, and I hold officials with great responsibility to a higher standard, not a lower one (Due Process and Rule of Law). Guilt still needs proof: I would require proof beyond a reasonable doubt for every conviction (Repeat Offenders and Forfeiture of the Right to Life), and a warrant is not a charge, so nothing here is proven. The Justice Department's 60-day pre-election restraint should be a fixed written rule, binding in every case, with an exception only for an immediate threat or evidence about to be lost (Federal Enforcement Near Elections); a search of a sitting candidate 22 days before the election should meet that bar and be explained. Her religion is a separate question. My excluded-ideologies rule would bar adherents of Islam, as it bars adherents of Nazism, communism, and socialism, from public office by constitutional amendment (Role of Religion in Government); that is my proposal, not current law, and it has no bearing on whether she committed a crime.

Haiti's Justice Minister Patrick Pélissier said Prime Minister Fils-Aimé is preparing meetings with Salvadoran authorities on extending the operation. Vice President Félix Ulloa said the terms of the security agreement will be released only "when diplomatic conditions allow." The four are still missing. head: What happened
topic: Case: Salvadoran troops abducted in Haiti, October 2026

body: What happened (sourced): The rescue's outcome is still unknown, gangs control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince, and the UN counted more than 5,700 people killed or injured by gang violence from January to mid-September 2026. As of 3 November 2026, El Salvador has sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti, most of them outside the Gang Suppression Force. The four hostages' status is disputed: Haitian authorities treat them as missing, El Salvador believes they are alive, and the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang has claimed they are dead. The UN distanced itself from his letter seeking talks. AP via Al Jazeera – El Salvador's Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers (2026) · UN News – Haiti gang leader seeks UN talks as El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to hunt for missing soldiers (2026)

head: My view
topic: Case: Salvadoran troops abducted in Haiti, October 2026

body: My view: If the captors refuse to release the hostages or cooperate, Bukele ought to use extreme force against those responsible. U.S. airlift for a partner's rescue force is the kind of joint operation with a cooperating government I prefer (Mexico and Latin America). Trying for release first and keeping 200 special forces ready is the order I want. His domestic record—the collapse of El Salvador's official homicide rate after the gang crackdown, with confrontation-exclusion and custody-death caveats noted in Gun Crime and Violence—is why I take the threat seriously when he says the gangs there can be finished the way MS-13 was at home. Counting and custody disputes do not erase the direction of that drop.
topic: Case: Salvadoran troops abducted in Haiti, October 2026

body: Destroying the headquarters of a gang tied to the ambush is the force I said Bukele ought to use once the captors refused to release the men. Friendly fire reaching the U.S. Embassy is what a single chain of command with the Gang Suppression Force prevents, so the coordination Washington asked for helps the mission rather than restraining it.

These are individual reported events, not statistics; they illustrate the position and do not measure a trend.

France, 17 Oct 2026: a nationwide day of protest against the cost of living and school conditions (authorities estimated about 550,000 marchers) turned violent in several cities. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said about 1,800 people were arrested, including a "record" 855 in the Paris region. Masked groups looted shops in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, and Limoges's 19th-century town hall was destroyed by a fire the prefect said was set deliberately. AFP – France counts cost of violent protests, 1,800 arrested By 18 Oct, Ouest-France reported more than 2,000 arrests nationwide and more than 600 police and gendarmes injured. Ouest-France – Violences du 17 octobre : quel est le bilan

France, 17 Oct 2026: the BBC reported that the main Paris march was largely peaceful in the afternoon before fires, torched vehicles and looting in the evening. Riot police used tear gas and water cannon, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 officers were injured. The interior ministry blamed "targeted acts of violence" by "hooded individuals". Includes BBC Verify–authenticated footage (labeled: footage) of the Limoges town hall spire collapsing. BBC News – Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as more than 1,200 arrested after protests

Paris, 18 Oct 2026: the morning after, the BBC reported burnt-out cars and shattered glass on the streets around Place de la République. BBC News – Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting

France, 6–17 Oct 2026: the student unions USL, Union étudiante, UNEF and FAGE called the national lycée days. On 6 Oct the interior ministry counted 256,000–266,000 marchers and organizers counted 450,000. The 17 Oct day began as a social-media "gilets jaunes" call that belonged to no party or union. The CGT, Solidaires, the Confédération paysanne, the student and lycée unions, LFI and the PCF then joined it. The interior ministry counted 550,000 marchers and organizers counted 800,000. PCF leader Fabien Roussel urged communists to accompany the lycéens and said "no violence is legitimate". LFI deputy Louis Boyard backed the blockades. franceinfo – la mobilisation des lycéens a réuni 450 000 manifestants; Euronews – Mobilisation du 17 octobre, qui manifestera en France; franceinfo – 800 000 selon les organisateurs, 550 000 selon le ministre; La Croix – Roussel appelle à soutenir les lycéens; BFMTV – Roussel, « aucune violence n'est légitime »; franceinfo – comment le blocage de quelques lycées s'est transformé en mouvement

19 Oct 2026: Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez conceded that police had "lost control" in some cities, citing a "lack of anticipation"; intelligence had predicted 200,000 marchers and more than 500,000 came. He offered his resignation, and Macron refused it and ordered a security review and "new operational methods." Partial curfews were imposed in parts of Paris and four northern cities, Marseille banned gatherings, and Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 2,513 people had been arrested and 67 imprisoned. Unions called new strikes and rallies for 5 November. The Guardian – France imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of Paris (2026)

22 Oct 2026: Darmanin said 2,700 people had been detained, more than 1,000 had appeared in court, and 217 had been jailed after fast-track trials. CNA (Reuters) – French justice minister says 217 people jailed over riots (2026) · Euronews – Violences du 17 octobre en France : 2 700 gardes à vue et 217 personnes incarcérées (2026)

24–27 Oct 2026: the Interior Ministry's provisional national figures for the weekend of 24–25 October counted 1,314 arrests, against 2,628 a week earlier, and 24 businesses looted. Nice ended its overnight curfew for minors on 26 October and said it could reimpose it; in Paris the curfew around Place de la République ended at 6 a.m. on 27 October, while a separate overnight curfew for unaccompanied minors and bans on unauthorized gatherings in parts of the city run to 29 October. The CGT, CFDT and Snes-FSU unions are calling a general strike for 5 November. Sortiraparis – Curfew in Paris: will it be extended again this Tuesday, October 27? (2026) · Nice Premium, citing the City of Nice – Nice: the curfew for minors lifted on October 26 (2026)

Spain, 24–26 Oct 2026: RTVE reports that riots in Barcelona on 24 October led to at least 128 arrests, and that on 26 October, after several thousand self-described "antifascists" protested outside the University of Deusto in Bilbao against a talk by the right-wing content creator Vito Quiles, which he cancelled for security reasons, several hundred people burned about half a dozen cars, a municipal police motorcycle and dozens of bins, threw stones at police and looted shops. The Basque police arrested 19, seven of them minors. RTVE links the calls to a social-media movement called "Blocus" that started in France and has called new actions in Madrid and other cities for 31 October. Bilbao's mayor, Juan Mari Aburto, said of the rioters, "they are not antifascists; they are real fascists." RTVE – Al menos 19 detenidos tras los violentos disturbios en Bilbao (2026) · Europa Press – Un total de 19 detenidos, siete de ellos menores, por los disturbios tras una manifestación contra Vito Quiles en Bilbao (2026)

5 Nov 2026: Five unions held a nationwide strike and marches over wages, living costs, public services and school conditions. CGT said more than 250,000 people had joined in 73 cities by lunchtime. About 70,000 police were deployed. A Paris court approved an alternate route from Place de la République to Place de la Nation; Paris had no citywide curfew, with unauthorized gatherings banned in designated areas from 7 a.m. to 11:59 p.m. Interior ministry reported violence near high schools in Rennes, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Strasbourg and Paris (mortar fire, fires, projectiles). Riot police used tear gas in Lyon; a high school near Toulouse was set on fire (BFM TV via France 24). The Eiffel Tower closed. France 24 – Live: Paris march begins as unions unite for nationwide strikes (2026)

10 Nov 2026: On a new day of lycée and teacher protests, Angela Pascoa Dos Santos, a deputy mayor of Chelles (Seine-et-Marne), was hit in the chest by a closed, full bottle of gasoline outside the Gaston-Bachelard lycée while trying to help classes resume; prosecutors opened an attempted-murder investigation. President Macron said the acts "must be punished with the greatest firmness," and the lycée union USL condemned the violence. In Paris about 5,900 marched by the police count (10,000 by organizers), chanting "À bas l'État, les flics et les fachos." The education ministry counted 49 of 3,700 lycées blocked and 1.6% of teachers on strike. An arson fire damaged 40 classrooms at the Émile-Zola lycée in Aix-en-Provence, which had been blockaded repeatedly; prosecutors have not linked it to the movement. Youth unions called a march for Saturday and a national day on 17 November, which the CGT has joined. France 24 / AFP – Nouvelle journée de mobilisation dans l'éducation, une élue agressée (2026)

12 Nov 2026: Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 lycées, about 5%, were blocked that morning, and that about a hundred had switched to remote classes on 10 November for safety. He condemned "violence débridée" and said all violent acts near lycées should be prosecuted, not just reported. After a meeting with principals and prosecutors, the government said offenses against school staff would be "judiciarisés" and their authors arrested, and that disciplinary action would be brought against those who disrupt schools. It counted 609 injured in schools, 364 pupils and 245 staff (81 of them principals or deputy principals), and 1,190 injured among police and gendarmes. Fires were set deliberately at two Montpellier lycées, and one person was arrested. Valérie Pécresse, president of the Île-de-France region, said pupils expelled for violence or damage would lose optional regional aid, put the damage at €10 million, and said there had been violent intrusions at 50 lycées. Youth unions kept their calls for Saturday and for 17 November. Le Dauphiné / AFP – Colère lycéenne : 24 établissements bloqués, des départs de feu, le ministre promet « des sanctions » (2026) · Public Sénat / AFP – Violences en marge des blocus lycéens : le gouvernement durcit le ton (2026)

14 Nov 2026: On the fifth national day ("acte V") of protests against the cost of living, the Interior Ministry counted 106,000 marchers nationwide and unions 200,000; in Paris, between 24,000 (ministry) and 100,000 (unions) marched from République to Nation. Police arrested 404 people nationwide, 126 of them in Paris, including 40 minors; 108 were held in custody in Paris, 38 of them minors, mainly for joining groups formed to commit violence. The Paris police prefecture said the marches went "globalement dans le calme," and two unauthorized marches in the evening were stopped. franceinfo / AFP – Manifestations du 14 novembre : un total de 404 personnes interpellées dans toute la France, dont plusieurs dizaines de mineurs (2026)

17 Nov 2026: On a national day of public-sector strikes over wages, the Interior Ministry counted 146,000 marchers nationwide, 28,000 of them in Paris; the CGT said more than 500,000, including 175,000 in Paris. The Paris police prefecture said the city was calm, and in Lyon the march returned to Place Bellecour for the first time since 17 October, with about 1,000 police and gendarmes deployed and no incidents reported. Europe 1 – Manifestations du 17 novembre : 146.000 manifestants en France, selon le ministère de l'Intérieur (2026). The same day Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told the National Assembly's law committee that the cost-of-living protests since 17 October had produced 7,184 police custodies, 2,661 of them of minors, leading to 3,053 prosecutions, 466 prison sentences (195 without suspension) and 356 people held in custody or jail as of 16 November, two-thirds of them from 17 October alone; 263 cases were opened with the aggravating circumstance of organized gangs, notably in Marseille and Lille. BFMTV (AFP) – Colère sociale: 7.184 gardes à vue et 356 personnes incarcérées depuis le 17 octobre (2026)

What happened (sourced): The 17 October protests, started by lycée students over school conditions and joined by unions and cost-of-living protesters, were largely peaceful by day; from the afternoon into the night they turned to looting, arson, vandalism and attacks on police by masked and hooded groups, which the interior ministry called "hooded individuals" and the interior minister described as "several thousand far-left individuals" joined by "delinquents". Of the 517 people held in Paris, 171 were minors. France 24 – 17 Octobre : des pillages en marge des manifestations contre la "vie chère" (footage); BBC News – Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting; actu.fr – Voitures incendiées, magasins pillés, affrontements : Paris plongé dans le chaos lors des manifestations (footage)

Marseille, 17 Oct 2026: in the late morning, several dozen protesters, most of them young, forced the 1673 wooden doors of the city hall on the Vieux-Port, shouting "c'est la Révolution, on prend la Bastille". AFP reported that some wore yellow vests or carried Palestinian flags. TV footage shows a protester carrying a Palestinian flag through the doorway. A police source told BFMTV there was "no more occupation" afterward. sub: Data: immigration and France's public finances

body: In the OECD's International Migration Outlook 2021 (Table 4.1, 2006–18 average), immigrants' net contribution in France is −0.85% of GDP when pure public goods such as defence and debt interest are shared per head, +0.25% when they are left out, and +1.02% counting only individual taxes, benefits, health and education. Defenders of France's immigration record point out that natives come out at −3.25% in the same accounting and that the total stays within about 1% of GDP. Per head, the picture runs the other way: in France each immigrant pays 12% less than a native-born resident while public spending per immigrant is only 6% lower, and the OECD singles out France for a relative fall in immigrants' fiscal ratio in the latest years. Chojnicki, Ragot & Sokhna find immigrants' net contribution to France's primary budget generally negative from 1979 to 2011, though within 0.5% of GDP, with their share of the primary deficit rising from 8.3% in 1995, about their weight in the population, to more than 17% in 2011. EU immigrants' per-head contribution declined markedly after 2000 and is now similar to that of immigrants from outside the EU. OECD – The fiscal impact of immigration in OECD countries since the mid-2000s, International Migration Outlook 2021 (2021); Chojnicki, Ragot & Sokhna, Revue économique – L'impact budgétaire de trente ans d'immigration en France : une approche comptable (2022); Chojnicki, Ragot & Sokhna, LEM working paper – L'impact budgétaire de 30 ans d'immigration en France : (I) une approche comptable (2018)

body: My view (17 October 2026 riots): These riots aren't really about school funding or the cost of living. France is deeply dissatisfied, with weak growth, inflation and a president in power for nearly ten years. The high school protests gave the left an opening, but what set these protests apart was the violence. French protests organized by unions are usually controlled. What broke this one open was spontaneous organizing on social media, with far-left groups and delinquents joining to burn and loot — the attribution Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez gave at the time. Not all rioters or marchers are non-assimilated, immigrant-background, and I do not claim they are, but from extensive video of the marches and the night violence, a sizable, clear presence of non-assimilated, immigrant-background people - mostly men - is visible among the rioters and among protesters in the disorder. That street composition is not measured by the Justice Ministry's jailed sample (data above): a custody profile of 186 people later incarcerated is not the movement, nationality is not ethnicity, and French authorities do not publish ethnicity in these bilans. The organizations that called and backed the day — LFI, PCF, CGT and Solidaires wings, student unions, Bloquons tout networks, Urgence Palestine and the rest listed above — are largely pro-immigration and collectivist. The violent layer is opportunistic: looters and chaos-seekers who do not follow the country's laws and do not respect its heritage because they were never assimilated into it. They are angry at a country they or their parents migrated into without knowing why, and without understanding that France is already among the world's top-tier welfare states. Where Islamist and far-left anger share the same street, recruiters work that ground. The state contains the violence instead of stopping it, because politicians fear a death at police hands would set off wider riots. The courts are too lenient and overwhelmed, the prisons are full, and the country is broke. This is the product of France's mass immigration, an abject assimilation and fiscal failure (OECD and Chojnicki data above), and exactly the erosion of culture I want the U.S. to avoid through heavy assimilation requirements and restricted immigration. France also needs a Nuremberg for communism. Communist parties and youth groups helped call these marches (above), yet French law treats only the crimes judged at Nuremberg as beyond denial (data above). France ought to recognize the crimes of communist regimes, the Holodomor, the Gulag and the Khmer Rouge killings among them, as crimes against humanity, teach them alongside the Holocaust, and hold glorifying them to the same standard as glorifying Nazi crimes. In the United States my rule is different: the government teaches, remembers and refuses honors, and praising either stays legal (Communism). France's postwar model is also colliding with itself: mass immigration was sold as a way to sustain pensions for an aging population, but non-EU immigration has added fiscal burden instead, and young newcomers with no shared identity with the French state have no reason to accept a deal that takes from the young to pay the old. Violent rioters should get serious prison time. Legacy outlets that lead with "largely peaceful" while the same day's reporting counts tear gas, water cannon, and more than a thousand arrests are soft-framing, not inventing the marches. The violence is still the story; the headline should not wash it out. BBC – France protests coverage using "largely peaceful" framing (2026) (Language and Assimilation; Immigration and Borders)

When a mob burns cars to stop a talk and the talk is cancelled, the mob has used force to silence a speaker. Free speech is held absolutely (Free Speech and Censorship), and the state's job is to protect the event and prosecute the force, not to let the threat of violence decide who may speak.

Throwing a bottle of gasoline at an elected official who is trying to reopen a school is attempted murder, and it should be prosecuted and punished as one. A march that chants against "the state, the cops and the fascists" while schools burn shows the same anti-state current I describe above.

Prosecuting every act of violence, instead of filing complaints that go nowhere, is the right policy, and it should hold for the adults behind the movement as much as for the pupils. Nearly 1,200 injured police officers show these are not school protests that got out of hand.

body: AI: close to my view: national rules on AI's security risks set by Congress in statute, with government regulation (AI and Automation). Basic income conflicts with my minimal floor. A pause on frontier research conflicts with my pro-AI position, and government-appointed seats on private companies' boards conflict with my property rights (Property Rights). His line that AI should not fire a weapon is close to my rule that autonomous weapons should be developed with human judgment kept over lethal force (Cyber Warfare and Autonomous Weapons).

body: Elections: we agree on opposing Citizens United and limiting money to individual donations (Election Administration). My limits apply to contributions to candidates and campaigns, not to independent speech (Voting and Elections), so the $300,000 his father-in-law gave a super PAC backing him is spending my rule allows and his own platform would ban. Voters must show ID, so his opposition to voter ID conflicts (Voting and Elections). I support ranked-choice voting by constitutional amendment (Ranked-Choice Voting). I found no stated position from him on it. I have no position on the filibuster, Supreme Court term limits or redistricting commissions.

body: Status as of Nov 8, 2026: Open. Chapter 188 is in effect as of November 6 under Healey's emergency preamble; suspension pending the 2028 vote is blocked. Galvin's office is reviewing the filed sheets (typically one to two weeks). The repeal question can still reach the 2028 ballot if enough signatures are certified.

22 Jul 2026: the House passed H.5595 119–33 (Roll Call 236); every Republican voting and nine Democrats voted no. Rep. Michael Day (D): "We've decided to get away from all the exceptions and trust our medical professionals." GBH – State lawmakers move to scrap limits on 24-week abortions and let doctors decide (2026)
31 Jul 2026: the Senate passed it on a 15–4 standing vote, and the House enacted it 121–35 (Roll Call 262). Massachusetts Legislature – Bill H.5595

10 Aug 2026: Governor Healey signed it as Chapter 188, saying "these situations are incredibly rare, and the decisions should be made between patients, their families, and their doctor — not by politicians and the government." Mass.gov – Governor Healey signs legislation strengthening abortion protections
Massachusetts Citizens for Life president Myrna Maloney Flynn said "this law crosses a fundamentally different line." GBH reported 99 abortions at or after 24 weeks in Massachusetts in 2024.

1 Sep 2026: opponents filed a referendum petition ("Repeal 188"). About 37,300 certified signatures put repeal on the 2028 ballot, and about 49,700 suspend the law until then; signatures are due to local clerks by 23 October and to the Secretary of State by 6 November. Governor Healey could block suspension with an emergency preamble and has not said whether she will. WBUR – Massachusetts abortion law faces 2028 referendum (2026); State House News Service – Healey noncommittal on shielding new law for abortions later in pregnancy (2026)

1 Oct 2026: the Massachusetts Medical Society urged Governor Healey to adopt an emergency preamble so the law takes effect at once and cannot be suspended, saying several patients had already left the state for abortion care since it was signed. Massachusetts Medical Society – Letter to Governor Healey Urging Adoption of Emergency Preamble to Chapter 188 of the Acts of 2026 (Oct. 1, 2026)

Oct 2026: Massachusetts' four Catholic bishops backed the petition to suspend the law, and on 16 Oct organizers said they were "very confident" of gathering enough signatures to pause it. The Boston Pilot – Mass.
